0.label: Player ignores that their queen is undefended on an open file, allowing immediate capture by the opponent's queen with check.
0.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase blunders where the player makes a secondary developing move (typically a bishop move to g4 or along a diagonal) while their queen sits undefended, usually on the e-file. The material signature shows 100% hanging moves (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -9.0 (a queen's worth), and Maia's response is always capturing the hanging queen with check. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses (median 596 centipawns), converting drawn or even winning positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis tags—hanging_queen, undefended_piece, opening_blunder—all converge on the same pattern: the player attends to a secondary concern (developing a bishop, threatening an opponent's piece, or repositioning) while completely overlooking that their queen is directly capturable. The boards confirm queens left exposed on e4/e5 squares along open e-files where the opponent's queen can sweep in with capture and check simultaneously.

6.label: Player moves a piece aimlessly while overlooking a free or easily winning queen capture available on the board.
6.description: This feature fires when players leave material on the table by failing to capture an available queen. The material signature shows that in 86% of cases the player captures nothing, while Maia's recommended move captures a queen 86% of the time—indicating a massive missed opportunity. The 'hangs' outcome (50%) reflects that the player's actual move often leaves their own piece en prise, compounding the error. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of positions, and the per-position analysis explicitly identifies 'missed_queen_capture' and 'same_diagonal_oversight' patterns where queens sit on open lines ready to be taken. The median eval loss of 322 centipawns confirms these are catastrophic oversights, and the trajectory shows that 43% of the time the player remains winning (suggesting the position was so good they survived despite the blunder), while 14% swing from winning to losing. The positions consistently show queens in plain sight on open diagonals, ranks, or files that the player simply fails to notice.

2.label: Player moves a piece (often retreating or capturing) while missing a decisive knight check that would win material or deliver mate.
2.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful knight check or knight fork that was available. The key integrated signals are: (1) Maia's recommended move is a knight move with check in 100% of cases, indicating the missed best move was always a knight delivering check; (2) the material signature shows 76% missed winning material with a median eval loss of 274 centipawns, confirming a serious tactical oversight rather than a positional inaccuracy; (3) the Opus analysis highlights king_safety (75%) as the dominant motif, with recurring themes of missed mates and missed tactics involving knight forks to exposed kings. The top boards consistently show positions where a knight on a central square can deliver check while simultaneously attacking a queen or rook (e.g., Nf6+ patterns, Ng5+ discoveries). Players instead make plausible-looking moves—capturing material, retreating pieces, or repositioning—while missing the forcing knight check that would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (92%), where king safety is most critical and knight forks to exposed kings are most potent.

14.label: Player moves queen aimlessly in endgame instead of capturing opponent's hanging queen.
14.description: This feature detects a specific and recurring endgame blunder where the player moves their queen (100% queen moves, 0% captures) while the opponent's queen is completely undefended and capturable. Maia consistently identifies the correct move as a queen capturing a queen (100% queen captures). The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (67%) meaning the player doesn't immediately lose material on the move itself, but misses winning the opponent's hanging queen — confirmed by the 'missed winning material' tag firing 100% of the time. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (88%), 'missed_capture' and 'queen_hanging' tags, and explicit descriptions of players ignoring trivially available queen captures. The eval trajectory (median 724cp lost, 67% winning->drawn) shows these are game-throwing mistakes in won endgame positions. The positions are exclusively endgames with queens still on the board, where the player makes a purposeless or aggressive-looking queen move while completely overlooking that the opponent's queen is en prise.

12.label: Player makes a quiet, materially safe move that misses the only drawing or winning resource, turning a holdable or won position into a loss.
12.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-capturing, materially 'safe' move (no pieces are hung or traded) yet suffers a catastrophic eval swing (median ~578cp), typically converting drawn positions into losing ones (75%) or winning positions into drawn ones (25%). The tactical analyses reveal a unifying thread: in each case there was exactly one critical resource—a promotion enabling perpetual check, a back-rank defense, a key capture maintaining an advantage—and the player instead temporized or redirected a piece to an irrelevant square. The motifs (promotion_error, king_safety, back_rank) and tags (perpetual_check_missed, drawn_position_missed, critical_tempo) all point to failing to recognize a narrow, forced saving or winning line in positions that superficially look stable. The piece diversity (bishop, knight, king, rook moves) confirms the mistake is not about a specific piece type but about missing the unique tactical obligation of the moment—often in late middlegame or endgame positions where one tempo decides the outcome.

3.label: Player makes a quiet developing or repositioning move while missing a free capture, often compromising king safety in the opening.
3.description: This feature fires when players make non-capturing moves (100% no capture) with queens, bishops, or pawns in the opening/early middlegame (70% opening, 30% middlegame) while Maia's recommended move captures significant material (70% rook captures, plus bishop/knight captures). The positions consistently show hanging pieces available for capture that the player ignores (missed winning material: 100%). The eval trajectory shows substantial cost (median 249cp lost), frequently converting winning positions to drawn or drawn to losing (30%/30%). The tactical motifs reveal the player's move often worsens king safety (50%) or loses tempo (17%), while a free piece hangs uncollected (33%). The concrete positions confirm this: knight forks on f7 with pieces available to capture, undefended pieces on open lines, and situations where the player plays prophylactic or developmental moves instead of simply taking hanging material—sometimes even blocking their own king's escape squares in the process.

15.label: Voluntarily trading a bishop for a knight on f3 in the opening, surrendering the bishop pair and positional compensation for no concrete gain.
15.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player captures a knight on f3 with their bishop (100% bishop moves capturing knights) during the opening phase (100% opening). The material outcome is always a trade (net 0.0), so this is not a material blunder but a poor exchange decision. The eval trajectory shows these trades are catastrophic positionally: 83% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 251 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core error: players surrender their bishop pair (tagged in all examples), lose tempo, and often remove their own defensive piece (e.g., a bishop guarding the long diagonal) without obtaining any compensation. Maia's suggested alternatives (knight moves 50%, pawn moves 33%) indicate the engine preferred developing or maintaining tension rather than resolving it with this premature exchange. The positions universally show fianchettoed or developed bishops on g4 or b7 capturing the f3 knight too early, conceding lasting structural and activity advantages to the opponent.

7.label: Player makes a natural-looking move while missing a knight fork with check that wins significant material.
7.description: This feature consistently fires when players overlook a knight fork delivering check (Maia's move is knight 86% of the time, gives check 100%, and captures high-value pieces like queens and pawns). The player's actual moves are diverse (pawns, knights, bishops, queens) and often involve trades or hanging pieces, but the critical pattern is that 100% of positions have missed winning material. The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly positions where the player was already winning (57% winning->drawn, 14% winning->losing), with a median loss of 294 centipawns—indicating they threw away a decisive advantage by failing to spot the tactical shot. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs: knight forks, missed tactics, and tempo loss. Concrete examples include missing Nxc7+ winning a queen, missing Nxe7+ with check, and missing Bxc6+ winning material—all cases where a forcing check-capture sequence was available but the player chose a slower, non-forcing continuation. The positions cluster in the opening/early middlegame (opening 57%, middlegame 43%) where kings are still centralized or recently castled, creating fork targets.

9.label: Capturing or checking in a won endgame that converts the position into a theoretical draw due to insufficient mating material.
9.description: This feature detects endgame positions where a player with a winning advantage makes a capture (always taking a pawn) with check that inadvertently eliminates the mating potential from the position. The material signature shows checks with captures that result in net material loss (-2.0 median), while the eval trajectory uniformly shows winning positions collapsing to drawn ones (median 534cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: promotions mishandled, pieces traded that were essential for checkmate (e.g., rook for pawn leaving K+N vs K), and passed pawns neutralized. The top boards confirm this—nearly all are deep endgames where the winning side captures material that simplifies into a theoretically drawn position (insufficient material, wrong-colored bishop, etc.). The common tags (insufficient_material, drawn_endgame, endgame_technique, passed_pawn) reinforce that these are not positional subtleties but fundamental endgame knowledge failures where greedy or impulsive captures with check destroy a won game.

1.label: Player captures or moves a major piece when a stronger tactical continuation (pin, fork, or tempo gain) was available.
1.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable move—often a capture (bishop 46%) or a major piece redeployment (rook/queen 46%)—but misses a superior tactical opportunity. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 400 centipawns, with 38% going from winning to still winning (squandering decisive advantage) and 15% dropping from winning to drawn, indicating these are moves that throw away a crushing position rather than outright blunders. The dominant motifs (pin 33%, tempo_loss 33%, fork 17%) combined with tags like missed_tactic, pin, and move_order reveal the core pattern: players grab material or make natural-looking moves without first checking whether a pin, fork, or precise move order would have won significantly more. The position summaries confirm this—capturing a hanging piece instead of setting up a lethal pin, taking on a square before eliminating a queen, or opening a file that benefits the opponent. The material outcome being mostly 'safe' (54%) shows these aren't blunders that immediately lose material, but rather missed tactical sequences where the player settled for something ordinary when a forcing continuation existed.

8.label: In a losing pawn endgame, makes a pawn exchange that accelerates defeat by destroying key pawn structure or losing tempo.
8.description: This feature fires on pawn exchanges in king-and-pawn endgames that dramatically worsen an already losing position (median 426cp lost, always losing->losing). The material signature shows 100% pawn captures resulting in trades (net material 0), yet these exchanges are catastrophic positionally. The board positions are exclusively pawn endgames (endgame 100%) with dominant motifs of pawn_endgame, passed_pawn, and tempo_loss. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows players capturing pawns that break critical blockades (d4xc5 allowing recapture with check/tempo), choose the wrong capture direction (exf6 vs gxf6 destroying a wedge pawn), or exchange pawns that were serving defensive functions (holding passed pawns back, maintaining structure). The Maia response is always a king move (100%), indicating the opponent simply improves king activity after the ill-advised trade. These are not material blunders—nothing is hung—but rather structural/tempo concessions disguised as 'equal' exchanges that collapse the defender's position in pure pawn endings.

13.label: Unsound bishop sacrifice on f7 with check in the opening, lacking sufficient compensation.
13.description: This feature fires exclusively on the classic beginner's trap of playing Bxf7+ (or ...Bxf2+) in Italian Game-type positions during the opening phase. All top activations show a bishop capturing a pawn on f7/f2 with check (bishop 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%), but the material outcome is consistently 'slightly down' (median -2.0), confirming the bishop is sacrificed for only a pawn. The eval trajectory is devastating: every instance transforms a drawn position into a losing one (median 342cp lost), equivalent to roughly a full minor piece deficit. The tactical analysis confirms these are unsound sacrifices (tagged in 7/7 positions) where the player lacks sufficient piece coordination or development to generate a real attack against the displaced king. Maia's recommended alternatives are quiet developing moves (knights and pawns, no captures), highlighting that solid development was readily available. This is the quintessential 'fried liver wannabe' mistake where players prematurely lunge at f7/f2 without the supporting pieces (particularly lacking Ng5 or equivalent pressure) that make such sacrifices theoretically sound.

4.label: Moving the king instead of addressing a tactical threat, leaving a piece or pawn undefended.
4.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) without capturing anything, and in doing so hangs material (82% hangs, median net material loss of -5.0, i.e., roughly a full rook). The eval trajectory shows these moves overwhelmingly occur in already-losing positions (82% losing->losing) but deepen the deficit by a median of 206 centipawns—making a bad situation catastrophically worse. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (50%) and king_safety (38%), and the per-position analyses confirm the pattern: the king moves to escape perceived danger or reposition, but the player fails to first resolve a hanging piece (often a rook) or exchange material that would neutralize a threat. The best moves identified by engines are typically rook exchanges or recaptures that the player skips in favor of a reflexive king move. The phase is predominantly middlegame (73%), where such neglected tactics are most punishing. This is not a trade gone wrong or a positional misjudgment—it is a concrete tactical oversight where king movement leaves friendly material en prise.

11.label: Advancing a kingside pawn in the opening that weakens the king's shelter or misses a tactical opportunity.
11.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening-phase mistake (85% opening) where a pawn is pushed (92% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) that weakens the player's own king safety or squanders a tempo while missing a superior tactical continuation. The eval trajectory shows these moves are devastating—median 302 centipawns lost, with 35% converting a winning position to drawn and 31% turning a drawn position into a losing one. The dominant motifs (king_safety 38%, hanging_piece 38%) combined with tags like 'opening_blunder' and 'missed_capture' reveal the pattern: players push pawns like g4, g5, b4, or b5 in the opening, either ripping open their own king's pawn cover (the g4/g5 pushes in front of a castled king) or making premature flank moves that ignore development and miss immediate captures. Maia's recommended moves (27% knight, 19% bishop, 38% capturing bishops) confirm that the correct play involved developing pieces or capturing hanging material rather than pushing pawns. The concrete positions repeatedly show g2-g4 weakening a castled king or b-pawn pushes that lose tempo while pieces remain undeveloped.

10.label: Player makes a seemingly reasonable move while missing a devastating knight or piece fork that would win significant material.
10.description: This feature fires when players overlook powerful forking opportunities in middlegame positions. The material signature shows 100% missed winning material with moves that are often 'safe' (50%) or 'hang' pieces (40%), meaning the player chose a move that either does nothing special or actively drops material, when a fork was available. The eval trajectory is severe (median 431cp lost), with many cases converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones. The tactical motifs are dominated by forks (33%), discovered attacks (33%), and hanging pieces (33%), with tags like 'knight_fork', 'king_and_queen_fork', and 'geometric_blindness' recurring. The per-position analysis confirms players chose greedy captures or passive moves instead of recognizing geometric patterns — e.g., taking a pawn with check instead of playing a crushing king+queen fork, or missing Ng6+ discoveries. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve knights (30%) and bishops (30%) delivering checks (50%), confirming the missed moves were forcing tactical shots. The player's actual moves (kings 30%, queens 30%, knights 20%) suggest they were focused on their own king safety or queen activity rather than spotting the opponent-targeting geometry available.

5.label: Moving a knight to an aggressive but undefended square in the opening, where it is won by a forcing reply like a queen check.
5.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase knight moves (100% knight moved, 100% opening) that jump to aggressive-looking but tactically vulnerable squares. The material signature shows 69% are initially 'safe' but 31% outright hang the piece, and 38% miss winning material—indicating the knight lands where it appears active but is tactically refuted. The eval trajectory is devastating: 85% of cases swing from a drawn position to losing, with a median loss of 283 centipawns (roughly a full piece). The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 60%, tempo_loss 40%) and tags (opening_trap, premature_attack, development) confirm the pattern: players launch premature knight attacks (Ng5, Nb5, Nb4) that leave the piece undefended and exploitable by queen forks, checks, or simple attacks that win the knight outright. The top boards vividly illustrate this—repeated Nf3-g5 and Nc3-b5/Nc6-b4 jumps in standard openings that are punished by Qa5+, Qa4+, or similar forcing moves recovering the piece with tempo.

17.label: In drawn rook/pawn endgames, making a safe but passive rook move that surrenders the balance by neglecting activity or critical defensive duties.
17.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame error where the player makes a rook move (100% rook moves, 0% captures, 0% checks) that appears materially safe (net material 0.0) but converts a drawn position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing, median 282cp lost). The top boards are overwhelmingly rook endgames and simplified pawn endgames (tags: rook_endgame 7/10, tempo_loss 4, rook_activity 3, passed_pawn 3). The tactical analyses repeatedly cite violations of core endgame principles: choosing passive defense over active counterplay, losing critical tempi, failing to activate the rook on open ranks, or neglecting passed pawn threats. The moves are not blunders in the sense of hanging material—they are quiet, 'safe-looking' rook repositionings that fatally misunderstand the dynamic requirements of the position, squandering a holdable draw by ceding activity, tempo, or key defensive coordination in simplified positions.

18.label: Moving a bishop to a square where it becomes a target of a knight fork that also checks the exposed king.
18.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where a player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves) to a seemingly natural development square, but critically overlooks a knight fork that simultaneously checks their exposed king (usually on f7/f2) and attacks the newly placed bishop. The material signature shows these are non-capture moves that hang a piece (67% hangs, median -1.0 material), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders converting winning positions to drawn or lost (median 540cp lost). The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies fork motifs (86%) with recurring tags of exposed_king, knight_fork, and tactical_oversight. In nearly every top-activating position, the king sits vulnerably on f7 or f2 (having lost castling rights or moved early), and the bishop develops to e6 or e3 where a knight can deliver check while simultaneously attacking the undefended bishop. The pattern is a classic opening trap where piece development is prioritized over recognizing the king's tactical vulnerability to knight geometry.

16.label: Knight captures a pawn in the opening that exposes a critical diagonal or tactical vulnerability, losing significant material.
16.description: This feature fires when a player uses a knight to capture a pawn in the opening phase, only to fall into a well-known tactical trap. The material signature shows knight captures pawn 100% of the time with a net material outcome of slightly down (median -2.0), indicating the knight capture itself triggers a sequence where the player loses more than they gained. The eval trajectory is devastating: 75% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 486 centipawns—essentially a full piece or more. The positional analysis reveals the recurring pattern: the knight capture (most commonly Nxd5) opens critical diagonals (especially a2-g8 toward f7) for the opponent's pieces, enabling queen-bishop batteries, exploitation of the uncastled king, and attacks on f7. The top boards confirm this is overwhelmingly the classic Italian/Scotch-style opening trap where Nxd5 or similar knight captures invite devastating discovered attacks. Tags like 'opening_trap', 'f7_pressure', 'diagonal_opening', and 'queen_bishop_battery' all point to the same archetype: a greedy or routine knight recapture that ignores the opponent's latent tactical resources along newly opened lines.

30.label: Player makes a developing or tactical move while overlooking that the opponent's queen is hanging and can be captured.
30.description: This feature fires when a player makes a seemingly reasonable move (often a knight or bishop development/capture) while completely missing that the opponent's queen is undefended and capturable. The material signature shows that the played moves are mostly 'safe' (not hanging material themselves), yet Maia's recommended moves capture a queen 83% of the time—indicating the queen capture was available but overlooked. The eval trajectory confirms massive centipawn losses (median 531cp), often converting a winning position into merely a drawn one. The tactical analysis tags reinforce this: 'hanging_piece' dominates at 83%, with 'queen_capture' and 'missed_tactic' appearing repeatedly. The per-position summaries describe a 'recapture reflex' or tunnel vision where players focus on a local exchange or development while a free queen sits elsewhere on the board. This is not a trade error but a pure tactical oversight—the queen is simply hanging and the player doesn't see it.

23.label: Moving the queen to a square that disrupts or abandons a winning mating attack against the opponent's king.
23.description: This feature detects positions where a player moves their queen (62%) or rook (38%) to a safe square (no material is immediately lost in most cases), but in doing so abandons a decisive king-safety attack. The Maia analysis confirms that the best moves overwhelmingly involved delivering check (88%) and winning material (88% missed winning material). The eval trajectory shows these moves throw away winning or drawn positions (62% winning->drawn, 25% winning->losing), with a massive median eval loss of 411 centipawns. The tactical analysis uniformly identifies king_safety as the dominant motif (100%), with recurring tags like queen_misplacement, missed_mate_threat, and missed_sacrifice. The concrete examples illustrate the pattern precisely: a queen moves to a nearby square that looks active but misses the one critical mating or forcing continuation (e.g., Qh4 instead of Qh6 missing Qg7#, Qf6 blocking the knight's mating square, Qe4 abandoning a Qxf2+ winning sequence). The player's queen relocation appears reasonable but fatally disrupts the coordination needed to execute the winning attack on the opponent's king.

20.label: Player captures material or makes a 'safe' move instead of delivering an available checkmate in one.
20.description: All three signals converge on one clear pattern: players have a forced checkmate available (almost always via a queen check, as shown by Maia's 93% queen moves and 100% check rate) but instead play a rook, knight, or bishop move that is materially 'safe' or even wins an exchange. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic missed opportunities—median eval lost is ~9829 centipawns (i.e., a missed mate), and 43% of cases flip from losing to winning for the opponent. The Opus analysis explicitly tags 'missed_mate_in_one' and 'greed_over_mate,' with examples showing queens capturing pawns/pieces instead of delivering checkmate, or pieces moving away from mating squares. The motifs (back_rank, king_safety) and tags (back_rank_checkmate, queen_checkmate, pattern_blindness) reinforce that the checkmate was typically a simple queen delivery on an open file or diagonal that the player overlooked in favor of a tempting but irrelevant material grab or positional move.

25.label: Player makes a costly queen move or exchange that abandons a dominant queen's attacking potential or defensive duties.
25.description: This feature fires when players misuse their queen—the moved piece is always a queen (100%), and the material outcome is predominantly losing (67%, median -4.0 pawns). The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 421 centipawns, turning already-difficult positions worse or throwing away winning chances (winning->drawn 33%). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the queen is either traded prematurely when it was the player's most active piece (queen_trade_error, initiative_loss, development_advantage_squandered), moved to a square that abandons critical defensive duties (hanging_piece, the Qf3 example leaving a1 undefended), or captured into a tactical trap (back_rank mate after Qxd8). The dominant motifs of king_safety (40%) and positional_mistake (20%) confirm these aren't simple calculation errors but failures to appreciate the queen's role in the position—whether maintaining pressure on an uncastled king, covering back-rank threats, or preserving initiative. The common thread across all examples is that the queen had an outsized positional role that the player failed to recognize before committing it to a inferior square or exchange.

21.label: In the opening, player makes a developing or recapturing move that leaves a piece undefended and freely capturable.
21.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening-phase blunder (71% opening, 29% middlegame) where the player makes a move—often with a bishop, knight, or queen—that leaves a piece hanging with no compensation. The material signature is stark: 55% of moves hang a piece outright (non-capture that drops material), with a median net loss of 3.0 material units (roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 45% go from winning to drawn and 16% from winning to losing, with a massive median cost of 414 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (89% of positions), with tags like missed_tactic, development, and recapture_error. The concrete pattern visible in the top boards shows players making natural-looking developing moves (Nc6, Nf6, Qd2, Qe2, Kd7) that ignore an immediate tactical threat, leaving a knight or bishop en prise to a simple capture. Maia's recommended moves (48% knight, 29% bishop) typically address the threat directly—recapturing correctly or moving the threatened piece. This is not a complex positional error but a basic tactical oversight during development where the player fails to notice their piece is undefended.

28.label: Player makes a passive or unrelated move while a piece is left hanging to an existing enemy attack.
28.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their king or another piece without addressing an immediate tactical threat, leaving material en prise. The material signature shows 75% of moves result in 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece), with the player predominantly moving their king (50%) in situations where a piece is already under attack. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly blunders (median 414cp lost), often converting drawn positions into lost ones or making losing positions decisively worse. The Opus tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (80%) as the dominant motif, with 'ignored_threat' appearing repeatedly in the tags. The concrete examples consistently show the same pattern: a king retreats or sidesteps while a knight, bishop, or pawn sits undefended under direct attack (e.g., Kd2 ignoring Rxc4, Kg2 ignoring the attack on Nd3, f3 unguarding e3). These are not complex tactical oversights but rather cases where the player fails to recognize or prioritize an existing, straightforward threat to their own material.

19.label: Moving the queen to a passive square when an active queen trade or tactical continuation was available, hanging material in the process.
19.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (80%) to a passive or aimless square, hanging material (80% hangs, median -3.0 material) while Maia's recommended response is to capture the now-vulnerable queen (100% queen capture, often with check at 60%). The eval trajectory shows this mostly occurs in already-losing positions (60% losing->losing) but also converts drawn positions to losing ones (20%), with a median cost of 152 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: rather than trading queens via an active simplification (tagged missed_simplification, endgame_avoidance), the player retreats or relocates the queen passively (passive_queen_move, tempo_loss), leaving it on a square where it is immediately captured or trapped. The boards confirm this—queens moved to g1, h4, g6, g7, h2, e2 are all retreating or sideways moves that abandon piece activity and allow the opponent to win the queen outright. The mistake is fundamentally positional: failing to recognize that the queen trade was the correct defensive resource, instead choosing a passive continuation that loses the queen entirely.

27.label: Playing a routine pawn move while opponent's queen hangs undefended, converting a winning position into a losing one.
27.description: This feature detects a specific and devastating opening blunder pattern: the player makes a seemingly natural pawn move (80% pawn, 20% knight) that is a non-capture ('hangs' at 100%), while completely overlooking that the opponent's queen (or sometimes bishop) is hanging and can be captured for free. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase (100%), and the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing from winning to losing (median 1010 centipawns lost, 100% winning->losing). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' across all examples, with 'missed_capture' (4/5), 'queen_loss' (3/5), and 'tempo_loss' (3/5) as recurring tags. Examining the concrete positions, we see cases like a queen on h5 that can be taken by Rxh5, a bishop on c7 capturing toward d8's queen, or a bishop on g5 with a clear diagonal to d8 — yet the player makes a development or pawn-push move oblivious to the free material. This represents a fundamental failure of board awareness where the player follows routine development instincts while a massive tactical opportunity sits in plain sight.

26.label: Knight moves in the opening that leave a piece undefended on a critical diagonal or square.
26.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase knight moves (100% knight, 100% opening) that are non-captures yet hang material worth approximately a full piece or more (median net material: -6.0 centipawns x100, i.e., ~6 pawns / a queen-equivalent loss). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders turning drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 558cp lost). The tactical motifs reveal the mechanism: 80% hanging_piece combined with tags like 'exposed_queen', 'diagonal_vulnerability', and 'fianchetto_power' indicate that the knight move removes a critical defender from a diagonal, exposing a high-value piece (often the queen) to an enemy bishop. The concrete positions confirm this—knights leaving f6, jumping to e5, or relocating to d7 inadvertently unblock long diagonals or pin-lines, allowing the opponent's fianchettoed or developed bishop to win material. These are classic opening traps where a seemingly natural knight development or repositioning fatally neglects piece coordination along key diagonals.

24.label: Minor piece or pawn move in the opening that ignores a lethal queen invasion on f2/f7, allowing checkmate or decisive material loss.
24.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player moves a knight, bishop, or pawn (non-capture, non-check) while completely overlooking a devastating queen attack exploiting the f2 (or f7) weakness. The material signature shows 83% of moves 'hang' something—not by dropping the moved piece itself, but by leaving the king fatally exposed. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 9719 centipawns lost), with positions collapsing from survivable to immediate checkmate or decisive disadvantage. The tactical analysis confirms king_safety as the universal motif (100%), with recurring tags like 'f2_weakness', 'king_in_center', and 'checkmate_threat'. The top boards consistently show Italian Game / Scholar's Mate family positions where a bishop on c5 and queen on f6/f3 coordinate against f2/f7, and the player ignores this threat to make a developing or aggressive-looking move (Nd5, Be2, Nb4, etc.). Maia's recommended move is always a queen move—specifically the queen delivering or threatening checkmate on f2/f7. This is a classic pattern-recognition failure in the opening where the player fails to see the opponent's mating coordination against the weakest square near their king.

31.label: Moving a piece (often queen) into a position where it becomes geometrically trapped, squandering a large advantage.
31.description: This feature fires on moves where a player places or leaves a piece in a square where it becomes trapped, typically costing several hundred centipawns. The material signature shows 'safe' moves (nothing is immediately hanging), yet the eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 446cp), indicating the damage is latent rather than immediate. The dominant motif is overwhelmingly 'trapped_piece' (75% of annotations, appearing in 6+ of the top 10 boards), with supporting tags like tempo_loss and piece_activity confirming that the piece ends up without escape squares. The phase is exclusively the opening, where development choices can lead to geometric traps—most commonly a queen venturing to a square (e.g., Qa8, Qh1, Qa2) where coordinated minor pieces or pawns cut off all retreats. The positions show both colors making this error: White's queen trapped on a8/a7, Black's queen trapped on h1/a2/b2, and occasionally a knight placed where it has no productive future. The move itself appears routine or even aggressive (a capture, a developing move, an invasion), but it ignores the opponent's ability to seal off the piece with tempo.

29.label: Knight moves to a seemingly active central square (often d5 or e4) but hangs because it lacks adequate support.
29.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: a knight is moved (93% of activations involve knight moves) to what appears to be an active or aggressive square—most commonly e4 or d5 in Slav/QGD-type pawn structures—but the piece is inadequately defended and hangs material (100% hangs, median -1.0 material loss). The eval trajectory confirms these are not minor inaccuracies but game-changing errors: 89% swing a drawn position to losing, with a median cost of 233 centipawns (roughly a full piece's positional value beyond the pawn). The tactical analysis reinforces that the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (62%), with the knight being captured via recapture sequences that win a clean pawn or exploit insufficient support. The phase is predominantly opening/early middlegame (59% opening, 41% middlegame), consistent with premature central knight lunges before adequate piece coordination. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show ...Nfe4 or Nd5 played in closed/semi-closed positions where the knight appears to threaten something but is simply lost after forced exchanges.

22.label: Failing to recapture an enemy piece (typically a bishop on f6) that has landed on a square where it can be taken, instead making a developing or quiet move that leaves material hanging.
22.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where an opponent's piece (almost always a bishop) has intruded onto a square where it can and should be captured, but the player ignores the threat and plays a quiet developing move or pawn push instead. The material signature shows 67% of moves result in hanging a piece (non-captures that drop material), with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory is devastating: 83% of these mistakes swing a drawn position to losing, with a median cost of 524 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 80% of cases, supplemented by tempo_loss. The top boards make the pattern crystal clear: positions like ...Bxf6 structures where the opponent's bishop sits en prise on f6, and instead of recapturing (gxf6, Bxf6), the player plays Be7, h6, or castles—moves that ignore the free capture and often allow the opponent to win material. Similarly, positions with a bishop sitting on f3 (having captured a knight) where White plays d3, Be2, or castles instead of simply recapturing. The Maia recommendations confirm that bishop captures were available in every case. This is fundamentally a failure to recognize that recapturing hanging material takes priority over development in the opening.

33.label: King moves that ignore doubled-rook pressure on an open file, hanging a piece.
33.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet king move (75% king, 25% pawn) that completely ignores a critical tactical threat on an open file—most often doubled rooks bearing down on an undefended or under-defended piece. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a rook), and Maia consistently responds by capturing a rook (100%). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders: 75% turn a winning position into a losing one, with a median loss of 561 centipawns. The tactical analysis repeatedly identifies the same pattern: the c-file (or similar open file) has doubled rooks attacking a piece that is defended zero times or only illusorily defended, and instead of addressing this crisis the player wastes a tempo on king centralization or a weakening pawn push. Tags like 'doubled_rooks_pressure', 'tempo_loss', and 'hanging_piece' converge on the same story—the player prioritizes a positional idea (king activity, pawn structure) while a concrete tactical threat on an open file goes unresolved, immediately dropping major material.

34.label: Player makes a quiet developing move instead of capturing a hanging piece with a bishop, throwing away a winning advantage.
34.description: This feature fires when players miss a straightforward piece-winning capture, almost always a bishop taking a rook (Maia's recommended move is bishop captures rook 100% of the time). The player instead makes a quiet move—often a bishop retreat, pawn push, or knight maneuver (88% non-captures)—that is objectively safe in isolation but misses the critical tactic. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly cases of throwing away a winning position (53% winning->drawn, 6% winning->losing), with a massive median cost of 271 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms hanging pieces and missed tactics as the dominant motifs, with multiple examples citing 'Bxf1' or 'Bxb7' as the single winning move. The players appear to overlook that an enemy piece is en prise, choosing instead moves focused on development, repositioning, or pawn structure that ignore the immediate tactical opportunity. This is a pattern of tactical blindness to available captures rather than a positional misjudgment or trade error.

37.label: Trading an active bishop or knight for a less valuable piece exchange that surrenders a tactical or positional advantage.
37.description: This feature detects positions where a player exchanges a bishop (76%) or knight (20%) for an opponent's knight (87%) in what is materially an even trade (94% trade outcomes), but the exchange costs a median of 291 centipawns in evaluation—typically converting a winning or drawn position into a drawn or losing one (winning->drawn 22%, drawn->losing 30%). The dominant motifs (fork 33%, king_safety 33%, hanging_piece 17%, tempo_loss 17%) reveal that the traded piece was either defending critical squares, maintaining tactical pressure, or the player missed an intermediate move (like a check or fork) that would have won material outright. The Maia suggestions (87% non-captures, often pawn or queen moves) confirm that the engine preferred maintaining piece activity or executing a tactic rather than simplifying. The top boards consistently show active bishops or knights being exchanged when superior alternatives existed—removing defenders of key pawns, abandoning diagonals that pressured the opponent's king, or missing intermediate checks that would have won material. This is fundamentally a trade error: the exchange itself is even in material but catastrophic in context, as it relieves the opponent's tactical problems.

35.label: Minor piece moves that fatally weaken king protection, typically dropping material or allowing mating attacks.
35.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where a player moves a bishop (52%) or knight (34%) in a way that critically compromises their own king's safety. The material signature shows these moves are predominantly non-captures (77%) that hang material (32%) or appear superficially safe (58%) but miss critical tactical consequences—53% of the time a winning tactic was available. The dominant motif is king_safety (56%), with tempo_loss (22%) and back_rank (11%) as secondary themes, indicating that the moved piece was either a key defender of the king or the move wasted time while the opponent had a dangerous attack brewing. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors (median 264cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (20%) or throwing away wins (11%). The top boards consistently show positions where the opponent has pieces aimed at the king (knights on e5, queens on the 7th rank, bishops on diagonals), and the player's minor piece move either removes a critical defensive piece (e.g., Bxb2 abandoning kingside defense) or places a piece on an irrelevant square while the king faces imminent threats.

32.label: Placing or leaving a minor piece on an undefended square in the opening, allowing it to be won for free.
32.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where the player moves a bishop or knight (80% combined) to a square that immediately hangs it, transforming a drawn position into a losing one (drawn->losing 100%, median loss ~426cp). The material signature confirms these are not trades—60% are outright hangs (non-capture moves that drop a piece) and 40% are slightly-down exchanges, with zero captures in most cases. The tactical analysis reinforces this: 62% hanging_piece motif, with recurring tags like 'undefended_knight', 'tempo_loss', and 'opening_blunder'. The concrete positions show knights jumping to unguarded squares (Ng6-f4 with no support, Nf3-e5 into a capture), bishops venturing to vulnerable diagonals (Bc5xe3 losing material, Bb7xg2 walking into a trap), and pawns pushed without support (e4-e5 hanging to a knight). In each case the player misjudges a seemingly active developing move as safe or forcing, failing to notice the piece lands on or remains on a square with no defenders against an obvious recapture or attack.

40.label: Player ignores a free capture of an opponent's piece in the opening, playing a routine or developmental move instead.
40.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening-phase mistake where the player makes a non-capturing move (94% no capture, 61% pawn moves) while a hanging enemy piece is available to be taken. The Maia engine confirms this by showing it would capture a bishop (67%) or knight (33%) in those positions. The 'missed winning material' rate is 100%, and the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (62%) combined with 'tempo_loss' (25%). The eval trajectory shows these errors are catastrophic—typically converting a drawn position into a losing one (83% drawn->losing) with a median cost of 451 centipawns (~a full piece). The concrete board examples reinforce this: a bishop sitting on b8/d6 goes uncaptured, a centralized knight on e4/d5 is ignored, as the player instead develops a piece, pushes a pawn, or makes a positional move. The common tags 'missed_capture', 'missed_recapture', 'hanging_piece_ignored', and 'development_over_tactics' all confirm that the player prioritizes routine development or positional ideas while completely overlooking an immediately available free piece in the opening.

43.label: Knight captures on f7/c7 without sufficient compensation, turning equal or manageable positions into losing ones.
43.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring chess mistake: premature or unsound knight sacrifices on f7 (and occasionally c7). The material signature shows 92% knight moves with the player capturing a pawn 58% of the time or making a non-capture that hangs material (27%), resulting in a median loss of 2.0 material points. The eval trajectory is devastating—54% of cases swing from drawn to losing and another 12% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 332 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are unsound sacrifices (tagged 6 times) where the knight lands on f7 hoping for a fork or king attack, but the position lacks the tactical prerequisites for the sacrifice to work. The top 10 boards almost universally show Nxf7 or Nxc7 played from g5, e5, or b5 in opening/early middlegame positions where the king safety motif (75%) tempts the player into a speculative attack that simply drops material. Better developing moves consistently existed within 50cp of the engine's best choice.

41.label: Moving the king to an exposed square where it walks into a forced mating net or lethal attack.
41.description: This feature fires on positions where a player voluntarily moves their king (60% king moves) into a fatally exposed position, typically in the opening or middlegame phase. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense (no piece is directly hung), but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences with a median loss of 430 centipawns, often converting drawn positions to lost or even flipping evaluations entirely. The tactical analysis is unanimous: 100% king_safety motif with tags including exposed_king (5/5), forced_mate (4/5), and king_walk/king_march_to_doom. The concrete positions show classic patterns—kings walking to g6 in Italian Game refusals, kings marching to g3 without pawn shelter, or queens abandoning king defense. In each case, the player's move appears locally reasonable but places the king on a square where opponent piece coordination (queen+bishop batteries, knight forks, pawn storms) creates an inescapable mating net. Maia's suggested alternatives (pawn moves, rook moves, checks) indicate defensive resources existed that would have maintained king safety.

39.label: Developing or moving pieces in the opening that ignore critical central tension or positional demands, costing significant evaluation.
39.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players move bishops (36%), pawns (27%), or knights (9%) in ways that are nominally 'safe' (55%) or hang material (36%), but critically fail to address the position's demands. The eval trajectory shows these moves are devastating: 73% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 248 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are not calculation errors but positional misjudgments—the dominant motifs are positional_mistake (40%), tempo_loss (20%), and king_safety neglect (20%). Common tags like tempo_loss, piece_activity, central_tension_ignored, and premature_development paint a consistent picture: players make natural-looking developing moves (Bc4, Bg7, f6, Re8) that ignore the concrete central tension or tactical obligations of the position. Meanwhile, Maia's suggested moves are exclusively pawn captures (100% pawn moving, 100% capturing pawns), indicating the correct response was to resolve central tension with a pawn exchange rather than continuing passive development. These are opening errors where players prioritize general principles over the specific positional demands of the moment.

45.label: Advancing a pawn in the opening that leaves a piece undefended, dropping roughly a full piece worth of material.
45.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) during the opening phase (100%) that immediately hangs a piece (100% 'hangs' outcome, median -2.0 material). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: positions go from drawn to losing (67%) or worsen an already losing position (33%), with a median loss of 418 centipawns—nearly a full piece. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (62%), with tempo_loss and development tags appearing frequently, indicating the pawn advance neglects piece safety. The top boards confirm this: moves like d2-d3 or d7-d6 in open positions leave knights or bishops en prise. Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%) instead, suggesting the correct response was a developing or repositioning knight move rather than a pawn push. The mistake is fundamentally tactical—the player advances a pawn (often seemingly natural development) without noticing it removes a defense or opens a line that drops material.

38.label: In winning or complex endgames, the player makes a non-forcing move (often king or rook) that misses a decisive tactical opportunity like a back-rank mate, queen capture, or forcing check sequence.
38.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (100% no capture) with a rook or king (80% combined) that fails to convert an advantage or exploit a critical tactical vulnerability. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic cost (median 9156cp lost), with 40% of cases going from winning to still winning but missing forced mates, and 20% throwing a win entirely. Maia consistently recommends forcing moves—checks (100%), captures of major pieces (60% rook/queen captures)—revealing that the optimal continuation involved aggressive, forcing play. The motifs (back_rank 25%, hanging_piece 25%, passed_pawn 25%) and tags (endgame_technique, rook_endgame, king_safety, back_rank_mate) confirm these are positions where concrete calculation was needed to exploit specific vulnerabilities (back-rank threats, hanging pieces, promotion chances), but the player instead made a passive or aimless move, failing to find the decisive blow in a technically demanding endgame.

36.label: Capturing a piece that removes a critical defender or opens lines, allowing devastating king attacks or back-rank tactics.
36.description: This feature fires on moves where a player captures a bishop or knight (78% bishop captures, 22% knight captures) but in doing so fatally compromises king safety or back-rank integrity. The material signature shows these are often 'trades' (44%) or nominally 'safe' (26%), meaning the capture itself isn't obviously losing material—yet the median eval loss is 104 centipawns and 93% of the time the player misses winning material (Maia captures nothing 93% of the time, suggesting the correct move was non-capturing). The dominant tactical motifs—king_safety (40%), back_rank (40%), and hanging_piece (20%)—reveal the true cost: the captured piece was defending the king, guarding a critical square, or the act of capturing opens lines for the opponent. The eval trajectory shows 37% losing→losing (making a bad position worse by grabbing material instead of defending) and 26% losing→winning (cases where the opponent had been winning but the position was complex). The per-position analyses consistently describe scenarios where capturing an attacking or defending piece (exf5 removing the e6 pawn, Qxg3 abandoning f3 defense, hxg3 opening the h-file) creates immediate mating threats or decisive tactical sequences the player failed to foresee.

42.label: Hanging a piece in a simplified endgame position by moving it to an undefended square attacked by the opponent.
42.description: This feature captures a highly specific and costly endgame blunder pattern. The material/position signature shows that 100% of activating moves are non-captures that hang a piece (median -5.0 material), occurring exclusively in endgame positions with kings and rooks as the primary pieces moved. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic swings—winning positions collapsing to losing or drawn ones, with a median cost of 504 centipawns—indicating these are throws of won or holdable endgames. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (89%), with rook endgames being the typical context. Examining the top boards, we see stripped-down positions (often just kings, rooks, and maybe one other piece) where the player carelessly moves a piece directly into an opponent's line of attack (e.g., rook moving to a square controlled by the opponent's rook, or a king stepping into a fork/skewer). These are positions where the player likely has a straightforward winning or drawing technique but instead blunders by placing a piece on an unprotected square, instantly losing the game. The simplicity of the positions makes these errors particularly egregious—there are few pieces on the board, yet the player overlooks a basic capture threat.

47.label: Player makes a passive king or queen move that abandons a winning attack, allowing perpetual check or counterplay.
47.description: This feature detects positions where a player, typically in the middlegame or endgame with a winning advantage, makes a passive king or queen move (king 38%, queen 38%) that critically neglects king safety and defensive coordination. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic—median loss of 462 centipawns, with 50% converting wins into draws and 25% converting draws into losses. The dominant motif is king_safety (60%), and Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (88%) that maintain attacking pressure or provide defense. The concrete positions reveal a recurring pattern: the player's king retreats or sidesteps passively (e.g., Kg8, Kh8, Ka1) or the queen wanders to grab material on the rim (Qa5, Qa2, Da5), abandoning its critical defensive/attacking role. This leaves the king vulnerable to perpetual checks or forced mates. The 88% 'missed winning material' rate confirms these players had winning tactics available but chose passive moves instead, throwing away decisive advantages.

44.label: Player gives a queen check that hangs material instead of capturing or maintaining a winning position.
44.description: This feature detects a specific and recurring tactical mistake: the player delivers a queen check (queen moved 100%, check given 100%) that hangs material (net median -6.0 centipawns lost, 'hangs' 100%) instead of executing a stronger move like a capture or quiet continuation. The eval trajectory shows these checks squander winning or strong positions (60% winning->winning but with massive centipawn loss, 20% winning->losing, 20% winning->drawn, median 1045cp lost). The OPUS analysis confirms the 'checking disease' pattern — premature checks given reflexively ('patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check') that lose tempo or allow the opponent to reorganize. Tags like 'premature_check', 'checks_arent_free', 'hanging_piece_ignored', and 'missed_capture' all point to players prioritizing a flashy check over a materially decisive continuation. Maia's recommended moves (captures of knights, pawns, queens, or quiet bishop moves) confirm that simple captures or non-checking moves were far superior. This is the classic 'checking disease' where the allure of giving check blinds the player to hanging pieces or winning captures.

46.label: Developing a piece in the opening to a square where an enemy pawn can immediately capture it for free.
46.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring opening blunder pattern. The material signature shows pieces (bishops 43%, knights 43%) being hung 100% of the time with no capture involved — these are not trades but pure one-move oversights where a piece lands on or remains on a pawn-attacked square. The phase is exclusively opening (100%), and the tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece in every case, with development and central_tension as common tags. The concrete positions reveal the classic pattern: moves like 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4?? (where ...e5 wins the bishop), or 1.e4 d5 2.Bc4?? (where ...dxe4 isn't even needed — dxc4 is not it, but the pattern involves pawns capturing pieces), or ...Bf5?? where e4xf5 wins immediately. The eval trajectory shows massive swings (median 551cp lost), typically converting drawn or slightly better positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 71%, winning->losing 29%). Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly pawn captures (100%), confirming the opponent simply takes the hung piece with a pawn. This represents the elementary tactical oversight of placing or leaving a piece on a square controlled by an enemy pawn in the opening phase.

49.label: Playing an early d5 pawn push that hangs material in opening positions.
49.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: premature d5 pawn breaks that leave material hanging. The material signature shows 94% pawn moves with no captures, where 82% result in hanging material (median -1.0 pawn net). The eval trajectory confirms these are serious blunders—71% convert drawn positions to losing ones, with a median cost of 250 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players push d5 prematurely in Italian Game and similar e4-e5 structures, undermining their own pawn chain or allowing forced pawn captures that win material. The top boards uniformly show Black (or occasionally White) playing d5 in the opening against a Bc4/Nf3 setup, where the push is tactically refuted. Tags like 'premature_central_break', 'tempo_loss', and 'development' confirm these are cases where the player attempts an active central break before completing development, only to find the push is tactically unsound due to hanging pieces or undermined pawn structures.

53.label: Player moves a piece to an irrelevant square instead of capturing an undefended or available enemy queen.
53.description: All three signals converge on a single recurring blunder: the player fails to capture a hanging or available enemy queen. The material signature shows that Maia's recommended move captures a queen in 100% of cases, while the player's actual move captures nothing 73% of the time and hangs material 42% of the time—indicating they moved a piece to an undefended square instead of taking the queen. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: median loss of 471 centipawns, with 27% of cases swinging from winning to losing and 38% making a losing position even worse. The tactical analysis explicitly identifies 'hanging_piece' (75%) and 'hanging_queen' motifs, with per-position summaries describing failures like 'captured a bishop when the queen was hanging' or 'moved a bishop instead of simply capturing White's undefended queen.' The piece distribution of player moves (rooks, bishops, knights, pawns) versus Maia's queen captures confirms the player consistently prioritized an inferior piece move over the highest-value available capture.

48.label: Playing a quiet, passive move that wastes critical tempo in a position demanding immediate tactical action.
48.description: This feature captures moments where players make passive, non-capturing moves (96% no capture) with kings, rooks, or queens that squander vital tempo in positions that demand urgent tactical responses. The material signature shows 33% of moves hang material — not through exchanges but through neglect, as the player's quiet move allows the opponent to execute threats. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 275 centipawns, with 30% converting drawn positions into losing ones and 37% making already-losing positions worse. Crucially, Maia's recommended moves involve captures 37% of the time (bishops, pawns, knights) that the player completely missed, and 56% of positions had winning material available. The dominant motifs — tempo_loss (43%) and hanging_piece (43%) — tell a unified story: the player plays a 'do-nothing' move (Kh8 instead of cxd5, Kg2 instead of a critical defense, Rf2 walking into a capture) while the position screams for the one active move that addresses concrete threats. The positions span middlegame and endgame roughly equally, suggesting this is a general pattern of passivity under pressure rather than phase-specific confusion.

51.label: Playing a passive pawn move (usually d3) that ignores the opponent's pawn attacking an undefended bishop on c4 in the opening.
51.description: This feature fires on a very specific opening blunder pattern: White has developed a bishop to c4 (typically in Italian Game or similar e4 openings), and Black's d-pawn advances to d5, directly attacking the bishop. Instead of addressing this threat (e.g., capturing on d5 or retreating the bishop), White plays a passive pawn move like d2-d3 or c2-c3 that fails to defend or move the hanging bishop. The material signature confirms this: 100% of moves are pawn pushes with no captures, yet they 'hang' material (median -2.0, consistent with losing a bishop). The eval trajectory shows drawn positions collapsing to losing (median 520cp loss), reflecting the catastrophic cost of leaving a piece en prise. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, with tags emphasizing tempo_loss and opening_blunder. All top positions feature a Bc4 under attack from a d5 pawn, with the player ignoring this threat to make an otherwise logical-looking developmental pawn move.

59.label: Player makes a passive king or rook move instead of capturing an undefended enemy rook.
59.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a simple one-move capture of an enemy rook that is hanging or undefended. The material signature shows the player moved their king (50%) or rook/pawn (36%) — all quiet, non-capturing moves (94% no capture) — while Maia's recommended move involves capturing a rook 100% of the time, typically with a bishop (54%) or knight (28%). The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of positions, with 'capture_blindness' and 'missed_capture' as recurring tags. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly oversights: the median centipawn loss is 501, with many positions going from winning to drawn (20%) or winning to losing (22%), reflecting how failing to collect a free rook squanders decisive advantages. The board positions consistently show endgame/middlegame scenarios where an enemy rook sits undefended on an open file or rank, and the player makes an irrelevant king shuffle or pawn push instead of the trivial capture.

52.label: Moving the king into a mating net when opponent's pieces are already coordinated for checkmate.
52.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a catastrophic king move (king 50% of played moves, with pawn moves being the other half—often promotion attempts that ignore the threat) that walks directly into a forced mating net. The material signature shows these are non-captures (captured: none 100%) where 50% hang material and the median eval loss is enormous (9573 centipawns, indicating forced mate). The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly losing->losing (75%) situations where the player makes a bad position terminal, plus one drawn->winning case viewed from the wrong side. The Opus analysis is definitive: dominant motifs are king_safety (60%), back_rank (20%), and promotion_error (20%), with recurring tags of mating_net, king_walk_blunder, and exposed_king. The concrete positions show kings on f7, f6, and similar exposed squares walking into coordinated queen-rook or queen-knight mating patterns. Maia's recommended moves (queen 75%, rook 25%) delivering check 75% of the time confirm that the correct response exploits the exposed king immediately. The player consistently fails to recognize that their king is fatally exposed and that the opponent's heavy pieces are already coordinated for a mating attack.

54.label: Moving the queen to an ineffective square that wastes a critical tempo in a position requiring immediate tactical action.
54.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (100% queen moves) to a square that either hangs material (60%) or is merely safe but ineffective (40%), when a decisive tactical continuation existed. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 509 centipawns, with 80% of cases missing winning material—often forced checkmates (missed_mate appears 3 times). The dominant motifs are king_safety (44%) and tempo_loss (33%), revealing that these queen moves squander a critical tempo in attacking positions where the opponent's king is vulnerable. The concrete examples confirm this: players move their queen to threatening-looking squares (Qh5, Qh4, Qh6) that appear aggressive but give the opponent exactly one tempo to defend, when an immediate non-queen move (like a rook sacrifice or piece capture) would have delivered checkmate or won decisive material. The trajectory (60% winning->winning but with huge eval drops, 20% winning->drawn) shows players who were already winning but threw away their attack by choosing a flashy but slow queen move over the killing blow.

57.label: Trading rooks into a losing pawn endgame where the opponent's king activity or pawn structure is decisive.
57.description: This feature fires when players trade rooks (82% rook trades, 18% queen trades) in endgame positions (82% endgame), simplifying into pawn endgames that are objectively lost. The material signature shows 100% trades (net material median 0.0), confirming these are voluntary exchanges rather than blunders. However, the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional cost: median 315 centipawns lost, with 46% going losing->losing and 43% going drawn->losing. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'pawn_endgame' (90%) as the dominant motif, with recurring tags of passed_pawn, piece_activity, and positional_mistake. The pattern is clear from the top boards and summaries: players trade their rook—often their key defensive or counterattacking piece—failing to recognize that the resulting pawn endgame is lost due to the opponent's superior king position, passed pawns, or pawn majority. Maia's recommended moves (100% non-captures) confirm that maintaining the rook on the board was correct, and 68% of positions had winning material available that was missed. The rook provided dynamic compensation or defensive resources that evaporated upon simplification.

50.label: King moves that allow stalemate or lose a won endgame by approaching incorrectly in KQ vs K or similar endings.
50.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (86%) in theoretically won or drawn positions with queen vs lone king or similar simplified material. The top boards reveal a clear pattern: KQ vs K, KQ vs Kq, or K+pawn endgames where the player's king move either creates stalemate, allows the opponent's queen to gain a critical tempo, or loses coordination with their own queen. The Maia engine consistently recommends queen moves (100%), suggesting the correct approach was to use the queen rather than the king at that moment. The motifs (tempo_loss, hanging_piece, king_safety) and tags (tempo_loss appearing 3 times, move_order_error) confirm these are move-order mistakes where the king steps into the wrong square before the queen has corralled the opponent, often resulting in stalemate or loss of a winning technique. The drawn->losing trajectory and massive centipawn losses in some cases (495cp median, one showing immediate checkmate) indicate these king moves catastrophically mishandle won or drawn endgame positions.

55.label: Player makes a non-forcing move when a forced checkmate or decisive king attack via checks was available.
55.description: This feature captures positions where the player has a winning mating attack but plays a quiet or non-forcing move instead of delivering the decisive blow. The material signature shows the moves are overwhelmingly 'safe' (85%) with no captures (69%), meaning the player isn't blundering material but is simply failing to finish the game. The Maia best-move signal is striking: 100% of recommended moves give check, predominantly with the queen (69%) or rook (31%), confirming that forcing sequences were available. The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the median eval loss of 246 centipawns reflects the cost of letting a forced mate slip into merely a winning position. The motif analysis confirms this with king_safety (57%), tempo_loss (29%), and back_rank (14%) as dominant themes, along with tags like missed_mate, mating_attack, and exposed_king. The trajectory (69% winning->winning) shows these players remain winning but have squandered a forced conclusion. The per-position summaries consistently describe scenarios where a player had mate-in-N but chose a slow repositioning move, a quiet attack on a piece, or a non-checking queen move instead of the immediately decisive check sequence that exploits the exposed enemy king.

56.label: Rook moves in lost endgame positions that allow immediate forced mate or catastrophic material loss.
56.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where a player in an already losing endgame position makes a rook move (100% rook moves, 100% non-captures) that catastrophically worsens their situation—typically converting a losing-but-defensible position into immediate forced mate. The material signature shows these moves hang material (median -5.0 net), while the eval trajectory confirms massive centipawn losses (median 9443) within already-losing positions. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging pieces (43%), king safety (29%), and back-rank threats (14%), with tempo loss appearing frequently (5/7 examples). The concrete positions show endgame configurations (100% endgame phase) where the rook move either blocks a critical escape square for the king, removes a defensive piece from a vital file, or walks into a forced mating net. The Maia response is always a king move (100%), suggesting the opponent's king activates decisively after the blunder. These are not positional misjudgments but rather final tactical collapses in technically lost but complex endgames where the player's rook move precipitates immediate catastrophe.

61.label: Player makes a seemingly safe move while missing a critical tactical opportunity involving back-rank or king safety themes.
61.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a materially 'safe' move (no piece is immediately hung or lost) but misses a powerful tactical continuation, typically involving back-rank threats, discovered attacks, or exploiting an exposed king. The material signature shows safe moves (median net material: 0.0) that aren't trades, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 377 centipawns), with 50% going from winning to drawn. The Opus analysis consistently tags back_rank, king_safety, exposed_king, and missed_tactic themes—the player retreats or repositions passively (Qf3, Qe2, Kb1, Bc4) when a decisive attacking blow was available (often a bishop or queen move exploiting king vulnerability). The common thread is that the player's move looks reasonable but abandons a winning attack or fails to exploit a critical king-safety weakness, allowing the opponent to consolidate or even turn the tables.

58.label: Player makes a non-defensive move while an enemy knight on a dominant square hangs or wins material.
58.description: Across the top activating positions, a consistent pattern emerges: the opponent has a powerful knight placed on an aggressive square (often N on f6, g6, c6, e4, or similar outpost) that threatens forks, captures, or checks. The player's move ignores this knight entirely—moving a king, rook, or queen to a square that either hangs material to the knight or fails to address its dominance. The material signature shows 78% of moves hang a piece (median loss of 3.0 material / 292 centipawns), and Maia's recommended moves almost universally capture the threatening knight (100% knight captures). The Opus analysis confirms motifs of hanging_piece (67%) and tempo_loss (33%), with tags like knight_geometry_oversight, dominant_knight, and piece_counting_error. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly already-losing positions made catastrophically worse, where the player overlooks the knight's tactical radius and pays an immediate material price. The boards consistently show an enemy knight on a central or attacking square (N on g6, f6, c6, e4, f3) that the player fails to neutralize or respect.

63.label: Moving the king into an exposed position, missing a critical capture or defensive resource that leaves the king vulnerable to tactical threats.
63.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player moves their king (48% of moves) in a non-capturing way (91% no capture) that hangs material (72% hangs) with a massive median eval loss of 312 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (57%), hanging_piece (29%), and back_rank (14%), with tags like 'exposed_king', 'king_walk_blunder', and 'king_safety' recurring throughout. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing pieces (67% knight, 24% bishop), indicating the player missed a critical capture opportunity and instead made a passive or actively harmful king move. The trajectory shows these mistakes occur across various eval states (losing->losing 33%, drawn->losing 15%), suggesting the player reflexively moves the king when under pressure rather than finding the concrete tactical resource (a capture or counter-threat). The board positions consistently show kings walking into crossfires, discovered attacks, or mating nets—transforming survivable positions into lost ones.

60.label: Player develops or repositions a piece while ignoring a critical Bxf6/Nxf6 kingside pawn-structure shattering threat in the opening.
60.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player moves a piece (most often queen, bishop, or knight) while completely ignoring a looming tactical threat involving the exchange on f6 that damages their kingside pawn structure. The material signature shows moves that are nominally 'safe' (88%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet 100% of the time a winning continuation (typically involving Bxf6 or Nxf6 with structural damage) is missed. The eval trajectory is devastating: 75% of cases go from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 252 centipawns. The positional layer reveals a consistent pattern: a bishop on h4/g5 or knight on d5 threatens to capture on f6, shattering the kingside, but the player makes a developing or repositioning move (Bg4, Qd7, Qe2, Ne6, etc.) that loses tempo and fails to neutralize the threat. Tags like 'tempo_loss', 'kingside_weakness', 'open_g_file', and 'pawn_structure_damage' recur throughout. The boards consistently show Italian Game / Classical setups where one side has Bh4 or Bg5 eyeing f6, and the opponent plays a move that allows the structural blow on optimal terms.

62.label: Player makes a move that leaves a piece undefended and capturable, overlooking an opponent's attacking line.
62.description: This feature fires on moves where the player leaves a piece hanging — 83% of positions show the 'hanging_piece' motif, and 42% of moves result in material being hung (non-captures that drop a piece). The player's moves are distributed across rooks (30%), pawns (24%), bishops (18%), and kings (14%), indicating they are making routine developing or repositioning moves while failing to notice that a valuable piece elsewhere is undefended. Critically, 100% of these positions miss winning material (Maia wanted rook 55%, queen 23%), meaning the correct move was typically to save or activate the hanging piece. The median eval loss of 233 centipawns confirms these are serious blunders — often losing a full piece. The per-position analysis reinforces this: queens left on attacked squares, rooks captured via open diagonals, and pieces sitting on squares controlled by enemy minor pieces. The trajectory (20% losing->losing, 12% drawn->losing) shows these mistakes frequently convert holdable or even winning positions into lost ones.
