The common thread is not a bad exchange or positional misjudgment, but pure tactical oversight — the player simply doesn't see that a piece is en prise after their move.

64.label: Queen captures a bishop but loses the queen in a position that was already losing, worsening the deficit significantly.
64.description: This feature identifies positions where a player uses their queen to capture a bishop (queen moved 100%, captured bishop 100%) but loses significant material in the process (net material median: -6.0, consistent with losing the queen for a bishop). The eval trajectory shows these occur in already-losing positions (losing->losing 100%) where the mistake deepens the deficit by a median of 265 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players grab an available bishop with their queen while missing that the queen itself becomes en prise or trappable after the capture (tags include 'queen_en_prise', 'pawn_captures_queen', 'capture_priority'). The motifs show hanging_piece and positional_mistake patterns, where players prioritize an immediate material grab over maintaining queen safety or pursuing better defensive resources. Maia recommends quiet knight moves instead (knight 100%, no capture), suggesting the correct approach was developing/repositioning rather than greedily snatching material with the queen in tactically unsafe circumstances.

65.label: Player makes a developing or active-looking move in the opening that walks into a concrete tactic, hanging material or allowing a devastating combination.
65.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in the opening phase (75% opening) make seemingly natural moves—often with knights (50%) or queens (25%)—that fail to address an immediate tactical threat, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (median 369 centipawns lost). The positions consistently show missed tactics involving hanging pieces, trapped pieces, or overloaded defenders. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding errors: 50% turn drawn positions into losing ones, and 25% throw outright wins. The boards reveal a common thread: players prioritize development or activity (Nb4, Ng4, Qf4, Kd7) while overlooking that their opponent has a zwischenzug, deflection, or simple capture available. In 75% of cases the player missed winning material themselves (Maia captures a bishop 75% of the time as the correct alternative). These are not positional misjudgments but concrete tactical oversights during the critical opening-to-middlegame transition where piece placement creates vulnerable geometries.

66.label: Moving a knight to an undefended square where it can be captured with a discovered attack or pawn fork, losing material.
66.description: This feature detects a specific opening-phase tactical blunder where the player moves a knight (100% knight moves, no captures) to a square that appears safe but walks directly into a tactical refutation. The key signal is that Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing the knight with check (bishop 100%, captures knight 100%, gives check 100%), indicating the knight landed on a square where it can be taken with a forcing recapture that also delivers check or creates a fork. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 380cp), turning drawn positions into losing ones or making losing positions far worse. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 60%, fork 40%) and the per-position analyses confirm the pattern: knights are placed on undefended squares (Ng4, Ne5, Nd5) where they are immediately captured by a pawn or bishop that simultaneously forks other pieces or gives check. The common tags—missed_tactic, hanging_piece, undefended_piece—reinforce that players fail to see their knight is tactically vulnerable despite the square appearing materially 'safe' at first glance. This is a pure tactical oversight in the opening where development tempo and piece coordination punish the misplaced knight.

67.label: Knight captures on f7 or f2 that trade a knight for a pawn while fatally compromising the player's position.
67.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early-middlegame pattern: a knight captures a pawn on f7 (for White) or f2 (for Black), resulting in a material trade (knight for pawn, net ~0 since the knight is typically recaptured or trapped). The material signature confirms 100% knight moves capturing pawns classified as trades. However, the eval trajectory reveals these are severe mistakes—88% shift a drawn position to losing and 12% turn a winning position to drawn, with a median cost of 186 centipawns. The tactical analysis shows these are unsound sacrificial combinations: players attempt Nxf7 fork tricks or Nxf2 attacks against the castled king, but the tactics don't work—the opponent's king safety is not actually compromised enough to justify the piece investment. The dominant motifs (king_safety 57%, positional_mistake 29%, fork 14%) confirm players are attempting speculative attacks or forks near the king that simply fail upon accurate defense. Maia's recommended moves (quiet pawn moves, queen moves, king moves) indicate that patient development or consolidation was correct instead of the aggressive but unsound knight sacrifice.

71.label: King moves in endgames that abandon defensive duties, hanging pieces or losing drawn positions.
71.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make king moves (60% of activations) in endgame positions (60%) that catastrophically misplace the king, turning drawn positions into losses (80% drawn->losing trajectory) with a massive median eval drop of 585 centipawns. The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly 'hangs' (80%) rather than bad captures—the player isn't trading poorly but rather moving a piece (usually the king) that abandons critical defensive responsibilities. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and pawn_endgame (33%), with tags like 'king_move_blunder', 'drawn_position_thrown_away', and 'compensation_loss'. The concrete examples show kings walking away from squares where they provided indirect protection to pieces (e.g., Ke6 abandoning protection of a bishop, Kg5 leaving a knight undefended), or moving into positions where coordination collapses. The bishops and knights that hang are typically left undefended after the king wanders, converting technically drawn endgames into immediate losses.

68.label: Player makes a routine developing move while ignoring an undefended enemy piece that could be captured for free.
68.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player moves a minor piece (bishop or knight) in a natural developing pattern but completely overlooks that an enemy piece is hanging and could be captured for free. The material signature shows 50% hangs (the player's own piece becomes vulnerable) and 50% safe moves, but critically Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a bishop — indicating a free capture was available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic, with a median loss of 1029 centipawns, swinging from winning to losing or drawn positions. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (90%) as the dominant motif, with tags like 'missed_capture', 'capture_oversight', and 'opening_blunder' reinforcing the pattern. The top boards show a recurring concrete scenario: an enemy bishop sits undefended (often on a6 after Bxa6 in Scandinavian-like structures, or on h3/h6 in fianchetto lines) and the player castles, develops a knight, or makes another routine move instead of simply taking the free piece. This is a pure tactical oversight — not a positional misjudgment or a trade gone wrong — where tunnel vision on development causes the player to miss an elementary capture.

70.label: Moving the king to an unsafe square in the opening, forfeiting castling rights or inviting attacks, instead of developing or capturing actively.
70.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase moves where the player voluntarily moves their king (67% king moves) to an exposed square, forfeiting castling rights and blocking development. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 198 centipawns across a range of situations (winning->drawn, drawn->losing, losing->losing), indicating these are consequential positional errors rather than outright tactical blunders. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), with tags like exposed_king, tempo_loss, and castling_rights_forfeited appearing repeatedly. Maia's recommended alternatives almost always involve capturing with a bishop (Bxd6) or retreating the king to a safer square, often winning material (missed knight captures in 100% of Maia's suggestions). The concrete positions confirm the pattern: multiple Ke7 moves in Fried Liver / Scotch-type openings where the king walks into the center, and Kg6 moves that expose the king to attack. The material outcome is mostly 'safe' (67%) because no piece is immediately lost, but the positional damage—permanent king exposure in an open center during the opening—costs nearly two pawns of evaluation on average.

72.label: King moves away from the critical square or piece coordination needed to convert a won endgame, allowing opponent counterplay via skewer or perpetual.
72.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a king move (80%) or pawn move (20%) that is materially safe but tactically catastrophic, converting winning positions into draws (80% winning->drawn trajectory, median 445cp lost). The positions are all simplified endgames—rook endgames, pawn endgames, or promotion scenarios—where the player's king drifts to the wrong square, abandoning coordination with their winning asset. The Opus analysis reveals the opponent consistently had a check-based tactic available (Maia gives check 100%), typically a skewer or back-rank resource exploiting the king's misplacement. The recurring motifs (skewer 30%, king_safety 30%, promotion_error 20%) all stem from the same root cause: the king steps away from the one square that maintains control, enabling the opponent's rook or promoted piece to deliver a saving skewer, perpetual check, or stalemate trick. Promotion errors (underpromoting to knight or promoting at the wrong moment) fit the same pattern of misjudging the critical coordination in a technically won ending.

73.label: Advancing a passed pawn with check in the endgame that squanders a tempo advantage or allows the opponent's king to reach an ideal square.
73.description: This feature captures a specific endgame error where a player pushes a pawn delivering check (100% pawn moves, 100% checks, 90% endgame phase) but the check is counterproductive—it either drives the opponent's king to a better square or wastes a critical tempo. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (79%), meaning no piece is immediately lost, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional damage: a median of 273 centipawns lost, with 34% of cases remaining winning but 24% collapsing from winning to drawn and 10% from winning to losing. The tactical analysis confirms 'tempo_loss' as the dominant motif (43%), with passed_pawn and pawn_endgame themes recurring. The concrete positions show patterns like d5-d6+ allowing the king to centralize on a blockading square, or premature pawn advances that fix structure and gift the opponent defensive resources. The key insight is that checking with a pawn feels forcing but actually surrenders the initiative by improving the opponent's king placement, turning technically won pawn endgames into draws or losses.

76.label: Moving the queen away from a critical king-defense role, allowing the opponent's king to escape danger or exposing one's own king.
76.description: This feature fires on endgame and middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (100% queen moves, no captures, no checks) to a square that loses its defensive or attacking coordination around the king. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (67%) meaning nothing is immediately hanging, yet the eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 377cp lost), with 50% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one. The dominant motifs are king_safety (57%) and tempo_loss, with perpetual_check appearing in 4/10 cases—suggesting the queen move often abandons control of squares needed to prevent perpetual checks or fails to maintain pressure on the opponent's exposed king. The concrete positions confirm this: in nearly every case, a king move (Kh6, Kf7, Kf6, Kg1, Ke2) was the correct choice instead of the queen relocation, indicating the player prioritized queen activity over urgent king safety needs. The queen moves look active but fatally neglect the king's vulnerability, throwing away winning or drawn positions.

69.label: Playing a tempting knight fork check that loses material by neglecting a more critical defensive or tactical priority.
69.description: This feature fires on positions where a player executes a knight check (100% knight moves, 100% checks) that appears tactically tempting—typically a fork—but is objectively disastrous, costing a median of 411 centipawns. The material signature shows the move either hangs material or ends slightly down (median net -2.0), indicating the knight check itself doesn't win material and often loses it. The Opus analysis reveals the core pattern: players prioritize a flashy Nc2+ (or Nc7+) fork/check over a more critical task—whether that's saving a hanging piece (trapped_piece tag appears 4 times), maintaining king safety (3 occurrences), or executing the correct move order (3 occurrences). The eval trajectory (drawn->losing 50%, losing->losing 50%) shows these are positions where the player either throws away a tenable or winning position by grabbing the wrong target first. The recurring theme across all examples is 'greed overriding strategy'—the knight check looks forcing and attractive but ignores that the resulting position leaves the player worse off, often because a defensive piece is removed from a critical square or because an intermediate move was required first.

75.label: Developing a minor piece to a square where it becomes vulnerable to a central pawn fork in the opening.
75.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening mistake where a player develops a minor piece (bishop 35%, knight 33%) to a square that allows the opponent to gain tempo or win material via a central pawn advance, most commonly d5. The material signature shows 37% of moves 'hang' a piece despite 92% being non-captures—the player isn't trading, they're placing pieces on vulnerable squares. The phase is overwhelmingly opening (96%), and the eval trajectory is devastating: 63% of cases shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 257 centipawns (roughly a minor piece). The tactical motifs—fork (33%), tempo_loss (33%), hanging_piece (22%)—all converge on the same pattern visible in the top boards: moves like ...Be6 in the Italian/Scotch where d5 creates a pawn fork hitting the bishop and a knight simultaneously, or premature knight placements that allow tempo-gaining pawn thrusts. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies d5 as the punishing move that attacks two pieces at once. The common tags (central_pawn_advance, pawn_fork, development, opening_principles) confirm this is a failure to respect how central pawn levers punish prematurely placed minor pieces in the opening.

78.label: Queen checks that squander forced mates or winning attacks by giving the opponent's king an escape route.
78.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that hangs material (75% hangs, median -1.0 net material) by choosing a flashy but incorrect checking sequence. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic cost (median 9285 centipawns lost), typically converting a winning position into a drawn or merely advantageous one (75% winning->winning with reduced advantage, 25% winning->drawn). The tactical analysis confirms the 'patzer sees a check' pattern: the dominant motifs are king_safety (60%) with recurring tags of missed_mate, forced_mate_in_3, and checks_not_always_best. The per-position summaries explicitly describe players who had forced checkmates in 3 but played checks in the wrong order, allowing the king to escape. Rather than calculating the precise mating sequence (often involving a rook lift or quiet move), the player reflexively fires a queen check that displaces their own attacking piece or gives the enemy king a flight square. Maia's preferred alternatives (rook 50%, pawn 25%, bishop 25%) confirm that the correct move was typically a non-queen, non-checking move that maintained the mating net.

74.label: King captures a pawn in a drawn endgame, abandoning a critical defensive duty and allowing opponent's passed pawn to promote.
74.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame mistake pattern: the player's king captures a pawn (100% king moved, 100% pawn captured) in what was objectively a drawn position, but the capture costs roughly 2 pawns net (material outcome slightly_down, median -2.0) and transforms the game from drawn to losing (100% drawn->losing, median 470cp lost). The missed move is consistently a knight maneuver (Maia's move: knight 100%, no capture), suggesting the correct plan involved piece activity or blockade rather than grabbing material. The tactical analysis reveals the core theme: these are pawn endgames or near-pawn-endgames (pawn_endgame 43%, passed_pawn 29%) where the king's capture abandons a critical defensive post—either leaving a piece unprotected (hanging_piece), breaking a blockade of a passed pawn, or losing a crucial tempo (tempo_loss). The concrete positions confirm this: Kxa2 abandons knight protection allowing a passed pawn to queen, Kxb6 captures in the wrong order destroying pawn structure, and Rxg7 similarly trades away defensive resources. The unifying error is a greedy king capture that looks natural but fatally compromises the player's ability to stop a passed pawn or maintain a drawn fortress.

77.label: Player makes a passive or misdirected move that squanders a significant tactical advantage by failing to find the one critical continuation.
77.description: This feature captures positions where players hold a strong (often winning) advantage but play a move that hangs material or misses a decisive tactic, typically costing ~286 centipawns. The material signature shows 50% of moves hang a piece and 86% are non-captures, indicating the player made a quiet, passive move when a forcing continuation was required. Maia's recommended moves heavily favor captures (queen captures 23%, bishop 23%, rook 14%) and checks (32%), confirming the missed opportunity was a concrete tactical shot. The eval trajectory shows 32% winning->winning (slight squander) and 18% winning->drawn, meaning these are predominantly cases of throwing away or significantly diminishing a winning position. The Opus analysis reveals recurring themes of missed tactics (tagged 3 times), tempo loss (3 times), and hanging pieces—players move a piece to a passive square (like Qd7 instead of Qxg5, or Rc7 instead of Qxd4+) abandoning the one critical attacking line. The middlegame dominance (82%) and piece_activity/king_safety tags confirm these are complex attacking positions where the player lost the thread of their initiative.

79.label: Ignoring concrete piece-capturing threats in sharp opening positions, typically losing a full piece to known tactical patterns.
79.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players move minor pieces or pawns into tactically vulnerable squares, missing that their opponent has an immediate capturing or forking threat. The material signature shows 24% of moves outright hang a piece and 20% are slightly down, with the median eval loss of 321 centipawns confirming full-piece-level blunders. The eval trajectory (64% drawn->losing, 12% winning->losing) shows these mistakes typically transform balanced or good positions into lost ones. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (44%), fork (22%), king_safety (22%)—combined with tags like 'opening_trap', 'missed_tactic', and 'unsound_sacrifice' reveal a consistent pattern: players develop or reposition pieces without calculating the opponent's immediate tactical replies in well-known opening lines (e.g., placing a knight where exd5 wins it, putting a bishop on a square attacked by a knight, or ignoring a fork on c2). Maia's 100% pawn moves suggest the correct alternatives were often simple developing or prophylactic pawn moves rather than the ambitious piece maneuvers chosen.

80.label: Developing a bishop to an undefended square where the opponent's queen can immediately capture it in the opening.
80.description: This feature consistently fires on a specific opening blunder pattern: the player develops their bishop (100% bishop moves) to an aggressive-looking but completely undefended square (g5, g4, or h6) very early in the game (100% opening phase). The material signature confirms these are non-capture moves that hang a piece (100% hangs, median -3.0 material = a full minor piece lost). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones 100% of the time, with a median cost of 486 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (100%), with recurring tags of premature_development, undefended_bishop, and queen_capture. The concrete positions reveal the archetypal pattern: Bc1-g5 or Bc8-g4 on move 2-3, placing the bishop where the opponent's queen on d8/d1 has an immediate unobstructed capture path. Players appear to be mimicking familiar development patterns (like the London or Trompowsky) without verifying the prerequisite pawn structure that would make the bishop safe.

81.label: Playing a rook check that leaves material hanging, squandering a winning or drawn position.
81.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where a player delivers a check with their rook (100% rook moves, 100% checks) but the move hangs material (100% hangs, median net material -1.0). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: positions go from winning or drawn to losing, with a median loss of 883 centipawns. The Opus analysis reveals that players are overlooking opponent piece activity (knight captures queen, hanging pieces) while fixated on delivering check. The common thread across examples is that the checking move either exposes a piece to capture or moves the rook to a square where it can be taken, often when a much stronger non-checking move (like mate or decisive material gain) was available. The players appear seduced by the forcing nature of a check while failing to verify that their position remains tactically sound after the opponent's forced reply.

82.label: Player moves a piece while leaving their queen undefended or exposed to capture, resulting in catastrophic material loss.
82.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a move (most often with the queen itself, but also with knights, bishops, or rooks) that leaves their queen en prise or removes a critical defender of the queen. The material signature is stark: 94% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -6.0 pawns, which corresponds precisely to queen value. The queen is the moved piece 50% of the time, suggesting the player relocates their queen to an undefended square or moves a supporting piece away. The Opus analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging_piece (80%) and overloaded_defender (20%), plus tags like 'blundered_queen' and 'removing the guard.' Concrete examples show patterns like Ne7 removing a knight that was defending the queen, or Be3 ignoring an attack on the queen. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 460cp), with 26% of cases turning drawn positions into losing ones. These are elementary one-move oversights in the middlegame where the player fails to notice their queen is attacked or unprotected after their move.

87.label: Player retreats or repositions a piece, abandoning a winning tactical resource that was the foundation of their advantage.
87.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'safe' move (94% no material lost immediately) that nonetheless costs a median of 317 centipawns by abandoning a critical tactical opportunity. The SEE signature shows the player moves rooks (50%) or minor pieces (31%) to passive squares while Maia identifies captures of major material (rook 81%, queen 19%) as the correct continuation—meaning the player missed winning material 100% of the time. The eval trajectory confirms these are predominantly thrown advantages (38% winning→drawn, 19% winning→losing), not errors from already-bad positions. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring motif: moves like Rb7 abandoning a crushing file, Bh5 retreating instead of capturing an undefended rook, or quiet king moves when decisive tactics existed. Tags like 'abandoned_open_file', 'wasted_tactical_pressure', and 'tempo_loss' reinforce that the player voluntarily releases tension by repositioning pieces rather than executing the available winning blow.

83.label: Moving a rook to a square where it can be captured by the opponent's queen via a tactical motif, throwing away a winning position.
83.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player moves their rook (100% rook moves) to a square where it becomes a hanging piece (100% hangs material, median -1.0 net material), allowing the opponent's queen to capture it (Maia plays queen 100%, capturing rook 50% or knight 50%). The tactical motifs are dominated by hanging pieces (67%) with discovered attacks and overloaded defenders also present. The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic blunders that throw away winning positions (winning->drawn 50%, winning->losing 50%, median 1072 centipawns lost). The concrete examples confirm this: Re3 placed on a square where a discovered check wins it, Rb2-e2 left the rook hanging to a queen, and other rook moves ignored that the opponent's queen had direct access to capture the misplaced rook. King safety tags (5 occurrences) suggest the rook often moves in positions where the player's king is already under pressure, making the oversight more likely. The common thread is a rook relocation that overlooks a simple queen capture or tactical shot exploiting the rook's new vulnerability.

85.label: Player makes a non-queen move that overlooks a critical queen check or queen-based tactic available to them, resulting in massive material or positional loss.
85.description: This feature fires when a player moves a piece (queen 33%, knight 19%, pawn 19%, bishop 16%) in the middlegame while completely missing that Maia's recommended move was a queen check (Maia: queen 100%, gives check 100%). The material signature shows 37% of moves hang a piece and 9% lose material outright, with a median net material loss of -1.0 and median eval loss of 454 centipawns—indicating catastrophic oversights. The missed winning material rate is 100%, confirming the player always had a strong tactical resource available. The eval trajectory shows wins converting to losses (9%) or draws (12%), and draws becoming losses (9%), consistent with throwing away a position. The Opus analysis reveals hanging pieces (50%), king safety issues (25%), and concrete examples of players moving queens to wrong squares or moving other pieces while missing back-rank threats, checkmate-in-one, or piece-winning queen checks. The boards confirm positions where powerful queen checks (often combining threats to king and hanging pieces) were available but the player chose an inferior move, frequently dropping material or allowing immediate decisive tactics.

84.label: Queen captures a central pawn early in the opening, losing tempo to minor piece development attacks.
84.description: This feature detects a specific opening mistake where a player uses their queen to capture a central pawn (typically on d5 or d4), placing the queen on an exposed central square too early. The material signature shows queen moves capturing pawns with a net loss of ~2 pawns worth of material (slightly_down), while the best move was consistently a bishop recapture (Bxe2/Bxb5). The eval trajectory is devastating: drawn positions become losing by ~424 centipawns, essentially dropping a full minor piece. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread - the centralized queen becomes a target for tempo-gaining development moves (Nc3, etc.) or direct forks (g4 hitting queen and bishop). The top boards confirm this is overwhelmingly an opening pattern (100% opening phase) where players greedily recapture with the queen instead of maintaining piece coordination, violating the classical principle against early queen development. The tags 'premature_queen_development', 'tempo_loss', and 'development' all reinforce that the queen sortie allows the opponent to develop with tempo, converting a balanced position into a strategically lost one.

89.label: King moves away from critical pawns in won pawn endgames, allowing the opponent to draw.
89.description: This feature detects king moves in pawn endgames that throw away a winning position by drifting to the wrong square. All activating positions are endgames where the player moves their king (100%) without capturing, while the best move (Maia's suggestion) was to capture a pawn. The material outcome appears 'safe' because nothing is immediately lost, but the eval trajectory shows a consistent winning->drawn collapse (median 537cp lost). The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (75%) and promotion_error (25%)—along with recurring tags like passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and king_activity confirm the pattern: the player's king wanders to an incorrect square, abandoning a critical capture or optimal blocking position, which allows the opponent to equalize in a pawn race or reach a theoretical draw. The concrete examples show kings stepping away from capturable pawns (Kf3 instead of Kxh4, Kc4 leaving b6 undefended) or failing to address promotion threats, turning textbook wins into draws.

92.label: Player makes a quiet or retreating move that hangs material, missing a powerful discovered attack or fork that would have won decisively.
92.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player overlooks a crushing tactical shot—most often a discovered attack or fork—and instead plays a passive or irrelevant move (frequently a king move or quiet piece retreat) that hangs material. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in hanging a piece with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece), while Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly checks (86%) involving knights or bishops delivering forks or discoveries. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding errors: 36% turn wins into draws, 21% turn draws into losses, and 21% turn wins into losses, with a massive median eval loss of 440 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with discovered_attack (25%) and fork (25%) as dominant motifs, alongside tags like missed_tactic (appearing in 7/14 positions) and exposed_king. The concrete positions show patterns like missing Ne7+ forks, Bxg7+ discovered attacks opening files, and Nc6+ saving resources—all cases where a forcing tactical blow was available but the player chose a quiet move instead.

86.label: Trading the bishop for a knight on e5 opens the f-file against one's own uncastled or vulnerable king.
86.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early middlegame mistake: the player captures a knight on e5 (or e4) with their bishop, initiating an equal-material exchange that is positionally catastrophic. All 14 top activations show a bishop capturing a knight (100% bishop moved, 100% knight captured, 100% trade by material). The eval trajectory reveals the true cost: 64% of these moves convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 214 centipawns—far too large for a simple inaccuracy. The tactical analysis explains why: the recapture (typically fxe5) rips open the f-file directly against the player's king, which in 79% of cases is still in the center (opening phase). The Opus summaries consistently highlight that the bishop being traded was a key defensive piece guarding critical squares, and its removal combined with the opened f-file and the resulting pawn on e5 displacing a knight defender creates a devastating attack. Tags like 'premature_capture', 'king_in_center', 'piece_displacement', and 'open_f_file' all converge on this pattern. Maia never recaptures (100% Maia captures: none), confirming the engine would not initiate this exchange. This is not a material blunder but a positionally ruinous trade that surrenders king safety for no compensation.

93.label: Player chose an indirect or flashy move instead of immediately capturing a hanging or vulnerable piece, throwing away a winning position.
93.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position plays an indirect move (a check, a threat, or a pawn push) instead of simply capturing material that is already available. The material signature shows the player's move is often safe (75%) and frequently delivers check (50%), yet Maia's recommended move captures a rook or queen 100% of the time — indicating the correct move was a straightforward capture the player ignored. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes (median 940cp lost), often converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones. The tactical analysis repeatedly highlights 'hanging_piece' and 'indirect_vs_direct' motifs, with example summaries describing textbook cases of threatening instead of taking, placing a queen on a vulnerable square instead of capturing, or pushing a pawn when a hanging piece could be won immediately. The pattern is consistent: the player sees something fancy (a check, a threat, a discovered attack) and plays it reflexively, missing that the simple direct capture was decisively winning.

88.label: Rook moves to an advanced square where it becomes tactically vulnerable due to overloaded defenders or simplification errors.
88.description: This feature captures a recurring middlegame mistake where players aggressively advance their rook (75% rook moves) to a far square—often the back rank or deep into enemy territory—without adequate support, resulting in the piece being hung (64% hangs material). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: median 283cp loss, with positions frequently shifting from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-losing. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying mechanisms: overloaded defenders that cannot simultaneously protect the rook and other duties (deflection), simplification errors where forced exchanges leave the player materially down, and king safety issues exposed once the rook commits forward. The top boards consistently show rooks lunging to the 8th rank (c1c8, d3d8, a7a8, b1b8, e3e8, e4e8) or 1st rank (d5d1, d7d1, d3d1) where they are either immediately hanging or trigger unfavorable forced sequences. Maia's preferred moves often involve quiet non-rook moves or pawn captures, suggesting the AI recognizes that the aggressive rook thrust is premature. The common thread is misjudging that an advanced rook placement is tactically sound when in reality the supporting pieces are overloaded or the simplification sequence favors the opponent.

90.label: Player makes a move that ignores a critical king safety threat, allowing the opponent a devastating tactical blow (often checkmate or near-checkmate).
90.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that catastrophically neglects king safety. The material signature shows that 42% of moves 'hang' material and 84% involve no capture—these are quiet, non-forcing moves that fail to address an urgent threat to the king. The piece moved is often a pawn (27%), queen (25%), or rook (20%), suggesting the player is making a 'normal' developing or repositioning move while their king is under siege. Maia's recommended move (78% pawn) suggests simple defensive pawn moves or pawn-shield repairs were available. The motif analysis is unanimous: 100% king_safety, with tags like checkmate_in_one, exposed_king, removed_defender, and pawn_shield_weakness. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 200 centipawns, with many positions going from drawn or even winning to losing, indicating the player threw away the game by ignoring the king's vulnerability. The top boards confirm this: positions feature exposed kings (e.g., kings on e2, k1, h2) where the opponent has rooks, queens, or knights aimed at the monarch, and the player makes an irrelevant move (like g2g3, a2a4, or moving a piece away from king defense) instead of addressing the mating threat.

91.label: Giving a check that wastes tempo by allowing the opponent's king to escape to a better square, often throwing away a winning attack or forced mate.
91.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) — predominantly with the queen (67%) or rook (21%) — that constitutes a tempo loss rather than a productive forcing move. The material signature shows these checks are overwhelmingly 'safe' (86%) and non-capturing (93%), meaning the player isn't blundering material directly but is squandering initiative. The eval trajectory reveals that 45% go winning->winning (maintaining advantage but extending the win unnecessarily) while 5% go winning->losing and 17% losing->winning, with a median eval loss of 0.0 — consistent with checks that are often technically non-losing but miss far stronger continuations. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (70%) with tags like 'premature_check', 'pointless_check', and critically 'missed_mate' — the player delivers an impulsive check that drives the king to safety, abandons a mating net, or misplaces their own piece (especially the queen). Maia's recommended moves (rook 40%, pawn 24%) with 0% checks and 67% missed winning material confirm that the engine wanted quiet building moves or decisive non-check tactics rather than the flashy but counterproductive check the player chose.

94.label: Developing or moving a piece in the opening while ignoring an imminent knight fork on f7 that wins material.
94.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake where the player (almost always Black) makes a developing move—typically a bishop move (57%)—that completely ignores a tactical threat against the f7 square. The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (100% hangs, median -1.0), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: every instance transitions from a drawn position to a losing one with a median loss of 313 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is a fork (67%), with recurring tags of f7_weakness, two_knights_defense, and knight_fork. The top boards confirm the pattern: the vast majority arise from the Two Knights Defense or similar Italian Game positions where White has Bc4 + Ng5 aimed at f7, and Black plays natural-looking but fatally passive moves (Be7, Bd6, d6, Nd4) instead of the critical d5 counterstrike. The Maia signal (100% pawn moves recommended) aligns with d5 being the standard theoretical defense. This is a classic case of prioritizing development over addressing an immediate tactical threat in well-known opening theory.

95.label: Capturing a queen on the back rank while exposing the king to a back-rank mate.
95.description: This feature fires when a player captures an opponent's queen (100% queen captures) using a rook (73%) or other piece, completing what appears to be a material trade (100% trade outcomes with median net +4.0), but fatally exposes their own back rank to a mating combination. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: median 9561 centipawns lost, with positions collapsing into forced checkmate. The Opus analysis and motif tags (back_rank 100%, back_rank_mate, trapped_king, pawn_coffin) reveal the consistent pattern: the player's king is hemmed in by its own pawns, and by recapturing the queen on the back rank (or moving a defensive piece to capture it), the player either removes a critical back-rank defender or places their piece on a square where a mating pattern is enabled. The top boards consistently show positions where a queen sits on the 8th rank offering itself as bait, and the recapture allows a devastating back-rank mate in 1-2 moves. Maia's recommended moves (91% non-captures) confirm the correct response was to decline the queen trade entirely.

97.label: King moves into a fork or tactical shot in a won endgame, hanging a major piece.
97.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (100% king moves) into a square that allows an immediate tactical blow—most commonly a knight fork or skewer—hanging a queen or rook (100% hangs material, median -5.0 material loss). The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing from winning to losing (100% winning->losing, median 896cp lost), meaning these are positions that were trivially won before the king stepped onto the wrong square. The dominant motifs (fork 30%, hanging_piece 20%, skewer 10%) and tags (tempo_loss, missed_tactic) confirm that the king inadvertently walks into a tactical pattern that the opponent's remaining piece can exploit. The boards show sparse endgame positions—Q vs N, R vs R, K+R—where king placement is the decisive factor, and a single careless king move exposes the superior piece to a decisive tactic.

98.label: Player ignores a hanging enemy piece in a winning position, allowing the opponent back into the game.
98.description: This feature fires when a player, holding a winning or clearly superior position, plays a quiet or passive move while an enemy piece (most often a rook) is hanging and can be captured for free. The material signature shows that 67% of the moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave something en prise) with a median net loss of -5.0 (approximately a full rook), while Maia's recommended move captures a rook in 100% of cases. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 67% swing from winning to losing and 33% from winning to drawn, with a staggering median eval loss of 1119 centipawns. The tactical analysis universally tags 'hanging_piece' and 'missed_capture' — the opponent's piece was undefended and freely capturable, but the player chose a slow king move, pawn push, or rook repositioning instead. These occur predominantly in simplified middlegame/endgame positions (rook endgames) where calculation demands are low, suggesting the player simply failed to scan for undefended enemy pieces before committing to a plan-based move.

96.label: Player makes a rook or king move that misses a winning back-rank tactic or checkmate, squandering a decisive advantage.
96.description: This feature fires when players overlook back-rank mating threats or tactics in rook-heavy middlegame and endgame positions. The material signature shows the player mostly moves rooks (51%) or kings (20%) without capturing (74% non-capture), while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a rook delivering check (71% rook moves, 71% checks). The 89% missed-winning-material rate confirms these are positions where a concrete tactical shot existed. The dominant motifs—king_safety (30%), back_rank (20%), and tags like back_rank_mate—reveal the recurring geometric theme: the opponent's king is vulnerable on the last rank, and a forcing rook check or mate was available. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 109 centipawns with many positions collapsing from winning or drawn to losing (23% losing->winning reflects opponent's perspective gaining), indicating players are throwing away wins or draws by playing passive or misdirected moves instead of exploiting the back-rank weakness. Concrete examples include missing Ra1# with perfect back-rank geometry, missing Rb1+ for mate in 2, and playing quiet rook moves when forcing checks would have been decisive.

99.label: Knight moves to e5 in the opening ignoring a pin from Bg4 to the queen, losing the queen or major material.
99.description: This feature fires almost exclusively on knight moves (94%) during the opening phase (100%) where the player moves a knight—typically Nf3-e5—while that knight is pinned by a bishop on g4 to the queen on d1, or where the knight move otherwise exposes a hanging queen or major piece. The material signature confirms catastrophic losses (71% loses, 29% hangs, median net material -5.0, i.e., roughly a queen's worth), and the eval trajectory shows positions swinging from drawn or winning to losing by a median of 550 centipawns. The dominant motifs are pin (44%) and hanging_piece (56%), with recurring tags like queen_hanging, pin_exploitation, and opening_trap. The top boards consistently show the pattern: a Bg4 pins the Nf3 to the Qd1, and the player plays Ne5 thinking it's an aggressive developing move, but instead allows Bxd1 or leaves major material undefended. Maia's recommended moves (pawn 53%, bishop 35%) suggest quiet developing alternatives that respect the pin rather than walking into it.

102.label: Developing or advancing pieces without capturing, missing concrete tactical opportunities and hanging material in the opening/middlegame.
102.description: This feature captures moves where players develop pieces (bishops 34%, pawns 31%, knights 12%) without making captures (81% non-captures) that end up hanging material (44% hangs) while missing winning tactical opportunities (69% missed winning material). The eval trajectory shows these are costly mistakes (median 272cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (28%) or worsening already losing positions (25%). The phase is predominantly opening (53%) and middlegame (38%), and the motifs of tempo_loss and passed_pawn combined with tags like 'unnecessary_check' and 'missed_material_win' suggest players are making natural-looking developing moves or pawn advances that ignore concrete tactics available on the board—such as the example of playing a pointless check instead of capturing an undefended pawn, or advancing a pawn when a piece capture was available. The pattern is one of passivity or routine development when the position demanded immediate tactical action.

101.label: In a winning endgame, the player simplifies or makes a passive move that dissipates a decisive advantage into a draw.
101.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player holds a winning advantage but makes a move that converts the position from winning to drawn, losing a median of 655 centipawns of evaluation. The material signature shows a mix of hanging pieces (50%) and trades (50%), indicating moves that either leave material en prise or exchange into a losing simplified position. The tactical analysis reveals themes of missed mates, unnecessary simplification (piece_exchange_error, positional_mistake), and tempo loss. Concrete examples include castling instead of delivering a forced checkmate sequence (O-O instead of Qxh7), and trading an active rook on the b-file to enter a hopeless bishop endgame. The common thread is that in technically winning endgames, the player either trades off their most active piece, makes a passive king move, or allows a simplification that eliminates their winning chances—essentially failing to convert a won endgame by choosing routine or simplifying moves over the decisive continuation.

100.label: Moving the queen to an undefended square where it can be captured or trapped, typically turning a drawn position into a losing one.
100.description: This feature fires on queen moves (81% of activating positions) that leave the queen hanging or lost (50% hangs, 19% loses material, net median -1.0 indicating loss of a full piece). The eval trajectory is devastating: 56% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 538 centipawns, indicating these are game-deciding blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), where the queen is placed on a square controlled by the opponent—often on a diagonal covered by a fianchettoed bishop (board 2: Qd5 into Bg2), or centrally where it can be attacked with tempo (boards 5, 6, 10: Qd4, Qe4, Qh5). The positions are predominantly in the opening/middlegame (94%), where piece activity is high and tactical lines punish exposed queens immediately. Maia's recommended moves are typically modest pawn or piece moves (pawn 38%, knight 12%), suggesting the correct approach was quiet development rather than aggressive queen sorties into danger.

103.label: Moving a piece (often the queen) to a square where it becomes vulnerable to a knight fork.
103.description: This feature identifies moves where the player places a high-value piece—most often the queen (30% of activations)—on a square that allows a devastating knight fork. The tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'fork' (89%), with tags like 'knight_fork' (9), 'queen_loss' (3), and 'geometric_vulnerability' (3) dominating. The material signature shows 73% 'safe' outcomes on the move itself (no immediate capture or loss), yet 19% result in a hang—consistent with the piece being lost on the subsequent fork. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: a median of 561 centipawns lost, with 14% converting winning positions to losing and another 14% converting drawn positions to losing. The concrete positions confirm this repeatedly: queens land on squares like c3, d7, d4, or d5 where an enemy knight delivers a simultaneous check and queen attack. The player's move is typically a non-capturing repositioning or a seemingly natural capture that overlooks the knight's geometric reach, transforming a favorable or balanced position into a decisive material deficit.

105.label: Moves that ignore critical king safety threats, turning tenable positions into lost ones.
105.description: This feature captures moves where the player neglects king safety considerations, resulting in catastrophic positional collapses. The material signature shows 90% 'safe' moves (no immediate material loss), yet the median eval drop is a devastating 371 centipawns—indicating the damage is positional/tactical rather than a simple piece hang. The trajectory shows 39% drawn->losing and 10% winning->losing, meaning these moves frequently throw away holdable or even advantageous positions. The dominant motifs (king_safety 38%, hanging_piece 38%) combined with tags like back_rank, exposed_king, and overloaded_defender reveal the mechanism: players make quiet-looking moves (king moves 26%, rook moves 26%, castling into danger) that fatally compromise their king's safety or fail to address existing king vulnerabilities. The concrete positions confirm this—castling into a bishop diagonal, moving rooks away from king defense, or playing queen moves that ignore back-rank/king exposure. These aren't captures or trades gone wrong; they're positional decisions that catastrophically underestimate threats to the king.

104.label: Player makes an irrelevant move while their own piece is left undefended and en prise.
104.description: This feature consistently fires when a player makes a move that completely ignores an existing tactical threat to one of their own pieces. The material signature shows 83% of moves result in a 'hang' (a non-capture move that drops a piece), with a median material loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors: 75% of cases convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median eval loss of 389 centipawns — consistent with dropping a minor piece. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (60%), and tags like 'undefended_piece', 'piece_loss', and 'ignored_threat' appearing repeatedly. The concrete examples show the pattern clearly: playing an irrelevant pawn push while a bishop is attacked, moving a piece into an undefended square on an open file, or removing a defender from a critical square. The player's moves are typically quiet (pawns 33%, bishops 33%, kings 17%) with almost no captures (92% non-captures), indicating these are passive or purposeless moves made while a concrete tactical threat demands immediate attention.

109.label: A bishop check in the opening that wastes tempo and hangs the piece.
109.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: playing a bishop check (100% bishop moves, 100% checks) that serves no constructive purpose and results in hanging material (100% hangs, median -2.0 material loss). All positions occur in the opening phase, and the trajectory consistently shows a drawn position collapsing into a losing one (median 276cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with tags like 'pointless_check' and 'development' appearing repeatedly. The concrete pattern across the top boards is unmistakable: premature bishop sallies (Bb5, Bb4, Bg5) delivering checks that are trivially blocked or parried, after which the bishop becomes trapped, attacked, or simply misplaced—losing a full piece's worth of compensation. The recommended moves (knight retreats like Nb1, Nce7, Nb8) suggest the player should have been consolidating development rather than chasing a check. This is the classic beginner trap of 'a check is always good' applied to bishop development in the opening.

107.label: Passive or retreating moves that waste critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with forcing tactics on open files.
107.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a move that is objectively safe (71% safe, no captures) but catastrophically wastes tempo. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (57%), with open_file_exploitation and piece_activity as recurring tags, indicating that the player's slow move allows the opponent to activate rooks on open files with forcing sequences. The eval trajectory is severe—57% of cases transition from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 319 centipawns—showing these are not subtle inaccuracies but game-deciding mistakes. Maia consistently finds rook moves (100%) that deliver check (100%), confirming that the opponent punishes the wasted tempo with immediate tactical forcing on the e-file or other open lines. The top boards reveal a recurring structure: semi-open positions with rooks on the e-file, where retreats (Bh5, Bg6), pawn pushes (b5), or aimless rook shuffles (Rb1) ignore the urgent tactical demands of the position, allowing the opponent to crash through with decisive rook activity.

110.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move while an enemy piece is hanging and freely capturable.
110.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a free capture that is clearly available. The material signature shows the player's move hangs a piece 67% of the time (median net material -1.0), while Maia's recommended move captures a high-value piece (queen 67%, bishop 33%) — indicating the best move was simply taking undefended material. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' in 100% of cases, with 'missed_tactic' tagged in 5 of 6 positions, confirming the player failed to notice an opponent's piece was en prise. The eval trajectory (median 464 centipawns lost, with 67% staying winning but bleeding huge advantage) shows these are positions where the player had a dominant stance but failed to cash in the simplest tactical gift. The Opus analyses consistently describe scenarios where a bishop could capture an undefended queen or major piece along a clear diagonal or open line, but the player instead made a quiet developing or centralizing move, gifting the opponent time to rescue the hanging piece. This is not a complex combination — it is a one-move oversight of freely available material.

106.label: King moves to a passive square in a drawn endgame, losing control of critical squares and allowing opponent's passed pawn to promote.
106.description: This feature detects king moves in pawn endgames (and simplified rook endgames) that convert a drawn position into a lost one. All activating positions are in the endgame phase (100%), involve king moves with no captures (safe material outcome), yet suffer a catastrophic eval drop (median 554cp, drawn->losing 100%). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs: passed pawns (40%), pawn endgames (30%), and tempo loss (20%). Examining the concrete positions confirms the pattern: in positions like KP vs K, rook+pawn endgames, or minimal piece endgames, the player's king steps to the wrong square—losing opposition, abandoning blockade duty on a passed pawn, or losing a critical tempo. These are positions where only one or two king moves hold the draw, and the player selects a plausible-looking but fatally passive square, typically losing control of the promotion path or ceding opposition. The narrowness of these positions (often a single drawing move exists) combined with the king activity/tempo themes confirms this as a classic endgame king positioning error.

108.label: Player makes a routine recapture or quiet queen move instead of a critical intermediate capture that wins material or tempo.
108.description: This feature fires when players move their queen (78%) in routine fashion—typically a recapture or retreat—while missing a critical zwischenzug (intermediate move) that Maia identifies as a bishop or knight capture (61%/30%). The top boards consistently show positions where an intermediate capture (often Bxe7 or similar) exploits mutual threats, pins, or overloaded defenders before completing an expected exchange sequence. The eval trajectory is devastating: 44% of cases convert winning positions to drawn ones, with a median loss of 367 centipawns, indicating these are game-changing oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (33%), tempo_loss (22%), and the recurring tags 'missed_tactic' and 'intermediate_move'—confirm the pattern: the player follows the 'obvious' move order (recapturing immediately or retreating) without recognizing that inserting a capture-with-tempo first would exploit the opponent's tactical vulnerability. The 30% 'hangs' rate reflects that by skipping the zwischenzug, the player's piece becomes undefended or the opponent gains a free tempo to consolidate.

111.label: Moves that catastrophically open lines to the player's own king, turning winning or equal positions into immediate losses.
111.description: This feature fires on moves where the player fatally compromises their own king safety, typically by capturing a piece (often a queen) that simultaneously removes a critical defensive pawn or piece shielding the king. The material signature shows captures (queen 50%, pawn 25%) that appear 'safe' or even winning materially, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: winning->losing 50%, winning->drawn 25%, drawn->losing 25%, with a staggering median centipawn loss of 10,417. The dominant motif is king_safety (38%), and the concrete positions confirm this pattern — the top two boards show Black capturing gxh5 which opens the g-file/diagonal to the king allowing immediate checkmate, while another shows a speculative sacrifice (Bxf7+) that opens lines but has no follow-up. The common thread is that the player makes a superficially attractive or greedy capture/move without recognizing that it opens fatal lines (diagonals, files) to their own monarch, often in the opening phase (75%) when pieces are undeveloped and cannot provide emergency defense. The passed_pawn and tempo_loss sub-motifs reflect cases where the player prioritizes material or peripheral goals while their king position collapses.

112.label: Premature bishop sacrifice on f7/f2 with check that lacks sufficient tactical follow-up in the opening.
112.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake: a bishop captures a pawn on f7 (or f2) with check, sacrificing material without adequate compensation. All 11 top activations involve a bishop capturing a pawn (100%) with check (100%), resulting in a net material loss of approximately 2 points (slightly_down 100%). The positions are exclusively in the opening phase (100%), predominantly in Italian Game or similar e4-e5 structures with bishops on c4/c5. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (91%) with a massive median eval loss of 358 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is king_safety (100%), with recurring tags of 'unsound_sacrifice,' 'premature_attack,' and 'insufficient_compensation'—the player attempts a pseudo-Fried Liver or similar attacking sacrifice but lacks the piece coordination (typically missing a knight on g5 or other supporting attackers) to generate real mating threats. The displaced king finds safety quickly, leaving the sacrificer down a full piece with no compensation.

116.label: Giving a check that forces trades or loses material in an already losing position, worsening rather than improving survival chances.
116.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player in a losing position delivers a check (100% check rate) that appears active but is counterproductive. The material signature shows these checks predominantly hang pieces (67%) with a median net material loss of -5.0, and the pieces used are rooks (67%) or queens (33%). The eval trajectory confirms these are exclusively losing->losing transitions with a substantial median loss of 181 centipawns—making bad positions significantly worse. The tactical analysis reveals the unifying theme through tags like 'patzer_sees_a_check' and 'pointless_check,' combined with motifs of tempo_loss and simplification_helps_opponent. The concrete positions show back-rank or file checks that force exchanges (unnecessary_exchange appears twice), converting active piece positions into hopeless endgames or allowing forced mates. Rather than seeking defensive resources, the player reflexively plays a check that hands the opponent favorable simplification or piece coordination.

113.label: In a losing endgame, moves a bishop (or leaves it) where it can be simply captured by the opponent's king.
113.description: This feature detects a specific recurring endgame blunder where a player, already in a losing position, moves their bishop to a square where it is directly en prise—most commonly to the opponent's king, which simply captures it. The material signature is unambiguous: 100% bishop moves, 100% hangs (non-capture that drops a piece), with the opponent's king recapturing the bishop in every case (median net material loss of -3.0, i.e., a full bishop). The eval trajectory confirms these are not game-deciding throws but rather cases of making a bad position worse (losing→losing, median 199cp further lost), suggesting players in desperate endgame positions lose focus or miscalculate piece safety around the opponent's active king. The tactical analysis reinforces this: dominant motifs are hanging_piece and passed_pawn pressure, with tags like tempo_loss, bishop_endgame, and missed_tactic. The concrete positions show sparse endgame boards (pawns + minor pieces or rooks) where the player overlooks that the opponent's king covers the bishop's destination square, often while distracted by passed pawn threats or other positional concerns.

117.label: Moving the queen away from a critical defensive role, leaving pieces or pawns unprotected in the opening.
117.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where the player moves their queen (100% queen moves, 0% captures) away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function—guarding a piece, controlling a key square, or maintaining coordination. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%) and pin (20%), indicating that the queen's departure exposes undefended material to immediate tactical exploitation. The eval trajectory shows this is a game-changing error: 50% of cases shift from drawn to losing and 30% from winning to drawn, with a median cost of 247 centipawns. Occurring predominantly in the opening (75%), the pattern involves premature or speculative queen sorties (e.g., Qg4 pursuing a kingside attack, Qb6 abandoning central defense, Qb4 leaving a knight unprotected) that prioritize activity over the queen's essential coordinating role. The tags—piece_coordination, tempo_loss, queen_misplacement, undefended_knight—all reinforce that the queen is relocated without appreciating that its previous square was the linchpin holding the position together.

114.label: Bishop captures a pawn in the opening, abandoning defense of a critical long diagonal and allowing devastating exploitation.
114.description: This feature fires on a specific opening mistake where a player moves their dark-squared bishop to capture a pawn (typically ...Bxb4 or similar), trading material equally in isolation but catastrophically abandoning the defense of the g7 pawn and the long h8-a1 diagonal. The material signature shows bishop captures pawn as a trade (net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals a massive cost: drawn positions become losing by a median of 383 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the mechanism: the opponent's fianchettoed bishop on b2 (or bishop on e5) was already aimed down the long diagonal, and removing the defensive bishop exposes a hanging rook on h8 or allows decisive penetration. Tags like 'pawn_grab_punished,' 'opening_trap,' and 'long_diagonal' recur consistently, and the top boards all show early-game positions (phase: opening 100%) where Black's bishop leaves f8 for a tempting pawn capture, falling into a prepared diagonal trap. The Maia recommendation of a knight move (non-capture) suggests the correct plan involved development rather than the greedy but structurally ruinous pawn grab.

115.label: In drawn endgames, player moves king or knight passively instead of capturing a critical piece or stopping a passed pawn, turning a draw into a loss.
115.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame blunder pattern where the player, in a theoretically drawn position, makes a 'safe' move (no material is immediately lost or traded) — typically a king move (75%) or knight move (25%) — while failing to capture a critical piece that Maia's engine line would take (Maia captures a queen 75% of the time, a pawn 25%). The eval trajectory is uniformly drawn->losing with a median loss of 589 centipawns, indicating these moves throw away the draw entirely. The tactical analysis reveals that in nearly every case there was exactly one good move available (often a capture like Nxb6 or Kxb6), and the player instead made a tempo-losing passive move. The dominant motifs — passed pawns (44%), hanging pieces (33%), and pawn/rook endgames — combined with tags like tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and king_activity confirm that the mistake is failing to address an urgent tactical obligation (capturing a hanging piece or blockading/capturing a passed pawn) in simplified endgame positions where precise calculation is required.

118.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a rook endgame that squanders a critical tempo and allows the opponent to seize activity.
118.description: This feature fires on middlegame-to-endgame transitions (100% middlegame phase) where the player makes a 'safe' but passive move (pawn 50%, king 33%, rook 17%; no captures, no checks) while the engine strongly preferred an active rook move (Maia's recommended move is rook 83% of the time, often capturing or exploiting the seventh rank). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with rook_endgame appearing in 4 of 6 positions and missed_tactic in 3. The eval trajectory shows these passive moves are devastating: 67% convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 234 centipawns. The concrete positions all show simplified rook endgames or near-endgames where the player chose a slow pawn push (h4, b3, a5, f3) or a passive rook move (Rbc1, Rec3) instead of the one forcing continuation that maintained activity or initiated a favorable exchange. The pattern is consistently one of failing to recognize the urgency of rook activity in simplified positions, allowing the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative with a single lost tempo.

119.label: In won endgames, player makes a non-capturing move while an enemy rook hangs undefended and capturable.
119.description: This feature fires consistently in endgame positions where the player has a winning advantage (often forced checkmate) but fails to capture a completely undefended enemy rook. The material signature shows Maia consistently recommending a bishop capture of a rook (Maia's move: bishop 100%, Maia captures: rook 100%), while the player instead makes safe but irrelevant moves (pawn pushes, king moves, or rook moves that ignore the free material). The eval trajectory shows these positions flip from losing (for the opponent) to winning for the opponent — a massive median eval loss of ~105 pawns (i.e., converting forced mates into merely advantageous or even losing positions). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' with tags like 'missed_capture' and 'material_oversight.' The concrete positions consistently show an enemy rook sitting undefended on an open square where the player's bishop has a clear capture path, but the player overlooks it entirely, squandering a trivially won position through a simple oversight in the endgame.

123.label: Player makes a developing or routine move instead of capturing an undefended bishop with a knight.
123.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing move (typically with a knight, bishop, or pawn) in the opening or middlegame while completely overlooking that their knight could capture an undefended enemy bishop. The material signature shows 100% safe non-captures by the player, while Maia's recommended move is always a knight capturing a bishop—confirming a missed free piece. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of cases, and the Opus analysis consistently describes scenarios where a bishop (often on f4, c4, or similar squares) is left undefended and a knight is already attacking it, but the player opts for a routine developing move (castling, Nd7, etc.) instead. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 470 centipawns, frequently converting a winning position into a drawn one (53% winning->drawn), indicating the player is throwing away a decisive advantage by prioritizing general development or positional goals over an elementary tactical capture.

120.label: Neglecting a critical capture or recapture sequence in the opening, playing a natural developing move instead of the tactically optimal move order.
120.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players make seemingly natural moves—typically pawn advances (56%) or knight moves (22%)—that miss available tactical opportunities. The eval trajectory shows these are costly errors (median 295cp lost), often converting winning positions to drawn (56%) or drawn to losing (33%). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and hanging_piece (33%), with 'missed_tactic' and 'move_order_error' as the most common tags. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: players play routine developing or central pawn moves (like ...d5, O-O, Bg2) when a specific tactical sequence was available—often a pawn capture or piece capture that exploits a temporary vulnerability. The Maia analysis confirms the correct moves frequently involve captures (pawn 56%, knight 22%) that the player bypassed. This is fundamentally a move-order issue in the opening where the player follows general principles rather than calculating the concrete tactical justification for an immediate action.

122.label: Moving the bishop to a passive square in the endgame while missing a concrete tactical opportunity (capture, check, or mating net).
122.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves a bishop (67% of moves are bishop moves) to a square that appears safe (67% safe, 33% hangs) but misses a winning tactical opportunity (100% missed winning material). The Maia-suggested moves frequently involve capturing a rook (67%) or delivering check (33%), indicating that concrete forcing moves were available. The dominant motifs—king_safety, hanging_piece, and tempo_loss—combined with the board positions show a consistent pattern: the player repositions their bishop aimlessly (e.g., Bg6-f7, Bf7-d5, Ae6 retreats) when a much stronger tactical continuation existed. The eval trajectory (67% losing->losing, 33% losing->winning) suggests these occur in already difficult positions where the missed tactic was the critical resource. The common thread is a purposeless bishop maneuver that squanders tempo and ignores concrete threats in simplified positions.

124.label: Player makes a quiet, purposeless move instead of executing a winning tactical combination involving forks or pins.
124.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position plays a safe but aimless move (king retreat, rook shuffle, pawn push) while a concrete tactical strike was available. The material signature shows 100% 'safe' moves with no captures—these aren't blunders that hang pieces, but passive non-capturing moves that squander tactical opportunities. Maia consistently recommends a rook capture of a bishop (100%), indicating the missed tactic typically involves winning material through a forcing sequence. The dominant motifs are forks (62%) and pins (12%), confirming that the available tactics involve double attacks or pins that the player completely overlooked. The eval trajectory (median 312cp loss, 67% winning->drawn) shows these passive moves throw away winning advantages. The Opus analysis repeatedly describes players retreating pieces from active posts or making purposeless king moves when immediate tactical strikes (Rxa2 with a fork, Rxe6 with a pin) would have won material decisively. The pattern is consistent: the player 'plays it safe' with a quiet move, missing a one-move-deeper combination.

125.label: Trading away a critical defensive bishop in a lost endgame, transitioning into a hopeless pawn ending or bare-piece position.
125.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player who is already losing (losing->losing 100%) makes a bishop move (100% bishop played) that trades or exchanges pieces (67% trade, 33% slightly down), typically capturing a knight (67%) or pawn (33%). The key pattern across all positions is that the bishop being traded was the player's last or most critical defensive piece. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of positional mistakes, pawn endgame transitions, and passed pawn themes, with frequent tags of simplification_error, bad_trade, and piece_activity loss. The board positions consistently show sparse endgame material where one side's bishop is essential for creating a fortress or blockading passed pawns, and by exchanging it the player removes their only defensive resource, worsening an already difficult position by a median of 302 centipawns. This is not a tactical blunder but rather a failure of endgame technique—the player simplifies when they should maintain piece tension, fatally entering a theoretically lost pawn or minor-piece ending.

121.label: In rook endgames with advanced passed pawns, pushing the pawn instead of delivering a critical intermediate rook check that secures promotion or decisive advantage.
121.description: This feature identifies a specific rook endgame mistake where the player advances a passed pawn (67% pawn moves) or makes a king move (33%) when the correct continuation was a rook check (Maia's move is always a rook delivering check). The positions are uniformly endgames with passed pawns near promotion, and the material outcome of the played move is technically 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet the median eval cost is 409 centipawns—indicating a massive squandering of winning or drawing chances. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (38%), tempo_loss (25%), and king_safety/back_rank themes, all pointing to the same pattern: the player fails to use an intermediate rook check to either force the enemy king to a worse square before promoting, or to gain a crucial tempo that makes the pawn advance decisive. The eval trajectories (winning->drawn 33%, drawn->losing 17%) confirm these are 'threw a win' or 'blew a draw' situations. The concrete examples (g3 instead of Ra1+, g2 instead of Rh1+, e2 without back-rank awareness) all show the player impatiently pushing material forward without the preparatory checking sequence that the rook provides.

127.label: Suboptimal king or pawn moves in pure endgames that lose critical tempi, often squandering a winning advantage into a draw.
127.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes king moves (60%) or pawn moves (40%) that are materially safe but positionally costly due to tempo loss. The eval trajectory shows 40% of cases convert winning positions into drawn ones (median loss ~4cp, but with catastrophic outliers losing 500+ centipawns). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (50%) and tempo_loss (40%), with king_activity and opposition as recurring tags. The concrete positions are pure king-and-pawn or minimal-piece endgames where the player either advances the king to the wrong square (losing the opposition), pushes a pawn prematurely (giving the opponent a crucial tempo), or makes an aimless king move when precise calculation was required. The feature captures the classic endgame error of playing 'natural-looking' moves that fail to maintain the delicate tempo balance needed to convert or hold these positions.

126.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty, leaving another piece or square unprotected for the opponent to exploit.
126.description: This feature detects positions where a player moves a piece (most often the queen, but also knights, bishops, or kings) that was serving a crucial defensive role, leaving another piece hanging or a critical square uncontrolled. The material signature shows 36% of moves result in a hang (a non-capture that drops a piece) and 79% involve no capture—indicating the player isn't trading but simply relocating a defender. The Maia-recommended moves are overwhelmingly rook moves (86%), suggesting the correct plan involved activating or repositioning a rook (often to contest an open file or defend a back rank), but instead the player moved a different piece away from its defensive post. The eval trajectory is severe (median 347cp loss) with 32% of cases flipping from winning or drawn into losing, confirming these are game-changing errors. The tactical analysis tags are dominated by tempo_loss (50%), hanging_piece (25%), and recurring themes of 'removing the guard' and 'undefended piece'—the player's own move effectively removes their own guard. Concrete examples include a queen leaving a rook undefended (Qh5), a knight abandoning rook protection (Nd1), and queens shifting to aggressive squares while leaving back-rank or piece-defense duties unfulfilled.
