The pattern is unified: the player prioritizes an attacking or seemingly active move while fatally neglecting a defensive obligation.

128.label: Moving a major piece to a square where it is immediately captured by an opponent's piece, throwing away a winning position.
128.description: This feature detects positions where a player places a piece (most often a rook or queen) on a square that is directly attacked by an opponent's piece, leaving it completely undefended and hanging. The material signature shows 30% hangs and 20% loses with a median net loss of -2.0 (a full piece), and 80% of the time a winning move was available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 50% winning->losing and 20% winning->drawn, with a median eval drop of 535 centipawns, confirming these are won positions being thrown away in a single move. The tactical motifs overwhelmingly point to 'hanging_piece' (75%) with tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'rook_blunder'/'queen_blunder'. The concrete examples show rooks placed on squares attacked by kings (Rf4 into Ke5), queens moved onto diagonals controlled by bishops (Qg3 into Bd6), and wrong capture orders that leave pieces unprotected. These are not complex tactical oversights but simple one-move blindness where the player fails to notice the destination square is already controlled by the opponent.

129.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy rook that can be captured for free, making an unrelated move instead.
129.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a completely undefended enemy rook that is available for immediate capture. The material signature shows the played moves are mostly 'safe' (no material exchanged), while Maia's recommended move captures a rook in 100% of cases—indicating the missed opportunity is always a free rook capture. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), and the tags consistently show 'missed_capture' and 'hanging_piece' as the core error. The tactical analyses describe nearly identical scenarios: an enemy rook sits unprotected, often adjacent to the player's king or bishop, yet the player makes a quiet or irrelevant move (king retreat, pawn push, bishop repositioning) instead of simply taking the rook. The eval trajectory confirms this costs a median of 231 centipawns—roughly a full rook's value—though many positions remain winning because the player had a large advantage beforehand. The positions span middlegame and endgame, often rook endgames where king activity is critical, and the free rook is sitting en prise to the king or a minor piece. The mistake is purely one of tactical oversight: failing to notice the simplest possible capture on the board.

131.label: Moving a piece away from a defensive duty, leaving another piece hanging or unprotected.
131.description: This feature identifies moves where a player relocates a piece (most often a queen or knight) without capturing anything, inadvertently leaving another piece undefended or removing a critical guard. The material signature shows 46% of moves result in a hang (a non-capture that drops a piece) and 90% involve no capture by the player, with a median material loss of -1.0 (i.e., a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors: 32% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 329 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'overloaded_defender' and 'removing_the_guard' as dominant motifs—the moved piece was serving a defensive function that the player overlooked. The concrete examples show patterns like a rook leaving c8 (exposing a knight on c6 to capture), or a queen repositioning that abandons protection of a key square or piece. These are primarily middlegame errors (73%) where piece coordination is complex and defensive responsibilities are easy to misjudge.

130.label: Trading a bishop when the exchange surrenders a winning or balanced position by losing piece activity or structural advantage.
130.description: This feature fires on positions where a player initiates a bishop exchange (bishop moved 96%, capturing bishop 47% or knight 34%) that is materially neutral (trade 77%, median net material 0.0) but positionally catastrophic (median eval lost 345cp). The eval trajectory shows these trades frequently throw away winning or balanced positions (winning->drawn 34%, drawn->losing 19%, winning->losing 8%). The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: these are not calculation errors but positional misjudgments—the dominant motifs are positional_mistake (33%) and tempo_loss (33%), with recurring tags of piece_activity and king_safety. The concrete positions confirm this: players exchange bishops on squares like f3, f6, d5, c6 where the trade relieves pressure on the opponent's position, surrenders the bishop pair, or allows the opponent to recapture with improved piece coordination. Maia's preferred moves (bishop 30%, knight 23%, queen 21%) with mostly non-captures (77%) suggest that maintaining tension or developing elsewhere was far superior to the committal exchange. The opening/middlegame phase split (47%/53%) indicates these premature exchanges typically occur when the position still has significant dynamic potential that the trade squanders.

134.label: A rook check that squanders a winning position by giving the opponent's king a tempo to escape danger.
134.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player delivers a rook check (94% rook moves, 100% checks) that is objectively harmful—frequently hanging material (56% hangs) with a median cost of 349 centipawns. The eval trajectory confirms these are position-squandering moves: winning→drawn (28%) or losing→winning for the opponent (17%), indicating the player was throwing away a significant advantage. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: these are 'patzer checks'—tempo-losing rook checks (tempo_loss 56%, king_safety 44%) that look aggressive but actually drive the opponent's king to safety, abandoning a mating attack or winning continuation. The Opus tags (premature_check, wrong_check, missed_mate_in_one, missed_tactic) confirm that in nearly every case, a much stronger quiet move or queen-based attack existed. Maia's preferred moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (83%), often delivering the correct check or maintaining the mating net. The top boards show rooks sliding to files to deliver check against exposed kings, when the position demanded a more precise continuation.

132.label: Trading rooks into a hopeless pawn endgame where the opponent has decisive passed pawns or superior king position.
132.description: This feature detects a specific endgame error where a player in an already losing position trades rooks (100% rook captures rook, net material 0.0 indicating a clean exchange), transitioning into a pure pawn endgame that is even more decisively lost. The eval trajectory confirms all positions go from losing to more losing (median 200cp further deterioration), meaning the rook was the player's last source of counterplay or defensive activity. The dominant motifs (pawn_endgame 62%, passed_pawn 25%) and tactical summaries confirm the pattern: the rook exchange eliminates the only piece that could fight against the opponent's passed pawns, superior king activity, or connected pawns. Maia's preferred moves (100% pawn captures pawn) suggest quieter pawn play was available rather than forcing the simplification. The board positions consistently show late middlegame/early endgame scenarios with few pieces where one side's rook was providing critical defensive or active resources that vanish upon the trade, leaving a technically lost king-and-pawn ending.

133.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a square where it is immediately capturable by an opponent's piece or pawn.
133.description: This feature fires on moves that leave a piece completely unprotected on its destination square, resulting in its immediate loss. The material signature is decisive: 62% of moves are classified as 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -3.0 (roughly a minor piece or more). The queen is the most frequently moved piece (48%), and critically, 83% of these moves involve no capture—the player simply places a piece where it can be taken for free. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: drawn→losing (41%) and winning→losing (14%) with a median eval loss of 467 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (71%), and example summaries describe queens placed on squares covered by pawns, knights moved to undefended squares attacked by bishops, and similar elementary oversights. The phase split (48% opening, 52% middlegame) suggests these occur when the board is still complex enough that players lose track of piece safety. Unlike trade errors or positional misjudgments, these are pure one-move tactical oversights where the player fails to notice a direct threat to the piece they just moved.

136.label: Queen lunges to f7/f2 with check in the opening but hangs to a defender, losing the queen for a pawn.
136.description: All three signals converge on one specific pattern: a premature queen attack in the opening (phase: opening 100%) where the queen delivers check on f7 or f2 (player moved queen 100%, played a check 100%) while capturing a pawn (player captured pawn 86%), but the queen is immediately lost because a defending piece recaptures (material outcome: loses 57%, net median -8.0, i.e., losing a queen for a pawn). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 520cp lost, drawn->losing 86%), and the Opus analysis explicitly tags this as premature_attack, scholars_mate_attempt, and queen_blunder. The concrete boards show classic Scholar's Mate setups (Qf3-f7, Qb3-f7, Qf6-f2) where the attacker overlooked a knight or king defending the target square. This is not a positional misjudgment or a trade—it is a tactical oversight where the player assumes the check wins material but the queen simply hangs to a recapture.

139.label: Advancing a pawn in the opening instead of capturing a freely hanging enemy piece, throwing away a winning advantage.
139.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player has a piece hanging en prise (or can capture one for free) but instead plays a quiet pawn move that ignores the tactical opportunity. The material signature shows the player always moves a pawn without capturing, while Maia consistently identifies a pawn-takes-knight as the correct move—confirming a free piece was available. The eval trajectory uniformly shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (median 529cp lost), indicating the player squandered a full piece advantage. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (89%) with supporting tags like 'missed_tactic' and 'opening_blunder', and the concrete positions confirm this: e.g., failing to play dxe4 capturing a knight on e4, or failing to play cxd5 capturing a hanging piece on d5, instead pushing the pawn forward to a square where it gains nothing. The consistent pattern is a developing or advancing pawn move that looks natural but catastrophically overlooks an immediately available free capture in the opening.

137.label: Player makes a quiet developing move instead of delivering a winning queen check.
137.description: This feature consistently fires when a player plays a slow, non-forcing move (typically a bishop development or retreat) while missing an immediately winning queen check. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (nothing hangs directly), but Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100%). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase, where the opponent's king is exposed or has lost castling rights, creating a tactical window that demands immediate exploitation. The dominant motifs are king_safety (75%) and tempo_loss (25%), indicating the player squanders a critical tempo by not striking at the vulnerable king. The eval trajectory is severe—median 312 centipawns lost—with 40% of cases converting a winning position into a losing one and 20% into a draw. The per-position analyses confirm the pattern: in each case, a powerful Qh5+, Qh4+, or Bxf7+ sacrifice/check was available that would have won material or delivered a decisive attack, but the player chose a passive developing move (Bc4, Be4, Bb3, castling, or a bishop retreat) that allowed the opponent to consolidate or block the tactical threat. This is a pure tactical oversight where the player fails to recognize the forcing nature of a queen check in an open position.

135.label: Trading or moving minor pieces while leaving another piece undefended, converting advantageous positions into losses.
135.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where players execute minor piece exchanges (knight 41%, bishop 35% moved) or king moves that inadvertently leave a piece hanging. The material signature shows 53% trades and 35% hangs with a median net of 0.0, indicating these are exchange decisions that go wrong rather than pure blunders—the player often captures something but loses more in return, or moves a piece while forgetting another is undefended. The eval trajectory is devastating: 35% drawn->losing and 29% winning->drawn, with a median loss of 444 centipawns, showing these mistakes squander significant advantages. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (33%), alongside tags like 'unprotected_bishop' and 'material_advantage_squandered'. The concrete positions reveal the pattern clearly: king moves that abandon bishops (FENs with c4/c2 bishops left en prise), knight exchanges that simplify into lost endgames, and captures that overlook a resulting vulnerability. The phase (65% middlegame, 35% endgame) and Maia's non-capturing alternatives (88% no capture) suggest the correct moves were quiet defensive or repositioning moves rather than the exchanges/trades chosen.

141.label: Player makes a passive or routine move instead of capturing an undefended piece with a queen check.
141.description: This feature fires when a player has a devastating queen capture available — typically capturing an undefended piece with check (often exploiting back-rank geometry) — but instead plays a quiet, non-capturing move with the queen, a pawn, or a bishop. The material signature shows the player's move is 78% non-capture and 30% hangs material, while Maia's recommended move is 96% a queen move that delivers check 100% of the time, frequently capturing a rook (35%), bishop (26%), or knight. The eval trajectory confirms these are enormous blunders (median 396cp lost), with 100% of cases representing missed winning material. The tactical analysis reinforces this: 75% involve a hanging piece motif, with recurring tags of missed_tactic, undefended_piece, capture_with_check, and back_rank threats. The concrete positions consistently show scenarios where Qx[piece]+ was available but the player chose a developmental or retreating move instead, squandering decisive tactical opportunities in the opening or middlegame.

138.label: Playing a slow or routine move while overlooking an immediate tactical threat against the king, typically along a vulnerable diagonal or weak f-pawn.
138.description: This feature detects moves where a player makes a natural-looking, often developmental or positional move (pawns 39%, rooks 20%) while completely ignoring an immediate king safety threat. The material signature shows 74% of these moves hang material (median loss of ~1 pawn equivalent), and 78% are non-captures—indicating passive moves rather than active miscalculations. The eval trajectory is devastating: 47% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 408 centipawns, confirming these are game-altering oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies king_safety (100%) as the dominant motif, with recurring tags like f7_weakness, queen_bishop_battery, king_displacement, and ignoring_threats. The concrete positions consistently show scenarios where an opponent has a queen+bishop battery aimed at f7/f2 or an open diagonal toward the king, and the player responds with a slow rook move, a routine pawn push like d7-d6, or a developing move that fails to address—or even worsens—the tactical vulnerability. Maia's preferred moves (69% pawn moves, 94% non-captures) suggest the 'correct' response was often a simple defensive pawn move or prophylactic action that the player neglected in favor of their own plans.

140.label: Moving a minor piece to an ineffective square while leaving material undefended or ignoring a critical tactical obligation.
140.description: This feature fires when a player moves a knight or bishop (63% combined) in a way that hangs material (26% hangs) or is nominally safe but misses a critical rook move (Maia recommends rook 90% of the time). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic cost (median 258cp lost, 33% drawn->losing), indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-changing blunders. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (44%), king_safety (33%), tempo_loss tags—reveal the common thread: the player wastes a tempo relocating a minor piece (e.g., Bc2, Nh5, Ne4) or makes a pawn move that opens lines for the opponent, when the position urgently demanded a rook move to contest a file, defend a piece, or maintain structural integrity. The concrete examples confirm this: Bc2 ignores the need for Rd1, a5 allows b5 with tempo trapping a knight, bxa5 removes a key defensive pawn. In each case, the player neglects a pressing defensive/active rook deployment in favor of a minor piece or pawn move that either directly hangs material or fatally loses tempo in a critical middlegame position.

142.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move, missing a devastating discovered check or fork that wins significant material.
142.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful discovered check or knight fork that would have won substantial material. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (67%) — the player isn't hanging pieces directly, but is making innocuous developing or prophylactic moves instead of executing a crushing tactic. Maia consistently recommends knight moves (82%) that deliver check (100%), confirming the missed tactic is almost always a discovered check or knight fork/check combination. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 460cp), frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 30%, winning->losing 11%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are discovered attacks (50%), forks (25%), and tempo losses (25%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, discovered_check, and exposed_king. The concrete positions show patterns like Nc7+ forking king and rook, dxc4+ discovering a check winning the queen, and similar knight-based tactical shots that the player completely overlooked in favor of passive alternatives.

143.label: Playing routine moves (h3, castling) instead of the winning Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice exploiting an uncastled king.
143.description: This feature fires consistently on opening positions where White has a bishop on c4 aimed at f7, Black's king remains in the center (often with a bishop on g4), and White plays a routine developing move (h3 to ask the bishop, castling, or retreating the bishop) instead of the crushing Bxf7+ sacrifice. The material signature shows safe non-captures (pawn/king moves) while Maia consistently recommends a bishop capturing a pawn with check (Bxf7+). The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins—71% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 270 centipawns. The tactical motifs (70% fork, 20% discovered attack) reflect that Bxf7+ typically initiates a combination involving a follow-up knight fork (e.g., Ng5+) or discovered attack to win back material with interest. The common tags (bishop_sacrifice, king_in_center, missed_tactic) and example summaries all describe the same Italian Game/Two Knights pattern where the concrete Bxf7+ combination disrupts castling rights and wins material, but the player instead makes a 'polite' move that squanders the tactical opportunity.

145.label: Player makes a move that walks into or fails to address a discovered attack, typically allowing a mating net or catastrophic material loss.
145.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player overlooks a discovered attack or king safety threat, resulting in massive evaluation swings (median 789 centipawns lost). The material signature shows pieces being hung (44%) rather than traded, with the best move (Maia's recommendation) being a check 89% of the time—indicating the player missed that their opponent had a devastating discovered check or mating continuation available. The dominant motifs are discovered_attack (50%) and king_safety (50%), with recurring tags of back_rank threats and mating nets. The trajectory shows most cases occur in already-losing positions (56% losing->losing) where the player's move converts a difficult but survivable situation into immediate catastrophe (forced mate or decisive material loss). The concrete positions confirm this: pieces are moved to squares that either expose the king to a discovered attack or ignore an existing one, while the engine's recommended move was almost always a check exploiting exactly that geometric alignment.

144.label: Unsound knight sacrifice on f7 in the opening that exposes the opponent's king but lacks sufficient follow-up, turning a balanced or favorable position into a losing one.
144.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring opening mistake: a knight captures a pawn on f7 (Nxf7 or occasionally Nxf2 from Black's perspective), targeting the king's vulnerable f-pawn. The material signature shows knight captures pawn 100% of the time with a net material outcome of slightly_down (-2.0), indicating the knight is lost or traded unfavorably after the capture. The eval trajectory is devastating—80% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 20% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 340 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are unsound sacrifices (tagged 7/10 times) motivated by king_safety attacks (80% dominant motif) that lack sufficient tactical justification. The top boards reveal this is almost exclusively the classic Fried Liver / Lolli-style Nxf7 sacrifice in Italian Game and Petroff positions (e.g., Ng5xf7 or Ne5xf7), played prematurely without the supporting pieces or tempo needed to convert the attack. Maia's suggested alternatives (quiet developing moves like knight retreats, pawn pushes, or bishop moves) confirm that patient development was correct rather than the speculative sacrifice.

147.label: Player makes a neutral trade or quiet move, missing a devastating check or checkmate that Maia consistently finds.
147.description: This feature fires when players execute exchanges or quiet moves (trades 71%, safe 29%) while completely missing a forcing check or mate. The most striking signal is the contrast between the player's moves (0% checks, pieces traded at material neutrality) and Maia's recommended moves (100% checks, 100% missed winning material). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights—median 564cp lost—often converting winning positions into drawn ones (29% winning->drawn). The tactical motifs reinforce this: tempo_loss (67%) indicates the player's move surrendered initiative, while back_rank themes (33%) and tags like missed_mate and king_safety reveal that the available checks exploited concrete king vulnerabilities. The concrete positions show patterns like missing Qe1# for a pawn push, or missing Rb7+ for a rook trade. Players are drawn to 'reasonable' exchanges or positional moves while a single forcing check—often with devastating consequences like back-rank mate or king exposure—goes unseen.

146.label: Giving a check in an endgame that wastes tempo and throws away a winning or drawn position.
146.description: This feature captures endgame positions where the player delivers a check (100% of moves are checks) with a rook or queen that serves no constructive purpose. The material signature shows nothing is captured or lost immediately ('safe' 100%), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: a median loss of ~10,595 centipawns, typically converting a losing-but-holdable or winning position into something far worse (67% losing->winning for opponent). The tactical tags consistently flag 'pointless_check', 'tempo_loss', and 'piece_activity' issues—the check looks active but actually squanders critical tempo needed for promotion races, king centralization, or defensive setups. The positions are universally endgames with passed pawns where every tempo matters enormously. Rather than advancing pawns, activating the king, or blockading, the player gives a flashy but purposeless check that allows the opponent to improve their king position or advance their own pawns. Maia's recommended moves (rook repositioning or king moves, never checks) confirm that quiet constructive play was required. The Opus analysis explicitly identifies several as 'pointless checks' that convert forced wins or draws into losses by gifting the opponent critical tempi in pawn races.

150.label: Player moves their queen to an attacked square, often giving check, resulting in immediate queen loss.
150.description: This feature captures a specific and devastating tactical oversight: the player moves their queen (83% of activations) to a square that is directly controlled by an opponent's piece, frequently while delivering check (50% of moves are checks). The material signature is catastrophic—median net loss of 8.0 points (consistent with losing a queen), with 100% of positions involving a hanging piece and the Opus analysis tagging 'queen_blunder' in 5 of 6 cases. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding errors: 67% convert winning positions into losing ones, with a median eval swing of 984 centipawns. The recurring pattern visible in the boards is 'check blindness'—the player is attracted to giving check or making an aggressive queen move without noticing the queen lands on a square defended by a rook, king, or minor piece. Maia's recommended moves are all queen moves with check (100%), indicating that a safe checking move existed but the player chose the wrong square or wrong tactical sequence, hanging the queen instead.

148.label: Player makes a queen or piece move that ignores a critical back-rank vulnerability, allowing the opponent a decisive tactical blow.
148.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (57%) or another piece while overlooking a back-rank threat or related tactical motif. The material signature shows moves that are slightly down, hang material, or outright lose it (median net: -2.0), indicating the player's move is not an exchange but a genuine oversight. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 401cp lost), with 43% of cases turning drawn positions into losing ones and others deepening an already bad situation. The dominant tactical motif is back_rank (50%), complemented by hanging pieces and overloaded defenders. The per-position analysis confirms the pattern: players choose natural-looking moves (captures, central knight maneuvers, queen repositioning) while missing forcing sequences—often rook-based—that exploit back-rank weakness or piece coordination. The consistent thread is that Maia's recommended moves heavily favor rook activity (57% rook moves, 57% rook captures), suggesting the missed resource is almost always a rook infiltration or back-rank tactic that the player's chosen move fails to address or prevent.

151.label: Player makes a quiet move while missing a strong knight capture or fork with check.
151.description: This feature fires when players make quiet moves (predominantly pawn, bishop, or knight moves, with 69% being non-captures) while Maia consistently identifies a knight move (100%) that captures material (67% knight captures, 33% bishop captures) with check (100%). The material signature shows 34% of moves hang a piece and another 13% are slightly down, confirming the player left material vulnerable. The eval trajectory is severe (median 379cp lost), with 34% going from drawn to losing and 16% from winning to drawn, indicating these missed knight forks/captures fundamentally shift the game's outcome. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece (50%) and tempo_loss (50%) motifs, with tags like knight_geometry, missed_capture, and calculation_error. The top boards consistently show knight(s) positioned to deliver devastating forks or captures with check (e.g., Nxf3+, central knight forks) that players overlook by playing routine developing or prophylactic moves instead.

149.label: Player ignores critical king safety threats while having a winning or defensible position, allowing catastrophic tactical consequences.
149.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a move (typically with the queen or king) that neglects urgent king safety concerns, resulting in massive evaluation losses (median 700cp). The material signature shows diverse outcomes—some moves hang material, some trade, some look superficially safe—but the unifying thread is the king_safety motif appearing in 57% of tactical analyses and 'exposed_king' tagging in 3/4 of positions. The eval trajectory reveals these are predominantly thrown wins (50% winning->losing, 25% winning->drawn), indicating the player had a strong position but made a move that catastrophically exposed their own king or failed to address threats against it. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), suggesting the correct play involved defensive or prophylactic rook placements to shore up king safety. The per-position analyses confirm: moves that transform winning positions into lost ones by walking into discovered attacks, allowing forced mating nets, or abandoning defensive duties around the king. The common 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' tags suggest these moves often waste time on irrelevant objectives while the king burns.

153.label: Moving the queen to a passive or exposed square while missing a discovered attack or hanging piece that wins major material.
153.description: This feature fires when players move their queen (71% of cases) to an inferior square, missing a powerful tactical opportunity—typically a discovered attack or capture of a hanging piece (the two dominant motifs at 50% each). The material signature shows these moves frequently hang material (43%) or are otherwise suboptimal (median net material: -1.0), while Maia's recommended moves capture rooks (71%) or bishops (29%), often with check (43%). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes: 43% turn winning positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 391 centipawns. The OPUS analysis reinforces this pattern—players overlook simple captures with check, discovered attacks that win major material, or bishop sacrifices initiating forced sequences. Instead, they play quiet queen moves (Qf2, Qh6 into a trap, Qf6/Qf7 retreats) that squander decisive advantages. The common thread is that the queen's repositioning either exposes the king, loses tempo, or simply ignores a concrete winning tactic that was available on that move.

155.label: Exchanging pieces that dissipate a winning or drawn position by removing tactical tension.
155.description: This feature fires when players make exchanges (material outcome 'trade' in 50% of cases) or slightly losing captures that dissolve their advantage. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 299 centipawns, converting winning positions to drawn or drawn to losing (33% each). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%) and tempo_loss (50%)—reveal the mechanism: by initiating an exchange or recapture at the wrong moment, the player either leaves another piece undefended (as in the queen left hanging on h5 after capturing on g1) or loses a critical tempo that allowed the opponent to capture a strong advanced piece (as in Nc3 instead of f7+ letting Black take the f6 pawn). The tags reinforce this: forcing_moves_missed, move_order errors, and queen_loss all point to players choosing a simplifying trade or recapture when a forcing sequence was available. The positions are predominantly middlegame (67%) where tactical tension is high, and in 83% of cases the player missed winning material—suggesting they saw an exchange but not the stronger non-trading continuation that maintained pressure.

154.label: Player makes a quiet or materialistic move instead of delivering a forced checkmate sequence starting with a check.
154.description: This feature fires when a player has a forced checkmate available (often beginning with a queen check) but instead plays a non-checking move—typically a knight retreat, a pawn capture, or a bishop move that appears logical but squanders the mating attack. The material signature shows the player's moves are mostly safe or slightly losing (not hanging pieces outright), yet Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen delivering check (100% check rate, 75% queen moves). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic missed wins: 83% of positions involve missed winning material, with a staggering median loss of ~88 pawns (i.e., missed mates converting to merely advantageous positions). The dominant motifs are king_safety (60%) with recurring tags of missed_mate, forced_mate, and checks_before_captures. The pattern across the top boards shows exposed enemy kings (often uncastled in the opening/middlegame) where the player retreats a piece, captures a peripheral pawn, or makes a developing move instead of initiating the forcing check sequence that leads to mate. The player prioritizes material gain or piece repositioning over the critical tempo of checking first.

152.label: Player makes a move while leaving a valuable piece (often the queen) undefended and capturable by the opponent.
152.description: This feature fires on positions where the player completely ignores a tactical threat to one of their own pieces, typically a high-value piece like the queen. The material signature shows that 50% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave a piece en prise) with a median net loss of 3.0 (roughly a minor piece to queen's worth), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings—50% go from drawn to losing and 33% from winning to losing, with a median 572 centipawns lost. The Opus analysis unanimously identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (100%), with recurring tags of 'ignored_threat', 'hanging_queen', and 'missed_tactic'. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern: a player makes a natural-looking developing or pawn move (dxc5, castling, pawn captures) while completely overlooking that an enemy piece already attacks one of their undefended pieces—particularly knights forking or attacking queens. Maia's recommended moves frequently capture knights (67%), confirming the opponent's knight was the threatening piece that should have been addressed. This is fundamentally a blindness-to-threat error occurring predominantly in the opening phase (67%).

156.label: In pawn endgames, the king moves away from the critical squares, ceding tempo in a pawn race or promotion contest.
156.description: This feature consistently fires on king moves in pawn endgames (89% endgame phase) where the player retreats or sidesteps with the king instead of advancing a pawn (Maia always recommends a pawn move). The material signature shows no captures and mostly 'safe' outcomes, indicating this isn't a material blunder but a subtle positional/tempo error. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (60%) and pawn_endgame (40%), with recurring tags for passed pawns, pawn races, and king activity. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 75 centipawns, often worsening an already losing position (67% losing->losing) or occasionally squandering a win (11% winning->drawn). Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: positions with passed pawns where precise king placement is critical, and the player drifts the king to a passive square (e.g., Kd7, Ke7, Ke6, Kf2) rather than contesting the promotion path or supporting their own passer. The mistake is fundamentally about misunderstanding which tempi matter in king-and-pawn endings.

157.label: Player makes a non-capture move that hangs a piece by failing to address an opponent's queen invasion or threat.
157.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions where the player moves a minor piece or pawn (knight 42%, bishop 25%, pawn 25%) while completely ignoring a critical threat from the opponent's queen. In nearly every top-activating position, the opponent's queen has infiltrated to a dangerous square (often b2 or g2) and is threatening material (rook captures, piece captures, or checkmate motifs). Instead of addressing this urgent threat—typically by trading queens, blocking, or counterattacking the queen—the player makes a developing or positional move that hangs a piece outright (100% hang rate, median -5.0 material). The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 387 centipawns), with half the cases going from already-losing to deeper trouble, but a significant portion throwing away drawn or winning positions. The recurring tags (hanging_piece, queen_infiltration, ignored_threat) and position analysis confirm the pattern: the opponent's queen is rampaging and the player plays a move as if the queen isn't there, resulting in immediate material catastrophe. Maia's suggested moves (queen 58%, bishop 42%) often involve addressing the queen threat directly through exchange or repositioning.

158.label: Ignoring a critical open h-file tactic (usually Rxh8+ with check) in favor of a greedy or tempo-losing piece move, throwing away a winning position.
158.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a decisive tactical opportunity on the h-file—typically Rxh1+ or Rxh8+ with check winning material—but instead plays a knight, queen, or bishop move that either grabs lesser material (a pawn or knight) or loses tempo. The material signature shows the player's move results in a net loss (median -4.0 centipawns lost in material, with outcomes split between 'loses', 'slightly_down', and 'hangs'), while Maia consistently identifies a rook capture on the h-file with check as the correct move. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 100% of cases go from winning to losing with a median swing of ~13.5 pawns. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece, back_rank, king_safety) and tags (open_file_race, king_in_center, capture_with_check, greedy_pawn_grab) all converge on the same pattern: both sides have tension on the h-file with castling rights still available, and the player fails to prioritize the forcing rook check that wins immediately, instead opting for a materialistic but non-forcing capture or a developing move that hands the initiative to the opponent. The positions overwhelmingly occur in the opening phase with kings still in the center, making the h-file race particularly lethal.

160.label: Hanging a major piece by ignoring back rank and king safety threats in the middlegame.
160.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a major piece (rook 35%, queen 24%) without capturing anything (82% non-captures) and immediately hangs material worth a median of 5 pawns (82% 'hangs' outcome). The eval trajectory shows devastating swings—18% go from winning to losing and 11% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 655 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are back_rank (33%), king_safety (33%), and hanging_piece (33%), indicating the player relocates a major piece that was serving a critical defensive role (often guarding the back rank or the king), leaving it or another piece undefended. The top boards confirm this: many feature a king on g1/g8 with rooks on open files, where the moved piece either abandons back-rank defense or steps into a tactically vulnerable square. Maia's recommended moves (52% rook moves, often quiet) suggest the correct play was to address the back-rank or king-safety issue rather than the speculative piece relocation that was played.

159.label: Moving a piece that abandons king defense, missing critical tactical threats to the exposed king.
159.description: This feature captures moves where players neglect king safety by moving defenders (especially bishops and knights) away from critical defensive duties, allowing devastating tactical exploitation of the exposed king. The material signature shows 63% non-captures with bishop (37%) and knight (16%) moves predominating—these are repositioning moves rather than exchanges. The 'hangs' (26%) and 'slightly_down' (16%) outcomes confirm pieces are being lost as a consequence. The Opus analysis is decisive: king_safety dominates at 67% of positions, with tags like 'removed_defender,' 'exposed_king,' and 'deflection_sacrifice' reinforcing that the player's move strips a key defender from the king's vicinity. The missed Maia moves (queen 26%, knight 26% with 21% checks) indicate strong tactical replies exploiting the newly exposed king. The eval trajectory (median 270cp lost, with winning->losing and drawn->losing representing 26% combined) shows these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders. The concrete examples confirm this: Qxh7 grabs a pawn while abandoning defense of a key piece, f7f6 weakens the king shelter allowing invasion, and multiple positions show kings becoming fatally exposed after the defender moves away. This is the pattern of a player who fails to recognize their piece serves a critical defensive role for king safety.

161.label: In Italian Game positions, Black prematurely captures on d4 with the bishop instead of recapturing with the knight on c4, losing a winning advantage.
161.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake occurring almost exclusively in Italian Game / Two Knights Defense positions. The material signature shows the player always moves a bishop capturing a pawn (Bxd4), resulting in a slight material loss (median -2.0), while the engine recommends a knight move capturing a bishop (Nxc4). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (100%), and the eval trajectory shows a consistent pattern of converting a winning position into a drawn one (100% winning->drawn, median 343cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: by capturing the d4 pawn with the bishop, Black neglects the hanging white bishop on c4 that could be captured by the knight, effectively missing a tactic (Nxc4) that would win material. The motifs of hanging_piece and tempo_loss confirm that the bishop move both misses the hanging piece and loses developmental tempo, as the bishop becomes exposed or misplaced on d4. This is a classic move-order/prioritization error where the player grabs a less valuable pawn instead of exploiting a tactical opportunity to win a piece.

162.label: Moving a bishop to an unprotected square where it or another piece is immediately lost to a tactical shot.
162.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where the player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves, 0% captures) that hangs material worth approximately 5 pawns (median net material -5.0), converting a winning position into a losing one (100% winning->losing, median 960cp lost). The bishop move is not a capture itself but leaves a piece en prise or creates a tactical vulnerability — the opponent's best response consistently involves a rook capturing a knight (Maia: rook 100%, captures knight 100%). The Opus analysis reveals the underlying motifs: hanging pieces (40%), back-rank weaknesses (20%), trapped pieces (20%), and positional errors (20%), with recurring tags around piece activity and missed tactics. The pattern shows players making seemingly active or repositioning bishop moves that overlook the opponent's concrete tactical reply exploiting the changed geometry — whether it's opening a file for a rook, leaving a knight undefended, or creating a back-rank threat. The catastrophic eval swing confirms these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding oversights where a consolidating or defensive move was required instead.

164.label: Bishop moves in the opening that leave a knight undefended, turning a winning position into a losing one.
164.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves) in the opening phase (100% opening), making a non-capture that hangs a piece (100% hangs, median -3.0 material = one full piece). The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing from winning to losing (100%, median 346cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (90%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, development errors, and tempo loss. The concrete positions reveal the pattern clearly: in Scotch/Vienna/Italian-type openings, a knight on e5 or e4 is left tactically vulnerable when the player makes a developing or repositioning bishop move (Bb4, Cb3, Bc4) that ignores the immediate tactical threat to their own knight. The player prioritizes a strategic concept (pinning, development, piece placement) over the urgent need to protect or retreat a tactically exposed knight, resulting in the immediate loss of a full piece.

165.label: Advancing a pawn in a won endgame while leaving a piece undefended, allowing the opponent's rook to capture it.
165.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where a player, holding a winning position, pushes a pawn (often toward promotion) instead of playing the tactically critical move—typically capturing with a bishop or rook (Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a rook). The material signature shows the player's pawn move is technically 'safe' (nothing immediately hangs on that move alone), yet it leaves a piece undefended or misorders the sequence, costing a massive median of ~93 pawns worth of evaluation (converting forced mates into merely winning positions). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%) and promotion_error (20%)—confirm that players either rush a promotion without neutralizing the opponent's active rook first, or advance a pawn while their own rook or bishop is left en prise. The boards consistently show rook endgames or bishop+rook endgames where the critical resource (an undefended piece on an open file) is ignored in favor of a tempting but premature pawn advance. The trajectory (winning->winning with enormous eval loss) indicates these are not game-losing blunders but severe imprecisions that squander forced mates or clean conversions.

169.label: Player makes a random move in the endgame while missing a forced back-rank checkmate in one.
169.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a winning back-rank mate in one move during an endgame position. The material/position signature shows the player making safe-looking moves (king moves, pawn captures, rook moves) while Maia consistently recommends rook or queen moves that deliver check — specifically back-rank mates. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: 100% of positions involve missed winning material, with a median loss of 212 centipawns, often flipping from losing to winning (meaning the mate was the saving resource) or converting a drawn/winning position into a loss. The Opus analysis unanimously tags 'back_rank' as the dominant motif with 'missed_mate_in_one' appearing in every analyzed example. Players are distracted by material greed (capturing pawns) or making aimless moves while a lethal Rg1# or Rc8# sits on the board. The endgame phase (100%) is critical: simplified positions with open files create back-rank vulnerabilities that players fail to exploit.

166.label: Hanging a rook (or king move) in a winning endgame position by missing the opponent's ability to capture a queen.
166.description: This feature detects a specific recurring endgame blunder pattern where a player with a winning or salvageable position gives away their rook (75% of moves are rook moves) without capturing anything in return (100% non-captures), effectively hanging material (75% 'hangs' outcome, median net material -1.0). The positions are exclusively endgames where Maia's recommended move captures a queen (100%), meaning the player consistently misses a queen capture that would win or maintain their advantage. The eval trajectory shows these moves often flip a losing position into a winning one for the opponent (75% losing->winning), with catastrophic centipawn losses (median -10,319cp, often leading to forced mate). The tactical analysis reveals exposed kings, hanging pieces, and missed captures as dominant themes—players make seemingly active moves (checks in 50% of cases, rook lifts, king walks) that look purposeful but overlook that the opponent's queen is en prise or that a simple queen capture solves everything. The common thread is tunnel vision in endgames: players focus on their own plans (promotion threats, checks, king activity) while completely missing an available queen capture that would decisively resolve the position.

163.label: Failing to correctly address passed pawn threats in endgames, allowing promotion or losing critical tempo.
163.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (67% endgame, 33% middlegame) where passed pawns dominate the tactical landscape (78% passed_pawn motif, 9/10 top boards showing passed pawns on the 7th rank or advanced positions). The moves themselves appear materially 'safe' (100% safe, no pieces immediately hanging), yet they cost a median of 248 centipawns—often converting drawable or winning positions into lost ones (winning->losing 17%, drawn->losing 17%, losing->drawn 17%). The key error is a tempo loss (tagged 9 times) in handling promotion races: players make natural-looking rook or pawn moves that fail to address the critical promotion threat, missing the one precise defensive or offensive continuation. The top boards consistently show positions with pawns on the 7th rank (c7, a7, d6, f6) where the correct move requires exact calculation of promotion sequences, but the player instead makes a passive or misdirected move (e.g., Cb8 instead of promoting defense, Kg3 instead of blocking, Qxh4 instead of stopping promotion). The promotion_error tag (22% motif, 4 occurrences) confirms that the subset of worst blunders involve outright miscalculation of who promotes first.

167.label: In winning endgames with passed pawns, player makes a piece move that abandons the coordination needed to promote or support the passed pawn.
167.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (86%) where the player has a winning advantage but makes a piece move (bishop/knight/king/rook) that squanders the tactical or positional coordination around a passed pawn. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (75% of positions), and the recurring tag 'tempo_loss' (4 occurrences) reveals that these moves waste critical time in positions where pawn promotion is the key winning plan. The eval trajectory shows that 57% remain winning->winning but with a median loss of 179 centipawns, while 28% transition from winning to drawn or losing — indicating these are serious inaccuracies that throw away decisive advantages. The concrete examples reinforce this: a bishop retreating away from a promotion-supporting diagonal (Be1), a knight abandoning a post that threatened promotion (Nc3 instead of maintaining the Nb5/a6 battery), and rook moves that fail to support advancing passers. The material signature shows 100% non-captures that are mostly 'safe' — these aren't blunders that hang pieces, but positional mistakes where the player loses the thread of the endgame by moving pieces away from their optimal passed-pawn-supporting roles.

168.label: Wasting a crucial tempo on a passive or irrelevant move, allowing the opponent to seize a decisive initiative or execute a winning tactic.
168.description: This feature captures moves where a player squanders a critical tempo during a tense middlegame position, typically by moving a piece (most often the queen, at 42%) to a passive or irrelevant square rather than addressing an urgent tactical threat. The material signature shows 58% of moves hang a piece and the median material loss is -1.0 (a full piece), indicating these tempo losses directly result in material catastrophe. The eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences: 25% swing from winning to drawn, 21% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 419 centipawns—these are game-deciding errors that often throw away winning or equal positions. The Opus tactical analysis and tags consistently identify tempo_loss (33%) and king_safety (33%) as dominant motifs, with examples showing moves like Ba6 wasting tempo on a passive square while the opponent launches a breakthrough, or b6 ignoring an urgent queen threat. The missed winning material rate of 62% further confirms that these players had strong moves available but chose time-wasting alternatives. The common thread is not a miscalculation of a tactical sequence, but rather a positional misjudgment about urgency—playing a slow, purposeless move in a position that demanded immediate action.

171.label: Knight moves to passive square, enabling opponent's tactical combination (often a fork or infiltration).
171.description: This feature fires when a player moves a knight (93% of activations) to a square that appears safe (77% safe, no captures made) but critically weakens the position by enabling the opponent's tactical shots. The median eval loss of 234 centipawns with 36% of cases going from drawn to losing indicates these are serious mistakes that shift the game's outcome. The dominant motifs—fork (33%), king_safety (22%), and overloaded_defender (11%)—reveal that the knight retreat typically abandons a defensive duty or vacates a key square, allowing the opponent to exploit newly created vulnerabilities. The top boards confirm this pattern: moves like Nf3-d2, Nf6-d7, and Nc6-e7 pull knights away from active posts (especially f3/f6 which guard critical squares around the king), creating tactical opportunities the opponent can exploit through forks, queen infiltrations, or attacks on weakened diagonals. Maia's preferred responses (25% pawn, 23% knight, 20% queen) suggest the engine wants active piece play or pawn grabs that exploit the newly passive knight's absence from key squares.

172.label: Playing a knight check instead of simply capturing a hanging piece in a won endgame, throwing away the win.
172.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player plays a knight check (knight moved 100%, check given 100%) instead of the obvious knight capture of a hanging piece (Maia's recommended move is always a knight capturing a pawn, 100%). The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe' — nothing is immediately lost — but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic damage: positions swing from winning to drawn (50%) or winning to losing (50%) with a median loss of 1049 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: the correct move was always a simple capture (e.g., Nxa4, Nxd6 capturing a hanging rook or pawn), but the player chose a superficially attractive check that accomplishes nothing. The motifs (tempo_loss, hanging_piece, trapped_piece) and concrete board positions (all endgames with knights, passed pawns, and minimal material) show that players are seduced by the 'active-looking' check while ignoring the concrete requirement to collect material or execute a won technique. The check often allows the opponent to escape or create counterplay around passed pawns.

173.label: Trading a rook for a minor piece in a position where the exchange sacrifice removes critical defensive or offensive resources, often enabling unstoppable passed pawns.
173.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a disadvantageous rook-for-minor-piece exchange that catastrophically simplifies the position. The material signature shows rooks moved 71% of the time, capturing bishops 57% of the time, with the outcome being 'slightly_down' (57%) or 'trade' (29%) — indicating these are deliberate exchange decisions rather than blunders, but ones that lose material value (median -2.0, consistent with rook-for-bishop). The eval trajectory reveals massive costs (median 414cp lost), with positions going drawn->losing (29%) or even winning->losing (14%), showing these exchanges throw away games. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: players are 'seduced' into capturing minor pieces with rooks (often with check or apparent tactical justification), failing to recognize that the resulting simplified position is lost due to passed pawns, loss of defensive resources, or removal of their only active piece. The top boards consistently show endgame/late-middlegame positions where the rook exchange enables unstoppable passed pawns or fatally simplifies into a lost ending. The common tags (passed_pawn appearing 5 times, rook_for_bishop_exchange, unstoppable_pawn) reinforce that these are structurally catastrophic simplifications rather than mere material miscalculations.

174.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move while their queen has an unobstructed path to capture an undefended enemy rook.
174.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a free queen capture of an undefended rook, typically on a8. The material/position signature shows that the player's actual move is safe and non-capturing (82% no capture, 82% safe outcome), while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capturing a rook. The tactical analysis confirms that in 100% of cases a hanging piece is present (specifically an undefended rook, tagged in 4/7 examples), and the queen has a clear diagonal or file to take it. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 243 centipawns, often converting a winning position into a drawn one (36%) or even a losing one (18%). The concrete board positions consistently show an undefended rook on a8 with the player's queen (often on f3 or similar diagonal) having direct access, yet the player instead makes a developing move, recapture, or positional shuffle—completely missing the tactical opportunity to win significant material for free.

170.label: Retreating or repositioning a piece (usually a bishop) that abandons a critical defensive or tactical function, causing positional collapse.
170.description: This feature fires on moves where a player retreats or relocates a piece—most often a bishop (42%) but also rooks and kings—that was serving a crucial tactical or defensive role in the position. The material signature shows 58% of these moves hang material (median net loss of -1.0, i.e., a full piece), yet 88% involve no capture, confirming these are non-forcing repositioning moves rather than failed exchanges. The Opus analysis reveals the unifying theme: the moved piece was a linchpin maintaining tactical justification or king safety, and its removal causes piece coordination to collapse (tags: tactical_justification_removed, piece_coordination_collapse, bishop_retreat_error). The eval trajectory shows a severe median cost of 222 centipawns, with many positions transitioning from drawn to losing or even winning to losing, indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but position-destroying decisions. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves/captures instead, suggesting the correct plan involved concrete pawn action rather than passive piece shuffling. The dominant motifs—king_safety (50%), hanging_piece (25%), and tempo_loss (25%)—confirm that these retreats simultaneously weaken the king, leave other pieces undefended, and waste critical tempo in middlegame positions where dynamic coordination is paramount.

176.label: Avoiding a decisive queen exchange in a won endgame, exposing the king to counterplay instead.
176.description: This feature detects positions where a player in a won endgame (100% endgame phase, typically queen endgames or pawn endgames) refuses a winning queen trade that would simplify into a trivially won position. The material signature shows the player moves the king (75%) or pushes a pawn (25%) rather than capturing, while Maia consistently recommends capturing the queen (Maia's move: queen 100%, captures queen 100%). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes—median 511 centipawns lost, with positions going from winning to winning (75%) or winning to losing (25%). The tactical analysis is remarkably consistent: tags like 'queen_trade_missed', 'pawn_endgame_conversion', and 'passed_pawn' dominate, with summaries explicitly describing players who 'threw away a completely won position by avoiding the decisive queen trade' that leads to a trivially won pawn endgame. Instead, they make king moves that expose themselves to perpetual check threats or counterplay. The board positions confirm queen-and-pawn endgames where simplification wins but the player sidesteps it.

175.label: Giving a check in a won endgame that wastes tempo without improving the position or advancing a winning plan.
175.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check (100% of activations) with a rook or queen in an endgame (100% endgame phase) that is objectively safe (no material lost) but subtly suboptimal. The eval trajectory shows these moves occur in already-winning positions (67% winning->winning, 33% winning->drawn), with a small median eval loss of -2.0 centipawns—indicating the check itself isn't a gross blunder but a technical imprecision. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with passed_pawn and promotion_threat tags recurring, revealing that the player gives a check that allows the opponent's king to reposition favorably instead of pursuing the concrete winning plan (typically promoting a passed pawn or restricting the king). The Opus analysis confirms this: checks like Rh8+ or Qd6+ let the opposing king escape to better squares, potentially complicating or even throwing away a win. Maia's response is always a king move (100%), often gaining activity. The pattern is a human instinct to 'keep checking' in won endgames rather than executing the precise technique required—a tempo-wasting check that either does nothing or actively helps the defender's king find counterplay.

177.label: Advancing a pawn that fatally compromises the king's protective pawn shield, allowing tactical exploitation.
177.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves (100% pawn played, 100% no capture, 100% safe material outcome) that catastrophically weaken the player's own king shelter. The top boards show a clear pattern: moves like ...g6 or ...b6 played in the middlegame (100%) that open lines or create holes around the castled king, typically in response to an opposing queen already aimed at the kingside or queenside. The eval trajectory (83% drawn->losing, median 358cp lost) confirms these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-losing positional errors that immediately hand the opponent a decisive attack. The Opus analysis unanimously identifies king_safety as the dominant motif, with pawn_structure and exposed_king as supporting tags. In every case, the player had reasonable alternatives (like ...f5, ...h6, or developing moves) but instead chose a pawn advance that created fatal weaknesses—whether it's ...g6 weakening the kingside dark squares in front of a castled king facing a queen on h5, or ...b6 collapsing the queenside shelter against a queen on a5/a6. The opponent typically already had pieces trained on the king position, and the pawn advance provides the final tactical trigger for a devastating breakthrough.

178.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while ignoring an immediate tactical threat (often a forced mate or hanging piece) against their own king.
178.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a move (typically a pawn push or king move) that hangs material or walks into a forced mate, while a critical defensive or capturing move was available. The material signature shows 69% of moves hang something and the median cost is -3.0 (often a full piece or more), with 274 centipawns median eval loss. The king_safety motif dominates (57%), with back_rank and hanging_piece themes also present. The tactical analysis reveals repeated patterns: players ignore free captures (like taking a hanging queen with Kxg8), miss the only defensive move against forced mate, or play meaningless pawn pushes while pieces hang near their king. The trajectory shows 38% losing->losing (making a lost position immediately terminal) and 31% losing->winning for the opponent, indicating these are often final catastrophic oversights. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (bishop 31%, queen 31%, rook 15%), confirming that the missed best move was usually a critical capture or defensive resource that the player completely overlooked in favor of an aimless move.

179.label: Moving a major piece to a square where it is immediately captured by an opponent's piece, hanging material in the middlegame.
179.description: This feature captures a recurring blunder pattern where players move a rook or bishop to a square where it is directly attacked and can be captured for free. The material signature is stark: 73% of moves result in a 'hang' (non-capture that drops a piece) with a median net material loss of -3.0, indicating full pieces being left en prise. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 462 centipawns lost), often turning drawn positions into losing ones (36%) or squandering winning advantages. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (50%), with recurring examples of rooks placed on squares controlled by enemy queens or other pieces. King safety and tempo loss tags (5 each) suggest these moves often occur in complex middlegame positions where the player is focused on other threats—attacking or defending—while overlooking that the destination square is already covered. The Maia alternatives frequently involve captures (pawn 27%, rook 18%, queen 9%), indicating the correct moves were often tactical continuations that the player missed in favor of a careless piece placement.

181.label: Premature f-pawn capture in King's Gambit structures that fatally exposes the king along the e1-h4 diagonal.
181.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake: playing fxe5 (or similar f-pawn captures) in King's Gambit and related f4-pawn structures during the opening phase. The boards overwhelmingly show positions where White has played f4 and then captures on e5 with the f-pawn, or Black makes the analogous error. While the material outcome is technically a trade (pawn for pawn, net 0), the positional catastrophe is severe—median 425 centipawns lost, consistently turning drawn positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis reveals the punishment comes through king safety (75% of motifs), specifically diagonal weaknesses (often the e1-h4 diagonal opened by the f-pawn's departure) enabling queen checks. Maia consistently recommends knight development (Nf3/Nf6) instead, showing the correct approach was to support the center without compromising king cover. The move represents a tempo loss and development failure: rather than completing piece development, the player makes a structurally weakening capture that invites immediate tactical punishment against the exposed king.

180.label: Moving the king passively in a lost endgame instead of finding an active defensive resource like a fork or check.
180.description: This feature identifies positions where a player in an already losing endgame moves their king passively (king moved 100%, no capture, no check, material outcome 'safe') when the engine recommends an active knight move that delivers check (Maia's suggestion: knight 100%, gives check 100%). The eval trajectory confirms these are losing->losing positions where the passive king move costs a median of 447 centipawns—not turning a win into a loss, but making a bad position dramatically worse by missing a last-chance tactical resource. The tactical analysis reveals the missed resources are typically knight forks (Ne2+ winning a queen), checks that gain tempo, or moves that maintain activity against passed pawns. The boards consistently show endgame positions with limited material where the player's king wanders aimlessly while a critical knight check or fork existed that could have complicated the position or salvaged material. The common thread is choosing king 'safety' movement over a desperate but objectively superior active piece tactic.

183.label: Moving the queen away from critical defensive duties in a lost position, accelerating mate or decisive material loss.
183.description: This feature fires on positions where a player in an already losing position makes a queen move that catastrophically worsens their situation (median 9086 centipawns lost, all losing->losing). The material signature shows the player moves their queen (100%), sometimes capturing a bishop but often making a non-capture 'safe' move, while the engine recommends a queen move that captures a pawn with check—indicating the player missed a defensive or counterattacking resource involving check. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the queen abandons essential defensive responsibilities (covering back-rank threats, blocking invasion squares, or maintaining piece coordination) and relocates to a tactically vulnerable square where it falls to forks, discovered attacks, or simply allows unstoppable mating sequences. Key tags of king_safety, tempo_loss, and back_rank_mate confirm that these queen moves expose the player's own king fatally. Examples include Qxa2 abandoning d-file defense, Qc4 walking into a knight fork, and Qxh6 leaving f7 unguarded for a mating attack. The player is already lost but dramatically shortens their survival by misplacing their most powerful defensive piece.

186.label: Moving a valuable piece to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured by the opponent.
186.description: This feature detects positions where players move high-value pieces (queens 36%, knights 27%, rooks 27%) to squares where they are left unprotected and immediately capturable. The material signature shows 55% of moves result in a piece being hung outright, with a median material loss of -5.0 (roughly a full piece or more). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders—46% convert a winning position into a losing one, and 18% turn wins into draws, with a median cost of 589 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (67%), and the per-position summaries consistently describe pieces placed on undefended squares in the line of fire of opponent pieces (rook placed where a bishop captures it, queen moved to a square attacked by a rook, knight moved to a square losing the queen). These are non-forcing, non-checking moves (0% checks) that squander tempo and activity, giving the opponent a free capture of material that was previously safe.

185.label: King moves to suboptimal squares in endgames, losing critical tempo in pawn races or promotion sequences.
185.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where the player moves their king (86% king moves) to the wrong square, wasting a crucial tempo. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (86%) with passed pawns (9 occurrences) and pawn structures being the central concern. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly losing->losing (86%) situations where the player makes their position slightly worse (median 41cp lost), indicating missed defensive resources rather than thrown wins. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (44%), with concrete examples showing kings walking into promotion-with-check lines (Kg3 allowing g-pawn to promote with check), chasing irrelevant pawns instead of centralizing (Kb4 instead of Kd4), or retreating when advancement was necessary (Ke6 instead of maintaining active positioning). The material signature confirms these are safe non-captures (57%) or moves that hang material (43%) — the king simply walks to the wrong square, either allowing an opponent's passed pawn to advance decisively or failing to contest a critical file/diagonal in time.

184.label: Pawn moves in the opening that allow a knight fork on c7 winning the exchange or more.
184.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening trap pattern where a player makes a seemingly natural pawn move (c5, c6, a6, or similar) while a White knight sits on b5, inadvertently allowing Nc7+ — a devastating knight fork targeting the king and rook (or queen). All positions occur in the opening phase with White's knight already aggressively posted on b5 alongside a Bf4 development scheme. The pawn moves appear logical (attacking the knight or gaining space) but fatally overlook that the knight can jump to c7 with check. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: every instance transitions from a drawn position to losing, with a median loss of 363 centipawns — consistent with losing the exchange or more. The motif analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'fork' (90%), and tags like 'opening_trap', 'knight_fork', and 'missed_tactic' dominate. The material signature shows 'safe' in most cases because the pawn move itself doesn't immediately hang material — the punishment comes on the opponent's next move when the fork lands.

182.label: Giving a flashy check (usually with a knight or queen) that hangs or sacrifices the piece, converting a winning position into a much worse one.
182.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers check (92% of cases) with a knight (42%), queen (26%), or bishop (21%), but the checking move hangs the piece (42%) or results in a net material loss (median -1.0). The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly cases of throwing away a winning or drawn position — winning→drawn (18%), winning→losing (13%), drawn→losing (13%) — with a massive median eval loss of 434 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: players execute a tempting check or fork prematurely without proper preparation (tempo_loss, move_order_error tags), sacrificing material for a check that doesn't actually accomplish anything because the opponent can simply recapture or sidestep. The top boards illustrate this vividly — premature Nf6+ forks where preparatory moves were needed, queen sacrifices for checks that the opponent easily parries, and knight checks that allow simple recaptures. The Maia baseline (only 21% checks) confirms that the engine would not have chosen these impulsive checking moves, instead preferring quieter piece development or proper tactical preparation. This is the classic amateur mistake of being seduced by a check that looks forcing but actually squanders a winning advantage.

188.label: Player captures material instead of delivering available checkmate.
188.description: This feature fires when players choose to capture high-value pieces (queen 50%, rook 43%) rather than delivering checkmate that was available on the board. The key signals align perfectly: Maia's recommended move gives check 100% of the time and captures nothing (86% no capture), while the player's move is a trade/capture of material. The tags 'missed_mate_in_one' (4 occurrences), 'material_over_checkmate' (3), and 'material_greed' (3) directly describe this pattern. The eval trajectory shows median 0.0 centipawns lost because both the played move and the missed mate lead to winning positions — the cost is practical (delayed mate) rather than evaluative collapse. The king_safety motif (67%) reflects that the opponent's king was already fatally exposed, making mate available. Concrete examples confirm this: Black missed Re1# by capturing a rook on f7, Black missed Qxg2# by playing Nxc2 to grab material, and White missed back-rank mates by capturing pieces instead. The phase is predominantly middlegame (79%) where mating attacks are most common alongside available material captures that tempt players away from the killing blow.

187.label: Moving a knight to capture or occupy a square where it becomes undefended and lost to a simple recapture or attack.
187.description: This feature identifies knight moves (94% of activations) that leave the knight hanging or inadequately defended on its destination square. The material signature shows 34% of moves outright hang the piece and another 12% lose material, with a median eval loss of 313 centipawns — consistent with losing a full knight. The tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'hanging_piece' (100%), and the top boards reveal a recurring pattern: knights jump to active-looking central squares (e5, d4, f4) that appear aggressive but where the knight is immediately captured by a pawn or piece with no adequate compensation. The Opus analysis confirms players chose flashy knight moves over concrete alternatives (like capturing undefended material elsewhere), seduced by the apparent activity of the knight's destination. The eval trajectory (19% drawn->losing, 15% winning->drawn, 4% winning->losing) shows these moves frequently throw away advantageous or equal positions. The better moves identified by Maia are diverse (bishops, pawns, queens), suggesting the knight move was chosen impulsively over a variety of superior alternatives that maintained material balance.

189.label: Playing a quiet pawn move in the opening instead of capturing a hanging knight, converting a winning position into a drawn one.
189.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player has a knight hanging for capture (Maia consistently recommends capturing with a knight, taking a knight) but the player instead makes a quiet, non-capturing pawn move (100% pawn moves, 0% captures). The material outcome of the move itself is 'safe'—nothing is immediately lost on that move—but the missed tactic (100% missed winning material) means the opponent's hanging piece escapes, costing a median of 441 centipawns and converting a winning position into a drawn one. The top boards confirm this: positions like r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/8/5N2/PPP1PPPP/RNBQKB1R where Nxe5 wins a piece but the player plays g3 or Bg2 instead. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 50%, fork 17%) and tags (missed_tactic, tempo_loss, development) all point to the same pattern: the player prioritizes a slow developmental or fianchetto pawn push while ignoring a free or tactically winning capture that was available right now.

190.label: Player moves a piece to a square where it is immediately captured for free, worsening an already losing position into a hopeless one.
190.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player in an already losing position (67% losing->losing trajectory) makes a move that hangs a piece outright (83% 'hangs' in material outcome, median net material loss of -5.0). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (62%), with Opus analyses consistently describing pieces moved to squares where they are immediately captured by enemy pawns or pieces for nothing in return. The enormous median eval loss (9256 centipawns) reflects that these blunders often convert difficult-but-playable disadvantages into completely resignable positions.
