The moves themselves are mostly safe (63%) or hang material (29%), but critically, 100% of activations miss winning material. The median eval loss of 313 centipawns and trajectories like winning->drawn (16%) and drawn->losing (12%) confirm these are game-altering blunders. The tactical layer reveals themes of back-rank threats, tempo loss, and missed tactics—players reposition pieces or make pawn moves while a decisive rook check (often exploiting back-rank weakness, exposed kings, or enabling a forcing sequence) goes unplayed. The top boards consistently show positions where a rook delivery check wins material or forces a decisive advantage, but the player instead makes a non-forcing move that squanders the opportunity.

320.label: Pushing the e-pawn forward without adequate support, hanging it to an opposing piece.
320.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: an unsupported e-pawn advance (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) that hangs material (92% hangs, median -1.0 material loss). The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, and the tactical analysis consistently identifies 'premature_advance' and 'development_neglected' as recurring tags, with the e5 push being the dominant concrete move across the top activating boards. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically convert a drawn position into a losing one (67% drawn->losing, median 240cp lost), indicating the advance is not a speculative gambit but rather a positional blunder where the player lacks piece coordination to sustain the advanced pawn. The opponent's best response often involves a simple knight or pawn capture of the undefended advanced pawn, explaining why Maia's recommended moves are frequently knight moves (42%) that exploit the hanging pawn.

317.label: Player makes a quiet developing bishop move in the opening, missing a free capture of an undefended enemy knight.
317.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions where the player moves a bishop (100%) without capturing anything, while the best move (Maia's recommendation) is capturing an undefended knight. The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet 100% of activations involve missed winning material, with a median eval loss of 447 centipawns — converting a winning position into a drawn one. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (62%), indicating an enemy piece is en prise but the player fails to notice it. The common tags emphasize piece_activity, development, and autopilot_error, painting a picture of a player who reflexively continues their development plan (fianchettoing a bishop, developing to e2, etc.) without scanning for the opponent's tactical vulnerability. The top boards confirm this: positions like Bg2 ignoring the hanging knight on e5, or Nf3 ignoring a hanging knight on d4. This is fundamentally a one-move tactical oversight where routine development autopilot overrides board awareness.

318.label: Player makes a non-forcing move that misses a decisive mating attack or tactical sequence involving king safety.
318.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player (mostly moving queens or pawns) plays a 'safe' or speculative move while missing a powerful tactic—almost always involving a rook delivering check or exploiting king exposure. The material signature shows 100% missed winning material, with Maia consistently recommending rook moves (often with check, 71%) that would have won decisively. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 282cp lost), with 43% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The tactical motifs center on king_safety (50%) and mating attacks: positions feature back-rank threats, queen infiltration paths, decoy sacrifices, and mating nets that the player overlooks in favor of moves that either lose tempo, weaken their own king, or grab irrelevant material. The boards consistently show tactically rich positions where coordinated piece attacks on exposed kings are available but ignored.

321.label: Failing to recapture or capture a hanging bishop in the opening, turning a drawn or better position into a losing one.
321.description: This feature fires when players in the opening phase make a minor piece or pawn move that ignores a hanging bishop on the board. The material signature shows the player moves a knight or bishop (often developing or capturing a pawn) while Maia's recommended move is to capture a bishop with a pawn — indicating a free piece was available. The boards consistently show positions where a bishop has landed on an aggressive square (often c6 or c3 after an exchange) and is left hanging, but the player either develops another piece, grabs a less valuable pawn, or makes a positional move like ...d6 instead of simply taking the free material. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: every instance converts a drawn position into a losing one with a median loss of 442 centipawns (roughly a full piece). The tactical analysis tags — hanging_piece, failed_recapture, material_oversight — all converge on the same pattern: the player overlooks that an opponent's bishop is undefended and can be captured immediately, often because it just completed a capture and the recapture seems non-obvious or the player is distracted by development or counterplay ideas.

319.label: Minor piece or pawn moves in the opening/middlegame that lose tempo and expose king safety weaknesses, costing roughly a full piece worth of evaluation.
319.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make seemingly natural developing moves (knights 33%, pawns 29%, bishops 19%) that are non-capturing (93% no capture) and appear safe (74% 'safe' material outcome), yet cause catastrophic evaluation swings (median 256 centipawns lost). The trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions to losing (31%) or winning positions to drawn (21%), indicating the player is throwing away a previously tenable or advantageous position. The tactical analysis reveals the core mechanism: these moves neglect king safety (29%), leave pieces hanging (29%), or lose critical tempo (29%), often allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting weakness with forcing sequences like checks or attacks on exposed kings. The top boards consistently show early/middlegame positions where a knight or piece move to an apparently active square actually removes a key defender or allows a tactical refutation—the player develops or repositions a piece without recognizing that the move creates a concrete vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit. Maia's preferred moves (98% pawn moves) suggest the correct approach was typically a quiet pawn move maintaining the position's integrity rather than the ambitious piece maneuver that backfired.

323.label: Player makes a quiet move while their bishop has a free rook capture available on the long diagonal.
323.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a free rook capture along an open long diagonal. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (no material changes) while Maia consistently recommends a bishop capturing a rook — a completely free piece worth substantial material. The eval trajectory confirms this is a winning position squandered into a draw (median 380cp loss), consistent with missing a clean tactical shot rather than a complex positional misjudgment. The tactical tags reinforce this: hanging_piece appears in 100% of cases, with 'long_diagonal', 'hanging_rook', 'undefended_rook', and 'missed_capture' as recurring themes. The concrete positions show fianchetto or early bishop development scenarios where the opponent's rook is left undefended on h8, a8, or h1 after a premature pawn move (like ...g6 or ...b6) opens the diagonal without proper protection. Instead of seizing the free material, the player makes a quiet developing or prophylactic move, wasting the critical tempo needed to exploit the tactical opportunity.

325.label: Promoting a pawn when the opponent's king can immediately capture the new queen.
325.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame blunder where a player promotes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% checks in some cases) but the newly created queen is immediately captured because the opponent's king is adjacent to the promotion square. The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (median -9.0, consistent with losing a queen worth 9 points). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: positions swing from winning to drawn or losing to drawn, with a median loss of 619 centipawns — reflecting that the player squanders a decisive passed pawn advantage. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'promotion_error' (60%) with tags like 'premature_promotion' and 'tempo_loss,' where the recurring theme is failing to first reposition the king to defend the promotion square or to drive the opponent's king away before queening. The correct technique in these positions is typically a preparatory king move to support the new queen, rather than rushing the promotion into the jaws of the opposing king.

322.label: Rook moves that fatally abandon back-rank defense in already-losing middlegame positions.
322.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player in an already-losing position moves their rook (100% rook moves, 100% middlegame) in a way that catastrophically worsens their situation, primarily by abandoning back-rank defense. The material signature shows these are non-capturing rook moves (no captures 100%) that are mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense (67%) but devastate the position strategically. The eval trajectory confirms these occur in losing->losing contexts with an enormous median eval loss of ~93 pawns, indicating moves that convert a difficult defense into immediate catastrophe (forced mates). The dominant motif is back_rank (50%), supported by tags like king_safety, exposed_king, and back_rank_mate. The concrete positions show rooks moving away from the 8th rank (Rff6, Rg6, Rb8) leaving kings fatally exposed, while Maia's recommended moves capture material or deliver checks exploiting the newly undefended rank. This is a positional collapse—the player's rook retreats or repositions without recognizing that it was the last piece preventing immediate tactical exploitation of the back rank.

324.label: Advancing or exchanging a pawn in a king-and-pawn endgame that fatally compromises the player's pawn structure or abandons a critical asset.
324.description: This feature fires on pawn moves in pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase, 62% pawn_endgame motif) where the player pushes or captures with a pawn in a way that destroys their own position. The material signature shows 75% of moves hang material (a pawn advance that drops a pawn or allows the opponent's king to penetrate) with a median net loss of -1.0. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 566cp lost), with moves converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (50% already losing but made worse, 25% drawn→losing, 25% winning→losing). The tactical analysis reveals a consistent pattern: players break their own pawn chains (self_destructive_break), sacrifice passed pawns for meaningless checks, advance pawns that create weaknesses rather than progress, or neglect king activity in favor of premature pawn pushes. The recurring tags—passed_pawn, tempo_loss, pawn_structure, king_activity—paint a picture of players who misunderstand the critical principles of pawn endgames: maintaining pawn integrity, preserving passed pawns, and prioritizing king centralization over impulsive pawn advances.

326.label: In won endgames, player makes a non-capturing move that leaves a piece or critical pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it for free.
326.description: This feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (100%) where the player has a winning evaluation but makes a move that leaves material hanging (hanging_piece motif in 100% of cases). The material signature shows the player's move is mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense (80%), meaning the moved piece itself isn't lost, but the move neglects to defend or capture an existing hanging piece—Maia's recommended moves capture material (rook 80%, bishop 10%, queen 10%) that the player simply missed. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% winning->drawn and 50% winning->losing, with a median loss of 892 centipawns, indicating complete game-outcome reversals. The boards show sparse endgame positions (rook endgames, minor piece endgames) where the player makes a quiet king, knight, or pawn move while an elementary capture or defense was available. Tags like missed_capture, tempo_loss, and piece_activity confirm the player lost focus on material safety in simplified positions, throwing away won games by overlooking undefended pieces.

328.label: Moving the queen to a passive or vulnerable square, overlooking opponent's tactical threats involving king safety or forks.
328.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (53%) to a square that appears safe but critically overlooks a tactical opportunity for the opponent. The material signature shows 42% of moves hang a piece and 47% are superficially safe, yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 284 centipawns, with 53% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The tactical motifs (king_safety 43%, hanging_piece 29%, fork 14%) combined with tags like missed_tactic and tempo_loss indicate that the queen move neglects defensive duties or walks into tactical patterns—knight forks winning the queen, pins exploiting the king's position, or leaving pieces undefended. Maia's recommended moves (queen 58%, rook 21%) suggest the correct continuation typically involved an active queen deployment or rook move that addressed the tactical threat. The concrete examples confirm this: queens retreating to passive squares (Qb5, Qb6), kings stepping into fork patterns, and pawn moves that ignore hanging pieces, all in positions where a tactically alert move would have maintained the balance.

330.label: Player makes a quiet developing or retreating move while an undefended enemy pawn or piece is available for capture.
330.description: This feature fires when a player plays a safe, non-capturing move (99% no capture, 96% materially 'safe' in isolation) — typically a pawn push, knight retreat, or bishop development — while Maia's recommended move overwhelmingly involves capturing a pawn (94% pawn capture). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 222 centipawns, often swinging from winning to drawn or drawn to losing (24% and 16% respectively). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (50%) with frequent tags like 'missed_tactic', 'missed_capture', and 'development_over_tactics_error'. The concrete positions show patterns like playing Be7 or Bd7 passively when Nxe4 or Qxd5 wins an undefended central pawn, or retreating a piece when a simple capture was available. The player prioritizes quiet positional development or prophylaxis over an immediately available free capture, a classic pattern of under-valuing concrete tactics in the opening and middlegame.

327.label: Player makes a passive developing move instead of exploiting an undefended bishop with Nxe5, throwing away a winning advantage.
327.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where the player has an available Nxe5 tactic that exploits a hanging bishop (usually on g4) but instead plays a passive bishop or pawn move (71% bishop moves, 29% pawn moves). The top activating positions almost all share the same structure: Black has played ...Bg4 pinning a knight on f3, and a knight on e5 is available to capture or a knight can move to e5, leaving the Bg4 undefended and capturable by the queen. The material signature shows 'safe' moves (71%) meaning the player's move doesn't immediately lose material, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic cost—86% go from winning to drawn and 14% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 437 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (83%) with tags like missed_tactic and tempo_loss. The player consistently chooses Be2 or similar passive development instead of the devastating Nxe5! combination that wins material through the now-undefended bishop. This is a pure tactical miss in the opening phase (100% opening positions) where the player fails to recognize that the pin on f3 can be broken tactically rather than passively tolerated.

329.label: Rook moves that grab material but overlook tactical consequences, leaving pieces hanging or the position collapsing.
329.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make aggressive rook moves (81% rook moves) to capture minor pieces (33% knight, 24% bishop captures), but the move results in a net material loss (median -2.0, with 52% slightly_down, 19% hangs, 14% loses). The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic—median 304 centipawns lost—often converting winning or drawable positions into losing ones (winning->losing 19%, drawn->losing 10%). The tactical analysis reveals the core problem: players 'cash in' prematurely with their rooks, grabbing tempting material while leaving other pieces hanging (hanging_piece 50%) or exposing king safety weaknesses (king_safety 50%). The top boards confirm this: rooks plunge into enemy territory (Rxd7, Rxf7, Rxb7, Rxc3) capturing pieces but creating tactical vulnerabilities—undefended pieces left behind, back-rank issues, or allowing the opponent's pieces to activate decisively. Maia's preferred moves (often quiet pawn/queen moves, 86% non-captures) suggest the correct approach was maintaining piece coordination rather than grabbing material.

331.label: Failing to resolve critical central pawn tension allows opponent's pawn fork or tempo-gaining advance that wins material.
331.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a developing or quiet move (bishop, pawn, knight, or king move—none capturing) while ignoring unresolved central pawn tension (e4/d4 vs d5/e5 structures dominate the boards). The material outcome of the played move itself is 'safe'—nothing is immediately hung—but the position collapses from drawn to losing (median 285cp loss) because the opponent punishes the timing error with a pawn advance (Maia always plays a pawn capturing a pawn, i.e., the e5 or e4 break). The recurring tactical motif is a pawn fork (appearing in 3/7 analyses) that displaces or wins a piece, combined with tempo loss and positional errors. The boards consistently show classical d4/e4 vs d5/e5 central structures in the opening or early middlegame where one side needed to capture or challenge the center immediately but instead played a slow developing move (Bb7, O-O, Bd7, c5, Cb2), allowing the opponent to seize the center with a tempo-gaining pawn thrust that forks pieces or creates overwhelming central dominance.

332.label: Knight trades away a strong/active knight for inferior material, squandering a winning or drawn position.
332.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player uses a knight (84% of moves) to capture a pawn or minor piece, resulting in a slight material loss or even exchange (median net -2.0, with 52% 'slightly_down' and 39% 'trade' outcomes). The eval trajectory shows these moves are costly—median 320cp lost, with many transitions from winning→drawn or drawn→losing—indicating that the knight being traded away was far more valuable positionally than the material gained. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motifs are king_safety threats and forks that were abandoned, with recurring tags like 'piece_for_pawn', 'missed_fork', 'knight_superiority', and 'wrong_capture'. The top boards show knights on powerful outpost squares (e6, f6, d6) being exchanged for pawns or passive bishops, throwing away attacking potential or fork threats. Maia's preferred moves (61% non-captures, 23% checks) suggest the correct continuation was to maintain the knight's dominance rather than cash it in prematurely. This is fundamentally a trade error where the player undervalues their knight's positional superiority.

334.label: Failing to capture undefended pieces in endgames by playing aimless or impulsive moves instead.
334.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player has a winning advantage but throws it away (75% winning->losing, 25% winning->drawn, median eval loss 638cp) by missing simple captures of hanging or undefended pieces. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), with recurring tags of missed_capture and tempo_loss. The player's moves are typically rook or knight moves that accomplish little (75% no capture), while Maia's recommended moves frequently capture undefended bishops or rooks (50% capture bishop, 25% capture rook). The tactical analyses consistently describe scenarios where an opponent's piece is completely undefended, but the player either plays a pointless check, makes a tempo-losing move, or advances a pawn instead of simply taking free material. This is a pattern of tunnel vision in endgames—players fixate on their own plans (checks, pawn pushes, rook lifts) while ignoring that the opponent has left a piece en prise.

335.label: Trading rooks when an opponent's advanced passed pawn promotes decisively after the exchange.
335.description: This feature fires when a player initiates a rook trade (rook moved 100%, captured rook 92%) that is materially equal (net 0.0, classified as a trade) but catastrophically overlooks an opponent's advanced passed pawn that promotes immediately after the exchange. The top boards consistently show positions with pawns on the 2nd rank (c2, d2, h2, a2) ready to promote, and the Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of promotion_error (50%) and back_rank (40%), with passed_pawn as the most common tag. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 167 centipawns, with many positions swinging from losing-to-winning (33%) or drawn-to-losing (17%), indicating that the rook recapture enables an unstoppable promotion or mating sequence. Maia's recommended responses (king 50%, rook 42%) suggest the correct move was often a defensive king move or rook repositioning rather than the reflexive recapture. The player sees an equal trade but misses that the resulting position is decided by the queening pawn, often combined with back-rank mating threats.

333.label: Middlegame moves that ignore king safety, losing tempo and allowing devastating attacks.
333.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeless or slow move (typically a knight or pawn move that doesn't capture or give check) while neglecting critical king safety concerns. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (67%) that don't immediately hang material, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 356cp lost), with positions swinging from drawn or winning to losing. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and the recurring tags emphasize tempo_loss (4 occurrences), king_safety (3), and missed_tactic (3). Examining the top boards confirms this: many positions feature exposed kings (e.g., Black's king on g7 with an open h-file, or White's king on g1/h1 facing a pawn storm) where the player plays a slow positional move instead of addressing the urgent tactical threats. The opponent (Maia's moves capturing bishops 67%) typically exploits the tempo loss to land decisive blows against the weakened king position. These are not material blunders per se but positional oversights where the player fails to recognize the urgency of king safety, allowing the opponent to convert attacking chances.

337.label: Developing or repositioning a piece while leaving another piece hanging to an existing pawn threat.
337.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase blunder where a player moves a knight (50%) or minor piece into position while ignoring an immediate tactical threat—typically an advanced pawn that attacks one of their pieces. The material signature is stark: 71% of moves hang a piece outright (median loss of ~241 centipawns), and the dominant motif is hanging_piece (44%) combined with tempo_loss (22%). The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: players develop or reposition pieces (e.g., Nf6, Bd7, Be7) while an enemy pawn on the 5th or 6th rank directly attacks one of their existing pieces. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing that threatening pawn (93% pawn captures), confirming the missed response was simply taking the dangerous pawn. The eval trajectory shows these are typically game-defining mistakes—64% turn drawn positions into losing ones—occurring predominantly in the opening (79%) when players prioritize development routine over addressing concrete pawn threats on the board.

336.label: Playing a knight check that loses material by removing an active piece from a strong position.
336.description: This feature captures knight moves that deliver check but are objectively terrible, typically losing significant material (median -6.0 pawns, with 60% hanging the piece and 40% losing material outright). The pattern is consistent across all three signals: (1) the material signature shows 100% knight moves giving check with devastating material consequences, while Maia's recommended moves rarely involve checks (0%), suggesting these checks are impulsive rather than sound; (2) the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 497 centipawns, often worsening already difficult positions (60% losing→losing) or throwing away advantages (20% winning→losing); (3) the tactical analysis reveals the recurring theme of 'false check'—a check that appears aggressive but actually removes the player's best-placed knight from a dominant square, surrendering piece activity, tempo, and positional compensation for nothing. The tagged motifs (tempo_loss, hanging_piece, premature_attack) and example summaries consistently describe players lured by the allure of giving check while sacrificing their most active piece without adequate compensation, often in the opening phase (80%) where piece activity is paramount.

338.label: In the opening, player makes a non-capturing move that leaves a piece completely undefended and capturable.
338.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player makes a seemingly natural developing move (castling, a knight hop, a pawn push, or a queen reposition) that neglects a critical tactical vulnerability: an undefended piece left en prise. The material signature shows 81% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -3.0 (approximately a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings—94% going from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 400 centipawns. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), with tags like undefended_piece, piece_loss, and missed_tactic reinforcing that the player simply overlooked that a piece (usually a knight) had no defender. Maia's suggested moves consistently involve capturing the hanging knight, confirming the missed tactic was straightforward. The concrete examples show patterns like castling while a knight on d5 is unprotected, moving a queen away from defending a knight, or developing a piece while ignoring that a previously-placed piece has become tactically loose due to the opponent's last move.

339.label: Moving the queen into a tactically vulnerable position, missing forks or hanging pieces that lose significant material.
339.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a queen move (46% of cases) that catastrophically misses a tactical threat, typically involving hanging pieces (67% motif) or forks (33% motif). The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 484 centipawns), with 45% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->losing 27%, drawn->losing 18%). The material signature shows that while 46% of moves appear 'safe' on the surface, 55% of the time the player misses winning material that was available. Maia (representing the correct move) would often capture a queen (36%) or make a queen move (55%), suggesting the player's queen move either fails to capture when it should or places the queen where it can be won by fork/attack. The example positions confirm this: queens placed on squares vulnerable to knight forks (Nf4+), queens captured for insufficient compensation (Qxe6+ allowing dxe6 recapture), and queen moves that ignore hanging pieces elsewhere. The common thread is a queen move that looks active but overlooks a concrete tactical refutation.

340.label: Player makes a developing or routine move while leaving a piece undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it for free.
340.description: This feature detects positions where a player makes a natural-looking developing or positional move (typically a bishop or rook move) while neglecting that one of their own pieces is hanging or has become unprotected as a consequence of the move. The material signature shows 41% of moves result in a hang (non-capture that drops a piece), with a median material loss of -1.0 (a full piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (26% drawn->losing, 8% winning->losing, median 344cp lost). The Opus tactical analysis consistently identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (40%), with pins and forks as secondary mechanisms that explain WHY the piece is hanging—the player either blocks a defensive line (e.g., Bd3 blocking the queen's defense of Nd4), ignores a pin that prevents recapture, or plays a developing move without noticing an undefended piece can be taken immediately. The missed captures by Maia (knight 31%, bishop 8%) confirm the opponent's best reply was simply taking the free piece. The positions cluster in the opening/middlegame (98%) where development tempo can mask tactical oversights.

341.label: Player makes an equal-material trade that dissipates a winning position by relieving tactical tension or ignoring a critical threat.
341.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a materially equal exchange (100% trades, median net material 0.0) that catastrophically collapses their evaluation—median loss of 379 centipawns, with 67% of cases going from winning to drawn. The trades involve bishops and rooks capturing roughly equal pieces, but the tactical analysis reveals the player is overlooking immediate threats (checkmate-in-one, forks, king safety issues) or committing move-order errors while simplifying. The dominant motifs of tempo_loss (40%) and missed_tactic tags indicate these are exchanges that release pressure—the player trades off an active piece or captures a less important target while a devastating tactic (often involving king safety or a mating pattern) goes unnoticed. Maia's recommendations frequently involve non-captures (50%), suggesting the engine saw quiet moves maintaining tension as superior. The pattern is a player in a winning position who reflexively captures an available piece of equal value, failing to recognize that the exchange itself destroys the attacking potential or ignores an immediate tactical refutation.

343.label: Trading major pieces (especially rooks) when winning, throwing away a decisive advantage into equality or worse.
343.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player with a winning position initiates a major piece trade (rook 50%, queen 30%) that catastrophically simplifies the position, squandering their advantage. The material signature shows 70% trades (exchanges of roughly equal material, median net 0.0) combined with checks (60%), suggesting the player is attracted to forcing-looking moves that appear active but actually relieve pressure. The eval trajectory is devastating: 60% winning->drawn and 20% winning->losing, with a median loss of 412 centipawns—consistent with throwing away a full winning advantage. The Opus analysis confirms this with dominant tags of 'premature_simplification', 'positional_mistake', and 'piece_activity', where the better move typically maintained tension or exploited the opponent's weaknesses (dead pieces, exposed kings, back-rank issues). The player repeatedly chooses a concrete-looking trade or check over maintaining a strategically crushing position, simplifying into positions where their advantage evaporates. Examples include trading queens when the opponent's pieces are trapped, or exchanging rooks when the endgame no longer offers winning chances despite the middlegame being dominant.

346.label: King moves passively in the endgame instead of capturing a freely available major piece.
346.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) but fails to capture a hanging or available major piece (Maia's suggested moves capture queens 50% and rooks 50%). The material signature shows 'hangs' 50% of the time, meaning the king move itself sometimes leaves material en prise, while the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing from winning to losing (median 1045cp lost) in 100% of cases. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), and the most common tags are 'missed_capture' and 'hanging_piece.' The concrete examples consistently show a king fleeing or making a quiet move when it could simply take an undefended queen, rook, or checking piece—e.g., moving the king away from an undefended queen on d4, or fleeing a check instead of capturing the checking rook. All positions are endgames where the board is simplified enough that the capture should be obvious, yet the player reflexively moves the king rather than taking freely available material.

344.label: Moving the knight away from defending the bishop on c4, allowing it to be captured for free.
344.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early middlegame pattern where White has a knight on e4 and a bishop on c4 (often in Italian Game or similar structures), and the player moves the knight to a square that leaves the bishop undefended and capturable. The material signature shows 100% knight moves that result in 'hangs' (80%) — meaning a non-capture that drops a piece — with a median material loss of 3.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings: 80% drawn->losing and 20% winning->losing, with a median loss of 269 centipawns. The top boards overwhelmingly show the same FEN position (Bc4/Ne4/Nf3 structure) where the only good move is Bd3 (retreating the bishop to safety), but instead the player moves the knight (to g5, c3, e5, f6, or other squares), leaving the c4 bishop hanging to ...d5xc4 or similar captures. The dominant motifs — hanging_piece, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic — all confirm the player overlooks that the knight was the bishop's sole defender. This is a classic 'removing the guard' self-inflicted blunder in the opening phase.

345.label: Developing or passive move in the opening that ignores an available tactical capture (usually Qxg4/Qxg5), leaving a piece hanging.
345.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player makes a natural-looking developing or pawn move (bishop deployment, f-pawn advance, castling, or rook shuffle) while missing a strong queen capture of a knight. The material signature shows the player's move hangs a piece or is merely safe (no capture made), while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capturing a knight—confirming the missed tactic. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (62%) and fork (25%), with tags emphasizing missed_tactic, development, and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of ~199 centipawns, often converting a winning or balanced position into a drawn or worse one (winning->drawn 50%, drawn->drawn 50%). The recurring concrete pattern involves Italian/Fried Liver-style positions where a knight lands aggressively on g4 or g5 and can be captured by the queen, but the player instead continues with routine development (Be6, Be3, f3, castling), overlooking the free material. The mistake is fundamentally tactical—ignoring an available capture of a hanging or inadequately defended piece—rather than a positional misjudgment or trade error.

342.label: Playing a passive queen or rook move that ignores an urgent tactical threat, hanging material or missing a forced win.
342.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a queen (59%) or rook (41%) to a square that appears natural but fatally ignores an immediate tactical obligation. The material signature shows these moves overwhelmingly hang a piece (53%) rather than being exchanges, with a median cost of -1.0 material and 194 centipawns of eval lost. The motif analysis reveals the underlying theme: king safety (44%), back-rank vulnerabilities (22%), and tempo loss (22%) dominate—the player's move is too slow given the tactical urgency of the position. Maia's recommended moves (often rooks or queens to different squares, frequently with check at 29%) show that the correct response involved addressing an immediate threat or delivering a decisive blow. The per-position summaries confirm this pattern: players choose 'natural but fatally slow' moves (e.g., Rah8 missing mate in 2, Rdd1 ignoring a critical capture, Qf2 instead of Qd3 abandoning a vital diagonal). The eval trajectory is scattered (losing->losing 29%, losing->winning 18%, winning->winning 18%, winning->losing 12%), indicating this mistake occurs across all evaluation contexts—what unifies them is that a concrete, urgent tactic was available but the player chose a developing or repositioning move that lost critical tempo against active threats.

348.label: Player makes a reasonable move but misses a stronger continuation involving an immediate check or forcing sequence.
348.description: This feature identifies positions where the player's move is often objectively safe (64% safe, median 0cp loss) but misses a much stronger forcing continuation. The key signal is that Maia's recommended move gives check 100% of the time, predominantly with the queen (69%), while the player's actual move almost never gives check (5%). The players typically move rooks, pawns, or queens in non-forcing ways. The tactical analysis confirms this: positions involve king safety themes, tempo loss, and missed forced mates being extended or converted into mere advantages. The eval trajectory shows many positions remain winning->winning (43%), consistent with the player maintaining an advantage but failing to deliver the knockout blow via a checking sequence. The motif tags (tempo_loss, king_safety, forced_mate, exposed_king) all point to situations where the opponent's king is vulnerable and an immediate check would exploit this decisively, but the player chose a slower continuation instead.

347.label: Moving a major piece (usually rook) to an undefended square where it becomes tactically vulnerable to enemy pieces.
347.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move a major piece—most often a rook (50%) or queen (18%)—to a square where it becomes tactically exploitable. The material signature shows 50% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece), with a median eval loss of 418 centipawns, indicating severe tactical oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The trajectory (27% drawn->losing, 14% winning->losing) shows these moves frequently convert playable or even advantageous positions into lost ones. The tactical motifs confirm the mechanism: hanging_piece (33%), overloaded_defender (22%), and fork (11%), with recurring tags like 'undefended_rook' and 'undefended_piece'. The concrete positions illustrate this clearly—Re1-d1 placing a rook in a knight fork's crosshairs, Qf5-f2 leaving a queen hanging, Rf8-b8 dropping the rook to a tactical shot, and Qf3-f2 overloading defensive duties. Players typically make passive or repositioning moves without noticing their piece lands on an unprotected square that the opponent can immediately exploit through discovered attacks, forks, or simple captures.

349.label: Failing to capture a hanging bishop in the opening, squandering a winning advantage into equality.
349.description: This feature fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player has a winning advantage (median ~500cp) but plays a developing or repositioning move (knight 50%, bishop 33%, queen 17%) instead of capturing an available bishop (Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a bishop). The material outcome of the played move is 'safe'—nothing is immediately lost—but the player misses winning material 100% of the time, and the evaluation collapses from winning to drawn (median 502cp lost). The top boards reveal a consistent pattern: Slav/Semi-Slav and similar d-pawn structures where bishops land on d6/d3 and become tactically vulnerable, yet the player continues normal development (Nf3, Nd2, Bg3, O-O, etc.) rather than executing the critical capture (Bxd6 or Bxd3). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (50%), with tempo_loss and positional_mistake also prominent, reflecting that the missed capture often also gains a tempo. The tactical theme is narrow: exactly one move maintains the advantage, and any alternative—however natural—throws away the win.

351.label: Developing a knight to a natural square that hangs material, squandering a winning position into equality.
351.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern where players develop knights (100% knight moves) in the opening phase (100% opening) to seemingly natural squares, but the move actually hangs material (100% hangs, median -1.0 net material). The trajectory is consistently winning->drawn (100%, median 253cp lost), meaning these are positions where the player had a clear advantage but threw it away with a careless developing move. The top boards confirm this: positions like Nf3 in King's Gambit or Italian Game structures where the knight development looks routine but overlooks a tactical shot — often an en prise pawn capture (Maia's response is 100% pawn captures pawn). The dominant motifs of tempo_loss and missed_tactic reinforce that these are automatic developing moves that ignore concrete threats, particularly failing to capture on e5 (fxe5 appears repeatedly as the missed best move). The player prioritizes piece development over material awareness, losing a pawn and their winning edge.

350.label: Failing to convert a winning or drawn endgame by missing the critical move, often allowing the opponent's piece activity or promotion chances.
350.description: This feature captures catastrophic endgame mistakes where a player, holding a winning or clearly favorable position, plays a king or rook move that throws away the game. The material signature shows no captures (100% non-capture moves) that frequently hang material (50%), while Maia consistently recommends rook captures—indicating missed winning recaptures or simplifications. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 896 centipawns, swinging from winning to losing (50%) or winning to drawn (50%). The tactical analysis reveals hanging pieces (60%), promotion errors (30%), and tempo losses (10%) as dominant motifs, all occurring in pure endgames. The top boards confirm this: rook endgames (K+R vs K+R), queen vs knight positions, and rook vs pawn promotion races where exactly one correct move existed. Players either fail to stop a passed pawn's promotion, misplace their king allowing counterplay, or give a pointless check from the wrong square that grants the opponent's king a critical escape route. The common thread is that these are technically demanding endgame positions where one imprecise move—often looking reasonable—completely reverses the evaluation.

353.label: Player makes a quiet move missing a checkmate or crushing queen attack on a diagonal.
353.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe-looking pawn, bishop, or knight move while missing a devastating queen attack—most often a checkmate in one or two moves. The material signature shows the player's move is materially 'safe' (73%) with no checks, while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen move (87%), frequently delivering check (53%) and often capturing a pawn (47%). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic missed wins: 93% of positions involve missed winning material, with a staggering median eval loss of ~9940 centipawns, indicating missed forced mates. The tactical analysis tags reinforce this: missed_mate_in_one (3), queen_diagonal (3), king_safety (5), and catastrophic_blunder (3) dominate. The concrete positions show recurring patterns of queens with open diagonals toward weakened kings (especially the c7-h2 or analogous diagonals), where the player chose routine positional or recapture moves instead of delivering mate. The phase is predominantly middlegame (80%) where king safety tactics are most acute.

354.label: Player makes a move that allows immediate or near-immediate checkmate by ignoring a lethal king safety threat.
354.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move—typically a king move, rook move, or queen move (83% hang material)—that walks directly into a forced checkmate or ignores an immediate mating threat. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median ~100 pawns lost, with 42% going winning->losing and 33% drawn->losing), confirming these are game-ending blunders rather than gradual positional errors. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies king_safety (86%) as the dominant motif, with recurring tags of checkmate_in_one (4 instances), ignored_threat (3), and king_walk_blunder. The concrete positions show kings stepping onto fatally exposed squares (e.g., Kg8-h7 into Rxh5#), players ignoring back-rank or h-file mating patterns, and moves that completely overlook queen-bishop batteries or discovered attacks targeting the king. The player's move is almost never a capture (92% non-capture), meaning they play a quiet or developing move while a lethal mating attack is already in progress, failing to recognize the immediate tactical emergency.

352.label: Advancing a pawn or king in a king-and-pawn endgame that throws away the win by losing the opposition or critical tempo.
352.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring pawn endgame mistake where a player with a winning position (typically a single pawn advantage or a decisive king position) makes a pawn push or king move that immediately converts the win into a draw, losing roughly 534+ centipawns. The material signature shows all moves are 'safe' (no piece is literally hanging or traded), yet the eval trajectory shows 56% go from winning to drawn, with the remainder staying winning but losing significant advantage. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is pure pawn_endgame with tags emphasizing tempo_loss, opposition, and king_activity — the classic endgame concepts that determine whether such positions are won or drawn. The concrete positions all feature king-and-pawn(s) vs king-and-pawn(s) endings where the player pushes a pawn prematurely (e.g., b5, f5, g4, g6, c5, b4) or misplaces the king (Kf3, Kf4, Kh6), surrendering the opposition or allowing the opponent's king to reach a drawing square. Maia's recommended moves are always king moves, indicating that maintaining or seizing the opposition with the king was the critical resource.

355.label: Delivering a check that leaves the checking piece undefended and immediately capturable, throwing away material in the endgame.
355.description: This feature captures a specific and costly endgame blunder pattern: the player delivers a check (100% of activating moves are checks) with a rook or bishop, but the checking piece is left hanging with no support (material outcome: 'hangs' 100%, median net material loss of -3.0, i.e., roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic collapses (median 9220 centipawns lost), often converting a winning position into a losing one. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), reinforced by tags like 'pointless_check', 'undefended_piece', and 'piece_activity'. The concrete positions confirm this: a rook moves to an undefended square giving check but is immediately captured (e.g., Rf4 taken by Rf7, Rxd8+ recaptured by the queen), or a bishop delivers a check on a square where it has no escape. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check without verifying that the piece survives after the opponent's obligatory response. This is a tactical oversight specific to pointless checks in endgame positions where piece safety should be paramount.

356.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that ignores an immediate tactical threat, leaving a piece hanging for free capture.
356.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, often cosmetically purposeful move (king repositioning, pawn advance, rook lift) that completely ignores an existing tactical obligation, resulting in a piece being left en prise. The material signature is stark: 75% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median material loss of -3.0 (roughly a full piece), and 100% involve no capture by the player. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (62%) combined with 'tempo_loss' tags — the player wastes a critical tempo on a secondary plan while a piece sits undefended. The eval trajectory shows this mostly occurs in already-losing or drawn positions (losing->losing 42%, drawn->losing 25%), suggesting players under pressure lose focus on immediate threats and play 'hope chess' moves. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing the hanging piece (bishop 50%, queen 42%), confirming the opponent had a free take available. The concrete positions show patterns like rook placed on undefended squares accessible to enemy queens, bishops left unprotected while playing flank pawns, and king moves that ignore queen tension — all cases where a simple threat was overlooked in favor of an irrelevant improving move.

361.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player retreats their king to a passive square instead of maintaining or advancing king activity, losing tempo in a critical race.
361.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames (80% endgame phase) where the player is already in a losing position and makes it slightly worse (losing→losing, median 46cp lost). The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures or checks—these are pure positional king maneuvers. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (56%), with king_activity and pawn_endgame as recurring tags. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: positions like Kd2 instead of Kd4, Ke2 instead of staying centralized, Kc1 instead of maintaining opposition—all cases where the king retreats or sidesteps to a passive square rather than contesting key squares, losing critical tempo in pawn races involving passed pawns. The player consistently chooses a 'safe-looking' but passive king move that surrenders opposition or allows the opponent's king to infiltrate, rather than the one active move that maintains maximum resistance.

360.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move, missing a devastating check sequence (often a fork or skewer) that would have won material or maintained a decisive advantage.
360.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player had a winning or clearly better position but played a slow, non-forcing move instead of exploiting a tactical check sequence. The material signature shows the player's move is mostly 'safe' (77%) with no checks played (0%), while Maia's recommended move delivers check 58% of the time—highlighting that the missed best move was almost always a forcing check. The dominant motifs (fork 33%, skewer 11%, discovered_attack) confirm the check would have won material via a tactical combination. The eval trajectory shows severe consequences: winning->drawn (38%) or winning->losing (8%) with a median loss of 304 centipawns, indicating these are game-changing missed opportunities. The concrete positions reinforce this: Bb3+ skewers winning the exchange, Re3+ deflection tactics, and other check-based combinations were available but the player chose quiet moves like a4, c4, or g3 instead. The 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss' tags confirm that by playing non-forcing moves, the player squandered tempo and allowed the opponent to consolidate.

358.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move while a major piece capture (often a hanging queen) goes unseen, throwing away a winning position.
358.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a straightforward winning capture—most often a hanging queen or major piece available along an open file—and instead plays a quiet, non-capturing move (75% no capture, pieces moved are knights/rooks/kings rather than attacking pieces). The material signature shows 50% of moves hang material and 92% miss winning material, while Maia's recommended moves frequently capture queens (42%). The eval trajectory is devastating: 42% of cases flip from winning to losing with a median loss of 663 centipawns, and many others drop from winning to drawn. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 60%, missed_capture, hanging_queen tags) and the Opus summaries confirm the pattern: players fail to see that an opponent's major piece is en prise—often a queen sitting on an open file with no defenders—and instead play a panicked king move, a quiet developing move, or an irrelevant tactical idea. The result is a catastrophic squandering of a won position due to pure tactical blindness rather than a complex positional misjudgment.

363.label: King or pawn moves that waste a critical tempo in pure pawn endgames, allowing the opponent to seize a decisive advantage.
363.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions (90% pawn_endgame motif, 100% endgame phase) where the player makes a king move (67%) or pawn move (33%) that squanders a crucial tempo. The dominant tags—tempo_loss (7), king_activity (6), pawn_structure (6)—reveal that these errors center on retreating the king when a pawn breakthrough was needed, advancing the wrong pawn to create a frozen structure, or abandoning defense of a critical pawn. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences (median 621 centipawns lost), with positions flipping from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-losing, confirming these are narrow-margin endgame positions where exactly one move draws or wins and any tempo waste is fatal. The material signature (safe 67%, no captures) confirms these aren't blunders of hanging pieces but rather subtle positional/tempo errors invisible without deep endgame understanding. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting the engine sees pawn breakthroughs or advances the human missed.

366.label: Knight captures a pawn but leaves the queen hanging or undefended, losing far more material than gained.
366.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a knight to capture a pawn (knight 100%, captures pawn 100%) but the move results in a severe material loss (net median -8.0, consistent with losing a queen). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), and the tactical tags repeatedly reference queen_trapped_or_lost, greed, and intermediate checks that exploit the newly undefended queen. The eval trajectory shows these occur in already-losing positions (losing->losing) where the player compounds their disadvantage by approximately 205 centipawns — a 'making a bad position worse' pattern rather than throwing a winning position. The concrete positions confirm: the knight greedily snatches a pawn (e.g., Nxf2, Nxc3) while the queen is left en prise to an intermediate tactic (discovered attack, check, or simple capture). The player is lured by a small material gain but fails to see that the knight move removes a critical defender or creates a tactical sequence that wins their queen.

359.label: Ignoring an undefended knight on g5 by playing a premature queen move or castling in the opening.
359.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where White has placed a knight aggressively on g5 (typically in Italian/Fried Liver-adjacent structures) but then plays a move—most often Qf3 or O-O—that completely ignores the fact that the g5-knight is hanging. The material signature shows 80% of moves are non-captures that hang a piece (median loss ~3 pawns / a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory consistently shows a drawn position collapsing into a losing one (median 397cp lost). The top 10 boards are nearly identical: White has a bishop on c4, knight on g5, and undeveloped queenside, yet instead of retreating or supporting the knight, White makes a premature developing or attacking move (Qf3 hoping for f7 threats, or O-O ignoring the piece entirely). Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (86%) with recurring tags like 'undefended_knight', 'premature_attack', and 'development'. The intended Maia move (always a pawn move) suggests that even simple responses by Black exploit the hanging piece. This is a classic amateur trap-seeking error: overcommitting to a cheap tactic while leaving material en prise.

357.label: Moving a piece that fatally exposes the king to back-rank or mating threats.
357.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes a move (often with the queen or king) that catastrophically exposes their king to mating threats or devastating tactical sequences. The material signature shows 60% hangs and a median net material loss of -1.0, but the eval trajectory reveals a staggering median loss of 9515 centipawns—indicating these aren't simple piece drops but game-ending blunders that allow forced mates or decisive combinations. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%), back_rank (25%), and tempo_loss (25%), confirming the pattern: the player's move removes a critical defensive piece, misplaces the king, or allows the opponent to deliver checks that gain decisive tempo. Maia's recommended moves give check 50% of the time, indicating the engine sees immediate king attacks that the player missed. The concrete positions show kings walking into mating nets (Kf8 allowing Qxe7+ and Qg7#), kings moving to squares where pawns can be captured with check (Ke6 allowing c6 capture with tempo), and pawn captures that strip critical kingside shelter (fxe3 exposing g2). Despite 40% of cases starting from winning positions, the king exposure turns wins into immediate losses.

365.label: In a losing endgame, the king wanders to a passive or exposed square instead of addressing the critical threat (passed pawns, piece activity, or pawn defense).
365.description: This feature captures king moves in lost endgame positions that worsen an already losing situation by a substantial margin (median 276cp lost). The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures and no checks — purely repositioning decisions. The positions are universally endgames (100%) where the player is already losing, and the key motifs are king_safety (62%) and tempo_loss. The tactical analyses repeatedly describe the king moving away from critical duties: abandoning pawn defense (Kd3 leaving g2 unguarded), walking into exposed squares (Kf4 moving away from passed pawns), or losing tempo in pawn races. Rather than keeping the king active near the critical sector — defending key pawns, blockading passed pawns, or maintaining opposition — the king drifts aimlessly, accelerating the loss. The 'hangs' outcomes (50%) reflect cases where the king's departure leaves material undefended, while 'safe' cases still hemorrhage positional value through lost tempi in critical pawn races.

364.label: Moves that fatally weaken king protection or abandon defensive duties, allowing decisive attacks.
364.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions (90%) where players make moves that compromise their king's safety or abandon critical defensive responsibilities. The material signature shows that 68% of these moves are non-captures, with 35% hanging material—indicating the player makes a move that leaves something undefended rather than actively blundering via a bad capture. The dominant motifs are king_safety (33%), tempo_loss (17%), and trapped_piece (17%), all pointing to moves that ignore the opponent's attacking potential. The eval trajectory is severe (median 288cp lost), with many positions going from drawn to losing (16%) or from already losing to completely lost (22%), suggesting players either misjudge the danger to their king or prioritize other plans while their position collapses tactically. The top boards confirm this: Kg7 walking into a mating net, Qf5 abandoning kingside defense, capturing on h5 removing a key defensive piece. Maia's preferred moves (55% rook moves, 0% checks) suggest the correct responses were typically consolidating or defensive rook moves that maintained king safety, which the players failed to find in favor of seemingly active but positionally catastrophic alternatives.

368.label: Capturing a piece that eliminates a key defensive piece controlling a passed pawn's advance path.
368.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes where the player captures a bishop (100% bishop captures) but in doing so removes a piece that was either critically defending against a passed pawn or abandons a defensive function. The positions are universally endgames (100%) with passed pawns as the dominant motif (80%), and the tactical analyses reveal a consistent pattern: pieces performing irreplaceable defensive roles (like controlling key squares in front of passed pawns) are exchanged away. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 380cp), often transforming drawn positions into lost ones, because the capture - while materially safe or even winning material (median net +3.0) - eliminates the only piece capable of stopping a passed pawn's promotion. The Opus analysis explicitly identifies cases where a knight controlling e6 was removed, or where the 'only move' was ignored in favor of a tempting capture. The combination of 'safe' material outcome with massive eval loss confirms these are not material blunders but strategic errors where winning material is irrelevant compared to the lost defensive function.

370.label: Sacrificing a bishop for a pawn with check on f2/f7, gaining no real compensation and losing material.
370.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: the player captures a pawn on f2 or f7 with a bishop (giving check), but the sacrifice is unsound—trading a bishop (~3 pawns) for merely a pawn plus a tempo from check that leads nowhere meaningful. The material signature confirms bishop captures pawn with check, resulting in a net loss of approximately 2 pawns (slightly_down). The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 365 centipawns, converting winning or drawn positions into drawn or losing ones. The tactical analysis confirms these are 'unsound sacrifices' and 'piece_for_pawn' errors where the check creates an illusion of attack but the opponent simply recaptures or sidesteps, leaving the sacrificing side down a clean piece for a pawn. The top boards overwhelmingly show Italian Game and similar open-game positions where Bxf2+ or Bxf7+ looks aggressive but lacks follow-up, while Maia's preferred moves (knight captures knight) maintain material balance through sound development.

369.label: In completely winning positions, player captures material instead of executing a shorter forced checkmate.
369.description: This feature fires when a player with an overwhelming advantage (typically in the endgame with queen or rook) makes a 'safe' capture or trade rather than delivering a forced mate sequence. The material signature shows queen/rook moves capturing pieces (rook, pawn, bishop) with net material gain, yet Maia's recommendation is always a checking move—revealing that the optimal line involved checks leading to mate. The eval trajectory confirms these are won positions staying won (winning->winning), but the massive median centipawn loss (9262cp, i.e., going from mate-in-few to merely winning or longer mate) indicates missed forced mates. The tactical analysis tags ('missed_mate', 'checks_before_captures', 'missed_tactic') and example summaries explicitly describe players instinctively grabbing material when a shorter checkmate was available—a classic 'checks before captures' violation. The 100% 'missed winning material' rate combined with 100% Maia-gives-check confirms the pattern: the engine sees a mating net via checks, but the player defaults to the greedy capture.

367.label: In endgames, the player moves the king to a square that allows a tactical blow (fork, hanging piece, or lost tempo), squandering a draw or advantage.
367.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) to an unsafe square that enables the opponent to exploit a tactical motif—most commonly a fork, hanging piece, or critical tempo loss. The material outcome of the move itself appears 'safe' (nothing is immediately captured or dropped), but the positional consequence is catastrophic: the median eval loss is 530 centipawns, with trajectories showing drawn positions turning into losses and even losing positions becoming hopeless. The dominant tags (tempo_loss, missed_tactic, king_safety) and motifs (hanging_piece, fork, passed_pawn) reveal that the king lands on a square that either allows a fork winning material, leaves a piece undefended, or fatally loses a tempo in a pawn race. The top boards consistently show king moves like Ke3, Kb2, Kg6, Kb7, Ke1, and Kf7 that walk into concrete tactical problems—forks from knights, loss of coordination defending passed pawns, or blundering a drawn pawn endgame. This is fundamentally an endgame king-placement error where the player fails to calculate the opponent's tactical response to their king's new square.

371.label: Losing tempo or misplaying move order in won pawn endgames, allowing the opponent to neutralize passed pawns or improve king activity.
371.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player has a winning advantage but squanders significant value (median 107cp lost) through tempo loss or move-order errors, while remaining in a winning position. The material signature shows 'hangs' at 100%, meaning the moves are non-captures that leave something undefended, but the real cost is positional/temporal rather than outright piece loss. The dominant motifs—passed_pawn (38%), pawn_endgame (25%), and tempo_loss (12%)—combined with recurring tags like king_activity, move_order, and pawn_structure reveal a pattern of misplaying critical endgame tempi. Concrete examples include playing Kc4 instead of the correct move order (allowing White to capture a pawn), pushing a5 instead of maintaining a connected pawn advantage, and advancing b5 which dissolves a winning pawn structure. The trajectory (winning->winning with ~107cp lost) confirms these are not game-losing blunders but costly inaccuracies that significantly complicate the conversion of won endgames.

372.label: King moves away from critical pawn tensions in endgames, allowing opponent to create unstoppable passed pawns.
372.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames that ignore critical pawn captures or tensions, resulting in catastrophic material loss. The material signature shows 100% king moves that hang material (median -1.0, meaning a pawn is lost) with no captures played, while the optimal move was consistently a pawn capture (Maia recommends pawn takes pawn 100% of the time). The eval trajectory is devastating: 67% of positions go from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 693 centipawns — essentially converting a holdable endgame into a completely lost one. The positional analysis confirms these are pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where passed pawns, tempo, and pawn structure are paramount. The top boards all show pure or near-pure pawn endings where the player moves their king (Kh2, Kf2, Kg7, Kg3, Kc5, Ke4, Kd6) instead of making the one critical pawn capture that maintains the balance. The recurring tactical theme is that by drifting the king rather than resolving pawn tension, the opponent gains a tempo to advance or create an unstoppable passed pawn.

373.label: Moving the queen away from a dominant or defensive position, forfeiting decisive tactical resources like back-rank threats or mating attacks.
373.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player relocates their queen (or occasionally rook) away from a critical square, abandoning a tactical or defensive function that was holding the position together. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' or 'hangs' outcomes with no captures (78%), indicating these aren't greedy captures but voluntary repositioning errors. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 422cp lost, with 39% converting winning to drawn/losing), confirming these moves throw away winning or stable positions. The tactical analysis reveals the unifying theme: back-rank vulnerabilities (40%), king safety collapse (40%), and tempo loss (20%). In concrete examples, queens leave dominant central posts to grab meaningless pawns, abandon diagonals that enabled back-rank mate threats, or vacate defensive squares protecting the kingside. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), suggesting the correct continuation involved activating rooks to exploit the very threats the player's queen was enabling—particularly back-rank attacks. The player's queen move disconnects the coordination that made those rook tactics possible.

375.label: Rook moves to a passive or ineffective square, surrendering tempo or abandoning an active post in the endgame.
375.description: This feature fires on rook moves (80% of activations) that are objectively safe (87% don't hang material) but cost substantial evaluation (median 239cp loss). The positions are split between endgames and middlegames, with the dominant motifs being tempo_loss (29%), positional_mistake, and rook_misplacement. The common tags reinforce this: piece_activity and tempo_loss appear most frequently, alongside rook_endgame and rook_misplacement. The eval trajectory shows these moves often convert drawn positions to losing ones (27%) or throw away wins (winning->drawn 13%), indicating the rook relocation squanders a critical dynamic advantage. The per-position examples consistently describe rooks voluntarily leaving powerful posts (e.g., abandoning first-rank harassment, moving to squares where they get challenged with tempo), allowing the opponent to seize the initiative. Maia's recommended moves often involve king activation or checks (33%), suggesting the player missed that the position demanded active play rather than passive rook repositioning.

374.label: Player makes a slow or misguided move that squanders a winning attacking position, losing critical tempo against the opponent's king.
374.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player holds a significant attacking advantage but plays a move that fatally loses tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate. The material signature shows mostly safe or trade-level moves (not outright piece drops), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses—median 747cp lost, with 31% going from winning to losing and 15% from drawn to losing. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and tempo_loss (38%), with recurring tags like rook_lift, missed_tactic, and attack_continuation, indicating the player had crushing continuations available (often rook lifts or direct queen/rook attacks) but instead played structurally-motivated pawn moves, premature captures, or positional consolidations. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly rook moves (77%), confirming that the missed best moves were typically aggressive rook deployments. The concrete positions show open files toward exposed kings, queens already on attacking squares (like h6), and strong piece activity that demanded immediate follow-through rather than the slow moves actually played.

377.label: Moving a knight that was defending the queen, leaving it hanging for capture.
377.description: This feature fires when a player moves a knight (80%) or bishop (20%) that was serving as a critical defender of their own queen or other high-value piece. The material signature shows the move predominantly 'hangs' (60%) or 'loses' (40%) material with a devastating median loss of -8.0 (approximately a queen's value), and the eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders converting winning positions to losing ones (100% winning->losing, median 852cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), with tags emphasizing 'removing_own_defender', 'queen_hanging', 'piece_dependency', and 'undefended_piece'. The concrete positions consistently show knights being moved away from squares where they protected the player's queen—often to aggressive-looking squares like d5—only for the opponent (Maia captures queen 80%) to immediately exploit the now-undefended queen. The pattern is a player making a 'flashy' or aggressive knight move without recognizing it was the sole guardian of a more valuable piece.

379.label: Playing a routine developing knight move instead of capturing a free hanging piece with the queen in the opening.
379.description: This feature fires when a player makes a routine developing move (Nf3 or Ne7) in the opening while completely overlooking a free piece capture available to their queen. The material signature shows knight moves that are objectively safe (not hanging anything) but miss winning material 100% of the time. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors, converting winning positions into drawn ones with a median loss of ~397 centipawns—essentially a full piece. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is a hanging piece (89%), with tags consistently indicating missed captures of undefended bishops (particularly on g4). The concrete board positions show a recurring pattern: an opponent's bishop has ventured to g4 early in the opening and is left undefended, the queen has a clear capture path (Qxg4), but the player reflexively develops their knight instead. This is a classic case of autopilot development trumping board awareness—the player follows general opening principles (develop pieces) without scanning for immediate tactical opportunities that would win free material.

376.label: Releasing critical tension or resources in endgames, allowing winning advantages to evaporate.
376.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in simplified positions (middlegame-to-endgame or pure endgame) make moves that release critical tension—abandoning key tactical resources, prematurely advancing pawns, or moving active pieces to passive squares. The material signature shows the moves themselves are mostly 'safe' (no immediate material loss in 67% of cases), yet Maia's recommended moves involve captures and checks (100% check rate, capturing rooks/queens), indicating the player missed forcing continuations that maintained their advantage. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 341 centipawns spanning winning->losing, winning->drawn, and drawn->losing transitions—classic 'throwing away the game' patterns. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of pawn_endgame (33%), passed_pawn (22%), and rook_endgame (22%), plus recurring tags of tempo_loss, piece_activity, and missed_tactic. Concrete examples show rooks moving away from critical files (losing Rxc2+ resources), premature pawn pushes (d4-d5 releasing a latent threat), and king moves that abandon coordination. The common thread is failing to maintain the one critical resource (active rook, restrained pawn, forcing sequence) that held the position together in a simplified setting.

383.label: In lost endgame positions, the player moves their king away from capturing an undefended piece, allowing the opponent to force checkmate.
383.description: This feature captures a specific endgame catastrophe pattern where a player, already in a losing position, moves their king passively instead of capturing available material (most notably undefended rooks). The material signature shows 100% king moves that hang material, while Maia consistently identifies a rook capture as the correct move. The eval trajectory confirms these are losing->losing positions where the mistake is catastrophic (median 9418 centipawns lost), typically converting a difficult but defensible endgame into forced mate. The tactical analysis reveals passed pawns, hanging pieces, and tempo loss as dominant motifs — the king retreats waste critical tempo in positions where promotion races or piece captures are the only defensive resource. The boards consistently show rook endgames and pawn endgames where the king walks away from a concrete capture or defensive duty, immediately allowing a forced mating sequence. This is not a positional subtlety but rather a failure to recognize the urgency of the position in the endgame phase.

378.label: Advancing a passed pawn while missing a critical bishop capture that wins material or defends a decisive threat.
378.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame/middlegame mistake where the player advances a pawn (100% pawn moves, no captures, materially 'safe' in isolation) while the engine strongly preferred a bishop capture of a pawn (Maia's move is bishop capturing pawn 100%). The eval trajectory shows these moves transform drawn positions into losing ones (median 468cp lost), indicating the pawn advance is not just suboptimal but catastrophic. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are passed pawns and king safety—players become fixated on pushing a passed pawn toward promotion but overlook that the opponent has a concrete tactical resource (often involving piece activity, exposed kings, or counter-promotion threats) that the bishop capture would have neutralized. The tags 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic' confirm that the pawn push wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a winning plan. The board positions consistently show late-middlegame or endgame scenarios with advanced passed pawns on both sides, where the player's tunnel-vision push ignores a simple winning capture or essential defensive move.

382.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move, missing a winning tactic involving hanging pieces or back-rank threats that would have converted a decisive advantage.
382.description: This feature identifies positions where a player, typically in the middlegame with a winning or equal position, plays a quiet pawn or piece move (56% pawn moves, no checks, 78% no captures) while missing a concrete tactical blow. The eval trajectory shows massive cost: 78% of the time Maia identified a winning material capture (queen captures in 44% of Maia's suggestions), and the median eval loss is 349 centipawns, with 44% of cases converting winning positions to drawn and 33% going to losing.
