The dominant motifs—hanging pieces (50%), back-rank vulnerabilities (25%), and king safety issues—reveal that opponents had concrete weaknesses ripe for exploitation. The per-position analyses confirm the pattern: players miss forced checkmates, fail to capture undefended queens, or choose intermediate threatening moves instead of clean winning captures. The player's moves are materially 'safe' (89%) precisely because they are passive non-committal moves that ignore the opponent's vulnerabilities, choosing prophylaxis or positional ideas over decisive tactical finishes.

381.label: Player makes a safe but passive king/rook move, missing a devastating knight fork or check that wins material.
381.description: This feature fires when players make safe, non-capturing moves (typically king retreats or passive rook moves) while completely missing a powerful knight tactical shot—almost always a fork or discovered attack with check. The material signature shows 100% safe moves (nothing hangs immediately) but 100% missed winning material, indicating the error is one of omission rather than commission. Maia consistently recommends knight moves that deliver check (100% check rate), frequently involving knight forks or sacrifices that win an exchange or more. The eval trajectory (median 150cp loss, winning->winning or winning->drawn) confirms these are positions where the player squanders a clean tactical opportunity rather than blundering into a loss. The dominant motifs—fork (43%), tempo loss (29%), discovered attack, and back-rank themes—all revolve around the knight's unique tactical geometry. Examining the boards, we see repeated patterns: centralized or well-placed knights (e4, d5, f3 squares) ready to deliver devastating checks, while the player instead shuffles a king to e7 or slides a rook passively, losing the critical tempo needed to execute the tactic.

380.label: Moving the queen into a square where it is captured or trapped due to king safety vulnerabilities, often overlooking checks or forks.
380.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves their queen (79%) or rook (21%) to a square where it is immediately hanging (92% hangs, median material loss of -9.0, i.e., a full queen). The dominant motif is king_safety (86%), with recurring tags including exposed_king, queen_blunder, and back_rank threats. The tactical pattern is consistent: the player moves their queen to a seemingly active or defensive square but overlooks that the opponent can capture it with check, fork it via a knight (fork motif at 14%), or exploit back-rank/king-safety weaknesses to win the piece outright. Maia's best response is typically a king move (79%), suggesting the opponent's king was already under pressure and the queen move was an attempt to address threats that instead fatally misplaced the queen. The eval trajectory shows this occurs across all game states—sometimes throwing away a winning position (winning->losing 12%), sometimes missing a chance to flip a losing game (losing->winning 29% reflects the missed opportunity from the opponent's perspective)—with a steep median cost of 196 centipawns confirming these are decisive blunders rather than marginal inaccuracies.

385.label: Player makes a safe but passive move in the endgame, missing a devastating bishop check along a diagonal that wins material or dominates the position.
385.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions where the player makes a materially safe pawn or minor piece move (75% pawn pushes, 25% bishop moves, 100% safe material outcome) while missing a crushing bishop check (Maia's move is 100% bishop, 100% giving check). The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 398 centipawns lost, with 75% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant tags include diagonal_exploitation, missed_check, and exposed_king, with multiple example summaries explicitly describing missed intermediate bishop checks (e.g., Bd4+ exploiting the long diagonal). The top boards show repeated positions where bishops have clear diagonal access to the enemy king, and the player instead pushes pawns (g2g4, h3g4, g4g5, g5g6) that accomplish nothing urgent. The pattern is a player who fails to recognize the forcing power of a diagonal check in simplified positions, opting for slow non-forcing moves that squander decisive advantages.

384.label: Critical tempo or move-order error in a winning pawn endgame that allows the opponent to equalize.
384.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player makes a seemingly safe pawn or king move that squanders a winning advantage, typically converting it into a draw (83% winning->drawn trajectory with a median eval loss of 358 centipawns). The material signature shows no captures and no material is immediately lost ('safe' 100%), yet the move is catastrophic because of tempo loss or incorrect move order in a razor-sharp pawn ending. The tactical analysis confirms this: tempo_loss appears in all 6 tagged positions, pawn_structure and pawn_breakthrough are common, and the positions consistently have only ONE winning move available (e.g., a precise pawn break like g4 or f5). The boards show locked or semi-locked pawn structures in king-and-pawn endgames where calculating the exact sequence of pawn advances and king maneuvers is critical. The player repeatedly chooses a 'natural' but imprecise move (like advancing the wrong pawn or moving the king passively) when only one specific continuation maintains the win.

386.label: Player overlooks a simple capture of an undefended enemy piece, hanging material instead.
386.description: This feature fires when players make moves that hang their own material (54% hangs) while completely missing a free capture that was available. The Maia best-move analysis shows 85% of the time the correct move was capturing a rook and 15% capturing a queen—major pieces left undefended. The 'missed winning material: 100%' signal confirms every single activation involves overlooking a concrete material win. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%) with recurring tags like 'missed_capture', 'undefended_rook', and 'material_oversight'. The eval trajectory is devastating: 54% swing from winning to losing with a median cost of 820 centipawns, indicating these aren't subtle positional errors but catastrophic oversights. The concrete positions confirm the pattern—players move kings, rooks, or knights to irrelevant squares (often creating threats like checks that accomplish nothing) while an enemy rook or major piece sits completely undefended and capturable. This is a pure tactical blindness pattern: the player fails to see an elementary hanging piece, often because they are distracted by an aggressive-looking but ultimately losing alternative move.

387.label: Player makes a move that leaves a major piece (usually the queen) hanging to an undefended pawn capture.
387.description: This feature detects positions where a player moves a piece—often the queen—to or leaves it on a square directly attacked by an enemy pawn, allowing a simple pawn capture that wins the piece for nothing. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -9.0 (approximately a queen). The eval trajectory reveals these are catastrophic blunders (median eval lost: -10424 centipawns), often turning losing positions into winning ones for the opponent (67% losing->winning flips). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (56%), with common tags including 'queen_blunder', 'en_prise', and 'oversight'. Examining the top boards, the recurring concrete pattern is strikingly consistent: queens placed on squares controlled by pawns (e.g., Qe6 attacked by f5 pawn, Qc5 attacked by d4 pawn, queen on f6 attacked by e5 pawn after its defender moves away). Maia consistently identifies the queen relocation as the correct move. These are not complex tactical oversights but simple one-move hanging pieces to pawn captures that the player failed to notice.

388.label: In a king-and-pawn endgame, the player moves their king away from the critical squares needed to escort or stop a passed pawn, turning a decisive result into a draw.
388.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring endgame blunder: in pure king-and-pawn positions (endgame 100%), the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures) in a way that abandons control of the promotion-critical squares. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert decisive advantages into draws (winning->drawn 50%, losing->drawn 50%, median loss 542cp, with several showing mate-to-draw swings of ~9995cp). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'promotion_error' (80%), with tags emphasizing tempo_loss, passed_pawn, and opposition—all hallmarks of failing to maintain the geometric relationship between king and pawn required for promotion or blockade. The concrete positions (e.g., Kd6e5 with pawn on e6, Kf6f5 with pawn on g6, Kb6c5 with pawn on c6) show kings stepping away from the key escort squares or opposition, releasing the opponent's king to reach the drawing zone. Maia consistently recommends the pawn push instead, confirming the king move is a tempo-wasting retreat from the winning technique.

391.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended square where it is immediately capturable in the opening, losing a full piece.
391.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder where a player moves their bishop to a square where it has no protection and can be captured for free. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves that are non-captures resulting in a hung piece (median -3.0 pawns, consistent with losing a minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones, costing a median of 487 centipawns — exactly what you'd expect from dropping a bishop. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly flags 'hanging_piece' (86%) with supporting tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'free_material.' The top activating positions make the pattern concrete: bishops placed on a6 where they're capturable by knights or pawns, bishops on h3 capturable via the f1-g2-h3 diagonal, and bishops on a3 with no support. All occur in the opening phase, often violating basic development principles (e.g., the Ruy Lopez bishop on a4 being left hanging after an incorrect move order). Maia's suggested knight moves indicate a simple developing alternative was available rather than the reckless bishop sortie.

390.label: Non-urgent flank pawn advances in the opening that waste tempo and create tactical vulnerabilities.
390.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening/early middlegame mistake where players push flank pawns (a-pawns, b-pawns, c-pawns, or h-pawns) when development or central action is critical. The material signature shows 93% pawn moves with no captures, and 79% are objectively 'safe' in that no piece immediately hangs—yet the median eval loss is 272 centipawns, indicating severe positional consequences. The eval trajectory (50% drawn->losing, 36% winning->drawn) reveals these moves frequently throw away half-point advantages or convert holdable positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: tempo_loss and development are the most common tags, with players choosing non-urgent flank advances (a5, c5, b5, h4, a4) instead of addressing central tension, completing development, or resolving tactical threats. The top boards consistently show positions from established openings (Ruy Lopez/Italian structures with Bb3) where the opponent has active central play, and the flank push either leaves pawns undefended (hanging_piece motif), weakens king safety, or squanders a critical tempo that the opponent exploits immediately.

392.label: Player captures with bishop before executing the correct sequence, leaving a piece hanging due to move-order error.
392.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a bishop capture (100% bishop moves, 100% capturing a rook) but in the wrong order, resulting in a catastrophic material loss (median -4.0 net material, median 798 centipawns lost). The eval trajectory shows these are consistently winning positions thrown away (100% winning->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant pattern: the player captures with the bishop first when they should have played a queen move (Maia recommends queen 100%, capturing a pawn). The Opus summaries explicitly identify 'fatal move-order errors' — for example, playing Bxf8 before Qxd8, leaving the queen undefended. The recurring tags (move_order_error, hanging_piece, undefended_queen, intermediate_move) confirm that by capturing in the wrong sequence, the player either leaves their own queen en prise or allows a devastating intermediate tactic (fork, capture with check) that wouldn't have been possible with the correct move order. This is not a simple blunder of hanging a piece, but a sequencing error in a multi-move tactical combination.

389.label: Losing a winning advantage by making an aimless move instead of executing the one critical continuation in a won endgame.
389.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a large advantage (median eval lost: 710 centipawns) in late middlegame or endgame pawn structures, yet plays a 'safe' non-capturing move (typically a knight retreat or king shuffle) that squanders the win. The material signature shows no captures and nothing immediately hanging—the move looks innocuous—but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: winning positions collapse to drawn (50%) or merely shrink dramatically (50%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (67% of cases), confirmed by the tag analysis (tempo_loss appears 7 times across examples). The board positions are almost exclusively locked pawn endgames with bishops or knights, where there is exactly one winning continuation (often a capture of a hanging piece or a critical pawn advance like f5 or Nxc7), and the player instead makes a purposeless developing or prophylactic move that allows the opponent to consolidate. The Maia suggestions consistently involve capturing material (pawn 50%, bishop 50%), confirming that the missed best move was a concrete action, not a quiet improvement. In essence, the player 'passes' in a position that demands immediate action, wasting the tempo needed to convert a won endgame.

398.label: Player develops a knight instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece in the opening, turning a winning position into an equal one.
398.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player moves a knight (100% knight moves, 0% captures) while a simple bishop capture was available (Maia recommends bishop captures bishop 100% of the time). The material outcome of the played move is 'safe'—nothing is immediately lost—but the player misses winning a free or insufficiently defended piece, as shown by the dominant 'hanging_piece' motif (86%) and tags like missed_tactic, missed_capture, and material_advantage_missed. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: 100% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 474 centipawns. The concrete positions consistently show early-game scenarios where an enemy bishop sits undefended (e.g., Bg4, Bf5, Bg5, Bd6) and the player reflexively develops a knight (Nf3, Nf6, etc.) or retreats rather than simply taking the hanging piece. This is a pattern of development-over-material tunnel vision in the opening.

393.label: A pawn advance that creates tactical vulnerabilities, often exposing the king or allowing discovered attacks.
393.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make pawn pushes (98% pawn moves) that are not captures (98% no capture) but frequently hang material (41%) or create severe positional weaknesses. The median eval loss of 235 centipawns is substantial, with trajectories showing positions going from drawn to losing (16%) or maintaining a losing trend (16%). The tactical analysis reveals a triad of motifs: positional mistakes, king safety compromises, and discovered attacks (each 33%). The top boards consistently show pawn advances like ...b5, ...g6, ...h6, b4, c4, d5 that weaken the pawn structure or open lines against the player's own king in middlegame positions (80%). These are not trades or captures but prophylactic or space-gaining attempts that backfire by creating tactical holes. The common tags reinforce this: piece_activity, king_safety, pawn_structure, and tempo_loss all point to pawns being pushed when the position demanded piece coordination or defensive consolidation. Maia's suggested moves (queen 24%, knight 22%, king 20%) indicate that piece moves—often defensive or actively improving—were the correct responses rather than these committal pawn advances.

395.label: Moving a piece to a square where it is immediately captured, hanging material in the opening or early middlegame.
395.description: This feature identifies moves where a player relocates a piece (most often a knight or bishop) to a square where it can be immediately captured, effectively hanging it. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in a 'hang' (a non-capture that drops a piece) with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors: median 346 centipawns lost, often turning winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->drawn 30%, winning->losing 20%, drawn->losing 10%). The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (50%), with 'missed_tactic' appearing in 4 of 10 cases—players overlook that the destination square is controlled by an opponent's piece. Concrete examples include placing a knight on d5 where it is captured by a bishop (position 2), or moving a king to f2 where material is lost (position 3). The phase is predominantly opening (70%), suggesting players are developing pieces carelessly without checking whether destination squares are adequately defended. Maia's recommendations typically involve capturing material (pawns 50%, pieces 30%) that the player ignored, confirming the player missed obvious tactical opportunities while blundering their own piece.

399.label: Losing player makes a fatal simplification or piece trade in a lost endgame, accelerating defeat.
399.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player who is already losing (75% losing->losing, 25% drawn->losing) makes a move that dramatically worsens their position (median 302cp lost). The material signature shows pawns and bishops being moved, with 38% resulting in hanging material and 38% in trades—often bad exchanges that eliminate key defensive pieces. The tactical analysis reveals themes of positional mistakes (33%), passed pawn mishandling (33%), and tempo loss (17%), with recurring tags of piece_activity, endgame_technique, simplification_error, and bad_trade. The concrete positions show players trading away their only minor piece (bishop for knight), making pointless pawn advances that create weaknesses, or losing tempo with their king—all accelerating an already difficult endgame into a hopeless one. The Opus summaries confirm the pattern: players eliminate their sole defensive piece, enter theoretically lost positions, or allow forced mates where resistance was still possible.

397.label: Knight jumps to an aggressive square but loses tempo when the opponent's piece retreats to a stronger position or delivers check, costing significant evaluation.
397.description: This feature fires on opening/early-middlegame positions (70% opening, 30% middlegame) where the player moves a knight (100% knight moves) to an apparently active square—often attacking a queen or occupying an outpost—but the move backfires tactically. The material signature shows these are not direct blunders of pieces (87% safe, no captures 97%), yet the eval trajectory is devastating: 43% of positions go from drawn to losing, 17% from winning to drawn, and 7% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 252 centipawns. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (62%), with fork (25%) and trapped_piece (12%) as secondary consequences. The Opus analysis consistently describes knights jumping to b4, d4, d5, or f4 that appear to win a tempo against a queen or create a threat, but the opponent's response (often a queen retreat to a stronger square like Qa4+ or Qa3, or a piece recapture that traps/displaces the knight) turns the 'attack' into pure tempo loss. Tags like premature_attack, piece_activity, and development reinforce that these are pseudo-active moves where the knight's aggression is strategically premature, violating opening principles and granting the opponent initiative.

394.label: Giving a check with the queen that loses material or tempo because the check is not actually forcing.
394.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a queen check (96% checks, 83% queen moves) that turns out to be ineffective or self-destructive. The material signature shows these moves predominantly hang the queen (56%) or are otherwise unsafe, with a median net material loss of -1.0 (roughly a piece or the queen itself). The Opus tactical analysis confirms the recurring motif: 'pointless_check' and 'check_is_not_forcing' tags appear alongside 'queen_blunder' and 'tempo_loss.' Players assume a check must be dangerous, but the opponent simply blocks, captures, or sidesteps while gaining tempo or winning the exposed queen. Maia (the human-like engine) gives check 0% of the time in these positions, confirming these checks are uniquely human errors born from the heuristic that 'check is always good.' The eval trajectory shows these blunders are devastating—median 202cp lost—and they occur across all game states (winning->losing 22%, drawn->losing 4%, drawn->winning only when the opponent had already been worse). The concrete positions repeatedly show queens flying to checking squares (Qa5+, Qd3+, Qh4+) where they accomplish nothing forcing and often land on undefended or tactically exposed squares.

396.label: Player makes a quiet or developing move that walks into a tactical fork, hanging material in a previously winning position.
396.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in the middlegame with a winning or comfortable position, plays a quiet move (most often a pawn push or rook move) that ignores an existing or imminent fork threat. The material signature shows 91% non-captures with 43% of moves hanging material—indicating the player isn't trading but is simply leaving pieces en prise. The median eval loss of 325 centipawns and the trajectory (winning->drawn 26%, winning->losing 11%) confirm these are positions where a substantial advantage is squandered. The dominant motifs (fork 33%, hanging_piece 33%, king_safety 33%) combined with tags like missed_tactic and tempo_loss reveal the mechanism: the player makes a slow or irrelevant move while the opponent has a concrete tactical shot available—often a knight fork hitting multiple pieces. Maia's suggested moves (rook 54%, bishop 34%) are consistently piece moves that address the tactical threat, indicating the correct response was to reposition or safeguard hanging material. The concrete positions confirm this: Rf1 walks into Nxe3 forking rook and bishop; Nf5 allows a fork; pawn pushes like g5 or h4 ignore tactical vulnerabilities. The pattern is a player who has built a winning position but loses focus on opponent counterplay, making a 'natural' move that overlooks a simple tactical motif.

400.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in the opening, missing a queen check that simultaneously forks an undefended piece.
400.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where the player has a winning queen check available (Maia's move is queen 100%, gives check 100%) that forks an unprotected piece—typically a bishop on b4 or b5—but instead plays a routine developing move (bishop 40%, pawn 25%, knight 15%). The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, often arising from Benoni/Indian structures or Ruy Lopez-type positions where a bishop has moved to an exposed square (b4/b5) without adequate support. The material signature shows the played move is 'safe' (90%)—nothing is immediately lost—but the missed tactic costs a median of 363 centipawns, converting a winning position into a drawn one (75% winning->drawn). The dominant motifs (fork 29%, hanging_piece 43%) and tags (queen_fork, missed_tactic, undefended_piece) consistently point to the same pattern: a queen sortie with check that simultaneously attacks a loose minor piece. The concrete examples (Qa4+ forking king and Bb4, Qa5+ winning Bb5) confirm this is a single recurring tactical oversight where players prioritize development over a decisive intermediate check.

401.label: Bishop develops while ignoring a concrete pawn-captures-knight threat in the opening, leaving a piece en prise.
401.description: This feature detects a recurring opening mistake where the player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves) in a developing or prophylactic fashion while completely ignoring an immediate tactical threat to one of their pieces—typically a knight that can be captured by a pawn. The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (100% 'hangs'), with a median cost of -2.0 material (approximately a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these blunders convert drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 279cp loss). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (56%), with 'ignored_threat' appearing as the most common tag (5 instances). The concrete positions consistently show French Defense and Alekhine-style structures where an advanced e-pawn threatens a knight on f3 or f6, and the player ignores this threat to make a quiet bishop move (Be7, Bg2, Be2, Bb4) or a prophylactic pawn move. The mistake is fundamentally one of opening tactical awareness: prioritizing development or prevention over an immediate material threat that should be addressed first.

402.label: Trading away a powerfully placed or tactically critical piece for a passive one, squandering a winning advantage.
402.description: This feature fires when a player voluntarily exchanges a dominant, actively-placed minor piece (most often a centralized knight or strong bishop) for an opponent's passive or less important piece of equal material value. The material signature shows 100% trades (net material ~0) involving knights (50%) and bishops (33%), so no material is literally lost—yet the median eval cost is 258 centipawns, with 45% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one. The Opus analysis repeatedly highlights 'dominant_piece_trade', 'wrong_exchange', and 'premature_exchange' tags: players remove the very piece generating all their pressure or tactical threats, relieving the opponent's defensive burden. In 79% of cases a concrete winning tactic (often a fork or combination using that same piece) was missed in favor of the routine trade. The checks in 43% of moves suggest the trade often comes with a superficially attractive check that masks its strategic cost. This is not a blunder of material but a catastrophic positional simplification—cashing in a dominant piece for its nominal equivalent while forfeiting the attacking initiative that piece sustained.

403.label: Trading or capturing when a hanging piece or tactic was available, turning a favorable position into a losing one.
403.description: This feature captures positions where the player initiates an exchange or makes a move that appears active (often capturing with a bishop or knight) but overlooks a concrete tactical opportunity—typically a hanging piece or fork—resulting in a catastrophic evaluation loss (median ~398 centipawns). The material signature shows 56% trades and 33% hangs, meaning the player either swaps pieces at the wrong moment or leaves material undefended. The trajectory (33% winning→drawn, 33% drawn→losing) confirms these are moves that throw away an advantage or cross into a lost position. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (60%) with missed_tactic appearing in most positions: players ignore free captures or place pieces on squares where they are immediately taken. Maia's recommendations (knights, pawns, rooks) suggest simpler developing or capturing moves were available. The boards show a consistent pattern: the player has a concrete tactical resource (a free capture, an undefended piece to exploit) but instead makes an exchange or 'active-looking' move that either drops material or allows the opponent's tactic to succeed.

404.label: Sacrificing a knight for a pawn (or nothing) in endgames where the piece was the last source of counterplay.
404.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player sacrifices their knight (60% knight moves) to capture a mere pawn (60% pawn captures) or makes a king move that allows material loss, resulting in a slightly negative material outcome (median -2.0, consistent with losing a knight for a pawn). The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic decisions—median 254 centipawns lost—often turning drawn or winning positions into lost ones (40% losing->winning from opponent's view, 40% drawn->losing). The phase is 100% endgame, and the tactical analysis consistently identifies hanging_piece (62%) as the dominant motif: the knight moves to an undefended square where it is immediately captured, or captures a pawn only to be recaptured, eliminating the player's last active piece and all counterplay. The Opus summaries repeatedly describe trading 'the only piece capable of creating complications' for a single pawn, creating trivially lost endgames. Maia's recommended moves (60% knight, but to safe squares or capturing higher-value pieces) confirm that better knight deployments existed.

405.label: King captures a pawn in an endgame but fatally loses tempo in a critical pawn race involving passed pawns.
405.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player's king captures a pawn (king moved 100%, captured pawn 100%) in a materially 'safe' way (no immediate material loss), but the tempo spent on the capture is catastrophic in the context of a passed pawn race. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 531 centipawns), often converting drawn positions to lost ones or deepening already losing positions. The dominant motif is passed pawns (100%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, promotion_error, and pawn_race. The concrete positions all show pure pawn endgames where connected or advanced passed pawns require precise king positioning and move counting—the king detours to grab a pawn that looks free but abandons a critical blockade, loses a tempo in a promotion race, or steps to the wrong side of the board. The Opus analysis confirms this: one example shows abandoning a blockade of a g6 passer to capture on f5, another shows a dead-equal position thrown away by a greedy king capture when simpler pawn moves held the draw.

408.label: Player makes a quiet developing move while overlooking a devastating knight fork that wins material.
408.description: This feature fires when a player misses a powerful knight fork opportunity in the opening phase. The material/position signature shows the player making safe, non-capturing moves (pawns 36%, bishops 36%) while Maia consistently identifies a knight move (100%) that delivers check (91%) and wins material (often capturing a pawn or queen). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly oversights—median 331 centipawns lost, with 55% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one and 18% turning wins into losses. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies fork motifs (83%), with knight_fork appearing in 5 of the top examples and the tag 'missed_tactic' appearing in 6. The concrete positions consistently show a knight poised to deliver a fork (often Nxc2+ or Nxc7+) exploiting a centralized king, while the player instead develops a piece passively (Be2, Be6, e5) completely overlooking the tactical shot. This is a classic pattern of opening-phase tactical blindness where routine development trumps concrete calculation.

406.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn or queen move in a closed middlegame position, squandering a winning or drawn advantage by losing critical tempo.
406.description: This feature captures a recurring positional mistake where players make passive, non-capturing moves (100% no capture) — predominantly pawn pushes (50%) or quiet queen/rook repositioning — in closed, locked middlegame structures. The positions universally feature blocked pawn chains and closed centers, where precise move order and timing are paramount. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and king_safety (33%), indicating that the player wastes a critical turn on an aimless move instead of executing the one accurate continuation (often a pawn break, en passant, or piece activation). The eval trajectory is severe: median loss of 287 centipawns, with 35% of cases converting a winning position into a draw and 12% turning a win into a loss. Maia's recommended moves are almost always pawn captures (77%), suggesting the player missed a concrete pawn break or tactical sequence that demanded immediate execution. The top boards confirm closed structures where a single tempo decides the game — the player drifts with a quiet move while the opponent's counterplay becomes unstoppable.

414.label: King moves in pawn endgames that are often optimal or near-optimal technique for escorting passed pawns.
414.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the material outcome is safe (no hanging pieces, no captures). The positions are overwhelmingly pawn endgames or simple piece endgames with passed pawns and promotion threats. The median eval loss is 0 centipawns, and the Opus analysis confirms that many of these moves are optimal or near-optimal (e.g., 'Kb6 is not a blunder—it is one of three optimal moves' and 'Kd3 was the absolute best move'). The dominant motifs are passed_pawn and promotion_threat, with king_activation also tagged. The boards show positions with advanced passed pawns where kings are actively escorting pawns or maneuvering for promotion. While most activations represent correct endgame technique, occasional costly errors appear (h4 losing 268cp by missing an immediate promotion tactic, Kf4 walking into a knight fork). The feature broadly captures the pattern of king activation moves in simplified endgame positions with passed pawns, regardless of whether the move was correct or erroneous.

407.label: Player makes an irrelevant move instead of delivering a short forced checkmate, typically missing a back-rank or king-safety mating pattern.
407.description: This feature fires when a player has a forced checkmate in 2-3 moves but plays an entirely unrelated move instead. The material signature shows mostly safe or hanging moves (pawns 33%, knights 27%, queens 20%) that are strategically aimless rather than pursuing the winning attack. The Maia best-move signal is overwhelming: 93% queen moves, 100% giving check, with 60% capturing a pawn (often a sacrificial queen move initiating the mating sequence). The median eval loss of 9822 centipawns confirms these are missed mates, not ordinary inaccuracies. The Opus analysis reveals a dominant pattern of king_safety (67%) and back_rank (33%) motifs, with recurring tags like missed_mate, mate_in_2, queen_bishop_battery, and catastrophic_blunder. The top boards show a strikingly specific recurring position: a Ba6+Qb3 battery aimed at b7 with the Black king on b8, where Qxb6+ Ka8 Qb7# is available but the player instead pushes central pawns (c4), plays defensive moves (g3, f3), or repositions knights (Nh4). The trajectory (47% winning->winning) suggests some positions remain won despite the miss, but the critical 20% that shift to drawn or losing confirm the catastrophic cost of overlooking short mates.

410.label: Ignoring or walking into a pin (often on the Nf3-Qd1 diagonal) during the opening, losing significant material.
410.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (90% opening) where the player makes a piece move (knight 21%, bishop 21%, pawn 28%, king 14% including castling) that ignores or exacerbates a pin, most commonly along the g4-d1 diagonal targeting Nf3 and the queen. The dominant tactical motif is 'pin' (43%), supported by 'hanging_piece' (29%) and tags like 'pin_exploitation', 'opening_trap', and 'exposed_knight'. The material outcome is mostly 'safe' (69%) meaning the move itself isn't a capture-gone-wrong but rather a positional/tactical oversight that allows the opponent a devastating reply—hence 18% 'hangs' a piece. Critically, 100% of these positions miss winning material (Maia always recommends a simple pawn move instead), and the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 281 centipawns with 35% going from drawn to losing. The top boards consistently show the Bg4 pinning Nf3 to the queen, and the player either castles into the pin, moves the knight away exposing the queen, or develops a piece ignoring the pin's consequences. This is a classic opening trap pattern where the player neglects the tactical implications of an existing or imminent pin.

417.label: Trading major pieces into a lost pawn endgame by misjudging the resulting king-and-pawn position.
417.description: This feature fires on moves where a player initiates a trade of major pieces (rooks or queens) with check, resulting in a materially equal exchange but a catastrophically worse pawn endgame. The material signature shows 100% trades (net material 0.0) delivered with check, yet Maia's recommended moves avoid the trade entirely (Maia captures: none 100%), indicating the trade itself is the mistake. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 245 centipawns—consistent with transforming playable middlegame positions into technically lost endgames. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags pawn_endgame_misjudgment (appearing in 4/6 positions) alongside simplification_error and queen_trade_error. The concrete positions confirm this: players trade rooks or queens, often with a seemingly forcing check, only to land in pawn endgames where the opponent's king activity, superior pawn structure, or passed pawn dynamics are decisive. The core error is misjudging the resulting king-and-pawn position—overestimating one's own passed pawns or underestimating the opponent's king proximity and pawn majority.

411.label: Moving a minor piece to a passive or retreating square in the opening, allowing the opponent a forced queen capture with check that wins material.
411.description: This feature detects a specific opening blunder pattern where the player moves a knight (67%) or bishop (33%) to a seemingly reasonable square—often developing or repositioning—while completely overlooking that the opponent has a forcing queen capture with check (Maia's response is 100% queen capturing queen with check). The positions are all in the opening phase (100%), and the moves are non-captures (83%) that frequently hang material (33%) or appear safe but enable a devastating tactical sequence. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes typically swing the position from drawn to losing (67%), with a median cost of 276 centipawns. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%) and tempo_loss (38%)—reveal the underlying pattern: the player wastes tempo on piece moves (Nfd2, Bg5, Ng4 retreats) that neglect central pawn defense or ignore forced exchanges, allowing the opponent to win the queen exchange favorably or pick up undefended pawns after the forced simplification. The concrete examples show moves like Bg5 ignoring that after Qxd1+ the e4 pawn hangs, or Nfd2 retreating when the position demanded maintaining tension.

409.label: Rook moves away from a defensive obligation, allowing back-rank mates, piece captures, or losing key endgame positions.
409.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves their rook (80% of cases) away from a square where it was performing a critical defensive or positional function—guarding the back rank, protecting a hanging piece, or maintaining control of a key file/rank. The material signature shows these aren't simple blunders of the rook itself but rather that moving it creates downstream catastrophes: the median eval loss of 706 centipawns and 40% winning->losing trajectory confirm these are game-losing mistakes. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 38%, back_rank 12%, overloaded_defender) combined with tags like tempo_loss and missed_tactic reveal that the rook was serving as a defender, and its relocation—often for greedy purposes like capturing a pawn (b8b2 example) or advancing a passed pawn—leaves critical squares unprotected. Maia's recommended moves (60% rook, 40% bishop, with 80% giving check) suggest the correct moves often involved active counterplay or maintained defensive coordination. The concrete examples reinforce this: Rb8b2 abandons back-rank defense allowing Rh8#, Rc8b8 misorders before a forcing knight check, and Kf4 walks into a discovered check after a rook exchange. The common thread is a rook (or king) move that neglects a defensive responsibility for an apparently attractive but ultimately losing objective.

413.label: Giving a check that leaves the checking piece or another piece hanging, sacrificing material for a useless tempo.
413.description: This feature captures positions where a player delivers a check (100% of activating positions involve check) but the move results in material loss (median net material: -3.0, with 40% hanging a piece and 20% losing material outright). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: 60% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 40% flip from losing to winning for the opponent, with a median loss of 343 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern—players are seduced by the forcing nature of a check but fail to calculate the opponent's response, which often includes a recapture with check or simply winning the undefended checking piece. The dominant tags (hanging_piece 60%, tempo_loss, calculation_error) and example summaries ('gave away the Rook with a check that Black can simply capture with the Queen with check back') reinforce that these are impulsive checks where the player prioritizes forcing moves over material safety, typically in endgames (60%) where piece activity matters but hanging material is immediately decisive. The checking piece (usually a rook at 60%) ends up en prise or the check enables a devastating counter.

416.label: Moving a piece to a square where it hangs to a tactical shot (fork, pin, or capture on an open line), losing significant material.
416.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a piece (bishop, pawn, rook, or knight) to a square where it becomes undefended or tactically vulnerable, resulting in material loss (69% hangs, median -1.0 material, median 217cp eval loss). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (50%), tempo_loss (25%), and fork (25%), with recurring tags like knight_fork, exposed_king, and undefended_piece. The player consistently overlooks that their moved piece lands on—or vacates defense of—a square exploitable by the opponent's tactical threats (forks gaining material with check, captures on open files, or simple takes of undefended pieces). The eval trajectory shows these are largely positions where the player was winning or equal (56% winning->winning with reduced advantage, 12% winning->drawn, 12% winning->losing), meaning the mistake squanders a good position by ignoring a concrete tactical threat. Maia's recommended moves (primarily pawn and king moves) suggest the correct approach was often a quiet defensive move addressing the threat rather than the active but tactically blind piece placement the player chose.

415.label: Trading queens when the opponent has an unstoppable passed pawn or near-promotion threat.
415.description: This feature fires on positions where a player trades queens (100% queen moved, 100% queen captured, 100% trade outcome) but the exchange critically enables the opponent's passed pawn to promote or become decisive. The eval trajectory shows positions going from drawn to losing or worsening an already losing position (median 46cp lost), indicating the trade itself is the mistake rather than a material blunder. The dominant motifs—passed_pawn (appearing in 7/9 tagged positions), promotion_error, pawn_endgame, and simplification_error—all converge on the same theme: by simplifying into a queen-less position, the player removes their best defensive piece against an advanced passed pawn. The concrete positions confirm this: multiple boards show pawns on the 2nd/7th rank ready to promote, and the queen trade eliminates the very piece that could blockade or check to prevent promotion. Maia's recommended moves (queen 67%, king 33%) with no captures suggest maintaining the queen on the board or making a king move to address the pawn, rather than simplifying. This is fundamentally an endgame/trade error where the player fails to recognize that the queen is their primary tool for stopping a promotion threat.

418.label: Moving a piece in the opening that leaves another piece or pawn undefended, allowing a devastating fork or capture.
418.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player moves a bishop or knight (bishop 67%, knight 33%) without capturing anything, and the move hangs material 67% of the time (median net material: -1.0). The eval trajectory shows these are costly errors converting drawn positions to losing (67%) or winning to drawn (33%), with a median loss of 317 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: the moved piece was serving a defensive duty, and by relocating it the player exposes a fork (40%) or leaves a piece hanging (40%). Common tags include knight_fork, piece_moved_from_defensive_duty, and opening_trap. The concrete positions confirm this — a bishop moves away from defending a pawn allowing Nxd6+ fork, a knight repositions overlooking a fork with check, or a pawn push ignores a mutual attack. In each case, Maia's recommended move captures a knight (100%), exploiting the newly undefended square. The unifying theme is a developing or repositioning move in the opening that neglects the defensive role of the moved piece, immediately allowing the opponent a tactical shot.

419.label: Moving a minor piece to a passive or misplaced square, hanging material while losing critical tempo or positional assets.
419.description: This feature fires on moves where a player relocates a minor piece (bishop 38%, knight 38%) to an inferior square, resulting in material being hung (67%) with a median loss of ~2 pawns worth of material (median net -2.0). The eval trajectory shows these mistakes frequently convert winning positions to drawn (24%) or drawn to losing (19%), with a steep median eval loss of 283 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are fundamentally positional errors (50% positional_mistake motif) characterized by tempo loss (most common tag), creating passive pieces, and surrendering key positional assets—such as trading a dominant centralized piece for a peripheral pawn, retreating a bishop to a square where it becomes permanently blocked, or overextending pawns beyond piece support. The pattern is not a simple tactical oversight but rather a strategic misjudgment where the player voluntarily worsens their piece placement, inadvertently leaving material en prise as a consequence of the positional misunderstanding. These occur predominantly in the middlegame (62%) and opening (33%), where piece activity and tempo are most critical.

420.label: Player abandons a winning attacking position by missing a forcing continuation, allowing the opponent to equalize or win.
420.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player holds a winning or at least drawn position but makes a move that catastrophically abandons their attacking momentum (median eval lost: 364 centipawns). The material signature shows the player's moves are mostly 'safe' (67%) — they aren't blundering pieces outright but rather making quiet or misdirected moves when sharp tactical continuations were required. The dominant motifs (discovered attacks, back-rank threats, king safety, promotion errors) all point to positions rich in tactical potential that the player fails to exploit. The common tags (tempo_loss, hanging_piece, queen_loss, forced_queen_trade) confirm that by ignoring the critical forcing move, the player allows the opponent to seize the initiative or simplify into a tenable position. The eval trajectory (winning->drawn 33%, drawn->losing 33%, winning->losing 33%) shows these are consistently positions where the player was objectively better or at least holding but threw away the game by choosing a passive or irrelevant move instead of the concrete tactical blow. Examples include ignoring a hanging piece to make an aimless king move, allowing a forced queen trade when attacking, and failing to deliver a back-rank mate sequence.

422.label: Moving a piece to an ineffective square that loses critical tempo in positions requiring urgent action.
422.description: This feature captures moves where pieces drift to squares that waste tempo in positions demanding immediate action. The material signature shows the player mostly moves rooks or knights without capturing (40% no capture), yet the net outcome is negative (median -2.0 centipawns material, with significant eval drops of ~495cp). The trajectory shows these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones (40%) or worsen already losing positions (60%), indicating the player fails to recognize urgency. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), supported by tags like decentralization and piece_activity—the moved piece lands on a square where it accomplishes nothing immediate while the opponent's threats (passed pawns advancing, king attacks materializing) go unaddressed. The Maia analysis confirms the computer wanted active captures (bishop 40%, queen 20%, rook 20%) often with check (40%), meaning the player bypassed forcing moves that maintained counterplay. Concrete examples include Ng5 removing a knight from a useful post, Ke5 failing to stop a passed pawn, and h7 giving the opponent time to consolidate. The common thread is prioritizing a seemingly active-looking move over the position's true demands.

423.label: Safe-looking moves that miss a winning knight fork or invasion, squandering a significant advantage.
423.description: This feature fires when a player makes a materially 'safe' move (no piece is hung, no exchange occurs) but misses a decisive knight tactic—almost always a fork or knight invasion (Nb5, Nd5, etc.) that would have won material or delivered a crushing positional blow. The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly winning positions collapsing to drawn (88%), with a median loss of 292 centipawns, indicating a squandered winning advantage. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'fork' (60%) combined with tempo loss (40%), and the missed_tactic tag appears in nearly every case. The top boards consistently show positions where a knight jump (Nb5, Nd5) threatened devastating forks on c7/d6 winning rooks or creating unstoppable dual threats, but the player chose routine developing or prophylactic moves (h3, Nf3, Bb5, g4) instead. The player's piece variety (bishop, rook, pawn, knight equally) reflects that any piece can be the 'wrong' move when the knight tactic is the critical one-move window.

421.label: Retreating or repositioning a piece to a passive square, abandoning critical defensive or attacking duties in the middlegame.
421.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a major or minor piece (queen 32%, knight 26%, rook 16%, king 10%) to a passive or inferior square, typically without capturing anything (79% non-capture) and without giving check. The material signature shows 37% of these moves hang a piece and 53% appear superficially safe, yet the median eval loss is a devastating 328 centipawns—indicating the cost is positional/tactical rather than a simple material drop. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: 47% shift from drawn to losing and 10% from winning to drawn. The tactical motifs (king_safety, hanging_piece, fork, overloaded_defender) combined with tags like tempo_loss, piece_coordination, centralization_loss, and piece_activity reveal the consistent pattern: the player retreats or redeploys a piece away from a critical square, losing tempo and coordination, which allows the opponent (Maia consistently recommends a rook capture, 100%) to exploit newly undefended material or launch a decisive tactical blow. The concrete examples reinforce this—Ng3 retreats a centralized knight, Kh1 wastes a critical tempo, Qb6 abandons a key square, Qe7 leaves a rook unprotected. The mistake is fundamentally one of misjudging which piece belongs where, sacrificing activity and coordination for an illusory improvement.

426.label: Playing a pawn move in the opening instead of capturing a free or hanging piece with the queen.
426.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where the player advances a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% non-captures, 100% materially 'safe' in isolation) while a free piece — typically a knight — is available for capture by the queen (Maia's recommendation is 100% queen capturing knight). The eval trajectory shows massive cost (median 483cp lost), with half the cases converting a winning position into a losing one. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 67%, missed_capture, free_material) and Opus analysis confirm the pattern: players see an undefended or hanging piece but choose a developing or attacking pawn push instead of the elementary queen capture. This is a classic opening tactical oversight — the player either doesn't notice the piece is en prise, overvalues pawn structure/development, or miscalculates that the pawn move 'attacks' the piece when a direct capture was immediately available and safe.

412.label: In a won endgame, the player makes a safe but aimless move instead of delivering an immediate checkmate or decisive conversion.
412.description: All positions are endgames where the player already has a winning advantage. The moves played are materially 'safe' (nothing is lost or hung) yet miss winning material 62% of the time, and Maia's suggested moves deliver check 62% of the time — indicating available checkmates or forcing sequences. The top boards confirm this: positions with immediate mates (K7/2qk4, Kd8 instead of Qc1#), promotions delayed (b5b6 instead of a forced promotion), and rook captures missed. The eval trajectory shows 0cp median loss because the position often remains winning, but the player squanders the immediate knockout, prolonging the game unnecessarily with passive king or pawn moves.

424.label: Moving the queen (or major piece) to an aggressive square while leaving critical defensive duties unmet, hanging material.
424.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their queen (70% of activations) to an apparently active square but in doing so abandon a crucial defensive responsibility, leaving a piece or critical square unprotected. The material signature shows 80% of these moves hang material (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median cost of -1.0 material units and ~346 centipawns of eval loss. The eval trajectory (50% drawn→losing, 40% losing→losing) shows these mistakes typically convert a holdable or already difficult position into a clearly lost one. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs: hanging_piece (60%) combined with tempo_loss (20%) and king_safety (20%). The per-position summaries repeatedly describe pieces being moved away from defensive duties — 'Qh4 catastrophically abandons the defense of f2', 'Ne5 removes the f3 knight's defense of d4', 'moving the f1 bishop away left g2 undefended'. The positions occur in opening/middlegame (50/50) where piece coordination is critical, and players are seduced by seemingly active piece placement while overlooking that their piece was the sole defender of a key square or piece.

425.label: Critical move-order or tempo mistakes in pawn endgames that squander decisive advantages or defensive resources.
425.description: This feature detects a highly specific class of pawn endgame errors where the player (usually moving a pawn or king) makes a tempo or move-order mistake that costs substantial evaluation (median 222cp). The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (81% safe, 97% no capture) with pawns and kings in endgame positions (74% endgame), confirming these aren't tactical blunders but subtle positional/timing errors. The eval trajectory reveals a mix of positions going from drawn to losing (23%) and already-losing positions collapsing further (36%), indicating missed defensive resources or squandered drawing chances. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags these as pawn_endgame (67%) with tempo_loss (11%) and passed_pawn (22%) motifs. The concrete examples show classic patterns: advancing the wrong pawn first (h5 before axb5), missing en passant windows, making king moves that cede critical tempi, and push-order errors that allow the opponent to create superior pawn structures. Maia consistently recommends pawn captures (100% pawn takes pawn), suggesting the correct moves often involve timely exchanges the player avoided in favor of seemingly natural but tempo-losing alternatives.

429.label: Moving the king to an exposed square while ignoring a winning tactical opportunity for the opponent.
429.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their king (38% of moves are king moves) into an exposed or unsafe square, completely overlooking devastating tactical threats. The material signature shows 44% of moves hang material and 94% miss winning material, while Maia strongly recommends capturing with the queen (62%) or rook (38%) — indicating clear tactical wins were available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 50% swing from winning to losing and 25% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 672 centipawns. The OPUS analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif (50%), with exposed_king tagged repeatedly. Concrete examples show kings walking to fatally exposed squares (Ka2 allowing Rxa3+, Kb3 into tactical nets, Kxf1 missing queen captures) where the player's king move either created or failed to address an immediate tactical crisis. The pattern is a player who reflexively moves their king — often looking like a natural escape or recapture — while completely blind to the opponent's forcing tactical sequences exploiting that very king exposure.

430.label: Player plays a quiet or non-forcing move instead of delivering a check or checkmate that was available.
430.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in the middlegame with an exposed enemy king, plays a quiet rook or queen move instead of a forcing check or mating sequence. The key integrated signals are: (1) Maia's recommended move gives check 100% of the time and frequently captures material (46% pawn captures, plus pieces), while the player's move gives check only 34% and captures nothing 66% of the time—indicating the player chose a passive move over a forcing one. (2) The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 683 centipawns, with 20% of cases flipping from winning to losing, consistent with missing a decisive tactical blow. (3) The Opus analysis confirms dominant king_safety motifs (80%), with tags like missed_tactic, mating_net, forced_mate_missed, and exposed_king appearing repeatedly. The example summaries explicitly describe missed checkmates in one, missed forced mates in three, and missed discovered checks. The player had a winning attack against an exposed king but played a non-forcing move (often a rook or queen repositioning), allowing the opponent to escape the mating net entirely.

427.label: Player makes a greedy or impulsive capture/check instead of executing a clearly winning continuation, throwing away the game.
427.description: This feature fires on positions where a player in a winning or advantageous position makes a superficially attractive move—often a check (44% checks) or a queen/rook capture—that loses massive material (median net -5.0, median eval lost 1073cp) by overlooking a simpler, decisive continuation. The eval trajectory shows 44% winning->losing and 11% winning->drawn, indicating these are predominantly thrown wins rather than errors in already-lost positions. The Opus analysis reveals the core pattern: players grab a rook or give a flashy check when a trivially winning move (like capturing an undefended queen, or maintaining a mating attack) was available. Tags like 'checks_without_purpose', 'unnecessary_sacrifice', 'missed_simple_win', and 'undefended_queen' all point to the same cognitive error—the player is seduced by an immediate tactical reward (a capture or check) rather than calculating the objectively strongest line. The 67% missed-winning-material rate confirms these positions had clear wins available. This distinguishes it from positional errors or endgame technique failures; these are middlegame/endgame positions where greed or impulsiveness overrides a winning plan.

432.label: Passive king or pawn moves in endgames that waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or advance.
432.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a slow, non-forcing king move (67%) or pawn push (25%) that squanders a vital tempo. The positions are overwhelmingly endgame (92%), and the material signature shows no captures — these are 'safe' moves in the immediate sense (83%) but strategically catastrophic. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (38%), passed_pawn (25%), and king_safety (25%), with rook_endgame and endgame_technique as recurring tags. The eval trajectory shows most positions were already losing (75% losing->losing) but the median cost of ~298 centipawns indicates these moves dramatically worsen the situation or extinguish any remaining defensive chances (17% drawn->losing). The concrete examples consistently show kings retreating when they should capture or advance, and pawns pushing without creating threats when the opponent has a passed pawn requiring immediate attention. The Maia engine's preferred moves frequently involve captures (75% pawn captures), confirming that the mistake is choosing a passive temporizing move over an active one in time-critical endgame positions.

431.label: Passive or structurally misguided pawn moves in the opening that surrender central control or block key development.
431.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn (and occasionally bishop) moves that appear safe materially (86% safe, median net material 0.0) but cause severe positional damage, costing a median of 245 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert winning positions to drawn (35%) or drawn positions to losing (35%), indicating squandered advantages through positional misunderstanding rather than tactical blunders. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are positional mistakes (38%), tempo loss (25%), and missed tactics (25%), with recurring tags of blocked d-pawns, failed development, and surrendered center control. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: players make seemingly quiet pawn advances (e5-e4 closing the center, b6 weakening the king, b6xa5 taking the wrong pawn) or passive bishop placements (Bd6 blocking own pawn) when Maia consistently recommends active pawn captures (100% pawn captures). These are opening decisions where players choose structure-damaging passivity over the available dynamic pawn captures that would maintain tension or win material.

433.label: Queen captures a pawn and becomes trapped or allows a devastating tactical response.
433.description: This feature identifies positions where the player's queen (86% of moves) captures a pawn (93% of captures) in the opening or middlegame, only to find itself trapped or exposed to tactical punishment. The top boards overwhelmingly show queens venturing to grab b2, d4, or c3 pawns—classic 'poisoned pawn' scenarios. The tags confirm this: 'pawn_grab_punished' appears repeatedly alongside 'trapped_piece' (40% of motifs) and 'tempo_loss'. The eval trajectory is devastating: 93% of the time a winning tactic was missed (Maia's preferred moves are quiet developing moves like knight, bishop, or king moves), and the median cost is 322 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions into losing ones (41% drawn->losing). The material outcome appears 'safe' (48%) or a 'trade' (36%) because the queen successfully takes the pawn, but the positional consequence—being trapped or allowing forks/discovered attacks—is catastrophic. The example summaries explicitly describe queens abandoning critical squares to grab pawns, enabling forcing tactical sequences.

428.label: A pawn move that fatally weakens the defense of a key knight, allowing tactical exploitation through overloaded defenders or pins.
428.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a seemingly quiet pawn move (42% pawn moves) that catastrophically undermines their piece coordination, specifically the defense of a critical knight. The material signature shows 62% 'safe' moves with 31% 'hangs'—these aren't captures gone wrong but quiet moves that leave pieces tactically vulnerable. The eval trajectory is severe (median 322cp lost, with 35% drawn->losing and 15% winning->drawn), indicating these are game-deciding mistakes. The Opus analysis reveals the core mechanism: overloaded defenders (50%) and pins (50%) are the dominant exploitation motifs. The top boards show a striking pattern—Italian Game and similar opening structures where b2-b3 or similar pawn pushes remove critical support from c3/f3 knights, or moves like f7-f6/d7-d6 that weaken king-side structure. Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%), suggesting the correct plan involved active knight play rather than the passive pawn moves chosen. The positions are predominantly opening (69%) and middlegame (31%), where piece coordination is paramount and a single weakening pawn move can expose tactical catastrophes.

434.label: Player wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent pawn or piece move while an active enemy rook demands immediate tactical response.
434.description: This feature captures a highly specific recurring mistake pattern: in middlegame positions where the opponent has an active rook (often invading on the 2nd/7th rank or controlling open files), the player makes a slow, non-urgent move—typically a pawn push (25%) or quiet piece move—that constitutes a pure tempo loss. The material signature shows these moves are roughly split between 'safe' (50%) and 'hangs' (46%), meaning about half the time the tempo waste directly allows the opponent to win material. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'tempo_loss' as the dominant motif (57%), supported by tags like rook_on_seventh, rook_invasion, and piece_activity. The eval trajectory is severe (median 251cp lost), with many positions swinging from drawn-to-losing (23%) or winning-to-losing (12%), indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-decisive blunders. Critically, Maia's recommended move is almost always a rook move (98%), suggesting the correct response involves engaging one's own rook to counter the opponent's active piece, but instead the player ignores the threat with a passive pawn push (a4, h3, b3, a3) or positional sideline. The boards consistently show enemy rooks on the 2nd rank or invading files, and the player's move fails to address this urgent tactical reality.

436.label: Playing a flashy check instead of capturing a hanging piece or finishing a forced mate.
436.description: This feature fires when players deliver a check (100% of activations) — usually with the queen (70%) — that either hangs material (50%) or is merely safe but suboptimal (30%), while the best move (Maia's recommendation) was to capture a major piece (rook 50%, queen 40%, knight 10%). The eval trajectory shows most cases remain winning->winning (60%), indicating the check doesn't always throw the game, but the 'missed winning material' flag fires 100% of the time, confirming a concrete capture was available. The Opus analysis tags ('unnecessary_check', 'checks_arent_always_best', 'hanging_piece') and example summaries explicitly describe players choosing spectacular checks over simple winning captures — sometimes delaying a forced mate, sometimes throwing it away entirely. The boards show positions rich with undefended enemy pieces where the player opted for a check rather than collecting free material, embodying the classic amateur mistake that 'not all checks are good checks.'

435.label: In losing endgames, plays a safe pawn move while overlooking an obvious free capture of an opponent's hanging piece.
435.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern in endgame positions where the player, already in a losing position, pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% safe/non-hanging) while completely missing an available capture of a hanging piece. The Maia analysis confirms that the best move was consistently a king capturing a bishop (100% king moves, 100% bishop captures), and the missed winning material flag fires at 100%. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (83%), with tags like 'missed_capture' and 'endgame_technique' reinforcing that these are straightforward one-move oversights rather than deep tactical misses. The eval trajectory shows these occur in already-losing positions (losing->losing 100%) but the median 338cp further loss indicates these missed captures would have significantly improved defensive chances or even created holdable positions (e.g., transitioning into defensible pawn endgames). The concrete positions show scenarios like a king directly attacking an undefended bishop, or a piece sitting en prise, where the player instead makes a routine-looking pawn advance, seemingly on autopilot in a difficult endgame rather than scanning for tactical opportunities.

438.label: Premature bishop sacrifice with check that wins a pawn but loses the piece with no compensation.
438.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake pattern: the player sacrifices a bishop (100% bishop moves) to capture a pawn (100% pawn captures) while delivering check (100%), but ends up slightly down in material (median -2.0, consistent with losing a bishop for one pawn). The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 283 centipawns, often turning drawn positions into losing ones (67%). The tactical analysis confirms these are unsound sacrifices — the check creates the illusion of a dangerous attack, but the opponent's king easily finds safety, leaving the sacrificer down a full minor piece with insufficient compensation. The top boards reveal the classic patterns: Bxf2+ or Bxf7+ in the opening, where the bishop grabs an f-pawn with check but the resulting position offers no real attacking chances. Maia's recommended moves (knight moves, no captures, no checks) represent solid developing alternatives that maintain material equality. This is a tactical miscalculation where players overestimate the value of a check and underestimate the cost of a full piece.

437.label: Player leaves their queen en prise on an open diagonal, allowing a bishop to capture it.
437.description: This feature captures a specific and recurring blunder pattern in the opening and early middlegame (72% opening phase) where the player places or leaves their queen on an undefended square that lies on an open diagonal controlled by the opponent's bishop. The material signature is stark: 78% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median loss of 6.0 material units (i.e., a queen), and the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 504 centipawns. The piece moved is overwhelmingly the queen (54%), and the tactical motif is 100% hanging_piece with recurring tags like queen_hanging, undefended_piece, and open_diagonal. The Opus analysis consistently describes the same scenario: the player overlooks that a long diagonal (often c1-h6 or a3-f8) is completely open and their queen sits directly in the crosshairs of the opponent's dark-squared bishop. Maia's recommended moves (75% queen moves) suggest the correct play was simply to move the queen to safety. This is not a complex tactical oversight but an elementary one-move blindness to diagonal geometry, predominantly punished in opening positions where bishops still command their natural diagonals.

441.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move instead of an available forcing continuation that exploits the opponent's vulnerability.
441.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a safe but passive piece move (no capture, no check, nothing hangs) that squanders a significant advantage—median 209 centipawns lost, with 50% of cases going from winning to drawn. The material signature shows diverse piece moves (rook, bishop, king, knight) that are all 'safe' but miss Maia's recommended forcing moves (75% rook moves, 50% giving check). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (40%) and missed_tactic (20%), with recurring tags like second_rank_invasion, missed_check, and timing_error. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: the player had an available check or invasion (e.g., Rd2+ invading the second rank) that would have maintained a winning tempo, but instead chose a passive retreat or repositioning move (e.g., Rd7, Bf6, Kh4) that allowed the opponent to consolidate. This is fundamentally a timing/tempo error—choosing a 'quiet' move when the position demanded immediate forcing action.

446.label: Player moves a piece away, leaving a bishop hanging on a key diagonal.
446.description: This feature fires when a player makes a non-capturing move (85% no capture) that hangs a piece (56% hangs outcome, median -1.0 material loss), while the best move was consistently to capture or save a bishop (Maia's move: bishop 100%, Maia captures: bishop 100%). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (70%), with recurring tags like undefended_piece, long_diagonal, and removal_of_defender. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 412cp lost), often turning drawn positions into losing ones (38% drawn->losing). The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: the player relocates a knight, pawn, or other piece without first resolving diagonal tension or defending a bishop that is en prise or about to become so. In many cases an overloaded defender or tempo loss compounds the error, leaving a bishop (often on a long diagonal like a1-h8 or a8-h1) fatally exposed after the move.

442.label: Moving the king instead of capturing or defending, leaving a piece en prise to a queen capture.
442.description: This feature captures a specific recurring blunder pattern: the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a non-capture, non-check manner that hangs material (net median -2.0 pawns), while the best move involved a bishop capturing an opponent's queen (Maia's recommendation: bishop captures queen 100%). The positions are all middlegame (100%) where the player was already winning but missed a tactic—typically a hanging piece (75% motif) or back-rank theme (25%). The eval trajectory shows winning->winning with a median loss of 210 centipawns, meaning these are significant missed opportunities that squander advantage without immediately losing the game. The common tags (missed_tactic, tempo_loss, hanging_piece, piece_activity) confirm the player made an unnecessary or defensive king move when a forcing capture was available, losing critical tempo and material. The boards consistently show positions where a piece is left undefended after the king sidesteps, allowing the opponent to recover material they should have lost.

440.label: Player mishandles pawn promotion or advancing passed pawns, losing critical tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
440.description: This feature captures positions where players make errors related to pawn promotion and tempo in late middlegame/endgame positions. The material signature shows pawns as the most common piece moved (36%), with 46% of moves hanging material and a high median eval loss of 331 centipawns. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (50%) and tempo_loss (50%), with recurring tags of passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and king_safety. The trajectory shows wins being thrown away (winning->drawn 18%, winning->losing 18%, drawn->losing 18%), indicating these are decisive mistakes in otherwise manageable positions. The top boards confirm this: positions with advanced passed pawns (c7c8q promoting to wrong piece, g6g7 losing tempo, positions with pawns on the 6th/7th rank) where the player either promotes incorrectly, advances without proper preparation, or loses a crucial tempo that allows the opponent to activate. Maia's preferred moves frequently involve captures of major pieces (rook 36%, queen 18%), suggesting the correct moves often involved winning material that the promotion/tempo error missed.

445.label: In rook endgames, a purposeless king move wastes critical tempo and hangs material to an opposing rook check.
445.description: This feature captures a specific rook endgame mistake where the player makes a non-improving king move (king moved 100% of the time, no captures) that hangs material (net median -5.0, typically a whole rook). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 444cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (43%) and hanging_piece (29%), with rook_endgame appearing as the most common tag (5 occurrences). The Opus summaries consistently describe the same mistake—moving the king aimlessly when the rook needed immediate attention, allowing the opponent's rook to deliver a winning check (Maia's response is always a rook check, 100%). The concrete positions show endgames with rooks and pawns where the player's king wanders while their rook or a critical pawn is left en prise, allowing the opponent to win decisive material with a forcing rook move.

439.label: Moving the queen to a passive square instead of capturing or continuing a winning tactical sequence.
439.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves their queen (75%) or rook (25%) to a passive or irrelevant square, abandoning an active tactical threat. The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe' (nothing is immediately hung), yet 75% of the time the player misses winning material — typically a capture (Maia recommends capturing a bishop 75% or pawn 25%). The eval trajectory reveals a massive median loss of 494 centipawns, with positions going from winning to drawn or remaining winning but with drastically reduced advantage.
