The tactical motifs—missed_tactic, back_rank threats, tempo_loss, and king_safety—reveal that the missed bishop moves would have exploited concrete attacking themes (back-rank mates, checks, discovered attacks on open files). The players were distracted by materialistic pawn grabs or routine queen repositioning when a forcing bishop move would have been decisive.

570.label: Moving a major piece away from a critical defensive task, leaving the king or key squares fatally unguarded.
570.description: This feature captures moves where a player relocates a major piece (rook 46%, queen 38%) to an irrelevant or ambitious square while neglecting an urgent defensive obligation—typically king safety or protection of a vulnerable piece. The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly non-captures (85%) that are nominally 'safe' (69%) or outright hang material (23%), meaning the piece itself isn't lost but the repositioning creates a tactical catastrophe elsewhere. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 324cp lost), frequently flipping drawn positions to losing (31%) or throwing wins (15% winning→drawn), confirming these are game-deciding errors rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical motifs—king_safety (29%), hanging_piece (14%), discovered_attack (14%), fork (14%)—along with tags like 'exposed_king', 'tempo_loss', and 'queen_offside' reveal the mechanism: the moved piece was performing a defensive function (guarding the king, covering a square, maintaining back-rank pressure) and its departure allows immediate tactical exploitation. The Opus analyses consistently describe queens moved away from defensive duties (Qc6 leaving f2 unguarded, Qa6 ignoring an undefended bishop), rooks sent to irrelevant files (Rce1 when the king needed Ne5), and pieces repositioned where they can be attacked with tempo. Maia's suggested moves (knight 38%, queen 23%) indicate the engine wanted defensive consolidation or counterplay maintenance rather than the ambitious but misguided redeployment the player chose.

576.label: Unprepared pawn advances in the opening that hang material or lose critical tempo.
576.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players make pawn moves (56% pawn, plus bishop development to bad squares at 33%) that are not captures (100% no capture) but hang material (78% hangs, median net material -2.0). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions to losing ones (67%) or worsen already losing positions (33%), with a median cost of 249 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: 'premature_pawn_advance' appears repeatedly in the tags, with examples like 8...b5 and 4...b5 being flank operations that ignore development, leave pieces exposed to tempo-gaining attacks, or simply drop pawns. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 33%, positional_mistake 33%, tempo_loss 17%) and tags (development, piece_activity, premature_pawn_advance) all converge on the same theme: players push pawns too early without adequate piece support, neglecting fundamentals like castling and development, resulting in material loss through tactical vulnerabilities created by the advance itself.

572.label: Giving a check with the queen in an endgame that allows the opponent to capture or neutralize it, throwing away a winning position.
572.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player delivers a check (100% check rate) predominantly with the queen (67% queen moves), but the check is catastrophically ill-conceived—resulting in material loss (44% loses, 44% hangs) with a median net material of -8.0 (roughly a queen's worth). The eval trajectory confirms these are predominantly thrown wins: 44% winning->winning (still damaged), 22% winning->drawn, 11% winning->losing, with a massive median eval loss of 506 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: premature promotions to queen that immediately hang to adjacent kings (30% promotion_error), pawn endgame simplification errors (30%), and queen checks that leave the queen en prise (hanging_piece 20%). The common thread across all positions is delivering a tempting check—either via promotion (d7d8q+, c7c8q+, g2g1q+) or queen movement (g4g5+, h2h8+, g1g8+)—without verifying that the checking piece survives. Tags like king_proximity and tempo_loss confirm the opponent's king is close enough to simply capture the offending piece. The player prioritizes the lure of check over basic piece safety in simplified positions.

574.label: In won endgames with passed pawns, the player makes an aimless king or pawn move instead of executing the critical promotion sequence.
574.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (88%) where the player has a passed pawn ready to promote but squanders the win through a tempo-losing king move (75% king moves) or passive pawn push (25%). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 888cp lost), with 50% converting wins into losses and the rest deepening already-lost positions. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are passed_pawn (50%) and promotion_error (25%), with tempo_loss appearing in 7/8 tagged positions. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: the player has an advanced passed pawn (often on the 6th or 7th rank) but plays a king shuffle or irrelevant move instead of the single critical tempo move needed to promote—whether that's pushing the pawn, supporting it with the king on the correct square, or executing a promotion tactic like an underpromotion fork. The Maia suggestions (50% pawn, 38% knight) confirm the engine wanted direct pawn promotion or a knight maneuver supporting the queening plan. This is fundamentally a failure to calculate the promotion race correctly in simplified endgames.

575.label: Misplacing a bishop on a square where it hangs to a simple pawn capture, squandering a drawn or winning position.
575.description: This feature detects a specific recurring blunder pattern where a player develops or repositions a bishop (67% bishop moves) to a square that is immediately vulnerable to a pawn capture or simple tactical sequence. The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly 'hangs' (67%) — non-capture moves that drop a piece — with a median cost of -1.0 material and a massive 548 centipawn eval loss, typically converting drawn positions into losing ones (67%) or winning positions into drawn ones (33%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (57%) with recurring tags like 'bishop_misplacement' and 'undefended_piece'. The concrete examples are strikingly consistent: Be6 hanging to cxd5/exd5, Bd3 hanging to dxe4, Be2 missing a capture on an undefended queen — all cases where the player ignores central pawn tension or immediate tactical threats and places a bishop on a square controlled by an enemy pawn. Maia's recommended moves (67% pawn captures) confirm that the refutation is typically a straightforward pawn take. This occurs predominantly in the opening (67%), suggesting players are following familiar development patterns without recognizing the specific tactical vulnerability created by unresolved central tension.

577.label: Player makes a safe-looking move while missing a simple back-rank checkmate in one.
577.description: This feature fires when players miss a trivially available back-rank mate (or mate in one) by playing a move that appears reasonable but throws away an instant win. The material/position signature shows the played moves are materially safe (80% safe outcomes) and involve no captures (40% capture nothing), while Maia consistently identifies a rook capture delivering check — pointing to a missed Rx?# back-rank pattern. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 60% of cases flip from losing to winning (from the opponent's perspective the player handed back a won game), with a median eval loss of ~103 pawns (i.e., missed mate). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is back_rank (80%), with tags like missed_mate_in_one, back_rank_mate, and trapped_king appearing repeatedly. Players are seduced by 'strong-looking' infiltrations, reflexive captures of hanging pieces, or purposeless moves while a simple rook or queen delivery on an open file against a pawn-entombed king goes completely unseen — a classic case of pattern blindness to the most elementary mating pattern in chess.

578.label: Moving the king to an inferior square that loses tempo or hangs material in positions that are already difficult.
578.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their king (67% of moves are king moves) to a suboptimal square, typically in endgame positions (67% endgame), resulting in material being hung (67% hangs) or a significant eval loss (median 286cp). The trajectory shows these are positions already difficult (67% losing->losing, 33% drawn->losing), meaning the king move converts a holdable or slowly-losing position into a hopeless one. The tactical analysis confirms this: in pawn endgames, the king retreats away from the critical action (e.g., Ke4 instead of Kg6 to contest passed pawns), surrendering the only saving plan. The dominant tags—tempo_loss (5), king_activity (3), and pawn_structure (4)—all point to the king moving to an irrelevant or dangerous square rather than maintaining active king placement. Even in non-endgame examples, pieces are placed on undefended squares (hanging_piece motif), but the unifying thread is a passive or misdirected piece placement that immediately drops material or positional compensation.

579.label: Advancing a pawn in the endgame that overlooks tactical threats, hanging material or missing critical defensive/offensive tactics.
579.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players push pawns (93% pawn moves) in endgame or late middlegame positions, and the move hangs material (57% hangs) rather than addressing urgent tactical threats. The median cost is 313 centipawns, frequently converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (29% drawn->losing, 21% winning->drawn, 14% winning->losing). The tactical motifs reveal that these pawn pushes ignore king safety issues (33%), forks (17%), back-rank threats (17%), and promotion errors (17%). The tags reinforce this: tempo_loss and passed_pawn appear frequently, suggesting players are fixated on advancing passed pawns or making 'progress' while overlooking that their king or pieces are tactically vulnerable. Maia's best moves are often rooks or knights delivering check (50% check rate), indicating the opponent had powerful tactical resources that the passive pawn push completely ignored. The concrete positions confirm this—players push pawns like e3, a3, b6, h3, f7 while missing captures with check, knight forks, or mating threats that punish their exposed kings.

582.label: Player overlooks a winning fork or combination, allowing the opponent a devastating tactical sequence.
582.description: This feature fires when players make moves that overlook critical tactical opportunities involving forks, king safety exploitation, and hanging pieces. The material signature shows 46% safe moves and 27% hangs—these aren't exchanges but rather moves that either passively allow tactics or directly blunder material. The median eval loss of 343 centipawns is substantial, with the trajectory showing positions transitioning from winning/drawn to losing (winning->losing 10%, winning->drawn 10%, drawn->losing 12%), indicating players are throwing away advantageous or equal positions. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are forks (33%), king safety (33%), and hanging pieces (33%), with tags like knight_fork, exposed_king, capture_with_check, and missed_tactic. The concrete positions confirm this: players make quiet or irrelevant moves (like f8g8, a8c8, or piece retreats) while missing that their opponent has a fork, a check-and-capture sequence, or that their own king is fatally exposed. The 68% missed winning material rate further confirms these are positions where a strong tactical blow existed but the player chose a passive or misdirected move instead, failing to recognize the geometric threats on the board.

581.label: Knight delivers a check that hangs the piece to an obvious recapture, squandering a winning position.
581.description: This feature identifies a specific and recurring blunder pattern: a player in a winning opening position impulsively plays a knight check (100% knight moves, 100% checks) that leaves the knight en prise with no compensation. The material signature shows the piece is simply 'hung' (not a trade or exchange) with a median loss of 3.0 material points (a full knight). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic damage — every instance flips from winning to losing, with a median swing of 518 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying cognitive error: players see a tempting check or apparent fork (tags: premature_attack, check_is_not_always_best, failed_fork, piece_sacrifice_unsound) but overlook that the target square is defended by a piece they failed to account for — typically a queen or bishop that simply recaptures. The boards confirm this in the opening phase, where knights leap aggressively to squares like c7, e5, f5, or b5 delivering check or threatening forks, only to be captured immediately. The player overestimates the value of giving check and underestimates the defender's straightforward recapture resources.

583.label: Knight captures or moves that expose critical tactical vulnerabilities, turning equal or winning positions into lost ones.
583.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves a knight (50%) or queen (38%) to capture an enemy knight (62%), but the capture exposes a devastating tactical flaw—typically a hanging piece (50%), discovered attack (25%), or king safety issue (25%). The material signature shows these moves are frequently trades (38%) or outright losses (38%) with a median net material of -2.0, indicating the player captures something but loses more in return. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 38% go from drawn to losing and 38% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 504 centipawns. The concrete positions confirm this pattern—knights are moved away from defensive duties (e.g., unblocking a diagonal for an enemy queen, abandoning protection of key squares) in exchange for capturing a piece, only to find the resulting position tactically collapsing. The Opus analysis repeatedly notes missed tactics and the theme of pieces that were serving critical defensive or blocking roles being exchanged away prematurely.

580.label: Retreating a bishop to a passive square instead of executing a forcing tactical sequence, allowing the opponent a devastating fork or trap.
580.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening mistake pattern where a player retreats their bishop (49% bishop moves) to a passive square—most commonly Ba5—instead of playing a forcing continuation like a capture or check. The Maia best move is universally a bishop capture on a knight with check (100% bishop, 100% captures knight, 100% check), indicating the player missed a forcing tactical sequence. The dominant motifs (fork 33%, trapped_piece 33%, tempo_loss 33%) and recurring tags (tempo_loss, hanging_piece, trapped_piece) confirm that these passive retreats squander critical tempo, leaving the bishop vulnerable to being trapped or allowing the opponent to execute a fork. The eval trajectory is severe: 49% of cases convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 352 centipawns, indicating these are not minor inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders. The phase is overwhelmingly opening (92%), and the concrete positions repeatedly show the pattern of Ba5 retreats in Nimzo-Indian or similar structures where Bxc3+ was the correct forcing move. The material signature shows 38% 'hangs' because the passively-placed bishop frequently becomes a tactical target.

584.label: Trading a powerfully placed knight for a passive piece, surrendering a winning tactical advantage.
584.description: This feature fires when players voluntarily trade away a dominant knight that holds critical tactical pressure (forks, outposts, or attacking potential). The material signature shows knight moves (50%) that are mostly 'safe' or 'trade' outcomes—not outright blunders but suboptimal exchanges. Maia consistently recommends keeping the knight (90% knight moves that maintain position), and 95% of activations miss winning material. The eval trajectory is severe: median 325cp lost, with 40% of cases converting a winning position to drawn, indicating the trade dissipates a decisive advantage. The tactical analysis confirms this: 'fork' and 'missed_tactic' dominate the motifs, with tags like 'piece_activity', 'knight_superiority', and 'tempo_loss' recurring. The example summaries explicitly describe trading dominating knights (e.g., a knight on e6 with a fork on c7, or a pressuring knight on c5) for passive bishops, collapsing winning positions into equality. The boards show knights on powerful central/advanced squares (e6, d7, c5, d5) being exchanged or relocated when they should be maintained for tactical domination.

585.label: Giving a purposeless check with the queen that loses tempo and allows the opponent to improve their position.
585.description: This feature identifies positions where a player delivers a check with their queen (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that accomplishes nothing strategically. The material signature shows these are non-captures (100% capture: none) that are often safe in material terms but wasteful in tempo. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags these as tempo_loss (80%) with 'pointless_check' being the most common tag (3 occurrences). The eval trajectory reveals that while the median cost is only 8 centipawns, 44% of the time winning material was missed—often including forced mates. The concrete examples show a recurring pattern: in queen-vs-rook endgames or winning positions, the player impulsively checks the king rather than executing the winning plan (capturing hanging material, maintaining a mating net, or coordinating pieces). The check displaces the queen from an active post, allows the opponent's king to centralize or escape, and lets hanging pieces find safety with tempo. Maia's suggested moves (67% pawn moves, 22% queen, 11% rook) confirm that quiet consolidating or capturing moves were far superior to the flashy but hollow check.

586.label: Neglecting critical central development in the opening by playing non-developing or flank moves that forfeit initiative.
586.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (87% opening) where the player makes a move that is materially safe (93% safe) but catastrophically wasteful in terms of tempo and development. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 344 centipawns, frequently converting winning or equal positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 40%, drawn->losing 27%, winning->losing 13%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (56%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, development, and piece_activity. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: players make flank pawn pushes (b4), passive piece moves (Qe2, Be7, Qc7), or premature piece sorties (Na5) when urgent central action (typically d4 or d5) was required. The Maia baseline (100% pawn moves) confirms that simple developing pawn moves were the natural best responses. The positions almost universally feature Italian Game or similar open-game structures where the center is contested and one tempo of delay allows the opponent's pieces to seize critical diagonals or central squares.

587.label: Black makes a developing or non-defensive move in the opening while White's Qh5+Bc4 battery threatens checkmate on f7.
587.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: Black faces a Scholar's Mate threat (White's queen on h5 combined with bishop on c4 targeting f7) and plays a move that completely ignores the immediate checkmate or winning tactical threat. The top 10 boards all show the identical Qh5+Bc4 battery structure, with Black responding with developing moves like Nc6, Qf6, Nf6, Ke7, or Nh6 instead of addressing the f7 vulnerability. The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions turning decisively losing (median 338cp loss), consistent with missing a forced tactic rather than a gradual positional error. The dominant motifs (king_safety 62%, with tags like scholars_mate, checkmate_in_one, missed_tactic) confirm the pattern is specifically about failing to defend against the classic f7 mating attack. The material signature shows these are non-captures (100% no capture) in the opening phase (100%), where the 'best' move according to Maia would have been a simple pawn move (likely ...g6 or ...Qe7) to address the threat.

588.label: Placing a minor piece on an undefended square where it is immediately captured for free in the opening.
588.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: during the opening phase (72% opening, 28% middlegame), the player moves a bishop (56%) or knight (22%) to a square that is directly attacked by an opponent's piece, leaving it completely undefended and hanging. The material signature confirms this with 83% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) and a median net material loss of -3.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings—37% of cases go from drawn to losing—with a median loss of 438 centipawns, consistent with dropping an uncompensated piece. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies the 'hanging_piece' motif (100%), with supporting tags like 'opening_blunder', 'development_error', and 'undefended_piece'. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: bishops placed on e5, f5, c5, or d6 where opponent knights on known squares capture them immediately. This is not a complex tactical oversight but a simple one-move piece-safety blindspot during development, where the player fails to verify that the destination square is adequately defended.

589.label: Trading an advanced attacking pawn for a passive defender's pawn, dissipating a winning kingside initiative.
589.description: This feature fires when a player trades an advanced, strategically powerful pawn (almost always on the 6th or 7th rank) by capturing a defender's pawn sideways, rather than maintaining the pawn's pressure or finding a stronger tactical continuation. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves capturing pawns in an equal exchange (net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 315cp), with positions going from winning to drawn or losing. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: dominant motifs are king_safety and promotion_error, with tags like tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and advanced_pawn_misuse. The boards show a recurring theme of f6xg7 or f3xg2 captures where the advanced pawn was a spearhead of the attack (e.g., a pawn on f6 threatening the king), and trading it off relieves all pressure on the opponent's king. The correct moves were typically tactical strikes (Nxg5, Bxh7+, f2+) that exploited the pawn's advanced position rather than cashing it in for an equal trade that eliminates the attacking potential.

591.label: Neglecting development or central tension in the opening, allowing opponent to win material through simple captures.
591.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player makes a pawn or bishop move that hangs material (71% hangs, median -1.0 material) instead of addressing immediate tactical threats. The eval trajectory is consistently drawn->losing with a median loss of 278 centipawns, indicating these moves turn equal positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis reveals tempo_loss (43%) and hanging_piece (29%) as dominant motifs, with recurring tags of development violations, missed tactics, and central tension mismanagement. The concrete positions show a clear pattern: in open e-pawn positions (Scotch, Philidor, Italian structures), the player makes a slow or misguided pawn push (c6, c5, h6, f6) or retreats a piece (Bb6) that ignores an undefended central pawn or allows a clean capture. Maia consistently identifies simple pawn captures as the refutation (100% pawn captures). These are not complex tactical oversights but fundamental opening principle violations—making non-developing moves while material is tactically loose in the center.

590.label: Giving a wasteful rook check in a winning endgame instead of executing the winning plan (capturing material or promoting).
590.description: This feature detects a specific recurring endgame mistake where a player delivers a rook check (rook moved 100%, check given 100%) that is materially safe but tactically purposeless. The positions are uniformly endgames (100%) where the player is winning, yet the opponent's best reply captures the rook (Maia takes rook 100%), meaning the check either allows an unwanted trade or squanders a decisive advantage. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 438 centipawns, typically collapsing a winning position into merely winning or drawn (75% winning->winning, 25% winning->drawn). The tactical analysis reveals the core motifs: unnecessary checks that lose tempo (tempo_loss tagged in all 4 positions), missed promotions (promotion_error in 33%), and failure to capture hanging pieces. The top boards confirm the pattern — positions with advanced passed pawns or undefended enemy pieces where the player reflexively gives check with the rook instead of executing the straightforward win (capturing a free piece, promoting a pawn, or simplifying). This is the classic 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' syndrome in technically won endgames.

592.label: Player captures or moves a major piece to grab material (often a pawn) while neglecting a stronger tactical continuation or positional priority, allowing the opponent to exploit tempo, forks, or king safety.
592.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a queen or rook (69% combined) to grab a pawn or pursue a minor material gain, but the move hangs the piece or loses significant value (44% hangs, 6% loses outright). The median eval cost is 291 centipawns, and 81% of the time the player missed winning material via a superior tactical shot. The Opus analysis confirms motifs of tempo loss (33%), fork vulnerability (33%), and king safety neglect (33%), with tags like 'material_grab_punished', 'misplaced_queen', and 'back_rank'. Concrete examples show a queen stranding itself on a7 to capture a pawn when Qxc8 won a rook, and a rook grabbing the a2 pawn while ignoring defensive needs. The eval trajectory shows these aren't just deepening already-lost positions—12% go from winning to drawn or drawn to losing—indicating the greed actively squanders advantages. The pattern is a player prioritizing a small material gain over the stronger tactical or positional move, leaving their piece misplaced and vulnerable to punishment.

593.label: Player makes a developing or pawn move in the opening that leaves a piece undefended, allowing a simple capture or tactical exploitation.
593.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern where players in the opening phase (70% opening) make moves—primarily pawn pushes (35%) and knight moves (25%)—that hang material (60% of moves result in a hang, median net material loss of -1.0 piece). The eval trajectory is devastating: 60% of the time a drawn position becomes losing, with a median loss of 418 centipawns. The tactical layer reveals that players overlook hanging pieces (29%), king safety threats (43%), and forks (29%), often losing tempo or missing simple tactics. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly knight moves (90%), suggesting the correct response was typically a knight retreat or repositioning to address the hanging piece. The top boards confirm the pattern: castling without addressing an undefended knight (position 1), making an illusory fork that actually loses material (position 2), removing a defensive piece that exposes the king (position 3), and pushing pawns that allow tactical exploitation of undefended pieces. The common thread is that players make natural-looking developing moves or pawn advances without noticing that a piece is left tactically vulnerable, transforming otherwise playable positions into lost ones.

594.label: Capturing on e7 with a pawn in the opening instead of continuing development, fatally weakening king safety.
594.description: This feature fires on a specific opening mistake where a player uses a pawn to capture a knight on e7 (or similar square) as a trade, but in doing so squanders a winning position by neglecting development and king safety. The material signature shows pawn captures knight as a 'trade' (net ~2.0, suggesting approximate material equality after recapture), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic swing from winning to losing (median 513cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the core error: king_safety dominates (83% of motifs), with tags emphasizing missed tactics, development, tempo loss, and piece activity. The top boards consistently show early opening positions (move 5-9) where the player greedily captures material (often dxe7) instead of playing simple developing moves like Nc3, Nf3, Bf4, or e3. The Opus summaries confirm that 3+ solid developing moves were available, each within 1 centipawn of optimal. The player chose a superficially tempting pawn capture that disrupted their own development tempo and exposed critical king-safety weaknesses, transforming a comfortable opening advantage into a lost position.

598.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured for free.
598.description: This feature detects moves where a player places a piece (typically a knight, rook, or bishop) on a square where it is immediately en prise, resulting in the loss of material. The material signature is stark: 90% of moves are classified as 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -3.0 (approximately a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing blunders, with 24% converting winning positions to drawn and 21% converting drawn positions to losing, with a median eval loss of 305 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs are 'hanging_piece' (40%) and 'tempo_loss' (40%), with common tags including piece_loss, undefended_bishop, and threats_ignored. The concrete examples show pieces moved to squares where they can be trivially captured—a knight jumping to a square covered by a pawn, a bishop placed where it is en prise, or a rook moved to a tactically vulnerable square without noticing the threat. These are single-move oversights where the player simply fails to check whether their destination square is safe.

595.label: Losing critical tempo in won or drawn endgames by allowing the opponent counterplay or escape squares.
595.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a move that appears safe (67% safe, no captures) but loses substantial evaluation (median 495cp lost), often converting wins into draws or draws into losses. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (appearing in 3/3 tagged examples) and hanging_piece, with passed_pawn context recurring. The concrete positions show players making moves that fail to maintain the precision required in simplified positions: checking from the wrong square allowing a king escape (b4 instead of b3), moving a knight while leaving the queen hanging, promoting to a queen that allows a fortress, or making a rook move that surrenders a winning endgame. The common thread is that each move squanders a tempo-critical moment—the player had a winning or holding continuation but chose a move that gave the opponent just enough time or space to equalize or win. Maia consistently finds forcing moves (queen captures, checks) that the player missed.

596.label: Bishop or minor piece moves away from blocking or stopping a critical passed pawn in the endgame, allowing it to promote or decide the game.
596.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where a player moves a bishop (62% of the time) away from a critical defensive task related to a passed pawn. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (70% of positions, tagged in all 8 top examples), and the phase is overwhelmingly endgame (88%). The moves are typically 'safe' in material terms (75%) — nothing is immediately hung or traded — but the positional cost is catastrophic, with a median eval loss of 234 centipawns. The trajectory shows most cases go from losing to deeper losing (62%) or from drawn to losing (25%), indicating these are positions where precise technique was required and the player abandoned the one critical defensive resource (usually blockading or intercepting a passed pawn). The Opus analysis repeatedly highlights abandoned blockades, tempo losses, and narrow drawing margins where only one move held. The opponent's best response typically involves the king (75%), consistent with king-march promotion plans in pawn endgames. This is a failure of endgame understanding — not seeing that the minor piece's only job was to restrain the passed pawn.

597.label: Defensive moves that fail to address king vulnerability in already-losing positions.
597.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in losing positions make passive, non-capturing moves (100% no capture) — typically rook retreats or king moves (75% combined) — that fail to adequately address king safety concerns. The dominant motif is king_safety (62%), and the eval trajectory shows these occur predominantly when already losing (44% losing->losing), with a modest median cost of 24 centipawns but occasional catastrophic collapses into forced mate. The boards reveal kings under pressure (exposed on h6, g3, h5, g1 behind weakened pawns) where the player shuffles a rook or makes a quiet king move instead of finding the one critical defensive resource. Half the moves hang material outright, suggesting the 'safe-looking' retreat actually leaves pieces or squares undefended. The tempo_loss tag (most common) confirms these moves waste time when urgent action was needed, and Maia's alternatives often involve active piece play (knight moves 31%, captures 25%) rather than passive defense.

600.label: Player makes a passive or retreating move that wastes critical tempo, allowing the opponent's attack to intensify in already difficult positions.
600.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in already difficult positions (50% losing->losing, 17% drawn->losing) make passive moves that squander tempo rather than addressing concrete threats. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (58%) — these aren't outright blunders of material but positional mistakes where the player fails to find the one active defensive resource. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and king_safety (33%), with Maia consistently recommending queen moves (62%) as the correct alternative — suggesting the best defense required active counterplay with the queen rather than the passive piece shuffles actually played. The median cost of 326 centipawns reflects how a single wasted tempo in a tense opening/middlegame position (54% opening, 46% middlegame) can collapse a defensible position into a lost one. Concrete examples like Kd8 instead of developing, or retreating a bishop when the queen needed to act, illustrate players choosing 'safe-looking' but fundamentally passive moves when only sharp, precise activity could hold the position together.

599.label: Advancing a pawn in the opening that hangs material by ignoring a concrete tactical threat or weakening a critical square.

The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic—converting winning positions to drawn or drawn to losing (median 282cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players push pawns that either ignore an existing tactic (missed_tactic, ignored_tactic tags) or create fatal weaknesses (weakening_pawn_move, king_safety), while better developing or capturing moves were available. The top boards confirm this: 3.d4 ignoring a hanging pawn, 4...f5 weakening the kingside instead of capturing, and e2-e3/d2-d4 type moves that overlook concrete piece-level threats. The consistent pattern is a seemingly natural or developing pawn push in the opening that overlooks an immediate tactical reality, leaving a piece or pawn undefended.

602.label: Unsound knight sacrifice on f7 in the opening without sufficient compensation.

The material signature shows knight moves 100% of the time, often capturing a pawn (62%) but resulting in material loss (slightly_down 62%, hangs 38%, median -2.0), confirming the knight is sacrificed without adequate return. The eval trajectory is devastating—75% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 326 centipawns—indicating this isn't a marginal inaccuracy but a game-changing blunder disguised as an attack. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: tags like 'unsound_sacrifice' (5 occurrences), 'insufficient_compensation' (3), and 'premature_attack' (2) reveal that players launch a flashy Nxf7 hoping for king-side chaos or a fork, but the opponent's king simply captures and escapes safely, leaving the attacker down a full piece with no follow-up. All top 10 positions show this exact pattern in the opening phase, typically around moves 4-6, where development is insufficient to support the sacrifice.

605.label: Moving a bishop deep into enemy territory where it hangs to the opponent's queen.

The material signature shows 50% hangs and 50% slightly_down outcomes with a median net loss of -2.0 (a full piece minus a pawn in some cases). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes: 100% of cases transition from drawn positions to losing ones, with a median cost of 514 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (100%), with supporting tags like opening_blunder, piece_for_pawn, and queen_recapture. The top activating boards show a remarkably consistent pattern: the London System bishop on f4 being played to c7 (or analogously Bf5-c2) on move 3, walking directly into the opponent's queen on d8/d1. This represents a pattern recognition failure where the player sees an 'active' square for the bishop without noticing it is guarded by the queen.

Maia consistently finds the correct rook move that delivers check (100% Maia gives check), confirming these are missed mating attacks. The tactical analysis reveals dominant back_rank (50%) and king_safety (38%) motifs, with recurring tags of missed_mate, back_rank, and king_exposure. The examples paint a vivid picture: players capture pawns greedily, retreat rooks passively, or reposition aimlessly while a forced checkmate (often in 1-7 moves) sits on the board via check sequences exploiting the opponent's trapped or exposed king. The 'greed' tag appears where players prioritize material over mating patterns.

601.label: Player misses a critical forcing continuation in the opening, wasting tempo on passive development instead of exploiting a tactical opportunity.
601.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening mistake pattern where a player has built up a promising attacking position—often involving pressure on f7, aggressive piece placement, or a pawn breakthrough opportunity—but fails to play the one critical forcing move that capitalizes on the initiative. The material signature shows mostly safe, non-capturing moves (91% no capture, 96% safe) with bishops, pawns, and knights, indicating passive development choices rather than the sharp tactical strikes that were available. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 232 centipawns, confirming these are positions where a concrete advantage was squandered. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), likely the key pawn thrusts (e5, e6) that would have maintained the initiative. This is fundamentally a failure to convert opening preparation into concrete action—choosing quiet development when the position demanded immediate tactical follow-through.

604.label: Player retreats or passively moves their queen in the opening, missing a hanging piece or tactic that would have won significant material.

The material signature shows the player moves their queen 50% of the time without capturing anything (100% no capture), while Maia's recommended move would have captured material 57% of the time (mostly pawns, but also knights and rooks). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), indicating that opponent pieces are undefended and freely capturable, yet the player ignores them. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: 93% of positions involve missed winning material, with a median loss of 496 centipawns, typically converting a winning position into a drawn one (64% winning->drawn). The concrete positions show queens being retreated to passive squares (Qd8, Qd1, Qd3, Qe7, Qd7) while enemy pieces sit en prise. The tempo_loss tag (5 occurrences) reinforces that these moves waste time in critical opening positions where piece activity and development are paramount.

606.label: Player makes a safe-looking developing move in the opening that misses a concrete tactical blow, throwing away a winning advantage.
606.description: This feature captures opening-phase positions (71% opening) where the player has a significant advantage but plays a quiet, 'natural' move—often a queen, knight, or bishop development—instead of the one critical tactical continuation. The material signature shows the move itself is usually 'safe' (59%) meaning nothing is immediately lost, yet the eval trajectory reveals a massive cost: 41% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 269 centipawns. The Opus analysis consistently identifies missed concrete tactics (pins, hanging pieces, central pawn breaks like e5! or f4!) that would have exploited the opponent's vulnerable position. Maia overwhelmingly suggests simple pawn moves (94%), confirming these are positions where the engine's recommended aggressive pawn thrust (exploiting pins, attacking pieces, opening lines) is the unintuitive but crushing choice that the player overlooks in favor of routine development. The dominant motifs—pin exploitation, hanging pieces, tempo loss—all point to squandering a concrete opening initiative by playing passively when a forcing blow was available.

607.label: Player moves queen non-optimally in a winning endgame, missing a forced checkmate or immediate decisive continuation.
607.description: This feature fires when a player with a dominant queen in a won endgame plays a slow, non-forcing queen move instead of delivering a forced mate or immediately decisive blow. The material/position signature shows queen moves (70%) that are technically safe (80%) but miss winning material 100% of the time, while Maia consistently finds queen checks (100%) that would finish the game. The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly won positions (winning->winning 60%, plus others converting to winning for the opponent's perspective), with a staggering median eval loss of 9116 centipawns—consistent with missing mate. The tactical analysis tags (missed_mate, checkmate_in_one, exposed_king, tempo_loss) and example summaries describing 'threw away a trivial forced mate in 3 by playing a slow king move' and 'prioritizes a speculative mating trap over concrete winning continuation' confirm the pattern: in queen endgames with passed pawns and exposed kings, the player drifts with aimless queen maneuvers or king moves instead of calculating the short forced mate sequence available.

608.label: Premature pawn advance in the opening that abandons central tension and leaves material or positional weaknesses.
608.description: This feature detects a specific opening mistake where a player pushes a pawn forward (100% pawn moves, no captures) in a way that overextends or releases central tension, converting a drawn/equal position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing, median 249cp lost). The top boards all show early opening positions (100% opening phase) where the pawn advance creates hanging pieces or tactical vulnerabilities (hanging_piece 43%, fork 14%) rather than maintaining flexible pawn structure. Common tags emphasize pawn_structure, development, and tempo_loss — the pawn moves violate opening principles by advancing without purpose (c5-c4, f5-f4, g7-g5) when better developing moves or captures were available. Maia consistently recommends a pawn capture instead (100% pawn captures pawn), indicating the correct move was to take in the center rather than push past it. The pattern is a player prematurely closing or bypassing central tension with an aggressive-looking but strategically misguided pawn thrust that creates concrete tactical problems.

610.label: King moves ignore an undefended enemy piece that could be captured for free.
610.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe king move (100% king moves, 100% materially 'safe') while leaving an enemy piece completely undefended and capturable. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (88%), and Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing an unprotected piece (bishop 67%, queen 33%). The eval trajectory shows these oversights are catastrophic: median 831 centipawns lost, with 67% of cases turning a winning position into a drawn one. The positions are predominantly endgames (67%) where the board is simplified enough that the hanging piece should be trivially visible. The concrete examples confirm the pattern: missing Kxa3 to take a hanging bishop, missing Kxe6 to capture a critical undefended bishop, or overlooking a free queen capture. The player's king wanders aimlessly instead of stepping toward or onto the square of an unprotected enemy piece, squandering a decisive material advantage.

609.label: Player misses a forced checkmate (often via promotion) and allows the position to simplify into a draw.
609.description: This feature fires in endgame positions where the player has a decisive advantage—typically a forced mate—but plays a 'safe' move (no capture, no check) that squanders the win entirely. The material signature shows the move itself doesn't lose material (100% 'safe'), yet Maia's recommended moves are almost always checks (100%) and frequently involve the queen, suggesting the engine sees a mating attack the player missed. The dominant motif is 'promotion_error' (100%), indicating the mistake revolves around mishandling promotion-related tactics: either failing to promote with check, promoting to the wrong piece, or making a quiet move when a promotion-based mating net was available. The eval trajectory confirms the catastrophic nature—positions swing from totally won (mate in a few moves) to drawn, costing thousands of centipawns. The top boards confirm this: nearly all are simplified endgames with overwhelming material advantages (multiple queens, rooks + queens) where the player makes a passive or aimless move instead of delivering the forced mate, often involving pawn promotion sequences.

612.label: Unsound bishop sacrifice on f7 with check in the opening, lacking sufficient attacking support.
612.description: This feature fires almost exclusively on the classic Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice in the opening phase (100% opening, 100% bishop moves, 100% checks, 98% capturing a pawn on f7). The material signature shows the move is 'slightly_down' (median net -2.0, i.e., losing a full piece for a pawn), confirming an unsound sacrifice rather than a simple exchange. The eval trajectory is devastating: 72% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 327 centipawns—indicating the sacrifice has no real compensation. The top 10 boards all show the identical pattern: a bishop on c4 capturing on f7 with check (c4f7) in Italian/King's Pawn type openings where the opponent's king is still on e8. The tactical analysis confirms these are premature sacrifices with insufficient piece support—typically the queen is uninvolved, a knight is undeveloped, and there is no follow-up attack. Maia's preferred alternatives (pawn moves 43%, knight development 27%) are quiet developing moves, underscoring how unnecessary and unsound the sacrifice is.

611.label: Moving the rook (or king) away from a critical defensive or attacking duty in an endgame, leaving material or positional assets unprotected.
611.description: This feature captures endgame mistakes (69% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (42%) or rook (27%) away from a critical square, hanging material 60% of the time without capturing anything (60% non-captures). The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly thrown wins (42% winning->drawn), with a median loss of 282 centipawns—consistent with squandering a decisive endgame advantage. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 33%, king_safety 33%, passed_pawn 22%) and recurring tags (rook_endgame, piece_activity, tempo_loss) reveal the underlying pattern: the player relocates their active piece to a less relevant square, abandoning defense of a pawn, control of a file, or blockade of a passed pawn. The top board examples reinforce this—Rxh7 leaving g3 unprotected, Rb6 abandoning defense of c7, cxd3 releasing a critical pawn structure. Maia's recommendations (95% non-captures, 11% checks) suggest the correct moves maintain piece activity or pressure rather than grabbing peripheral material. This is fundamentally an endgame piece-activity error where the player misjudges which square or task their rook/king should prioritize.

614.label: Player ignores a back-rank threat or tactic, hanging major material or allowing mate.
614.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that overlooks a critical back-rank vulnerability. The material signature shows that 71% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a rook), and 86% of the time the player missed winning material—specifically, Maia's recommended move captures a rook in 100% of cases. The Opus tactical analysis confirms back_rank as the dominant motif (60%), with king_safety and missed_tactic recurring tags. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings: winning→losing, drawn→losing, and even positions collapsing, with a median loss of 515 centipawns. Concrete examples reinforce this: a player grabs a pawn while back-rank mate is threatened (Bxb2 instead of Rxe8), a player plays a passive rook move instead of capturing first on the back rank (Rd2 instead of Rxd3), and a player ignores mutual rook attacks allowing the opponent to exploit the back rank. The pattern is consistently one of tunnel vision—making a 'normal' developing or defensive move while completely blind to the opponent's immediate back-rank tactical resource.

613.label: Player makes a plausible-looking move that abandons a winning king attack, missing checkmate or devastating back-rank tactics.
613.description: This feature fires when players in middlegame positions overlook lethal king-safety threats—particularly back-rank mates and forcing sequences involving checks. The material signature shows pieces are often not captured (63% no capture) yet the move 'hangs' material 32% of the time or is merely 'safe' but catastrophically wrong strategically. The key signal is that Maia's recommended moves deliver check 46% of the time (vs. player's 12%), indicating the missed continuation involved a forcing attack on the king. The dominant motifs (king_safety 50%, back_rank 33%) and tags (missed_mate, exposed_king, back_rank) confirm the player failed to exploit or defend against king vulnerabilities. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 325 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or worse—the player had a decisive attack but played a natural-looking move (often a queen relocation or bishop development) that let the opponent escape. The per-position analyses reinforce this: players grab material out of 'instinct' while missing back-rank checkmates, or place pieces on seemingly logical squares while overlooking knight checks and deflections that crack open the king position.

617.label: Capturing a pawn with a rook that allows the opponent's passed pawn to promote or transforms a drawable endgame into a lost pawn endgame.
617.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder where a player uses their rook to capture an enemy pawn (rook moved 100%, pawn captured 100%) but in doing so loses far more material than gained (net material median -4.0, meaning the rook itself is typically lost or trapped). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 1318cp lost), converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones. The dominant motifs—promotion_error (40%), pawn_endgame (30%), passed_pawn (10%), rook_endgame (10%)—combined with tags like tempo_loss and piece_activity reveal the core pattern: the player trades away their rook by capturing a pawn (often a dangerous passed pawn near promotion), transforming the position into a hopeless pawn endgame. The concrete positions confirm this: rooks capturing advanced pawns on the 7th rank (g1g7, d4d7, a8a6, g3g7, a4a7) where the rook is exchanged for a single pawn while the opponent retains unstoppable passed pawns. The rook was the key defensive piece providing drawing chances through activity, and its removal leaves the player in a lost king-and-pawn ending.

618.label: Player makes a passive or misguided move (often pawn push or queen retreat) instead of executing a winning queen maneuver, hanging material in the process.
618.description: This feature fires when players overlook a strong queen move that would win material or maintain a critical advantage. The signature is clear: Maia recommends a queen move 91% of the time, yet the player instead plays a pawn (38%), queen to the wrong square (35%), or minor piece move (12%). The result is catastrophic—50% of moves hang material outright, with a median loss of 303 centipawns and 97% of positions involving missed winning material. The eval trajectory shows positions collapsing from drawn to losing (29%) or winning to losing (9%), indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 40%, pin 20%, fork 20%) confirm that the missed queen moves would have exploited concrete tactical vulnerabilities. The concrete examples reinforce this: retreating a queen from a square where it could capture a hanging piece (Qxb5), pushing pawns when only Qe2 holds the position, or playing passive knight moves when the queen had a decisive tactical shot. Players are distracted by prophylactic or developing moves while the queen's tactical potential goes unexploited.

616.label: Player trades or sacrifices their queen when it was the key piece maintaining their advantage, converting a superior position into a lost one.
616.description: This feature fires on positions where the player voluntarily exchanges or sacrifices their queen (queen moved 67% of the time, often capturing) in situations where the queen was essential to maintaining winning chances. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 1290 centipawns), with positions going from winning to losing (33%), drawn to losing (33%), or accelerating a loss (33%). The tactical analyses consistently highlight 'queen_trade_blunder' as a recurring tag — in one case a won Queen vs. Pawns endgame was thrown away by trading the queen for a pawn, in another the queen needed for perpetual check was exchanged away. The motif distribution (hanging_piece 43%, promotion_error 29%) reflects that after the queen disappears, remaining pieces become vulnerable or pawn promotions become unstoppable. The boards confirm this: multiple positions show Bxh2-type pseudo-sacrifices where the bishop (or queen) is simply lost without compensation, and endgame positions where exchanging the queen eliminates the only winning resource (perpetual check, promotion prevention). The common thread is removing one's most powerful piece from the board when it was the linchpin of the position's advantage.

619.label: King or pawn move in a won pawn endgame that squanders the win by losing critical tempo or opposition.
619.description: This feature fires on moves in pure pawn endgames (90% pawn_endgame motif, 100% endgame phase) where the player makes a 'safe' move—no material is hung or traded—yet catastrophically converts a winning position into a draw (100% winning->drawn trajectory, median 555 centipawns lost). The moves are predominantly king moves (67%) or pawn advances (33%) that forfeit essential endgame principles: opposition, tempo, or proper timing of pawn advances. The tactical analysis consistently tags tempo_loss as the dominant error, with king_activity and opposition frequently cited. The concrete positions show minimal-material king-and-pawn endings where a single inaccurate step (e.g., moving the king to the wrong square or pushing a pawn prematurely) immediately surrenders the winning technique, allowing the opponent to reach a theoretical draw.

621.label: Hanging a rook in an endgame by moving it into the capture path of the opponent's rook.
621.description: This feature identifies a specific and recurring endgame blunder where a player moves their rook directly into the line of fire of the opponent's rook, hanging it for free or allowing a losing rook trade. The material signature shows 86% rook moves with 68% resulting in a hang and a median loss of 5 points (approximately a full rook). The phase is predominantly endgame (68%), and the tactical analysis confirms dominant motifs of 'rook_endgame' (60%) and 'hanging_piece' (40%), with tags like 'rook_trade_blunder' and 'lost_pawn_endgame' reinforcing that these moves either drop the rook outright or force a trade into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn ending. The eval trajectory shows most cases occur in already-losing positions (55% losing->losing), suggesting these are desperation or fatigue-driven errors in technically difficult rook endgames, though the median 225cp loss indicates the blunder substantially worsens the position beyond what was already lost. The concrete board positions consistently show open files or ranks where both rooks operate, and the player carelessly places their rook where it can be immediately captured.

620.label: Passive or irrelevant moves that waste critical tempo while the king faces mounting tactical threats.
620.description: This feature captures moves that squander a crucial tempo in positions where king safety is the dominant concern. The material signature shows mostly non-capturing moves (88% no capture) that are nominally 'safe' (58%) or hang material (33%), typically pawn pushes or quiet piece moves that fail to address immediate tactical crises. The eval trajectory reveals a median loss of ~198 centipawns, with the most common pattern being positions that go from losing to deeper losing (30%) or from drawn to losing (15%), indicating these tempo-wasting moves allow the opponent to convert or escalate an attack. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags king_safety (75%) and tempo_loss (25%) as the dominant motifs—players make moves like f3, Bd2, Qe2, h4, or f4 that ignore urgent kingside threats, fail to resolve tactical confrontations, or displace defenders from critical squares. Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve active captures (pawns, knights, rooks) or piece development that addresses the attack, confirming the human error is choosing a passive, tempo-losing continuation when the position demands immediate defensive or counterattacking action.

622.label: Player ignores a decisive tactical blow (often a back-rank mate or winning capture) in favor of an aimless or flashy but inferior move.
622.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player has a crushing tactical shot available—frequently a back-rank mate, a simple winning capture, or a promotion-forcing advance—but instead plays a move that hangs material or squanders the advantage. The material signature shows 67% of the played moves hang a piece (median net material: -1.0), while Maia's suggested moves capture a rook 67% of the time, indicating a clean winning capture was on the board. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 33% go from winning to losing and 33% from drawn to losing, with a median eval loss of 939 centipawns. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are back-rank threats (40%) and hanging pieces (20%), with recurring tags of missed_mate, passed_pawn advancement ignored, and attraction_to_checks—suggesting players are seduced by superficially active moves (checks, harassment, pawn grabs) while overlooking the immediately decisive tactical continuation. The positions consistently show a single clean winning move (Qxd8#, Qxa8, e2 promotion push, Qxb1+ mating sequence) that the player bypasses.

624.label: Bishop captures pawn on h3/h6 as a speculative king attack sacrifice that lacks sufficient compensation.
624.description: This feature fires on a highly specific recurring mistake: a bishop captures the h-pawn (h3 or h6) near the castled king as a speculative sacrifice intended to open the king's shelter. The material signature shows bishop moves capturing pawns 100% of the time, with the outcome classified as a 'trade' (the bishop is captured back, netting ~-1 material), but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional consequences—53% of cases convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 235 centipawns. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies king_safety as the dominant motif, with recurring tags of 'unsound_sacrifice', 'premature_attack', and 'insufficient_compensation'. The top boards confirm the pattern: in closed/semi-closed positions during the opening or early middlegame, players sacrifice their bishop on h3 (as Black) or h6 (as White) hoping to strip the king's pawn cover and launch an attack, but the opponent's defensive resources (piece rerouting, central counterplay) far exceed the attacker's remaining forces, leaving them down material with no real threats.

625.label: Player advances a pawn instead of capturing a hanging queen, turning a losing position into a forced loss.
625.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) while Maia's recommended move captures a queen (100% queen captures). The material signature shows the move 'hangs' material (net -1.0 median), but the real catastrophe is revealed by the eval trajectory: positions shift from losing to winning (100%), with a staggering median eval loss of -10,517 centipawns — meaning the player had a single saving/winning resource (capturing the opponent's queen) and missed it entirely. The Opus analysis confirms this with recurring tags like 'missed_queen_capture', 'hanging_piece', and 'forced_mate', with example narratives describing players who left completely undefended queens on the board. The concrete board positions show endgame scenarios where an enemy queen is en prise to a pawn capture (e.g., cxd5 capturing a Queen on d5, fxe6 capturing a Queen on e6, Bxc3 capturing a Queen on c3), but the player instead makes an irrelevant pawn push or king move, converting what would have been a won position into immediate forced checkmate.

623.label: Knight captures a pawn in the opening only to be left hanging or vulnerable to a fork, costing significant material.
623.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where a knight greedily captures a pawn (knight moved 100%, pawn captured 100%, opening phase 100%) but leaves itself tactically vulnerable. The material outcome appears 'safe' at first glance (91%), meaning the knight isn't immediately lost on that square, but the position collapses because the knight lands on an exposed square where it can be attacked via a fork (30% fork motif, including Qa4+ queen forks) or simply left hanging to a subsequent attack (70% hanging_piece motif). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: 73% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 282 centipawns—essentially a piece. The concrete pattern is remarkably specific: Nxe4 or Nxd4 captures in well-known opening structures (Scandinavian, French, Sicilian) where Maia's best move was a quiet developing move (bishop 55%, pawn 18%) rather than the tempting pawn grab. The common tags (development, piece_activity, tempo_loss) reinforce that these players sacrifice development and tempo for a pawn that proves poisoned.

626.label: Capturing a safe but irrelevant pawn instead of pursuing the fastest winning technique (checks, promotion, or eliminating key defenders).
626.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player captures a pawn (100% player captured pawn) that is materially 'safe' (nothing hangs, net +1.0) but strategically wasteful, costing a median of 369 centipawns. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and promotion-related errors, with king_safety tags suggesting the missed moves often involved delivering checks (Maia gives check 67%) or eliminating critical defenders rather than grabbing peripheral pawns. The eval trajectory shows these are mostly winning→winning (67%) but the win becomes dramatically less decisive or slower—doubling the path to mate or allowing counterplay. The boards confirm this: taking a g6 pawn instead of the e6 bishop preventing mate, capturing on f6 instead of delivering immediate checks, or grabbing a-file pawns instead of advancing passed pawns. The player consistently chooses a 'safe' pawn capture that looks productive but squanders decisive tempo in positions where precise technique (promotion threats, checks, key piece elimination) would win quickly.

627.label: Trading queens when the queen itself provided critical dynamic compensation or attacking chances, converting into a lost or drawn endgame.
627.description: This feature fires on positions where a player initiates a queen trade (92% queen moves, 100% capturing a queen, 92% with check) that objectively costs significant evaluation (median 235cp lost). The material signature shows a clean trade (net 0.0), so no material is blundered outright—yet 85% of the time the player missed a winning alternative. The eval trajectory reveals this is predominantly a 'throwing' mistake: winning→drawn (23%), drawn→losing (23%), and winning→winning but with severe eval loss (15%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is entering a pawn endgame (71%) via queen exchange where the player's queen was the sole source of dynamic counterplay—perpetual check threats, king harassment, or promotion prevention. Tags like queen_trade_error, passed_pawn, and pawn_endgame_conversion recur, showing players misjudge the resulting pawn structure. The concrete positions consistently show one side trading queens with check, only to find the resulting king-and-pawn ending is technically lost due to passed pawns, promotion races, or tempo issues that the queen had been papering over.

630.label: Player makes a developing or pawn move in the opening while leaving a piece hanging to an obvious capture.
630.description: This feature detects opening-phase blunders where the player pushes a pawn or makes a knight move (50% pawn, 50% knight) that is itself materially 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost on the moved piece), but critically ignores an opponent's piece that is already hanging or a simple capture that wins material. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic damage (median 524cp lost), shifting from winning to drawn or drawn to losing. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), and the per-position analyses consistently describe scenarios where a piece (often a knight on f4) is completely undefended and capturable by a pawn, yet the player makes an irrelevant developing move (c4, d5, h6, or castling) instead of taking the free material. The tags reinforce this with 'opening_blunder', 'tempo_loss', and 'missed_tactic'. The key pattern is not that the player hangs their own piece, but that they fail to capture the opponent's hanging piece, effectively gifting material by omission during the opening phase.

632.label: Queen captures a defended pawn in the opening, immediately losing the queen.
632.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring beginner mistake: in the opening phase (100%), the player moves their queen to capture a pawn (queen moved 100%, captured pawn 100%), but that pawn is defended by a piece the player failed to notice—typically a rook along an open file or a pawn on an adjacent square. The material signature shows a catastrophic net loss (median -8.0, consistent with losing a queen for a pawn), and the eval trajectory confirms the position collapses from drawn to losing (median 618cp lost). The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (86%) and recurring tags like 'pawn_grab_punished', 'queen_blunder', and 'pawn_captures_queen'. The concrete board positions show queens venturing to h5, a5, h7, or g3 early in the game to snatch pawns that are clearly protected, resulting in immediate queen loss. This is a fundamental piece-safety oversight where greed overrides board vision.

628.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet king or minor piece move while the opponent's queen hangs undefended, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
628.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions where the opponent's queen is left completely undefended (hanging_piece motif in 100% of cases, hanging_queen tagged repeatedly), yet the player moves their king (75%) or bishop (25%) instead of capturing it. Maia's recommended move captures the queen in every instance (Maia captures: queen 100%), confirming that a simple winning capture was available. The material signature shows the played move itself is mostly 'safe' or 'hangs' — meaning the player didn't lose material directly on that move but missed the free queen capture, which constitutes the massive eval swing. The trajectory (winning->losing 75%, drawn->losing 25%, median loss ~1023cp) confirms these are game-deciding oversights that convert winning or holdable endgames into lost ones. The summaries explicitly describe missing elementary queen captures (e.g., Nxd4 capturing the Queen, Rxd4 winning White's undefended Queen). The common thread is tunnel vision in the endgame — players focus on pawn races, king activity, or minor threats while completely overlooking that the opponent's queen is en prise.

629.label: Aggressively moving a bishop or piece into an attack that hangs material by overlooking the opponent's tactical resources.
629.description: This feature captures positions where players—most often with bishops (50%) or rooks (19%)—make aggressive-looking moves that hang a piece (50% of outcomes) or lose material outright, resulting in a median loss of ~3 pawns worth of material and ~315 centipawns of evaluation. The moves frequently deliver check (31%) or target the opponent's king, suggesting the player is pursuing an attack, but the execution is flawed: the piece is left en prise or the tactic simply doesn't work. The Opus analysis confirms motifs of hanging_piece, tempo_loss, king_safety, and fork—indicating these are pseudo-attacks where the player invests a piece expecting initiative or mating threats but miscalculates. The trajectory shows many positions go from winning to drawn or worse (winning→drawn 19%, drawn→losing 12%), meaning the player was already ahead and threw away the advantage by overextending. Maia's recommendations (rooks, bishops, knights without capturing) suggest quieter consolidating moves were available. The concrete positions reinforce this: bishops lunging to attack squares, rooks capturing with apparent threats, but all leaving material hanging because the aggressive continuation was tactically unsound.

631.label: Premature pawn advance in a won pawn endgame that allows the opponent to reach a theoretical draw.
631.description: This feature fires on pawn advances in pure king-and-pawn endgames that throw away winning positions by creating drawn theoretical positions. All activating examples are pawn moves (100%) in endgame positions (100%) that are materially 'safe' (no pieces hang), yet the eval trajectory shows the player going from winning to drawn 78% of the time with a massive median eval loss of 480 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the motif: pawn_endgame (90%) with recurring tags like 'opposition', 'theoretical_draw', and 'king_and_pawn_endgame'. The concrete pattern across boards shows players pushing pawns (e5, d6, g5, h4, f4, g5, a4, f4, g4) when the correct plan required maintaining pawn structure flexibility or prioritizing king activity. These advances typically destroy connected pawn advantages, create rook-pawn draws, or allow the opponent to seize the opposition, converting textbook wins into book draws through ignorance of endgame theory.

635.label: Sacrificing a well-placed piece for a showy check that loses material without compensation.
635.description: This feature captures positions where a player delivers an attractive-looking check (55% of moves are checks) that actually hangs or sacrifices a major/minor piece without adequate compensation. The material signature shows 55% hangs and median net material loss of -3.0 (roughly a full piece), with rooks (46%) and knights (27%) being the most commonly sacrificed pieces. The eval trajectory is devastating: 55% of these moves convert a winning position into a draw, and 27% turn a win into a loss, with a median cost of 445 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this pattern—example summaries describe sacrificing a dominant knight for a 'meaningless check,' throwing away a winning rook for a pawn with check, and placing pieces en prise after flashy but unsound moves. The common tags 'unnecessary_check,' 'piece_sacrifice_without_compensation,' and 'hanging_piece' all converge on the same theme: the player is seduced by the visual appeal of giving check rather than maintaining their material or positional advantage.

634.label: Player makes a safe-looking move while missing a winning knight fork that would have won material outright.
634.description: This feature fires when players miss decisive knight forks in middlegame and endgame positions. The material signature shows the played moves are 'safe' (no material lost immediately) — the player moves their king or knight without capturing anything — but they miss Maia's recommended move which invariably delivers check (100% check rate). The dominant motif is 'fork' (60%), with 'knight_fork' appearing in 3 of 4 analyzed positions, and the per-position analyses consistently describe missed Nf3+, Ne1+, or Nc7 forks that would have won a piece outright. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed wins: median 426 centipawns lost, with players going from winning to losing or drawn in 50% of cases. The players choose quiet repositioning moves (king walks, slow knight retreats like Nb4) instead of the crushing tactical blow, suggesting a failure to calculate forcing sequences involving check + fork.

633.label: Pieces moved away from back-rank defense, allowing mating threats or catastrophic tactical exploitation.
633.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders where players move major pieces (rooks 42%, knights 33%, queens 17%) in ways that fatally compromise back-rank security. The material signature shows 67% of moves hang a piece (median -2.0 material loss), yet the true cost is far greater—median eval loss of 479 centipawns with several positions swinging from defensible to forced mate. The dominant motifs are back_rank (50%) and king_safety (50%), confirmed by the Opus analysis showing pieces removed from defensive duties on the first rank, exposing the king to mating combinations. The best moves (Maia's choices) were typically rook moves (67%) that maintained back-rank coverage or actively captured material, often with check (25%). The concrete positions consistently show cramped king positions on g1/g8/h1/h8 with rooks needed for defense being moved elsewhere—either capturing tempting material or relocating to seemingly active squares—while opponents have heavy pieces aimed at the back rank. This is not a simple hanging piece but a failure to recognize that the moved piece was performing a critical defensive function against back-rank or king-safety threats.

639.label: Player makes a routine capture or trade instead of delivering a forced checkmate exploiting the back rank or exposed king.
639.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player has a forced checkmate (often in one or two moves) exploiting back-rank weaknesses or exposed king geometry, but instead plays a natural-looking capture or exchange. The material signature shows trades and routine captures (median net material 0.0) rather than blunders of material—the player isn't losing pieces, they're simply choosing a mundane move over a winning tactical blow. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly checks (100%) using bishops and rooks, confirming the missed forcing sequences. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of back_rank (50%) and king_safety (50%), with recurring tags of missed_mate and missed_mate_in_one. The eval trajectory shows a massive median cost of 217 centipawns, with positions shifting from winning to drawn/losing (34% combined) or remaining losing—indicating the player threw away a decisive advantage by tunnel-visioning on material exchanges rather than calculating the lethal mating pattern available via checking sequences along ranks and diagonals.

637.label: Opening pawn captures/advances that trade material but surrender tempo and positional advantage.
637.description: This feature fires on pawn moves in the opening (100% opening phase) that execute or initiate exchanges (76% trades) but cost enormous positional value (median 271cp lost). The moves are overwhelmingly pawn captures of other pawns (90% capture pawns), yet the eval trajectory shows these trades convert winning positions to drawn (43%) or drawn to losing (29%). The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: these are premature pawn advances or captures that lose tempo (29% tempo_loss motif), expose pieces to attack (29% hanging_piece), or miss superior tactical alternatives like capturing active pieces. The concrete positions confirm the pattern—players mechanically recapture or advance pawns (exd6, exf6, d4d3, d5d6) when a developing move or piece capture was far stronger, often leaving their own pieces undefended or opening lines that favor the opponent. Maia's recommendations (bishops 29%, knights 29%) suggest piece development was the correct approach rather than these reflexive pawn exchanges.

636.label: Player makes a slow or self-blocking move instead of delivering the crushing queen check/mate that was available.
636.description: This feature fires when a player has a queen poised for a decisive check or mating attack (Maia's best move is always a queen check, 100%) but instead plays a non-checking move with a minor piece or pawn that either hangs material (48%) or is merely safe but purposeless (36%).
