The tactical motifs (fork 20%, king_safety 20%, back_rank 20%) combined with tags like missed_tactic(4) and missed_queen_check(1) confirm that concrete winning tactics were available but overlooked. The concrete positions reinforce this: abandoning Qe3+ to castle, missing mate-in-3, and retreating pieces when decisive blows were available.

765.label: Player makes a non-rook move that allows the opponent's rook to seize a dominant file or rank, typically the 7th rank.
765.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where the player moves a knight, pawn, or other piece (knight 28%, pawn 26%, rook 22%) without capturing anything (90% non-captures), while the best move was overwhelmingly a rook move (Maia's recommendation is rook 85% of the time). The material signature shows 40% of these moves hang a piece and 53% are nominally 'safe' but miss a critical tactical opportunity—99% miss winning material. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 250 centipawns, often converting drawn positions to losing ones (14%) or worsening already losing positions (21%). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and king_safety (33%), with tags emphasizing tempo_loss and open_file_exploitation. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: opponents have rooks poised to invade on open files or the 7th rank (e.g., Rf7 invasions, rook lifts), and the player ignores this threat by making a non-urgent move elsewhere, losing critical tempo and allowing devastating rook penetration that wins material or creates mating threats.

766.label: Knight recapture ignoring a forcing bishop sacrifice with check that wins material or maintains a winning attack.
766.description: This feature fires in opening positions where the player captures a knight (typically on e4) instead of playing a devastating Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice with check. The material signature shows knight captures that appear 'safe' (median +3.0 material), but the eval trajectory reveals these moves collapse a winning position into a drawn one (median 296cp lost). The Maia signal confirms the correct move was consistently a bishop capturing a pawn with check (Bxf7+). The tactical analysis highlights king safety (40%) and fork/discovered attack motifs, with 'missed_tactic' as the dominant tag. The recurring pattern is a known opening trap (particularly in the Two Knights/Italian Game complex) where Bxf7+ exposes the king and wins back material with interest or creates a mating attack, but the player instead makes a superficially logical knight exchange that squanders the tactical opportunity. The positions consistently show only one good move within 50cp of the best, indicating a narrow critical moment that the player fails to recognize.

764.label: In endgames, the player moves their king passively instead of capturing available material or occupying critical squares, turning drawn or manageable positions into losses.
764.description: This feature identifies a specific endgame mistake where the player moves their king (100% king moves, 0% captures) in a 'safe' manner—nothing is immediately hung—yet misses a winning capture that Maia consistently finds (Maia captures a pawn 67% or rook 33% of the time). The positions are exclusively endgames with minimal material, where the critical resource is tempo and king activity rather than raw piece safety. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 67% of the time a drawn position becomes losing, and the median centipawn loss of 589 (with several positions reaching forced checkmate) confirms these are decisive errors. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs of passed pawns, pawn endgames, and tempo loss—the player retreats or sidesteps with the king when the only winning move was to advance toward or capture a key pawn. The board positions confirm this: kings in sparse endgames where one precise king move (often a capture like Kxb6 or an active advance) was required, but the player chose a passive or retreating king move that surrendered the opposition or allowed a passed pawn to promote.

767.label: Giving check with a piece that ends up trapped or hanging, squandering a winning or equal position.
767.description: This feature fires on moves where the player delivers check (100% of activations) predominantly with a queen or knight (71% combined), but the checking piece ends up hanging (42%) or in an unsafe trade (17%). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 234 centipawns, with many cases converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 8%, drawn->losing 17%). The Opus analysis reveals the core pattern: players are seduced by the forcing nature of a check, but the checking piece lands on a square where it becomes trapped (trapped_piece motif 14%), hangs to a recapture (hanging_piece 29%), or critically weakens king safety by abandoning a defensive role (king_safety 43%). The classic example is Nxc7+ where the knight wins material with check but ends up permanently trapped on a8, or Nxc2+ where greed overrides the defensive value of the piece. Maia's preferred moves (often quiet queen or pawn moves, rarely giving check at 8%) confirm that the correct approach was typically a non-forcing consolidating move rather than the flashy but self-destructive check.

768.label: Playing a flashy check that misses a stronger quiet capture or recapture, losing significant material or advantage.
768.description: This feature captures the classic 'patzer sees a check' syndrome in middlegame positions. The material signature shows the player delivering check 100% of the time while the move typically hangs material (50%) or loses material (25%), with a median net loss of -1.0 piece value. Meanwhile, Maia's recommended moves capture a queen 100% of the time with no check—indicating that the player chose an inferior checking move over a simple winning capture. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 190 centipawns, with positions ranging from throwing away a winning advantage to converting a drawn position into a losing one. The Opus analysis explicitly identifies 'unnecessary_check' and 'tempo_loss' as recurring tags, with one summary directly calling out the 'give check first fallacy' where a player plays a flashy discovered attack or check instead of calmly taking hanging material. The boards confirm this: pieces (bishops, knights, rooks) deliver checks that look forcing but allow the opponent to escape or consolidate, when a quiet queen capture was available.

769.label: Giving a purposeless queen check instead of trading queens into a won pawn endgame.
769.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame mistake pattern: the player has a winning position with queens on the board and a clearly superior pawn structure, where the correct move is to trade queens (Maia's recommended move is always a queen capture) to enter a trivially won pawn endgame. Instead, the player gives a queen check that accomplishes nothing—no material gain, no improved position—merely delaying the conversion and often allowing the opponent to escape into a drawn position. The material signature shows a safe queen move delivering check (no capture, nothing hanging), while Maia consistently recommends capturing the opponent's queen. The eval trajectory uniformly shows winning→drawn with a massive median loss of 497 centipawns, confirming these checks squander decisive advantages. The tactical analysis tags (pointless_check, unnecessary_check, queen_trade_missed, missed_simplification, pawn_endgame_conversion) and the dominant pawn_endgame motif all converge on the same story: players resist the decisive simplification, perhaps instinctively preferring active-looking checks over the 'boring' winning technique of trading into a won ending.

774.label: Delivering an unnecessary queen check that leaves the queen en prise, instead of trading queens into a winning simplified position.
774.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a queen check (played a check: 100%) that hangs the queen (hangs 100%, net material median: -1.0) instead of capturing the opponent's queen (Maia's response is always Qxq, 100%). The eval trajectory shows these moves collapse winning positions into draws or losses (median 301cp lost), consistent with the tags 'unnecessary_check' and 'hanging_queen'. The positional layer reveals the player had a simple queen trade available (Qxf7+, Qxd5) that would convert into a trivially won endgame—often with connected passed pawns—but instead played a showy or aimless check that placed the queen on an undefended square where it is immediately captured. The combination of 'hanging_piece' motif (50%) and 'pawn_endgame' motif (38%) confirms the recurring pattern: the player avoids a winning simplification in favor of a flashy but tactically unsound check.

770.label: Playing a flashy knight or bishop check that hangs the piece or loses significant material instead of executing the correct tactical sequence.
770.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers check (100% of activations) with a minor piece—predominantly a knight (66%) or bishop (26%)—but the check is catastrophically costly: 46% of the time the piece is simply hung, and 40% of the time material is lost on net (median net material: -4.0, i.e., roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 270 centipawns, often converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (23% drawn->losing, 17% winning->drawn). The tactical analysis reveals the core mistake: these are move-order errors and premature intermediate checks (tags: move_order, zwischenschach, intermediate_move, knight_check) where the player plays a spectacular-looking check before executing the correct continuation (e.g., capturing a queen or completing a mating net). Maia's recommended moves are typically queen moves (49%) or rook moves (26%) that would have maintained the tactical advantage without sacrificing the piece. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (83%) with rich tactical complications where the temptation to check first—rather than play the quiet winning move—proves ruinous.

773.label: Trading rooks in an endgame that transitions into a lost pawn ending.
773.description: This feature fires when a player exchanges rooks in an endgame position, transforming a defensible (or at least complex) rook endgame into a hopelessly lost pawn endgame. All top activations occur in endgame positions (100%), involve rook moves (100%), and the material signature shows trades (50%) or safe moves that invite forced exchanges (50%), with a median eval loss of 191 centipawns. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (80%) and passed_pawn (20%), with recurring tags like 'wrong_exchange' and 'pawn_endgame_transition' confirming the strategic error. The Opus analyses consistently describe scenarios where the rook was the only piece holding the position together, and once exchanged, the opponent's passed pawns or superior king position become decisive. The eval trajectory (67% losing→losing, 17% drawn→losing) shows these are mostly positions already under pressure where the rook trade eliminates the last defensive resource, though some cases involve throwing away drawn positions entirely.

772.label: In drawn endgames, the king moves to the wrong square, converting a holdable position into a lost one.
772.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern: the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) in a position that is objectively drawn, but the move converts it into a losing position (100% drawn->losing trajectory, median loss of 658 centipawns). The material outcome is 'safe'—nothing is immediately hung or traded—yet the positional damage is catastrophic. The top boards reveal pure pawn endgames and king-and-piece endgames where the correct king placement was the only way to hold the draw (e.g., needing ...e5 instead of a king move). Opus analysis confirms extremely narrow positions with only one drawing move available, and tags like tempo_loss and king_safety reinforce that the king stepped to the wrong square, losing a critical tempo or abandoning a key defensive post. Maia's recommendation of pawn moves (100%) further confirms that the engine wanted a pawn break or advance rather than the passive/misguided king move that was played.

775.label: Developing or repositioning a minor piece to a square where it loses tempo and allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
775.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a knight or bishop (53% combined) to a square that appears safe (89% safe material outcome) but constitutes a serious positional error costing a median of 278 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions into losing ones (47%) or throw away wins (17%), indicating significant strategic damage without immediate material loss. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (38%), positional_mistake (25%), and fork vulnerability (25%)—combined with recurring tags like piece_activity, piece_coordination, and inefficient_defense reveal the core pattern: the player repositions a minor piece to an inefficient square, wasting a critical tempo. This allows the opponent to execute tactical shots (forks, captures of now-undefended pieces) that were not possible before. The top boards confirm this: pieces move to squares like b4, c3, g4, or f4 where they either block coordination, invite tactical refutations, or abandon key defensive/attacking duties. Maia's recommended moves (47% bishop, 25% knight) suggest the correct approach was maintaining piece activity rather than passively repositioning.

771.label: Player makes a passive or aimless move that abandons a promising kingside attack, allowing the opponent to consolidate or exploit back-rank weaknesses.
771.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player has a winning or strong attacking position (median eval lost: 426cp, with 28% winning->drawn and 11% winning->losing trajectories) but plays a passive piece move—often a rook relocation or quiet bishop/queen move—instead of executing the available tactical blow. The material signature shows 78% of the moves are non-captures that are either safe or hang material (33% hangs), while Maia strongly recommends capturing a pawn (94%) with a bishop (67%) or knight (22%), indicating a concrete tactical continuation was available. The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and back_rank (33%), with tags like attack_dissipation, missed_tactic, and sacrifice_missed appearing frequently. The concrete positions confirm this: players retreat rooks to passive squares (Rhe8, Rf8d8, Ra1e1) or make aimless moves (Rg3g4, Nf3) when sharp attacking moves like Bxh3, Nxg4, or captures exploiting king safety were available. The player effectively releases the tension in a position where they had a powerful initiative, allowing the opponent to escape or counterattack.

777.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move that overlooks a critical tactical threat, leaving pieces hanging or pinned.
777.description: This feature fires when players make moves that ignore available tactical resources, resulting in severe evaluation drops (median 415 centipawns). The material signature shows that while 50% of moves appear 'safe' superficially, 33% immediately hang material, and the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (43%), pin (29%), fork (14%), and overloaded_defender (14%). The key pattern is that Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve checks (83%) or captures of significant material, meaning the player chose a quiet or non-forcing move when a powerful tactical blow was available. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: 33% convert winning positions to losing ones, and 17% turn drawn positions into losses. The concrete positions show knights placed on undefended squares, queens left in pins, missed zwischenzugs, and exchanges that ignore intermediate tactical shots. The common thread is that players made 'natural-looking' moves (developing, trading, pushing pawns) while completely missing forcing tactical sequences that their opponents can exploit.

776.label: Recapturing bxc6 in the opening allows a devastating bishop fork on c6 hitting king and rook.
776.description: This feature detects a specific opening trap pattern predominantly arising from Ruy Lopez or Scotch-type positions where a knight has been sacrificed or placed on c6. In all top activating positions, the player recaptures with the b-pawn (bxc6), trading a pawn for the knight on c6 (material signature: pawn captures knight, 'trade' with median +2.0 net). However, this recapture is a move-order error that exposes the king to a Bxc6+ fork from the b5-bishop, winning the exchange (rook for bishop) or leaving critical pieces undefended. The eval trajectory confirms this is devastating: 80% of cases convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 236 centipawns. The dominant motif is 'fork' (60%), with recurring tags of bishop_fork and opening_trap. Maia consistently recommends a queen move (Qd7) instead, which blocks the fork diagonal or prepares proper recapture. The mistake is tactical rather than a simple trade error—the player fails to recognize the latent bishop fork geometry before committing to the pawn recapture.

778.label: Knight jumps to capture a pawn in the opening, trading itself for inadequate compensation while abandoning development.
778.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase positions where a knight (100% of cases) captures a pawn (100%) in what amounts to a trade (net material ~-1), typically losing the knight for only a pawn or two. The dominant pattern shows knights jumping to b5 or b4 to snag a pawn, but the resulting exchange leaves the player with inferior piece activity, lost tempo, and compromised development. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly decisions: 86% shift from drawn to losing positions with a median loss of 298 centipawns—far exceeding the material exchanged, revealing the positional damage. Maia consistently recommends quiet bishop development moves instead (bishop 100%, no captures), emphasizing that maintaining piece coordination was critical. The tactical analysis tags (piece_activity, development, tempo_loss) confirm the knight sortie disrupts the player's own setup while gaining only a pawn, and the positional_mistake/hanging_piece motifs indicate the knight often becomes stranded or the remaining pieces are left vulnerable after the premature exchange.

780.label: Trading a bishop for a defended pawn in the opening, losing a full minor piece worth of material.
780.description: This feature detects a recurring opening mistake where a player captures a pawn with a bishop, but the pawn is defended, resulting in a net material loss of approximately two pawns (median -2.0 centipawns equivalent to losing a minor piece for a pawn). The material signature shows bishop moves capturing pawns 100% of the time with a 'slightly_down' outcome, consistent with trading a ~3-point piece for a ~1-point pawn. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: positions shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 443 centipawns, indicating the bishop sacrifice provides no compensation. The tactical analysis tags ('bishop_for_pawn', 'capturing_defended_pawn', 'bishop_misuse', 'opening_mistake') and example summaries consistently describe scenarios where a bishop captures a pawn that is adequately defended by multiple pieces, with no tactical justification—no lasting check, no fork, no positional compensation. The boards confirm this: Bxe7, Bxd7, and similar captures where the bishop ventures onto a square to grab a pawn only to be recaptured cleanly, squandering a minor piece in the opening phase.

782.label: Trading a bishop for a knight in the opening that worsens an already losing position by misplacing pieces or creating tactical vulnerabilities.
782.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player, already in a losing position, initiates a bishop-for-knight exchange in the opening phase that further deteriorates their situation by a significant margin (median 318cp lost). The material signature shows bishop captures knight as a trade (net 0), but Maia consistently prefers a quiet pawn move instead, indicating the exchange was unnecessary. The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: these bishop trades create hanging pieces, move-order errors, and positional weaknesses—such as leaving other pieces undefended (e.g., the Bxc6 example where the e3-bishop becomes hanging) or abandoning key diagonals. The losing->losing trajectory confirms these aren't game-deciding blunders from a winning position, but rather impatient exchanges that accelerate defeat by surrendering the bishop pair, ruining pawn structure, or enabling tactical zwischenzugs that the opponent can exploit.

781.label: Quiet non-threatening moves in the opening that waste a winning advantage by ignoring concrete tactical opportunities.
781.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (81% opening) where the player makes a safe, non-capturing minor piece or pawn move (pawn 42%, knight 31%, bishop 15%) that costs a median of 267 centipawns, frequently converting a winning position into a drawn one (58% winning->drawn). The material outcome is overwhelmingly 'safe' (96%), meaning no pieces are exchanged or hung—the mistake is purely one of omission rather than commission. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (33%) and fork (33%), with tags like missed_tactic (8 occurrences) and development_advantage_squandered confirming that the player had concrete tactical strikes available (forks, Nxg5-type attacks, Nb5 jumps) but instead chose routine developing or retreating moves. The top boards show positions with kings still in the center, open files, and overextended pawns—exactly the contexts where a single tempo of initiative is decisive. The player consistently fails to convert their development lead or piece activity into a forcing blow, instead making 'logical-looking' quiet moves that allow the opponent to consolidate.

783.label: Moves in already-difficult positions that overlook tactical threats, causing catastrophic evaluation swings through king safety neglect or missed discoveries.
783.description: This feature fires on moves where players in already-compromised or roughly equal positions make moves that catastrophically worsen their situation by overlooking concrete tactical threats. The material signature shows 42% of moves simply hang material (non-captures that drop pieces) with a median net loss of -1.0, while the eval trajectory shows 42% go from drawn->losing and 42% from losing->losing, with a massive median eval loss of 261 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals dominant motifs of king_safety (29%), discovered_attack (14%), and trapped_piece (14%), with 'missed_tactic' being the most common tag. The moved pieces are diverse (knights, pawns, bishops, queens) suggesting no single piece-type blunder but rather a pattern of making natural-looking developing or defensive moves that fail to address immediate tactical dangers in the position. The positions are predominantly middlegame (50%) and opening (42%), where tactical complexity is highest. The 75% missed-winning-material rate confirms these players had strong moves available but chose passive or structurally-motivated moves that walked into opponent's tactical resources.

784.label: Playing a visually tempting check that leaves the checking piece undefended and capturable.
784.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player delivers check (100% of cases) with a knight, rook, or queen, but the move hangs the piece (71% hangs, median material loss of -3.0). The eval trajectory shows these checks frequently convert winning positions into losing ones (29% winning->losing) with a median cost of 275 centipawns. The Opus analysis consistently describes 'flashy' or 'visually appealing' checks—often forks or attacks on multiple pieces—where the checking piece lands on an undefended square and is simply captured. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 38%, fork 25%, king_safety 25%) confirm these are pseudo-tactical shots that look forcing but overlook a basic refutation: the opponent captures the unprotected attacker. Maia's recommended moves (often rook or queen captures, 35% non-captures) suggest quieter continuations that maintain material and positional advantage rather than grabbing a showy but unsound check.

779.label: Ignoring knight fork threats on f7 in the opening by playing a passive bishop move instead of addressing the tactical threat.
779.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: the player moves a bishop (often a passive developing move or a pointless check) while completely ignoring a knight fork threat, typically targeting the f7 square. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves that hang material (median -3.0, consistent with losing a full piece), and the eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions turning into losing ones (median 364cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is a knight fork (67%), with recurring tags like 'knight_fork', 'f7_weakness', and 'two_knights_defense' — pointing squarely to the classic Two Knights Defense and Blackburne-style traps where Ng5/Nxf7 forks are the critical threat. The boards confirm this: most positions feature the Italian Game or similar setups where Bc4+Ng5 target f7, and the player plays a bishop move (Be7, Bd6, Bd3, Bf5, Bg4) that ignores the imminent fork. Maia's recommended moves (knight capturing a pawn) represent the correct defensive or counterattacking responses. This is a quintessential opening trap pattern where development is prioritized over addressing a concrete tactical threat.

785.label: Capturing a piece with king or pawn while leaving the queen undefended on an open file.
785.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where the player captures a bishop (100% of cases) with a pawn or king, but in doing so neglects the defense of their own queen. The material signature shows a net loss of ~6.0 (median), consistent with losing a queen after winning only a bishop. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%) with recurring tags of 'undefended_queen', 'open_file_exploitation', and 'queen_capture'. The example summaries explicitly describe scenarios where hxg6, hxg3, Kxf7, or Kxf2 captured a bishop but fatally abandoned queen defense, allowing the opponent to take the queen with no recapture. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 348 centipawns, reflecting the catastrophic queen-for-bishop imbalance. Maia's recommended moves (all king moves, no captures) suggest the correct response was to sidestep the bishop sacrifice and maintain queen coverage rather than greedily recapturing.

788.label: Player makes a move that leaves one of their own pieces undefended and en prise.
788.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that leaves a piece hanging — undefended and capturable by the opponent. The material signature shows 33% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) and 36% 'trade' outcomes where the player initiated an exchange but left something else unprotected, with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full minor piece). The moved pieces are predominantly bishops (44%) and knights (22%), suggesting players relocate minor pieces without noticing they've left them or other pieces unguarded. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the motif in 100% of cases, with tags like missed_tactic, piece_activity issues, and tactical_oversight. The eval trajectory is severe — median 363 centipawns lost — with many positions flipping from winning to losing (17%) or drawn to losing (17%). The top boards consistently show positions where a player made a natural-looking developing or capturing move while completely overlooking that a piece was left en prise elsewhere on the board. Maia's suggested moves (knight 28%, queen 25%) often represent simply capturing the hanging piece or making safe developing moves, confirming the opponent had an obvious target available.

787.label: Player retreats or makes a passive move instead of delivering a decisive kingside attack, squandering a winning position.
787.description: This feature fires on positions where the player holds a significant attacking advantage—often in the opening or early middlegame with the opponent's king exposed (king on g6 or f6 in many examples)—but plays a passive, retreating, or non-forcing move instead of the winning tactical blow. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (knights retreating, quiet pawn pushes, queen repositioning) rather than aggressive continuations, while Maia consistently recommends a checking move with a pawn (often a pawn break like f5+ or h5+). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic—60% go from winning to losing and 40% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 508 centipawns. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss at 60%, plus discovered_attack and pin) and tags (king_safety, exposed_king_ignored, missed_king_attack, retreating_blunder) all converge on the same pattern: the player had a devastating attack in progress but voluntarily surrendered the initiative by retreating a piece or making a slow move, giving the opponent time to consolidate or escape. The boards consistently show exposed enemy kings (frequently on g6/f6) with White's pieces aggressively posted but the played move backing away from the attack.

786.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves when immediate tactical action or counterplay is urgently required.
786.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a passive, tempo-losing move instead of the one forcing continuation that maintains their position. The material signature shows 50% of moves hang material and 77% miss winning material, with a massive median eval loss of 420 centipawns. The eval trajectory reveals these aren't just minor inaccuracies—they convert winning positions to losing (19%), drawn to losing (19%), and represent catastrophic collapses. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with recurring tags like 'slow_move_punished' and 'counterplay_required'. The concrete positions show the pattern clearly: playing g5 instead of addressing a tactical threat, playing g6 prophylactically when Qc2 forces a won endgame, moving the king passively when a queen needed to be active. The player's moves span various pieces (queen 27%, rook 19%, king 19%) but Maia consistently recommends queen moves (54%), suggesting the best move was almost always a forcing queen action. These are critical moments demanding concrete calculation where the player instead plays a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move that squanders the position's tactical demands.

790.label: Failing to address opponent's passed pawn promotion threats in rook endgames, allowing unstoppable queening.
790.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a rook or king move that appears safe (80% safe, no captures) but catastrophically misses the urgency of passed pawn promotion races. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 555 centipawns), often converting drawn positions into lost ones (40%) or making already-losing positions hopeless (60%). The dominant motifs—passed_pawn, promotion_error, rook_endgame, and tempo_loss—paint a consistent picture: the player makes a passive or misdirected rook move (Ra8, Rc1, Rd3) when the critical task was stopping or racing an advanced passed pawn. Maia's recommended moves (80% rook moves, 20% captures) indicate that active rook placement addressing the promotion threat was available. The boards confirm this: positions feature pawns on the 2nd/7th rank about to queen, and the player's move ignores or inadequately addresses this threat, often losing a critical tempo in the promotion race.

789.label: Knight moves to an aggressive-looking but unsound square, abandoning its defensive or positional duties for a superficial attack.
789.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move a knight (95% of activating moves) to a seemingly active square—often delivering a check or creating a fork threat—but the move is fundamentally unsound because the knight either hangs (31% of cases) or abandons a critical defensive function. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 247 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (28%) or throwing away winning positions (11%). The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant motif is positional_mistake (60%), with common tags including tempo_loss, piece_activity, and premature_attack. The top boards reveal a concrete pattern: knights jumping to d4, d5, f5, or e5 in the opening/early middlegame (62% opening phase), where the move looks aggressive but either leaves the knight hanging, sacrifices it for insufficient compensation (e.g., Nf5+ unsound sacrifice), or removes a piece that was performing a vital defensive role (e.g., Nc6 blocking a diagonal). Maia's preferred moves tend to be quieter developing moves (pawns 29%, bishops 19%), suggesting the model detects that the human is choosing flashy knight activity over sound positional play.

791.label: Giving check that allows forced trades or counterplay, squandering a winning position.
791.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers check (100% of cases) with a major or minor piece—most often a queen (50%) or bishop/rook—but the check is ill-timed and costly (median material loss of -4.0, net eval lost ~703 centipawns). The eval trajectory shows these moves predominantly occur from winning positions that deteriorate to drawn or losing (75% of cases start from winning). The tactical motifs (discovered attack, tempo loss, hanging piece) combined with tags like 'move_order_error', 'premature_simplification', and 'unnecessary_exchange' reveal the common thread: the player rushes to give check—perhaps seeing a flashy discovered attack or a forcing sequence—without realizing the check allows the opponent to simplify favorably, trade off critical attacking pieces, or expose the checker to capture. The board positions confirm this: endgames and middlegames where one side has a clear advantage but throws it away by prioritizing a check that either hangs a piece, forces an unfavorable queen trade, or loses tempo. The Maia baseline (0% checks) suggests the engine recognized that quiet moves were superior, while the player was seduced by the forcing nature of a check.

792.label: King captures a knight in a lost endgame, mishandling passed pawn dynamics and promotion threats.
792.description: This feature fires on positions where a player's king captures a knight in an already-lost endgame, resulting in a position that is materially 'safe' (no immediate hanging pieces) but strategically worsening. The material signature shows king takes knight 100% of the time with a net material gain (median +3.0), yet the eval trajectory confirms the player was already losing and the capture costs roughly 18 centipawns median—sometimes catastrophically more (631cp in one example). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are promotion errors (38%), passed pawn mishandling (25%), and pawn endgame technique failures (12%). The recurring pattern is that the knight being captured was actually serving a critical defensive function—blocking a promotion square, restraining passed pawns, or maintaining piece activity—and removing it via capture unleashes the opponent's passed pawns or promotion threats. The player sees a 'free' piece but fails to recognize the knight's positional value in holding the endgame together, converting a difficult-but-holdable position into a hopeless one.

793.label: Developing a bishop to an undefended square where it is immediately captured or trapped in the opening phase.
793.description: This feature captures a recurring opening/early-middlegame mistake where the player develops a bishop (75%) or knight (25%) to a square where it hangs with no compensation. The material signature shows 67% of moves result in a hung piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median cost of -1.0 material (i.e., a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses (median 355 centipawns), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (42%) or throwing wins (25% combined). The tactical analysis unanimously identifies the hanging_piece motif (100%), and the concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: bishops are developed to apparently active squares (Bb4, Bb5, Bh3) where they are immediately captured or trapped because the player overlooks a simple recapture or the square is controlled by the opponent. The opening phase dominance (75%) and development/piece_activity tags confirm these are premature or careless developing moves rather than complex middlegame blunders.

794.label: Player moves a non-queen piece or retreats the queen, leaving it undefended and capturable.
794.description: This feature detects middlegame positions where the player makes a move (most often with the queen itself, but also knights, bishops, or pawns) that leaves their queen hanging or fatally unprotected. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in a 'hang' (a non-capture that drops a piece) with a median material loss of -1.0 (consistent with losing a queen), while Maia's recommended response is universally to capture the queen (Maia's move: queen 100%, Maia captures: queen 100%). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: positions shift from drawn-to-losing (27%), winning-to-drawn (23%), or winning-to-losing (12%), with a median cost of 236 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (62%), supplemented by tempo_loss and move_order_error tags—indicating players often play the right idea in the wrong sequence (e.g., developing a piece before securing the queen, or retreating the queen to a passive square where it becomes tactically vulnerable). The top boards consistently show queens on exposed squares that become capturable after the blundering move.

795.label: Moving a minor piece that overlooks an opponent's immediate tactical shot, hanging material.
795.description: This feature fires when a player moves a bishop or knight (73% combined) in the middlegame and immediately loses significant material (median -4.0 pawns worth, with 48% 'loses' and 26% 'hangs'). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (56%), supplemented by forks (22%) and back-rank threats (11%). The player's move typically ignores or creates a tactical vulnerability—opening a critical file, leaving a piece undefended, or failing to address an opponent's threat—while the engine's recommended move (often a queen move, 50%) would have maintained the position or exploited a tactic first. The eval trajectory shows these are game-decisive errors: 18% throw a winning position into a loss, 24% turn a drawn position into a loss, and the median centipawn cost is 366. The per-position analysis confirms a recurring pattern: the player executes a natural-looking developing or tactical move without first addressing or noticing the opponent's concrete reply (a fork, a file-opening capture, or an attack on an undefended piece), resulting in immediate material catastrophe.

796.label: Moving the king to an unsafe square where it becomes vulnerable to mating attacks or tactical exploitation.
796.description: This feature captures king moves that walk into danger, predominantly in endgame and middlegame positions where the player is already losing or in a drawn position. The material signature shows 77% king moves with a median loss of 260 centipawns, and 46% of moves hang material (the king walks to a square that allows tactical exploitation). The dominant motifs are king_safety (60%), hanging_piece (20%), and back_rank (20%), with recurring tags like 'king_walk_blunder' and 'king_hunt' confirming the pattern. The engine (Maia) frequently recommends rook or queen moves (often with check at 46%), indicating the player missed that their king needed to stay put while active pieces handled threats. The eval trajectory shows 62% losing->losing (making a bad position worse by exposing the king further) with 15% drawn->losing (a survivable position thrown away by a careless king move). Concrete examples include walking into queen-knight mating nets, stepping onto squares vulnerable to back-rank mates, and moving the king while leaving pieces undefended. The critical error is prioritizing king activity or escape when the destination square is tactically compromised.

799.label: In a winning middlegame position, the player makes a passive or tempo-losing move instead of the one critical tactical continuation, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
799.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player holds a winning middlegame position (median eval loss of 456 centipawns, with 43% winning->losing and 43% winning->drawn trajectories) but plays a quiet, non-forcing move (0% checks, 71% no captures, 71% safe material outcome) instead of the single critical tactical continuation—most often a knight maneuver or capture (Maia's move is knight 86%, capturing a knight 57%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with king_safety and missed_tactic as recurring tags. The top boards show positions where the player makes developing or repositioning moves (Qb6, hxg6, Bb7, b5, Qa5, Qf2) that squander a concrete tactical opportunity. The positions typically feature complex middlegames with opposite-side castling or active piece play where only one move maintains the advantage, and the passive choice hands tempo back to the opponent, collapsing the position from winning to drawn or losing.

798.label: Incorrect pawn advance order or premature push in a won pawn endgame that throws away the win or creates stalemate.
798.description: This feature detects a specific recurring mistake in pawn endgames where a player, already in a winning position, pushes the wrong pawn or advances prematurely, squandering a decisive advantage. All activating positions are endgames (100%) involving pawn moves that deliver check or advance toward promotion. The massive median eval loss of ~9484 centipawns (winning->winning but often converting a forced win into a draw/stalemate) reveals these are catastrophic technique errors despite the position still being nominally 'winning' by raw eval in some cases. The dominant motifs—promotion_error (38%), pawn_endgame (38%), and tags like premature_advance and drawn_endgame—confirm the pattern: players push a7+ before b6 (wrong move order blocking promotion), advance pawns that create stalemate traps (h3-h2 boxing in the king), or break connected pawn structures (g4-g5 allowing counterplay). Maia never gives check in these positions (0%), suggesting the check-giving pawn push is a tempting but incorrect human impulse that violates proper endgame technique.

801.label: Player leaves a piece undefended and hanging on a square attacked by the opponent, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
801.description: This feature fires on moves where the player leaves a piece (most often a rook) completely undefended and vulnerable to capture, typically by ignoring an existing threat. The material signature shows 40% of moves 'hang' a piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median net loss of -2.0 (roughly a full piece), while the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic swings: 60% convert a winning position into drawn and 40% turn drawn into losing, with a median cost of 503 centipawns. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (83% of motifs, appearing in 5 of the top examples) alongside 'undefended_rook' and 'ignored_threat', confirming these are not complex tactical oversights but straightforward failures to notice a piece is left en prise. The concrete positions reinforce this: rooks left on diagonals attacked by bishops (FENs 1-2), pieces moved without addressing direct capture threats, and exchanges that inadvertently leave remaining material undefended. The endgame-heavy phase (60%) suggests players relax vigilance in simplified positions where a single hanging piece is immediately decisive.

797.label: Slow or passive bishop/pawn moves in the opening that waste critical tempo when dynamic action was required.
797.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening-phase mistake where the player makes a 'safe' bishop move (75%) or pawn move (25%) that is materially sound but catastrophically slow. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 304 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions to drawn ones (50%) or drawn to losing (25%). The tactical analysis overwhelmingly flags tempo_loss (57%) as the dominant motif, with tags like missed_tactic, missed_pawn_break, and dynamic_advantage_squandered appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: advanced pawn-chain structures (often Caro-Kann/French-type setups with e5+d4 space advantages) where White has a temporary initiative based on Black's cramped, underdeveloped position. Instead of exploiting this with sharp moves (e6 breakthroughs, Ng5 attacking f7, immediate pawn breaks), the player retreats to passive development (Bd2, Bf4, b4 pawn grabs, Be3) that allows Black to consolidate with ...e6 or complete development. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting the engine sees critical pawn breaks as the correct continuation. The mistake is fundamentally positional—understanding when a position demands urgency over routine development.

800.label: In won or advantageous endgames, plays a slow or aimless pawn/king move instead of the precise continuation that maintains or converts the advantage.
800.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players with winning or significantly better positions make seemingly safe pawn or king moves (pawn 55%, king 27%) that are materially 'safe' (100% safe, no pieces hang) but catastrophically imprecise. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically squander large advantages (median 271cp lost), with 55% going winning->winning but at huge cost, and 27% collapsing from winning to drawn or losing. The tactical analysis reveals dominant pawn endgame motifs (44%) with passed pawns (7 instances), where the critical resource is tempo and precision rather than material. Maia's recommended moves often involve active rook checks (64% give check) or piece activity that concretely converts the advantage, while the player instead makes a passive pawn advance or king shuffle. The top boards consistently show simplified endgame positions with passed pawns where one precise move (often a check, a rook activation, or correct king march) wins decisively, but the player chose a 'natural-looking' but ineffective continuation that allows the opponent to activate or reach a drawable structure.

804.label: In pawn endgames, the king retreats or sidesteps losing a critical tempo in a pawn race.
804.description: This feature detects king moves in pawn endgames (100% endgame phase, 100% king moves, pawn_endgame tag in 9/10 positions) where the player wastes a tempo by moving the king in the wrong direction or retreating unnecessarily. The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly 'safe' moves (89%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet the eval trajectory reveals a consistent loss (median 103cp) in already-losing positions (100% losing->losing). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (80%), with passed_pawn concerns underlying most decisions. The concrete positions show kings stepping backward (Kd3, Ke2, Kd7, Ke6) instead of advancing toward critical pawns or optimal squares, costing exactly the one tempo that decides whether an enemy passed pawn promotes or a friendly pawn can be saved. The Maia alternatives (56% king, 44% pawn) confirm that the correct move often involves either a better king path or an immediate pawn push to exploit the tempo.

802.label: Moving the king into a forced mating net when a saving move existed.
802.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their king (60% of activations) into a square that allows forced checkmate, typically in the middlegame (85%). The material signature shows these moves 'hang' material 80% of the time with a median loss of -3.0 (often the king itself via mate), and Maia's recommended move captures a queen 100% of the time—indicating the player missed a critical capture that was the only way to survive. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders (median 9177 centipawns lost), with 60% occurring in already-losing positions where the player still had defensive resources but instead walked into immediate mate. The tactical analysis tags (exposed_king, mating_net, king_walk_blunder, king_safety) and example summaries consistently describe kings stepping into coordinated mating attacks—Ke5 into checkmate, Ka3 into a queen-rook battery, Kd7 into a mating net—when exactly one alternative move (usually capturing a piece) would have kept the game alive. The pattern is a king move that ignores an urgent tactical obligation, converting a difficult-but-defensible position into forced mate.

806.label: In won endgames, playing purposeless checks or passive moves instead of capturing hanging pieces or queens that would clinch the win.
806.description: This feature fires on a specific endgame mistake pattern where players have a winning position (100% endgame phase) but fail to convert by missing simple captures. The material signature shows the played move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet the trajectory reveals catastrophic eval drops (median 497cp, 67% winning->drawn), meaning the player squandered a decisive advantage. The moves are predominantly queen moves or king moves that deliver purposeless checks (67% give check) rather than capturing available material. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing (queen takes 67%, rook takes 33%), confirming that a straightforward winning capture was available. The tactical analysis tags reinforce this: hanging_piece appears in 50% of motifs, missed_capture is tagged 4 times, and example narratives describe giving 'purposeless checks instead of capturing the queen' or moving the king 'away from the undefended rook.' The common thread is players in completely won endgames who reflexively give check or make 'active-looking' moves while overlooking that a simple capture immediately wins.

803.label: Playing a flashy check or capture that overlooks a stronger tactical continuation, often throwing away a winning or tenable position.
803.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes an impulsive forcing move—typically a check (44% of moves give check) or capture with a rook/knight/queen—that looks aggressive but actually loses significant material (median net material: -1.0, with 39% losing and 22% hanging material). The eval trajectory shows these moves are devastating: median 353 centipawns lost, with 34% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->drawn 17%, winning->losing 17%). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players fixate on a check or capture ('unnecessary_check' tag, 'hanging_piece' motif) while missing a much stronger tactic nearby—a back-rank mate, a skewer, or a simple winning recapture. The Opus examples crystallize this: Nh7+ removes a knight from a critical square for no gain, Rf7xf1 misses a back-rank mate (Rf8#), and Qd8 walks into a skewer. The common thread is threat-fixation: the player sees ONE forcing idea (a check, a capture) and plays it reflexively without scanning for the opponent's tactical resources or their own superior alternatives.

807.label: Capturing a pawn with the rook that simplifies into a hopeless pawn endgame, surrendering the rook's activity advantage.
807.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player in a losing endgame captures a pawn with their rook (rook captures pawn 100%), but in doing so either allows or forces a transition into a pure pawn endgame where the position becomes significantly more hopeless. The material signature shows the capture itself is 'safe' (80%) — the rook isn't lost — but the dominant motif is pawn_endgame (78%), and the tactical analysis repeatedly describes transforming 'a difficult but resource-rich rook endgame into a completely hopeless pawn endgame.' The tempo_loss tag (7/10) and piece_activity tag (8/10) confirm the rook was the player's key active piece providing counterplay, and exchanging it (or allowing its exchange) eliminates defensive resources. The trajectory (losing→losing, median 120cp lost) shows these aren't game-losing blunders from good positions but rather critical errors that deepen an already difficult situation by removing the one piece that provided drawing chances. The FENs confirm endgame positions with passed pawns where rook activity was the defender's lifeline.

808.label: Player makes an aimless move while an opponent's piece hangs undefended and capturable for free.
808.description: This feature fires in positions—predominantly endgames (78%)—where the player has a winning advantage but overlooks an opponent's completely undefended piece that could be captured immediately (hanging_piece motif in 88% of cases, missed_capture tagged in 5/9). The material signature shows the player's move itself often hangs something (44%) or is merely safe but pointless (56%), while Maia's recommended move captures a bishop in 100% of cases, confirming the missed opportunity. The eval trajectory (median 337cp lost, with 78% staying winning but at greatly reduced advantage, and 22% dropping to drawn or losing) indicates these are not game-losing blunders in the strictest sense but massive squanderings of a dominant position. The concrete board examples repeatedly show an undefended bishop sitting en prise while the player makes a slow king move, pushes a pawn, or captures something far less valuable—classic 'tunnel vision' away from a free piece in a simplified position.

805.label: Moving the queen (or other major piece) to a passive or tactically vulnerable square, abandoning critical defensive or attacking duties and allowing devastating tactical punishment.
805.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a major piece move (often queen or rook) that catastrophically misplaces it, ignoring urgent tactical obligations. The material signature shows the moves are mostly non-captures (83% capture nothing) yet frequently hang material (33%) or lose it outright (17%), with a massive median eval loss of 1134 centipawns—indicating game-deciding blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The trajectory (50% winning->losing, 50% losing->losing) shows these often throw away winning positions entirely. The tactical motifs reveal the underlying pattern: exposed kings (back-rank weaknesses ignored), hanging pieces left en prise, and simplification errors where necessary exchanges are avoided in favor of passive or misguided piece repositioning. Maia's suggested corrections consistently involve queen captures (100%), often with check (33%), showing that the correct move was to engage tactically rather than retreat or reposition. The common thread across positions is abandoning a critical tactical obligation—whether defending a back rank, trading when forced, or avoiding a vulnerable square—in favor of a queen/rook move that looks active but catastrophically fails.

810.label: Player makes a passive or positional move while a straightforward winning capture sits on the board.
810.description: This feature fires when players overlook an available capture that would win material outright. The material signature shows 92% of the played moves are non-captures, while Maia's recommended moves capture a piece 67% of the time (knight 42%, bishop 17%, pawn 8%)—confirming the player consistently chose a quiet move over a winning capture. The 'hanging_piece' motif dominates at 86%, with 'missed_capture' as the most frequent tag, reinforcing that an enemy piece was simply available to take. The eval trajectory is severe (median 327cp lost), with 29% of cases turning a drawn position into a losing one and 12% throwing away a winning position entirely. The played pieces are predominantly rooks (50%) and knights (21%), suggesting players made developmental or repositioning moves—Re2, Rd1, Kf1—while a concrete tactical capture (often a pawn or piece recapture) was sitting right there. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (83%), where board complexity evidently causes players to overlook hanging material in favor of 'logical-looking' but inferior quiet moves.

809.label: In the Italian Game with d4, Black plays a tempo-losing or irrelevant move instead of recapturing on d4, hanging the e5 pawn.
809.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: Black faces the Italian Game position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d4 (or similar move orders) where White has played d4 challenging Black's center. Instead of the critical recapture on d4 (exd4), Black plays passive or irrelevant moves like ...h6, ...a6, ...Na5, ...f6, or ...g6—moves that lose a tempo and hang the e5 pawn to dxe5. The material signature confirms this: 100% of moves are non-captures that hang material (median -1.0, i.e., a pawn), and Maia's response is always a pawn capture (taking the free e5 pawn). The eval trajectory shows all positions going from drawn to losing (~232cp swing), consistent with dropping a clean pawn plus positional compensation for White in the opening. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece, tempo_loss, development) confirm Black is making a development-irrelevant move when the central tension demanded immediate resolution. This is a classic beginner opening trap where the urgency of the d4 tension is not recognized.

811.label: Passively retreating the queen in the opening instead of capturing a tactical piece, losing critical development tempo.
811.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: in Scandinavian-type positions where Black's queen is on d5 with a bishop on g4 and knight on c6, the player retreats or repositions the queen (to d8, d7, e6, or a5) instead of executing the tactically necessary Bxf3 capture. The material signature shows the queen move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately hung), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic cost of ~311 centipawns, typically converting a drawn position into a losing one (88% drawn->losing). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (80%): by moving the queen passively, the player wastes a critical tempo in the opening while missing the only good move (Bxf3), which would exploit the hanging/exposed f3 knight. The positions are almost exclusively from a single opening tabiya, making this a recurring pattern of choosing a quiet queen retreat over an active tactical capture that was the sole way to maintain equality.

814.label: Player moves a queen or rook to an unprotected square, hanging it to an opponent's capture and causing a catastrophic evaluation swing.
814.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a major piece (queen 46%, rook 36%) without capturing anything (100% non-captures), and the move hangs material 82% of the time with a median net loss of -3.0 (roughly a minor piece to queen's worth). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing mistakes: 36% swing from winning to losing, 27% from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 389 centipawns. Maia's recommended moves predominantly involve capturing a rook (91%), confirming that the opponent had a strong piece available to take that the player overlooked. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (40%), king_safety (40%), and tempo_loss (20%)—reveal that players are moving their major pieces to squares where they become tactically vulnerable, often ignoring back-rank threats or failing to account for the opponent's attacking resources. The concrete positions show queens and rooks being placed on squares where they are immediately won by the opponent's minor or major pieces, frequently in positions where the player was distracted by king safety concerns or positional aims rather than calculating concrete threats to their own pieces.

813.label: Passive or non-developing moves in the opening that squander a significant advantage by ignoring urgent tactical demands.
813.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material is immediately lost or traded) but critically misallocates tempo. The material signature shows 100% safe moves with no captures, yet 100% of cases miss winning material — indicating the player chose a quiet continuation when a forcing tactical opportunity existed. The eval trajectory (median 239cp lost, with 60% winning->drawn and 20% drawn->losing) confirms these moves throw away substantial advantages. The tactical analysis reveals a consistent pattern: pieces are self-blocked (especially bishops behind pawns like ...Qe7 blocking Bf8), development is obstructed, and tempo is wasted on slow pawn moves (like ...b6 or ...d6) when the position demands immediate action such as checks, captures, or piece development. The top boards consistently show early middlegame positions (moves 6-15) where one side has active pieces and central control, and the mistake involves retreating, blocking, or making a positionally passive move instead of meeting the opponent's initiative with concrete counterplay.

812.label: Wasting a critical tempo on an irrelevant kingside pawn move while a major tactic or hanging piece demands immediate attention.
812.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player pushes a kingside pawn (h3, g3, g6, h4 — always a pawn move, 100%) in situations where a far more urgent tactical issue exists. The material signature shows these are non-captures (100% no capture) that are either safe (56%) or outright hang material (44%), indicating the pawn push itself sometimes directly allows a piece to be taken. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 405 centipawns, with 44% going from winning to still winning (but much worse), 33% collapsing from winning to drawn, and 22% falling into a losing position. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring theme: in nearly every case, the player ignores a hanging piece (50% of motifs), wastes a crucial tempo (38%), or overlooks a back-rank threat. Maia's recommended moves are active pieces — rooks (56%) and queens (33%) — often delivering check (56%) or capturing material. The pattern is unmistakable: the player reflexively plays a 'quiet' kingside pawn move (typically h3 or g3) as if improving king safety or luft, while the position screams for an immediate tactical response to defend or exploit hanging pieces.

815.label: Trading an actively-placed bishop for a passive piece in the opening, squandering a winning or equal position.
815.description: This feature fires on opening/early middlegame positions (70% opening, 30% middlegame) where the player uses their bishop to capture a knight (90% bishop moved, 90% captured knight) in what is objectively an equal material exchange (median net material: 0.0, 90% classified as 'trade'). However, the eval trajectory reveals these trades are catastrophic positionally: 50% go from winning to drawn and 20% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 268 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are not calculation errors but strategic misjudgments—trading an actively-placed bishop (controlling key diagonals, supporting attacks) for a passive or undeveloped piece. Tags like 'helping_opponent_develop', 'tempo_loss', 'piece_activity', and 'king_safety' indicate the player relieves pressure on the opponent's position. Several concrete examples show bishops on strong diagonals (e.g., Bc4xg8, Bf4xb8) being exchanged for knights that were passive or trapped, but the trade itself releases tension and abandons attacking potential. Move-order errors compound this: in some cases the player should have delivered checks or maintained threats before committing to the exchange.

817.label: Player makes a safe-looking move that squanders a concrete tactical opportunity, often losing a winning or drawn position.
817.description: This feature fires on moves where the player had a strong tactical resource available (69% missed winning material) but instead played a quiet, non-capturing move (77% no capture) that appeared safe but hemorrhaged evaluation (median 277cp lost). The moves are predominantly in the middlegame (85%) and involve pieces like rooks, bishops, and queens being repositioned passively rather than exploited aggressively. The eval trajectory shows positions transitioning from drawn-to-losing (23%) or winning-to-drawn (19%), indicating squandered advantages. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: king safety threats left unexploited, hanging pieces not captured (Qxa8 missed, Bxh7+ missed), tempo lost by retreating or castling when immediate action was required (Nf2 fork abandoned, Ne7+ check ignored). Maia's recommended moves heavily favor queen moves (50%) and checks (31%), confirming that the computer sees forcing continuations the player failed to find. The dominant motifs—king_safety (40%), hanging_piece (20%), and tempo_loss (20%)—paint a picture of players who sense danger or opportunity but choose cautious development over concrete calculation, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counter-attack.

816.label: Knight captures the e5 pawn in Italian/Four Knights openings, losing material after the piece is recaptured with a tactical refutation.
816.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake where a knight captures the e5 pawn (Nxe5 or Nxe4) prematurely in Italian Game and Four Knights positions. All activating positions show knight moves capturing a pawn (100%), with a net material outcome of -2.0 (slightly_down), indicating the knight capture is punished — the player loses more than the pawn they grabbed. The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn->losing with a median loss of 276 centipawns, meaning a roughly equal position collapses into a decisive disadvantage. The tactical analysis confirms this is a 'pawn grab punished' pattern: the knight move removes a key defender (often the f3 knight protecting kingside squares), and the opponent exploits the resulting tactical vulnerability — typically a fork recovering the piece with interest, or an attack on an undefended bishop (e.g., Bc5). Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly pawn moves (88%), suggesting quiet development was correct rather than the greedy capture. This is a classic opening trap that appears repeatedly in the Italian Game and related e4-e5 openings at amateur level.

821.label: Player makes a routine or passive move while an opponent's piece is hanging and freely capturable.
821.description: This feature fires when players make safe but strategically irrelevant moves (pawn pushes, castling, quiet development) while a concrete tactical opportunity—typically a free piece capture—is available. The material signature shows the player's move is mostly safe (50%) or even hangs material (33%), while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen capture (89%) taking an undefended bishop (72%) or knight (11%). The missed winning material rate of 94% confirms these are clear tactical oversights. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 420 centipawns, with positions swinging from winning/drawn to losing. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%), and the per-position analyses consistently describe scenarios where an enemy piece sits undefended on an open square while the player makes a routine pawn move, castles, or develops passively. The opening/middlegame phase (100%) indicates these occur in complex positions where the abundance of pieces creates opportunities that players overlook in favor of 'natural' moves.

819.label: King or pawn moves in pawn endgames that lose critical tempo, allowing the opponent's passed pawns or king to gain decisive activity.
819.description: This feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player, usually moving the king (57%) or a minor piece/pawn, makes a move that is materially safe (71% safe) but positionally costly. The dominant motifs are passed pawns (44%), pawn endgames (33%), and tempo loss (22%), with the most frequent tags being passed_pawn and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically worsen already-losing positions (57% losing->losing) or squander advantages (14% winning->drawn, 14% drawn->losing), with a median cost of 82 centipawns. The concrete positions confirm king retreats or advances to wrong squares (Kd7, Kc8, Ke7, Kb6) and pawn pushes (h4) that cede tempo to the opponent's king or passed pawns. The mistake is not about hanging material or bad trades, but about misjudging the race dynamics and king opposition in simplified endgames, where a single tempo determines whether a passed pawn promotes or a king reaches a critical square.

822.label: Player retreats or repositions a bishop instead of delivering a winning king attack with the queen.
822.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe bishop move (no capture, no check, no material loss) while having a winning position, but misses a decisive queen move (often a capture or mating sequence). The eval trajectory shows a consistent pattern of remaining winning but hemorrhaging ~273 centipawns of advantage—indicating a forced mate or crushing attack was available but not executed. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and back_rank threats (33%), with tags heavily featuring missed_mate, king_hunt, and attack_abandoned. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows positions where the player's pieces are actively aimed at the enemy king, but instead of delivering the killing blow (typically a queen infiltration, back-rank mate, or king hunt), the player makes a quiet bishop development or retreat move that relieves the pressure. This is not a material blunder—nothing is hung—but a tactical failure to recognize and execute a winning attack, defaulting instead to a 'safe' positional move that lets the opponent survive.

820.label: Player makes a safe-looking move that fatally weakens their own king's defenses, turning a drawable or winning position into a losing one.
820.description: This feature fires on moves that appear materially safe (96% safe, no captures, no checks) but catastrophically compromise king safety. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%), hanging_piece (33%), and overloaded_defender (17%), indicating that the player's move either removes a key defensive piece from the king's vicinity, pushes a critical pawn shield forward, or relocates a piece that was serving double duty protecting the king. The eval trajectory is devastating: 48% of cases shift from drawn to losing and 17% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 326 centipawns—consistent with opening up fatal attacking lines against one's own king. The concrete examples reinforce this: Nc7 abandons kingside defense leaving h3 fatally weak, h4 removes pawn cover from a knight on g3, hxg3 opens the h-file catastrophically. The moved pieces are diverse (queen 22%, pawn/bishop/knight 17% each), suggesting the common thread isn't WHAT piece moves but that it leaves the king exposed. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve the king itself (30%), confirming that the best response was often a defensive king move rather than the aggressive or repositioning move the player chose.

823.label: Player makes a quiet or inferior move when a strong queen capture was available, squandering a large advantage.
823.description: This feature fires when a player, usually in the middlegame with a winning or at least equal position, plays a queen move, rook move, or pawn push that is 'safe' or outright 'hangs' material—while Maia's recommended move overwhelmingly involves a queen capturing a major or minor piece (rook 55%, knight 31%). The median eval loss of ~491 centipawns is enormous, and the trajectory shows wins collapsing into draws or losses (winning->drawn 14%, winning->losing 12%, drawn->losing 7%). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), meaning the opponent had an undefended piece that the player simply failed to take. The example summaries reinforce this: a player checks with a knight instead of capturing a free rook, takes with the wrong piece removing attacking potential, or plays a passive move when a decisive queen capture existed. The pattern is a player overlooking or ignoring a concrete winning capture—typically a queen taking an inadequately defended piece—and instead making a move that looks active or safe but throws away material and the game.

824.label: Moving a rook passively when the king faces immediate mating threats or tactical dangers, missing a critical check or defensive resource.
824.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a rook (78% of cases) in a way that ignores urgent king safety concerns. The material signature shows these moves frequently hang material (56%) without capturing anything, while Maia's recommended move is always a rook delivering check (100%), indicating a missed checking resource that was either defensive (perpetual check) or tactically necessary. The dominant motifs are king_safety (62%) and tempo_loss (25%), with back_rank and mating_net tags recurring, suggesting the player's rook move fails to address immediate mating threats or misses a forcing check that would have saved/improved the position. The eval trajectory (56% losing->losing, 33% losing->winning) combined with a median 0cp loss indicates these are mostly small inaccuracies in already-decided positions—the player makes a passive or misdirected rook move when the only resource was an active checking sequence. The concrete positions confirm this: Rc8 instead of exploiting a knight fork, Rd7 ignoring a mating net, Rh8 walking into a discovered attack, all while a forcing check was available.

825.label: Knight moves that ignore king safety threats or remove critical defenders, allowing devastating tactical refutations.
825.description: This feature captures a specific pattern of erroneous knight moves (63% of activations) during the opening and middlegame (97% combined) where the player aggressively repositions or sacrifices a knight while overlooking critical king safety issues. The dominant motif is king_safety (80%), with tags revealing exposed kings in the center, ignored threats, and even missed checkmates. The median eval loss of 230 centipawns confirms these are serious tactical errors, not minor inaccuracies. The material signature shows a mix of hanging pieces (26%), unsound trades (23%), and slightly losing exchanges (14%) with a net median of -1.0, indicating the knight moves typically cost material or allow devastating counterplay. Maia's recommended moves (queen 23%, knight 23%, pawn 20%) suggest the correct responses were often quiet developing moves or exploiting the opponent's weakened king position rather than the speculative knight lunges played. The per-position analysis consistently shows knights being moved aggressively (Nd5, Nxf7, Nd4) while critical defensive duties or lethal opponent coordination (especially queen-bishop batteries targeting f2/f7) are ignored, resulting in immediate tactical punishment.

827.label: Pushing a passed or advanced pawn too early in a pawn endgame, allowing it to be blockaded or exchanged, squandering a winning advantage.
827.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player pushes a pawn forward (pawn moved 100%, no capture) in a way that costs significant evaluation (median 490cp lost), often converting a winning position into a drawn or much worse one (50% winning->drawn, 50% winning->winning but with massive eval loss). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (67%) and passed_pawn (17%), with recurring tags of king_activity loss, tempo_loss, and crucially premature_advance. The concrete positions consistently show pawn pushes (e4-e3, d4-d3, f4-f3, a5-a4, c4-c3) that either advance into easily blockaded squares, allow the opponent to exchange and neutralize a pawn majority, or abandon the pawn's role as a spatial restraint. The material signature shows 50% 'safe' and 50% 'hangs', meaning the pushed pawn itself sometimes becomes lost. This is a classic endgame technique error: advancing a pawn when patience (maintaining tension or improving the king first) was required.

826.label: Player moves a piece to an unsafe square, leaving it or another piece undefended against an existing threat.
826.description: This feature captures moves where the player hangs a piece (56% of moves result in a hang) by failing to notice an existing tactical threat. The material signature shows queen (30%) and knight (26%) moves that are non-captures (82%) yet lose approximately a piece worth of material (median -1.0, ~256 centipawns lost). The Maia recommendations strongly favor queen captures (63%), indicating that a simple winning capture was available that the player ignored. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (60%), with recurring tags like 'blunder_ignoring_threat' and 'missed_tactic'. The examples illustrate a consistent pattern: players make developing or seemingly active moves (like gaining tempo or repositioning) while overlooking that their move either removes a critical defender or leaves a piece unprotected. The eval trajectory shows these errors are catastrophic—converting wins to draws/losses (40%) or worsening already difficult positions (22%)—because the player prioritized their own plan over board awareness of opponent threats.

828.label: Trading the queen for a rook via check when a forced checkmate sequence exists, converting a won game into a merely advantageous endgame.
828.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced checkmate (often within 1-8 moves) but instead plays a queen capture of a rook with check—a superficially aggressive move that actually squanders the mating attack. The material signature is unambiguous: queen moves 100%, captures a rook 100%, delivers check 100%, yet the outcome is classified as 'loses' (net material median -4.0, consistent with trading queen for rook). The eval trajectory is catastrophic: a median loss of 9,274 centipawns, representing the difference between forced mate and a 'merely' winning endgame. The Opus analyses confirm the pattern repeatedly—forced mates in 1-8 moves are abandoned because the flashy queen-takes-rook-with-check feels decisive but actually removes the key attacking piece. The dominant tags (missed_mate, missed_tactic, king_safety, tempo_loss) all point to the same story: the player sees a tempting check/capture combination but fails to calculate the shorter mating line, prematurely simplifying into a position where the mating net has dissolved. This occurs overwhelmingly in endgame positions (75%) where the queen's dominance should be leveraged for mate rather than exchanged for material.
