893.description: This feature fires on positions where the player (usually moving their queen, 57%) makes a 'safe' move that doesn't lose material immediately but misses a critical tactical opportunity involving a fork or tempo-gaining check. The eval trajectory shows severe cost (median 359cp lost), with 29% going from drawn to losing and 29% from winning to drawn—classic 'threw the win/draw' patterns. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are forks (33%) and tempo loss (tagged twice), with deflection appearing frequently. Maia's recommended moves often involve checks (43%) or queen captures (29%), confirming that the engine saw forcing continuations the player overlooked. The concrete examples reinforce this: Black misses Qb4+ winning a rook via fork, White misses Bc8+ gaining decisive tempo, Black places the queen on a square vulnerable to a tempo-gaining attack. The positions span middlegame (57%) and endgame (43%), but the unifying thread is a quiet queen move when a forcing tactical blow (check/fork/deflection) was available.

891.label: Moving a piece (often the queen) to an ineffective square that loses tempo and allows the opponent's queen to exploit tactical weaknesses.
891.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a move—most often with the queen (52%) but sometimes with minor pieces or pawns—that fails to address the critical tactical demands of the position, while the opponent's queen (Maia recommends Qx captures 100% of the time) is poised to exploit hanging pieces or king safety issues. The material signature shows 41% of these moves hang a piece and 44% appear superficially safe, yet the median eval loss is a devastating 304 centipawns, with 24% of cases converting drawn positions to losing ones and 14% throwing away wins. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss 30%, hanging_piece 30%, king_safety 30%) reveal the common thread: the player's move ignores an immediate threat or fails to consolidate, often relocating a piece to a square where it loses coordination or abandons defense of a critical square. The top boards consistently show queens or pieces retreating to passive squares (Qb3+, Qg6, Nf3 retreats, Gc7 grabs) while the opponent's queen has a devastating capture or invasion available. These are not exchange errors but tactical oversights where piece placement priorities are misjudged under concrete pressure.

896.label: Premature flank pawn moves in the opening that lose tempo and allow tactical punishment.
896.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves during the opening phase (100% opening) that are non-captures (100%) and frequently hang material (60% hangs, median -1.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions to losing (60%) or winning to drawn (40%), with a substantial median loss of 278 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players push flank pawns (a3, b4, b5, h3, h6, a6) instead of addressing central tension or completing development. The dominant motifs are forks (40%) and tempo loss (40%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, pawn_structure, central_tension, and development. The concrete positions show classical opening structures (Italian, Ruy Lopez, King's Indian) where the opponent has strong central presence, and the erring player wastes a critical tempo on a wing pawn move that either walks into a tactical fork, allows the opponent to seize the initiative, or violates the principle of resolving central tension before flank play. Maia consistently suggests capturing a central pawn instead (100% pawn captures), confirming these were moments where concrete central action was required rather than prophylactic or expansive flank moves.

897.label: Moving a knight away from a critical defensive post, leaving pieces or king vulnerable to tactical exploitation.
897.description: This feature captures knight moves (89% knight) that are overwhelmingly non-captures (93%) yet result in hanging material (54%) with a median loss of 256 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (50%), reflecting that the knight was serving a crucial defensive role—guarding key squares, protecting other pieces, or shielding the king. The per-position analyses consistently describe the knight leaving a critical post (e.g., abandoning defense of f2, leaving a bishop undefended, vacating a square that prevented queen infiltration). The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic across all game states (winning->losing 11%, drawn->losing 14%), indicating the knight's departure triggers immediate tactical consequences like forced mates, captures with check, or removal-of-guard sequences. The tags (forced_mate, removal_of_guard, defensive_piece_removal, diagonal_weakness) confirm the knight was the linchpin of a defensive structure, and its departure collapses the position. This occurs almost entirely in the middlegame (89%) where piece coordination around the king is most critical.

895.label: Player abandons coordination with a dangerous passed pawn, allowing the opponent to neutralize a winning or drawn position.
895.description: This feature fires when a player makes a passive or irrelevant move (often a rook retreat, king move, or piece relocation) that severs the critical connection between their pieces and a dangerous passed pawn. The material signature shows mostly non-captures (90% no capture) that frequently hang material (40%) or are otherwise safe but pointless, with Maia strongly preferring rook moves (80%) that maintain pressure—often with check (40%). The eval trajectory is devastating: 40% winning->drawn, 30% drawn->losing, 20% winning->losing, with a median loss of 374 centipawns, indicating these are game-changing errors that throw away significant advantages. The tactical analysis reveals passed pawns and tempo loss as recurring tags, with examples consistently showing players moving pieces away from passed pawn support (Re8 instead of Rc1+ to protect b2 pawn, Re1 abandoning the c-file connection to b7 pawn, Kg2 instead of queen activity). Back-rank themes appear because the passed pawns often threaten promotion on the back rank, and the missed tactics involve exploiting that promotion threat. The positions consistently feature advanced passed pawns (a2, b2, b7, e7) where the player needed to maintain piece coordination for promotion but instead made a tempo-losing or passive move.

898.label: King captures an irrelevant pawn instead of maintaining optimal centralization or supporting passed pawns in a winning endgame.
898.description: This feature identifies a recurring pawn endgame mistake where the player's king deviates from the correct path to capture a tactically insignificant pawn, throwing away a winning position. The material signature shows trades (king or pawn capturing a pawn for roughly equal material exchange), but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 530 centipawns), often converting wins into draws or losses. The phase is exclusively endgame, and the dominant motifs (pawn_endgame 75%, passed_pawn, tempo_loss, king_activity) all point to the same error: the king wanders off to grab a pawn that could be won later (or is irrelevant), while the correct move was to centralize, support a passed pawn, or maintain a critical tempo. The Opus analyses confirm this pattern repeatedly—Kxc4 abandoning e5, capturing on f4 activating the opponent's king, h5xg6 releasing pawn tension. Maia's recommended moves are typically king centralizations (Ke4, Ke5, Kc6) that maintain dominance. The mistake is not a material blunder in the traditional sense but a positional/tempo catastrophe disguised as a 'free' pawn capture.

899.label: Rook captures a pawn but is immediately lost, sacrificing a full exchange with no compensation.
899.description: This feature identifies positions where a player captures a pawn with a rook but loses the rook in the process, resulting in a catastrophic material imbalance (net material median: -4.0, consistent with losing a rook for a pawn). The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (100%), often rook endgames with passed pawns, where the player misjudges that eliminating a pawn is worth sacrificing the rook. The eval trajectory shows these are already losing positions made significantly worse (losing->losing, median 275cp lost), indicating the player is desperately trying to address a threat (often a passed pawn) but chooses a self-destructive method. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant pattern: 'rook_for_pawn' tags, 'exchange_sacrifice_error', and summaries describing players who give up a full rook for a single pawn without adequate compensation. Maia's recommended moves are non-capturing rook moves, suggesting the rook should have been repositioned rather than sacrificed. The boards show rooks lunging at defended pawns or passed pawns where the resulting pawn endgame or material deficit is hopeless.

900.label: King or rook moves in endgames that lose critical tempo, allowing opponent to exploit passed pawns or win material.
900.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (75%) or rook (25%) in a way that loses significant tempo. The material signature shows these are not capture-related blunders—100% involve no captures—and most moves appear 'safe' (75%) in the immediate material sense, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional consequences (median 425cp lost), with 75% going from losing to deeper losing and 25% converting drawn positions into lost ones. The dominant motifs are passed pawns (29%), rook endgames (29%), and tempo loss (tagged in 3/4 positions), indicating the player misplaces their king or rook at a critical moment when precise timing was needed to handle passed pawns, maintain piece activity, or prevent deflection tactics. The concrete positions show kings walking into pawn checks that deflect them from defending pieces, kings failing to invade at the right moment, and rooks being passively placed when active moves were required. The common thread is a failure to appreciate the urgency of tempo in simplified positions with passed pawns.

902.label: Moving a major piece to a square that converts a drawable endgame into a lost one by hanging material.
902.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves a queen or rook to a square that either hangs the piece outright or loses significant material (median -5.0 material, with 50% hangs and 50% loses). The eval trajectory is devastating: 75% of the time a drawn position becomes losing, with a median loss of 777 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals rook endgames and hanging pieces as dominant motifs, with recurring themes of missed perpetual checks, poisoned pawns, and piece activity errors. The concrete positions show players making seemingly active rook or queen moves (Ra4, Ra6, Qg4, Ra8) that fail to maintain drawing resources — often missing perpetual check opportunities or capturing poisoned pawns on controlled squares. The key unifying pattern is a player in a holdable endgame who makes an impatient or greedy major-piece move that immediately drops the piece or decisive material, converting a theoretical draw into a trivial loss.

903.label: Trading rooks on a back rank that allows a mating attack or devastating back-rank tactic.
903.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern where a player initiates a rook trade (93% rook moves, 79% capturing a rook, 100% trades) on the back rank, failing to recognize that the recapture or resulting position enables a lethal back-rank mating sequence. The Opus analysis confirms back_rank as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with tags including king_safety, forced_mate, and back_rank_mate. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 360 centipawns, with many positions collapsing from playable (or even winning) into forced checkmate in 2-3 moves. The top boards all show contested back ranks with rooks lined up, where the player mechanically recaptures or initiates an exchange without recognizing that the resulting open file or removal of a defending rook exposes their own king to an unstoppable mating pattern. Maia never captures in these positions (100% non-capture), suggesting the correct move was typically a defensive or evasive move rather than the seemingly natural trade.

901.label: Developing or moving a piece in the opening that leaves an undefended queen en prise, turning a drawn position into a lost one.
901.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player makes a non-capturing developing move (knight or pawn, 50% each) that inadvertently hangs a major piece—specifically the queen. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' with a median net loss of -6.0 (approximately queen value), and the eval trajectory confirms a drawn position collapses into a losing one (median 464cp lost). The tactical analysis consistently identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, with 'hanging_queen' appearing frequently in the tags. Examining the top boards reveals a recurring pattern: positions from well-known opening lines (Scandinavian Defense, Philidor, Caro-Kann) where the player's queen is actively placed or exposed, and a routine developing move (like ...Nf6, ...e6, Bg5, Nc3, Bf4) neglects that the queen is left undefended on an open diagonal or file. Maia's recommended move is always a queen move (100%), confirming the queen needed to relocate to safety. These are classic beginner-level oversights where the player focuses on development or a plan while forgetting their queen's vulnerability.

904.label: Exchanging a well-placed minor piece for an inferior opponent's piece, surrendering tactical or positional dominance.
904.description: This feature fires on positions where the player initiates a minor piece trade (bishop or knight captures knight or bishop) that is materially equal but positionally catastrophic. The material signature shows 100% trades with net material of 0.0, yet the median eval loss is 249 centipawns—indicating the exchange itself destroys significant positional value. The Opus analyses consistently describe trading a 'dominant' or 'tactically essential' piece for the opponent's worst or most passive piece (tagged 'good_piece_for_bad_piece', 'premature_capture'). The boards confirm this: active knights on outposts (e6, d4, c5) or bishops performing vital restraining/attacking functions are swapped off for undeveloped or passive enemy pieces. The eval trajectory shows this costs wins (winning->drawn, drawn->losing) because the traded piece was the linchpin of the player's attacking or tactical pressure. King safety and pin motifs appear because the traded piece was often contributing to an attack or defensive structure. This occurs predominantly in the opening/early middlegame (60%/40%) where piece activity differentials are most consequential, and the player impulsively captures rather than maintaining the tension with their superior piece.

906.label: Moving a knight to a square where it obstructs a vital defensive or offensive line, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical weakness.
906.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves a knight (50% of activating moves) into a square that fatally disrupts coordination among their own pieces—typically blocking a queen's defensive path, removing a key defender, or abandoning control of critical squares. The material signature shows these moves predominantly hang material (67%) with a median loss of ~1 pawn equivalent, while the eval trajectory reveals massive cost (median 269cp lost), often making already-losing positions decisively worse (67% losing->losing) but sometimes throwing away drawn or winning positions entirely. The tactical analysis confirms the recurring pattern: pieces become overloaded or undefended (hanging_piece 43%), positional coordination collapses (positional_mistake 29%), and the opponent's queen gains infiltration routes (queen_infiltration tag). The concrete examples repeatedly show Nbd2 blocking queen paths, knights moving to squares that unguard pawns, and piece moves that inadvertently create tactical sequences the opponent can exploit. These are not simple one-move blunders but coordination failures where the knight move disrupts the defensive architecture of the position.

905.label: Playing a passive or tempo-losing move that leaves a piece undefended, resulting in significant material loss.
905.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make passive repositioning moves or tempo-losing retreats that leave pieces hanging. The material signature shows 79% of moves result in hanging a piece (non-captures that drop material), with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The pieces moved are predominantly bishops (36%) and kings (21%), suggesting passive redeployments or king walks that abandon defense of other pieces. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (43%), tempo_loss (29%), and passed_pawn (29%)—paint a clear picture: instead of addressing urgent tactical demands (capturing material, advancing/blocking passed pawns, or defending attacked pieces), players waste a tempo on an aimless move. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors (median 385cp lost), with 21% converting wins to losses and 21% converting draws to losses. The concrete examples reinforce this: Bc2 wastes tempo when Rd1 was critical; Kf5 abandons the knight on d5; Kg3 ignores a passed pawn situation. In each case, the player had a concrete obligation (defend a piece, capture material, or address a passed pawn) but instead played a move that looked natural yet left material en prise.

907.label: Choosing a slow or wrong pawn move in a winning pawn/rook endgame, losing a critical tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
907.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (59% middlegame, 41% endgame, but the tactical analysis reveals 67% pawn_endgame motif and 33% passed_pawn motif) where the player makes a tempo-losing pawn or rook move that squanders a winning or drawn position. The material signature shows the moved piece is often a pawn (33%) or rook (30%) with no capture (93%), and the move is nominally 'safe' (67%) yet results in catastrophic eval swings (median 574cp lost), with 26% going winning->losing and 15% winning->drawn. The recurring tags—passed_pawn, tempo_loss, pawn_race, pawn_breakthrough—combined with the Opus examples (e.g., choosing a slow flank push instead of an urgent kingside breakthrough, or pushing a passed pawn one square too early giving the opponent a key tempo) paint a clear picture: the player misjudges the timing in a pawn-centric endgame, plays a move that looks natural but loses the race by exactly one tempo, handing the win to the opponent.

908.label: Player moves a piece (often rook or king) that leaves another piece undefended and hanging, throwing away a winning position.
908.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player makes a non-capturing move (70% no capture) that hangs a piece (70% 'hangs' outcome), resulting in a catastrophic median material loss of -3.0 and a median eval swing of 575 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly thrown wins: 50% go from winning to losing and 30% from winning to drawn. The dominant tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' (83%), with tags emphasizing undefended pieces and material oversight. The concrete positions confirm this: a king move that leaves a bishop en prise (Kd2 leaving material loose), a rook move that ignores an attacked piece (Rf8-a8 leaving material hanging), or a king move that abandons defense of a critical piece (Kc4 leaving the c2-bishop to be captured). The player's attention is drawn elsewhere—repositioning a rook, moving the king—while failing to notice that a piece is left without protection. Maia's suggested moves (which often involve knight, queen, or rook) frequently address the tactical threat directly, confirming that the error is pure oversight rather than a calculated sacrifice.

909.label: Trading pieces or pawns that releases tension and worsens an already difficult defensive position.
909.description: This feature identifies exchanges (79% trades, median net material 0.0) where the player captures a piece—typically a knight (47%) or pawn (42%)—that releases critical tension in the position, accelerating their decline. The eval trajectory shows these moves predominantly occur in already-losing positions (58% losing->losing) but cost a substantial median of 209 centipawns, transforming holdable or difficult positions into clearly lost ones. The tactical motifs (king_safety 33%, discovered_attack 17%, back_rank 17%) reveal that these trades remove defensive resources or open lines that benefit the opponent's attack. Concrete examples like fxe6 opening the f-file for Black's rook, or axb5 creating back-rank vulnerabilities, illustrate the pattern: the player initiates a seemingly natural exchange that resolves pawn or piece tension prematurely, but the resulting open lines, discovered attacks, or weakened king position far outweigh the superficially equal material transaction. Maia's preferred moves (84% non-captures) suggest the correct approach was usually to maintain tension rather than trade.

910.label: Giving a purposeless check with the queen in a queen endgame that either hangs the queen or allows a fatal queen trade into a lost pawn endgame.
910.description: This feature fires on queen checks in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the check serves no constructive purpose and causes severe damage. The material signature shows the player always moves their queen (100%) and always gives check (100%), yet Maia's recommended move was consistently a queen capturing a pawn (100% Qxpawn, 0% check), indicating the check was chosen over concrete material gains. The tactical tags 'pointless_check' and 'tempo_loss' appear repeatedly, confirming these checks gain nothing positionally. The consequences are catastrophic: 100% missed winning material, with a median eval loss of 254 centipawns, and trajectories showing positions collapsing from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-losing. The concrete boards reveal the mechanism: checks that allow queen interpositions forcing trades into lost pawn endgames (e.g., Qe4+ allowing Qe5!), checks that land on defended squares hanging the queen outright (e.g., Qb4+ where a3 captures), or checks that waste tempo while passed pawns needed immediate attention. The common thread is a reflexive check impulse overriding the critical endgame task of capturing or blockading passed pawns.

911.label: Player makes a bishop capture/trade while ignoring a more urgent tactical threat, typically a hanging piece elsewhere.
911.description: This feature fires when players move their bishop (55% of activations) to make a trade or capture that is objectively inferior because it ignores a critical threat on the board. The material signature shows trades (36%) and hangs (27%), with a median net loss of -1.0 material, while the eval trajectory reveals a massive median cost of 341 centipawns—often converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->losing 18%, winning->drawn 18%). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (80%), and Opus analysis consistently describes scenarios where the player captures with their bishop (often taking a knight on a natural-looking square like Bxc6 or Bxf6) while completely overlooking that a more valuable piece—frequently a queen or bishop—is hanging elsewhere. Maia's recommended moves (queen 36%, bishop 36%) confirm the engine wanted to address the hanging piece or play a more forcing continuation. The positions cluster in the opening/early middlegame (55%/46%) where piece development creates multiple tactical obligations, and the player's bishop move represents a tunnel-vision capture that misses the board's most urgent demand.

912.label: Player hangs a major piece in a clearly winning position, allowing opponent to capture it for free.
912.description: This feature captures a devastating and recurring blunder pattern: a player with a winning position (62% winning->losing trajectory) makes a move—most often a king or knight move—that leaves a major piece completely unprotected (62% 'hangs' material, 100% hanging_piece motif). The median eval loss of 1261 centipawns confirms these are catastrophic swings. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing a queen (75%) or rook (25%), confirming that the opponent's piece was freely available but the player instead made an aimless or misguided move. The boards show patterns like king moves abandoning defensive duties over pieces (Kh8 leaving a rook unguarded), knight moves abandoning rook defense, or moving pieces away from critical squares. Tags like 'tempo_loss', 'false_sacrifice', and 'check_is_not_always_best' reinforce that players are making moves that feel active but actually neglect basic piece safety. The 88% missed winning material rate confirms these players had strong positions and simply failed to notice their own piece was en prise after their move.

915.label: Advancing a passed or key pawn too early in the endgame, squandering a positional advantage.
915.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves in endgame positions (73% endgame, 27% middlegame) where the player pushes a pawn forward without capturing, and the move either hangs material (35%) or is nominally safe but positionally devastating (62%). The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly cases of throwing away a win or drawing chance: 35% go from winning to drawn, 19% from drawn to losing, and 4% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 289 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are passed pawns (44%) and pawn endgames (33%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, king_activity, and pawn_structure. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: players advance passed pawns (d5-d6, g5-g6, e5-e6, a5-a6) or push pawns prematurely (b4-b3, c7-c5, f5-f4, f4-f3, e4-e3) when patient king maneuvering or piece activity was required. The pawn advance often destroys a critical restraint, loses a tempo, or allows the opponent's king to become active, converting what was a winning or tenable position into one that is drawn or lost.

913.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that ignores a critical king safety threat, allowing the opponent a strong attacking continuation.
913.description: This feature fires on moves where the player neglects king safety in the middlegame, typically by making a pawn, bishop, or knight move that fails to address an imminent mating attack or king-side threat. The material signature shows 96% non-captures with 36% of moves hanging material, indicating the player is making quiet moves when urgent defensive or counter-attacking action is needed. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 273 centipawns, with positions shifting from drawn-to-losing (23%) or losing-to-more-lost (23%), confirming these are mistakes that allow the opponent's attack to become decisive. The Opus analysis is unambiguous: 100% of positions are tagged with king_safety as the dominant motif, with mating_attack, exposed_king, and missed_tactic as supporting tags. Maia's recommended moves are predominantly piece captures (bishop/knight captures at 77%), indicating the correct response was to eliminate attacking pieces or contest key squares around the king. The top boards consistently show positions with exposed kings (castled or otherwise) where the player makes a developing or spatial move (like b6-b5, c3-c4, e4-e5) instead of addressing the opponent's gathering kingside forces.

914.label: Moving the rook to a passive or irrelevant square instead of exploiting an active opportunity in simplified positions.
914.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame/late-middlegame mistake where the player moves a rook (49% of activations) to a passive square, squandering a concrete tactical or positional opportunity. The material signature shows these moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (88%) and nominally 'safe' (70%), yet Maia consistently recommends a rook move instead (89%), indicating the correct plan involved an active rook deployment. The eval trajectory is severe (median 218cp lost), with 36% of cases converting drawn positions into losing ones—suggesting these passive rook retreats or lateral shuffles surrender critical tempos in simplified positions. The motif analysis confirms this: tempo_loss (30%) and hanging_piece (30%) dominate, while tags like rook_endgame, passed_pawn, and piece_activity recur. The top boards illustrate the pattern clearly—positions with few pieces where the rook needed to seize an active file, attack a pawn, or cut off the opposing king, but instead was moved to a square with no immediate threat or defensive purpose (e.g., Rh1-c1 instead of Rxh7, Rc6-c5 losing tempo, Re8-g8 abandoning back-rank pressure). The player repeatedly fails to recognize that in simplified positions, rook activity and tempo are paramount, defaulting to 'safe-looking' but strategically catastrophic passive placements.

916.label: Misplacing a rook or king in a passed-pawn endgame, losing critical tempo and allowing the opponent's passer to advance or promote.
916.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (71% endgame phase) where the player moves a rook (57%) or king (29%) in a way that is materially 'safe' (86% nothing hangs) but positionally catastrophic, costing a median of 269 centipawns. The dominant motifs are passed pawns (50%) and tempo loss (25%), with rook endgames appearing in most cases. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions into lost ones (29% drawn->losing) or throw away winning advantages (14% winning->drawn), indicating the player fails to respect the urgency of passed pawn races. The top boards consistently show advanced passed pawns (a-file, c-file promoters) where the correct move involves directly supporting or blockading the passer, but instead the player makes a passive rook shuffle or king move that loses a crucial tempo, allowing the opponent's pawn to queen or the opponent's pieces to achieve decisive activity. Maia's preferred moves (71% pawn moves) confirm that the engine wanted direct pawn advancement rather than the slow piece maneuvers chosen.

918.label: Player makes a quiet or materialistic move instead of delivering a forcing check/mate sequence exploiting the opponent's exposed king.
918.description: This feature fires when a player, typically with a queen (44% of moves played), makes a safe but non-forcing move (78% safe, 0% checks played) while Maia's recommended move is almost always a queen check (94% queen, 100% check). The dominant motif is king_safety (71%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, exposed_king, and missed_mate. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 203 centipawns, often converting winning positions into drawn or less advantageous ones (winning->drawn 6%, winning->winning 44% but with significant eval loss). The board positions consistently show an opponent's king on an exposed square (often h6/h-file) where a forcing check sequence would win material or deliver mate, but the player instead plays a passive continuation like advancing a pawn, capturing material greedily (Qxd5 instead of Qg7+), or repositioning without tempo. The per-position analyses repeatedly describe missed mate-in-3 patterns and forced tactical sequences beginning with checks that exploit geometric queen-rook coordination against a trapped king.

920.label: Player makes a quiet developing or non-capturing move while the opponent's queen is hanging and freely capturable.
920.description: This feature fires consistently on positions where the opponent's queen is en prise (undefended or inadequately defended) and the player fails to capture it, instead making a routine developing or positional move. The material/position signature shows the player's moves are non-captures (100% no capture) and mostly safe (93%), meaning they aren't blundering their own pieces—they're simply missing a free queen. Maia's recommended move captures a queen 93% of the time, confirming the missed opportunity. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 425 centipawns, often swinging from winning to drawn or even losing (33% winning->drawn, 13% winning->losing), reflecting the enormous cost of missing a free queen. The tactical analysis tags (hanging_piece 86%, hanging_queen, missed_capture, missed_tactic) and concrete examples all confirm the same pattern: the opponent's queen sits undefended on an open square, attacked by an available piece, and the player plays a development move (Nc3, Be3, h3, Nf3) completely ignoring the capture. This occurs predominantly in the opening phase (73%) where early tactical oversights around exposed queens are most common.

919.label: In winning or complex endgames, the player makes a quiet move that misses a forcing tactical sequence (fork, queen trade, capture) and squanders a decisive advantage.
919.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player, often in a winning or at least holdable position, plays a passive or aimless move (typically a rook or king move that is 'safe' in material terms—no captures, no checks) instead of finding a concrete forcing continuation. The phase is 100% endgame, and the eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 628cp), with moves turning winning positions into drawn or lost ones. The Opus analysis reveals that the best moves consistently involved forcing lines: queen trades into trivially winning pawn endgames, knight forks winning the queen, or captures of undefended pieces. Instead, the player's moves are characterized by tempo losses, self-blocks, or king moves that walk into checks. The dominant tags—queen_trade, simplification, bishop_endgame, missed_capture—all point to situations where the player needed to calculate a short concrete sequence to convert but instead played a 'natural-looking' quiet move. The motifs of king_safety and fork indicate that the missed lines often involved tactical geometry the player failed to see under endgame simplification pressure.

917.label: Pawn moves in the opening that fatally weaken king safety, especially along diagonals, allowing tactical punishment.
917.description: This feature captures a specific recurring opening-phase blunder (74% opening) where the player makes a pawn or minor piece move that catastrophically weakens their king's position. The material signature shows 62% 'safe' and 32% 'hangs'—the moves don't immediately lose material but create vulnerabilities that the opponent exploits tactically. The eval trajectory is devastating: 56% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 288 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: king_safety is the dominant motif (44%), with weakened diagonals, missed tactics, and development issues as recurring tags. The top boards make the pattern vivid—multiple instances of ...f6 against a knight on e5, removing the f-pawn and exposing the e8-h5 diagonal to Qh5+ ideas, or f2-f3 weakening the king's position. Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%), suggesting the correct continuation was developing or repositioning a knight rather than making the weakening pawn push. The player ignores king safety in pursuit of attacking or displacing the opponent's well-placed knight, but the 'cure' proves far worse than the disease.

921.label: Player makes a quiet/developmental move in the opening, missing a forcing queen check sequence that wins material.
921.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing move (often castling or a pawn push) in the opening phase, while missing a concrete queen check sequence that would have won material. The material signature shows 100% safe moves (nothing hangs immediately) yet 100% missed winning material, indicating the player chose a positionally reasonable but tactically inferior move. Maia consistently recommends queen moves (100%), often delivering checks (75%), revealing that the missed tactic involves a forcing check-and-capture combination. The eval trajectory is severe (median 398cp lost), typically converting a drawn position to losing (75%) or a winning position to drawn (25%). The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs include tempo_loss and hanging_piece, with recurring tags of missed_tactic, exposed_king, and queen_check. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows positions where the opponent's king is exposed (often on f7 after early king moves in open games), and the player opts for development (castling, pawn moves) instead of exploiting the exposed king with a forcing queen check sequence that picks up undefended material.

923.label: Failing to capture a knight (often on c3/c6) in the opening, losing tempo and squandering a winning advantage.
923.description: This feature fires when players in the opening (80%) make moves—often pawn pushes or quiet piece moves—that ignore a critical knight capture available on the board. The material signature shows the played move hangs material 60% of the time (median net -1.0), while Maia consistently recommends capturing a knight (100% knight moves, 80% knight captures). The eval trajectory is devastating: 80% of the time a winning position collapses to drawn, with a median loss of 332 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (60%) and missed_tactic (20%), with recurring tags around development, piece activity, and king safety. Examining the concrete positions, many arise from Sicilian/Italian/Spanish-type openings where a knight lands on c3 or c6 and the opponent plays a slow move (c6, O-O, Bxc3, Qf3) instead of the one critical capture (Nxc3, Nxc6) that maintains the advantage. The positions are narrow—typically only one good move exists—making the miss especially costly.

922.label: Playing an aggressive central pawn advance in the opening that overlooks a knight fork or tactical refutation, turning a balanced position into a losing one.
922.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn moves (100% pawn played, 100% opening) that are materially 'safe' in the immediate sense (nothing is directly hanging) but cause a catastrophic positional collapse, with the eval consistently shifting from drawn to losing by a median of 349 centipawns. The recurring pattern involves premature ...e5 or similar central pawn pushes (visible in the top FENs showing Sicilian Dragon and similar structures) where the player advances a pawn aggressively but overlooks that it creates tactical vulnerabilities—particularly knight forks or hanging pieces—that the opponent's already-developed knight (Maia's move is 100% knight) can exploit. The tags confirm this is a development/tempo/piece-activity mistake: the pawn push either loses tempo, weakens squares, or allows a tactical shot that the player missed. The motifs (fork 33%, hanging_piece 33%, positional_mistake 33%) show the refutation is tactical in nature but the root cause is a positional misjudgment—pushing a pawn before adequate development, creating exploitable weaknesses in the opening.

924.label: Developing a bishop to an undefended square where the opponent's queen captures it for free in the opening.
924.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring opening blunder: the player develops their bishop (100% bishop moves) to a square—almost always g4 or g5—where it is completely undefended and immediately capturable by the opponent's queen. The material signature confirms this is not a trade but a pure hang (96% hangs, median -3.0 material, i.e., a full piece). The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic, turning drawn positions into losing ones (91% drawn->losing, median 472 centipawns lost). The tactical analysis unanimously identifies the hanging_piece motif (100%), with tags like undefended_bishop, queen_capture, and opening_trap reinforcing the pattern. The top boards reveal the concrete recurrence: in standard opening positions (100% opening phase), players move their c-file bishop to g4/g5 prematurely, apparently expecting a pin on the knight/queen but overlooking that the opponent's queen on d1/d8 simply captures the unprotected bishop. This is a fundamental one-move tactical oversight common among lower-rated players in the opening.

925.label: Developing a bishop to an ineffective square in the opening, losing tempo and often hanging the piece.
925.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake: moving a bishop (100% bishop moves) to a square where it has no real target or function, typically Bg4 or Bg5 in the opening (98% opening phase). The material signature shows these moves hang a piece 55% of the time (median cost -1.0, i.e., a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences—51% of activations turn a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 370 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core motifs: tempo_loss (40%) because the bishop is immediately kicked back or trapped, hanging_piece (30%) because it lands on an undefended square with no support, and king_safety issues (10%) because the player ignores critical threats (like f7 attacks) to develop the bishop prematurely. The top boards consistently show Bg4 played without a piece on f3 to pin, or Bg5 played where it accomplishes nothing, allowing the opponent to gain tempi with f3 or h3 while simultaneously exploiting the neglected center or king position. Maia's recommended alternatives (pawns 31%, knights 27%) suggest proper developing moves or defensive resources were available.

930.label: Playing a slow or speculative move instead of cashing in with an immediate bishop capture winning material.
930.description: This feature fires when players make a non-capturing move (82% no capture) with a pawn, bishop, or knight instead of taking a concrete bishop capture that wins material (Maia's move is bishop 100%, capturing a pawn 71% or bishop 29%). The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the median eval loss is 250 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (32% winning->drawn, 11% winning->losing). The tactical analyses repeatedly describe scenarios where the player chose a speculative pawn advance (like f5) or a positional developing move (like Qe2, Bd7, Ne5) while a clean Bxb7 or similar bishop capture was available on a specific diagonal. Common motifs include tempo loss, blocking one's own bishop diagonal, and positional mistakes—all reflecting the failure to execute a time-sensitive capture. The positions are typically in the opening or middlegame with bishops aimed at vulnerable pawns, where a narrow tactical window demands immediate material collection rather than slow preparation.

928.label: Player makes a safe but passive move, missing a forcing knight tactic (often Nxf7+ or similar) that wins material.
928.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a materially safe move (no captures, nothing hangs) while missing a powerful knight tactic that wins the exchange or more, typically involving a check. The material signature shows 100% safe moves with no captures, while Maia consistently recommends a knight move capturing a rook with check (Nxf7+, Nxf3+, etc.). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 263 centipawns, with positions going from losing to worse or from winning to drawn—indicating these missed tactics represent critical turning points. The dominant motifs center on king safety and exposed kings: the missed tactics exploit vulnerable king positions (uncastled kings, weakened f7 squares, open files toward the king). The per-position analysis confirms players chose passive retreats or pawn pushes (Qd7, f6, Nh3, Bb5) instead of the forcing tactical blow. In several cases, the passive move actually worsens king safety (e.g., f6 opening the f7 square) compounding the error.

926.label: Player delivers a check or queen move that squanders a forced checkmate sequence, settling for a merely winning position.
926.description: This feature fires when a player has a forced mate available (typically mate-in-2 to mate-in-4) but plays an inferior queen move or check that throws away the mating sequence. The material signature shows queen moves (88%) that frequently give check (75%) but result in material loss or hanging pieces (net median -6.0), indicating the queen is often sacrificed or placed on a vulnerable square unnecessarily. The eval trajectory is striking: the median centipawn loss is 9226, reflecting the enormous gap between a forced mate and the resulting merely-winning position. Critically, 100% of positions had missed winning material, and the Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'missed_mate' and 'king_safety' themes, with specific examples describing forced mates in 2-4 being converted into won endgames. The dominant motif is king_safety (50%), consistent with positions where the opponent's king is already exposed and ripe for a mating attack. The player sees the attack and delivers a check, but chooses the wrong checking square or the wrong piece, often allowing the opponent to escape or trade down. The positions cluster in the middlegame (88%) where mating nets are most complex and easy to miscalculate by one critical square.

927.label: Unnecessary pawn advances in the opening that leave a piece undefended, typically losing material worth ~2 pawns.
927.description: This feature detects a specific opening-phase blunder where the player pushes a pawn (78% pawn moves, 22% bishop moves that similarly ignore threats) without capturing anything, yet the move leaves a piece hanging (100% 'hangs' material signature, median net material -2.0). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (100%) and the eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (89% drawn->losing), with a median cost of 245 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players advance h-pawns (h4, h5) or make passive developing moves (d6, Be2) when they should instead be retreating or repositioning a bishop that is under attack (Maia's suggested moves are 67% bishop, 33% knight—the pieces that needed attention). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (62%) and king_safety (38%), with tempo_loss and development as top tags, confirming these are wasted tempi in critical opening positions where a piece (usually a bishop on g4 or a knight) is en prise and the player ignores the threat to push an irrelevant pawn.

929.label: Minor piece moves in the opening that fatally abandon critical defensive duties, turning drawn positions into losing ones.
929.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (95% opening) where players move minor pieces (bishops 37%, knights 34%) to squares that look active or natural but critically abandon defensive responsibilities. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (66%) — nothing is immediately captured or hung in the obvious sense — yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: 58% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 348 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the mechanism: pieces are moved away from squares where they performed essential defensive functions (blocking diagonals, covering key squares, maintaining king safety). The motifs — hanging_piece (50%), king_safety (33%), trapped_piece (17%) — combined with tags like 'missed_tactic', 'uncastled_king', and 'lost_defensive_resource' paint a clear picture: players relocate minor pieces without recognizing that those pieces were the linchpin of their position's structural integrity. Examples include a knight leaving e7 (removing a critical diagonal block), a bishop going to a5 where it gets trapped, and castling queenside into an exposed position. The best move (Maia: bishop takes knight 100%) typically involves a concrete defensive exchange that maintains the position's balance, which the player bypasses in favor of a seemingly developing but fatally weakening move.

932.label: King moves that block or delay own passed pawn advancement in won endgames.
932.description: This feature identifies a specific endgame mistake where a player, holding a winning position with passed pawns, makes a king move that obstructs or delays their own pawn's promotion path. The material signature shows 56% king moves with 89% no captures, confirming these are non-capturing king maneuvers rather than tactical exchanges. The phase is 100% endgame, and the eval trajectory shows these errors convert winning positions into still-winning (78%) or drawn (22%) ones, with a massive median cost of 472 centipawns—indicating severe positional damage even when the result category doesn't always change. The tactical analysis reveals dominant motifs of promotion_error, passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and pawn_endgame, while the concrete positions (e.g., Kg7 blocking the g-pawn, Kb5 abandoning pawn support, Ka3 prioritizing capture over promotion) consistently show kings stepping into squares needed by their own pawns or wasting critical tempo that allows the opponent's king to reach key defensive squares. The common thread is a failure to coordinate king placement with pawn promotion plans in technically won endgames.

933.label: Capturing or chasing pawns with major pieces while abandoning critical defensive or attacking coordination.
933.description: This feature identifies moves where the player uses a major piece (queen 50%, knight 33%, rook 17%) to capture pawns (83% pawn captures) but at catastrophic positional and material cost (median eval lost: 753 centipawns). The trajectory shows these are decisive blunders—50% go from winning to losing, 33% from drawn to losing—indicating the player had a good or tenable position and threw it away. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying cause: the piece capturing the pawn abandons a critical defensive or coordinating role (king_safety x3, piece_coordination x2, defensive_piece_removal x1), leaving back-rank weaknesses, hanging pieces, or structural collapse. Examples include Qc3 grabbing a pawn while exposing the king, Qa2 snatching material while the queenside collapses, and Nf5 relocating from a key defensive post. Maia's recommended moves (50% non-captures) suggest the correct play was maintaining piece placement rather than grabbing material, confirming these as greed-driven positional catastrophes.

931.label: King moves that ignore critical passed pawn promotion threats in the endgame.
931.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (78% endgame phase) where the player makes a king move (67% king moves) that is objectively safe in terms of immediate material (67% safe, median net material 0.0) but misses winning material 89% of the time. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (30%) and tempo_loss (30%), with passed_pawn appearing in 9/9 top positions as a tag. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 100 centipawns, often in already-losing or already-winning positions where the player fails to address the critical passed pawn situation—either their own promotion opportunity or the opponent's. Examining the concrete positions, we see advanced passed pawns (on c2, a2, e7, d7, b7, c7) where the player's king wanders to an irrelevant square instead of supporting or stopping promotion. Maia's suggested moves frequently involve checks (44%) or more active piece play that directly engages with the promotion race. The mistake is fundamentally a tempo loss in a pawn race—moving the king to a square that doesn't contribute to the critical promotion dynamics, allowing the opponent to gain a decisive tempo advantage.

935.label: Player develops or retreats a minor piece instead of capturing an undefended knight with the queen.
935.description: This feature fires consistently in opening positions where the opponent has placed a knight on an exposed square (typically h4 or h5) that is completely undefended and capturable by the queen. The player, focused on routine development or retreating their own bishop, plays a 'safe' minor piece move (bishop 60%, knight 40%) that ignores the free material. Maia consistently identifies Qxh4/Qxh5 as the correct move (queen 100%, capturing knight 100%). The material signature shows the played move is technically 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), but the missed tactic costs a median of 472 centipawns, converting a winning position into a drawn one. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (78%), with tags like 'undefended_knight' and 'missed_capture' reinforcing that the player simply failed to notice or prioritize the free piece. The positions cluster around London System and similar d4/e3 openings where knights land on the h-file rim squares early and go unnoticed.

936.label: Player makes a quiet piece move instead of capturing a hanging minor piece with a pawn, squandering a winning advantage.
936.description: This feature identifies positions where the player has a winning or near-winning advantage and plays a quiet, seemingly active piece move (bishop 44%, rook 22%, pawn 22%) instead of a simple pawn capture that would win material. The material signature shows the played move is 'safe' (89%) — nothing is immediately lost — but Maia's recommended move is always a pawn capture taking a bishop (89%) or knight (11%). The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 67% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 258 centipawns. The board positions consistently show an enemy bishop or knight on g4/g5 that can be captured by an h-pawn (hxg4, hxg5), but the player instead develops a piece, repositions a rook, or makes a king move. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 30%, fork 20%) and tags (missed_tactic, missed_capture) confirm the player overlooks freely capturable material. The example summaries explicitly reference missing hxg4/hxg5 pawn captures. This is a pattern of neglecting simple pawn takes on pieces that appear active but are actually hanging.

934.label: Hanging a piece in the opening by ignoring tactical threats while already losing.
934.description: This feature captures a specific pattern of opening-phase blunders where a player, already in a losing position, makes a move that hangs material (median -3.0 pawns net loss, 100% hang rate). The moves involve queens (50%), bishops (25%), and kings (25%) but never capture anything—these are non-tactical moves that overlook immediate threats. The Opus analysis reveals the underlying motifs: hanging pieces (67%) and forks (33%), with recurring tags of capture sequences, opening disasters, ignored threats, and piece vulnerability. The player consistently fails to notice that their piece is undefended or that a forcing sequence (pin exploitation, deflection, fork) wins material. The eval trajectory shows these are already-losing positions made catastrophically worse (median 371cp lost), suggesting players in distress compound their problems by tunnel-visioning on their own plans while ignoring opponent threats. The top boards all show complex opening positions with multiple tactical tensions where one side plays a natural-looking developing or repositioning move while completely missing that a piece is en prise to a concrete tactical shot.

937.label: Player makes a non-critical move that overlooks an immediate tactical threat exploiting their exposed king.
937.description: This feature fires when players make moves that catastrophically ignore threats to their own king's safety. The material signature shows 54% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that leave material en prise) with a median loss of -1.0 material, and the pieces moved are often knights (33%) or kings (25%) — purposeless repositioning moves rather than addressing the crisis. The eval trajectory reveals devastating consequences: a median of 449 centipawns lost, with 17% converting winning positions to losing and 21% converting drawn positions to losing. The dominant tactical motif is king_safety (57% of positions), supported by tags like checkmate_in_one, exposed_king, and back_rank threats. The concrete examples confirm this pattern: players make seemingly reasonable developing or repositioning moves (Kh8, Bb6, b5, Ng6) while their king is critically exposed, allowing the opponent to execute mating attacks, queen invasions, or decisive combinations targeting the king. Maia's recommendations (50% knight moves, mostly non-captures) suggest the correct responses involved defensive piece placements or blocks that the players failed to recognize as urgent. The positions are predominantly middlegame (75%) where king safety is paramount but the board complexity masks the immediate danger.

938.label: Rook moves or captures that leave pieces hanging or walk into tactical traps, causing catastrophic material loss in the middlegame.
938.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a rook move (48% rook, with queen and bishop moves also represented) that results in severe material loss (43% loses, 19% hangs, median net -4.0 material, median 425cp eval drop). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), with passed_pawn and back_rank threats also present. The eval trajectory shows these aren't just worsening already-lost positions—19% swing from winning to losing and 19% from drawn to losing, indicating thrown games. The tactical analysis reveals a pattern of rook moves that either walk into traps (e.g., capturing a pawn on e7 only to have it recaptured decisively), miss hanging pieces elsewhere (e.g., taking a queen trade when a free knight is available), or fail to address immediate threats like back-rank mates and passed pawns. Maia's recommended moves are often king moves (24%) or quiet defensive moves (67% non-captures), suggesting the correct response was to address a tactical threat rather than pursue the active-looking rook move that was played.

939.label: Player hangs or poorly trades a piece in the opening by overlooking a tactical refutation involving undefended pieces.
939.description: This feature identifies opening-phase mistakes where the player moves a bishop or rook and either hangs material outright (50%) or enters a trade that loses significant net material (median 3.0 pawns worth). The eval trajectory shows severe consequences: half the time a drawn position becomes losing, and half the time a winning position remains technically winning but with a massive 400cp median loss. The tactical layer reveals the common thread: hanging pieces, tempo loss, and overloaded defenders. In the concrete positions, we see patterns like a bishop recapturing on d1 while overlooking that an undefended queen can be taken back, or a rook move that leaves another piece unprotected. The recurring tags of tempo_loss, king_safety, and piece_activity suggest these mistakes occur when players make developing or active-looking moves in the opening without calculating the immediate tactical consequences for their undefended pieces. Maia consistently finds bishop captures that exploit the newly hanging material, confirming these are missed tactical shots rather than deep positional errors.

940.label: In the opening, the player makes a passive or irrelevant move instead of playing a strong centralized knight that would win material or seize the initiative.
940.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (94% opening) where Maia consistently recommends a knight move (100% knight) that the player fails to find. Instead, players make seemingly reasonable but passive moves with queens (31%), pawns (25%), kings (19%), or bishops (12%) that lose significant evaluation (median 286cp lost), often transitioning from winning to drawn (50%) or drawn to losing (19%). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (60%), fork (20%), and hanging_piece (20%), reflecting that the missed knight move typically exploits tactical vulnerabilities—forks on key squares like d5 or d4 that simultaneously attack multiple targets (queen + undefended piece). The player's chosen moves are materially 'safe' (81%) in that nothing immediately hangs, but they squander a concrete tactical opportunity. Tags like premature_queen_development, exposed_queen, and uncastled_king_exploitation_missed confirm that players often develop or reposition their queen to a square where it becomes a target, when instead a knight jump would have decisively punished the opponent's position. The boards consistently show Italian Game / King's Pawn structures where Nd5 or Nd4 leaps are devastatingly strong.

941.label: Moving a piece while leaving an undefended knight en prise to a simple capture.
941.description: This feature detects positions where a player makes a move (most often with a knight or queen) that leaves a knight completely undefended and capturable. The material signature shows 63% of moves result in a 'hang' (non-capture that drops a piece) with a median material loss of -3.0 (consistent with losing a full knight). The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the universal motif (100%), with 'undefended_knight' appearing as a recurring tag. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes are devastating: 41% convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 327 centipawns—roughly one full piece. The concrete examples reinforce this: Rh3 ignoring a threat to the knight on g5, Qxe7 leaving the knight on g4 undefended for Bxg4. Players frequently relocate one piece (often the queen or another knight) while failing to notice that their knight elsewhere on the board lacks protection and faces an immediate capture threat. This occurs predominantly in the opening (52%) and middlegame (48%), suggesting players are still developing or maneuvering and lose track of piece safety.

943.label: Player makes a passive or slow move instead of capturing an available enemy queen.
943.description: This feature fires when a player moves their queen, rook, or other piece passively while missing a straightforward queen capture that was available. The material signature shows that 91% of moves involve no capture, yet Maia's recommended move captures the queen 93% of the time — indicating the player consistently overlooked an available queen take. The 'hanging_piece' motif dominates at 60%, with tags like 'undefended_queen' and 'missed_capture' reinforcing that the opponent's queen was en prise or could be won. The eval trajectory (median 341cp lost, with 23% drawn->losing and 20% winning->drawn) shows these oversights are catastrophic, converting favorable or equal positions into losses. The example summaries describe scenarios where a queen sits on an open diagonal or is mutually attacked, and the player retreats passively or plays a non-forcing move instead of simply taking. The 'hangs' outcome at 41% further confirms that by not capturing, the player often leaves their own piece vulnerable in the resulting position.

942.label: Moving a bishop in the opening that leaves a pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to win material.
942.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake (93% opening phase) where a player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves) that hangs material (62% hangs, median -1.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these are costly errors, with a median loss of 290 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing (41%) or winning to drawn (28%). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the bishop move (typically Bg4 or Bg5) removes a defender from a pawn (usually b7) or creates a tempo-loss opportunity, leaving material en prise. The top boards confirm this repeatedly — Black plays ...Bg4 pinning a knight but leaving b7 undefended for Qxb7, or White plays Bg5 attacking a queen but allowing a tactical refutation. The Opus tags (missed_tactic, opening_trap, undefended_pawn, development) reinforce that these are move-order errors where the bishop deployment is premature, neglecting defensive duties before the position is ready for such activity.

944.label: In already losing positions, player makes a rook/queen move that hangs material or removes a critical defender, accelerating the loss.
944.description: This feature captures a pattern where players in already losing positions (losing->losing 100%) make desperate or panicked moves that dramatically worsen their situation (median 574cp further lost). The material signature shows rook moves (75%) and queen moves (25%) that result in material loss—either hanging a piece outright (25%), losing material on an exchange (25%), or coming out slightly down (50%). The tactical motifs reveal the specific mechanisms: hanging pieces on undefended squares (50%) and back-rank vulnerabilities (50%), with tags highlighting king safety issues, undefended rooks, and overloaded defenders. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern: a player in a difficult defensive position makes a move that either places a major piece on an undefended square (e.g., Rf4-g4 where the rook hangs to the queen), or removes a critical defensive piece from its post (e.g., capturing with a queen that was guarding against back-rank infiltration). These are not calculated sacrifices but rather moves made under pressure in losing positions that collapse the defense entirely.

945.label: Player advances a pawn or makes a quiet move instead of delivering an available checkmate.
945.description: This feature fires when a player in a completely winning position (often with mate-in-one or mate-in-two available) plays a purposeless quiet move—most commonly a pawn push (57%) or minor piece move—instead of delivering the checkmate. The material signature shows the moves are predominantly non-captures (86%) that objectively hang material or are classified as safe only because the engine sees forced mate anyway. The eval trajectory reveals a massive median loss of 9155 centipawns, reflecting the difference between instant mate and a prolonged conversion, though the position usually remains winning (71% winning->winning). The Opus analysis consistently identifies missed_mate and checkmate_in_one tags, with king_safety and back_rank motifs dominating—these are positions where the opponent's king is trapped and a queen delivery square is trivially available. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (71%) that deliver check (86%), confirming the missed checkmate pattern. The player appears to 'autopilot' a pawn advance or quiet consolidating move while blind to the immediate tactical kill shot.

948.label: Player leaves their queen unprotected or makes a move that allows the queen to be captured for free.
948.description: This feature identifies middlegame blunders where the player makes a move that leaves their queen hanging or loses catastrophic material (median -8.0 material, median 732 centipawns lost). The material signature shows pieces being hung or lost rather than traded, with 50% of cases involving queen moves and the opponent frequently capturing the queen in response (Maia captures queen 50%). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (57%) and king_safety (29%), with 'hanging_queen' appearing as a common tag. The eval trajectory shows massive swings—positions going from losing to winning for the opponent (50%) or drawn to losing (50%)—consistent with catastrophic one-move blunders rather than gradual positional deterioration. The concrete examples confirm this: a queen left unprotected on c3 capturable by the opponent, a king move while the queen on b3 hangs to a bishop, and multiple positions where the player ignores a tactical threat to their queen while making an unrelated move. The core pattern is inattention to the queen's safety during complex middlegame positions.

949.label: Player makes a passive queen move in the opening, missing a winning tactical opportunity such as a free capture or a check that maintains advantage.
949.description: This feature detects opening-phase positions where the player moves their queen passively (no capture, no check) in a position where they were winning, and the engine's recommended move was also a queen move but one that delivers check. The material outcome of the played move is 'safe' (nothing immediately hangs), yet the player loses a median of ~259 centipawns, converting a winning position into a drawn one. The top boards reveal a consistent pattern: positions with active queen placement possibilities (especially Qh5 retreating to f3 instead of maintaining attacking pressure, or Qd5 retreating to d8 instead of exploiting hanging pieces). The tactical motifs—hanging pieces (40%), overloaded defenders (20%), and king safety themes (20%)—confirm that these are positions rich in tactical opportunities that the player ignores in favor of a quiet, non-committal queen retreat. The tempo_loss tags further indicate that these moves waste critical attacking time in the opening, allowing the opponent to consolidate and equalize.

946.label: Retreating or misplacing a knight in the opening, losing critical development tempo and often hanging the piece.
946.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a player moves a knight (90% of cases) to a passive or vulnerable square, losing crucial development tempo. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (90%), and the dominant motif is tempo_loss (60%), with development and piece_activity as the most common tags. The concrete pattern visible in the top boards is striking: in Italian Game and similar e4-e5 structures, a knight on f6 is challenged by e5 and instead of playing the strong d5 advance (consistently identified as the best move by Maia/engine), the player retreats the knight to passive squares like g8, e8, h5, or places it on tactically vulnerable squares like d5 or g4 where it hangs or accomplishes nothing. The eval trajectory shows these moves are devastating—median 266 centipawns lost, with 52% converting drawn positions to losing ones. The material signature confirms that while 62% are technically 'safe' (no immediate capture), 33% directly hang the knight. Maia's preferred moves are overwhelmingly pawn pushes (81%, typically d5 striking the center) rather than these knight retreats, indicating the AI recognizes the positional imperative to counterattack rather than retreat. This is fundamentally a tempo/development error in sharp opening positions where passivity is immediately punished.

951.label: Giving a check that wastes tempo and allows the opponent to seize the initiative or capture material.
951.description: This feature identifies positions where a player delivers a check (69% of activating moves are checks, predominantly with rooks) that appears safe in immediate material terms (69% 'safe' outcomes) but catastrophically loses tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or win material on the next move. The eval trajectory shows these checks typically swing the game from drawn to losing (46%) or deepen an already losing position (23%), with a median cost of 261 centipawns. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (67%) and king_safety (33%), indicating that the checking move fails to accomplish anything constructive—the opponent's king simply moves to a better square while simultaneously threatening or capturing pieces. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve captures (92% of Maia moves capture material: rooks, bishops, queens, knights), confirming that the correct approach was to take material rather than give a pointless check. The top boards show positions where a direct capture or positional move wins decisively, but the player instead gave a flashy but hollow check that squandered the advantage.

947.label: Player overlooks an immediate checkmate (typically Qxg2# or Qxh7#) and plays a non-forcing move instead.
947.description: This feature fires when a player misses a checkmate in one move during the middlegame. The material/position signature shows that the player typically moves a rook (53%) or other non-forcing piece without capturing anything (88% no capture), while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capture with check (queen 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%) — indicating the missed move is a queen taking a pawn that delivers mate. The 'missed winning material: 100%' confirms every activation involves overlooking decisive material/mate. The Opus tactical analysis unanimously identifies king_safety as the dominant motif with tags like 'missed_mate_in_one', 'back_rank_king', 'smothered_king', and 'king_entombed'. The concrete positions (e.g., Qxh7# with king entombed on h8, Qxg2# supported by a rook on g8) all show textbook one-move mating patterns. The eval trajectory (41% winning->winning, 29% losing->drawn) reflects that while the position remains favorable in many cases, the player squanders an immediate forced win, sometimes converting a losing position into merely drawn by missing the knockout blow. The median eval lost of 0.0 centipawns is misleading because missed mates are often scored as infinite rather than centipawn losses in engines.

952.label: Player leaves a major piece (queen or rook) undefended and it is captured for free or near-free.
952.description: This feature detects moves where the player catastrophically leaves a major piece hanging. The material signature shows 59% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median net loss of -8.0 (approximately a queen's value), and the pieces moved are predominantly queens (47%) and rooks (34%). The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 90% of cases, with common tags like 'undefended_piece', 'queen_blunder', and 'hanging_queen'. The eval trajectory shows massive evaluation swings—median 548 centipawns lost—with 22% converting drawn positions to losing and 19% converting winning positions to losing. The concrete examples illustrate the pattern clearly: a queen left en prise on f6 with two rooks attacking it, a king moving away from a rook it was protecting, and other cases where the player's move simply ignores that a major piece is under attack or becomes undefended. These are not exchange errors or positional misjudgments—they are pure tactical oversights where a valuable piece is left to be captured with no compensation.

950.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move, missing a decisive knight fork or knight tactic that would have won material.
950.description: This feature fires when players overlook a powerful knight fork or knight-based tactic available in the position. The material signature shows that 63% of the played moves are 'safe' (non-capturing, non-hanging moves) while 20% hang material — these are quiet, routine moves rather than active tactical attempts. Meanwhile, Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly knight moves (54%) that deliver check (69%), confirming the missed opportunity is typically a knight fork with check. The eval trajectory is severe (median 451cp lost), with 63% of cases converting a winning or drawn position into a drawn or losing one (winning->drawn 26%, drawn->losing 20%, winning->losing 17%). The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'fork' as the dominant motif at 40%, with 'missed_tactic' as the top tag (8 occurrences) and 'knight_fork' explicitly tagged. The concrete positions reinforce this: boards feature centralized or active knights (Nd5, Nf5, Ne7+) where a fork with check wins the exchange or significant material, but the player instead makes a passive king move, pawn push, or captures an unimportant piece, completely missing the decisive knight tactic.

953.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move when an immediate forced checkmate (often via back rank or check) was available.
953.description: This feature fires on positions where the player had a winning position (59% winning→winning trajectory) but threw away an immediate forced checkmate, as evidenced by the extraordinary median eval loss of 9260 centipawns—a signature of missing mate rather than merely losing material. The material signature shows the played moves are overwhelmingly safe non-captures (76% safe, 100% no capture) using rooks, pawns, or bishops, meaning the player chose a quiet developing or consolidating move instead of delivering the killing blow. Meanwhile, Maia's suggested moves are 76% queen moves that ALL give check (100% check rate), confirming the missed move was a forcing queen check or checkmate. The tactical motifs (back_rank 50%, hanging_piece 50%, missed_forcing_sequence, check_first) and the concrete examples—such as missing Rd1# for a merely winning position, or missing Qf4+ as a forcing check sequence—confirm that the recurring mistake is overlooking an immediate or near-immediate checkmate, typically involving back-rank themes or forcing checks that the player replaced with a slow, non-urgent move.

954.label: Player trades queens or captures major material instead of delivering a back-rank or king-safety checkmate.
954.description: This feature fires when a player makes a queen or rook capture (usually trading queens — 90% capture a queen, 80% classified as 'trade') while missing a devastating forced mate or winning tactic involving the opponent's exposed king. The material signature shows exchanges at roughly equal net material, but the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 320 centipawns, with 100% of positions having missed winning material. The dominant motifs are back_rank (50%) and king_safety (38%), and the Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'missed_mate_in_one', 'material_greed', and 'queen_trade_error' — the player grabs the opponent's queen or a seemingly attractive capture rather than recognizing an elementary mating pattern (often back-rank checkmate or king entombment). Maia's recommended moves give check 90% of the time, confirming that the correct continuation involved a forcing king attack rather than the materialistic trade the player chose. The trajectory (40% losing→winning, 40% winning→winning turning into missed opportunities) shows these are positions where a mate would have been decisive, but the player's pattern blindness toward back-rank and king-safety themes caused them to settle for a trade.

957.label: Player makes a safe-looking move in the opening/middlegame, missing a fork or double attack that would have won material and converted a winning position.
957.description: This feature captures positions where the player has a winning advantage (median eval swing of 435 centipawns, all cases going from winning to drawn) but plays a 'safe' move (83% safe material outcome) instead of finding a decisive tactical blow. The dominant motif is a fork (67%) or double attack pattern that would win a piece outright. The concrete examples consistently show missed pawn forks, missed piece-winning tactics, and geometric blindness—the player fails to see that a specific square allows a simultaneous attack on two enemy pieces. Notably, the player's moves are often quiet developing or pawn moves (50% pawns), while the engine/Maia recommendation involves active rook or bishop moves (rook 67%, bishop 33%) that exploit the tactical geometry. This occurs predominantly in the opening (67%) where players default to routine development rather than calculating concrete forcing sequences, squandering decisive advantages through pattern-recognition failure on fork/double-attack motifs.
