955.label: Player moves king or avoids a critical queen trade, leaving their own queen or pieces hanging to the opponent's active queen.
955.description: This feature detects positions where the player fails to execute a necessary queen trade (or simplification) and instead makes a passive king move or sidestep, leaving material hanging. The material signature shows 70% of moves 'hang' material (median net loss of -2.0, i.e., roughly a full piece), with king moves being the most common played move (50%) and queen moves second (30%) — yet Maia's recommended response captures the player's queen 80% of the time. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors (median 248cp lost), often making an already losing position decisively worse (60% losing->losing) or throwing away drawn/winning positions. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece and king_safety, with recurring tags like 'queen_trade_necessity' and 'undefended_piece.' The concrete positions consistently show scenarios where a queen exchange (e.g., Qxf6, Qxe7+, Qxe3) was mandatory to avoid the opponent's queen exploiting an exposed king or winning undefended material, but the player instead made a non-forcing king retreat or irrelevant move, walking into a forced loss.

956.label: Trading a well-placed pawn for a knight on e7, abandoning a strong central/advanced pawn and squandering a winning position.
956.description: This feature fires on positions where the player uses an advanced passed pawn (typically on d6) to capture a knight on e7, executing a trade that objectively costs massive evaluation (median 538cp loss, with 75% going from winning to losing). The material signature shows pawn captures knight (75%) in what registers as an exchange/trade rather than a blunder—the player gets material back but destroys their positional advantage. The recurring board pattern shows White with a powerful advanced d6 pawn in the opening facing a knight on e7, where capturing dxe7 trades away the dominant passed pawn that was paralyzing Black's development. Maia's suggested alternatives (developing moves like Nc3, Bf4, Nf3, or maintaining the pawn) preserve the crushing positional bind. The tactical motifs (king_safety, overloaded_defender) confirm the d6 pawn was creating multi-dimensional threats that evaporate once traded. The remaining activations in pawn endgames show the same pattern: prematurely exchanging an advanced passer when maintaining it would win. Tags like tempo_loss and missed_tactic reinforce that the trade surrenders initiative for insufficient compensation.

960.label: Advancing a pawn instead of capturing a piece, throwing away a won endgame by mishandling the promotion race or allowing a critical blockade.
960.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (67% endgame, 33% middlegame) where the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) instead of capturing an enemy piece (Maia recommends capturing a bishop 67% or knight 33% of the time). The material outcome of the move itself appears 'safe'—nothing is immediately hanging—but the missed capture costs enormously: 100% of cases miss winning material, with a median eval loss of 1120 centipawns, typically converting a winning position into a drawn or lost one (winning->drawn 67%, winning->losing 33%). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are promotion errors, passed pawn mishandling, and tempo loss. The player repeatedly chooses to advance a passed pawn (or preparatory pawn) when the correct move was to eliminate a defending piece, thereby allowing the opponent to establish blockades, gain tempo with checks, or neutralize the promotion threat. The boards consistently show king-and-pawn endgames with advanced pawns where capturing an enemy minor piece was the only path to victory.

959.label: Player makes a non-capture move that leaves a piece en prise, turning a playable or winning position into a losing one.
959.description: This feature detects moves where the player (using king or rook moves that are non-captures and non-checks) catastrophically hangs material worth approximately 3 pawns (median net material: -3.0). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders, with positions swinging from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-losing by a median of 812 centipawns. The tactical analysis consistently identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (60%), supplemented by 'tempo_loss' (40%), indicating the player made a move that either placed a piece on an attacked square or moved away from defending a critical piece, often when an obvious recapture or simplification was available. The board positions confirm the pattern: rooks left on attacked diagonals (e.g., Re4 attacked by Ba8), pieces abandoned without defense (e.g., Re2 attacked by Re3 and Bf3), or king moves that ignore immediate tactical threats to one's own pieces. In every case, Maia's recommended move was a simple capture (bishop or rook taking) that the player inexplicably missed.

961.label: In already losing positions, player makes a move that hangs a piece or allows a back-rank/king-safety tactic, accelerating defeat dramatically.
961.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player in an already losing position (78% losing->losing trajectory) makes a catastrophic defensive error that significantly worsens their situation (median 197cp lost, with several positions converting to forced checkmate). The material signature shows 67% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material, median net -3.0), indicating the player is not blundering through aggressive play but through passive or panicked defensive moves. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%), king_safety (33%), and back_rank (17%)—combined with tags like removed_defender, tempo_loss, and self_entombment, reveal that players are making moves that inadvertently expose their king or leave pieces unprotected while trying to survive. The concrete positions show rooks moved to vulnerable squares (Rf8-e8 hanging to Rxe8+), bishops moved off key defensive diagonals (Bb7-c6 unblocking an attack on a rook), and kings stepping into worse squares. Maia's suggested moves (89% rook moves, often capturing) confirm that simple, natural developing/active moves were available. This is the pattern of a defender cracking under pressure—making the 'second mistake' that turns a difficult but holdable position into an immediate catastrophe.

963.label: King moves that waste critical tempo in pawn endgames instead of executing decisive pawn breakthroughs.
963.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure pawn endgames (phase: endgame 100%, king moved 100%) where the player wastes a crucial tempo instead of playing the correct pawn advance. The material signature shows these are 'safe' moves—nothing is hung or traded—but the eval trajectory reveals a devastating cost (median 301cp lost), often converting winning positions into losses (winning->losing 12%, drawn->losing 25%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (30%) and pawn_endgame (60%), with recurring tags for king_activity, pawn_breakthrough, and passed_pawn. The concrete positions show kings shuffling (Kh6, Kg6, Kg7, Kg3) when immediate pawn breaks like f5! or pawn advances would have been decisive. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%) instead. The pattern captures a common amateur mistake: in critical pawn endgames where one tempo decides everything, the player makes an aimless king move rather than the forcing pawn advance that creates an unstoppable passed pawn.

964.label: Hanging a piece in the opening by overlooking a fatal king safety weakness or tactical shot.
964.description: This feature captures opening-phase blunders where the player moves a bishop or queen to a square that hangs material (median net loss of -1.0 piece, 100% non-capture moves that drop material). The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 9415 centipawns lost), often converting drawn or already-losing positions into immediately lost ones. The tactical motifs—king_safety, hanging_piece, trapped_piece—combined with tags like checkmate_in_one, overlooked_mate, f2_weakness, and king_in_center reveal the common thread: the player makes a developing or attacking move that fatally ignores their own king's vulnerability or leaves a piece undefended, allowing the opponent to exploit the position with a mating attack or simple piece capture. The top boards confirm this pattern: moves like Bf3 leaving f2 unguarded for Qxf2#, Be5 left hanging to a knight capture, or queen moves that overlook back-rank and central-king threats. These are opening-stage oversights where the player's attention to offense blinds them to a concrete tactical refutation rooted in their king's exposed position.

965.label: Player makes a developing or castling move in the opening instead of capturing a free bishop on h6/h3, throwing away a winning position.
965.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: a bishop (often White's) has ventured to h6 (or h3) where it is hanging and capturable, typically by a fianchettoed or developing bishop. Instead of taking the free piece, the player makes a 'natural' developing move—most commonly castling (king moves 43%) or fianchettoing the bishop toward g7 (bishop moves 43%)—which ignores the hanging piece entirely. The material signature shows 100% missed winning material with Maia consistently recommending a bishop capture (Bxh6, Bxh3, Bxb2, etc.). The eval trajectory is devastating: 71% of cases swing from winning to drawn and 29% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 520 centipawns—roughly a full piece. The top boards confirm the recurring pattern: White's bishop sits exposed on h6 and Black plays ...Bg7 or ...O-O instead of capturing it. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), reinforcing that this is a pure missed-capture tactical oversight in the opening phase where players prioritize development or king safety over a free piece.

967.label: Queen delivers a purposeless check that squanders a winning attack or forced mate.
967.description: This feature fires when a player uses their queen to give check (56% checks, 100% queen moves) in a middlegame position where a decisive king attack or forced mate exists but is missed (100% missed winning material, king_safety motif 100%). The tags consistently show 'wrong_check', 'premature_check', 'missed_mate', and 'forced_mate_missed' — the player reflexively checks the opponent's king rather than executing the precise winning continuation. Maia's recommended moves (rook 62%, bishop 19%, knight 12%) with 100% check frequency indicate that the correct path involved coordinating other pieces to deliver mate or maintain a mating net, rather than the impulsive queen check that allows the king to escape or enables defensive interpositions. The eval trajectory (median 199cp lost, with winning->winning 44% and winning->drawn 6%) confirms these are positions where the player was already winning but threw away significant advantage — or even a forced mate — by choosing a flashy but incorrect queen check that releases pressure on the enemy king.

962.label: Player trades or misplaces their queen, abandoning a winning or equal attack and allowing the opponent to consolidate.
962.description: This feature fires on queen moves (100% queen moved) that are predominantly non-captures (83% capture nothing) yet result in catastrophic evaluation drops (median 241cp lost), with 67% missing winning material. The dominant tag 'queen_trade_error' (4 occurrences) combined with 'attack_abandoned' (2) reveals the core pattern: players offer or allow queen exchanges at precisely the wrong moment. The eval trajectory shows 25% winning->drawn and 25% drawn->losing, indicating these moves frequently throw away advantages. The Opus summaries consistently describe scenarios where the queen was the linchpin of an attack against an exposed king, and exchanging it relieved all pressure, often leaving the opponent with dominant passed pawns or a safe position. The 58% check rate suggests these queen moves often look aggressive (giving check) but actually simplify the position fatally. This is a positional/strategic error dressed up as an active move — the player confuses activity with progress and trades away their most powerful attacking piece prematurely.

966.label: Capturing a pawn while ignoring critical king safety threats, turning a winning position into a losing one.
966.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player captures a pawn (100% pawn captures) but catastrophically overlooks tactical threats to their own king. The eval trajectory shows 80% of cases swing from winning to losing with a massive median loss of 685 centipawns, indicating these are not marginal errors but game-deciding blunders. The material signature shows the captures are mostly 'trades' or neutral-looking exchanges, suggesting the pawn capture itself seems reasonable in isolation. However, the tactical analysis reveals the true cost: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (43%), king_safety (29%), back_rank (14%), and overloaded_defender (14%), with recurring tags of exposed_king and missed_tactic. The concrete positions confirm this pattern—players grab material (like Rxf2 taking a pawn instead of Kxd2 capturing a hanging rook, or bxc4+ forcing the opponent's king to a better square) while their own king position collapses. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures of major pieces (rook 60%, knight 20%, queen 20%), confirming that the correct continuation exploited tactical vulnerabilities the player ignored in favor of the tempting pawn capture.

968.label: Advancing pawns in lost endgames that further weaken the position or allow forced sequences.
968.description: This feature fires on pawn moves in endgame positions where the player is already losing. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves, 67% of which hang material (typically the pushed pawn itself), with a median net material loss of -1.0. The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly losing->losing transitions (89%), meaning the player was already in a bad position and made it worse, though typically by only a modest amount (median 31cp lost). The positional analysis reveals passed_pawn and pawn_structure as dominant motifs—players are pushing pawns (often g-pawns or b-pawns) hoping for counterplay or promotion chances, but these advances are premature or tactically unsound, either dropping the pawn outright, losing tempo, or creating weaknesses that accelerate the opponent's winning plan. The board positions consistently show king-and-pawn or rook endgames where the desperate pawn advance fails to generate meaningful counterplay.

969.label: In a winning endgame, the player leaves their rook en prise to the opponent's king or pawn, turning a won position into a lost one.
969.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player makes a move that hangs a major piece—almost always a rook—resulting in catastrophic material loss (median -5.0, i.e., a full rook). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders: 100% go from winning to losing with a median eval swing of 1130 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%), occurring in rook endgames (tagged in 5 of the top examples) often involving pawn races and passed pawns. The concrete pattern across the top boards is remarkably consistent: the player either moves their king or pushes a pawn while their rook sits on a square capturable by the opponent's king (e.g., Kxf5, Kxd5) or pawn, or moves the rook itself onto an attacked square. Rather than a complex tactical oversight, these are simple one-move oversights where the player loses track of their rook's safety while focused on pawn promotion or king activity in the endgame.

958.label: In a won endgame, plays a quiet rook move instead of a forcing rook check that accelerates the win.
958.description: This feature fires when a player in a completely won endgame (material median +3.0) makes a safe rook move—sometimes capturing a piece—but misses a rook check (Maia's recommendation is always a rook check, 100%). The eval trajectory shows 0 centipawns lost because the position is already decisively won, but the player fails to find the most forcing continuation. All three board examples confirm this: the player has overwhelming material advantage and plays a passive or capturing rook move while a rook check was available that would hasten checkmate or simplify the technique. The mistake reflects imprecise endgame technique—choosing material gain or repositioning over the more forcing check that maintains maximum pressure on the opponent's king.

973.label: Moving a rook to an unprotected square in the opening, hanging it to minor pieces or pawns.
973.description: This feature detects a specific opening blunder pattern where a player moves their rook (100% rook moves) to an exposed square without adequate support, hanging material (100% hangs, median -2.0 material loss). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 306cp lost). The top activating positions reveal the concrete pattern: premature rook lifts like Ra1-a3, Rh8-h6, or Rd8-d4 in the opening phase (100% opening), where the rook lands on a square attacked by opponent's minor pieces or pawns. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece as the dominant motif (88%), with tags emphasizing tempo_loss, development issues, and premature_rook_development. In each case, the player had straightforward developing moves available (Bc4, Nf3, Nc3) but instead wasted tempo moving a rook to an undefended square where it becomes a target, violating basic opening principles about not developing rooks before minor pieces.

972.label: Player makes a quiet move while an enemy piece hangs free for the taking.
972.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing move (king or pawn advance) while a simple winning capture was available. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (nothing is hung or lost immediately), yet Maia consistently recommends a bishop capturing a knight — a clean piece win. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (83%), and the tags overwhelmingly point to missed_capture, capture_oversight, and material_win_missed. The concrete positions confirm this: in each case an enemy piece sits undefended (a bishop on d1, a rook en prise to a pawn, a knight capturable for free) and the player inexplicably plays a passive king move or pawn push instead. The eval trajectory (median 381cp lost, with winning→drawn or winning→winning but significantly worse) shows these oversights squander decisive advantages. This is classic 'piece blindness' — failing to notice that an opponent's piece is simply hanging and can be taken for nothing.

970.label: Player overlooks an immediate checkmate in one move, playing a quiet or irrelevant move instead.
970.description: All three signals converge on a single catastrophic pattern: the player misses a forced checkmate in one. The Opus tactical analysis explicitly tags 'missed_mate_in_one' and 'checkmate_threat_missed' repeatedly, with examples showing Qxh7#, Qxg7#, Qxb7#, and back-rank/king-exposure mates all overlooked. The eval trajectory confirms this—the median centipawn loss is enormous (9207 cp, i.e., a full mate lost), with 75% of positions involving missed winning material via Maia's suggested checks (75% check rate) and queen/rook captures. The material signature shows the played moves are mostly 'safe' non-captures (no material exchanged) because the player chose a quiet move (h4h5, Rb5, Rd7, Qxb6 capturing a pawn) instead of delivering the available checkmate. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), reflecting that the opponent's king was fatally exposed. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (88%), where mating attacks are most common. This is not a positional or trade error—it is a pure tactical oversight where an immediate forced mate exists and the player simply does not see it.

971.label: Player retreats or makes a passive move instead of maintaining a winning attack, catastrophically losing the initiative.
971.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a passive or defensive move—often retreating a piece to safety—when the position demanded maintaining aggressive pressure or even sacrificing material to continue an attack. The material signature shows a mix of piece types moved (bishop, rook, pawn, king) with no captures in 67% of cases, indicating passive non-engaging moves. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 441 centipawns, with cases swinging from winning to drawn, winning to losing, or even flipping forced mates. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (67%) and king_safety (33%), with tags emphasizing initiative_loss, passive_retreat, attack_maintenance, and sacrifice_required. The per-position analysis confirms this pattern vividly: Ba1 saves a bishop instead of playing the attacking Rh2 sacrifice; Kh8 is a passive king move that throws away a forced mate; pieces retreat when bold continuation was required. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), suggesting the engine sees active rook play as critical in these positions. The player instead chooses safety over aggression, collapsing their attack and handing the opponent the initiative or even a forced win.

974.label: Trading a key attacking piece (usually a rook) when a stronger tactical continuation exists, dissipating a winning attack.
974.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player executes a rook trade (often with check) that appears forcing but squanders a much stronger tactical continuation. The material signature shows rook moves 100% of the time, with 75% involving captures that result in roughly equal material exchanges — these are not blunders of material but premature simplifications. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic cost: a median of 533 centipawns lost, with positions going from winning to drawn or even drawn to losing. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: players choose the 'instinctive' forcing move (a check, a capture) rather than maintaining tension for a fork, back-rank mate, or coordinated attack. Tags like 'attack_dissipation,' 'premature_exchange,' 'missed_fork,' and 'missed_mate' all point to the same error — the player simplifies into an inferior position when a more complex but decisive continuation was available. The 75% check rate is telling: these moves feel strong (they give check!) but actually release pressure by eliminating the very piece needed to deliver the killing blow.

975.label: Castling or moving the king into a position where it becomes tactically vulnerable, often enabling discovered attacks or mating threats.
975.description: This feature fires on moves where the player relocates their king (67% king moves, with castling being the dominant action) into a square that critically compromises king safety. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic, with a median loss of 311 centipawns and 37% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies king_safety (83%) as the dominant motif, with castling_error and discovered_attack as recurring tags. The top boards confirm the pattern: players castle into positions where the opponent already has pieces aimed at the castled king's shelter (e.g., bishops on open diagonals, queens aligned for discovered checks, or pawns ready to be ripped open). Maia's recommended alternatives are typically quiet developing moves (pawns, rooks, knights) that keep the king centralized or address the tactical threats first. The material signature shows these aren't capture-related blunders—the moves are 'safe' in the immediate sense (no piece hangs on the move itself in 67% of cases), but they walk the king into a pre-existing tactical storm that the player failed to recognize.

978.label: Player makes a routine or passive move instead of executing a winning knight fork that wins the queen.
978.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a decisive knight fork, typically one that checks the king while simultaneously attacking the queen. The material/position signature shows that 100% of Maia's recommended moves are knight moves delivering check, while the player's actual moves are a mix of knight captures (30%), pawn moves (20%), bishop moves (17%), and queen moves (14%) — all routine or passive alternatives. The Opus analysis confirms the fork motif in 100% of cases, with tags like 'knight_fork', 'queen_win', and 'royal_fork' dominating. The eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 484 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing, indicating that the missed fork was often the critical turning point. The concrete positions show patterns like Ne2+ forking king and queen, or Nd6+ exploiting king-queen alignments, where players instead made exchanges (Nxf3, Bxf3), passive development (Ne2, Dd3), or quiet moves (Qc7, h3) that squandered the tactical opportunity entirely.

977.label: In endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player makes a safe but slow move instead of immediately promoting or executing the winning tactic involving promotion.
977.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player has a critical passed pawn ready (or nearly ready) to promote, but instead plays a passive rook or king move that squanders tempo and significant advantage. The material signature shows safe moves (no material lost immediately) with rooks and kings, while Maia consistently recommends pawn moves that deliver check—indicating the optimal line involved immediate promotion or promotion threats. The 'missed winning material' flag at 100% confirms concrete wins were available. The Opus analysis reinforces this with 'promotion_error' as the dominant motif (60%), and tags like 'passed_pawn', 'tempo_loss', and 'missed_tactic' recur heavily. The eval trajectory (median 115cp lost, with one case throwing away a forced mate) shows these are not trivial inaccuracies but consequential failures to convert. The player sees the endgame is favorable and plays a 'natural' move, but misses that the position demanded an immediate forcing sequence centered on pawn promotion.

976.label: Player makes a quiet pawn or rook move while missing a winning knight capture (typically Nxe/Nxc winning material).
976.description: This feature fires when a player makes a passive or tempo-losing move (75% pawn pushes, 25% rook moves) while completely missing a winning knight tactic. In every case, Maia's recommended move is a knight capturing a rook—indicating a concrete knight fork or knight tactic was available that wins significant material. The material signature shows the played move frequently hangs material (50%) rather than being safe, and 100% of positions involve missed winning material in the middlegame. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 258cp), transforming drawn or slightly losing positions into clearly lost ones. The tactical motifs (overloaded defender, pin, king safety, back-rank themes) suggest the knight tactic exploits existing positional weaknesses that the player fails to recognize. The top boards confirm this pattern: positions with White's rooks on the 7th rank or knight outposts where a knight capture (Nxe7, Nxc2, Nxe2, Nxe5) would win decisive material, but the player instead pushes a pawn or makes an aimless rook move, losing tempo and allowing the opponent to consolidate.

981.label: Moving a piece to a square where it is undefended and tactically vulnerable, effectively hanging material.
981.description: This feature captures moves where the player relocates a piece (most often a queen or knight) to a square where it becomes immediately or tactically hanging, resulting in a median loss of ~3 pawns worth of material. The material signature shows 55% of moves directly hang a piece with no capture involved, and 100% of the time the player missed a winning continuation (Maia consistently recommends a bishop move instead). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights — 46% shift from drawn to losing and 27% make a losing position decisively worse, with a median cost of 327 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 67% of cases, where the moved piece lands on an attacked square (e.g., bishop placed on b4 attacked by a queen on d4, or queen moved to e7 allowing a double attack). These are one-move tactical oversights in the opening/middlegame where the player fails to notice that the destination square is covered by an opponent's piece, rather than complex multi-move errors.

979.label: Moving a minor piece or pawn to an undefended square where it can be captured for free, typically squandering a drawn or winning position.
979.description: This feature captures moves where a player actively hangs a piece (45% of moves result in a hanging piece, with a median material loss of -1.0). The moved pieces are predominantly knights (30%), pawns (25%), and bishops (23%), yet 75% of these moves involve no capture—meaning the player isn't trading but simply placing a piece where it can be taken. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly blunders: 32% turn drawn positions into losing ones and 14% turn winning positions into drawn ones, with a median eval loss of 311 centipawns (roughly a full minor piece). The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (43%), and the concrete examples show pieces placed on squares directly attacked by opponent pieces (e.g., a bishop moved to f5 where a queen on e4 captures it freely, or a knight moved to a square where it's undefended). Maia's suggested alternatives are typically quiet bishop or rook moves (62% bishop, 27% rook) that maintain piece safety, confirming the player's error was failing to notice the piece lacked protection on its destination square.

982.label: Trading a powerfully placed knight for a lesser piece, squandering a winning or balanced position.
982.description: This feature fires when players voluntarily exchange a well-positioned knight (57% of moves are knight moves) for an opponent's bishop (43% capture a bishop) or knight (29%), typically in the middlegame (79%). The material signature shows these are trades (71%) rather than blunders—the player captures roughly equal material—but the eval trajectory reveals these exchanges are catastrophic positionally, costing a median of 248 centipawns and frequently converting winning positions to drawn (36%) or drawn to losing (21%). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: players trade away centralized, active knights that were generating attacking pressure (king_safety 29%, fork potential 14%) or dominating key squares, eliminating their best piece and all associated tactical threats. The Opus summaries repeatedly describe exchanging a 'magnificently centralized knight' or a 'primary attacking piece' for a passive bishop, collapsing the position's dynamic energy. Maia's preferred moves (bishop 43%, queen 29%) suggest quieter developing or repositioning moves were correct rather than the premature simplifying exchange.

983.label: Trading rooks into a losing pawn endgame by eliminating the piece providing dynamic compensation or pressure.
983.description: This feature fires when a player initiates a rook exchange (rook captures rook, 100% trade) that transforms a tenable or winning position into a lost pawn endgame. The material signature shows a clean trade (median net 0.0), so no material is blundered outright—yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional losses (median 537cp lost), with 50% going drawn->losing and 25% winning->losing. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags 'pawn_endgame' (86%) as the resulting motif, with recurring themes of 'premature_simplification', 'wrong_simplification', and 'rook_exchange_error'. The concrete positions show rook endgames where the player's rook was the sole piece maintaining blockades against passed pawns, exploiting king activity advantages, or generating dynamic threats (h-file pressure, breakthroughs). Once rooks come off, the opponent's passed pawns or superior king position become decisive. Maia's alternatives (75% non-captures, 50% giving check) confirm that keeping rooks on with active play was correct. This is a classic endgame misjudgment: simplifying when the rook was the irreplaceable source of counterplay.

980.label: Player makes a non-forcing, tempo-losing move that squanders a winning or favorable position in the middlegame.
980.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (77% no capture, 55% materially 'safe') that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or launch a decisive counter. The material signature shows diverse piece movement (pawns 38%, rooks 19%, queens 17%, kings 15%) but crucially, Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly pawn moves (85%) that often involve captures (51% pawn captures), suggesting the player missed concrete pawn breaks or central advances in favor of aimless piece shuffling. The eval trajectory is severe (median 239cp lost) with the dominant pattern being winning->drawn (23%), indicating these are positions where the player had a significant advantage but threw it away. The Opus analysis confirms this: the top motifs are tempo_loss (33%), king_safety (17%), and back_rank (17%), with tags emphasizing piece_activity and missed_tactic. The concrete positions show queen moves to passive squares (Qb3, Qa4), rook moves that ignore back-rank threats (Rf4, Re1), and exchanges that relieve tension (exd7) — all cases where a forcing continuation existed but the player chose a slow, non-committal alternative that handed the initiative to the opponent.

984.label: Pushing or capturing a pawn in a critical endgame position instead of prioritizing king activity or stopping a passed pawn.
984.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where players make fatal pawn-related decisions that convert drawn or winning positions into losing or drawn ones (median eval loss: 463 centipawns). The material signature shows pawn moves (67%) that frequently hang material (33%) or are otherwise suboptimal, while Maia consistently recommends knight or bishop moves (piece activity/king activity). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (57%) and passed_pawn (43%), with recurring tags of king_activity, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: players push their own passed pawns or capture irrelevant pieces when they should instead be using their king or minor pieces to stop the opponent's more dangerous passed pawn. The trajectory (drawn->losing 67%, winning->drawn 33%) confirms these are game-changing errors where players misjudge the resulting pawn race or king proximity calculation, often failing to recognize that the opponent's passed pawn is faster or that king centralization was the only way to maintain the advantage.

985.label: A non-capturing pawn or piece move that wastes tempo or weakens the position in closed/semi-closed structures, squandering an advantage.
985.description: This feature identifies moves in opening-to-middlegame closed or semi-closed positions where the player makes a non-capturing move (pawn 36%, bishop/queen/knight 18% each) that is materially 'safe' (77%) but positionally catastrophic, costing a median of 237 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically convert drawn positions to losing (32%) or winning positions to drawn (27%), indicating the player is throwing away an advantage or equilibrium. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (50%), king_safety (25%), and hanging_piece (25%)—combined with tags like pawn_storm_backfire, premature_attack, and diagonal_weakness reveal that the core mistake is an ill-timed pawn push or piece redeployment that either weakens the king's shelter (g5, g6-g5), wastes critical tempo (a3, Rb1), or blocks natural development (c3, Qb3). The Maia engine consistently preferred simple pawn captures (96%), suggesting the player ignored concrete pawn breaks in favor of slow or misguided plans. The top boards all feature locked pawn chains where the player chose a committal but aimless move instead of the thematic break or consolidation.

986.label: In winning endgames, plays flashy or aimless moves (checks, promotions, passive retreats) instead of the precise tempo-critical continuation needed to convert.
986.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player holds a winning advantage but squanders it through imprecise timing, typically losing 218+ centipawns and converting winning positions into draws (67% winning->drawn). The material signature shows safe or neutral moves (not blunders of material) — checks (67%), queen promotions, and passive king moves — that appear active but miss the single critical continuation. The tactical analysis reveals a consistent pattern: tempo_loss and missed_tactic tags dominate, with passed_pawn themes recurring. Players give aimless checks instead of advancing decisive passed pawns, promote to queen when a subtler move wins, or make passive retreats when only one precise move maintains the win. The positions (rook endgames, pawn races, king+pawn vs king+pawn) all demand exact calculation of tempi, and the mistake is choosing a move that looks natural or aggressive but fatally loses the critical tempo needed to convert.

990.label: Capturing a pawn in a won endgame that allows the opponent to force a draw or win through promotion or simplification.
990.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where a player with a winning position grabs a pawn (player captured: pawn 100%) with a major piece (queen/rook), but this capture loses significant material (net -4.0 median) and throws away the game (winning->drawn or drawn->losing, with catastrophic eval swings up to 10000cp lost). The boards are exclusively endgame positions featuring passed pawns and rook endgames. The tactical pattern is consistent: the player captures a seemingly free pawn without recognizing that the opponent's piece controls a critical square or rank, enabling an immediate recapture, forced exchange, or promotion threat. The Opus analysis repeatedly notes that safe king repositioning or patient moves were available, but the player was lured by the pawn grab. Maia's suggested moves (always giving check, never capturing) confirm that the correct approach was active play targeting the opponent's king or promotion threats rather than material collection. The positions all feature advanced passed pawns where tempo and piece coordination matter far more than an extra pawn.

988.label: Playing slow, passive developing moves in the opening instead of seizing the center with a critical pawn break or tactic.
988.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (93% opening) where the player makes a materially safe move (100% safe, no captures, no checks) but squanders a winning advantage into a drawn position (87% winning->drawn, median 242cp lost). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (80%), with the concrete pattern showing players choosing passive piece shuffles (Nbd2, b3, d3, Re1, Cb2) instead of the critical central pawn break (typically d4 or e4) that would have won material via a fork or maintained a decisive initiative. Maia consistently recommends a pawn move (100%), usually the central break the player missed. The OPUS analysis confirms this: players develop pieces to natural-looking squares or make preparatory moves that are one tempo too slow, allowing the opponent to consolidate, when an immediate forcing central advance would have exploited the opponent's king still in the center or unstable piece placement. The positions are almost exclusively Italian/Spanish-type openings where White has a space and development advantage that demands immediate action.

987.label: Moving the king into a mating net or back-rank catastrophe, often allowing immediate or near-immediate checkmate.
987.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their king (62% of moves are king moves) into a fatally unsafe square, frequently enabling back-rank mates or other king-safety catastrophes. The dominant motifs are king_safety (38%) and back_rank (25%), with the Opus analyses repeatedly describing 'catastrophic blunders' that walk into checkmate-in-one or allow immediate mating attacks. The material signature shows 44% of moves hang material (the king itself being trapped counts as the ultimate hang), and the median eval loss is a massive 388 centipawns, with several positions showing 9000+ cp losses (immediate mate). The trajectory confirms these are not positional subtleties but game-ending disasters: 50% go from losing to losing (making a bad position terminal), and 25% convert drawn positions into losses. The concrete boards show kings retreating to h1 into back-rank mates, kings stepping to unsafe squares like c6 or h8 where they face immediate tactical punishment, and queens being sacrificed on e1 in desperation. The pattern is a player under pressure who reflexively moves the king to an apparently safe square without recognizing the mating geometry already in place.

989.label: Retreating or misplacing a well-positioned knight instead of exploiting its tactical potential.
989.description: This feature fires when players make quiet, passive moves (often with knights or bishops, no captures, no checks) that abandon strong piece activity—particularly knight centralization or tactical threats—in favor of slow or retreating moves. The material signature shows 86% non-captures with 60% 'safe' outcomes yet 27% hanging pieces, indicating moves that aren't immediately losing material but critically miss tactical opportunities. The eval trajectory (median 250cp lost, with 18% winning->drawn and 13% drawn->losing) confirms these are game-changing mistakes that squander significant advantages. Maia's recommended moves are 100% knight moves, often with tactical intent (forks, captures), while the actual played moves are diverse quiet pieces moves. The dominant motifs—missed_tactic, tempo_loss, fork, and king_safety—combined with tags like piece_activity, knight_retreat, and development all point to the same pattern: players voluntarily give up active piece placement or miss forcing knight tactics (especially forks) in favor of slow positional moves. The concrete examples reinforce this: retreating a knight from d5 to f6, playing passive pawn moves instead of Ne5, missing Nf4 forks, and making quiet rook or pawn moves when knight tactics were decisive.

995.label: Moving the queen away from defensive duties, fatally exposing the back rank or king.
995.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders where the player moves their queen (43% of moves are queen moves) away from a critical defensive post, leaving the back rank or king fatally exposed. The material signature shows that 57% of these moves hang a piece and the median cost is 6 pawns (median eval lost: 525 centipawns), indicating catastrophic immediate punishment. The dominant motifs—back_rank (40%), hanging_piece (40%), and king_safety (20%)—combined with recurring tags like 'queen_abandons_defense' and 'back_rank_mate' confirm that the core pattern is a queen move (or other piece move) that removes a crucial defender from the back rank or king zone. The eval trajectory shows 29% go from winning to losing and 43% worsen an already lost position, meaning these are not subtle positional errors but instant tactical collapses triggered by neglecting defensive responsibilities. Maia's responses frequently involve queen or rook moves delivering check (29%) or capturing material, consistent with immediate back-rank exploitation or king attacks once the defense is vacated.

991.label: Developing or repositioning a piece to a square where it loses tempo to an opponent's pawn advance in the opening.
991.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (88% opening) where the player typically moves a bishop (38%) or pawn (25%) to a square that immediately loses tempo or allows the opponent to seize the initiative with a pawn thrust. The material signature shows no captures (100% none) and mostly 'safe' outcomes (75%), meaning the piece isn't literally hanging but the positional damage is severe—median eval loss of 241 centipawns, with 62% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The tactical analysis confirms tempo_loss as the dominant motif (40%), with tags like 'tempo_loss_to_pawn_advance' and 'center_opening_urgency' appearing repeatedly. Concrete examples show bishops developed to squares attacked by d5 or e5 pawn advances (Be6 hit by d5, Bb5 inviting c6), or quiet moves like Qd7/Qb6 that ignore critical central tension, allowing the opponent to execute a thematic pawn breakthrough. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100% pawn), suggesting the correct play was to address the central pawn structure directly rather than develop passively. The pattern is a premature or misplaced piece deployment in the opening that gifts the opponent a crucial tempo for central expansion.

993.label: Failing to address or exploit passed pawns, losing critical tempi in positions where promotion threats decide the game.
993.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a move that neglects the critical importance of passed pawns, resulting in a significant evaluation loss (median 245 centipawns). The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (100% no captures) that aren't outright blunders of pieces but miss the tactical demands of the position. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (78%) combined with tempo_loss (22%), and the trajectory shows these errors convert drawn positions to losing ones (67%) or throw away wins (33%). The top boards consistently show endgame or late-middlegame positions with advanced passed pawns on both sides, where the player makes a natural-looking move (pushing a pawn, repositioning a rook, capturing on the wrong square) that loses crucial tempi for stopping or advancing passers. The Maia analysis confirms 100% missed winning material, suggesting concrete tactical sequences involving promotion threats were available. The common tags (promotion_threat, rook_endgame, overloaded_defender) reinforce that these are positions where precise calculation around passed pawns was required but the player chose a move that allowed the opponent to gain decisive tempo in the pawn race.

992.label: Player ignores an imminent checkmate threat by making a passive or irrelevant move while Maia's response delivers a decisive check.
992.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player overlooks a critical king safety threat, typically a forced mate or devastating check sequence. The material signature shows the player making mostly 'safe' or non-capturing moves (pawns, kings, queens) that appear innocuous but fatally ignore the opponent's attacking resources—Maia's response is a check 100% of the time, often with a knight (67%) or bishop (33%) delivering the blow. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: a median loss of 758 centipawns, with most positions going from already-losing to deeply losing, or even converting wins/draws into losses. The tactical motifs (king_safety 67%, missed forks, back-rank vulnerability, exposed king) and the per-position analyses reveal a consistent pattern: the player either walks the king into a mating net (Kg7 into Qxh7+/Qh6#), panics about a secondary threat while leaving the king fatally exposed, or moves a defensive piece away from king protection. The top boards show kings on open files/ranks with heavy pieces bearing down, and the player's move fails to address the immediate mating attack, allowing forced checkmate or decisive material gain via check.

997.label: Developing or attacking while leaving own bishop en prise in the opening.
997.description: This feature fires when a player makes a knight or bishop move in the opening that ignores an urgent threat to their own undefended bishop, resulting in hanging a piece (median net material loss of -3.0, i.e., a full minor piece). The eval trajectory consistently shows drawn positions collapsing to losing (median 396 centipawns lost). The top-activating boards all share a common structure: Italian/Gambit-style openings where a bishop on c4 or c5 is attacked by a pawn (often d5 or b4), and the player instead develops a knight, plays a premature attack, or makes a tempo-losing move rather than addressing the threat. The dominant tags—hanging_piece, tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and development—confirm that the player prioritizes piece development or speculative aggression over the concrete need to save or retreat their threatened bishop. Maia consistently identifies the simple bishop capture (taking the free pawn while preserving material) as the correct alternative.

994.label: Promoting or advancing a pawn prematurely in an endgame, allowing immediate capture or losing a won position due to move-order error.
994.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake where players rush to promote pawns (or advance them prematurely) without proper king support or move-order consideration. The material signature shows 67% pawn moves and 100% hangs — the promoted piece or advanced pawn is immediately lost. The eval trajectory is dramatic: 67% of cases flip from losing to drawn and 33% from losing to winning (from the opponent's perspective, the player throws away a winning advantage), with a staggering median eval loss of ~100 pawns (including mate-to-near-draw swings). The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant 'promotion_error' motifs (56%), supported by tags like passed_pawn, tempo_loss, premature_promotion, and move_order. Concrete examples show queens being promoted directly into capture range of the opposing king (g1 next to Kf2), pawns pushed without king escort violating the 'king leads the pawn' principle, and promotions that allow counter-promotion or stalemate tricks. All positions are pure endgames where precise calculation was required but the player chose the impulsive advancing move instead of the patient preparatory one.

996.label: Trading a central pawn that releases tension and exposes positional weaknesses in the opening/early middlegame.
996.description: This feature fires on pawn exchanges (100% pawn moved, 95% capturing a pawn) in the opening (60%) and middlegame (40%) where the material outcome is overwhelmingly a trade (84% trade, median net material 0.0), yet the positional cost is catastrophic (median 247cp lost, 49% drawn->losing). The top boards consistently show premature captures like dxc5, exd4, exf5, and dxe5—releasing central tension when the player's pieces are underdeveloped or poorly coordinated. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 44%, tempo_loss 22%, positional_mistake 22%, discovered_attack 11%) and tags (development, piece_activity, tempo_loss, premature_exchange) reveal that the pawn trade itself is materially neutral but strategically disastrous: it opens lines for the opponent's better-developed pieces, surrenders central control, or exposes tactical vulnerabilities like discovered attacks on undefended pieces. Maia's recommendations (knight 23%, bishop 21%) confirm that developing moves were available. The player's error is choosing an apparently safe equal exchange that actually dissolves a favorable pawn structure and hands the initiative to the opponent.

998.label: Retreating or passively developing a piece in the opening that hangs material on a key central square.
998.description: This feature identifies opening-phase mistakes where the player moves a minor piece (knight or bishop) to a passive square—often retreating it or developing it to an innocuous location—while leaving material hanging elsewhere on the board. The material signature shows 100% hangs (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0, and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (median 349 centipawns lost), converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis highlights hanging_piece and tempo_loss as dominant motifs, with development, piece_activity, and center_control as recurring tags. The concrete positions reinforce this: knights retreating from dominant central outposts (e4 back to f6), bishops developing passively (Be2 instead of a more active continuation), and moves that surrender tempo in sharp opening positions where central pawns or pieces become undefended. In each case the player prioritized a seemingly natural developing or retreating move while missing that a concrete tactical vulnerability (usually a central pawn or piece left en prise) demanded immediate attention. Maia's suggested pawn moves confirm that simple pawn captures or advances would have addressed the hanging material.

999.label: Trading or moving a knight into a losing endgame by abandoning its critical defensive/blockading role.
999.description: This feature fires when players make knight moves (57% knight, 43% pawn) that result in trades or hanging pieces (43% each), costing a median of 259 centipawns. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (40%) and passed_pawn tags (appearing in 3/5 examples), revealing that the core mistake is voluntarily entering or worsening a pawn endgame by removing the knight from a critical blockading or defensive square. The eval trajectory shows wins being thrown (29% winning->drawn) or equality being lost (14% drawn->losing), consistent with premature simplification. The Opus analyses explicitly describe knights being removed from 'ideal blockade squares' and 'key defensive' roles, after which the opponent's passed pawns or superior king position become decisive. Maia's suggested alternatives (86% knight moves, 57% checks) indicate the knight should have stayed active rather than being exchanged or displaced. The boards confirm late-middlegame/endgame positions where connected passed pawns or king activity dominate after the knight disappears.

1000.label: Player moves a rook passively in a won position, missing an immediate checkmate delivery.
1000.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced mate-in-one (typically with a rook) but plays a different rook move or pawn move instead. The material signature shows rook moves (69%) that are overwhelmingly safe or non-capturing (75% no capture), while Maia's recommended move is a rook check 100% of the time—indicating the missed checkmate. The 'missed winning material' tag fires at 100%, and the median eval loss of 9044 centipawns confirms a catastrophic blunder (losing a forced mate is scored as losing infinite/very large eval). The dominant motifs are king_safety (70%) and back_rank (20%), consistent with mating patterns involving rooks on ranks/files near an exposed king. The tags 'missed_mate_in_one' (6), 'mating_net' (4), and 'catastrophic_blunder' (3) directly confirm this. The trajectory (winning->winning 50%, losing->winning 38%) reflects that even after missing mate, the position often remains technically won, but the blunder is still extreme. The concrete examples (Ra1#, Re3#, Re4#) all show textbook back-rank or mating-net mates overlooked in favor of aimless rook or pawn moves.

1002.label: Player makes a passive or purposeless move while an enemy piece hangs undefended, throwing away a winning or equal position.
1002.description: This feature identifies positions where the player overlooked a free capture of an undefended enemy piece. The material signature shows the player's moves are predominantly non-capturing king/rook/bishop moves (86% no capture), while Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing hanging pieces (knights 43%, rooks 36%, queens 14%). The tactical analysis confirms 100% hanging_piece motif with recurring tags of missed_capture and material_oversight. The eval trajectory shows these oversights are devastating—median 507cp lost, with 65% of cases converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones. The concrete positions reinforce this: players make quiet king retreats, development moves, or rook lifts while enemy pieces sit en prise, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack. This is not a complex tactical miss but rather a failure to notice freely capturable material already available on the board.

1005.label: Queen moved to an undefended square in the opening, leaving it hanging to opponent's capture.
1005.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where the player moves their queen (78% of cases) to an unsafe square during the opening phase (89%), resulting in the piece being hung (78% material outcome). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 284cp), typically converting drawn positions to losing ones (67%) or winning to drawn (33%). Maia's response is universally to capture the hanging queen (100% queen captures), confirming the tactical oversight. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (75%), tempo_loss tags, and development concerns—indicating these are premature queen sorties in the opening that land on tactically vulnerable squares. The positions show queens venturing out early (moves 6-15) without adequate support, where a single forcing response wins the queen outright or traps it.

1001.label: Pawn captures a bishop on a file adjacent to the king, destroying the pawn shield and allowing a devastating attack.
1001.description: This feature fires when a player uses a pawn to capture a bishop (88% bishop captures) that has been sacrificed on a square adjacent to their king (typically h6 or h3), destroying their own pawn shield. The boards overwhelmingly show a bishop sacrificed on h6 (or h3 for White), and the player reflexively recaptures with the g-pawn (gxh6, gxh3, hxg6), opening critical lines toward their king. The king_safety motif dominates (88%), and the eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 793 centipawns), often swinging from winning or drawn to completely lost. Maia's recommended moves (knight 50%, queen 25%) suggest the correct response was to ignore the sacrifice or develop counterplay rather than recapture. The 'trade' material outcome reflects that the pawn did capture the bishop (roughly equal exchange on paper), but the positional devastation of opening the g-file and destroying the pawn shield vastly outweighs the material balance. Tags like mating_attack, open_file, queen_infiltration, and pawn_shield_destruction confirm that the recapture enables a lethal kingside assault.

1003.label: Player makes a non-checking move that ignores an immediate checkmate threat or allows forced mate, when a defensive or checking move was required.
1003.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is critically exposed and they fail to address an immediate mating threat. The material signature shows 49% of moves hang material and 80% involve no capture—players are making quiet moves (rook relocations, king walks, pawn pushes) while their king is under lethal attack. The Maia best-move signal is decisive: 100% of recommended moves are checks (with rooks 36%, queens 33%, knights 16%), indicating the position demanded either delivering check to gain tempo or interposing/fleeing with check. The missed winning material rate of 99% confirms these are catastrophic oversights. The eval trajectory shows 31% losing->losing (making a lost position immediately terminal) and 18% losing->winning (from the opponent's perspective, gifting mate). The Opus analysis unanimously tags king_safety (100%), with exposed_king, forced_mate, and back_rank motifs dominating—players walk their kings into mating nets, abandon back-rank defense, or ignore forced mate sequences. The top boards consistently show kings on open files/ranks with queens and rooks poised to deliver mate, where the player's move was irrelevant to the mating pattern bearing down on them.

1004.label: Moving a minor piece or pawn while leaving the queen hanging on an open diagonal.
1004.description: This feature fires when players make developing or pawn moves (pawns 35%, knights 29%, bishops 16%) that ignore a critical diagonal threat to their queen. The material signature shows 41% of moves hang a piece with a median loss of -1.0 (consistent with losing a queen for nothing or near-nothing), and 100% of positions miss winning material that Maia identifies (typically a bishop move exploiting the open diagonal). The eval trajectory is devastating: 51% of cases convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median cost of 445 centipawns—consistent with losing a queen. The tactical analysis confirms this: 67% involve a hanging piece, with the most common tags being 'queen_hanging', 'ignored_threat', 'undefended_queen', and 'open_diagonal'. The concrete examples repeatedly show the same pattern: a player develops a knight (e.g., Nd2) or plays a pawn move while their queen sits unprotected on a diagonal attacked by an enemy bishop (Bg4-d1, Bg5-d8). The player fails to recognize that the diagonal is completely open and that no piece blocks the attack line. This is an opening/early middlegame phenomenon (59% opening, 41% middlegame) where rapid development causes tunnel vision about long-range diagonal threats to the queen.

1006.label: Moving or capturing without noticing that a piece is left undefended and can be taken for free.
1006.description: This feature captures middlegame positions (82%) where players make moves—often with knights (32%), pawns (26%), or bishops (21%)—that leave a piece hanging or lose material through a tactical oversight. The material signature shows 26% 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) and 18% 'loses' (gave up more than captured), with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%), with tags like 'undefended_piece', 'piece_safety', and 'capture_order_error'. Players frequently miss that their move leaves a piece en prise—e.g., placing a queen on a square attacked by an enemy bishop, or capturing in the wrong order so a piece is left undefended. The eval trajectory shows these are often costly blunders (median 261cp lost), with 28% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn or losing one. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (rook 24%, bishop 18%) that would have won the hanging material, and 79% of positions involve missed winning material. The concrete examples reinforce this: queen moved to an attacked square, knight sacrifice leaving pieces undefended, captures made in wrong sequence exposing an unprotected piece.

1007.label: Trading knights into a pawn fork that wins back material or attacks a remaining piece.
1007.description: This feature fires when a player makes a knight exchange (knight captures knight in 90% of cases) that superficially appears to be an equal trade but overlooks a tactical consequence—most commonly a pawn fork. The material signature shows trades (net 0.0 median), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 343cp), with 90% of cases turning drawn positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'fork' (67%), where the recapture (typically dxe5 or similar pawn recapture) creates a pawn fork attacking another piece. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (80%) in classical structures (often involving a knight on e5 being recaptured), and the Opus summaries consistently describe scenarios where the player captures on e5 without calculating that the pawn recapture attacks a second piece (often a bishop) with no safe retreat. The player sees an equal exchange but misses the intermediate fork that wins additional material.

1012.label: King moves backward in the opening, walking into tactical vulnerabilities that convert a winning position into a losing one.
1012.description: This feature detects a specific recurring opening-phase blunder where a player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) to a square that exposes it to devastating tactical consequences. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: every instance transitions from winning to losing with a median loss of 646 centipawns, indicating these are game-deciding mistakes. The positional analysis confirms the core issue is king safety (67% dominant motif), with exposed_king and tempo_loss tagged in nearly every example. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows kings retreating to back-rank squares (Ke8, Kg8, Kf8) or passive squares (Kg1, Ke2) during the opening, where they walk into discovered attacks, queen checks, or mating threats. Rather than maintaining an active king position or developing pieces, the player reflexively retreats the king, losing critical tempo and allowing the opponent's pieces to coordinate decisive attacks against the newly exposed monarch.

1009.label: Player moves knight passively in the opening, missing a forcing queen check or mating attack on the exposed king.
1009.description: This feature fires when a player makes a routine or passive knight move (95% knight moves, mostly non-captures) in the opening (95% opening phase) while missing a devastating queen check (Maia's best move is queen 95%, always giving check 100%). The positions consistently feature exposed kings (king_safety 83% motif, exposed_king and missed_mate tags) where a forcing queen check (often Qh4+ or Qh5+) would maintain or convert a winning advantage. Instead, the player retreats or repositions the knight—sometimes trading it off materialistically (37% trades) or simply developing it passively—abandoning the critical attacking pressure. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 302 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions into drawn or even losing ones (53% winning->drawn, 10% winning->losing). The concrete examples confirm this: players capture on d7 instead of playing Qh5+, play Nf3 instead of exploiting light-square weaknesses, or retreat knights that were essential components of mating nets. The fundamental error is prioritizing piece activity or material over a time-sensitive king attack.

1008.label: Failing to execute the one urgent move (usually promotion or perpetual check) by temporizing with a king move or passive piece move.
1008.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has exactly one critical tempo-sensitive resource available—typically an immediate pawn promotion or a perpetual check opportunity—but instead plays a passive or temporizing move (king moves 60%, rook/queen repositioning). The material signature shows 'safe' moves (nothing is immediately hung), yet the median eval loss of 558 centipawns reveals these are catastrophic strategic errors. The motifs (promotion_error 40%, king_safety 40%) and tags (promotion, tempo_loss, passed_pawn, perpetual_check_missed) consistently point to positions where one precise move was required NOW, but the player delayed. The trajectory is heterogeneous (winning->drawn, drawn->winning lost, etc.) because these tempo-critical moments arise in various eval contexts, but in each case the common thread is that a single-tempo delay allows the opponent to consolidate—whether by controlling a promotion square, activating a rook on an open file, or setting up a mating net. The boards confirm this: endgames with advanced passed pawns where Kh7/Kf2/Kb8 temporizes instead of promoting or giving perpetual check, and middlegame positions where a passive rook move surrenders the critical tempo needed to maintain a winning initiative.

1011.label: Playing a king move instead of capturing an available hanging piece.
1011.description: This feature fires when a player moves their king (100% king moves) in a position where an obvious capture is available — typically capturing an opponent's rook with a pawn (Maia recommends pawn captures rook 100% of the time). The material signature shows these king moves are either safe or hang material (50/50), but critically, 100% of activations miss winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these occur in already-losing positions (losing->losing) where the missed capture would have clawed back significant material (median 120cp lost). The tactical analysis consistently tags 'missed_capture' and 'hanging_piece' — the opponent has left a piece en prise (often a rook), and instead of simply taking it, the player makes an aimless king move that either attacks nothing meaningful or walks into further danger. Examples include moving the king to 'attack' a rook that easily escapes, or repositioning the king while an enemy rook sits undefended on a square attackable by a pawn or bishop. This represents a form of capture blindness where the player fixates on king activity rather than recognizing the concrete material available.

1010.label: Moving the queen to a square that creates tactical vulnerabilities (back-rank, diagonal pins, or deflections) around the player's own king.
1010.description: This feature fires on queen moves (94% queen moved) that are predominantly non-captures (93% no capture) in the middlegame (94%), where the queen lands on a square that critically weakens the player's king safety or creates exploitable geometric relationships. The material signature shows 64% safe and 33% hangs, meaning the queen itself isn't immediately lost but the resulting position collapses tactically. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 328cp lost), with 22% going drawn->losing and 13% winning->drawn, indicating these moves throw away half-points or full points. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety (25%) and back_rank (25%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, diagonal_vulnerability, and piece_activity. The concrete positions show queens landing on squares that create fatal alignments with their own king (e.g., queen and king on the same diagonal enabling deflection sacrifices, or queens moving away from back-rank defense). Maia's recommended moves are diverse (queen 20%, king 18%, bishop 18%), suggesting the correct responses often involve prophylactic king safety measures or maintaining defensive coordination rather than the aggressive-looking but self-weakening queen relocations that triggered the feature.

1013.label: Trading an active bishop for a knight, surrendering positional advantage and key diagonal control.
1013.description: This feature fires when a player voluntarily exchanges their bishop for a knight (bishop moved 98%, capturing a knight 95%) in a trade that is materially equal (93% trades, median net 0.0) but positionally catastrophic (median 226cp lost). The eval trajectory shows these trades frequently convert drawn positions to losing (37%) or winning to drawn (12%), indicating the player is throwing away a significant positional edge. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is positional_mistake (67%), with recurring themes of surrendering active bishops that controlled key diagonals, abandoning attacking potential, or relieving tension prematurely. The top boards consistently show bishops on active diagonals (g4, b7, c6, h4, f4, f5) being traded for knights, after which the opponent's position improves dramatically—often activating a previously passive piece or stabilizing a compromised structure. Maia's preferred alternatives (knight 44%, pawn 27%, bishop 22%) suggest the engine wanted to maintain tension or develop further rather than exchange. This is a classic case of releasing dynamic pressure through an ill-timed simplification.

1014.label: In lost endgame positions, playing passive king or pawn moves instead of capturing available material that could prolong resistance or shift the outcome.
1014.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where the player, already in a losing position, fails to make an available capture—typically with the king—that would either prolong the game or potentially shift the evaluation. The material signature shows the player moves kings (44%) and pawns (44%) while Maia consistently recommends king moves that capture pawns (56%) or rooks (33%). The 'missed winning material' tag fires 89% of the time, confirming these are positions where a capture was available but ignored. The eval trajectory (losing->losing 89%, median 144cp lost) shows these moves make already-bad positions significantly worse rather than throwing wins. The tactical analysis reinforces this: examples include failing to play Kxb3 to capture a rook, missing Kxa2 to stop a promotion, and pushing pawns while pieces hang. The dominant motifs—passed pawns, hanging pieces, and tempo loss—all point to the same pattern: in simplified endgame positions with critical captures or pawn races, the player makes an aimless or retreating move instead of the urgent capture that was required to maintain defensive chances.

1016.label: Player makes a non-forcing move that misses a crushing check-based tactical combination, losing significant material or position.
1016.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a passive or non-forcing move (typically with the queen, knight, or king) while Maia's recommended move is almost always a queen check (100% Maia gives check). The material signature shows the player's move is often safe or hangs material (59% safe, 29% hangs), but critically, 100% of these positions involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory confirms severe consequences with a median loss of 302 centipawns, spanning various starting positions (losing->losing 35%, drawn->losing 18%, winning->losing 12%). The tactical analysis reveals recurring motifs of tempo_loss, overloaded_defender, and king_safety, with common tags including missed_tactic, exposed_king, and missed_check. The concrete positions show uncastled or exposed kings where a forcing queen check (often Qxc3+ or similar) would exploit overloaded defenders or win decisive material, but instead the player chooses a passive retreat or developing move that surrenders the tactical initiative entirely. This is fundamentally a failure to recognize check-based tactical combinations that exploit king exposure.

1015.label: A pawn advance giving check that wastes tempo, fixes pawn structure, and often improves the opponent's king position.
1015.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake: advancing a pawn to deliver check when it is counterproductive. All top activations involve pawn moves (100%) that give check (100%), predominantly in endgame positions (57%) or late middlegame (43%). The material signature shows these checks frequently hang the pawn or create structural damage (57% hangs, median -1.0 material), while the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 350cp lost, with 43% converting drawn positions to losing ones). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern through recurring 'pointless_check' and 'tempo_loss' tags—the check superficially looks aggressive but actually improves the opponent's king placement (driving it to a better square like g6 or g1), permanently fixes pawn structure eliminating future tension, or releases critical control over key squares. The example summaries explicitly describe checks that 'actively improve' the opponent's king, 'permanently weaken' pawn structure, or 'fatally remove' pawn control over invasion squares. This is a classic pattern where players reflexively push a pawn with check without calculating whether the check actually helps.

1017.label: Capturing a pawn while overlooking a much stronger move that wins or preserves major material.
1017.description: This feature fires on positions where a player (usually with king or rook) captures a pawn but loses substantial material in the process, typically throwing away a winning position. The material signature shows 100% pawn captures that result in net material loss (median -4.0), while Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing a rook or making a more purposeful move. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 67% winning->losing and 33% winning->drawn, with a median loss of 892 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players fixate on removing a dangerous or tempting pawn (often a passed pawn on f2, g2, or similar) while completely overlooking that they could capture a hanging piece (57% hanging_piece motif) or execute a decisive tactic. The concrete positions confirm this — White takes on f2 instead of capturing a hanging rook on d2, White takes on g2 instead of capturing a rook on f1, and similar scenarios where pawn-grabbing blinds the player to far superior alternatives. These occur primarily in middlegame-to-endgame transitions where material imbalances and passed pawns create tunnel vision.

1018.label: Moving a piece that exposes a devastating discovered attack along a now-unblocked line.
1018.description: This feature fires when a player moves a piece (most often a king or knight) that inadvertently opens a line for the opponent's discovered attack. The material signature shows 83% non-captures with 30% hanging material and a median loss of 403 centipawns—indicating these aren't exchanges but outright tactical blunders. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings: 29% go from drawn to losing, 9% from winning to losing, and 8% from winning to drawn. The tactical analysis is emphatic: 90% of positions are tagged with the discovered_attack motif. The top boards illustrate the classic pattern—in the Stafford/Petroff-type positions, Black retreats the knight from e4 (e.g., Nf6 or Ng5), unblocking the e-file for White's queen on e2 to attack; in other cases, a king steps onto a diagonal or file that enables a devastating discovered check or attack. The player's natural-looking retreat or king move fails to recognize that the piece being moved was shielding a critical line, and once removed, the opponent's battery delivers a winning blow—typically netting a queen or decisive material advantage.

1019.label: Trading an active bishop for a poorly-placed knight in the opening, conceding tempo and activating opponent's pieces.
1019.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where the player uses their bishop to capture a knight (bishop moved 100%, knight captured 100%) in a trade (net material 0.0) that costs significant positional value (median 184 centipawns lost). The positions are all in the opening phase, and the common tags—premature_capture, helping_opponent_develop, bishop_pair_conceded, tempo_loss, and piece_activity—paint a clear picture: the player rushes to exchange their active, well-developed bishop for an opponent's knight that is either misplaced (e.g., on a6 or h5) or already in trouble. Rather than maintaining pressure or exploiting the knight's awkwardness with moves like g4 or d6, the player relieves the tension prematurely. The eval trajectory (winning->winning 50%, winning->drawn 50%) shows this isn't a game-losing blunder but a strategic error that squanders a significant advantage. Maia consistently prefers quiet pawn moves instead, suggesting the engine recognizes no urgency to capture.
