The trajectory (winning->drawn 30%, losing->winning 20%) shows these errors often throw away winning positions by exchanging into simplified, drawn endgames instead of finishing the opponent off.

1084.label: Player overlooks a pawn that can capture an enemy queen on an adjacent square, instead making a non-capturing move that hangs material.
1084.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring one-move tactical oversight: the player has an advanced pawn (typically the e5 pawn) that directly attacks the opponent's queen (typically on f6), yet the player completely fails to see the pawn capture and instead plays a quiet, non-capturing move (rook lift, queen retreat, bishop move, etc.). The material signature shows 100% hangs (non-captures that drop material) with Maia consistently recommending a pawn move that captures a queen. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders—100% winning-to-losing swings with a median loss of 882 centipawns, consistent with missing a free queen capture. The tactical analysis tags (pawn_captures_queen, pawn_takes_queen, hanging_queen, one_move_tactic) and the Opus summaries all converge on the same psychological blind spot: players systematically underestimate pawns as attacking pieces and fail to see that a lowly pawn can capture the most powerful piece on the board. The top 10 boards all share the structural motif of an e5 pawn facing a queen on f6, making this an extraordinarily specific pattern of chess blindness.

1083.label: Player makes a king or pawn move that leaves their queen completely undefended, allowing opponent to capture it for free.
1083.description: This feature captures positions where the player, often in a winning or clearly advantageous position, plays a seemingly purposeless king move (67%) or pawn move (33%) that hangs material — specifically their queen. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) with a devastating median loss of ~92 pawns worth of eval (reflecting queen loss or subsequent mate). The Maia analysis confirms the opponent's best response captures a queen 100% of the time. The tactical motifs overwhelmingly center on 'hanging_piece' (80%) with supporting tags like 'hanging_queen', 'missed_capture', and 'missed_tactic'. Examining the boards, the pattern is remarkably consistent: the player has a queen on the board that is either undefended or becomes undefended after their move, and they play a king shuffle or pawn push that ignores this vulnerability entirely. In several cases the player had forced wins (including mate) available but instead made an aimless move that left their queen en prise. The eval trajectory (67% winning->winning, 33% winning->losing) suggests that in some cases the position remains technically winning despite the blunder (perhaps due to advanced passed pawns or promotion threats), but in others it's immediately fatal.

1086.label: Player misses an immediate checkmate in one move during an endgame, making a non-forcing move instead.
1086.description: All three signals converge on the same pattern: players missing checkmate in one in endgame positions. The material/position signature shows queen moves (67%) that are 'safe' (not hanging anything) but miss Maia's recommended queen checks (100% check, 100% missed winning material), indicating the player moved their queen to a non-checking square when a mating move was available. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 222 centipawns but the Opus analysis reveals the true catastrophe—losses of 9000+ centipawns representing the difference between forced mate (#-1) and merely winning positions. The tags confirm this: checkmate_in_one (2/3), missed_checkmate, missed_tactic (3/3), and king_safety (3/3) as the dominant motif. The top boards show endgame positions where one side's king is exposed (often on the h-file edge) and a queen delivery of checkmate was available but missed, with the player instead making a quiet queen repositioning move or even a king move. This is a pure pattern-recognition failure in simplified positions where the mating net exists but goes unseen.

1088.label: Non-forcing pawn or quiet moves in the opening that miss tactical opportunities involving forks or checks, losing massive eval.
1088.description: This feature fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (100% no capture) — typically a pawn push (60%) — instead of exploiting concrete tactical opportunities. The dominant motif is fork (50%), with tempo_loss and king_safety as recurring tags. Maia consistently recommends piece moves (knights/bishops) that capture with tactical threats (80% bishop captures, 40% checks), indicating the player missed forcing sequences. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 373cp lost), with 40% swinging from winning to losing, showing these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders. The boards consistently show rich tactical positions with knights on active squares, exposed kings, and piece tension — yet the player retreats into passive pawn moves or quiet queen shuffles (like ...Qd6 instead of ...Nxf3+, or a3 walking into a fork, or ...h6 when the king is exposed). The unifying theme is prioritizing slow positional ideas over urgent forcing moves in sharp opening positions where tempo is decisive.

1091.label: Moving the queen to an ineffective square when immediate tactical action was required, losing significant material or positional advantage.
1091.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their queen (57% of activations) to a passive or irrelevant square while missing a critical tactical opportunity. The material signature shows these are predominantly non-capturing moves (82% no capture) that frequently hang material (37%) rather than being outright trades. The median eval loss of 235 centipawns is severe, with the trajectory showing positions transitioning from drawn to losing (20%) or winning to drawn (11%), indicating the player squandered a defensible or advantageous position. The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: the dominant motifs are hanging pieces (40%), tempo loss (20%), and king safety neglect (20%), with recurring tags of missed tactics and initiative loss. Maia's suggested moves are often rooks (35%) or quieter queen moves (30%) with no checks (0%), suggesting the correct response was typically a concrete developing or defensive move rather than the flashy but misguided queen maneuver the player chose. The concrete examples reinforce this: Qg7+ as a pointless check, Qe2 ignoring back-rank threats, slow queen retreats when sharp tactical responses were needed. The player's queen moves look active but miss the tactical demands of the position.

1089.label: Bishop or piece develops to a square that ignores central tension, hanging material and losing a critical tempo in the opening.
1089.description: This feature fires on opening-phase bishop moves (100% bishop played, 100% opening) that hang material (net -1.0, no capture made) by neglecting immediate central threats. The eval trajectory consistently shows a drawn position collapsing into a losing one (drawn->losing 100%, median 179cp lost), indicating these aren't positional gambles but genuine oversights. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (67%), hanging_piece (22%), and fork (11%)—combined with tags like 'central_tension_ignored,' 'premature_queen_development,' and 'missed_tactic' reveal a single recurring pattern: the player develops a piece (often a bishop to an active-looking square like Bb4, Bc4, Bd3, or makes a premature queen sortie) without first resolving central pawn tension, leaving a piece or pawn en prise. The opponent's best response (Maia plays a pawn capture 100%) simply wins the hanging material. Essentially, these are move-order errors where a developing move that might be correct one tempo later is played prematurely, gifting the opponent a free pawn or piece.

1090.label: Failing to capture a free or hanging pawn in the opening, instead making a passive or positional move that squanders material or structural advantage.
1090.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player overlooks a concrete opportunity to win material (usually a hanging pawn) and instead plays a passive or structurally dubious move. The material signature shows 50% of moves literally hang material while the other 50% are nominally safe but miss a clearly winning capture—Maia's recommended move is consistently a bishop capture or active piece move that wins material. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors (median 274cp lost), converting winning positions to drawn or drawn positions to losing. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (40%), tempo_loss (40%), and positional_mistake (20%)—along with recurring tags like missed_tactic, missed_material_gain, and development, all point to the same pattern: in a sharp opening position where a pawn (often on b5) or piece is en prise, the player retreats passively (Bb3), pushes a flank pawn (b4, a6, c6), or develops aimlessly instead of simply taking the free material. The concrete positions confirm this—multiple Italian/Sicilian/QGD-type openings where Bxb5 or a similar capture is available but ignored in favor of slow prophylactic moves.

1092.label: Advancing a central pawn (d4/d5/e5/g4) that disrupts the player's own pawn structure and cedes positional control in the opening.
1092.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn advances—100% pawn moves with no captures—that are positionally catastrophic despite appearing materially safe (94% 'safe' outcomes). The moves are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (79%) and involve premature central breaks (d5-d4, d4-d5, e4-e5) or misguided kingside pawn lunges (g5-g4). The eval trajectory reveals these are game-changing errors: 27% swing from drawn to losing and 21% from winning to drawn, with a median cost of 239 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms these are purely positional mistakes (100% positional_mistake motif) tagged with pawn_structure damage, tempo_loss, and reduced piece_activity. Maia's suggested alternatives (knights 30%, bishops 18%, pawns 36%) indicate that developing pieces or maintaining pawn tension was correct. The concrete positions show closed/semi-closed structures where the player prematurely releases central tension, gifting the opponent outposts, open lines, or initiative—classic premature central breaks that violate opening principles of maintaining flexible pawn structures.

1094.label: Player makes a quiet move while checkmate in one via back rank is available.
1094.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position has an immediate back-rank checkmate available (typically Rb8# or Qb8#) but instead plays an irrelevant quiet move—a pawn push, knight maneuver, or bishop repositioning. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (pawns 38%, knights 38%) while Maia consistently identifies a queen delivering check as the correct move. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain winning but at catastrophic cost (median 9340 centipawns lost), representing a squandered forced mate. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags back_rank (86%) with missed_mate_in_one appearing in 6 of 8 positions, and the concrete board positions all show a trapped king on a8 with the back rank fatally exposed. The player's pieces are well-positioned for the killing blow but the player fails to recognize the pattern, opting for slow positional improvements instead of the instant win.

1093.label: Moving the queen to a square controlled by an enemy pawn, immediately losing the queen for little or no compensation.
1093.description: This feature identifies a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: the player moves their queen (86% of cases) to capture a piece (knight 32%, rook 27%, bishop 14%) on a square that is directly defended by an enemy pawn, resulting in the immediate loss of the queen. The material signature confirms catastrophic losses (77% 'loses' with a median net material of -6.0, consistent with losing a queen for a minor piece or rook). The eval trajectory shows these are game-deciding errors (median 538 centipawns lost), frequently converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (27% winning→losing, 27% drawn→losing). The Opus tactical analysis is unambiguous: 100% hanging_piece motif, with recurring tags like 'queen_blunder', 'queen_trapped_by_pawn', 'piece_value_miscalculation', and 'recapture_oversight'. The concrete examples consistently show queens landing on squares where a pawn simply recaptures (e.g., queen takes on c5 where e5 pawn recaptures, queen goes to b5 where a4 pawn takes, queen captures on d6 where e5 pawn controls). This is not a complex tactical sequence but rather an elementary oversight of pawn coverage — the player is drawn by the material on the target square and fails to notice the humble pawn defending it.

1097.label: Trading away the last defensive piece in the endgame, entering a lost pawn ending or allowing a back-rank mate.
1097.description: This feature captures endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player trades or misplaces their critical defensive piece—typically a bishop or rook—resulting in a catastrophic swing from a drawn position to a lost one (drawn->losing 100%, median eval loss of 10000 centipawns). The material signature shows moves with bishops (50%) and rooks (50%) that either hang a piece or end up slightly down, with the common thread being the removal of the sole piece capable of holding the position. The tactical analysis tags (passed_pawn, pawn_endgame, bishop_vs_pawns, transition_error) and summaries consistently describe the same pattern: the player eliminates their only piece that can blockade passed pawns or defend a critical square, entering a hopelessly lost pawn endgame or exposing a fatal weakness like a back-rank mate. The FENs confirm sparse endgame positions with advanced passed pawns where one defender was the linchpin of the draw. This is not a simple material blunder but a failure to recognize that the last active piece is irreplaceable for defensive purposes.

1095.label: A pawn move in the opening that leaves a piece undefended, turning an equal position into a lost one.
1095.description: This feature captures a specific opening mistake pattern where a player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) that inadvertently hangs a piece (100% 'hangs' outcome with median -6.0 material loss, consistent with losing a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions collapsing into lost ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 604cp loss). The tactical analysis reveals the underlying mechanisms: the pawn move either blocks a defender, opens a line exposing a piece to a pin or fork, or wastes a critical tempo needed to address a tactical threat. Common tags include missed_tactic, hanging_piece, pin, and queen_loss. The top boards show classic opening scenarios—positions from the Italian, Nimzo-Indian, Scandinavian—where a seemingly natural developing pawn push (e6, e5, d6, d3, e3) overlooks that an existing piece (often the queen or a bishop) becomes tactically vulnerable. Maia also recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting these are positions where pawn play feels natural but the specific pawn chosen is catastrophically wrong.

1098.label: Moves that fatally compromise the player's king safety in middlegame/endgame positions, exposing it to tactical threats.
1098.description: This feature captures moves where the player neglects king safety, leading to significant evaluation drops (median ~193 centipawns). The material signature shows the moves themselves are often materially 'safe' (67%) — meaning the player isn't obviously hanging a piece — but the positional consequence is catastrophic. The dominant motif is king_safety (100% of analyzed positions), with tempo_loss as the most frequent tag, indicating moves that waste time or remove key defenders while the king is vulnerable. The eval trajectories are diverse (drawn->losing, winning->drawn, even losing->winning in one case), but the common thread is that the player's king becomes exposed or loses critical defensive resources. Board inspection confirms endgame/late middlegame positions where kings are active but vulnerable — moves like Kg6 walking into danger, Nxf4 removing a key defender enabling perpetual checks, or piece moves that open lines toward the player's king. The mistake is fundamentally positional: the player makes a move that appears safe materially but fatally weakens their king's shelter or removes defenders, allowing the opponent tactical resources (checks, mating threats, perpetuals) that shift the evaluation dramatically.

1099.label: Playing a passive or slow developing move when a concrete tactical opportunity (often a piece capture or forcing continuation) demands immediate attention.
1099.description: This feature captures positions in the opening and early middlegame where the player makes a non-forcing, often developmental move (knight 25%, queen 23%, bishop 22%) that fails to address or exploit a concrete tactical situation. The material signature shows 89% of these moves are non-captures, yet Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly captures (92% knight captures, 8% bishop captures), indicating a clear missed tactical opportunity. The eval trajectory is severe—median 267 centipawns lost, with 27% going drawn-to-losing and 25% winning-to-drawn—showing these slow moves squander significant advantages or allow opponents to seize the initiative. The motif analysis confirms this: tempo_loss (50%) is the dominant theme, with hanging_piece (25%) and king_safety (25%) rounding out the picture. The concrete positions show patterns like playing Nd2 blocking one's own pieces, Rfe1 instead of a forcing knight jump, or retreating a queen when a capture was available. The common thread is choosing a 'logical-looking' but non-forcing move when the position demanded immediate tactical action—typically capturing an exposed or hanging piece that gives tempo against the opponent's position.

1096.label: Playing a safe but passive piece move when the position demanded an aggressive tactical continuation, squandering a winning or significant advantage.
1096.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player with a strong position (often in the opening or middlegame) plays a natural-looking but passive piece move—typically a bishop or rook retreat/development to a non-threatening square—when a forcing tactical sequence was available. The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly non-capturing moves (93% no capture) that are technically 'safe' (75%) but cost a median of 292 centipawns. The eval trajectory confirms these squander winning positions: 39% go from winning to drawn, 21% from drawn to losing. Maia's recommended moves are predominantly knight moves (82%), often to aggressive outpost squares or capturing material, confirming that the missed opportunity involved an active piece deployment. The tactical analysis reveals tempo_loss as the dominant motif (50%), with tags like initiative_squandered and missed_tactic reinforcing that the player chose consolidation over exploitation. The concrete positions show a recurring theme: White has an established knight on e5, active bishops, and centralized pieces, but instead of pressing with tactics (Qxf7+, Nf5, captures), plays moves like Bd2, c3, Be3, Re1—developing moves that look reasonable but allow the opponent to stabilize. This is the classic 'one quiet move too many' mistake where the player fails to recognize their position has reached a critical moment demanding concrete action.

1100.label: Player retreats or repositions a piece, missing a forcing tactical continuation (often a check, capture, or mate) that Maia identifies.
1100.description: This feature fires when players move a knight, queen, or bishop to a passive or retreating square, missing a sharp tactical opportunity that typically involves a check or material-winning capture. The material signature shows the player rarely captures anything (75% no capture) and the moves are mostly 'safe' in isolation, yet the median eval loss is a devastating 314 centipawns—indicating the player squandered a concrete tactical shot. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve queens delivering checks (75% check rate) or capturing pawns/material, confirming that the missed opportunity was a forcing continuation. The trajectory (33% winning→losing, 17% drawn→losing) shows these are game-turning moments where an initiative or attack was abandoned. The Opus analysis reinforces this with tags like missed_mate, checkmate_in_one, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss—the player chose a quiet developing or retreating move (e.g., Nb5-a3, Qg4 left hanging after Bc4, knight retreating from active post) when a forcing blow was available. The dominant pattern is abandoning an attack at its climax by playing a non-forcing move instead of the critical tactical strike.

1103.label: Playing a passive pawn or piece move that wastes critical tempo, allowing the opponent to exploit undefended pieces or missed tactical opportunities.
1103.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player makes a slow, non-capturing move (predominantly pawn pushes at 60%) that squanders a crucial tempo. The material signature shows 40% of these moves hang material and 100% miss winning material opportunities, while Maia consistently recommends active bishop or knight moves instead. The eval trajectory is devastating—median 407 centipawns lost—with 40% of cases converting a winning position into a losing one. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss at 50%, hanging_piece at 33%, fork at 17%) reveal the mechanism: by playing a passive move, the player either leaves pieces undefended for the opponent to exploit, or misses a concrete tactic (fork, exchange-winning move) that the position demanded. The board positions consistently show complex middlegame/early endgame scenarios where active piece play was critical, but the player chose an aimless pawn push or piece retreat, giving the opponent time to strike at vulnerable targets.

1101.label: Player makes a losing move in a winning position where a forcing queen check sequence (perpetual or mate) was available.
1101.description: This feature fires when players miss a critical queen checking sequence. The material/position signature shows Maia consistently recommending queen moves with 100% check frequency, while the player instead moves rooks, kings, or pawns—none of which deliver check. The 100% 'missed winning material' rate combined with the catastrophic eval trajectory (median 927cp lost, with 43% winning->losing and 43% winning->drawn) confirms these are positions where a forcing queen check sequence (perpetual, mating attack, or winning tactical sequence) was available but the player chose a quiet or defensive move instead. The motifs of king_safety and hanging_piece, combined with tags like missed_perpetual and diagonal_vulnerability, confirm the opponent's king was exposed and tactically vulnerable. The example summaries explicitly reference missed Qf8+/Qd8+ sequences and catastrophic king moves onto vulnerable diagonals. The 'hangs' category (43%) reflects that the player's passive move leaves their own pieces undefended once the forcing sequence is missed, while the 'trade' category (43%) reflects exchanges that surrender the initiative needed to execute the check sequence.

1107.label: In already-lost pawn endgames, the king drifts to a passive square, allowing forced mate or decisive pawn promotion.
1107.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames where the player is already losing (losing->losing 100%) but the move catastrophically worsens the position (median eval lost: 9202 centipawns, indicating transitions from 'merely lost' to 'forced mate'). The material signature shows safe king moves with no captures or checks—these aren't tactical blunders in the traditional sense but fatal king placement errors. The dominant motifs (pawn_endgame, passed_pawn, tempo_loss, king_safety) and the concrete positions confirm the pattern: in simplified endgames with passed pawns, the king moves to the wrong square—losing opposition, allowing the opponent's king to centralize, or stepping into a mating net. The Opus analysis confirms several positions where the king move either enables forced checkmate or lets passed pawns promote uncontested. The phase is exclusively endgame, and the mistake is fundamentally about king activity and tempo in pawn races.

1102.label: Moving a rook away from a critical open file, surrendering control and allowing the opponent counterplay.
1102.description: This feature detects a recurring middlegame mistake where players voluntarily move their rook (50% rook moves) away from a strategically vital open file, surrendering positional dominance. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly game-changing errors: 50% go from winning to drawn and 19% from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 355 centipawns — enormous for non-tactical mistakes. The Opus analysis consistently describes abandoning critical files (c-file, d-file) where the rook was exerting pressure, often redundantly doubling on a less important file or retreating passively. The material signature confirms these are not tactical blunders in the traditional sense: 88% involve no captures, 56% appear 'safe' to the engine in immediate material terms, yet 31% actually hang material as a downstream consequence of losing file control. Maia's recommended moves (100% rook moves giving check along open files) reveal what was missed: active rook play exploiting the very files being abandoned. The common tags (piece_activity, rook_activity, open_file, tempo_loss) and board positions consistently show open file structures where one side's rook leaves its post, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.

1106.label: Moving the king passively in a won endgame instead of capturing with a rook to simplify decisively.
1106.description: This feature detects a specific endgame mistake pattern where a player with a clearly winning position (median eval ~+700) makes a passive king or pawn move instead of executing a decisive rook capture or tactic. The material/position signature shows the player moved their king (62%) or pawn (38%) without capturing anything, while Maia consistently recommends a rook move (100%) that captures a piece (knight 75%, rook 12%, bishop 12%) often with check (62%). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain winning but lose ~120cp of advantage — representing technique imprecision rather than game-losing blunders. The tactical analysis reinforces this: tags like tempo_loss (7), missed_tactic (7), and piece_activity (9) indicate the player chose a slow, non-forcing continuation when a clean tactical resolution (Rxf5+, Rxc6+, Rxe4, Rxd6) was available. The endgame phase (100%) and motifs (passed_pawn, tempo_loss, pawn_endgame) confirm these are all late-game positions where the player drifts with king shuffles or pawn pushes instead of using their rook actively to liquidate material and convert.

1104.label: Playing a natural but non-forcing rook move (typically to d8 or c1) that squanders a tactical opportunity by giving the opponent crucial tempo.
1104.description: This feature identifies a highly specific pattern: players move their rook to a seemingly logical square (78% rook moves, 97% non-captures) — most commonly placing a rook on an open file (Rad8, Rac1, Rad1) — while missing a sharp tactical blow that was available. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (95%) with uncastled or vulnerable kings, pins, and forks present. The median cost is 274 centipawns, with 62% of cases involving missed winning material. The eval trajectory shows these are often game-changing errors (27% winning→drawn, 8% winning→losing), meaning the player had a significant advantage but threw it away by playing a 'natural developing move' instead of a concrete forcing continuation. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies tempo_loss as the dominant motif — the routine rook placement gives the opponent the tempo needed to consolidate or escape. The missed tactics include discovered attacks, piece-winning combinations (Nxf3+, Bb5!, Bxf2+), and forcing checks. The Maia suggestions confirm the engine wanted checks (22%), captures (43%), and active piece play rather than quiet rook lifts. This is the classic amateur mistake of 'improving' a piece when a concrete tactical solution demands immediate attention.

1110.label: Failing to capture a hanging piece in a winning position, converting a win into a draw.
1110.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player, holding a winning advantage (median 883 centipawns lost), fails to capture an opponent's hanging piece — typically a bishop that could be taken by the king. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), but Maia's recommended move is always a king capturing a bishop, confirming the missed capture. The hanging_piece motif dominates (62%), and the eval trajectory is uniformly winning->drawn, meaning these oversights squander decisive advantages. The positions are locked endgame or middlegame structures where the opponent's piece is en prise but the player makes a passive king or bishop move instead, often losing tempo or choosing inferior king positioning. The pattern is not a complex tactic but a simple one-move capture oversight that throws away the game.

1105.label: Player moves their queen (or other major piece) to a square where it is immediately captured by an opponent's piece, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
1105.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a one-move blunder that leaves a major piece (most often the queen, 46% of moves) hanging on an undefended square, allowing immediate capture. The material signature is stark: 64% of moves are classified as 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -5.0 (approximately a queen's value). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes that throw away favorable positions—36% go from winning to losing, 18% from winning to drawn—with a median eval swing of 928 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms 100% hanging_piece motifs, with recurring tags like 'queen_blunder' and 'one_move_blunder.' Maia's recommended moves frequently capture a rook (46%) or nothing (41%), indicating the best move was often simply to take the opponent's hanging piece or make a safe developing move. The concrete board examples consistently show pieces placed on squares directly attacked by opponent pieces (e.g., queen moved to f6 where a rook captures it, queen moved to f3 where a bishop takes it, king moved to a file where a rook pins/captures the queen). These are not complex tactical oversights but single-move visualization failures in the middlegame (73%) where the player fails to notice a basic attack on the destination square.

1108.label: Recapturing on a bishop exchange without first exploiting an intermediate tactic, leaving a piece hanging.
1108.description: This feature fires on opening-phase bishop exchanges where the player recaptures (or initiates a trade) with a bishop or pawn, resulting in a materially equal exchange on the surface, but critically misses the correct move order. The material signature shows 100% trades (net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 416 centipawns—indicating the trade itself isn't the blunder, but the *sequence* in which it's executed. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), and the most frequent tag is 'move_order' (appearing in 6/10 cases), confirming that these players capture a bishop immediately rather than first inserting an intermediate move (often a check or fork) that would win material. Maia's recommended moves are bishop moves that give check 67% of the time—precisely the in-between tactic being missed. The positions are all in the opening with active piece play, where a tempo-sensitive intermezzo (like Bxd7+ before recapturing) would have preserved or won material. Instead, the automatic recapture leaves another piece undefended, converting drawn or slightly favorable positions into losing ones.

1109.label: Player makes a non-forcing move that fatally compromises their own king's safety, missing a forcing defensive or offensive continuation.
1109.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a quiet or non-forcing move (often a knight retreat, pawn push, or greedy capture) while their king is critically vulnerable, missing a forcing continuation (usually involving check) that was necessary to survive or maintain advantage. The material signature shows the player's moves are mostly non-captures (72%) that frequently hang material (33%), while Maia's suggested moves are almost exclusively knight moves delivering check (94% knight, 100% check), indicating a missed forcing defensive or counterattacking resource. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 579cp lost), with positions going from drawn/winning to losing. The tactical analysis confirms king_safety (50%) and tempo_loss (50%) as dominant motifs—players lose critical tempi by playing slow moves (like Nxa1 grabbing material, or f3 weakening the king shelter) when the position demanded an immediate forcing response. The common tags (discovered_attack, deflection, king_shelter_destruction, forced_mate) confirm that the missed moves exploit king vulnerability through tactical forcing sequences.

1113.label: Queen captures a defended pawn in the opening, hanging the queen to a hidden defender.
1113.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions where the player's queen captures a pawn but loses massive material (median -8.0, consistent with losing the queen). The eval trajectory shows drawn positions collapsing to losing (median 615cp lost), indicating these were balanced games destroyed by a single oversight. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (75%), with recurring tags like 'capturing_defended_pawn', 'queen_blunder', and 'basic_oversight'. The concrete positions show queens greedily snatching pawns that turn out to be defended by bishops or other pieces (e.g., Qxg7 where the g7-pawn is defended by Bf8), or pieces moving to squares where they are simply captured. The common thread is an overambitious capture—usually by the queen—that overlooks a straightforward defender, immediately dropping the queen for a pawn and converting a playable position into a lost one.

1115.label: Moving a rook to an undefended square where it can be captured for free, often due to a move-order error.
1115.description: This feature identifies a specific and costly tactical oversight: the player moves their rook (100% rook moves, 0% captures) to a square where it is completely undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it (Maia responds with rook captures rook 100%, often with check). The material signature confirms these are not exchanges but outright hangs (100% 'hangs' classification, median -5.0 material loss corresponding to a full rook). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 663cp lost), sometimes converting a winning position into a losing one. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant pattern: hanging_piece (67%) combined with move-order errors and undefended rooks. The concrete examples show players either moving their rook past an enemy rook without first exchanging (leaving it en prise), making prophylactic moves while a rook sits undefended, or attacking a piece while ignoring that their rook can be captured with a discovered attack or check. The common thread is failing to notice that after the rook move, no friendly piece guards the rook's new (or original) square.

1114.label: Player releases central or positional tension with a pawn or minor piece move, squandering a winning or balanced position.
1114.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a seemingly safe move (66% safe, 74% no capture) — typically advancing or exchanging a pawn (42%) or repositioning a minor piece (40% bishop/knight) — that releases critical tension and throws away a winning advantage. The eval trajectory is stark: 51% of cases go from winning to drawn and 11% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 304 centipawns. Maia strongly preferred quiet pawn moves (92%), confirming these are natural-looking but strategically costly decisions. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are positional mistakes (43%), tempo losses (14%), and missed discovered attacks/tactics (14%), with recurring tags around piece activity, tempo loss, and move order errors. The top boards reinforce this: moves like exd5 instead of the space-gaining e5, or axb6 leaving a piece hanging, or releasing pawn chains prematurely — all cases where the player chose a simplifying or tension-releasing move when maintaining pressure was critical. These are not tactical oversights in the traditional sense but rather failures to sustain positional advantages, collapsing winning positions into equality.

1112.label: Rook moves to a square where it becomes a tactical target via deflection or discovered attack.
1112.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player moves a rook (90% of activations) to a square that appears natural but creates a fatal tactical vulnerability. The material signature shows 71% 'safe' moves — meaning the rook isn't immediately hanging — yet 56% of the time a winning tactical shot is missed by the opponent or, more precisely, the player overlooked that the rook's destination enables a combination. The tactical motifs (king_safety 40%, deflection, hanging_piece, overloaded_defender) combined with the example analyses reveal the recurring theme: the rook lands on a square where a sacrifice (often Bxh7+ or Bxh6+) deflects the king, leaving the rook undefended, or the rook moves away from defending a critical square, or it lands where a fork/skewer picks it up. The eval trajectory (median 275cp lost, with 14% drawn->losing and 17% losing->losing) confirms these are serious tactical oversights rather than positional inaccuracies. Maia's suggested moves are diverse (rook only 37%), indicating the engine sees better alternatives. The concrete board positions repeatedly show rooks moving to f-file or e-file squares where they become targets of deflection sacrifices or are left undefended after forced sequences.

1111.label: Player makes a move that fatally compromises their own king's safety, allowing tactical exploitation.
1111.description: This feature fires on moves where the player neglects their king's vulnerability, leading to severe consequences. The material signature shows the player most often moves their king (43%) or a pawn (23%), rarely capturing anything (88% no capture), yet 40% of the time the move hangs material—indicating the move itself creates tactical vulnerabilities rather than being a direct blunder of a piece in hand. Crucially, Maia (the human-like engine) overwhelmingly recommends a king move (98%), suggesting the correct response was to address king safety directly, but the player chose a different piece move or an inferior king move that worsened their king's position. The Opus tactical analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif (57%), with tags like exposed_king and pawn_structure_weakening appearing repeatedly. The examples illustrate this clearly: castling into tactical pressure (e8c8 facing Nd6+), pushing pawns that destroy the king's shield (f5 opening diagonals, c5 exposing the king on c4), and king moves that walk into danger. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 215 centipawns, with the majority of cases being positions that were already losing getting worse (27%) or drawn positions collapsing into losses (8%), suggesting players under pressure make desperate or careless moves that further expose their king rather than addressing the defensive need Maia identified. The middlegame dominance (66%) aligns with king safety being most critical when pieces remain active on the board.

1118.label: Player makes a quiet, safe move in the opening/middlegame while missing a devastating knight fork that would win significant material.
1118.description: This feature fires when a player plays a non-committal, safe move (pawn, queen, or bishop moves that don't capture or give check) while completely missing a knight fork tactic. The material signature shows 100% safe moves with no captures—these aren't blunders that hang pieces, but passive moves that squander a winning advantage. The eval trajectory (89% winning->drawn, median 275cp lost) confirms the player is throwing away a won position. The tactical analysis is emphatic: 62% fork motifs, 5/8 positions tagged with knight_fork, and Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%). The example summaries repeatedly describe centralized knights delivering forks on queens, winning exchanges, or making consecutive captures. The positions cluster in the opening/early middlegame (67% opening) where the opponent's pieces are still congested and vulnerable to knight geometry. The player instead plays aimless prophylactic moves (h3, a3, Rb1, Bf3) that accomplish nothing while the knight tactic evaporates.

1116.label: Player makes a catastrophic move-order error in the opening that hangs a piece by ignoring an immediate tactical threat.
1116.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in the opening phase (73% opening) make moves that hang material (73% hangs) by failing to address an immediate tactical threat before proceeding with their intended plan. The moves are predominantly bishop (40%) and knight (20%) moves that ignore opponent threats, resulting in a median loss of 5.0 material units and 531 centipawns of evaluation. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (60%), tempo_loss (20%), and fork (20%)—combined with tags like 'ignoring_threat', 'castling_before_addressing_threat', and 'move_order' reveal players who execute a reasonable-looking developing move or castle without first resolving an urgent tactical issue. The eval trajectory shows these are frequently game-deciding mistakes: 40% turn winning positions into losing ones and 20% turn drawn positions into losing ones. Maia's recommended moves (73% queen moves, often captures) confirm the missed opportunity was typically to address or exploit the very threat being ignored. The concrete positions show patterns like castling into a bishop fork on the queen, playing a developing move while a piece is en prise, or executing a plan one tempo too late.

1117.label: In won endgames, the player moves their king to a passive or incorrect square, throwing away a decisive advantage.
1117.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player, typically moving their king (67%), makes a move that is objectively safe (67% safe, no material immediately lost) but catastrophically weakens their winning position—median eval loss of 892 centipawns, with the trajectory showing winning→winning (67%) or winning→drawn (33%). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (33%), hanging_piece (22%), and passed_pawn (11%), while the recurring tags emphasize king_activity and tempo_loss. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: kings retreat from active squares (Kf7→Kf6 abandoning a mating net, Ke7→Kf8 passively retreating instead of capturing a key pawn with Kxe6, Kf6→Ke7 allowing counterplay). The player consistently fails to use their king aggressively in the endgame, choosing quiet or retreating king moves that allow the opponent to equalize or escape what should be a technically won position. Maia's suggested alternatives often involve captures (rook 33%, pawn 33%) or more active piece placement, highlighting that the correct plan required engagement rather than passivity.

1119.label: Ignoring a tactically available knight capture in the opening to play a routine developing or non-critical move, throwing away a winning advantage.
1119.description: This feature fires when a player in the opening phase plays a knight move (or other quiet developing/preparatory move) instead of capturing an opponent's knight that is tactically vulnerable. The material signature shows the played move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet Maia's recommended move captures a knight, indicating there was a concrete tactical opportunity on the board. The eval trajectory confirms a catastrophic swing—positions go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 435 centipawns—consistent with squandering a decisive advantage. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 62%, tempo_loss 25%) and tags (missed_tactic, development, piece_activity) reveal that the player prioritized routine development or pawn moves (like ...a6, ...Nf6, ...e6) over exploiting a hanging or insufficiently defended knight, often in Sicilian or Italian-type structures where a centralized Nd4 or exposed piece was available for capture. The mistake is fundamentally tactical: the player sees a 'normal' developing move and misses that the position demanded an immediate concrete capture.

1120.label: Giving a rook check that hangs material instead of capturing a winning tactic in a won endgame.
1120.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a rook check (75% rook moves, 75% checks) in a winning endgame that hangs material (100% hangs, median -1.0 net material), while the correct move was a rook capture of a pawn (Maia: rook 100%, captures pawn 100%). The eval trajectory shows winning->winning with a median loss of 63 centipawns, but individual cases can be catastrophic (up to 1122cp lost). The top boards reveal a highly repetitive pattern: the same rook-on-the-7th-rank endgame position appears multiple times where the player shuffles the rook back and forth delivering pointless checks (Rh7-h8, Rh8-h7) instead of executing the one decisive tactical capture (like Rxf2+ or capturing a passed pawn). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (67%), tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and piece_activity—confirm the player is wasting tempi on non-constructive checks while leaving their own material unguarded and missing the concrete winning conversion. This is a classic endgame error of choosing flashy but pointless checks over precise material collection.

1122.label: King moves or passive rook moves that leave the back rank fatally unguarded or abandon critical coordination.
1122.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a king move (26%) or rook move (42%) that hangs material (68% of outcomes) with a median cost of ~200 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows most cases occur in already-losing positions (47% losing→losing) but also includes drawn→losing (10%) and even losing→winning reversals missed (16%), indicating the player fails to exploit or defend tactical threats. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and back_rank (33%), with recurring tags of piece_coordination breakdown and king_safety failures. The concrete positions confirm this: Kf1 walking into mate-in-2 via back rank, rook moves that abandon critical files breaking queen-piece coordination, and king moves to exposed squares where back-rank or hanging-piece tactics become decisive. The player consistently misjudges the safety of their back rank or first-rank squares, making 'quiet' king/rook moves that overlook immediate tactical vulnerabilities stemming from inadequate back-rank defense.

1124.label: Player makes a quiet or slow move, missing an immediate queen checkmate or devastating queen check that was available.
1124.description: This feature fires when a player makes a non-capturing, non-checking move (93% no capture, 0% checks) — often a knight move (37%) — while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen move (89%) that delivers check (100%) and frequently captures material (37% pawn, 22% bishop, 15% rook). The positions are middlegame (78%) with recurring motifs of back-rank vulnerability, king safety exploitation, forks, and hanging pieces. The tags confirm missed mate-in-ones, missed checkmates, and catastrophic blunders. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 264 centipawns, with many positions swinging from winning to drawn or losing. The concrete examples reinforce this: players chose slow developing or retreating moves (Ng3, Bd4, Nd7) when an immediate queen mate or winning queen check with capture was available. The pattern is consistently one of overlooking a forceful queen blow — often a back-rank mate or a queen capture with check — in favor of a quiet positional or prophylactic move.

1121.label: Player makes an aimless move while missing a forced checkmate or devastating tactic exploiting king safety weaknesses.
1121.description: This feature fires on positions where a player overlooks a winning tactical blow—most commonly a back-rank mate or king-safety exploitation—and instead plays a passive or irrelevant move (typically a pawn push or quiet rook move). The material signature shows the played moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (100% no capture) and often 'safe' in isolation, meaning the move itself doesn't hang anything but catastrophically misses the winning continuation. The eval trajectory is dramatic: 33% of cases flip from losing to winning (opponent's perspective) and 17% throw a win into a loss, with example positions showing missed mate-in-1, mate-in-2, and forced sequences worth thousands of centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety (43%) and back_rank (29%), with tags like missed_tactic, back_rank_mate, and missed_mate recurring. Maia's suggested moves consistently deliver check (100%), often with rooks or knights exploiting exposed kings. The pattern is a player making a 'do-nothing' move—a pawn advance, a rook shuffle—while a crushing king-safety tactic (often back-rank or fork-based) sits available on the board.

1123.label: Player makes a slow or passive piece move in the opening, missing a concrete tactical opportunity that wins material.
1123.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (bishop 40%, knight 24%, pawn 19%) in the opening phase (83%) that is objectively safe in isolation (83% 'safe' material outcome) but completely misses a sharp tactical blow. Maia's recommended moves are captures (bishop 38%, knight 31%, pawn 26%) often delivering check (19%), revealing that the position demanded concrete action. The dominant motifs—hanging pieces (33%), forks (17%), king safety (17%), overloaded defenders (17%)—combined with tags like missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and uncastled_king confirm the player chose a slow developmental or repositioning move when a forcing sequence was available. The eval trajectory is severe (median 257cp lost), frequently turning winning or equal positions into drawn or lost ones (winning→drawn 21%, drawn→losing 17%). The top boards illustrate this clearly: castling when a piece could be won, retreating an attacking knight to a passive square, or playing a routine pawn push instead of a tactical combination exploiting the opponent's uncastled king or loose pieces.

1125.label: Player captures a queen with a minor piece, trading queens prematurely while overlooking hanging pieces or tactical continuations that would have maintained a winning advantage.
1125.description: This feature fires when players execute a queen trade (100% trades, 100% capturing a queen, primarily with bishops at 58%) that costs them significant advantage (median 412 centipawns lost, with 92% missing winning material). The trajectory confirms these are 'throwing a win' situations: 31% winning->drawn, 19% winning->losing, 19% drawn->losing. The tactical layer reveals why: the dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), with move_order_error as a recurring tag. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern—players rush to capture an exposed queen (often Bxd1 or similar) before addressing other tactical opportunities like capturing hanging knights or exploiting pins. The Opus analysis explicitly identifies move-order catastrophes where taking the queen first allows the opponent to save hanging pieces or achieve symmetrical trades. Maia's recommended moves (46% queen moves, with 42% capturing bishops) suggest the correct continuation often involved maintaining queen activity rather than exchanging. These are not greedy captures but premature simplifications where the player's impatience to resolve queen tension blinds them to the fact that intermediate moves would have preserved their advantage.

1127.label: Squandering a winning endgame by making a slow or retreating move instead of executing the decisive tactical blow.
1127.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern in endgame positions where the player holds a winning advantage but throws away a large portion of it (median 306cp lost) through a tempo-wasting or passive move. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (knight 50%, pawn 50%) that don't immediately lose material but fatally squander the initiative. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss, passed_pawn, back_rank, and king_safety—combined with tags like missed_tactic and promotion_error reveal that in each case there was a concrete winning continuation (promoting a passed pawn, delivering a back-rank checkmate, exploiting a discovered attack) that the player missed in favor of a slow developing or retreating move. The positions are uniformly endgames where the player remains technically winning but has converted a forced decisive advantage into something far less clear. Examples include retreating an active rook from its dominant post, moving a bishop when a passed pawn needed immediate advancement, and playing a quiet king move when a tactical shot was available.

1126.label: Wasting a crucial tempo in positions where immediate action (capture, promotion, or tactical strike) was required to convert or defend.
1126.description: This feature identifies positions—predominantly in endgames or critical tactical moments—where the player squanders a vital tempo by making a passive or retreating move instead of executing an immediately winning or necessary action. The material signature shows that the player's move is often a non-capture (100% no capture) that either hangs a piece or is merely 'safe' but strategically catastrophic. The eval trajectory reveals enormous costs (median ~94 pawns lost, i.e., converting to losses or throwing wins into draws), consistent with missing forced wins like captures (Kxb3), tactical shots (Bxf7+), or promotion-related moves. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (33%), supported by tags like passed_pawn, endgame_technique, and missed_capture—indicating positions where a passed pawn demands immediate attention or a simple capture/promotion was available but the player instead made an aimless king move, knight retreat, or passive rook move. The common thread across all examples is that one wasted move in a time-critical position (often with passed pawns racing, or a one-move tactical window) collapses the entire evaluation.

1128.label: Developing a bishop to a square where an enemy pawn immediately captures it for free in the opening.
1128.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player develops a bishop (100% bishop moves, 0% captures) to a square where it is immediately captured by an enemy pawn, hanging a full piece (net material median: -3.0, consistent with losing a minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost — positions swing from drawn to losing by a median of 610 centipawns. The tactical analysis (62% hanging_piece motif, tags like 'pawn_captures_piece', 'opening_trap', 'move_order_error') and the concrete positions make the pattern unmistakable: players in Caro-Kann, Scandinavian, or Queen's Gambit-style openings place their bishop on f5 or f4 where an unblocked central pawn (e4 or e5) captures it immediately. Maia's response is always a pawn capture (100%), confirming the piece is simply taken. This is a pure one-move tactical oversight — a move-order error where the bishop development needed to be preceded by a pawn exchange on e4 or the bishop needed a different square.

1129.label: A developing move in the opening that allows an opponent's pawn advance to trap a bishop.
1129.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (100% opening) that are materially safe in themselves (no captures, no material lost immediately) but cause a dramatic drawn-to-losing evaluation swing (median 275cp loss, 85% drawn->losing). The dominant motif is trapped_piece (67%), with bishop_trapped appearing explicitly and piece_activity being the most common tag. The concrete pattern across top boards shows positions where a bishop has ventured to an aggressive square (g4, f5, g6) and the player makes a developing or pawn move that ignores an imminent pawn advance (h4-h5, g4-g5) that seals off the bishop's retreat squares. Rather than retreating the bishop or preventing the trapping advance, the player makes a natural-looking but catastrophic developing move (e6, Nf6, Bh5) that allows the opponent to permanently entomb the piece. The feature captures the specific pattern of positional negligence in the opening where piece activity is compromised by failing to recognize a trap closing around an exposed bishop.

1130.label: King moves that allow or walk into stalemate in won king-and-queen endgames.
1130.description: The top activating positions are overwhelmingly king-and-queen vs lone king (or near-equivalent) endgames where the stronger side plays a king move that either stalemates the opponent or drastically reduces the winning advantage. The material signature shows 86% king moves with no captures and 'safe' outcomes—nothing is hung or traded, yet the eval trajectory shows massive centipawn losses (including a missed checkmate-in-one). The Opus analysis confirms pattern blindness, missed tactics, and king safety issues in pure pawn/piece endgames. Maia's recommended moves are almost always queen moves (86%), suggesting the correct plan involved using the queen actively (to deliver check or restrict the opposing king) rather than advancing one's own king into a stalemate or drawing configuration. The positions in the top-10 boards are textbook KQ vs K or KQ vs K+pawn setups where careless king centralization ruins the win.

1131.label: Moving a piece to an unprotected square while missing an opponent's tactical reply that wins material.
1131.description: This feature captures positions where a player makes a non-capture move (100% no capture) that leaves a piece hanging (73% hangs material), with a devastating median loss of 307 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (60%), indicating the player places or leaves a piece en prise without adequate defense. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes frequently convert winning positions to losing ones (36%) or drawn positions to losing ones (18%), meaning these are often game-deciding blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The missed opportunities are telling: Maia's recommended moves frequently involve queen captures (64%) and other material-winning tactics, confirming that the opponent had a concrete tactical shot available that the player overlooked. The tempo_loss tags (6 occurrences) and king_safety concerns (5 occurrences) suggest players often make developing or prophylactic moves that look reasonable but fatally ignore an immediate tactical threat—the classic pattern of playing a 'normal' move when the position demands addressing a concrete hanging piece or tactical vulnerability.

1135.label: Trading a major piece before eliminating a tactically dangerous minor piece, allowing a devastating fork or hanging piece.
1135.description: This feature captures positions where the player initiates a major piece trade (rook or queen exchange) but does so in the wrong move order, leaving a piece hanging or enabling a fork. The material signature shows 100% trades (net material ~0), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 413cp), swinging from winning/drawn positions to losing/drawn ones. The tactical analysis consistently highlights that the player prioritized a simplifying exchange (rook trade, queen trade) without first neutralizing an active minor piece (typically a knight) that then executes a fork or captures a hanging piece. Tags like 'move_order', 'tempo_loss', 'simplification_error', and 'knight_fork' reinforce that the core mistake is sequencing—the trade itself isn't inherently bad, but doing it before removing the tactical threat is what collapses the position. The board positions confirm this: knights on active squares (d3, e3, d5) punish the premature exchange with forks or recaptures.

1133.label: Player captures material instead of delivering a forced back-rank checkmate.
1133.description: This feature fires when a player in the middlegame has a forced back-rank mate (typically in 1-2 moves) but instead makes a materialistic capture—usually taking a rook with their queen. The material signature shows the player capturing rooks 83% of the time with queens (50%) or other pieces, yielding a 'safe' or 'trade' outcome, while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen or rook delivering check (100% check rate). The tactical analysis confirms back-rank mate as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with tags like 'mate_in_2', 'missed_checkmate', 'material_greed', and 'queen_sacrifice_missed' recurring throughout. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: a median of 10019 centipawns lost, reflecting that a forced mate was available but the player settled for a routine capture, often converting a winning position into a drawn or even losing one. The concrete positions all show kings trapped on the back rank with mating patterns available via Qd8+, Re8#, Qe8+, or Rh8#, but the player reflexively grabbed material instead of calculating the short checkmate sequence.

1134.label: Bishop captures a pawn with check in a winning endgame, simplifying into a drawn position by removing necessary material.
1134.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a bishop capture of a pawn that gives check, but the resulting simplification converts a winning position into a draw (100% winning->drawn trajectory, median 310cp lost). The material signature shows a net loss of ~2 pawns worth despite capturing, indicating the bishop is subsequently lost or the resulting position is theoretically drawn due to insufficient material. The tactical analysis confirms this with tags like 'insufficient_material', 'endgame_technique', and 'passed_pawn_handling' — the key example explicitly notes 'failing to recognize that King + [insufficient pieces]' leads to a theoretical draw. Rather than maintaining winning technique (e.g., keeping the bishop to support a passed pawn or maintain a mating net), the player grabs a check that trades down into a known drawn endgame. Maia's recommended moves avoid the capture entirely (100% non-capture, 0% check), suggesting the correct approach was quiet prophylactic play preserving the winning material configuration rather than the tempting but drawing simplification.

1137.label: Voluntarily moving the king in the opening, forfeiting castling rights and wasting critical development tempo.
1137.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder where the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) early in the game (100% opening phase), permanently forfeiting castling rights. The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median loss of 278 centipawns), indicating a catastrophic positional concession rather than a tactical oversight. The dominant motifs—king_safety (88%), tempo_loss (12%)—along with recurring tags like 'exposed_king', 'castling_rights_forfeited', 'king_walk', and 'opening_principles_violation' confirm the nature of the mistake: the player voluntarily places their king on an unsafe square (e2, e7, f2, d2) when castling was still available, gifting the opponent free tempi and leaving the king vulnerable to tactical exploitation in an open center. The boards consistently show positions where standard development (castling, piece deployment) was both available and necessary, making these king moves pure positional self-destruction.

1136.label: Moving a piece to a square where it is immediately captured without compensation.
1136.description: This feature detects unforced moves that simply hang a piece. The material signature is stark: 71% of moves result in a hang (non-capture that drops a piece) with a median net material loss of -3.0 (roughly a full piece). The pieces moved are predominantly bishops (52%) and knights (24%), placed on squares where they are immediately captured. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of the Opus tactical analyses, and tags like 'no_compensation', 'unforced_error', and 'piece_for_pawn' reinforce that these are not sacrifices or miscalculated exchanges but simple oversights. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 209 centipawns, with 57% occurring in already-losing positions (losing->losing) and 14% turning drawn positions into losing ones—suggesting players in difficult or complex positions blunder tactically by placing pieces on undefended or attacked squares. The concrete examples confirm this: a bishop moved to e7 where it's captured by a pawn on f6, a knight check on c6 that's immediately recaptured with no follow-up, and a bishop move to g6 that hangs the piece. These are opening/early middlegame blunders (52% opening, 48% middlegame) where the player overlooks a simple one-move threat to the piece they just moved.

1132.label: Premature pawn advances in king-and-pawn endgames that fatally compromise pawn structure or tempo.
1132.description: This feature fires on pawn moves in pure pawn endgames (89% pawn_endgame motif, 80% endgame phase) where the player pushes a pawn prematurely, losing critical tempo or destroying their own pawn structure. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures and no material immediately lost ('safe'), yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 94 centipawns, typically worsening an already losing position (80% losing->losing) or converting a draw into a loss (20% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis consistently identifies tempo_loss and premature_pawn_advance as key tags—these pawn pushes either allow the opponent to liquidate the pawn structure (e.g., h4 allowing gxh4/hxg3 chain reactions), fix pawns on vulnerable squares (e.g., c4 creating a dysfunctional majority), or cede key squares to the opposing king. The top boards confirm the pattern: symmetrical or near-symmetrical pawn structures where one ill-timed push (g3, h4, h5, c4, g5, b5, g6) hands the opponent a decisive advantage in the resulting pawn race or king maneuver. Maia's preferred responses (80% king moves) show the opponent exploiting the tempo loss through superior king activity rather than pawn play.

1138.label: Player moves queen or rook instead of delivering a decisive knight check that wins immediately.
1138.description: This feature detects positions where the player had a winning knight check (Maia's move is knight 95%, giving check 100%) but instead moved their queen (48%) or rook (24%) to a square that fails to exploit the exposed enemy king. The king_safety motif dominates (86%), and the tactical analysis repeatedly shows the player choosing the wrong checking piece or abandoning a forcing sequence involving knight discoveries and checks. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median -9589 centipawns lost), often converting forced checkmates or decisive advantages into drawn or lost positions. The material signature shows 'missed winning material' at 100%, confirming these are not positional subtleties but concrete tactical oversights. The example summaries make it explicit: players move their queen to non-optimal squares (Qh6, Qc7, Qg5+) when a knight check (Nh5+, Nd5+, etc.) would have initiated an unstoppable mating attack or decisive material gain through a forcing sequence. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (95%) with exposed kings where the knight's unique geometry creates lethal discovered or double checks that the player overlooked.

1139.label: Rook moves to a passive square in rook endgames, abandoning active positioning or missing critical captures.
1139.description: This feature fires on rook endgame mistakes where the player moves their rook (71% of activations) to a passive or purposeless square instead of maintaining activity or executing a critical capture. The material signature shows 98% non-captures with 26% of moves hanging material, yet the median net material is 0.0—indicating the loss is positional rather than immediate material. The eval trajectory shows devastating costs (median 212cp lost), with 26% converting drawn positions to losing and 12% throwing wins into draws. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: players abandon dominant rook positions for aimless lateral moves (e.g., Rd2-a2, Rc8-c2, Rc5-h5), lose tempo, or fail to capture available material (62% missed winning material). Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (38%) or checks (19%), confirming the player chose passivity over concrete action. The top boards consistently show rook endgames with passed pawns where rook activity is paramount, and the player instead retreats or sidesteps to squares that accomplish nothing strategically.

1141.label: Placing or leaving a piece on a pawn-captured square in the opening, immediately losing material.
1141.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase moves (100% opening) where the player hangs a piece (100% hangs) by ignoring a simple pawn capture threat, turning a drawn position into a losing one (drawn->losing 100%, median ~473cp lost). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (78%), supported by tags like development errors, tempo loss, and opening traps. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows pieces (especially bishops via ...Bc5 or knights) being placed on squares directly attacked by a central d- or e-pawn, or catastrophic tempo-wasting moves like Ke2/Ke7 that forfeit castling and leave material loose. Maia's response is always a pawn capture (100%), confirming the piece was simply left en prise to a pawn. These are elementary one-move oversights in the opening where the player fails to notice that a central pawn directly attacks the square they just occupied.

1140.label: Mishandling won or drawn king-and-pawn endgames through tempo loss, premature pawn advances, or promotion errors that squander the advantage.
1140.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of errors in pure king-and-pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a move that is materially 'safe' (80% nothing hangs) but positionally catastrophic. The eval trajectory shows most cases go from winning to still winning but with significant leakage (median 32cp lost), with critical cases converting wins into draws (20%) or even rescuing draws from losing positions at the cost of winning chances. The dominant motifs—promotion_error, passed_pawn mishandling, pawn_endgame technique failures, and tempo_loss—all point to the same underlying mistake: the player lacks precise endgame technique. Concrete examples include promoting into an immediately capturable queen (g1=Q with the king on f2), advancing a passed pawn one square too early (g5-g6 instead of maintaining opposition), abandoning a mating king position (Kf7-f6 giving up control of key squares), and moving a knight away from a dominating post. The moved pieces are kings and pawns (80% combined), consistent with simplified endgame positions where every tempo and square matters enormously.

1143.label: Advancing a pawn that fatally weakens the position by hanging material or exposing the king.
1143.description: This feature captures middlegame pawn advances (87% pawn moves) that are overwhelmingly non-captures (87% no capture) and result in hanging material (73% hangs, median -1.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic, with a median loss of 277 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing (47%) or throwing wins (26% combined winning->drawn/losing). The tactical analysis reveals the underlying mechanism: these pawn pushes open critical diagonals, ignore immediate threats to the king, or leave pieces undefended—as seen in the dominant motifs of hanging_piece (44%) and king_safety (33%). The top boards consistently show aggressive-looking pawn advances (f5-f6, e5-e6, e6-e7, g5-g6, h3-h4) that appear threatening but actually create devastating tactical vulnerabilities, whether by opening diagonals to the king, leaving pieces without support, or ignoring urgent defensive needs. The Maia suggestions (queen 20%, rook 20%, bishop 20%) indicate the correct moves typically involved piece activity or addressing threats rather than pushing pawns forward.

1142.label: Player makes a developing or pawn move in the opening while completely ignoring an opponent's queen that is threatening to win major material.
1142.description: This feature fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player makes a move—typically a pawn push or minor piece retreat (pawn 40%, knight 40%, bishop 20%)—that hangs material (80% hangs) by failing to address an immediate queen threat. The top boards reveal a strikingly consistent pattern: the opponent's queen (Maia's piece is queen 40% of the time, and queen invasions are tagged) is actively threatening to capture a rook or deliver a devastating blow (e.g., Qxh1 winning a rook, Qxg7 threats), and the player instead plays a passive or developmental move that ignores this lethal threat. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 388cp, roughly a full rook), with positions going from drawn-to-losing (40%) or even winning-to-losing (20%). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (86%), and recurring tags include missed_tactic, king_safety, and tempo_loss—all pointing to a player who prioritizes their own plan (development, pawn structure) while being blind to the opponent's queen invasion. The positions consistently feature an enemy queen already penetrated into dangerous squares (Qb7, Qg7, Qf2) where immediate defensive action was required.

1144.label: Trading a rook for a queen while overlooking an immediate back-rank or tactical catastrophe that makes the position hopeless.
1144.description: This feature fires when a player uses their rook to capture an enemy queen (rook moved 100%, queen captured 100%) in what appears to be an exchange or trade (net material median +4.0, classified as 'trade'), but the recapture or resulting position exposes a devastating tactical vulnerability—most commonly a back-rank mate threat or a hanging piece left undefended. The eval trajectory shows the move costs a catastrophic median of ~91 pawns worth of evaluation, typically converting a drawn or already-losing position into immediate checkmate or total collapse (drawn->losing 50%, losing->losing 50%). The tactical motifs confirm back-rank threats (50%) and hanging pieces (50%), with tags including king_safety, missed_tactic, and undefended_piece. Maia would have preferred a quiet pawn move (100%), suggesting the engine saw that the 'tempting' queen capture was actually a trap. The player grabs the queen with their rook, believing they're winning material or simplifying, but the resulting position leaves them fatally exposed—often to an immediate back-rank mate or loss of their own queen that was left undefended during the capture sequence.

1145.label: Misplays in rook endgames and promotion decisions that worsen already difficult positions.
1145.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes (63% endgame phase) where players make critical errors in rook endgames and pawn promotion situations. The material signature shows moves that hang pieces (37%) or lose material (32%) with a median net loss of -4.0, predominantly involving pawns, rooks, and queens. The eval trajectory reveals these are mostly positions that are already losing (68% losing->losing) but the move makes things significantly worse (median 147cp lost), indicating failures to find defensive resources or conversion errors. The tactical analysis highlights rook endgame themes (50%), promotion errors (25%), and passed pawn mishandling (25%) — players trade rooks at the wrong moment (entering lost king-and-pawn endgames), promote to the wrong piece, or fail to maintain rook activity behind passed pawns. The top boards confirm this: multiple positions show premature rook exchanges (h2h3 allowing rook trade), incorrect promotions (promoting to queen when stalemate tricks or underpromotion was needed), and rook-vs-passed-pawn positions where the active piece is surrendered.

1146.label: Player retreats or repositions a piece, missing that an opponent's piece is hanging or a tactic is available, costing massive material.
1146.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a bishop, pawn, or queen in a non-capturing, non-checking way (86% no capture) that is objectively safe or hangs material, while Maia's suggested move is always a queen capture (100% queen moves, capturing pawns 57%, bishops 29%, knights 14%). The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the median eval loss is a catastrophic 465 centipawns—typically converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 36%, winning->drawn 29%, winning->losing 14%). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%), king_safety (20%), and trapped_piece (20%), with tags emphasizing missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and undefended_minor_piece. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows players retreating active pieces (e.g., Qa4->Qc2 abandoning attack on an undefended bishop), pushing pawns that remove support from key pieces, or making developing moves that ignore freely capturable enemy pieces. The player essentially turns away from a concrete tactical opportunity—often an undefended or trapped piece—by making a quiet repositioning move, allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape.

1147.label: Failing to find the only correct move in a critical position, turning a drawn or holdable game into a loss.
1147.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a critical decision—often in pawn endgames or simplified positions—and fails to find the single (or very few) saving move(s), resulting in a catastrophic evaluation swing. The material signature shows king and pawn moves (no captures, no checks), consistent with endgame maneuvering rather than tactical exchanges. The eval trajectory confirms massive losses (median 573 centipawns), predominantly converting drawn positions into lost ones or making losing positions far worse. The Opus analysis repeatedly emphasizes that only one or very few moves held the position, and the player chose a natural-looking but fatally flawed alternative.
