Common tags (opposition, passed_pawn, pawn_structure, tempo_loss) reveal that the mistakes involve subtle endgame concepts—losing the opposition, mishandling pawn races, or making tempo-losing moves that allow enemy passed pawns to promote. The boards confirm this: most are king-and-pawn endgames or simplified positions where precise calculation of pawn structures and king activity was required.

1148.label: Premature pawn or king moves in the opening that leave pieces hanging on vulnerable diagonals or squares.
1148.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake (75% opening) where players make pawn moves (50%) or premature king moves (12%, often castling into danger) that ignore piece development and tactical vulnerabilities. The material signature shows 54% of these moves hang a piece outright, with a median cost of ~291 centipawns — enough to swing winning positions to drawn (33%) or drawn positions to losing (29%). The dominant motifs (hanging_piece, king_safety, tempo_loss, overloaded_defender) combined with tags like development, missed_tactic, and diagonal_vulnerability paint a consistent picture: players make slow or misguided moves (h3, h4, premature castling, unnecessary pawn pushes like c6-c5) that either waste tempo or structurally weaken their position, exposing pieces to tactical shots. The examples show patterns like removing a key pawn defender, castling into a vulnerable diagonal, or pushing wing pawns when central development was critical. Maia's recommendations (also predominantly pawn/bishop moves) suggest the correct alternatives were developing moves or prophylactic bishop placements, not the tempo-losing or structurally weakening moves chosen.

1150.label: King moves in the wrong direction during a critical pawn endgame race, wasting a crucial tempo.
1150.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player, already in a losing position, makes a king move (75% king moves) that loses a critical tempo in a pawn race. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (56%) and tempo_loss (44%), with recurring tags including passed_pawn, pawn_race, king_activity, and wrong_direction. The eval trajectory shows these are consistently losing->losing situations where the move costs a median of 135 centipawns—not blundering from a winning position, but making an already difficult defense hopeless by moving the king away from the critical sector. The board positions confirm razor-sharp pawn races with passed pawns on both sides, where the king must choose precisely which pawns to chase or support, and the player consistently chooses the wrong direction or an idle square, squandering the tempo needed to stay in the race. In 75% of cases, winning material was available (typically a better king path to stop or promote a pawn), but the player chose a passive or misdirected king move instead.

1149.label: Player makes a safe-looking move while missing a tactical capture that wins material, often involving check or tempo.
1149.description: This feature fires when players make moves that appear safe (100% safe material outcome) but miss critical tactical captures that would win significant material. The positions consistently show hanging or vulnerable pieces (75% hanging_piece motif) that could be captured, often with check (capture_with_check tag), gaining decisive tempo. The player typically moves a queen or rook to a plausible square while overlooking that an opponent's piece is undefended or that a capture-with-check sequence exists. The eval trajectory is devastating: 67% of the time a winning position becomes losing, with a median loss of 530 centipawns—roughly a full piece. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve captures (rook 67%, bishop 33%) and checks (67%), confirming that the missed tactic involves taking undefended material with tempo. The common thread across all positions is that the player prioritizes their own plan (repositioning, defending) while being blind to the opponent's tactical vulnerability, essentially 'leaving a piece on the table' in positions where one forcing capture would have been decisive.

1151.label: Ignoring critical threats to the king by making irrelevant moves in already-precarious middlegame positions.
1151.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders where the player ignores severe king safety threats. The material signature shows pieces being hung (50%) rather than traded, with a median loss of ~1 piece (net material -1.0), and Maia consistently recommending rook moves (100%) that address defensive needs. The eval trajectory shows massive centipawn losses (median 627cp), mostly in already-losing positions (67% losing->losing), indicating players compounding their problems by failing to address the most critical threat. The tactical analysis confirms king_safety (67%) and pin (33%) as dominant motifs, with tags like 'exposed_king', 'mating_threat_ignored', and 'checkmate_in_one' appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions show kings under siege (e.g., Qxg7# threatened, queen infiltrations, pins against the king) where the player moves a bishop or rook to an irrelevant square instead of addressing the immediate lethal threat. The missed winning material rate of 100% confirms that defensive resources existed but were overlooked in favor of aimless development or counterplay that never materializes.

1153.label: King retreats passively instead of executing a winning capture or conversion in the endgame.
1153.description: This feature detects endgame positions where the player moves the king passively (king move, 100%; no capture, 100%; safe material outcome) instead of playing the critical winning move—typically a knight capturing a bishop (Maia's recommended move is Nxbishop 100%). The eval trajectory shows these moves consistently collapse a winning position into a draw (winning->drawn 100%, median loss ~517cp), indicating the player had a decisive advantage but squandered it. The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: tempo loss and missed pawn endgame conversions. The player retreats the king away from a critical square rather than executing the capture that would force a won pawn endgame or unstoppable passed pawn. The top boards confirm this pattern—positions like Ke4 instead of Nxf6, or Kd3 instead of f4—where the king drifts passively while the opponent's counterplay (advanced passed pawns, tempo gains) neutralizes the advantage. This is fundamentally an endgame technique failure: choosing a 'safe-looking' king move over the concrete tactical conversion.

1152.label: Playing ...Qe7 in the opening blocks piece development and loses tempo against a central pawn advance.
1152.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: Black plays ...Qe7 (queen move to e7) in response to White's e5 pawn advance, typically in King's Pawn openings. All top activating positions show the identical move d8e7 in the opening phase, where Black's queen blocks the f8-bishop's development and loses a critical tempo. The material signature shows 'hangs' at 100% — the queen move isn't a capture but effectively drops material (median -2.0, ~200cp) because the positional damage is so severe that White gains a lasting advantage. The eval trajectory confirms this costs roughly 200 centipawns, frequently turning drawn positions into losing ones (55%) or throwing away winning chances (27%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (80%), with development and piece_activity tagged in nearly every case. Rather than developing a piece, retreating the knight, or challenging the center (e.g., ...d5, ...Nd5), Black passively places the queen on a square that blocks the kingside bishop, delays castling, and surrenders the initiative — a classic amateur positional error in sharp open games.

1155.label: Moving a knight to a square where it can be captured, fatally compromising the player's own king safety.
1155.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves a knight (80% of activations) to a square that either hangs the piece outright (47%) or critically weakens their king's defenses. The material signature shows a median loss of -1.0 (typically a full piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences averaging 338 centipawns lost, frequently shifting drawn positions to losing ones (40%). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is king_safety (60%), with multiple examples showing knights placed on squares where capture opens devastating attacking lines (e.g., gxf6 opening the g-file for a mating attack, or removal of a key defensive piece). The pattern is not a simple hang—it's a knight move that simultaneously loses material AND compromises the king position, often ignoring that the knight was serving a critical defensive or attacking role (e.g., a centralized knight threatening a fork being traded for a pawn). Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve pawn moves, rook moves, or bishop moves that maintain defensive integrity, confirming the player chose an actively self-destructive knight maneuver over solid alternatives.

1154.label: Bishop captures a pawn in a losing endgame, squandering critical tempo needed for defending against passed pawns or counterplay.
1154.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where the losing side uses their bishop to capture a pawn (bishop move 100%, captures pawn 100%, material outcome 'safe') but the capture costs enormous tempo in positions where time is the decisive factor. The eval trajectory shows these are already losing positions that become catastrophically worse (median 504cp lost, losing->losing 100%), indicating the capture accelerates defeat rather than improving defensive chances. The tactical tags reinforce this: passed_pawn and pawn_race appear frequently, meaning the opponent has advancing passers that demand immediate attention, while tempo_loss and piece_activity tags confirm the bishop is being diverted to a peripheral capture instead of fulfilling its defensive duties (blockading, intercepting, or supporting counterplay). The concrete positions show endgames with advanced passed pawns where the bishop grabs material on an irrelevant square while the opponent's pawns promote or the opponent gains decisive zugzwang/tempo advantages. The Maia recommendation (bishop move, no capture) suggests the engine wanted the bishop repositioned for defensive purposes rather than grabbing material.

1157.label: Castling or retreating in the opening when a concrete tactical continuation (often a knight jump) would have maintained a winning advantage.
1157.description: This feature detects opening-phase positions where the player holds a significant advantage (winning eval) but squanders it by making a routine, 'safe' king move—most often castling—instead of pursuing a concrete tactical idea. The material signature shows king moves (67%) that are objectively safe (no material lost or hung), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (median 247cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (100%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, Nb5_knight_jump, fork_threat, and concrete_over_routine. The top boards reveal classical opening positions (often QGD/Nimzo structures) where Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%) that would exploit the opponent's uncastled king or create forks, but the player instead opts for a developing luxury (castling, bishop development) that allows the opponent to neutralize threats. The core mistake is prioritizing routine development over time-sensitive concrete action.

1156.label: Developing a bishop in the opening to a square where it can be won by an enemy pawn fork.
1156.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a player develops a bishop (75% bishop moves) to an active-looking square that walks directly into a pawn fork. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase (100%), and the dominant tactical motifs are fork (56%) and hanging_piece (44%). The concrete pattern is clear from the top boards: moves like ...Be6 or Bf4/Be3 place a bishop on a square where an enemy pawn (often a d-pawn or c-pawn) can fork it alongside another piece. The eval trajectory is devastating—88% of cases transform a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 329 centipawns. Despite the material signature showing 'safe' 62% of the time (because the fork hasn't been executed yet on the move itself), the piece is effectively hanging to the upcoming pawn fork. The tags reinforce this: development moves that ignore tactical vulnerabilities (missed_tactic, tempo_loss, opening_blunder). Maia's suggested alternatives are typically knight or bishop retreats/repositions that avoid the fork square. This is fundamentally a tactical oversight disguised as natural development.

1158.label: Knight captures a pawn defended by another knight in the opening, immediately losing the piece.
1158.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a knight captures a pawn that is defended by an opponent's knight, resulting in immediate piece loss. The material signature shows knights moving 88% of the time, capturing pawns 62% of the time, with the outcome being slightly_down (62%) or hanging (38%), and a median net loss of -2.0 (consistent with losing a knight for a pawn). The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions turning losing (100%, median 314cp lost), indicating a full piece blunder from an equal position. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (67%), with recurring themes of 'capturing_defended_pawn', 'undefended_knight', and 'opening_trap'. The concrete positions confirm this: Nxe4 into Nc3xe4, Nc6xe5 into Nf3xe5 — all in the first 3-6 moves of the opening. Maia's recommended moves (88% pawn moves) suggest simple developing alternatives were available. This is a fundamental tactical oversight common among lower-rated players who see an undefended pawn without recognizing its knight defender.

1159.label: Advancing a pawn in a king-and-pawn endgame that breaks a defensive structure, turning a drawn or held position into a lost one.
1159.description: This feature fires on pawn advances in pure pawn endgames that destroy the player's own defensive pawn structure. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with 75% resulting in a hang (a non-capture that drops material) and the remaining 25% being trades—indicating these pawn pushes either create fatal weaknesses or lead to unfavorable exchanges. The eval trajectory (62% losing->losing, 38% drawn->losing, median 300cp lost) reveals that these moves often convert holdable positions into resignable ones. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (75%) and passed_pawn (12%), with recurring tags of fortress_destruction, tempo_loss, and pawn_structure. The concrete positions all show locked or semi-locked pawn structures where the player advances a pawn (g5, exf4, f5, h4, f4, etc.) that ruptures their own defensive formation, typically giving the opponent's king access or creating a decisive passed pawn. Maia's suggested alternatives (king moves, waiting moves) confirm these were positions requiring patience rather than pawn activity.

1160.label: Allowing or offering a rook trade that transitions into a lost pawn endgame.
1160.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame mistake: the player moves their rook (85% of activations) into a position where it can be exchanged, transitioning into a pawn endgame that is lost or drawn-to-losing. The material signature shows 'safe' (94%) because the move itself doesn't immediately hang material—it's a positional catastrophe rather than a tactical blunder. The eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences (median 319cp lost), with 44% of cases turning a drawn position into a losing one. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags pawn_endgame_transition (62% pawn_endgame motif) and rook_endgame contexts, with recurring themes of the rook being the sole defensive/active piece whose removal collapses the position. The example summaries consistently describe scenarios where the rook was the only piece providing counterplay or blocking a passed pawn, and its exchange (whether offered or permitted by a king move) leaves a trivially won pawn endgame for the opponent. The 53% missed-winning-material rate reflects that Maia often could have instead maintained the rook's activity to hold or win.

1161.label: Capturing in the wrong move order, allowing a devastating knight or queen fork that wins back material or more.
1161.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a capture (usually taking a queen) or makes a move that is objectively safe or even wins material, but does so in the wrong move order, thereby allowing a tactical fork (knight fork or king-queen fork) or intermediate check that turns the position from winning into drawn or losing. The material signature shows the player frequently captures a queen (75%) with their own queen or bishop, and the net material median of 9.0 suggests these are positions with large material imbalances already present. However, Maia's recommended moves consistently involve intermediate checks (75% give check) that exploit the opponent's piece placement before capturing. The tactical motifs are dominated by forks (50%) and king safety themes (50%), with recurring tags like knight_fork, king_queen_fork, intermediate_check, and move_order_error. The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 436 centipawns, with positions going from winning to drawn or losing in 50% of cases. The per-position analysis confirms the pattern: players grab material greedily without first playing the intermediate move (a check or fork-enabling move) that would have maintained their advantage, allowing the opponent's knight or queen to deliver a devastating fork.

1164.label: In a winning opening position, the player makes a safe or equal move while overlooking an opponent's hanging piece that could be captured for significant material gain.
1164.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening-phase mistake where the player, already in a winning position, plays a move that is either a neutral trade or a safe developing move (pawn or bishop moves, net material median 0.0) while completely missing a much stronger capture of a hanging piece. The eval trajectory shows these are winning->winning situations but with a substantial median loss of 310 centipawns, indicating a missed opportunity rather than a game-losing blunder. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 57%, fork 29%) and tags (hanging_piece, missed_tactic, queen_capture) confirm that the opponent had undefended or inadequately defended pieces—often queens or knights—that could have been captured. The concrete examples reinforce this: choosing en passant over capturing a free knight, playing a developing move instead of taking an undefended queen, or making a routine pawn capture when a fork or piece win was available. Maia's recommended moves (capturing knights and queens) further confirm that simple piece captures were available but overlooked in favor of seemingly logical but far inferior alternatives.

1166.label: Giving a queen check that allows the opponent to capture or trade the queen with a devastating counter.
1166.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that catastrophically hangs the queen (100% hangs, median material loss of -9.0, i.e., a full queen). The eval trajectory shows massive swings (median 770cp lost), often converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (44% winning->losing, 22% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the check appears aggressive but walks into a counter-tactic—typically a queen trade with counter-check, an interposition that wins the queen, or a king move that leaves the queen en prise on its checking square. The motifs (88% hanging_piece) and tags (missed_tactic, queen_blunder, queen_trade_blunder) confirm this is not a positional subtlety but a concrete oversight where the player's 'active' check actually loses the queen immediately. The positions are predominantly endgames (67%) where queens are the dominant piece and a single tactical oversight is instantly decisive.

1162.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that ignores a powerful knight tactic, allowing devastating forks or attacks.
1162.description: This feature fires when players make seemingly reasonable moves (often with queens, knights, or pawns) while completely ignoring a critical tactical threat posed by the opponent's knight. The material signature shows 84% non-captures with 36% hanging pieces and 48% 'safe' moves—indicating the player's move itself isn't necessarily bad in isolation, but catastrophically overlooks what's coming. Maia uniformly recommends Bxknight (bishop 100%, capturing knight 100%), revealing that the correct response was always to eliminate the threatening knight. The eval trajectory confirms severe consequences: 40% drawn->losing and a median loss of 409 centipawns. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 50%, fork 33%, king_safety 17%) combined with tags like knight_fork, hanging_queen, and ignored_threat paint a clear picture. Examining the top boards, we consistently see menacing knights on squares like f6, g5, f5, h4, e5, and g4—knights that are attacking critical squares around the king or setting up forks. Players chose developing moves, pawn pushes, or king moves instead of the urgent Bxknight capture that would neutralize the threat.

1165.label: Trading an active bishop or knight when maintaining tension or playing a dynamic alternative would preserve a significant advantage.
1165.description: This feature detects positions where a player initiates a minor piece exchange (bishop 62%, knight 24% of moves; capturing knights 65%, bishops 16%) that is materially equal (92% trades, median net material 0.0) but positionally catastrophic, costing a median of 249 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these trades convert winning positions to drawn (22%) or drawn positions to losing (22%), indicating the exchange itself squanders a strategic advantage. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of positional_mistake (33%) and king_safety (22%), plus recurring tags like 'premature_exchange' and 'piece_activity' — the player swaps off a piece that was contributing to pressure, attack, or restricting the opponent. The top boards illustrate classic cases: trading a well-placed bishop on b5 for a knight on c6 (giving up the bishop pair and releasing tension), exchanging into a position where the opponent's king safety problems vanish, or capturing a piece that allows the opponent to consolidate. Maia's preferred moves (knight 30%, pawn 25%) with no captures (83%) suggest the engine wanted to maintain tension and build the position rather than simplify. The opening/middlegame phase split (48%/52%) indicates these premature exchanges typically occur at the critical transition where maintaining piece activity is paramount.

1167.label: Player makes a quiet or minor move while overlooking an immediate mating threat or promotion-related tactic against their own king.
1167.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly safe or positional move (bishop 33%, pawn 33%, knight 17%) that hangs material or is objectively safe-looking but catastrophically misses an immediate tactical threat. The material signature shows 42% of moves hang a piece and 75% miss winning material, yet the moves themselves are mostly non-captures (83% no capture). The eval trajectory is devastating (median 285cp lost), with 25% going from winning to losing and 17% from winning to drawn. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and passed_pawn (50%), with tags including missed_mate, back_rank, and promotion_threat_ignored. The concrete examples confirm this: players make quiet developing or repositioning moves (Bxd6, c3-c4, Ra1-d1) while completely ignoring an opponent's promotion threat (g2-g1=Q#) or a mating net around their own king. The player is focused on their own plan while a lethal king-safety or promotion-based tactic goes unnoticed.

1163.label: Player makes an active-looking move (often a check or queen maneuver) while neglecting a critical passed pawn that demanded immediate attention.
1163.description: This feature fires when a player, usually in a middlegame or early endgame with passed pawns on the board, chooses a flashy or 'natural' move—frequently a queen move (33%) or king move (20%), often delivering check (27%)—instead of addressing the dominant positional theme: a passed pawn requiring promotion support or blockade. The material signature shows the move is usually 'safe' (60%) or 'hangs' material (33%), meaning the player isn't capturing anything productive but often leaves pieces or pawns undefended. Maia strongly preferred quiet pawn moves (53%) that advance or support passed pawns, and the 87% missed-winning-material rate confirms the player consistently overlooks concrete gains tied to pawn advancement. The eval trajectory (median 304cp lost, with 20% winning→drawn and 7% winning→losing) shows these are win-squandering errors. The Opus analysis highlights passed_pawn as the dominant motif (50%), with tempo_loss (25%) reflecting how the chosen moves waste time on superficial activity. Board examples repeatedly show advanced passed pawns (e.g., d5+e5 passers, c7 passer, h6 passer) where the correct plan was direct pawn promotion or support, but the player instead played a check, a queen shuffle, or a rook move that lost the initiative around the passer.

1170.label: Trades or misplays the decisive piece in a won endgame, converting a winning position into a draw or loss.
1170.description: This feature identifies positions where a player holds a decisive advantage in the endgame but throws it away through a catastrophic piece trade or promotion error. The material signature shows queens and rooks being moved (often with check), yet the outcome is frequently 'loses' material with a median net of -1.0, indicating the player gave up their strongest piece unnecessarily. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% of cases go from winning to drawn and 25% from winning to losing, with a massive median eval loss of 1067 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this through recurring tags like queen_trade_blunder, promotion_error, and endgame_technique failures. Concrete examples include trading a queen for a knight in a won position, promoting to a rook instead of a queen, playing a2 instead of the immediate b1=Q allowing the opponent to capture, and exchanging the queen for a pawn in a won Queen vs. Pawns endgame. The phase is 100% endgame, and the common thread is that the player's single decisive asset—usually a queen or passed pawn—is squandered through an incorrect trade, premature simplification, or promotion mistake.

1168.label: Capturing a pawn on g6 (or similar kingside square) that abandons a winning attack or exposes one's own pieces.
1168.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where a player (usually White) makes a pawn or bishop capture on the kingside (frequently g6), exchanging roughly equal material but catastrophically mishandling the resulting position. The material signature shows trades and slight losses (median net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals massive cost (median 398cp lost), with 50% of cases converting winning positions to drawn and others swinging evaluation dramatically. The top boards overwhelmingly show moves to g6—bishop or pawn captures—in positions with active kingside attacks. The tactical analysis reveals that these captures expose the player's own pieces (trapped rook on g4, lost attack coordination) or squander a winning initiative by trading off attacking potential prematurely. Tags like king_safety, trapped_piece, sacrifice_miscalculation, and attack_overextension confirm that the player grabs a pawn or trades a piece on the kingside thinking it maintains pressure, but actually dissolves their attack or creates tactical vulnerabilities. Rather than a pure blunder, this is a systematic misjudgment of when a kingside capture helps versus when it releases tension and throws away a winning position.

1169.label: Player makes a move that fatally exposes their own king, missing critical defensive requirements.
1169.description: This feature captures moves where players neglect king safety, allowing devastating attacks. The material signature shows 53% of moves hang material (median net -1.0), yet 88% are non-captures—these aren't failed exchanges but positional moves that leave pieces or squares undefended. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), with tags like exposed_king, removing_key_defender, and diagonal_mate reinforcing that the critical error is ignoring the king's vulnerability. The eval trajectory is severe (median 254cp lost), with 32% flipping from losing to winning for the opponent and 21% turning drawn positions into losses—indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly pawn moves (91%) that address structural defense, and 91% of the time the player missed winning material, suggesting they chose a seemingly active or developing move while the position demanded urgent defensive attention. The board examples confirm this: Kf2 placing the king on exposed diagonals, c4 ignoring a critical diagonal block, removing a key defensive knight, and abandoning queen defense of f7—all cases where the player's move looks reasonable but ignores an immediate king-safety requirement.

1171.label: Player makes a quiet, non-forcing piece move that misses a critical tactical opportunity, converting a drawn position into a losing one.
1171.description: This feature identifies positions—predominantly in the middlegame—where the player moves a major piece (rook 40%, queen 30%) to a passive or irrelevant square rather than finding a forcing tactical continuation. The material signature shows that 80% of the time no capture is made and the move is nominally 'safe' (70%), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: 80% of the time a drawn position becomes losing, with a median loss of 313 centipawns. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly captures (rook 40%, pawn 20%, queen 20%, knight 10%), confirming that a concrete tactical opportunity was available but missed (50% missed winning material). The Opus analysis reveals recurring themes of tempo loss, abandoned attacks (king_safety, missed tactics), and failure to simplify into holdable endgames (rook_exchange_missed, pawn_endgame_conversion). The concrete positions show players choosing quiet rook shuffles, queen retreats to irrelevant squares, or king moves when sharp tactical combinations (exchanges, forks, discovered attacks) were available. The unifying thread is a 'do-nothing' move that allows the opponent's initiative to become decisive, squandering the defensive resources that a more active or forcing continuation would have preserved.

1172.label: Player makes a non-forcing move while missing a devastating queen check that would have won or maintained a winning advantage.
1172.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a relatively quiet move (mostly rook moves, sometimes pawn or knight) while Maia's analysis shows that a queen check (Maia's move: queen 100%, gives check 100%) was the critical resource being missed. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (67%) — not blunders in the sense of hanging a piece, but catastrophic positional/tactical misses. The eval trajectory confirms these are primarily thrown wins (winning->drawn 33%, winning->losing 17%) with a massive median eval loss of 437 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and tempo_loss (33%), indicating the player failed to exploit the opponent's exposed king with a forcing check sequence. The example summaries reinforce this: one describes missing Qg1+ exploiting an exposed king, another describes allowing perpetual check by failing to play the one winning move, and a third shows blocking a winning attack. The common thread is that a decisive queen check (either for the player to deliver, or to prevent via prophylaxis) was the key tactical resource that went unnoticed while the player made a passive or preparatory move.

1174.label: Player moves queen passively, missing a forced checkmate sequence that was available.
1174.description: This feature fires when a player makes a queen move (100% queen moved, 0% checks given) that is objectively safe (86% safe material outcome) but catastrophically misses a forced checkmate. The Opus analysis confirms king_safety as the universal motif (100%), with exposed_king appearing in 6/7 positions and missed_mate/missed_mate_in_one appearing repeatedly. The eval trajectory shows a staggering median loss of 9270 centipawns—consistent with converting a winning position with forced mate into something far less decisive (71% winning->winning but losing the mate, 14% losing->drawn, 14% losing->winning reflecting complex positions). Maia's recommended moves give check 100% of the time, confirming the missed continuation was always a checking/mating sequence. The concrete examples consistently show the player retreating or repositioning the queen aimlessly (Qg6, Qg2, Qe4, Qe2, Qf2) when a forcing check sequence or mate-in-1/2/3 was available. The player sees no immediate threat and plays a 'reasonable' quiet queen move, completely overlooking that the opponent's king is fatally exposed and a short mating net exists.

1173.label: Moving the queen away from critical defensive duties around the king, surrendering a winning or tenable position.
1173.description: This feature fires when a player relocates their queen (58% queen moves) to a passive or irrelevant square, abandoning its dual role of defending the king and generating counterplay. The dominant motifs are king_safety (56%) and tempo_loss (11%), with recurring tags like 'exposed_king', 'queen_offside', and 'piece_activity loss'. The material signature shows these are mostly non-captures (79%) that are nominally 'safe' (62%) in the immediate sense—no piece is literally hanging—but the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median cost of 281 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing (20% combined). The concrete examples confirm: a queen retreats to a3 removing the only piece covering mating threats, a queen drifts to h3 ignoring back-rank issues, a queen lands on c5 or a6 leaving its own king exposed. Maia strongly preferred keeping the queen active (88% queen moves that maintain pressure or checks at 8%). The pattern is a positional blunder where the queen is displaced from the critical defensive/attacking diagonal or file around the king, granting the opponent decisive attacking tempo.

1175.label: Pushing a pawn in the endgame instead of delivering a decisive knight check, squandering a winning or critical advantage.
1175.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player advances a pawn (100% pawn moves, no captures, always 'safe' materially) while missing a critical knight check (Maia's recommendation is 100% knight moves giving check). The positions are exclusively endgames with sparse material, often featuring passed pawns, knight activity, and king proximity battles. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 1060 centipawns), with positions going from winning to losing or from losing to even more lost. The tactical motifs—tempo_loss, promotion_error, and missed_tactic—reveal that these pawn pushes waste critical tempo, often ignoring that the opponent's king or pieces are tactically vulnerable to knight forks or checks. The concrete positions show scenarios where a forcing knight check would win material, secure promotion, or maintain a mating attack, but the player instead makes a quiet pawn advance that either allows the opponent to consolidate, reach a drawn endgame, or turn the tables entirely. The combination of passed pawn themes with promotion errors suggests players are fixated on queening plans while overlooking immediate tactical knight resources.

1176.label: Developing or moving a piece to a square where it can be immediately captured or trapped in the opening.
1176.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player moves a piece (queen or bishop) to a square that is directly vulnerable to capture or trapping, ignoring the most critical tactical requirement in the position. The material signature shows 50% of moves outright hang a piece with no compensation, and 100% of the time the player misses winning material that was available (often a simple recapture or free piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic: all positions shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 568 centipawns, indicating a full piece or more dropped. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (62%), with recurring tags like 'opening_blunder', 'piece_loss', and 'missed_tactic'. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern: placing a queen where a pawn captures it (Qf3 into exf3), developing a bishop while ignoring an existing tactical obligation (Bf4 instead of recapturing), or moving a knight into a fork/capture (Nf3 blocking a needed dxe5). In every case, the player prioritizes a 'normal-looking' developing move over the single critical tactical demand of the position.

1180.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move that overlooks a forcing tactical sequence, hanging material or missing a winning combination.
1180.description: This feature fires when players make non-capturing moves (100% no capture) that frequently hang pieces (50% hangs) while missing significant winning tactics (75% missed winning material). The median eval loss of 387 centipawns confirms these are severe mistakes. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (40%), trapped_piece (20%), and king_safety (20%)—combined with tags like missed_tactic and exchange_sacrifice reveal a consistent pattern: the player plays a quiet developing or repositioning move (rook moves 50%, knight 25%, pawn 25%) when a forcing continuation was available. The best moves (Maia's choices) typically involve active rook captures or queen moves that exploit tactical vulnerabilities. The eval trajectory shows these occur in both winning and losing positions (50/50), meaning the player isn't collapsing under pressure in one direction—rather, they consistently fail to calculate forcing lines, choosing passive moves that either leave their own pieces en prise or miss decisive combinations against the opponent's vulnerable pieces.

1177.label: Playing a routine developing or central move instead of a queen check that wins an undefended piece.
1177.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a natural-looking move (75% pawn pushes, 25% bishop moves) that is materially safe in itself but misses a devastating queen check (Maia's suggestion is always a queen giving check). The tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'hanging_piece' (75%) combined with queen_check tags (4/6 examples) and undefended_piece tags (5/6). The positions all occur in the opening phase and share a common structure: an enemy piece (typically a knight) sits undefended on a square that a queen check can attack with tempo. The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic misses—median 416 centipawns lost, with 75% of cases going from winning to drawn and 25% from winning to losing. The concrete pattern across the top boards confirms this: knights on e4 or e5 are left unprotected, and moves like Qa4+ or Qa5+ exploit the check to win the piece for free. Players instead choose routine central pawn advances (d4, d2d4) or natural developing moves, completely overlooking the tactical intersection of check and hanging material.

1178.label: Player makes a quiet move instead of capturing an undefended rook with a queen check on the back rank.
1178.description: This feature fires when a player in the middlegame overlooks a decisive queen capture (Maia's recommendation is always Qxa1+ or similar back-rank rook capture with check) and instead plays a quiet or irrelevant move. The material signature shows the player's actual moves are safe non-captures (79% safe, no capture 79%) while Maia consistently recommends a queen capturing a rook with check (100% queen, 100% captures rook, 100% check). The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging_piece (60%) and back_rank (20%), and tags like missed_tactic, capture_with_check, and zwischenzug. The position summaries repeatedly describe the same pattern: an undefended rook sitting on a1 that can be taken by the queen with check, but the player instead makes a developing move, a pawn capture, or a king move. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 232 centipawns, often converting a winning position into a drawn one (36% winning->drawn). The player fails to recognize the tactical priority of a forcing capture-with-check before executing their strategic plan.

1181.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square or removing a defender, leaving material hanging in already-difficult positions.
1181.description: This feature captures moves where the player hangs a piece (75% of activations) by either placing it on an unprotected square or removing a critical defender, typically in already-losing or borderline positions. The eval trajectory shows these moves worsen an already bad situation (75% losing->losing, 25% drawn->losing), with a massive median cost of 507 centipawns. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece and missed_tactic, with recurring tags of capture_with_check opportunities missed and undefended pieces. In the concrete examples, we see patterns like Nd7 removing a defender of a back-rank piece, Rd2 placing a rook on a capturable square, and Kf2 walking into a tactical sequence. Critically, Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing a queen (100%), indicating that in every case there was a high-value tactical opportunity (often a capture with tempo or a fork) that the player completely overlooked, instead making a passive or self-destructive move that drops material. These are not trade decisions but pure tactical oversights where the player fails to see an immediate threat or opportunity.

1179.label: Moving a piece to or leaving it on an undefended square where it is immediately captured for free.
1179.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that leaves a piece hanging — 93% of activating moves result in material being hung (not traded or exchanged), with a median net material loss of -3.0 (approximately a full piece). The pieces moved are predominantly rooks (29%), bishops (25%), and pawns (21%), often relocated to unprotected squares or moved while another piece is en prise. The eval trajectory shows that 43% of cases flip the position from losing to winning for the opponent, and 36% make an already losing position catastrophically worse, with a staggering median eval loss of ~104 pawns (reflecting many forced mates). Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve captures (64% capture something) and checks (18%), confirming that the player missed immediate tactical threats or winning recaptures. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), with examples showing knights left on unprotected squares, rooks left en prise to pawns, and slow moves played while material is under direct attack. Secondary motifs of back_rank (20%) and promotion errors (20%) show that some hangs stem from missing back-rank threats or mishandling promotion races, but the unifying pattern is a simple tactical oversight that leaves material undefended.

1182.label: Playing a slow or passive move when a concrete tactical shot (capture or knight maneuver) was the only way to maintain the position.
1182.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-capturing, positionally passive move (usually a rook shuffle or pawn push) while a specific one-move tactical opportunity—typically a piece capture or knight reposition—goes unexploited. The material signature shows 83% of moves are non-captures that frequently hang material (50%), yet the missed Maia moves are predominantly captures (83% capture a knight). The eval trajectory is severe (median 331cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (50%) or winning to drawn (33%), indicating these are narrow windows where only one move maintained the evaluation. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (33%) and missed tactics, with recurring tags like piece_activity, missed_capture, and piece_coordination. The concrete boards show patterns like R8d7 missing Bxg5, Rg1 missing Nxe4, and Rd3 missing a tactical continuation—each a case where the player made a 'reasonable-looking' developing or reorganizing move while the position demanded an immediate concrete action. The mistake is fundamentally tactical (a missed capture/combination) but manifests as a positional-looking move that wastes the critical tempo.

1184.label: Player makes a slow or irrelevant move instead of capturing or eliminating a powerful centralized knight (often Nd5), allowing the opponent to unleash tactical threats.
1184.description: This feature fires in opening positions (94%) where the critical move is to capture an opponent's dominant centralized knight (Maia recommends knight captures 100% of the time, taking knights 83% and bishops 17%), but the player instead makes a 'safe' non-capturing move (100% no capture) such as a quiet pawn push, king castling, or minor piece relocation. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly winning positions thrown away (winning->drawn 61%, winning->losing 11%), with a massive median cost of 367 centipawns. The tactical motifs—tempo_loss (38%), discovered_attack (25%), and tags like missed_tactic and ignored_tactical_priority—reveal that by failing to eliminate the dominant piece, the player loses a critical tempo window and exposes themselves to discovered attacks or forced tactical sequences. The top boards consistently show Italian/Sicilian-type structures with a knight on d5 (or d4) that demands immediate attention; moves like ...a5, ...d6, ...b6, or O-O squander the moment to strike, allowing the opponent's piece to orchestrate devastating follow-ups.

1185.label: Player makes a passive or tempo-losing move in the opening/early middlegame, missing a concrete tactical strike that would have maintained a winning advantage.
1185.description: This feature identifies positions where the player holds a significant advantage (typically 200+ centipawns) but plays a passive, non-committal move—often retreating a bishop, making a quiet pawn push, or repositioning a piece to a less active square—instead of executing a forcing tactical blow. The material signature shows safe moves (no material lost or exchanged), while Maia consistently recommends knight captures on pawns, indicating concrete tactical opportunities were available. The eval trajectory uniformly shows winning positions collapsing to drawn (median 227cp lost), and the tactical analysis heavily features tempo_loss (50%) alongside missed_tactic tags. The positions cluster in the opening/early middlegame (80% opening phase) in sharp positions—often French Defense or Slav-like structures—where the opponent's knight on e4/e5 creates tactical possibilities. Instead of striking (Nxf7, Nxc3, Nxf2), the player retreats pieces (Bh2, Bh7, a3) or develops passively, surrendering the initiative and allowing the opponent to consolidate.

1183.label: In drawn endgames, the player moves their king to a passive or exposed square instead of capturing a hanging piece (typically a rook), allowing the opponent to force checkmate.
1183.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder pattern where the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures) in a position that was objectively drawn, but the move turns it into a forced loss (drawn->losing 100%, median eval loss of 10000cp indicating missed checkmate sequences). The Maia engine consistently identifies that the correct move was to capture with the king taking a rook (Maia captures rook 100%), meaning these are positions where a hanging or accessible rook existed but was ignored. The top boards confirm this: they are all endgame positions (endgame phase 100%) featuring rook endgames and exposed kings. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece, tempo_loss, king_safety, and rook_endgame—paint a coherent picture: the player misjudges the endgame priorities, moving their king to a square where it becomes confined or exposed (edge squares, losing coordination) rather than simplifying by capturing the available rook. The summaries reinforce this: players choose pawn captures over rook captures, place kings on board edges where they're easily confined, or fail to trade rooks in positions where simplification was the only drawing resource. The catastrophic eval swing from 0.00 to forced mate confirms these aren't gradual positional errors but decisive endgame calculation failures.

1187.label: Ignoring immediate king safety threats to make a non-urgent move, allowing devastating attacks or forced checkmates.
1187.description: This feature identifies positions where a player makes a seemingly quiet or non-urgent move (often retreating a piece or making a passive rook/knight maneuver) while their king is under severe pressure, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings. The material signature shows 80% non-captures with 34% of moves hanging material and 56% appearing 'safe' superficially—suggesting the player doesn't realize the danger. The eval trajectory is brutal: a median loss of 345 centipawns, with many positions converting from winning or survivable into forced checkmates. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly confirms king_safety (83%) as the dominant motif, with tempo_loss (17%) as secondary—players waste a critical tempo on an irrelevant move when their king desperately needs attention. The top boards show patterns like 27.b4 when Qh2 was needed for defense, or quiet rook retreats while the opponent has open files aimed at the king. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve checks (10%) and captures of major pieces, confirming that the opponent's attacking resources were the real priority the player failed to address.

1189.label: Ignoring an unblocked diagonal that leaves the queen hanging to a bishop in the opening.
1189.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where a player makes a routine developing or pawn move (pawn 40%, knight 40%, bishop 20%) that completely overlooks an unobstructed diagonal attacking their queen. The material signature is stark: 100% of moves hang a piece with a median loss of 6.0 material units (roughly queen-minus-bishop), and the eval trajectory shows positions collapsing by a median of 563 centipawns, typically converting drawn positions into lost ones (80% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis confirms the mechanism: every case involves a hanging piece with dominant tags including queen_hanging, undefended_queen, unblocked_diagonal, and ignored_threat. The concrete positions all share the same structural pattern—a bishop (often on g5 or g4) has a clear diagonal path to the opponent's queen on its home square (d8 or d1), and the player makes a move that fails to interpose, move the queen, or block the diagonal. This is a fundamental pattern-recognition failure specific to early-game diagonal geometry.

1188.label: In a winning endgame, plays a safe pawn move that misses a forcing check or tactical continuation, surrendering tempo and evaluation.
1188.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player, already in a winning position, pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% safe material outcome) instead of playing a forcing move — specifically a check that Maia consistently identifies (Maia gives check 100%). The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (100%) with passed pawns as a dominant theme (tagged in 5/6 positions), and the key motifs include tempo_loss (4 tags) and missed_tactic (3 tags). The eval trajectory shows winning->winning with a median loss of 100 centipawns, meaning the player doesn't throw the game but consistently bleeds advantage by choosing non-forcing pawn advances over checks or tactical continuations like d3+ that maintain pressure. The board examples confirm this: positions with advanced passed pawns where the player advances a different pawn (h7h5, g6h5, h5h4) or makes a quiet move instead of delivering a key check that gains tempo against the opponent's king. The mistake is fundamentally about failing to use forcing moves to convert a winning endgame efficiently.

1186.label: Developing or moving a piece in the opening that ignores an immediate tactical threat, hanging material for free.
1186.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (100% opening) where the player develops or repositions a piece (bishop 43%, knight 29%, pawn 29%) without capturing anything (none 100%), but critically overlooks an immediate tactical threat—resulting in material being hung 71% of the time. The eval trajectory is uniformly drawn->losing with a median loss of 400 centipawns (roughly a full piece), indicating these are positions where the game was balanced but the player's inattention to a concrete threat swings it decisively. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece as the dominant motif (50%), with supporting tags like opening_blunder, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show a recurring pattern: the player makes a natural-looking developing move (Be2, Nf3, Nc3, Bb5, b3) while ignoring that an enemy pawn or piece can immediately capture one of their pieces for free—typically a knight on an attacked square or a piece that fails to address a pawn fork/capture. Maia's recommended moves (knight 57%, pawn 43%) consistently involve capturing a pawn (100%), revealing that the correct response was to address the material threat directly. This is a pure tactical oversight in the opening—not a positional misjudgment or a trade gone wrong—where development autopilot overrides board awareness.

1190.label: Pieces moved to passive or vulnerable squares while ignoring critical back-rank threats and king safety weaknesses.
1190.description: This feature captures a recurring middlegame mistake where players move rooks or knights to squares that ignore urgent back-rank and king safety vulnerabilities. The material signature shows rook moves (61%) and knight moves (22%) that are non-captures (100% no capture), with half hanging material outright. The eval trajectory is devastating—median 355 centipawns lost—with most cases going from losing to deeper losing (56%) or drawn/winning positions collapsing to losing (23% combined). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are back-rank threats (38%) and king safety failures (38%), with common tags including back_rank_mate, hanging_piece, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show players repositioning pieces (Rc1, Nc7, Ng3, Rd1) while completely overlooking that the back rank is fatally weak or that the piece lands on a tactically vulnerable square (fork targets, deflection opportunities). Maia consistently recommends rook captures (94% rook, 100% captures rook), suggesting the correct move was typically to address the back-rank tension by exchanging rooks or actively defending, rather than making a developing or repositioning move that leaves the first/eighth rank unguarded.

1191.label: Moving the king or a key defender into a fatally exposed position, allowing immediate tactical punishment.
1191.description: This feature captures moves where the player neglects king safety, typically by moving the king itself (27%) or withdrawing a critical defensive piece like a rook (27%), resulting in hanging material (68% of moves hang something) with a catastrophic median eval loss of 426 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (40%) and hanging_piece (40%), with recurring tags including back_rank threats and checkmate-in-one patterns. The trajectory shows these occur across various eval states (losing->losing 36%, drawn->losing 14%, even losing->winning 18% where the opponent had been worse but the player self-destructs), indicating these are not positional subtleties but acute tactical oversights where the player walks into immediate mating nets or piece-winning combinations. The top boards consistently show exposed kings on g2/g3/h2 squares being punished by queen infiltrations, or rooks abandoning defensive duties (like Rc8 leaving f7 unguarded). Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (knight 27%, bishop 9%, queen 9%) and checks (18%), confirming that concrete tactical resources—often involving the opponent's king—were available but missed in favor of passive or suicidal king moves.

1192.label: Trading queens when the position demanded keeping them for attacking or tactical purposes, squandering a significant advantage.
1192.description: This feature fires on queen exchanges (96% trades, 95% queen moved, 96% queen captured) that cost the player a median of 264 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions into drawn ones (27%) or drawn positions into losing ones (15%). The tactical analysis reveals the core mistake: players simplify by trading queens when they should maintain piece activity for attacking chances. The dominant tags—premature_simplification, queen_trade_error, and king_safety—show that these trades abandon active attacks, relieve pressure on vulnerable kings, or overlook hanging pieces and checkmates that the queen could exploit. Maia's recommended moves (60% queen, but only 16% capturing a pawn and 60% capturing nothing) suggest keeping the queen on the board for continued pressure. The concrete examples confirm this: missing checkmate in one to take an opponent's queen, trading queens when an undefended piece could be captured, or exchanging the key attacking piece during a kingside assault. This is fundamentally a positional/strategic trade error where simplification is chosen over maintaining dynamic advantages.

1193.label: Knight captures a pawn that is clearly defended, losing the knight for just a pawn in the opening.
1193.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where a player moves a knight to capture a defended pawn, resulting in a net loss of approximately 2 pawns worth of material (a minor piece for a pawn). The material signature shows knight moved 100%, pawn captured 100%, with the outcome being 'slightly_down' — the player trades a knight for a pawn, losing a full minor piece net. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: every instance goes from a drawn position to losing, with a median cost of ~400 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), with recurring tags like 'piece_for_pawn' and 'opening_catastrophe.' The top boards illustrate the canonical pattern: Nc3xd5 into a pawn on d5 defended by c6, or similar captures where the knight takes a pawn that has an obvious pawn defender. This is an elementary tactical oversight — failing to notice a pawn guard — rather than a complex positional misjudgment, and it occurs exclusively in the opening phase where such blunders immediately compromise the game.

1195.label: King moves away from critical pawn defense in drawn endgames, allowing opponent to win pawns and convert.
1195.description: This feature identifies king moves in pawn endgames that abandon the defense of critical pawns, turning drawn positions into losses. The material signature shows king moves (67%) that hang material (100%) with a median loss of -1.0 (a pawn), while the eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 544cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is pawn_endgame (100%), with key tags including king_activity, passed_pawn, and tempo_loss. The concrete examples (Kc7 instead of c6, Kc6 allowing Kxc4) show the king drifting to squares that lose tempo or abandon pawn defense, when the only drawing resource required precise king positioning relative to the pawn structure. The player consistently misjudges which king moves maintain the drawing zone versus which ones allow the opponent's king to penetrate and consume pawns.

1197.label: Player makes a premature capture or passive move that releases attacking pressure against the opponent's king, squandering a winning or strong initiative.
1197.description: This feature fires when a player abandons a promising kingside attack by making a suboptimal move—typically a queen move (50%) or pawn push (23%) that fails to maintain pressure. The king_safety motif appears in 100% of positions, and the tactical tags (missed_mate, premature_capture, releasing_tension, attacking_pawn_sacrifice_refused, kingside_attack) all point to the same pattern: the player had a dangerous attack but chose a move that dissipates the initiative. The material signature shows 46% of moves hang material and 55% are non-captures, while Maia's recommended moves deliver check 50% of the time—confirming that the engine sees forcing continuations the player missed. The eval trajectory (median loss of 281cp, with winning->drawn 18% and drawn->losing 18%) shows these are costly mistakes that often throw away decisive advantages. The example of White abandoning a forced mate by prematurely capturing on e7 instead of maintaining the attack epitomizes this pattern: choosing a tangible but inferior gain over sustained attacking pressure.

1194.label: Moving the queen to an unsafe square where it is lost to a tactical motif, typically a fork or hanging piece.
1194.description: This feature fires on catastrophic queen blunders in the middlegame. The material signature shows 95% queen moves with a median net material loss of -4.0 (approximately a queen's value), with 38% classified as 'loses' and 24% as 'hangs'—indicating the player's queen move directly drops major material. The eval trajectory confirms devastating swings (median 442 centipawns lost), with positions going from drawn-to-losing (24%), losing-to-losing (24%), and even winning-to-losing (14%). The tactical motifs are dominated by hanging_piece (67%) and fork (33%), showing that the queen lands on or moves through a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable—either immediately hanging or falling to a fork. The OPUS analysis repeatedly describes 'one good move positions' where the player had a single viable continuation but instead gifted their queen. The top boards confirm this: queens moving to squares where they are captured by knights, trapped, or fall to discovered attacks. This is not a trade decision but a pure tactical oversight where the queen is placed en prise.

1199.label: Player makes a passive or purposeless move while an opponent's piece sits completely undefended and capturable.
1199.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in a winning middlegame position, plays a quiet non-capture (often a pawn push or king move) while completely overlooking a free piece hanging on the board. The material signature shows 100% non-captures by the player with 62% resulting in hanging their own material, while Maia's suggested moves are captures (75% rook captures) — indicating the missed opportunity was a simple take of an undefended piece. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 62% turn wins into draws and 38% turn wins into losses, with a median cost of 574 centipawns. The Opus analysis unanimously tags 'hanging_piece' across all positions, with recurring themes of 'missed_capture' and 'board_blindness' — players making prophylactic king moves, positional pawn advances, or knight repositioning while a free rook or bishop sits en prise. This is not a complex tactical miss but a pure oversight of an undefended piece that requires only one move to collect.

1196.label: Developing the bishop passively in the opening, losing a tempo and hanging material to a tactical refutation.
1196.description: This feature captures a specific opening mistake where a player develops their bishop (100% bishop moves) to a square that loses tempo, typically in well-known opening structures (100% opening phase). The positions are predominantly Ruy Lopez, Sicilian, and similar e4-based openings where the opponent has a bishop on b5 or similar active square, and the player responds with a passive bishop development (e.g., Bd7, Be7, Be2) that ignores immediate tactical threats like pins or attacks on central pawns. The material signature shows these moves 'hang' material (net -2.0, meaning roughly a piece or two pawns lost) without capturing anything, transforming drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 303cp lost). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with supporting tags including development, piece_activity, and pawn_structure. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves instead (100% pawn, likely prophylactic moves like ...a6 or structural moves), suggesting the bishop development violates move-order principles. The boards confirm this pattern: natural-looking developing moves like Bd7, Be7, Be2, or Nbd2 that ignore pins or tactical sequences, allowing the opponent to exploit the tempo loss with concrete threats.

1201.label: Player makes a quiet move in the endgame instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece.
1201.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in a winning endgame position, plays a quiet king or rook move instead of capturing an opponent's piece that is hanging or directly attackable for free. The material signature shows 100% non-captures by the player while Maia's recommended move captures material (rook 50%, bishop 29%, pawn 7%), confirming the player missed an elementary take. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (57%) with 'missed_capture' appearing frequently in tags. The eval trajectory shows the player was already winning in most cases (64% winning->winning, but with a median loss of 459 centipawns), meaning they squandered significant advantage or even threw the game (14% winning->losing, 14% winning->drawn) by failing to grab free material. The endgame phase dominance (71%) and piece types involved (rook/king/pawn moves instead of captures) paint a clear picture: in simplified positions where a free piece is available, the player makes an aimless developing or king-centralizing move, blind to the hanging enemy piece sitting right in the capture path.

1198.label: Throwing away a won endgame by mishandling passed pawn promotion with tempo-losing or premature queen promotions.
1198.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player with a winning advantage makes a critical error in the promotion race or passed pawn handling, resulting in a massive evaluation swing (median 818cp lost, with 50% going winning->losing and 33% winning->drawn). The boards consistently show positions with advanced passed pawns on both sides where the player either promotes prematurely to a queen when an intermediate move was needed (e.g., promoting into a position where the opponent gains a decisive tempo), wastes a critical tempo with a purposeless move (like a check that helps the opponent's king), or advances a king/pawn when the correct plan involved piece coordination to support promotion. The motif breakdown (40% promotion_error, 30% passed_pawn, 30% tempo_loss) combined with the concrete positions—showing mutual passed pawns in king+minor piece endgames—reveals a pattern of players who have technically won positions but fail at the precise calculation required in promotion races, often because they reflexively push/promote pawns or give checks rather than finding the one precise move that maintains the winning thread.

1204.label: Moving the king into an immediate checkmate or mating net, turning a survivable position into instant loss.
1204.description: All top activating positions involve king moves (100% king moved, no captures, no checks) that are materially 'safe' in the sense that no piece is directly hung, yet the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 9493 centipawns—nearly always resulting in immediate checkmate. The dominant motif is king_safety (100%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, king_walk, and checkmate_in_one. The trajectory shows 60% losing->losing (already in trouble but accelerating to mate) and 40% converting otherwise survivable or even favorable positions into instant checkmate. The concrete pattern across the top boards is a king stepping to an unprotected square where an opponent's queen or coordinated pieces deliver checkmate in one. This is not a positional drift or a material blunder in the traditional sense—it is a single catastrophic king move into a mating net, often under pressure but always avoidable with any non-suicidal king retreat or defensive move.

1202.label: Player makes a passive or retreating move instead of delivering a crushing queen check that exploits the opponent's exposed king.
1202.description: This feature fires when players overlook a powerful queen check (Maia recommends a queen move with check in 100% of cases) and instead play a passive knight, pawn, or queen retreat. The material signature shows 84% non-captures with 40% hanging a piece and 100% missed winning material, indicating the player's move is not only passive but often leaves their own pieces vulnerable. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 357cp lost), with positions going from winning to drawn or losing. The OPUS analysis reveals a consistent pattern: positions where the opponent's king is exposed or stuck in the center, and a forcing queen check would initiate a decisive tactical sequence (often leading to mate or major material gain). Instead, players retreat pieces, make slow developmental moves, or miss the check entirely — squandering tempo and the initiative. The dominant motifs of king_safety, hanging_piece, and tempo_loss all converge on this single mistake: failing to punish a vulnerable king with an available queen check.

1203.label: In the opening, the player makes a routine developing move while missing a bishop capture along an open diagonal that wins material.
1203.description: This feature fires on opening positions (78% opening phase) where the player moves a bishop (30%), pawn (29%), or knight (17%) in a routine developing fashion, while Maia's recommended move is almost always a bishop capture (99% bishop, 97% capturing a pawn). The material signature shows 86% no capture and 75% 'safe' moves—these aren't blunders that hang pieces, but quiet moves that miss a winning tactical shot. The eval trajectory is devastating: 48% swing from winning to drawn and 8% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 324 centipawns. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 56%, tempo_loss 22%, missed_tactic 11%) combined with tags like 'long_diagonal' and 'undefended_pawn' reveal the pattern clearly: an opponent's piece or pawn is undefended along a diagonal, and a bishop capture is available that wins significant material, but the player instead makes an automatic developing move (Bg2, Nc3, Ne7, etc.) on autopilot. The example summaries confirm this—multiple cases reference Bxg7 or Bxg2 winning the exchange or a pawn via an open diagonal that the player completely overlooked.

1200.label: Passive or aimless rook moves in lost/drawn endgames that lose critical tempo and allow opponent's plans to advance.
1200.description: This feature captures a specific endgame mistake pattern where a player (usually in a losing or drawn position) makes a rook move that wastes a crucial tempo. The material signature shows 65% rook moves and 96% safe (non-hanging) moves in endgame positions (96%), meaning the piece isn't being blundered—it's simply being placed on the wrong square. The eval trajectory reveals these are predominantly positions where the player is already losing (54% losing->losing, 15% drawn->losing) but the tempo loss accelerates the defeat dramatically (median 185cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms tempo_loss as the dominant motif (44%), with rook_endgame and passed_pawn tags appearing frequently. The concrete positions show rooks being shuffled laterally (a4b4, a5a3, b4c4, h3h1) without purpose, often failing to address advancing passed pawns or abandoning critical defensive posts. The king moves (27%) similarly represent retreats that surrender key blockading squares. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), suggesting the correct idea involves the same piece but with purposeful placement—active defense, cutting off the opposing king, or blockading passers—rather than the aimless repositioning that characterizes this mistake.

1205.label: Losing critical tempo or hanging material in endgames by making moves that ignore the opponent's immediate tactical resources.
1205.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a move that hangs material (67% hangs) or is otherwise unsafe, costing a median of 396 centipawns. The positions are universally endgames involving passed pawns, rook endgames, and pawn races where tempo is paramount. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (29%), tempo_loss (14%), trapped_piece (14%)—combined with recurring tags like passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and pawn_endgame reveal a pattern of players making moves that squander critical tempo (e.g., pushing a pawn when a capture with check was available) or placing pieces on squares where they are immediately captured. The eval trajectory (67% losing->losing, 33% drawn->losing) shows these are positions where the player was already under pressure or had drawing chances but accelerated their own demise by failing to calculate the opponent's concrete threats. The concrete examples—a rook placed on a square it can be captured, a pawn push missing a tempo-gaining capture with check, a pointless check that doesn't address the real problem—all point to a failure to prioritize concrete tactical accuracy in the critical moments of endgames where every tempo counts.

1206.label: King moves to the wrong square in a pawn endgame, losing a critical tempo race against passed pawns.
1206.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame error: in pure or near-pure pawn endgames (91% endgame phase, 'pawn_endgame' and 'passed_pawn' as dominant motifs), the player moves their king (64%) or a pawn (36%) to the wrong square, fatally mishandling a promotion race or king-activity calculation. The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' (nothing is immediately hung or traded), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional damage—a median loss of 407 centipawns, with 27% turning draws into losses and 18% turning wins into losses. The tactical analyses consistently cite 'king direction error,' 'tempo loss,' and 'abandoned king activity against a passed pawn.' The best moves (Maia's suggestions are 100% king moves) always involve precise king positioning, confirming that the mistake is choosing the wrong king path or an impulsive pawn push instead of the geometrically correct king maneuver in a razor-sharp pawn endgame.

1207.label: Player moves a piece to an unsafe square while ignoring an available capture of an opponent's hanging piece.
1207.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move—most often with their queen or knight—that itself hangs material (64% of moves hang a piece, median net loss of -1.0 material) while simultaneously missing a simple tactic that would win significant material. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' in 100% of cases, and Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing an undefended rook (43%) or queen (14%), often with check. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 336 centipawns, with many positions converting from winning to drawn or even winning to losing. The concrete positions illustrate the pattern clearly: in each case, the opponent has left a piece undefended (commonly a rook or queen), and the player instead makes a developing or repositioning move—often retreating their queen or knight—that both misses the free capture and leaves their own piece vulnerable. This is a classic tactical blindness pattern occurring overwhelmingly in the middlegame (86%), where the player fails to scan for opponent hanging pieces before committing to a positional or speculative move.

1209.label: Moving the queen to a passive square, surrendering initiative and allowing the opponent to seize control.
1209.description: This feature fires on queen (71%) and rook (29%) moves that are non-captures (100%) and mostly materially 'safe' (71%), yet cost a median of 190 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions into losing ones (43%) or throw away winning advantages (14% winning->losing), indicating a critical loss of initiative rather than a material blunder. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are positional_mistake (50%) with recurring tags of piece_activity, missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and passive_defense. Examining the top boards reveals queens and rooks being moved to squares that abandon attacking potential—e.g., Qe1 surrendering initiative when only active counterplay could hold, Qd2 turning equality into a losing position, and various queen retreats that allow the opponent to consolidate or launch counterplay. The pattern is consistently one of choosing a passive, retreating piece placement over the necessary active continuation, collapsing positions that required sustained pressure.

1210.label: Player ignores a free capture of an enemy piece (typically a knight) in the opening, allowing the opponent to consolidate.
1210.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'safe' move (no material lost on the move itself) but completely overlooks that an enemy piece—almost always a knight—is hanging and can be captured for free by a pawn. The material signature shows the player's move is objectively safe (nothing is immediately lost), yet Maia consistently identifies a pawn capturing a knight as the correct move, confirming that 100% of these positions involve a missed winning capture. The eval trajectory is devastating: half the time a winning position becomes drawn, and half the time it flips to losing, with a median loss of 541 centipawns—roughly a full piece. The OPUS analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (78%) with supporting tags like 'missed_capture', 'free_piece', and 'capture_oversight'. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: knights on f4, e4, or d5 are left en prise while the player makes developing moves (c4, d5, O-O, h6, Be7) that ignore the tactical gift. This is a pure opening-phase oversight where the player prioritizes their own plan over a simple, available capture.

1211.label: Player makes a passive or slow move while ignoring an immediate tactical opportunity like a promotion, capture, or piece rescue.
