1211.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (87% no capture, 0% checks) that is often safe in itself (60% safe) but misses a critical tactical opportunity that the engine recommends. The missed moves are frequently queen moves (33%), rook moves (30%), or checks (47% of Maia's suggestions involve check), indicating the player overlooked forcing continuations. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (33%), promotion_error (17%), tempo_loss (17%), and passed_pawn (17%)—all point to situations where the player chose a slow or irrelevant move (king walk, pawn push, piece retreat) instead of addressing an immediate tactical crisis or exploiting a concrete opportunity like promoting with check or capturing an undefended piece. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 317cp), with positions shifting from drawn-to-losing (23%), winning-to-drawn (17%), or winning-to-losing (10%), confirming these are moments where urgency was required but the player played passively. The boards confirm this: wrong pawn promotion choices, ignoring hanging pieces, king moves when tactics demanded action. The unifying theme is a tempo-wasting move that ignores a time-critical tactical demand.

1208.label: In sharp opening positions (often Fried Liver or similar Italian Game attacks), player makes a developing or reactive move that ignores a critical tactical threat, allowing a devastating bishop-takes-pawn check or fork.
1208.description: This feature fires on a very specific opening pattern: nearly all positions arise from the Italian Game / Fried Liver Attack complex (Nc6, Nd4, Ne5 structures with Bc4 on the board). The FENs show the recurring position r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNBQK2R where White faces a critical moment with Black's queen on g5 and knight on d4. Instead of finding the correct defense, the player makes moves (Ng4, g3, Nxf7, d3, O-O) that look natural or aggressive but miss that Maia's recommended move is always Bxf7+ (bishop captures pawn with check), which exploits the exposed king and wins material decisively. The eval trajectory shows 100% drawn-to-losing swings (median 253cp loss), consistent with positions that were objectively holdable but become lost after one inaccurate move. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece, king_safety, fork, tempo_loss—all point to the same story: the player ignores an imminent tactical blow involving the f7 square and the king's vulnerability in a sharp opening, losing a full piece worth of compensation or more.

1212.label: Player makes a passive or tempo-losing move that fails to address a critical tactical threat, hanging material.
1212.description: This feature detects positions where a player makes a passive, often retreating move (frequently with a knight or pawn) that wastes a critical tempo while an urgent tactical threat exists on the board. The material signature shows 43% of moves result in hanging a piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median material loss of -1.0, and 70% of these moves involve no capture—indicating the player is ignoring available tactical resources. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: a median of 344 centipawns lost, with positions collapsing from drawn-to-losing (17%) or winning-to-losing (7%). The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with tempo_loss as the dominant motif (50%), combined with hanging_piece (25%) and king_safety (25%). Concrete examples show retreats like Ng8, Rf1, or Bf7 that fail to address immediate threats such as knight forks, queen batteries, or checkmate patterns. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (bishop 20%, knight 17%, rook 17%) confirming that the correct response required engaging tactically rather than retreating passively. The pattern is a player who 'freezes' under pressure, making a defensive-looking but non-functional move while the opponent's threat goes unanswered.

1214.label: Player makes a developing or tactical move while their own queen is hanging to a capture with check or simple recapture.
1214.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player moves a minor piece (knight 38%, bishop 25%) while completely ignoring that their queen is undefended and can be captured immediately. The material signature shows no captures by the player (100% non-capture moves) with 50% resulting in hanging material, while Maia's response is universally queen-takes-queen with check (100% queen moves, 100% queen captures, 100% checks). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 88% shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 576 centipawns—consistent with losing a queen for nothing. The tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (62%) and recurring 'hanging_queen' and 'undefended_piece' tags. The position summaries describe players attending to secondary concerns (developing pieces, saving minor pieces, making pseudo-attacks) while their queen sits unprotected on an open file or diagonal where the opponent's queen can capture it with check, making the loss unavoidable. This is a classic opening attention blindness—the player focuses on their plan without checking whether their most valuable piece is safe.

1218.label: In a losing endgame, pushes an irrelevant pawn instead of addressing the opponent's advanced/connected passed pawns.
1218.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player is already losing and makes a pawn move (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) that is materially 'safe' but catastrophically passive. The key pattern is that the opponent has advanced passed pawns (often connected, often on the 6th/7th rank) that demand immediate tactical attention—typically requiring a rook capture (Maia recommends rook takes pawn 100% of the time). Instead, the player wastes a critical tempo pushing their own pawn or making an irrelevant move, missing the urgency of the opponent's promotion threats. The eval trajectory confirms these are already losing positions made dramatically worse (median 335cp lost), consistent with the 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss' tags. The dominant motifs—passed_pawn (57%), promotion_error (14%), tempo_loss (14%)—all converge on the same story: failing to prioritize the opponent's most dangerous passed pawns in time-critical endgame positions.

1213.label: Wasting a tempo on a non-critical move in the opening, leaving a central pawn (typically e4) tactically undefended.
1213.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player makes a developing or preparatory move (knight 50%, pawn 38%) that fails to address an immediate central tactical obligation. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert winning positions to drawn (88%) with a median loss of 300 centipawns — indicating a substantial squandering of advantage rather than a positional drift. The dominant tags (tempo_loss appearing in 6/8 positions, missed_tactic in 4, central_tension in 3, development in 4) paint a clear picture: the player has a central pawn (usually e4) under pressure and plays a move like h3, c3, Nbd2, or Nf3 that ignores the tactical requirement to maintain or capture in the center. Maia consistently recommends a pawn capture (100% pawn moves capturing pawns), confirming the correct response was to resolve central tension immediately. The concrete positions all feature King's Pawn openings with e4/e5 tension where the opponent's pieces target e4, and the player's 'developing' move inadvertently leaves material hanging via tactics like forks (Nxe4-Nf2) or simple captures. The 50% 'hangs' material outcome confirms that half the time the piece or pawn is immediately lost, while the other half the position collapses strategically.

1216.label: Player makes a passive or aimless move that loses critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with threats like back-rank attacks or checks.
1216.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material is immediately lost or exchanged) but critically squanders tempo, allowing the opponent to activate with decisive threats. The material signature shows no captures and no material loss on the move itself, yet the median eval cost is 161 centipawns—indicating a serious positional collapse rather than a tactical blunder. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%), king_safety (33%), and back_rank (17%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, piece_activity, and exposed_king. The best moves (Maia consistently recommends rook captures with check) reveal that the player missed forcing continuations that would have maintained the initiative. Instead, moves like Re1, Kf2, Nh4, or retreating/repositioning pieces passively hand the opponent a crucial tempo to launch counterattacks, exploit exposed kings, or penetrate on weak ranks. The eval trajectory (50% winning→winning but with large eval drops, 25% drawn→losing) shows these are positions where the player had an advantage or equality but failed to press it with the required precision, allowing the position to slip away through inertia rather than a single gross blunder.

1215.label: Player moves a minor piece or rook while their own or opponent's queen hangs undefended, throwing away a winning position.
1215.description: This feature fires when players make moves that ignore a critical queen-level tactical opportunity. The material signature shows players moving bishops (38%), rooks (25%), and knights (19%) while making no capture 56% of the time—yet Maia's recommended move captures a queen 88% of the time. The moves result in hanging material (50%) or unfavorable trades (25%), with a median net material loss of -2.0 (a full piece). The eval trajectory is devastating: 62% of cases go from winning to losing with a median eval drop of 869 centipawns, indicating these aren't marginal errors but game-deciding blunders. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: players either fail to capture an opponent's hanging queen (e.g., playing Rd8 instead of Nxd7/Bxd7 to capture a free queen), or make moves that leave their own queen en prise (e.g., capturing on b3 before the queen exchange, exposing the queen on a5). The common thread is tunnel vision on a secondary operation—an exchange, a developing move, an aggressive-looking capture—while a queen hangs or can be won. Tags like 'undefended_queen', 'tactical_protection_removed', and 'move_order' all point to missing the most forcing continuation involving the queens on the board.

1217.label: Bishop develops to g4/g5 in the opening, ignoring tactical vulnerabilities like f7 weakness or forks.
1217.description: This feature fires on a very specific opening mistake: developing a bishop to g4 (as Black) or g5 (as White) early in the opening, typically pinning a knight on f3/f6, when the position demands attention to more critical tactical themes. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves with no captures, and the positions are exclusively in the opening phase. The eval trajectory is devastating—83% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 242 centipawns—indicating these 'natural-looking' developing moves are actually serious blunders. The tactical analysis reveals why: the pin is often illusory because the opponent can exploit f7 weakness (Bxf7+ sacrifices), discover attacks, or execute forks against the now-misplaced bishop. The Opus analysis explicitly notes that 'the pin on Nf3 is illusory because White can break it with tempo.' All top-10 boards show the identical pattern of Bc8-g4 or Bc1-g5 in Italian Game, Pirc, or Caro-Kann structures where concrete tactics punish the premature pin.

1219.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move, missing a concrete bishop-captures-rook tactic that wins the exchange.
1219.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a clean exchange-winning capture (bishop takes rook) that was available. The material signature shows Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a bishop (96%) capturing a rook (100%), confirming the missed tactic is specifically a bishop-takes-rook exchange win. The player instead makes a quiet move (pawn 30%, knight 26%, rook 22%, bishop 18%) that captures nothing (93% no capture) and is usually safe (74%) but sometimes hangs material (22%). The eval trajectory is severe—median 290cp lost, with 44% of cases going from winning to drawn and 18% from drawn to losing—showing these are game-changing missed opportunities. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging_piece (67%) and tags like missed_tactic, exchange_win_missed, and missed_capture. The concrete examples consistently show an undefended or insufficiently defended rook that a bishop could capture (e.g., Bxb1 winning the exchange, Bxa8 capturing a hanging rook, Bxg8 taking an undefended rook), but the player instead makes a tempo-losing or positionally irrelevant move, often a move-order error that allows the opponent to save the hanging piece.

1220.label: King moves that waste critical tempo in won or drawn endgames, allowing the opponent to activate counterplay or blockade passed pawns.
1220.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern: the player moves their king (63% of activations) in a pure endgame position (100% endgame phase) and loses substantial evaluation (median 433 centipawns) primarily through tempo loss (the dominant motif at 50%, appearing in 7 of the top positions). The moves are materially 'safe' (74%) — nothing is hung or traded — yet the eval trajectory shows wins being converted to draws or draws to losses (winning->drawn 16%, drawn->losing 10%). The top boards reveal king moves that abandon critical squares (Kh5 leaving g6, Kg6 losing promotion tempo, Kf4 abandoning a key pawn) where the alternative involved either advancing/supporting a passed pawn (30% passed_pawn motif) or executing a tactical finish. The Maia predictions (47% pawn moves) confirm that the correct continuation typically involved pawn advances rather than king wandering. This is the classic endgame error of moving the king 'actively' when precise pawn timing was required, squandering decisive tempi in positions that demanded calculation rather than general principles.

1222.label: Knight exchange in the opening that allows a tactical fork or leaves pieces hanging.
1222.description: This feature fires on opening-phase knight exchanges (90% knight moved, 95% knight captured) that appear materially neutral (95% trades, median net 0.0) but actually cost a median of 358 centipawns, typically swinging the position from drawn to losing (58%). The boards consistently show early middlegame positions where the player recaptures or initiates a knight trade on a central square (e4, d4, d5, e5) without accounting for the tactical consequences: the dominant motifs are forks (33%), hanging pieces (22%), and discovered attacks (11%). The common tags—piece_activity, development, pawn_structure, missed_tactic, tempo_loss—reveal that the knight exchange cedes critical tempo or exposes an undefended piece. Maia's preferred responses (knight 42%, king 32%) suggest the opponent exploits the resulting tactical vulnerability rather than simply recapturing. In essence, the player sees an apparently equal trade but misses that completing the exchange grants the opponent a devastating fork, discovered attack, or wins a now-undefended piece elsewhere.

1223.label: Moving the queen to an exposed square in the opening, losing tempo and allowing tactical punishment.
1223.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: developing or repositioning the queen prematurely (queen moved 100%) to squares like b3 or b6 in the opening phase (100%). The material signature shows the queen move hangs material 75% of the time—not because the queen itself is captured immediately, but because the misplaced queen allows the opponent to gain tempo with developing moves (tempo_loss 67%, development tag), often enabling forks (33%) or exploiting the queen's vulnerability. The eval trajectory is severe: positions shift from drawn to losing 75% of the time, with a median loss of 332 centipawns. The top boards confirm this pattern unmistakably—moves like Qf3-b3, Qd1-b3, and Qd8-b6 all represent early queen sorties to b-file squares that violate opening principles. The opponent's best response is typically a knight move (75%) that simultaneously develops with tempo against the exposed queen. Tags like 'premature_queen_development' and 'queen_misplacement' directly confirm this diagnosis. The queen isn't lost outright but its premature activity costs multiple tempi and collapses the position.

1224.label: Moving the knight away in the opening and allowing a discovered attack by the queen on e4/e5, losing major material.
1224.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern: positions arising from Petrov-like or Stafford Gambit structures where both sides have knights on e4/e5 and a queen on e2 creates a latent discovered attack along the e-file. The player moves their knight (100% knight moves), typically retreating it to f6, f3, or elsewhere, which unblocks the opponent's queen's discovered attack on the king or a major piece along the e-file. The material signature shows the move itself appears 'safe' (86%) — no immediate capture loss — but the eval trajectory universally shows drawn->losing with a median loss of 429 centipawns, indicating the queen is effectively won via the discovered attack on the next move. All positions are in the opening phase (100%), the missed move is always a queen move (Maia 100% queen), and the tactical motif is discovered_attack in every case. The common tags (king_safety, e-file_pressure, e-file_pin) confirm the geometric theme: the knight's departure opens a devastating line for the opponent's queen, typically winning the player's queen or delivering a decisive material advantage.

1225.label: Developing or repositioning a piece while ignoring a direct threat to an existing piece (usually the queen), hanging it for free in the opening.
1225.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player makes a routine-looking move (development, repositioning) while completely overlooking that one of their pieces—most often the queen—is already under direct attack. The material signature shows 100% hangs (non-captures that leave a piece en prise) with a median net loss of 6 pawns (~queen value), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings from winning to losing (median 984cp lost). The tactical motifs are unanimously 'hanging_piece', with dominant tags including 'ignored_threat', 'hanging_queen', and 'queen_blunder'. The concrete positions reinforce this: bishops invading c7 attacking queens on d8 that go unaddressed, queens placed on squares attacked by knights, and pawns left undefended while the opponent has tempo—all in the first 3-7 moves. The player simply fails to notice or respond to an existing tactical threat on the board, prioritizing their plan over board awareness.

1221.label: Moves a piece to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable due to geometric or tempo oversights.
1221.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a bishop, queen, or minor piece (often without capturing anything) to a square that hangs material due to an overlooked tactical relationship. The material signature shows 72% non-captures with 34% of moves hanging a piece, and the median eval loss of 351 centipawns confirms these are severe blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The trajectory (25% drawn->losing, 16% winning->drawn) shows these moves frequently throw away the game's result. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: 50% hanging_piece motifs combined with tempo_loss and geometric/diagonal vulnerability tags. The concrete positions illustrate this—castling into a diagonal check, advancing a pawn that loses tempo to a knight fork, or placing a piece on a square that allows capture with check. Maia's suggested alternatives (41% queen moves, 31% knight moves) indicate the engine wanted active piece play rather than the passive or misguided repositioning that created the tactical vulnerability. The player consistently fails to account for the opponent's forcing responses (checks, attacks with tempo) that exploit the newly-placed piece's geometric weaknesses.

1226.label: Weakening pawn moves in the opening that fatally compromise king safety, allowing immediate tactical punishment.
1226.description: This feature fires on early-game pawn moves (100% opening phase, player moved pawn 100%) that catastrophically weaken the king's position. The boards reveal a clear pattern: moves like ...f6, ...g5, ...a5 (when f-pawn is already gone), or passive pawn pushes like h2-h3 that ignore development and create fatal diagonal/file weaknesses around the king. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of ~9979 centipawns — effectively game-ending blunders that allow immediate checkmate or forced mate sequences. The dominant motifs (king_safety 67%, pin 22%) confirm these are not material giveaways but positional catastrophes where a seemingly 'safe' pawn move (material outcome: safe 100%) opens critical lines to the king. The tactical analyses consistently describe opened diagonals (h5-e8, f1-a6), exposed kings, and immediate queen checks. The 50% drawn->losing and 50% losing->winning trajectory split reflects that sometimes the player was already worse and sealed their fate, while other times the opponent's position flipped from equal to mating — both via the same fundamental error of weakening king shelter with careless opening pawn moves.

1227.label: Player makes a non-urgent or reflexive move while missing a forced checkmate or decisive tactical blow involving check.
1227.description: This feature fires on positions where the player had a winning or drawn position and made a move (often a king move, rook move, or quiet pawn push) while Maia's recommended move was a check (100% of Maia moves give check) that would have delivered checkmate or won decisive material. The material signature shows the player's moves are mostly 'safe' (71%) or 'hang' material (29%), meaning they aren't making obvious blunders in the traditional sense—they're simply playing elsewhere while a forced mating sequence or crushing check exists. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses (median 393cp lost), with positions going from drawn/winning to losing in 72% of cases. The tactical motifs (king_safety 43%, tempo_loss 29%, fork 14%) and tags (promotion_threat, exposed_king, knight_fork) reveal positions with rich tactical content where the opponent's king is vulnerable. The concrete examples confirm this: missing Qb1+ leading to checkmate, missing Nc2+ fork, and playing tempo-losing moves in positions where immediate checks win. The common thread is that players make 'reasonable-looking' quiet moves while overlooking that a forcing sequence starting with check wins immediately.

1228.label: Playing a slow or quiet move when an immediate forcing sequence (check, sacrifice, or mating attack) was available against an exposed king.
1228.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a non-forcing, often natural-looking move (rook repositioning, quiet bishop move, pawn push) while a powerful forcing continuation—typically involving checks, sacrifices, or a direct king hunt—was available. The material signature shows 74% non-captures with 35% of moves outright hanging material, yet the key signal is that Maia's recommended moves give check 50% of the time versus 0% for the played moves. The dominant motifs (king_safety 40%, tempo_loss 20%) and tags (exposed_king, back_rank, missed_mate, king_hunt, missed_check) confirm that the opponent's king was vulnerable and the player failed to exploit it. The eval trajectory (median 244cp lost, with 68% missing winning material) shows these are costly oversights—often converting decisive advantages into unclear or lost positions. The concrete examples reinforce this: missing Rxb2+ forcing mate, playing slow h5 instead of immediate checks, and choosing quiet rook moves when the opponent's king was fatally exposed. The core error is a failure to recognize urgency—prioritizing positional consolidation over available tactical violence against the king.

1229.label: Player makes a passive move in a rook endgame instead of unleashing a winning discovered attack or knight fork with check.
1229.description: This feature captures a specific endgame pattern where the player has a knight that can deliver check (often a discovered attack or fork) while simultaneously winning the opponent's rook or other material, but instead plays a passive or aimless move with the rook, pawn, or king. All positions are endgames (100%) where the player's move is materially 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet Maia consistently identifies a knight check (100% knight moves, 100% checks) as the winning continuation. The dominant motifs are forks (38%) and discovered attacks (25%), with the recurring tag 'missed_tactic' appearing in every case. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes cost a median of 430 centipawns, typically converting a winning position into a drawn one (67% winning->drawn). The concrete pattern across the top boards is strikingly consistent: a knight sits on a square where it can move with check, either forking the king and a rook or uncovering an attack on an enemy piece along a rank or file. Instead of executing this decisive blow, the player moves another piece passively, squandering the tactical opportunity and allowing the opponent to survive in a simplified position.

1231.label: Knight captures a central pawn in the opening, leaving it tactically exposed to forks or tempo-gaining attacks.
1231.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a knight prematurely captures a central pawn (typically on e4 or d5), appearing materially safe in the short term but creating tactical vulnerability. The material signature shows knight captures a pawn with no immediate material loss (safe, +1.0 median), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows the position shifting from drawn to losing (~242cp lost), indicating a delayed tactical punishment. The Opus analysis reveals the knight becomes a target for forks (30%), hangs to subsequent attacks (60%), or causes critical tempo loss (10%). The common tags—opening_trap, pawn_grab_punished, development, tempo_loss—paint a clear picture: the knight moves twice in the opening to grab material, neglecting development, and is then exploited by opponent responses like Qa4+ forks, Nb5 threats, or pawn recaptures that gain tempo on the queen. The top boards consistently show positions from well-known opening traps (Scandinavian, Sicilian, Alekhine structures) where the f6-knight rashly captures on e4 or d5 and faces devastating tactical consequences.

1230.label: A safe-looking non-capturing move that abandons a winning attacking initiative, allowing the opponent to equalize.
1230.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where a player makes a materially 'safe' move (67% safe, no captures 60%) that catastrophically squanders a winning advantage—the dominant trajectory is winning->drawn (60%) with a median loss of 269 centipawns. The moves are typically quiet developing or repositioning moves (bishops, rooks, pawns, queens moved to non-aggressive squares) rather than captures or trades. The tactical analysis reveals the player consistently misses concrete attacking continuations (missed_tactic appears 4 times, king_safety 3 times, piece_activity 3 times), often involving queen attacks on the kingside (Qh5, Qh4 patterns). The motifs of tempo_loss (20%) and hanging_piece (40%) suggest these quiet moves either waste a critical tempo or leave pieces uncoordinated, allowing the opponent's defense to consolidate. Maia strongly favors queen moves (87%), confirming that the natural/best continuation involved aggressive queen play that the player avoided in favor of a passive alternative. The positions are complex middlegames with pieces aimed at the enemy king, where one precise attacking move was needed but the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' retreat or regrouping move instead.

1235.label: Player makes a non-defensive move while an immediate checkmate threat exists along an open diagonal toward their king.
1235.description: This feature fires when a player completely overlooks an immediate or near-immediate checkmate threat exploiting an open diagonal aimed at their king. The material signature shows mostly safe, non-capturing pawn or piece moves (75% safe, 62% no capture), indicating the player is pursuing routine development or positional plans rather than addressing a lethal tactical threat. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median loss of 9625 centipawns), with positions swinging from drawn-to-winning for the opponent (38%) or winning-to-losing (25%), confirming these are game-ending oversights rather than gradual positional errors. The tactical analysis is definitive: 100% king_safety motif, with recurring tags including back_rank_adjacent, checkmate_in_one, h7_weakness, queen_bishop_battery, and diagonal_mate. The concrete positions consistently show open diagonals (c2-h7, d6-h2) where the opponent's queen can deliver immediate checkmate, but the player instead plays a pawn push, capture, or quiet move as if the threat does not exist. Maia's 100% pawn recommendations suggest the engine expected quiet play, but the critical defensive resource (like g3 or g6 blocking the diagonal) was the only survival move.

1234.label: In a lost pawn endgame, the king retreats or moves passively, losing critical tempo in the race to stop or support passed pawns.
1234.description: This feature detects king moves in pawn endgames where the player, already in a losing position, compounds the deficit by misplacing their king—typically retreating or moving sideways when the position demanded an active approach. The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures and no checks, confirming these are pure repositioning decisions rather than tactical exchanges. The eval trajectory (losing->losing, median 122cp lost) shows these moves deepen an already lost position rather than throwing a win, indicating the player misjudges the urgency of king activity in the pawn race. The dominant motifs (pawn_endgame 70%, tempo_loss 20%, passed_pawn 10%) and tags (king_activity, tempo_loss, passed_pawn) confirm the pattern: the king goes to a square that wastes a tempo—often retreating (Kd4 instead of Ke5, Kc3 instead of maintaining centralization, Kf3 instead of opposing the enemy pawns)—when precise king placement was the only defensive resource. The concrete positions show pure king-and-pawn endgames where a single wasted tempo converts a difficult defense into a hopeless one.

1232.label: An aggressive knight or queen move (often with check) that leaves the piece or another piece hanging, causing a major evaluation swing.
1232.description: This feature identifies positions where a player makes an aggressive-looking move—typically with a knight (42%) or queen (42%)—that frequently delivers check (42%) but critically leaves material hanging (67% of moves result in a hung piece). The median material loss is -1.0 (a full piece), and the median eval cost is a devastating 356 centipawns, often swinging from drawn or winning positions into losing ones (33% drawn->losing, 17% winning->losing). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and king_safety (33%), with tags like premature_attack, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic recurring. The pattern is clear from the top boards: players launch seemingly forcing attacks (checks, captures on key squares, piece invasions) but overlook that their aggressive piece or a piece left behind is undefended. The Maia baseline rarely gives check (0%) and often captures material instead, confirming that the correct moves were quieter defensive or consolidating moves rather than flashy attacks. This is the classic 'attacking move that forgets defense' blunder—the player sees the aggression but misses that the opponent can simply take the hanging piece.

1238.label: In drawn endgames, making moves that abandon critical defensive resources (hanging pieces, exposing the king, or trading away counterplay) to convert a drawable position into a loss.
1238.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes (100% endgame phase) where the player converts a drawn position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing trajectory, median loss of 279 centipawns). The material signature shows a mix of hanging pieces (50%) and trades (50%), suggesting the player either leaves material undefended or exchanges away critical defensive pieces. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging_piece (40%), king_safety (40%), and positional_mistake (20%), with recurring tags of piece_activity, king_safety, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern: players in drawable endgames make moves that either leave pieces en prise (Kc1 ignoring a hanging bishop, moving a rook to a square where it's captured), trade away their only source of counterplay (exchanging a dynamic bishop that provided all defensive chances), or expose their king fatally. These are not outright blunders from winning positions but rather failures to maintain the defensive discipline required to hold drawn endgames.

1237.label: Moving a knight to the rim (especially Na5) in the opening, hanging it or losing significant material while abandoning central control.
1237.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where the player moves a knight to the edge of the board (100% knight moves, predominantly ...Na5 attacking a bishop on c4) in Italian Game or similar structures. The material signature shows the knight move hangs material 78% of the time (median -1.0 material loss), and the eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 272cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the knight retreat to the rim neglects king safety (tagged 8/9 times), loses tempo (7/9), and misses better developing alternatives. The concrete pattern is almost exclusively ...Nc6-a5 in e4/e5 openings where the knight becomes vulnerable on the rim, the player falls behind in development, and White obtains a crushing initiative against the uncastled king. Rather than maintaining central tension or developing pieces, the player chases the bishop with a move that leaves the knight misplaced and the position collapsing.

1233.label: Active pieces are sacrificed or hung on moves that squander tempo or abandon attacking potential, typically costing a winning or drawn position.
1233.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves where a player's piece (most often a rook, but also bishops, knights, and queens) is hung or sacrificed without adequate compensation—41% of moves hang a piece and the median material cost is -1.0. The key unifying thread from the tactical analysis is tempo_loss (33%) combined with king_safety and discovered_attack motifs: the player makes an impulsive active-looking move (a check 31% of the time, a piece relocation, or a premature advance) that abandons a critical defensive or attacking role. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors (median 322cp lost), frequently converting winning or drawn positions into losses (33% combined winning→drawn or drawn→losing). Maia's recommendations show the engine wanted quiet moves capturing pawns or maintaining piece coordination (54% non-captures, 38% pawn captures), indicating the correct continuation was typically to consolidate rather than lash out. The example positions illustrate the pattern vividly: knights leaving dominant outposts for showy checks, bishops traded away that were shielding the king, and passive retreats that leave tactically critical pieces en prise. The common thread is an impulsive piece commitment that loses material while surrendering tempo or positional coordination.

1236.label: A quiet pawn move in the opening that overlooks a knight-based tactical opportunity, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1236.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player pushes a pawn (most often h6, h5, or e6) that appears safe—nothing is immediately lost or captured—but critically misses a stronger knight move identified by the engine. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures and no material lost directly (safe), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows a drawn position collapsing into a losing one (median 209cp lost). The Maia-suggested best moves are always knight moves, indicating missed piece activity or tactical responses. The top boards reveal a pattern of undeveloped or passively-placed pieces (often with a bishop on g6) where the player makes a slow, prophylactic pawn push (h6, h5, e6) instead of deploying or repositioning a knight to exploit the opponent's central presence. The OPUS tags reinforce this: piece_activity and development dominate, with tempo_loss and hanging_piece motifs indicating the pawn move either wastes time or leaves pieces undefended. The recurring scenario is an opening where active piece play was required but the player chose a 'safe-looking' pawn move that passively ignores the position's tactical demands.

1239.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move, missing a forcing tactical sequence exploiting the opponent's exposed king.
1239.description: This feature fires when a player makes a materially 'safe' but passive move (typically a rook or queen repositioning with no capture or check) while a powerful tactical opportunity involving king safety goes unexploited. The Maia engine consistently recommends captures (100% capture rate, often winning a queen) that exploit exposed king positions through check sequences, knight forks, or bishop checks. The dominant motif across all positions is king_safety (100%), with tags like exposed_king, missed_capture, check_sequence, and hanging_queen_ignored appearing repeatedly. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes—median 376 centipawns lost—frequently converting winning positions into losing or drawn ones. The concrete example of ignoring Nxd5 (capturing a queen) to instead flee with a king perfectly illustrates the pattern: the player fails to recognize that aggressive tactical punishment of the opponent's king vulnerability is available and instead plays defensively or aimlessly, squandering a decisive advantage.

1241.label: Moving a knight or bishop to an undefended square where it can be captured for free, turning a balanced or salvageable position into a losing one.
1241.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move minor pieces (knights 50%, bishops 32%) to squares where they hang without compensation. The material signature shows 55% of moves result in a hung piece with no capture involved (97% non-captures), and a median material loss of -1.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders: 34% convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 270 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (67%), alongside tempo_loss and missed_tactic tags. The concrete positions show knights and bishops being placed on squares that look active but are tactically undefended—often ignoring opponent's attacking resources on diagonals or central squares. Players appear to be making developing or repositioning moves without checking whether the destination square is adequately protected, resulting in immediate material loss.

1240.label: Playing a flashy check (usually with a bishop) that wastes tempo or sacrifices material instead of executing the stronger tactical continuation.
1240.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check—predominantly with a bishop (80% bishop moves, 80% checks given)—that appears forcing but actually squanders a winning or near-winning position. The material signature shows the move itself is often 'safe' (60%) meaning nothing is immediately lost, but Maia's recommended alternatives involve capturing high-value pieces (rooks 40%, queens 40%) or delivering more purposeful checks (60%). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain winning but leak a median of 174 centipawns—classic 'checks aren't free' scenarios where the player had a decisive continuation available. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'premature_check' and 'tempo_loss' as dominant motifs: the check forces the king to a square that actually improves its safety or activates the opponent's pieces, while the player's piece ends up misplaced or captured. Tags like 'piece_sacrifice_without_compensation' and 'checks_arent_free' reinforce that the mistake stems from the psychological lure of giving check rather than calculating the concrete best move (often a capture or quiet winning move). The boards show bishops checking on diagonals (Bd4+, Bf7+) when simple captures or queen maneuvers would have been decisive.

1244.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move instead of delivering a devastating check that wins material or forces checkmate.
1244.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful checking move (Maia recommends a queen check 98% of the time) and instead plays a passive or purposeless move. The material signature shows the player's move is often safe or hangs material (58% safe, 28% hangs), but critically, 98% of the time the best move involved giving check—a forcing move that would have won significant material or delivered checkmate. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: a median of 353 centipawns lost, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing. The tactical analysis reveals back-rank threats, king safety exploitation, and capture-with-check motifs that the player completely missed. The concrete examples consistently show positions where a check (Rd1+, Bxe5+, Rg6 leading to Qe4+) would have been crushing, but the player chose a quiet move (b3, Nc3, Kf1, g6) that squandered the forcing sequence. The common thread is failing to recognize that a check creates an unavoidable tempo advantage that wins the game.

1242.label: Player makes a move that fatally ignores an immediate tactical threat, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
1242.description: This feature fires on moves where the player overlooks a concrete tactical threat on the board, resulting in severe material or positional loss. The material signature shows 55% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -1.0, and the player's moves are typically rooks (36%) or pawns (27%) that serve no defensive purpose against the existing danger. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: 36% swing from winning to drawn and 18% from winning to losing, with a massive median eval loss of 475 centipawns—consistent with throwing away substantial advantages. The tactical motifs reveal the nature of the ignored threats: back-rank mates left unaddressed (f7f5 ignoring doubled rooks on the 7th), forks invited (f2f3 opening the knight fork), king safety emergencies neglected (Rc5c8 pointless check ignoring own king danger), and tempo-losing moves that allow the opponent's threat to execute. Maia's recommended moves (king 36%, queen 27%, knight 27%) suggest defensive or active responses were available. The common thread is not a specific tactical pattern but rather the player making a 'normal-looking' move while a lethal tactical threat (mate, fork, discovered attack) demands immediate attention.

1245.label: Player makes a non-pawn move (piece development or quiet move) when a critical pawn advance was required to maintain advantage.
1245.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a piece (knight 24%, pawn 24%, bishop 23%) but Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a pawn move (99%), indicating the engine strongly preferred a specific pawn advance. The material signature shows these are mostly safe moves (64%) or hanging moves (25%) — not captures or trades — meaning the player made a quiet developing or repositioning move instead of the critical pawn push. The eval trajectory shows severe consequences: median 265cp lost, with 13% going drawn->losing and 12% winning->drawn, indicating these pawn advances were often the only way to maintain a winning or drawn position. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss 25%, fork 25%, positional_mistake 25%, king_safety 12%) reveal that by failing to advance the pawn, the player either lost tempo, allowed opponent pieces to reach critical squares (enabling forks), weakened their king position, or missed a pawn break that would have constrained enemy piece activity. The top boards confirm this: positions where g4 would evict a powerful knight, f4 would maintain a winning attack, or pawn advances would secure space or open lines — all missed in favor of aimless piece shuffling.

1243.label: Pushing g-pawn in the opening weakens king diagonals, hanging material or allowing devastating queen checks.
1243.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: pushing the g-pawn (g7-g6 or g2-g3) when a queen is already active on a dangerous diagonal (typically h5 or h4). The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures, and 83% of these moves hang material—the pawn push itself doesn't lose the pawn but fatally exposes the king's position, opening diagonals that allow queen forks (capturing on e5 with check then taking h8), discovered attacks, or direct material wins. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: median 317cp lost, with 42% of cases swinging from drawn to losing and 17% from winning to losing. The tactical motifs (king_safety 33%, hanging_piece 33%, fork 22%) combined with tags like pawn_shield_weakened, opening_trap, and queen_fork all point to the same pattern. The top boards are almost entirely Scholar's Mate variations or similar early queen attacks where the defender plays ...g6 trying to chase the queen but instead opens the long diagonal and loses material on e5/h8 or elsewhere. This is a classic beginner trap where the 'natural' pawn push to attack the queen actually makes things catastrophically worse.

1246.label: Failing to find the only good move in positions where one precise continuation was required to maintain the evaluation.
1246.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a narrow decision point—typically only one move within 50cp of optimal—and fails to find it, resulting in a large evaluation swing (median 265cp lost). The material signature shows these are predominantly non-capturing moves (100% no capture) with rooks and bishops that appear safe on the surface (67% safe, 33% hangs), but the Opus analysis reveals the real cost: missed tactics (100% missed winning material), hanging pieces, tempo loss, trapped pieces, and promotion errors. The eval trajectories are diverse (winning→drawn, drawn→losing, losing→winning missed), suggesting this isn't a single positional theme but rather a failure at critical junctures where calculation was essential. The endgame-heavy phase (67%) combined with passed pawn and piece activity tags indicates these are positions requiring precise technique—often involving rook maneuvers near promotion squares or bishop retreats to maintain coordination—where the player chose a natural-looking but fatally imprecise continuation instead of the singular correct move.

1247.label: Moving a piece that was critically defending against tactics, hanging material in the process.
1247.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a queen, knight, or bishop (often non-capturing, 52% no capture) that results in hanging a piece (52%) or losing significant material (22%), with a median loss of 3 pawns worth and a massive eval drop (median 687cp). The trajectory shows these are game-deciding errors: 30% swing from winning to losing, 17% from drawn to losing. The Opus analysis reveals the core pattern: the moved piece was serving a defensive role (removing_defender tag), and relocating it exposes tactical vulnerabilities—often along diagonals toward the king (king_safety 25%) or leaving other pieces unprotected (hanging_piece 50%). The concrete positions confirm this: Na5 removes a knight from c6 leaving the king exposed to Bxe6+; pieces move to aggressive-looking squares but abandon critical defensive duties. Players are lured by activity or superficial threats while failing to recognize their piece was a linchpin holding the position together.

1249.label: Player ignores a strong queen move that addresses king safety, instead making a passive or misdirected move that allows the opponent to exploit the exposed king.
1249.description: This feature captures positions where the player's king is vulnerable (king_safety and exposed_king dominate the tags) and the best move involves an active queen deployment (Maia recommends queen moves 95% of the time), but instead the player makes a non-queen move (pawn 20%, queen 20%, king 20%, rook 20%) that fails to address the critical king safety issue. The material signature shows these aren't capture blunders—90% involve no capture—but 30% hang material as a consequence of the positional neglect. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic: median 295cp lost, with 25% converting wins into draws. The tactical analyses repeatedly show players retreating pieces passively, moving queens to irrelevant squares (Qxa7 abandoning king defense), or failing to centralize the queen when king safety demands it. The common thread is that an exposed or uncastled king required immediate attention via queen activity, and the player chose a move that ignored or worsened the defensive crisis.

1248.label: Player overlooks a critical intermediate or winning check, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or escape punishment.
1248.description: This feature fires when players miss a forcing check that would have decisively changed the position. The material signature shows moves that are mostly 'safe' (no immediate material loss in 83% of cases), yet Maia's recommended move gives check in 100% of examples—revealing that the engine consistently found a checking resource the player ignored. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 584cp lost), with positions swinging from winning to losing or drawn, indicating these are game-deciding oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical motifs (intermediate_check, back_rank, hanging_piece) and per-position analyses consistently describe scenarios where a check would have won material (often a queen) or delivered mate: Bb5+ saving a queen, Qxf5+ as an intermediate check winning the queen, Bc4+ winning Black's queen via tempo. Instead, players chose quiet or non-forcing alternatives (capturing without check, retreating, or developing passively), surrendering the tempo advantage that a check provides. The common thread is not a material blunder per se, but a failure to recognize that a check creates an unavoidable forcing sequence.

1250.label: A developing or routine move leaves a piece or pawn unprotected, allowing the opponent to win it via a knight fork or simple capture.
1250.description: This feature identifies positions where a player makes a seemingly natural move (pawn advance, piece development, castling) that overlooks a concrete tactical threat—most commonly a knight fork or the simple capture of an undefended piece. The material signature shows 88% of these moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave something en prise) with a median net loss of -1.0 (typically a pawn), and virtually none involve captures themselves (93% non-capture). The eval trajectory is devastating: 30% of cases flip from a drawn position to a losing one, with a median cost of 247 centipawns—indicating these are not minor inaccuracies but game-changing oversights. The tactical motifs are overwhelmingly fork (60%) and hanging_piece (40%), with recurring tags like 'undefended_pawn', 'knight_fork', and 'missed_tactic'. The concrete examples confirm the pattern: a bishop develops to e7 leaving d5 undefended for a knight capture with tempo; castling ignores a knight fork on c6; a pawn advance to b6 removes a defender enabling a devastating knight fork on both rooks. The phase split (48% opening, 52% middlegame) suggests these occur during development when players prioritize routine moves over tactical vigilance.

1253.label: Player makes a suboptimal move while missing a decisive capture or promotion that would win immediately.
1253.description: This feature fires on positions where the player overlooks a winning tactical opportunity—typically a capture or pawn promotion—that would have been immediately decisive. The material signature shows that in 100% of cases, Maia's recommended move captures a rook (often via promotion or a simple hanging piece), indicating a missed winning capture. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: a median of 9340 centipawns lost, with positions going from winning to still-winning (but missing forced mate) or from losing to handing the opponent a win. The tactical motifs are diverse but unified by the theme of ignoring an immediately available decisive action: hanging pieces left uncaptured (bishop takes undefended rook on a clear diagonal), promotion errors (recapturing with a rook instead of promoting to queen with check), and back-rank vulnerabilities. The boards consistently show endgame or late-middlegame positions with passed pawns near promotion or undefended pieces, where the player makes a passive or irrelevant move instead of executing the winning blow.

1251.label: Giving a check that loses significant material or ruins a winning position in the endgame.
1251.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player delivers a queen check that costs substantial material (median -8.0 net material, median 328 centipawns lost). The material signature shows the queen captures a pawn with check but loses far more in return — a classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' pattern. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain winning but with drastically reduced advantage (or in one case, complete collapse to equality). The Opus analysis repeatedly tags 'tempo_loss' and 'unnecessary_check' as dominant motifs: the check accomplishes nothing strategically while forfeiting the queen or disrupting a winning tactical geometry. The top boards show endgame positions (passed pawns, rook endgames, king-and-pawn scenarios) where quiet moves would secure the win, but the player impulsively checks, losing the queen or critical coordination. Maia's recommended moves are simple pawn pushes — no check, no capture — confirming that the correct approach was patient conversion rather than flashy but self-destructive checks.

1254.label: A rook check that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to activate their king and exploit passed pawns.
1254.description: This feature detects positions where a player delivers a rook check that catastrophically squanders a winning position. The material signature shows 100% rook moves that are checks but hang material (median -1.0), indicating the check itself creates a vulnerability or loses a critical asset. The eval trajectory is devastating: every instance goes from winning to losing with a median loss of 861 centipawns, meaning these checks throw away completely won games. The tactical analysis reveals the mechanism: the dominant motif is tempo_loss (56%), combined with passed_pawn (33%) and pawn_race contexts. The positions are consistently middlegame-to-late pawn race scenarios where the player has dangerous passed pawns but delivers a pointless check instead of advancing or supporting them. The check drives the opponent's king to an active square (often near the passed pawns), allowing the king to devour the pawns or the opponent's own passed pawn to advance decisively. Maia consistently finds the correct alternative: capturing a pawn rather than giving the flashy but counterproductive check.

1255.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move instead of capturing a hanging or vulnerable piece with their bishop.
1255.description: This feature identifies positions where the player's bishop could capture a piece (usually a knight) to win material, but instead the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (knight, pawn, rook, or queen move that is 'safe' but pointless). The material signature shows 86% non-captures with Maia consistently recommending bishop captures (100% bishop moves, 90% capturing knights). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: median 375cp lost, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' and 'capture_sequence' as dominant motifs—the opponent has an undefended or insufficiently defended piece that the player's bishop can simply take, but the player overlooks this elementary capture in favor of a tempo-losing or purposeless move. The concrete examples repeatedly show patterns like ...Bxg5 or ...Bxd4 winning a full piece being missed for moves like ...Qe8, ...h6, or ...Nxe5 (capturing the wrong piece).

1252.label: Ignoring immediate king safety threats (forks, back-rank, exposed king) in already-losing middlegame positions, resulting in catastrophic or fatal evaluation drops.
1252.description: This feature fires on moves where a player, typically already in a losing or precarious middlegame position, makes a move (most often a knight move, but also queen or bishop) that fatally neglects king safety. The material signature shows these are not primarily capture-related blunders—50% involve no capture at all and the moves appear 'safe' on the surface. However, the tactical analysis reveals dominant motifs of king_safety (43%), fork (29%), and back_rank (14%), with recurring tags of exposed_king and missed_tactic. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of ~9183 centipawns, with 67% of cases going from losing to losing (i.e., a survivable disadvantage collapses into immediate mate or catastrophic material loss) and 17% flipping from winning to losing. The concrete positions show kings on open files (d8, f2, f8) facing coordinated piece attacks, where the player's move either walks into a fork, ignores a back-rank threat, or develops passively while the opponent has a crushing tactical blow available. Maia's suggested alternatives (bishops, pawns) tend to address the immediate threat or exchange off attacking pieces. The pattern is a player failing to recognize the urgency of their king's vulnerability in a complex middlegame.

1256.label: Pawn exchange that opens a file toward the player's own king in opposite-side or sensitive castling positions.
1256.description: This feature fires on pawn captures (100% pawn moved, 100% pawn captured) that are materially neutral trades (91% trade outcome, median net material 0.0) but cause severe positional damage, with a median eval loss of 248 centipawns. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), and the recurring tactical tags include opposite-side castling, open files, and pawn structure degradation. The concrete pattern visible in the top boards is highly consistent: players recapture or initiate pawn exchanges (cxb4, axb4, hxg5, hxg4) that open lines directly toward their own king, handing the opponent attacking resources. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions to losing (33%) or winning positions to drawn/worse (12%), indicating that the player is throwing away their position by making a seemingly natural pawn trade that catastrophically compromises their king shelter. Maia's recommendations (knight 44%, non-capturing moves 100%) suggest the engine preferred piece development or repositioning rather than opening critical files.

1258.label: Moving a minor piece to a square where it is immediately captured by an enemy pawn in the opening.
1258.description: This feature detects a specific and recurring opening blunder where the player develops or repositions a minor piece (knight or bishop) to a square that is directly attacked by an enemy pawn, leaving it hanging with no compensation. All three signals converge clearly: the material/position signature shows 100% hanging moves (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -2.0 (a full minor piece), exclusively in the opening phase. The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions turned into losing ones, with a median loss of 515 centipawns—consistent with dropping a piece for nothing from an equal position. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies hanging_piece as the dominant motif, with tags like 'opening_blunder', 'ignored_threat', and 'pawn_captures_piece' reinforcing that the player simply places a piece where a pawn takes it. The concrete examples (Bd6 captured by e5 pawn, Bf4 captured by exf4, Bd3 captured by e4 pawn, Nd2 leaving a piece en prise) all show the same pattern: a minor piece lands on or remains on a pawn-attacked square with the player apparently blind to the immediate one-move threat.

1259.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended square where it is immediately capturable in the opening.
1259.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder where a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) to an aggressively-placed but completely undefended square, hanging it for free (100% hangs, median -3.0 material = one full piece). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic damage: positions shift from drawn to losing with a median cost of 549 centipawns, consistent with losing a minor piece for nothing. The top activating positions show a clear pattern: moves like Bc1-h6, Bf1-a6, Bc8-h3, and Bb2-g7 all represent early-game bishop lunges to long-diagonal squares that appear threatening but are immediately capturable by an opponent's piece already covering that square. Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (80%), with tags emphasizing premature attacks, tempo loss, and bishop blunders. The opponent's best response (Maia suggests pawn moves 100%) often indicates simple recaptures or that the bishop landed on a pawn-defended square. This is a classic beginner mistake of prioritizing an aggressive-looking move over basic piece safety in the opening.

1257.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move, missing that the opponent has a devastating queen check (often with discovered attack) that wins significant material or initiates a mating sequence.
1257.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a move that is objectively safe in terms of immediate material (60% safe, 30% hangs), but critically overlooks a powerful queen check resource available to the opponent. The Maia signal is striking: in 100% of cases the best move involves giving check, and 69% of the time it's a queen check, with discovered attacks, forks, and king safety motifs each appearing in a third of cases. The player's moves are diverse (pawns, queens, knights, bishops) and mostly non-capturing (81% no capture), suggesting tempo-losing or irrelevant moves that ignore the tactical vulnerability of their king. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 327 centipawns, with positions collapsing from drawn-to-losing (13%), winning-to-losing (6%), or winning-to-drawn (5%), indicating these are game-changing oversights. Tags like king_in_center, exposed_king, and discovered_check confirm that the player's king is tactically vulnerable, and by playing a non-urgent move (often a flank pawn push or premature exchange), they allow the opponent's queen to deliver a check that wins material or initiates a forced sequence. The concrete examples show pawn pushes (h4, a5, b3) and piece trades (Qxf4) that ignore imminent queen check threats exploiting open lines and exposed kings.

1260.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in the opening that squanders a winning tactical opportunity involving a strong knight on e5.
1260.description: This feature fires on opening positions where White has a powerful centralized knight (typically on e5) in a French Defense or Slav-like structure, and instead of exploiting a concrete tactical opportunity (often Nxf7 or maintaining pressure), plays a passive, non-forcing move such as castling (O-O), a quiet developing move (Ndf3), a pawn push (a3), or a bishop retreat (Bh2). The material signature shows 100% safe moves (nothing is hung or traded), yet the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic loss of advantage: 88% winning->drawn and 12% winning->losing, with a median loss of 227 centipawns. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (44%), king_safety concerns, and missed tactics—confirm that the player is surrendering the initiative by choosing comfort over concrete action. Maia consistently recommends knight captures on pawns (Nxf7 or similar), indicating the missed tactic was a forcing knight sacrifice that the player declined in favor of a 'normal' developing move, allowing the opponent to consolidate and neutralize the position.

1263.label: Moving king or rook into a position where an opponent's fork wins significant material.
1263.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes a king or rook move (50% each) that hangs material (75% of outcomes) by overlooking an opponent's forking opportunity. The median material loss is -2.0 (typically a full piece), and 100% of cases miss winning material that was available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 50% swing from winning to losing and 25% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 758 centipawns. The dominant motif is 'fork' (67%), confirmed by tags like missed_fork and knight_tactics. The concrete positions show patterns like Ke6 walking into exd5+ discovering successive knight captures, or Ra7 allowing a tactical sequence that eliminates a key knight. Players move their king or rook without recognizing that the destination square (or the resulting position) allows the opponent to exploit a fork—typically a knight fork—that wins back decisive material.

1261.label: Moving a knight or bishop to an inferior square where it hangs or loses tempo, squandering a strong position.
1261.description: This feature fires on moves where a player jumps a minor piece (knight 50%, bishop 36%) to a square where it is immediately hanging (71% hang rate, median -3.0 material loss), typically costing around 485 centipawns and frequently converting a drawn or winning position into a losing one (36% drawn->losing, 21% winning->losing). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and hanging_piece (25%), with tags like 'attacking_piece_traded_for_nothing' and 'premature_sacrifice' reinforcing the pattern. The concrete positions show players choosing flashy or aggressive-looking knight/bishop jumps (Nd5 vs Nb5, trading a dominant bishop for a passive piece, sacrificing a bishop for a meaningless check) when the piece was already well-placed or a better square existed. The Maia baseline (bishop 50%, pawn 21%) suggests the correct moves were typically quiet bishop repositions or pawn moves rather than the aggressive piece leaps chosen. This is fundamentally a tactical error where the player misjudges the piece's safety or value on its new square, losing a full piece to a simple capture or refutation.

1265.label: Player moves a rook passively instead of capturing the opponent's hanging queen with another piece.
1265.description: This feature consistently fires when a player moves a rook (100% rook moves) in a position where Maia identifies a queen capture as the correct move (Maia captures queen 100%). The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe' — nothing is immediately lost on that move — but the player misses winning material 100% of the time, resulting in a catastrophic eval swing (median 972cp lost, winning->losing 100%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is a hanging piece (80%), with tags like 'missed_tactic' and 'queen_capture' recurring. The concrete examples reinforce this: positions where a knight or rook could simply take an undefended queen, but the player instead makes a quiet rook move (repositioning, grabbing a pawn, or making a passive defensive gesture), completely overlooking the free queen. This is a pure tactical oversight — the opponent's queen is en prise to another piece, but the player's attention is drawn to a rook move that appears useful but costs the game.

1262.label: Moving a knight to an unprotected square where it can be immediately captured or leaving a piece hanging elsewhere.
1262.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a knight (60% of cases) to a square where it is undefended and immediately vulnerable to capture, or where the knight move neglects a more urgent tactical obligation (such as defending a hanging piece elsewhere). The material signature shows that 40% of moves hang a piece outright and 30% result in a net material loss, with a median cost of -2.0 material points—consistent with losing a full minor piece. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: a median of 409 centipawns lost, often turning drawn positions into losing ones (30%) or making already-losing positions decisively worse (30%). The Opus tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (67% of positions) and 'undefended_piece' as the dominant motif. Concrete examples reinforce this: Nd3 placed on an undefended square captured by an enemy knight, Nd3 played while ignoring an attacked queen, and knights moved to squares with no support. The pattern is a knight relocation that either places the knight en prise or ignores a hanging piece that the knight should have been defending—a one-move tactical blindspot around piece safety.

1264.label: Player makes a piece move (often capturing material) while ignoring a lethal attack brewing against their own king.
1264.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a piece (knight 33%, bishop 21%, queen/rook 17% each) — often capturing material or making a seemingly active move — while completely overlooking devastating threats to their own king. The material signature shows 50% non-captures and 33% pawn captures, with 62% 'safe' outcomes on the surface, yet 79% of moves miss winning material and the median eval loss is a massive 446 centipawns. The eval trajectory (25% winning->losing, 21% drawn->losing) shows these moves frequently transform playable positions into lost ones. The tactical layer is dominated by king_safety (67%) and fork (33%) motifs, with tags like 'king_hunt', 'exposed_king', 'greedy_pawn_grab', and 'material_greed' recurring. The top boards confirm the pattern: positions feature dark-square attacks (Bxg7/Qxh7+ combinations), exposed kings with pieces aimed at them, and players who grab material (Qxd7, Rxd8, Nxd5) or make peripheral moves while their king is under siege. Maia's suggested moves (54% pawn, 25% knight, 0% captures) indicate the correct responses were typically quiet defensive moves, not counter-captures — the player chose greed or activity over survival.

1267.label: Quiet pawn moves in drawn middlegames that overlook knight fork or king-attack threats, losing ~300cp.
1267.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly quiet or routine pawn move (67% pawn moves, mostly non-captures) that ignores a critical tactical threat—typically a knight fork or king safety issue. The material signature shows the moves are overwhelmingly 'safe' in the sense that nothing is immediately hung, yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic shift from drawn to losing (83% of cases), with a median loss of 302 centipawns. The dominant motifs are fork (40%) and king_safety (40%), and the top boards consistently show positions with a powerful knight on e5 combined with a queen on h5 creating dual threats. Maia's recommended moves involve bishop or rook captures of knights (67% knight captures), indicating the correct response was to eliminate the threatening piece. The common tags—missed_tactic, tempo_loss, piece_activity—confirm that these are cases where the player made a passive or irrelevant pawn move instead of addressing an urgent tactical threat involving forks or attacks on the king.

1268.label: In a losing endgame, playing a rook check that captures a pawn but loses significant material against a passed pawn.
1268.description: This feature identifies a specific endgame mistake pattern where a player in an already losing position plays a rook capture of a pawn with check (rook move 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%), but this move loses substantial material (net -4.0 median). The positions are universally endgames featuring passed pawns near promotion, and the rook check—while seemingly active—actually loses tempo or allows the opponent to recapture with a piece in an improved position. The eval trajectory shows losing->losing with a median 108cp further deterioration, indicating these moves make a bad position decisively worse. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players are lashing out with forcing moves (checks/captures) against advanced passed pawns rather than employing proper endgame technique like improving king position or blockading. The boards consistently show positions with advanced passed pawns (7th rank) where the rook desperately tries to interfere by capturing a supporting pawn with check, but this only accelerates the loss by removing the rook from a defensive post or allowing a favorable recapture.

1266.label: Player makes a rook move that misses a checkmate or decisive check, often greedily capturing material instead.
1266.description: This feature fires when a player moves a rook (79% of activations) in a position where a forced checkmate or devastating check was available (Maia's move is always a rook delivering check, 100%). The king_safety motif is universal (100%), and the tags consistently reference missed_mate, checkmate_in_one, mating_net, and exposed_king. The positions characteristically feature doubled rooks on the 7th rank or rooks with access to back-rank/file mates. Instead of delivering the killing blow, the player makes a 'safe' but non-checking rook move—often a greedy capture (42% capture a pawn) or a lateral rook slide that abandons the mating configuration. The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 37% go from winning to drawn, with a massive median loss of 241 centipawns. The concrete examples show patterns like Rxh7 instead of Rdf7#, or moving a rook off a critical file that enabled perpetual/mate threats. The mistake is fundamentally tactical—the player fails to recognize the immediate mating pattern their rook coordination enables.

1270.label: Moving a rook to an unprotected square where the opponent's queen can immediately capture it.
1270.description: This feature identifies a highly specific tactical blunder where a player moves a rook (86% of activating moves) to a square that is completely undefended, leaving it en prise to the opponent's queen. The material signature confirms this: 43% of moves are outright hangs and 43% are slightly_down, with a median material loss of -4.0 (consistent with losing a full rook). The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of Opus analyses, with 'undefended_rook' and 'queen_captures' as recurring tags. The eval trajectory is devastating—86% of cases shift from drawn to losing—indicating these are positions where the player was holding equality but threw it away with a single careless rook move. The concrete examples reinforce the pattern: Ra5 placed within capture range of a queen on d8, Rxh4 left undefended on a queen diagonal, Rc2 accessible to a queen on a4. Maia's recommended alternatives (57% knight moves, no captures) suggest quiet developing moves that maintain the balance, further confirming these rook placements are unnecessary and tactically oblivious rather than forced.

1269.label: Developing or moving a knight while ignoring an attacking pawn that wins it.
1269.description: This feature fires on opening-phase knight moves (75% knight, 100% opening) where the player ignores an immediate pawn threat against their piece. The material signature shows 50% hangs (the knight is left en prise to a pawn) and the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 303 centipawns—consistent with losing a minor piece. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (38%) with recurring tags of 'ignored_threat' and 'development', and multiple example summaries describe scenarios where a player makes a developing or repositioning knight move while a pawn (typically an advanced e5 pawn) is attacking or about to capture the knight. The positions are overwhelmingly French/Caro-Kann/Pirc-type structures where White has pushed e5 attacking a knight on f6, and Black either ignores the threat entirely or moves the knight to a poor square. The mistake is fundamentally tactical—the player prioritizes development or a positional idea while overlooking that their knight is hanging to a pawn capture.

1271.label: Trading or simplifying in the opening when a strong tactical continuation (often exploiting a pin) would have maintained a winning advantage.
1271.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (90% opening) where the player makes a premature exchange or simplifying move that squanders a winning advantage — the trajectory shows 70% winning→drawn with a median loss of 230 centipawns. The material signature shows 50% trades (exchanges of roughly equal material) and 30% knight moves, often capturing on f3 or f6, releasing central tension. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring motif: the player had a pin (often Bg5 pinning Nf6) or an overloaded defender to exploit, but instead chose a simplifying exchange or quiet move (premature_exchange, dominant_piece_traded, move_order_error tags). The boards consistently show Italian/Spanish-type structures with Bg5 pins on Nf6 and central knight outposts where the player traded off the tactical tension rather than exploiting it with moves like e5 or maintaining the pin pressure. The key unifying pattern is abandoning a concrete tactical advantage in favor of a seemingly natural but premature exchange during the opening.

1272.label: Player makes a slow or greedy move while ignoring an immediate tactical threat against their own king or hanging pieces.
1272.description: This feature fires on moves where a player ignores a critical, urgent threat in the position—typically involving king safety or a hanging piece—and instead plays a slow, passive, or greedy move. The material signature shows that 44% of these moves hang a piece outright, and the median eval loss is a massive 360 centipawns, with many positions transitioning from winning to drawn or losing. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of king_safety (50%), tempo_loss (25%), and hanging_piece (25%), with tags like self-block, escape-square-removal, and checkmate-in-one. The best moves (Maia's recommendations) frequently involve captures of bishops and rooks or delivering check (31%), indicating the player missed forcing tactical continuations.
