The concrete examples show a pattern: blocking a king's escape square while a mate threat exists, playing a slow rook move instead of a critical pawn break, missing a free capture, and grabbing a pawn with the queen while abandoning a mating attack. In each case, the player's attention drifts to a secondary goal while the position demanded an immediate, forcing response to a tactical crisis.

1274.label: In endgames, the player moves their king or another piece instead of capturing an undefended rook with a bishop.
1274.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player has a bishop that can freely capture an undefended or hanging rook, but instead plays a king move (100% king moves) that fails to collect the material. The material outcome of the played move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), but Maia consistently identifies bishop-takes-rook as the correct move (100% bishop capturing rook). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), with 'missed_capture' and 'undefended_piece' appearing frequently in the tags. The eval trajectory shows these were winning positions that became drawn (100% winning->drawn, median 892 centipawns lost), meaning the player threw away a completely won endgame by overlooking a free rook capture. The concrete board positions confirm this: bishops on diagonals attacking rooks, with the player opting for passive king moves instead of the decisive material grab.

1273.label: Aimless king or pawn moves in won pawn endgames that surrender a critical tempo for a necessary breakthrough.
1273.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a winning advantage in a pawn endgame (middlegame-to-endgame transition, all positions are pawn endgames or simplified minor piece endings) but plays a purposeless king move or non-critical pawn advance instead of executing the decisive pawn breakthrough. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (king 67%, pawn 33%) that don't lose material immediately but hemorrhage evaluation (median 493cp lost), typically converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones (winning->drawn 67%, winning->losing 33%). The tactical analysis consistently identifies tempo_loss as the dominant theme: the opponent is gifted an extra move to play a defensive ...c5 or similar pawn block that permanently prevents the winning break. The top boards overwhelmingly show king shuffles (Kg3, Kg4) or wing pawn pushes (h4, h5h4) when a central or queenside breakthrough (b4, f5+) was the only way to convert. This is a classic endgame technique failure—playing 'on the wrong side of the board' or making waiting moves in positions that demand immediate concrete action.

1276.label: In lost endgame positions with advanced passed pawns, the player retreats their king passively instead of capturing or blocking critical pieces, missing the last defensive chance.
1276.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player moves their king passively (king move 100%, no capture) in already-losing positions, missing a critical tactical resource—typically a knight capture (Maia recommends capturing a knight 100% of the time). The positions are uniformly endgames with advanced passed pawns (44% passed_pawn motif) where promotion threats are imminent. The eval trajectory shows these are already losing positions made catastrophically worse (losing->losing, median 9251cp loss), indicating the player had one last chance to fight but chose a passive king move that allows unstoppable promotion or checkmate. The dominant tags—tempo_loss, piece_activity, missed_tactic—confirm the king move wastes a critical tempo, failing to engage an active piece (usually a knight) that could delay or block the opponent's passed pawn. The boards show positions with pawns on the 6th/7th rank where the correct defense required an active capture rather than a retreating king move.

1277.label: Trading pawns in endgames that inadvertently creates or enables a dangerous passed pawn for the opponent.
1277.description: This feature fires on pawn exchanges in late middlegame and endgame positions (100% pawn moves, 100% trades, 77% middlegame / 23% endgame phase) where the player initiates a pawn capture that appears equal in material but is catastrophic positionally. The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (62%) and pawn_endgame (38%), with recurring tags of pawn_structure issues and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 358 centipawns, with 38% going from drawn to losing and 8% from winning to losing — indicating these trades often throw away half-points or full points. The concrete positions are almost exclusively king-and-pawn endgames where the player captures a pawn (e.g., fxg5, exd5, bxa5, axb3) that opens lines or creates a passed pawn for the opponent. The Opus analysis confirms move-order errors where the sequence of captures matters critically — for example, capturing in the wrong order grants the opponent a passed pawn rather than the player. Maia's responses are non-captures (100%), meaning the engine doesn't need to recapture — the damage is structural. This is a classic endgame pattern recognition failure: the player sees an equal trade but misses that the resulting pawn structure decisively favors the opponent's passed pawn.

1275.label: In won endgames, playing a slow move instead of advancing or promoting a passed pawn with check.
1275.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player has a winning or near-winning advantage but fails to execute the critical promotion or tempo-gaining move. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (100% safe, no captures) that aren't inherently losing material but miss a decisive tactical opportunity—specifically, Maia consistently recommends moves that give check (100% check), indicating the missed resource involves a tempo-gaining promotion or rook check. The dominant motifs (promotion_error 33%, passed_pawn, tempo_loss as the most common tag) confirm the player repeatedly fails to push or promote passed pawns with tempo, or misses underpromotion tactics (like h1=B+ winning a piece). The eval trajectory shows these are winning positions that either stay winning but with significantly reduced advantage (median 118cp lost) or slip to drawn, representing squandered wins rather than outright blunders. The concrete positions show advanced passed pawns on the 2nd/3rd rank in king+rook or king+pawn endings where the player makes a passive king or rook move instead of the forcing promotion continuation.

1280.label: Squandering a winning endgame by wasting tempo instead of executing a critical pawn breakthrough.
1280.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a winning endgame (83% winning->winning, 17% winning->drawn) but makes a catastrophic tempo error related to passed pawn play. The material signature shows mostly pawn moves (67%) that either trade or hang material, while the dominant motifs are passed_pawn (67%) and pawn_endgame (22%) with tempo_loss appearing in 5 of 6 cases. The concrete pattern across the top boards is remarkably consistent: positions with critical pawn tension (especially h-pawn vs g-pawn breakthroughs like hxg6) where the player plays a slow move (unnecessary king moves, f3, Rd8 instead of the immediate pawn capture/advance) that allows the opponent to resolve the tension favorably. The median eval loss of 9410 centipawns confirms these are positions where forced mates or trivial wins are being thrown away by missing that the pawn break must be executed immediately rather than after 'improving' the position. Maia consistently recommends the pawn move (100%), highlighting that the correct idea is straightforward but the player fails to recognize the urgency.

1281.label: A pawn advance in the endgame that fatally weakens the player's king position or destroys a critical pawn structure.
1281.description: This feature detects endgame pawn pushes (98% pawn moves) that create devastating king safety or pawn structure vulnerabilities. The material signature shows these moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (99%) that appear superficially safe (77%) but frequently hang material (22%), with a median eval loss of 214 centipawns. The trajectory reveals these are often game-deciding errors: 24% convert winning positions to drawn ones, while 34% make already-losing positions worse. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety (43%) and passed_pawn (43%), with recurring tags like tempo_loss, pawn_structure_destruction, and pawn_break_error. The concrete positions show pawn advances (c4, g5, h4, f5, b4) that either expose the player's king to checks on newly opened files/diagonals, or liquidate a pawn majority that was the sole winning advantage. Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve king moves (43%) or rook moves (16%), indicating the correct plan was to improve piece placement rather than rashly advance pawns. These are positional endgame blunders where a tempting pawn push destroys the structural or king-safety foundation of the position.

1278.label: Playing a passive or purposeless move that leaves a piece undefended against a concrete tactical threat.
1278.description: This feature identifies moves where the player makes a non-capturing, non-checking move (100% no capture, 0% check) — typically with the queen or king — that ignores an immediate tactical threat on the board. The material signature shows 38% of these moves directly hang a piece, while the remainder appear 'safe' only superficially before the opponent exploits the position. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 363 centipawns, with 38% going from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to drawn, indicating these are game-changing oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing material (queen captures 62%, rook 25%, knight 12%), confirming that the correct response was to address a tactical obligation — take a piece, defend against a fork, or otherwise respond to the threat. The Opus analysis reinforces this with tags like 'tempo_loss' (3 occurrences), 'hanging_piece' (3), and 'fork' — the player wastes a tempo on an aimless move (e.g., Ka3 instead of saving a knight, Ke4 walking into a check, Ne4 ignoring a knight fork) while the opponent has a concrete tactical shot available. The pattern is a player who drifts with a quiet move when the position demands immediate tactical attention.

1279.label: Playing a flashy check (often a pawn or bishop sacrifice) that leaves material hanging instead of pursuing a stronger continuation.
1279.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) — most often with a pawn (73%) or bishop (27%) — that results in material being hung (55%) or lost (64% net negative outcomes, median -1.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these checks are costly but not always game-ending: 64% remain winning→winning (suggesting a squandered advantage rather than immediate loss), while 36% cross critical thresholds (drawn→losing or winning→losing), with a median of 251 centipawns lost. The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and passed_pawn (33%), indicating the player is lured into delivering a check — often a Greek Gift Bxh7+ or a pawn advance like h5+ or f4+ — that appears to attack the enemy king or create threats, but is premature or misordered. The Opus analyses confirm this: one position shows a catastrophic move-order error with Bxh7+ before the necessary preparatory Nxf6+, another shows h5+ allowing a safe king retreat when a diagonal check was far superior. The player prioritizes the forcing nature of check over the soundness of the attack, hanging material in the process.

1283.label: Passive piece retreats or exchanges that squander a tempo-based advantage, turning winning or drawn positions into significantly worse ones.
1283.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes a positional retreat or simplifying exchange that loses critical tempo, costing a median of 252 centipawns. The material signature shows mostly safe or trade outcomes (no outright blunders of material), yet the eval trajectory reveals devastating positional consequences: 38% turn drawn positions into losing ones and 25% throw away winning positions. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (33%) and hanging_piece (33%)—combined with tags like rook_endgame, passed_pawn, and king_activity paint a picture of moves that voluntarily surrender initiative. The concrete examples reinforce this: a king retreating from an aggressive square (Kb3 instead of exploiting Re4), a bishop retreating to a passive square (Ba4-d7 missing Qxb4), trading away a key constraining piece (Bxc5 releasing positional pressure). These are not calculation errors per se, but failures to maintain tension and exploit tempo-sensitive advantages, particularly in middlegame positions (75%) where initiative is paramount.

1282.label: Moving a bishop (or knight) to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable, hanging material in the middlegame.
1282.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where the player moves a minor piece (bishop 67%, knight 33%) to a square that leaves it or another piece hanging, resulting in significant material loss (median net material: -2.0, with 50% classified as 'hangs'). The eval trajectory shows devastating consequences: 50% of cases shift from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 238 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), supported by tags like missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and piece_activity—indicating the player actively repositions a piece but overlooks that the destination square is tactically compromised (attacked, pinned, or forkable). The top boards confirm this: pieces land on squares attacked by opponent forces (e.g., Bb5 into a pin, Nc8 into a hanging square, Bg5 leaving material loose). In every case, a clearly superior tactical continuation existed (100% missed winning material), often a capture or check that would have maintained or improved the position. The error is fundamentally about piece placement that ignores immediate tactical threats to the moved piece.

1284.label: Advancing a passed pawn with check before it's ready, allowing blockade or neutralization and squandering a winning advantage.
1284.description: This feature fires on pawn advances (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) that often deliver check (86%) but result in hanging material (57%) or merely safe but ineffective moves (43%), with a median cost of 203 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently throw away winning positions (winning->drawn 14%, winning->losing 14%, drawn->losing 14%). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: premature advances of passed pawns (promotion_error 29%, premature_advance tag appears 3 times) that give tempting but hollow checks (premature_check tag, tempo_loss 43%). The concrete positions confirm this—e6-e7+ allowing permanent blockade by ...Ke8, h3-h2+ checks that drive the king to safety while the pawn becomes useless, and f3-f2+ enabling a saving bishop sacrifice. In each case, the player pushes a dangerous passed pawn one square too early (often with check), allowing the opponent to neutralize what was a decisive positional asset. The 'threat was stronger than the execution' principle applies throughout.

1285.label: Trading queens when a stronger tactical continuation (fork, diagonal attack) would have won decisive material.
1285.description: This feature fires on positions where the player initiates a queen trade (queen moved 100%, queen captured 100%, check delivered 100%) that results in an equal material exchange (net 0.0), but squanders a winning advantage—median eval loss of 342 centipawns, with trajectories going from winning to winning (diminished) or winning to drawn. The tactical analysis reveals that in each case a superior non-simplifying move existed: a knight fork winning the opponent's queen (tagged knight_fork, fork motif), a diagonal attack exploiting queen vulnerability (Ba3 type moves), or similar tactics that would have converted the advantage decisively. Instead, the player chose a routine simplifying queen exchange that eliminated the very target or tension that made the tactic work. The recurring tags—premature_simplification, missed_tactic, move_order_error—confirm this is a pattern of cashing in too early via a queen trade rather than first executing the winning combination. Maia's preferred moves (knight 67%, bishop 33%) represent exactly those missed tactical shots.

1286.label: Player makes a routine developing move in the opening while leaving a bishop completely undefended and en prise to an opponent's bishop.
1286.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player makes a natural-looking developing move (castling, pushing d4, playing Re8, or moving a knight) while completely ignoring that their bishop is undefended and directly attacked. The material signature shows 100% hangs with a median loss of 3.0 (a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (drawn->losing 88%, winning->losing 12%) with a median loss of 483 centipawns. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies hanging_piece as the motif, with tags like undefended_piece, undefended_bishop, ignored_threat, and opening_trap reinforcing the pattern. The concrete positions reveal a recurring Italian Game / Two Knights structure where a bishop on c4 or c5 is left unprotected while the player plays a standard move (d4, O-O, Re8, Ng4), allowing the opponent's bishop to simply capture it for free. Maia's response is always a bishop capturing a bishop. This is not a complex tactical oversight but rather a fundamental failure to notice a direct one-move threat to an undefended piece during the opening phase.

1288.label: King moves instead of capturing an undefended queen with a knight in drawn endgames.
1288.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures) in a position that is objectively drawn, but misses a critical knight capture of an undefended or hanging queen (Maia's move is 100% knight capturing queen). The material signature shows 'safe' moves (nothing immediately hangs from the move itself), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows drawn->losing swings (median 331cp lost), indicating the player failed to recognize the one saving/winning tactic available. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece as the dominant motif (40%), with tempo_loss as the most common tag—the king move wastes a critical tempo while the opponent's queen remains en prise to the knight. The boards show classic queen-vs-knight endgames where the knight has exactly one correct square (capturing the queen) but the player retreats or advances the king instead, transforming a theoretical draw into a hopeless loss.

1287.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move instead of delivering a check or checkmate sequence, squandering a decisive king-safety advantage.
1287.description: This feature fires when a player has a winning mating attack available (Maia's recommended move is a check 100% of the time, most often with the queen) but instead plays a quiet rook, knight, or pawn move that neither checks nor captures. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame scenarios (87%) where the opponent's king is exposed or vulnerable. The dominant motif is king_safety (62%), reinforced by tags like 'exposed_king', 'missed_mate', and 'mating_attack_missed'. The material outcome of the actual move is usually safe (56%) or outright hangs a piece (30%), meaning the player either did nothing useful or actively worsened their position. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 503 centipawns, with 22% of cases converting a winning position into a losing one and 13% going from winning to drawn—classic signs of throwing away a decisive attack. The concrete examples confirm this: players move rooks to irrelevant squares, grab peripheral pawns with their queen, or make king moves while a forced checkmate or devastating check sequence sits one move away. The mistake is fundamentally a failure to recognize and execute the available mating attack against an exposed king.

1289.label: Moving the queen to a passive square that exposes the king to tactical sequences involving forks or forcing checks.
1289.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves their queen (83% queen moves) to a square that appears safe (50% safe, 50% hangs) but fatally exposes the king to tactical punishment. The dominant motifs are forks (50%) and king safety issues (25%), with recurring tags of knight_fork, exposed_king, and forced_queen_exchange. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 363 centipawns), often converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones. Maia consistently responds with king moves (100%), suggesting the opponent's forcing sequences drive the king into vulnerable squares after the queen retreats. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows queens retreating to passive squares (e2, d2, g2, b3) where they no longer protect critical squares around their king, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly exposed monarch with forks, checking sequences, or piece-winning tactics. This is not a material blunder in the direct sense—the queen isn't immediately captured—but rather a positional-tactical error where the queen's relocation creates a tactical vulnerability the opponent exploits.

1291.label: In drawn endgames, the player moves their king to an unsafe square, leaving a piece hanging to a rook check or capture.
1291.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder pattern where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a drawn position, inadvertently leaving a major or minor piece undefended (hanging_piece motif 100%, material outcome 'hangs' 100%). The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions collapsing into lost ones (drawn->losing 100%, median loss ~869cp, roughly a full rook). Maia's response is always a rook capture with check (rook move 100%, captures rook 100%, gives check 100%), indicating the opponent exploits the hanging piece with a forcing move. The tactical pattern is clear from the board positions: in rook endgames, the player prioritizes king activity or captures a less important piece (tempo_loss, wrong_priority tags) while overlooking that their king move exposes a critical piece to a rook check-capture combination. The player's king wanders into a square that allows the opponent's rook to simultaneously check and win material.

1293.label: Delivering check or attacking a suboptimal target instead of finding the strongest continuation, often missing a winning tactic.
1293.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check or captures a less valuable target when a stronger tactical continuation exists. The material signature shows checks given 67% of the time with a median net material loss of -4.0, indicating these checks are not productive. The eval trajectory shows 67% losing->losing with a median 219 centipawns lost, meaning the player makes an already difficult position significantly worse by choosing a flashy but incorrect move. The tactical analysis reveals recurring tags of 'check_is_not_always_best', 'piece_priority', and 'missed_tactic'—the player is seduced by giving check or hitting an obvious target (like capturing a rook with check instead of taking a queen, as in the first example) rather than calculating the strongest line. The boards consistently show positions with active pieces where multiple forcing options exist, but the player picks the wrong one, often a check that allows the opponent to escape or a capture of the wrong piece. This is fundamentally a tactical pattern-matching error where the allure of check or an obvious target overrides proper calculation.

1292.label: Sacrificing the queen for a meaningless check that yields no follow-up attack or compensation.
1292.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: the player delivers a check with the queen (92% checks, 88% queen moves) that results in catastrophic material loss (median net material: -8.0, with 52% hangs and 44% loses). The checks are superficial—they look aggressive but lead to nothing: no mating attack, no sustained pressure, no tactical follow-up. The Opus analysis confirms this with tags like 'superficial_check', 'premature_simplification', and 'counterplay_elimination', where players trade away their most powerful piece for trivial material (a rook, knight, or nothing at all) simply because the move comes with check. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 209 centipawns, often converting playable or even winning positions into losses (winning->losing 12%, drawn->losing 12%), though many occur in already-losing positions (losing->losing 32%) where the player desperately throws in a flashy but futile check. The concrete positions confirm queens lunging to back ranks or king-adjacent squares, capturing defended pieces with check but allowing easy recaptures that leave the player down a full queen's worth of material.

1296.label: Trading queens when the opponent's king is exposed, squandering a winning attack.
1296.description: This feature fires on positions where a player initiates a queen trade (100% queen moved, 100% queen captured, net material median 0.0 confirming an exchange rather than a blunder) while holding a winning or near-winning position. The eval trajectory shows these trades cost a median of 267 centipawns, with 67% going from winning to drawn—classic 'threw a win' signatures. The tactical layer reveals the unifying theme: king_safety is present in 100% of dominant motifs, with tags like 'premature_queen_trade', 'exposed_king_exploitation_missed', and 'attacking_opportunity_squandered'. Maia's recommended alternatives (queen moves with checks 67%, or non-queen captures) confirm that maintaining the queen on the board was critical to exploiting the opponent's exposed king. The concrete positions show Black kings stranded on f6, open files against castled kings, and other attacking configurations where simplification relieved all pressure. The player chose a safe-looking equal trade instead of pressing the attack with pieces still on the board.

1290.label: Knight captures a pawn hoping for a fork or attack but loses material due to the piece becoming trapped or tactically refuted.
1290.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a player moves a knight to capture a pawn (often on f2/f7 or e5), lured by the apparent tactical promise of a fork or king attack, but the knight sacrifice is unsound. The material signature shows knight captures pawn with a net loss of ~2 pawns (slightly_down), meaning the knight is lost or trapped after the capture — it's not an even trade but a speculative sacrifice with insufficient compensation. The eval trajectory confirms these occur in already-losing positions that become significantly worse (median 183cp lost), so the player is desperately lunging for tactics rather than addressing their deficit. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: pseudo-forks on f2/f7 that look threatening but are refuted (the opponent's pieces can simply sidestep or counter-attack), trapped knights that have no retreat squares after the capture, and positional errors where occupying a square prematurely allows the opponent to win material back with tempo. The boards consistently show Nxf2 'fork' attempts against the king and rook that fail because the queen relocates with threats, or Nxe5 captures that allow recapture gaining a full piece. These are opening-phase errors driven by pattern-matching to fork motifs without calculating the refutation.

1295.label: Player leaves their queen on a square where it can be captured for free or near-free by an opponent's minor piece.
1295.description: This feature fires overwhelmingly on positions where the player's queen (53% of moves played) ends up on a square where it is immediately hanging, with 79% of activations showing a 'hangs' material outcome and a median loss of 6.0 points (roughly queen value). The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with 'hanging_queen' appearing as a common tag. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings—21% go from drawn to losing and 10% from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 535 centipawns—consistent with dropping a queen outright. The concrete board examples reinforce this: queens placed on squares attacked by knights or bishops that the player simply overlooked (e.g., queen on c4 taken by a knight on e5, queen left en prise after castling). These are not sacrifices or trades but pure one-move oversights in the opening or middlegame where the player fails to notice a piece attacking their queen's destination or current square.

1297.label: Playing a flashy but non-forcing check that leaves the queen hanging to a simple recapture.
1297.description: This feature identifies positions where a player delivers a check (44% of activations) with their queen (36% queen moves) that appears active but is tactically hollow—the queen lands on a square where it can be trivially captured. The material signature is stark: 42% of moves hang a piece outright, with a median net material loss of -4.0 (roughly a queen's worth minus what was captured). The OPUS analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the universal motif (100%), with recurring tags like 'pointless_check', 'check_is_not_a_threat', 'queen_blunder', and 'rook_captures_queen'. The eval trajectory shows these are often game-deciding errors: winning->losing (17%), winning->drawn (11%), and drawn->losing (11%), with a median cost of 540 centipawns. The concrete positions reinforce this pattern—e.g., a queen checking on d4 directly in front of a rook on d8, or a queen moving to c8 while a back-rank piece captures it. The missed winning material rate (61%) confirms Maia saw far better alternatives. The player is seduced by the psychological force of delivering check, failing to notice the queen has no safe square afterward.

1294.label: Player makes a quiet developing or prophylactic move in the opening, missing a devastating bishop pin or diagonal exploitation that would win major material.
1294.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening-phase mistake where the player (usually White) plays a safe, non-capturing move—often a pawn push (c3, a4, b5) or a routine developing move (castling, rook repositioning)—while completely overlooking a crushing tactical opportunity involving a diagonal pin or bishop exploitation. The material signature shows 90% safe moves (nothing is hanging), yet 100% of positions involve missed winning material, with a median eval loss of 361 centipawns, often converting winning positions into drawn ones (50% winning->drawn). The dominant motif is 'pin' (57%), supported by tags like pin_to_king, diagonal_exploitation, queen_trapped, and deflection. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly bishop moves (90%), confirming that the correct tactic nearly always involves placing a bishop on a key diagonal to pin a high-value piece (usually the queen) to the king. The positions consistently feature open diagonals in the opening where a bishop sacrifice or pin would win the queen or decisive material, but the player instead chose a slow positional or prophylactic continuation, blind to the one-move tactical shot.

1300.label: Advancing or exchanging a pawn that fatally ruptures the player's own pawn structure or chain in a winning/drawn position.
1300.description: This feature fires on pawn moves (62% of activations) in middlegame/endgame positions where the player destroys their own pawn structure or chain, converting a drawn or winning position into a losing one. The eval trajectory is devastating: 62% go from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 416 centipawns—indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but catastrophic positional collapses. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (50%) or hangs (25%), meaning the damage isn't from immediate piece loss but from structural deterioration that creates unstoppable passed pawns or breakthroughs for the opponent. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs include pawn_endgame (33%), positional_mistake (22%), and passed_pawn (22%), with recurring tags of pawn_structure, tempo_loss, and patience_required. Concrete examples include gxf6+ destroying a winning pawn chain, h5 throwing away a won pawn endgame, c5 allowing a forced pawn breakthrough with en passant, and b5 ruining a won king-and-pawn position. The common thread is impatience—pushing or exchanging a pawn that was the structural backbone of the position.

1299.label: Advancing a pawn in a king-and-pawn position that squanders a winning advantage by losing critical tempo or creating fixable weaknesses.
1299.description: This feature detects pawn advances in endgame and middlegame positions—particularly pawn endgames—where the player pushes a pawn (83% pawn moves) that appears safe (67% safe material outcome) but catastrophically mishandles the position. The eval trajectory shows these moves predominantly convert winning positions into draws (67% winning->drawn) with a massive median cost of 314 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (75%) and tempo_loss (25%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, pawn_structure, and positional errors. The concrete positions show king-and-pawn endgames where the player pushes g-pawns or h-pawns (g4, h5, g3) that either allow the opponent to equalize via king activity or destroy their own pawn structure's zugzwang potential. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves that deliver check (100%), suggesting the correct continuation involved more aggressive pawn advances with tempo, while the player's passive pawn push lost the thread of the position. This is the classic endgame mistake of playing a 'natural' pawn move that looks safe but irreversibly ruins the win.

1298.label: Knight (or minor piece) moves that look aggressive but fatally compromise position by losing tempo or abandoning key defensive duties.
1298.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make seemingly active minor piece moves—predominantly knight moves (67%) and occasional bishop moves (33%)—that appear aggressive or forcing but actually hemorrhage position value. The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' in the immediate sense (nothing is directly hung), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: median 381cp lost, with positions collapsing from drawn-to-losing (67%) or winning-to-losing (33%). The tactical analyses reveal the common thread: these are tempo-losing piece lunges (often checks or attacks that accomplish nothing) that either abandon critical defensive squares (enabling king-side attacks) or misplace pieces where they have no real follow-up. Examples include a knight jumping to h5 losing tempo, a bishop leaping to e4 where it gets chased, and a knight hopping to a5 away from the action. The boards confirm opening/early middlegame positions (67% opening phase) where development and piece coordination matter most, and one impulsive piece jump squanders the entire position despite no immediate material loss.

1301.label: Voluntarily moving a piece away from a square where it threatened or enabled a winning tactical fork.
1301.description: This feature fires when a player repositions a minor piece (knight or bishop, occasionally queen) away from an active square, unknowingly abandoning a concrete fork or combination that the piece enabled. The material signature shows non-captures (100% no capture) that are mostly 'safe' superficially (72%) but cost a median of 290 centipawns—indicating the move isn't an outright blunder of material but a missed tactical opportunity. The dominant motif is 'fork' (50%), and the Opus analyses repeatedly describe scenarios where the moved piece was the lynchpin of a fork threat (e.g., Nxd5+ fork, Bxe6 tactics). Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly captures (100% capturing a pawn), often with check (28%), confirming the player missed a concrete tactical strike. The eval trajectory (33% winning→drawn, 33% drawn→losing) shows these are game-changing moments where an advantage evaporates because the player passively retreated or repositioned a piece that was already optimally placed to execute a tactic. The positions cluster in Sicilian/Italian-type middlegames and openings with pieces aimed at e6/d5, where one precise capture would have exploited the position.

1302.label: Player makes a quiet or inferior move when a decisive tactic (back-rank mate, fork, or winning capture) was available, throwing away a winning or equal position.
1302.description: This feature fires on positions where the player had a concrete winning tactic available—most commonly a back-rank checkmate, a knight/queen fork, or a hanging piece capture—but instead played a quiet or suboptimal move (often a king move, rook retreat, or wrong capture). The material signature shows the moves themselves are mostly 'safe' or involve trades, meaning the player didn't necessarily blunder a piece outright, but the critical cost is in the missed opportunity: 85% of the time they missed winning material, and Maia's suggested moves frequently deliver check (62%). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-turning errors with a median loss of 252 centipawns, and 31% convert a winning position into a drawn one. The tactical motifs (back-rank mate, fork geometry, missed queen captures) reveal that the winning resource was sharp and concrete—a one-move tactic the player simply overlooked. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame, where complex positions mask these short tactical shots. In essence, the player had a knockout punch available but threw a jab instead, squandering decisive advantage.

1303.label: Developing or moving a minor piece to a square where it is easily expelled or accomplishes nothing, losing critical tempo and leaving central pawns undefended in the opening.
1303.description: This feature detects a recurring opening-phase mistake (94% opening) where players move minor pieces (bishops 34%, knights 26%) or pawns (28%) to squares that waste tempo and leave material hanging (62% hangs, median -1.0 material). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (62%), with hanging_piece (25%) as the consequence: the moved piece either gets immediately expelled (like Ng4 kicked by h3) or abandons defense of a central pawn (like Nf6 leaving e5 undefended). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-altering errors (median 265cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing (40%) or winning to drawn (18%). Maia consistently recommends simple pawn moves (100% pawn), suggesting the correct play was straightforward central pawn defense or advancement rather than the premature piece sortie. The top positions all share the pattern of a player ignoring concrete central tension to make a developing move that either hangs a center pawn or places a piece where it must immediately retreat, squandering opening tempo at a critical moment.

1305.label: Moving the knight away from e4 in Stafford-like positions, allowing White's queen on e2 to discover an attack winning the piece back with interest.
1305.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern: Black has a knight on e4 and White has a queen on e2 with a knight on e5, creating a latent discovered attack along the e-file targeting Black's king. In all top-activating positions, the player moves their knight (100% knight moves), retreating or redirecting it to squares like f6, g5, d2, or f2, failing to recognize that the queen on e2 will exploit the opened e-file once the knight vacates e4. The discovered attack motif dominates (80%), and the eval trajectory universally shows drawn->losing with a median loss of 458 centipawns—essentially losing a queen's worth of material. The phase is exclusively opening (100%), and Maia consistently recommends queen moves (100%), suggesting the correct defense required keeping the queen safe or addressing the e-file pin. The positions closely resemble the Stafford Gambit or Petrov's Defense traps where Black must find the only move (often ...Qe7) to block the discovered attack, but instead carelessly moves the knight, walking into catastrophic material loss.

1304.label: Player makes a safe but passive rook/king move in a winning endgame, missing a forcing check (often a skewer or back-rank tactic) that would have won decisive material.
1304.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player holds a winning or large advantage but plays a quiet, 'safe' move (100% safe material outcome, no captures in 76% of cases) instead of the critical forcing continuation. Maia consistently recommends a rook or queen move that delivers check (100% Maia gives check), typically exploiting a skewer along a rank/file or a back-rank vulnerability. The dominant motifs—skewer (33%), back_rank (22%), and tempo_loss (22%)—reveal that the missed resource is almost always a geometric tactic involving the rook checking the king and then winning material on the follow-up. The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly 'throwing a win' situations: 47% go from winning to drawn and 6% from winning to losing, with a massive median eval loss of 471 centipawns. The rook_endgame tag (7 occurrences) and endgame phase (59%) anchor this in simplified positions where the player's passive king or pawn move squanders a decisive advantage by giving the opponent time to consolidate, rather than delivering the decisive check that exploits piece alignment.

1308.label: Trading a well-placed piece that gifts the opponent dangerous passed pawns or strengthens their pawn structure.
1308.description: This feature fires on piece exchanges (100% trades, median net material 0.0) where the player initiates a knight or bishop capture that, while materially equal, creates or strengthens the opponent's passed pawns. The eval trajectory shows these trades are costly (median 207cp lost), typically worsening already difficult positions (67% losing->losing, 33% drawn->losing). The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (57%) and pawn_endgame (29%), with recurring tags of pawn_structure and piece_exchange_error. The concrete positions consistently show scenarios where a player trades off an active minor piece (knight on b6, bishop on e4, knight on strong outpost) only to discover the recapture creates connected passed pawns or removes a key blockader. Maia's alternatives (100% non-captures) suggest the correct approach was to maintain the piece rather than initiate the exchange. The mistake is positional/endgame blindness: failing to calculate the pawn structure consequences of an apparently equal trade.

1306.label: Pushing a pawn that ignores an urgent tactical demand elsewhere, surrendering tempo and allowing the opponent's pieces to dominate.
1306.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a pawn move (50% pawn, with bishop/knight moves also appearing) that is objectively safe in immediate material terms (75% safe, median net material 0.0) but catastrophically misses the point of the position. The eval trajectory shows massive damage (median 288cp lost), with 30% going from drawn to losing and 20% from winning to drawn — these are game-changing errors. The Maia recommendations (45% queen, 45% rook moves) reveal that the correct responses involved activating major pieces to address urgent tactical needs. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: tempo_loss and piece_activity are the dominant tags, with players making moves that ignore pressing threats (e.g., a trapped piece, an undefended bishop, a knight invading) in favor of irrelevant pawn advances or pawn captures that open dangerous lines. The examples consistently show pawn pushes (b5, e4, b4, c5, d6) that either open fatal diagonals, ignore urgent piece rescues, or surrender the initiative by failing to address active enemy pieces. The mistake is fundamentally positional/strategic — choosing a slow pawn move when the position demands immediate piece action.

1307.label: Developing a bishop to a fianchetto square in the opening while leaving material undefended, turning an equal position into a lost one.
1307.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase positions (100%) where the player moves a bishop (100% bishop moves) — typically fianchettoing to g7, b7, or b2 — without capturing anything, yet the move immediately hangs material (100% 'hangs' outcome, median -3.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these moves uniformly convert drawn positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 572cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (71%), with common tags including missed_tactic, piece_activity, and development errors. The concrete pattern from the top boards reveals players routinely fianchetto bishops (Bg7, Bb7, Bb2) or make other bishop development moves in the opening without noticing that the long diagonal or piece placement leaves something tactically undefended — often because the fianchetto square was already controlled by the opponent or because the move neglects a concrete threat. The positions show hypermodern/fianchetto structures where the natural-looking developing move is actually a blunder because it ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability elsewhere on the board.

1309.label: Promoting a pawn to a queen when an underpromotion or preparatory move was required, allowing the opponent to equalize or gain a decisive tempo.
1309.description: This feature fires on pawn promotion errors in endgame positions (66% endgame, 34% middlegame) where the player automatically promotes to a queen without considering the tactical consequences. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures, yet 91% of these moves hang material (median net loss of -4.0, i.e., roughly a queen's worth), indicating the newly promoted queen is immediately lost or the promotion allows a devastating counterattack. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing blunders (median 444cp lost), frequently collapsing winning positions into draws (28% winning->drawn) or converting drawn positions into losses (19% drawn->losing). The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'promotion_error' (88%) as the dominant motif, with the concrete positions showing patterns where promoting to a queen allows back-rank tactics, captures with check on key diagonals, or immediate rook captures of the new queen. Maia's recommended moves (59% rook moves, 12% king moves) suggest the correct approach was often to improve piece placement, neutralize enemy passed pawns, or choose an underpromotion before committing to the promotion.

1311.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square where it can be captured by an opponent's piece or pawn, losing significant material.
1311.description: This feature fires when players make moves (predominantly rook moves, but also knight and pawn moves) that leave a piece hanging on an undefended square, allowing the opponent to capture it for free. The material signature shows 40% of moves result in a hang (non-capture that drops a piece) with no captures being made by the player, while Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing material (knight captures 100%), confirming that the opponent had a winning capture available. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of positions, with tags including hanging_queen, undefended_piece, and queen_blunder. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 377 centipawns, with 40% of cases converting drawn positions to losing ones and 20% throwing away winning positions to draws—consistent with simply dropping a piece. The concrete examples confirm this: a queen moved to c4 overlooking it was attacked by both a rook and pawn, pieces relocated to squares controlled by the opponent without adequate defense. These are not exchange decisions or positional subtleties, but straightforward tactical oversights where the player fails to notice their piece is en prise after the move.

1310.label: Retreating an active piece instead of executing a winning fork or tactic, throwing away a winning or equal position.
1310.description: This feature fires on positions where the player retreats or passively repositions an active piece (often a knight or queen) instead of executing a devastating tactical blow—most commonly a fork. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (89% safe, 100% no capture) that aren't immediately losing material themselves, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional collapse: 56% winning->drawn and 22% winning->losing, with a median loss of 397 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is a missed fork (50%) combined with king safety neglect (50%), with tags like 'tactical_blindness', 'knight_retreat', and 'misplaced_knight' recurring. The concrete positions show knights pulled back from dominant outposts (e.g., Ne4->Nd6 missing Nd2 fork, Nf3->Nh2 creating a passive target), or queens/pieces relocated to inferior squares when a crushing tactic was available. The Maia recommendations (44% knight moves, often non-capturing) suggest the correct move involved keeping the piece active or delivering the fork. This is fundamentally a tactical blindness pattern where the player instinctively retreats rather than calculating the winning combination sitting on the board.

1312.label: King moves in endgames that hang material or fatally compromise the position due to elementary oversights.
1312.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of catastrophic king moves in endgame positions. The material signature shows 64% king moves that predominantly hang pieces (57%) with a median material loss of -1.0, occurring almost exclusively in endgames (93%). The eval trajectory reveals these mistakes are devastating—median 450 centipawns lost—often converting drawn positions into lost ones (36%) or making already losing positions hopeless (43%). The tactical analysis confirms this through king_safety and hanging_piece motifs: kings stepping onto attacked squares, making tempo-losing moves when immediate action (like promotion) was critical, or abandoning defensive duties. The concrete positions show kings wandering to unsafe squares (Kh2 losing a critical tempo, Ke7 delaying promotion, kings walking into discovered attacks), all representing elementary oversight-level blunders where the player's king move either directly hangs a piece or fatally misses a one-move threat in simplified positions.

1313.label: Moving a piece that was the sole defender of another valuable piece, leaving it hanging and losing massive material.
1313.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves a piece (most often a knight or queen) that was serving as the critical defender of another high-value piece, leaving that piece completely unprotected. The material signature shows 42% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full piece), while Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing a rook (55%) or delivering check (98%), confirming that the opponent immediately exploits the newly undefended piece. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 33% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 818 centipawns, indicating these are decisive blunders that throw away won games. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), with specific examples showing knights moved away from defending queens, queens moved away from defending knights, and bishops moved away from critical defensive squares. The back_rank motif (30%) represents a secondary pattern where the abandoning move also exposes a back-rank vulnerability that enables the winning tactic. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (89%) where piece coordination is complex and the defensive role of a piece is easy to overlook.

1315.label: Player makes a developing or king move in the opening that leaves a piece undefended, allowing the opponent to win material via tactics.
1315.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player makes a seemingly natural developing move (often a king move like castling, or a bishop move) but overlooks that it leaves a piece hanging or misses a critical tactical opportunity. The material signature shows 100% missed winning material, meaning the opponent always had a strong tactic available. The eval trajectory is devastating—67% of the time converting a winning position into a losing one, with a median loss of 363 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece and missed_tactic as the dominant tags, with tempo_loss and forks also appearing. The concrete positions reinforce this: castling into a position where a piece is hanging (e1g1 with queen exposed on the Italian), capturing a piece while leaving one's own queen undefended (Bxf3 allowing Nxd8+), or developing a knight to f3 while a piece hangs elsewhere. These are all opening-phase blunders where the player prioritizes development or king safety without noticing an immediate tactical vulnerability in their position.

1314.label: Player makes a passive move instead of playing a pawn fork that simultaneously checks the king and attacks a piece.
1314.description: This feature identifies positions where the player had a devastating pawn fork available (typically a pawn advance giving check while simultaneously attacking a rook or other piece) but instead played a slow, non-forcing move. The material signature shows the player's moves are predominantly pawns and rooks that are 'safe' (no material exchanged), while Maia consistently recommends a pawn move that delivers check — 100% of Maia's suggestions are pawn checks. The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the median eval loss is 295 centipawns, confirming these are significant tactical oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'fork' (50%) and 'pawn_fork' as the dominant motif, with concrete examples showing patterns like ...f5+ forking a king on e4 and a rook on g4, or c6+ exploiting an overloaded piece to force promotion. The top boards confirm a recurring structural theme: an enemy king exposed on a central file (often e4) with a rook nearby, where a single pawn advance creates a simultaneous check and piece attack. Players instead choose passive developing moves (Rbd8, a6, b6) that surrender the tactical opportunity.

1318.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that leaves a major piece en prise, converting a winning position into a losing one.
1318.description: This feature fires when a player holds a winning position but plays a passive, non-forcing move that hangs a piece (100% hangs in the material signature, median net loss of -5.0 material). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 83% of cases flip from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 1014 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (86%), and Opus analysis reveals a consistent pattern: the player had a decisive advantage but chose a slow or careless move (pawn push, king move, or misplaced bishop) while a critical piece—often a rook—was left undefended. Maia's responses are predominantly rook captures (67%) delivered with check (83%), indicating the opponent immediately exploits the hanging piece with tempo. Tags like missed_mate, rook_sacrifice_blunder, and move_order reinforce that these are positions demanding immediate tactical precision, where the player instead played a 'quiet' move that catastrophically overlooked a concrete threat to their own material.

1321.label: Player makes a quiet move while missing a knight fork that wins material.
1321.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful knight fork opportunity. The material signature shows that the player's actual moves are predominantly quiet (92% no capture) with rooks, knights, and queens, while Maia's recommended move is always a knight move (100%) that captures a pawn (88%) as part of a forking sequence. The tactical analysis confirms that forks are the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with knight forks specifically tagged. The eval trajectory shows a severe cost (median 319cp lost), with many positions shifting from winning to drawn (23%) or drawn to losing (15%), indicating these missed forks were decisive tactical opportunities. The top boards consistently show knight fork possibilities—often Nc2+ forking king and rook, or Nxe6 forking queen and rook—where the player instead made natural-looking but aimless developing or defensive moves. The middlegame phase (90%) is consistent with complex tactical positions where knight forks thrive amid piece congestion.

1317.label: In the opening, player makes a developing or pawn move while ignoring an undefended enemy piece that could be freely captured.
1317.description: This feature consistently fires on opening-phase positions (100%) where the player makes a seemingly natural developing move—typically a pawn push (57%) or bishop move (29%)—while completely overlooking a hanging enemy piece. The Maia engine confirms this by showing it would capture a bishop in 100% of cases, and the 'missed winning material' flag triggers at 100%. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' across all positions, with recurring tags of missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and development, indicating players are so focused on their own development plan that they fail to scan for free captures. The eval trajectory is devastating: 71% of cases convert a winning position into a drawn one, with a median loss of 302 centipawns—essentially throwing away a full piece advantage. The concrete positions reinforce this: moves like f2-f3, c7-c6, or Be2 are played 'on autopilot' for development or pawn structure while an enemy bishop or knight sits undefended and capturable. The material outcome shows 'safe' (86%) because the move itself doesn't hang anything—the error is one of omission rather than commission.

1319.label: Player makes a non-capture move that leaves a piece undefended, allowing the opponent to win material via a simple capture.
1319.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move (most often a pawn push, but also knight, rook, or bishop moves) that is not a capture, yet immediately hangs material worth a median of 3 pawns (100% 'hangs' in the material signature). The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic blunders—75% turn drawn positions into losing ones and 25% throw away winning positions, with a median eval loss of 575 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the universal motif (100%), where the player either moves a piece to an undefended square, removes a critical defender, or ignores a tactical relationship (like a mutual attack) that the opponent can immediately exploit. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing the hanging piece (bishop 62%, queen 38%), often with check (38%). The boards show early opening and middlegame positions where players make developing or positional-looking moves while completely overlooking that they leave a piece en prise or remove a key tactical justification for their piece placement.

1320.label: Player gives a showy check instead of executing a winning combination, throwing away a decisive advantage.
1320.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) with a major or minor piece (queen 50%, rook 25%, bishop 17%, knight 8%) that hangs material (67%) or is merely safe but misses a far stronger continuation. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 490 centipawns, with many cases converting forced mates or winning positions into draws or even losses (winning->drawn 17%, losing->winning 17% from opponent's perspective). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant pattern: players choose a 'flashy' or 'natural' check over a quiet killer move (often a capture or positional squeeze), with tags like 'aimless_check', 'missed_mate', and 'missed_tactic' recurring throughout. Maia's recommended moves are non-checking (0% check rate) and frequently involve captures (pawn 50%, knight 17%, bishop 8%), confirming that the correct idea was a concrete material/mating threat rather than a pointless check. The boards show positions where devastating wins (mates in 4-18) were available but the player reflexively checked, allowing the opponent to escape. This is the classic 'patzer sees a check' syndrome—prioritizing forcing moves over winning moves.

1322.label: Player makes an unnecessary move instead of immediately promoting a passed pawn that delivers checkmate or wins decisively.
1322.description: This feature fires consistently on endgame positions where the player has a pawn one square from promotion (often on the 2nd/7th rank) but plays an irrelevant piece move instead of promoting immediately. The material signature shows safe or slightly-down moves with no captures—the player isn't losing material directly but is squandering a decisive advantage. The eval trajectory is dramatic: median eval lost is -10,817 centipawns, meaning forced checkmates are converted into merely winning or even losing positions. The dominant motif is 'promotion_error' (56%), with tags heavily featuring tempo_loss (7 instances) and passed_pawn (5 instances). The concrete positions all show pawns on c2, e7, f7, or g2 ready to promote, while the player instead moves a knight, king, bishop, or rook. Maia's suggested moves are 100% pawn moves (the promotions), often with check (67%). This is a classic endgame technique failure where the player loses sight of the simplest winning plan—push the pawn—and instead makes a 'useful-looking' but catastrophically slow alternative move.

1316.label: In a won KQ vs K endgame, the player advances the king instead of delivering immediate checkmate with the queen.
1316.description: All activating positions are trivially won King+Queen endgames where the player moves their king toward the opponent's king rather than using the queen for an immediate mating sequence. The material signature shows king moves 100% with no captures and a 'safe' outcome (nothing is lost), while Maia consistently recommends a queen move. The eval trajectory shows 0 centipawns lost, confirming the position remains winning - this is purely a technique inefficiency, not a blunder. The player appears to be slowly walking the king up to assist with a mating net when the queen alone (or queen with minimal king support already in place) can deliver checkmate immediately. This is the classic amateur endgame mistake of not recognizing when the mating pattern is already available.

1325.label: Playing a safe-looking but passive move that squanders a winning advantage by missing a concrete tactical opportunity.
1325.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a materially safe move (91% safe, 0% captures) — typically a rook move (55%) or king move (18%) — that looks natural or consolidating but completely misses a winning tactic available to them. The eval trajectory shows these moves overwhelmingly throw away wins: 46% go from winning to drawn, 9% from winning to losing, and 18% from drawn to losing, with a massive median eval loss of 376 centipawns. The missed tactics (64% missed winning material) span multiple motifs — forks, hanging pieces, king safety exploits, and tempo gains — but the unifying pattern is that the player chose a passive, non-engaging move (like Rfd8 instead of capturing an undefended piece, or Rd7 instead of a crushing double attack, or Kg3 walking into mate) while Maia's recommended moves were active pieces making captures (36% bishop captures, 9% pawn captures, 9% rook captures) or delivering threats. The player consistently prioritizes quiet development or repositioning over concrete tactical resolution in the middlegame.

1326.label: Player captures a bishop with a pawn in the opening, missing a stronger tactical continuation that exploits a hanging or trapped piece.
1326.description: This feature identifies opening positions where the player makes a pawn capture of a bishop (pawn moved 100%, bishop captured 100%) that appears materially safe (net +3.0, consistent with winning a bishop) but misses a significantly stronger move—typically a knight capture (Maia recommends capturing a knight 100% of the time). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 328 centipawns, often converting a winning position into a drawn one (50% winning->drawn). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging pieces (80%) and trapped pieces (20%), with recurring tags of missed tactics, hanging pieces, and tempo loss. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: players grab an available bishop with a pawn while a more valuable tactical opportunity—such as exploiting a pinned, trapped, or hanging knight—goes uncollected. The move isn't a blunder in the traditional sense (material is gained), but it's the wrong capture order or wrong target, allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape with a piece that was otherwise lost.

1327.label: Player makes a passive or temporizing move instead of executing an available tactical capture that wins material.
1327.description: This feature detects positions where a player has a concrete winning capture available (typically a rook capture exploiting forks, overloaded defenders, or hanging pieces) but instead plays a passive, non-capturing move. The material signature shows 86% of the played moves capture nothing, while Maia's recommended moves capture pieces (bishop 34%, knight 31%, pawn 31%), confirming the player consistently missed available captures. The eval trajectory (median 286cp lost, with 28% winning->drawn) shows these are game-changing missed opportunities that squander winning advantages. The tactical analysis reinforces this: dominant motifs are forks (40%) and overloaded defenders (40%), with recurring tags of 'missed_tactic' and 'missed_capture'. The example positions consistently show a player choosing quiet queen retreats, temporizing rook moves, or pawn pushes when a forcing capture (often Rxd3 or Rxa2) would have won material through a tactical sequence. The player sees the tension but flinches from the critical blow.

1323.label: In a pawn endgame with passed pawns, the player wastes a critical tempo on an irrelevant move instead of racing their king or pawn to stop/promote.
1323.description: This feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (100%) where passed pawns are the dominant motif (80% of positions). The player's moves are predominantly pawn pushes (50%) or king moves (33%) that squander decisive tempo in pawn races. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences—median 669 centipawns lost—with games swinging from winning to losing (33%), winning to drawn (33%), or drawn to losing (33%), indicating these are game-deciding moments where one tempo determines whether a passed pawn promotes or is stopped. The tactical tags consistently show tempo_loss (6 occurrences), pawn_race (3), and wrong_capture (3). The concrete positions confirm this: capturing an irrelevant piece instead of racing the king to stop a passed pawn, taking with the wrong pawn and creating a passed pawn for the opponent, or pushing a pawn that allows the opponent's passer to queen first. The material signature shows 'safe' moves (67%) because these aren't hanging pieces—they're positionally catastrophic tempo wastes in time-critical pawn endings where the player fails to calculate the race correctly.

1324.label: Queen moves to an irrelevant square, abandoning a defensive or attacking duty near the king, allowing immediate mate or decisive tactical blow.
1324.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves their queen (100% queen moves) without capturing anything, and the move hangs material (net -1.0 median). The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%), back_rank (17%), and promotion errors (17%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, overloaded_defender, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show a consistent pattern: the queen is needed on a specific diagonal, rank, or square to prevent checkmate or maintain a critical tactical threat, but the player moves it elsewhere—often to capture a pawn or reposition unnecessarily. Examples include moving the queen off the a1-h8 diagonal allowing Qg7#, playing Qxc4 instead of Qc3, or delaying a promotion to make an irrelevant pawn push. Despite the eval trajectory showing winning->winning with 0.0 median centipawns lost (suggesting the engine still evaluates some as technically winning), the tactical analyses reveal catastrophic swings in several cases (forced mate, 9748cp swings), indicating the feature captures moments where the queen abandons its critical defensive or offensive function near the king.

1328.label: Player captures a queen immediately without first inserting a crucial intermediate check, losing significant material or positional advantage.
1328.description: This feature detects positions where a player executes a queen capture (material signature shows 100% queen capture resulting in a 'trade') but fails to insert a critical zwischenzug—typically an intermediate check—before completing the exchange. The OPUS analysis consistently identifies 'zwischenzug', 'intermediate_move', and 'move_order' as dominant tags, with tempo_loss as the primary motif. Players capture the queen directly when they should first play an in-between move (usually a check exploiting an exposed king) that saves an additional piece or gains decisive tempo. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 769cp), with positions going from winning to losing or becoming drastically worse, because by skipping the intermediate move the player effectively donates a piece for free. Maia's suggested moves frequently involve checks (100% give check), confirming that the missed resource was a forcing intermediate move before the trade. The net material median of 8.0 reflects that while both sides exchange queens, the failure to interpose the zwischenzug leaves a piece hanging, turning what should be a winning exchange sequence into a devastating material loss.

1329.label: Player makes a move completely ignoring an existing or imminent checkmate threat against their own king.
1329.description: This feature fires when a player executes a seemingly reasonable move—often a trade, capture, or positional maneuver—while completely overlooking a lethal mating threat already present on the board. The material signature shows 40% trades and 39% hangs, indicating the player is focused on exchanges or piece activity rather than defensive urgency. The king_safety motif appears in 100% of cases, with recurring tags like 'checkmate_in_one', 'checkmate_threat_ignored', 'ignored_mating_threat', and 'back_rank_adjacent' confirming the pattern. The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of -9324 centipawns—consistent with missing mate rather than a positional inaccuracy—and includes many winning->losing transitions. Maia's recommended moves (37% pawn, with 6% giving check and 84% non-captures) suggest the correct response was often a simple defensive move or block rather than a flashy tactic. The top board examples consistently show players capturing material, making queen moves, or pushing pawns while a forced mate along an open diagonal or back rank was already threatened and required immediate attention. This is fundamentally a tactical blindness to the opponent's mating geometry, not a material or positional misjudgment.

1330.label: Pawn or king moves that fatally weaken the player's own king position, squandering a winning or equal game.
1330.description: This feature fires when a player makes a pawn move (67%) or king move (17%) that catastrophically compromises their own king safety, typically in the middlegame. The material signature shows these are 'safe' non-captures (83%) — not blunders of hanging pieces, but positional self-inflicted wounds. The Opus analysis confirms king_safety as the universal motif (100%), with recurring tags like self_weakening_pawn_move, tempo_loss, and missed_mate. The concrete positions show moves like g2-g3 cracking open the king's pawn shelter, f4-f5 or g3-g4 advancing pawns that were shielding the king, and aimless king moves when forced mates were available. The eval trajectory (median 343cp lost, with winning→drawn 33% and drawn→losing 17%) confirms these moves throw away substantial advantages. Meanwhile, the engine's preferred move was consistently a queen move (100%), often delivering check (50%) — meaning the player ignored attacking continuations to instead make a passive or weakening move that invited the opponent's pieces (especially the queen) into the newly exposed king position.

1333.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move, missing a winning knight fork that checks the king and wins material.
1333.description: This feature consistently fires when a player overlooks a decisive knight fork. The material/position signature shows that the best move (Maia's recommendation) is a knight move delivering check 100% of the time, while the player instead makes a quiet pawn push, passive rook move, or irrelevant capture. The 'missed winning material' flag is triggered in 100% of cases, and the median eval loss of 194 centipawns confirms a significant tactical oversight rather than a subtle positional error. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'fork' as the dominant motif (83%), with tags like 'knight_fork', 'missed_tactic', and 'missed_knight_fork' reinforcing the pattern. The concrete positions show knight forks checking the king while simultaneously attacking a rook, winning material by force. The trajectory (66% winning->winning) indicates that these players are already ahead but fail to find the clean tactical blow, often choosing greedy pawn advances or passive moves instead of the crushing knight fork that would end the game decisively.

1335.label: Playing a slow, passive rook or king move that squanders a winning or drawn position by losing critical tempo.
1335.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'safe' move (94% no material lost immediately, 94% no capture) — typically a rook (39%) or king (32%) move — that loses substantial evaluation (median 224cp) primarily through tempo loss (50% dominant motif). The positions are concentrated in rook endgames and middlegame-to-endgame transitions (68% middlegame, 32% endgame), with recurring tags like rook_endgame, piece_activity, and passed_pawn. The trajectory shows these moves frequently convert winning positions to drawn (26%) or drawn to losing (13%), indicating the player had a concrete winning plan available (Maia recommends active rook moves 74% of the time, often with captures or checks) but instead chose a passive, non-committal move. The per-position analysis repeatedly highlights that the played move places a piece passively, surrenders invasion squares, or fails to centralize the king — all costing the tempo needed to convert an advantage in simplified positions.

1334.label: In endgames, plays a slow or purposeless move while leaving a piece (usually a rook) en prise to simple capture.
1334.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a non-capture move (100% no capture) that hangs material (71% hangs, median net material -5.0, i.e., roughly a rook). The tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'hanging_piece' (75%), and the OPUS summaries confirm the pattern: the player pushes a pawn, makes a king move, or repositions a piece while their own rook sits undefended and capturable. Maia's recommended move is almost always a rook capture (86% rook, 100% captures a rook), meaning the opponent's piece was freely available to take. The eval trajectory shows these are typically winning or at least tenable positions being squandered (median 243cp lost), with 43% winning->winning (still ahead but damaged) and 14% winning->losing. The common thread is a failure to notice or prioritize the most basic tactical requirement—defending or moving an attacked piece—while instead playing a slow positional or prophylactic move that ignores the immediate material crisis on the board.

1331.label: In open king positions during the opening, player develops quietly instead of delivering a crushing queen check that wins material.
1331.description: This feature fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player has a devastating queen check available (Maia recommends queen 100%, gives check 100%) but instead plays a non-forcing developing move (bishop 38%, pawn 19%, queen 19%, knight 19% — none giving check). The positions overwhelmingly arise from gambits like the Latvian where a pawn has been sacrificed, leaving the opponent's king fatally exposed on the e-file or h5 diagonal. The missed tactic (tagged in 7/8 examples) typically involves Qh5+ exploiting the absence of the f-pawn to win material via forced sequences (e.g., winning the h8 rook). The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 75% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 223 centipawns. The dominant motifs — king_safety (62%), tempo_loss (25%) — reflect that the quiet moves not only miss the kill shot but often allow the opponent to consolidate with tempo (e.g., d5 hitting a bishop on c4). The material signature shows these quiet moves are mostly 'safe' (81%) — the player isn't blundering a piece, they're simply failing to punish the opponent's exposed king with the available forcing check.

1336.label: Player makes a non-checking move that squanders a forced mate, typically choosing a capture or retreat instead of a decisive king attack.
1336.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position misses a forced checkmate sequence, instead playing a materially-oriented or passive move. The material signature shows the player moved minor pieces (bishop/knight) rather than the queen, while Maia consistently identifies the queen delivering check as the correct move. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic centipawn losses (median ~9471cp) while remaining nominally winning—consistent with converting a forced mate into merely a large advantage. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly flags king_safety (78%) as the dominant motif, with 'missed_mate' and 'missed_tactic' as recurring tags. The concrete positions show exposed enemy kings (often uncastled, hemmed in by their own pieces) where the player chose captures (Bxd8 instead of Qxd8#, Nxe4 instead of Qh5+) or retreats rather than prosecuting the attack with checks. The common thread is prioritizing material gain or piece repositioning over delivering the killing blow against a vulnerable king.

1332.label: In endgames with limited options, the player makes a king or minor piece move that appears safe but misses a forced winning capture or unique saving move, allowing immediate mate or decisive material loss.
1332.description: This feature captures a specific endgame catastrophe pattern.
