The material/position signature shows the player moved their king (67%) or bishop (33%) without capturing anything, and the move appeared 'safe' in material terms—nothing was immediately hung. However, Maia's suggested moves involved capturing a queen (67%) or making active moves, indicating a critical capture or tactic was missed (missed winning material: 100%). The eval trajectory is devastating: median loss of ~10,491 centipawns, with positions flipping from losing-to-winning (67%) or drawn-to-losing (33%), meaning the player had one narrow path to save or win the game and missed it entirely. The tactical analysis confirms this: positions featured hanging pieces that went uncaptured (43% motif), forced mates that were allowed, and scenarios where exactly one good move existed. The boards show simplified endgame positions (all endgame phase) where passive king retreats or bishop moves ignore hanging queens, miss promotion threats, or walk into forced mates. The common thread is a quiet-looking move in an endgame that catastrophically fails to exploit or defend against a concrete tactical resource.

1337.label: Moving a knight in the opening that leaves another piece (typically a bishop) undefended and hangable.
1337.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a knight (83% of activations) in a position where a bishop is left unprotected, causing a drawn position to become losing (100% drawn->losing, median 250cp loss). The top boards reveal a recurring scenario—most activations occur in Italian/Scotch-type positions (e.g., Bc4 on an open diagonal with knights on e4/f3) where the knight move abandons defense of the bishop. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (60%), with Opus summaries repeatedly noting that the bishop on c4 is left capturable by a pawn on d5. Rather than a positional subtlety, this is a concrete oversight: the player makes an aggressive or developing knight move without noticing it was the sole defender of a hanging piece. The phase is exclusively the opening, and Maia consistently recommends the bishop move (Bd3) that resolves the tension safely. The material signature ('hangs' 83%) confirms these are non-capture moves that simply drop material rather than losing exchanges.

1338.label: Slow king or piece moves in won endgames that squander tempo and allow the opponent to hold or complicate.
1338.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (most often a king move, sometimes a rook or pawn move) instead of the most efficient continuation. The material signature shows no captures and mostly safe moves (no material is hung), yet the median eval loss is 163 centipawns—indicating significant advantage is squandered through inefficiency rather than through dropping material. The phase is 100% endgame, and the dominant motif is tempo_loss (57%), with rook_endgame appearing in 6 of 7 tagged positions. The eval trajectory shows the majority go from winning to still-winning but with substantially degraded efficiency (e.g., mate-in-14 becoming mate-in-25), while some cross the threshold from winning to drawn or even losing. The concrete positions show simplified endgames (K+R, K+P, R vs R) where the player drifts with aimless king moves (Kd4, Ke3, Ke4, Kc6) or passive piece retreats instead of seizing the critical tempo with forcing moves like captures or promotion advances.

1340.label: King moves in endgame positions where capturing an enemy queen with a rook was the only winning move.
1340.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) instead of capturing a hanging or available enemy queen with a rook (Maia's recommended move is always rook captures queen, 100%). The material outcome of the actual move appears 'safe' in the immediate sense—nothing is lost on the move itself—but the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing from drawn to losing (median 9999 centipawns lost), indicating missed forced wins or draws turning into losses. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (57%), with tags like 'queen_capture_missed' and 'missed_tactic' reinforcing that a free or capturable queen was available. The top boards confirm this: simplified endgame positions with queens and rooks where the player's king temporizes while a rook capture of the queen was critical. In several cases, the missed queen capture was the unique path to a draw or win (e.g., enabling perpetual check or material dominance), and the king move instead allows the opponent to consolidate or deliver checkmate.

1339.label: Knight captures a pawn in the opening, leaving itself or another piece hanging and squandering a winning position.
1339.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a player's knight captures a pawn (material signature: knight moved 100%, captured pawn 100%) but the net material outcome is slightly down (median -2.0), indicating the knight or a supporting piece is lost in the aftermath. The eval trajectory consistently shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (100%, median 245cp lost), meaning these captures squander significant advantages. The tactical analysis confirms the core pattern: the knight lands on an exposed or unsupported square after the greedy pawn capture, leaving it hanging (67% hanging_piece motif) or trapped. Tags like 'material_greed' and 'released_tension' reinforce that the player is lured by a free pawn but overlooks that the knight becomes vulnerable — often recapturable by a pawn or attackable along a file/diagonal. The board examples consistently show knights jumping to central squares (e4, e5) to grab pawns in open positions, only to be immediately challenged or captured because supporting pieces were displaced or the knight's retreat squares are covered.

1344.label: Player moves a bishop while ignoring a knight fork that wins major material.
1344.description: This feature fires when a player makes a bishop move that completely ignores an active knight fork on the board, typically on f7. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves with no captures that hang material (median -6.0, consistent with losing a queen). The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% winning-to-losing swings with a median loss of 917 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: knight_fork appears in 5 of the tagged positions, and the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (56%) and fork (44%). The concrete positions overwhelmingly show a knight on f7 (or similar forking square) attacking the queen and rook/king simultaneously, where the player develops a bishop (Bb7, Bg7, Be6) or makes another bishop move instead of the only correct response—capturing the forking knight with the king (Kxf7). This is an opening-phase blunder where players prioritize development over addressing an immediate tactical threat.

1341.label: Moving the queen out early in the opening, losing tempo to opponent's developing attacks.
1341.description: This feature identifies a classic opening mistake: premature queen development that loses critical tempo. The material signature shows the player moves their queen 100% of the time, almost always without capturing (89% no capture), and the phase is overwhelmingly opening (98%). While 74% of moves are technically 'safe' in that nothing is immediately hanging, the eval trajectory reveals devastating positional consequences—a median loss of 276 centipawns with 55% of cases turning a drawn position into a losing one. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss 56%, with recurring tags like 'premature_queen_sortie', 'development', 'opening_principles_violation') confirm the pattern: the queen ventures out prematurely (Qh5, Qd5, Qf6, Qb6), gets attacked by developing minor pieces or pawns, and must retreat while the opponent gains multiple tempi for development. Maia's recommended alternatives are overwhelmingly minor piece moves (pawn 36%, knight 32%, bishop 19%), indicating the correct approach was calm development rather than aggressive queen forays. The top boards consistently show early queen moves to active-looking but strategically poor squares where they become targets.

1342.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive or active square, leaving another piece undefended and en prise.
1342.description: This feature captures moves where a player relocates a piece (often a bishop, knight, or pawn) without recognizing that the moved piece was performing a crucial defensive function—guarding another piece or controlling a key diagonal/square. The material signature shows 44% of moves result in a 'hangs' outcome (a non-capture that drops a piece), while Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing a bishop (71%) or knight (29%), indicating the opponent immediately wins the hanging material. The eval trajectory is severe: a median loss of 344 centipawns, with 28% of cases converting a drawn position to losing and 10% throwing a winning position to drawn. The Opus tactical analysis confirms this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (43%), supplemented by 'tempo_loss' (29%) and 'defensive_function_ignored' as a recurring tag. The concrete examples reinforce this: a bishop moves off a diagonal that was protecting a rook, a bishop lands on an unprotected square where it's immediately captured, or a piece relocates only to be trapped. The common thread is a single-move tactical oversight where the player fails to account for the defensive or protective role their piece was playing before moving it.

1343.label: King moves in lost endgames that worsen the position by losing tempo or abandoning defensive duties.
1343.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player is already losing (losing->losing 100%) and the move makes matters worse by a median of 80 centipawns. The material signature shows king moves (100%) that predominantly hang material (67%) rather than actively trading—indicating the king wanders to a square that allows the opponent to win material or gain decisive progress. The dominant motifs are king_safety (44%) and tempo_loss (22%), with tempo_loss appearing in 4/10 tagged positions, confirming that these king moves waste time rather than contributing to defense. The top boards show kings drifting to squares like b7, b6, a4, h4, and h2 where they either lose tempo in pawn races, expose themselves to tactical threats, or fail to contest critical squares. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%) instead—advancing or defending pawns—suggesting the correct plans involved pawn activity rather than king repositioning. This is a classic endgame error pattern: moving the king without purpose when concrete pawn play was required.

1345.label: Player makes a capture or move that leaves their own piece hanging to a tactical reply.
1345.description: This feature fires when players make moves (predominantly with rooks, bishops, or knights) that leave their own pieces en prise to tactical responses. The material signature shows 50% of moves 'hang' a piece and the median net material loss is -2.0, indicating substantial material hemorrhage. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly mistakes (median 461cp lost), often converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones (33% winning->drawn, 17% winning->losing). The Opus analysis unanimously identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (100%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, move_order errors, and premature checks. The pattern is consistent: players execute a superficially attractive move—a capture, a check, or a developing move—without first resolving or noticing that their own piece is tactically vulnerable. Maia's recommended moves typically involve captures (rook 33%, bishop 33%, knight 17%) that exploit the hanging piece, confirming the player overlooked a concrete tactical threat on the board before making their move.

1346.label: Minor tempo or move-order inaccuracy in a clearly winning endgame that doesn't meaningfully affect the outcome.
1346.description: This feature fires on positions that are already decisively winning (evaluations of +456 to +653) in endgames where the player makes a king or pawn move that is technically suboptimal but costs negligible material (median 0-1 centipawn loss). The positions are 100% endgame phase with the player maintaining a winning evaluation throughout. The material signature shows safe moves (nothing is hung or traded) where Maia recommends capturing a pawn with a bishop or making a different king move. The dominant motifs—passed pawns, tempo loss, pawn endgames, and move order—reveal that the 'mistakes' are almost always about optimal sequencing: whether to advance a passed pawn first, check before capturing, or position the king on the ideal square. The eval trajectory (winning->winning with ~1cp loss) confirms these are essentially irrelevant inaccuracies in positions where multiple moves win equally. The pattern captures the SAE detecting slight deviations from computer-perfect technique in trivially won endgames.

1347.label: Player makes an unsound sacrifice or exchange that trades away a key piece without sufficient compensation, turning a drawn or winning position into a losing one.
1347.description: This feature fires on positions where the player initiates an exchange or sacrifice (material outcome: 46% trade, 23% loses, 15% hangs) that is fundamentally unsound — typically trading away a critical defensive or attacking piece for inadequate compensation. The eval trajectory is devastating: 54% of cases swing from drawn to losing, and 23% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 318 centipawns. The moves involve knights (38%) and bishops (38%) being traded or sacrificed, often with a check (31%), giving the appearance of tactical activity. However, the dominant motifs — hanging_piece (43%), positional_mistake (29%), king_safety (29%) — combined with tags like unsound_sacrifice, trading_key_piece, and misjudged_exchange reveal that the player is misjudging the value of the exchange. Concrete examples include trading away a fianchettoed bishop that was the sole defender of light-square weaknesses, attempting a Greek Gift sacrifice without proper supporting pieces, and capturing pieces that leave other material hanging. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly quiet (77% non-captures, 0% checks), indicating that the correct approach was to maintain piece tension rather than force exchanges. The opening-heavy phase (77%) suggests these are premature tactical attempts before positions are ripe for combinations.

1349.label: Player moves a rook aimlessly when a decisive rook capture (often an exchange or hanging piece) was available.
1349.description: This feature fires in middlegame positions where the player is already winning but makes an aimless rook move instead of executing a clearly available rook capture. The material signature shows the player's rook move is technically 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet Maia consistently identifies a rook capturing a rook as the correct continuation. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain winning but hemorrhage a median of ~300 centipawns—substantial advantages squandered without the position flipping. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this: 60% of cases involve a hanging piece the player simply failed to take, and common tags include 'missed_exchange' and 'missed_tactic.' The concrete examples show patterns like missing Rxd1 to eliminate a defensive rook, ignoring Rxd7 capturing an undefended queen on an open file, or moving a rook away from the critical file. The player sees their rook, knows it should be active, but redirects it to a passive square rather than executing the winning capture that's right in front of them.

1350.label: Playing a passive or slow move when the position demands immediate concrete action, wasting a significant advantage.
1350.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a non-forcing, tempo-losing move that squanders a winning or drawn position. The material signature shows mostly safe moves (67%) with no captures (87%), indicating the player chose a quiet continuation rather than a forcing one. The eval trajectory is devastating: 53% of cases go from drawn to losing, and 27% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 228 centipawns—a massive positional squandering. The tactical analysis confirms tempo_loss as the universal motif (100%), with tags like 'attacking_chances_squandered' and 'concrete_over_slow' reinforcing that the player chose a slow plan (pawn pushes, piece retreats, or defensive regrouping) when the position demanded immediate tactical exploitation. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting the engine's recommended moves were also modest—but the key distinction is that the player's slow move was specifically the wrong slow move in a position requiring precision. The board positions show rich middlegame/opening positions with attacking potential (uncastled kings, piece activity) where the player drifted with a passive continuation instead of striking.

1351.label: Playing a slow or cosmetic piece move instead of executing or preventing a concrete tactical threat.
1351.description: This feature fires when players make seemingly reasonable but ultimately passive moves—often pawn pushes, knight redeployments, or bishop shuffles (pawn 25%, bishop 22%, rook 20%, knight 18%)—that miss a critical tactic available to them or their opponent. The material signature shows 83% non-captures with 35% hanging outcomes, indicating these moves frequently leave material undefended. Crucially, 100% of positions have missed winning material, and Maia consistently recommends bishop (55%) or knight (37%) moves that exploit concrete tactical opportunities like forks or captures. The eval trajectory (median 262cp lost, with 11% drawn->losing and 8% winning->drawn) confirms these are game-changing errors, not minor inaccuracies. The Opus analysis reveals the common thread: players choose moves that look active or logical on the surface (centralizing a knight, advancing a pawn, repositioning a rook) but miss forcing tactical sequences—knight forks, captures of loose material, or defensive necessities. Tags like 'wrong_piece,' 'pseudo_attack,' 'tempo_loss,' and 'missed_tactic' all point to the same syndrome: prioritizing cosmetic improvement over concrete calculation, allowing the opponent's threats to materialize or letting winning tactics slip away.

1348.label: King moves away from critical passed pawn duties (blocking or supporting) in endgames, allowing opponent's pawn to promote or one's own pawn to be lost.
1348.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player moves their king (62% of moves are king moves) in the wrong direction, abandoning its critical role relative to passed pawns. The positions are 100% endgame with passed pawns as the dominant motif (75%), and the common tags reveal blockade_failure (3), king_activity (4), and tempo_loss (3) as key themes. The material signature shows these are 'safe' moves (88%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 186 centipawns, indicating a severe positional/strategic cost rather than a tactical blunder. The player misses winning material 62% of the time, typically because the correct king move would have supported their own passed pawn or blocked the opponent's. The concrete positions consistently show king moves heading away from promotion squares (Ke4 instead of Ke6, Kc5 abandoning the kingside, Kd4 leaving b3 unblockaded), converting holdable or winning endgames into lost ones. The trajectory (75% losing→losing, 12% drawn→losing) confirms these mistakes mostly accelerate an existing disadvantage by misunderstanding the pawn race geometry.

1352.label: A passive pawn move that ignores a tactical opportunity, leaving material hanging or wasting a critical tempo.
1352.description: This feature detects pawn moves (95% of activations) in the opening and middlegame that fail to address urgent tactical demands on the board. The material signature shows 70% are 'safe' in isolation but 30% outright hang material, while Maia's recommended moves are diverse piece moves (knights 29%, bishops 19%, queens 12%) that would have captured or activated—indicating the player chose a slow pawn push over a concrete tactical solution. The eval trajectory is severe (median 276cp lost), with 17% dropping from drawn to losing and 13% from winning to drawn, confirming these are game-changing errors. The Opus motifs (67% hanging_piece, 22% tempo_loss) and example positions consistently show the player pushing a flank or secondary pawn (b4, b3, a3, f4, d4) while a piece is en prise or a critical capture/tactic was available. The pattern is a player defaulting to a 'developing' or space-gaining pawn move that completely ignores the tactical emergency, gifting the opponent material or decisive tempi.

1354.label: King moves that squander critical tempo in rook endgames with passed pawns, missing urgent rook activity.
1354.description: This feature fires on rook endgame positions where the player makes a purposeless king move (88% king moves) instead of the correct rook maneuver (Maia recommends a rook move 100% of the time). The positions universally involve passed pawns (either the player's or opponent's) where tempo is absolutely critical. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and passed_pawn (40%), and the tag 'rook_endgame' appears in nearly every example. The eval trajectory shows these tempo wastes are catastrophic—median 434cp lost—frequently converting drawn positions into losing ones (38%) or throwing away wins (12% winning->losing). The concrete pattern across all top boards is identical: a far-advanced passed pawn (often on the 7th rank) demands immediate rook action (checks, deflections, promotion support, or intermezzo tactics like Rg8+), but the player instead shuffles their king aimlessly, losing the one tempo that made the position tenable or winning.

1357.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square where it can be captured for free, overlooking the opponent's ability to take it.
1357.description: This feature identifies moves where a player relocates a piece (most often a bishop, but also rooks and knights) to a square where it is left undefended and can be captured outright. The material signature shows 'hangs' as the most common outcome (40%), with a median net material loss of -2.0, confirming that pieces are being given away without compensation. The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as a 100% dominant motif, with supporting tags like 'piece_left_undefended' and 'counting_error.' Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing the hanging piece (knight 60%, pawn 20%, rook 20%), showing the opponent has a trivial recapture available. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 372 centipawns, with outcomes spanning winning->losing, drawn->losing, and other catastrophic swings, indicating these aren't subtle positional errors but outright tactical oversights. The positions occur in opening and middlegame phases where piece activity is high and players fail to notice that their moved piece lacks protection or that their move leaves another piece en prise to a double attack.

1355.label: Rook or king moves in endgames that inadvertently leave pieces en prise to forks or tactical shots.
1355.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of endgame mistakes (67% endgame, 33% middlegame) where players move rooks (56%), queens (22%), or kings (22%) without capturing anything, yet hang material (56% hangs) with a median loss of 265 centipawns. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (33%), fork (22%), and tempo_loss (22%)—reveal that these moves either place pieces on undefended squares or walk into knight forks and tactical refutations. The eval trajectory shows these errors frequently throw away winning or drawn positions (winning->drawn 22%, winning->losing 22%, drawn->losing 11%), indicating players who had an advantage but made a careless non-forcing move that allowed the opponent a concrete tactical blow. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing material (knight 44%, bishop 33%, rook 22%), confirming that the missed resource was a simple capture or tactic the player overlooked. The concrete examples—a rook sacrifice check with no compensation, a king stepping onto a fork square, a rook move walking into mate, and passive rook maneuvers allowing the opponent favorable exchanges—all share the thread of aimless or impulsive piece movement in simplified positions that directly drops material to an elementary tactic.

1353.label: Player makes a slow or passive move that squanders a winning position by losing critical tempo.
1353.description: This feature captures positions where the player holds a winning or clearly advantageous position but plays a slow, non-forcing move (typically a rook or king move that captures nothing—88% no capture, 90% materially 'safe') instead of executing the decisive tactical blow. The eval trajectory confirms this: 34% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a massive median loss of 247 centipawns, indicating these are not minor inaccuracies but game-changing mistakes. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with players choosing passive repositioning moves over immediately decisive continuations. Maia's recommendations (66% rook moves, 27% giving check) show the engine wanted active, forcing play—often involving back-rank threats, exploiting overloaded defenders, or pushing promotion advantages—while the player drifted with quiet moves like pawn pushes (f5 instead of Rc2) or aimless piece shuffles. The endgame/middlegame phase split (29%/71%) and the concrete positions (rook endgames with passed pawns, positions with pins and back-rank motifs) confirm these are moments where one precise tempo decides the game, and the player fatally relaxes.

1356.label: Queen delivers a pointless or counterproductive check that abandons critical defensive/attacking duties, squandering a significant advantage.
1356.description: This feature captures a recurring middlegame mistake where the player moves their queen (59% of activations) to deliver a check (18%) or reposition it away from key squares, but the move is tactically hollow—typically a 'purposeless check' or an overextension that abandons king safety coverage (67% king_safety motif), back-rank defense (17%), or piece coordination. The material signature shows the move itself doesn't directly lose material in most cases (49% safe, 38% hangs), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional consequences: a median loss of 362 centipawns, with many positions shifting from winning to drawn/losing (10%+10%) or drawn to losing (18%). The Opus analysis consistently identifies deflection, tempo loss, and pointless checks as the mechanism—the queen check drives the opponent's king to a safer square or pulls the queen away from defending critical squares (back rank, kingside), allowing immediate tactical refutation. The best move (Maia's queen move 69%, often staying put or capturing) would have maintained the advantage by keeping defensive coverage intact rather than chasing illusory tactical gains.

1359.label: Playing a showy check that squanders a winning position by missing a stronger tactical continuation.
1359.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player delivers a check (86% of moves are checks) with a knight, rook, or queen, but this check is a suboptimal 'flashy' move that misses a much stronger tactic. The material signature shows that the checks themselves aren't always immediately losing material (43% safe), but 100% of positions have missed winning material, and the median eval loss is a massive 444 centipawns. The trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 57% winning->winning (still winning but much less so) and 29% winning->drawn, meaning the player had a dominant position and squandered it. The tactical motifs—king_safety, tempo_loss, and discovered_attack—reveal the mechanism: players are attracted to immediate checks that look aggressive but actually lose tempo or forfeit a stronger discovered attack or mating net. The Opus analyses explicitly describe choosing 'a flashy check over the superior move' and note how checks set traps but objectively ruin the position. Maia's preferred moves (queen 43%, rook 29%) often involve quiet but devastating continuations that the player overlooked in favor of the seductive check.

1358.label: Developing or moving a knight in the opening while leaving a more valuable piece (typically a queen) undefended, resulting in immediate material loss.
1358.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a knight (100% knight moves, 100% non-captures) that hangs material worth approximately a queen (median net material loss of -6.0 pawns). The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions collapsing into lost ones (100% drawn->losing, median 499cp lost), meaning the player had a tenable position and threw it away with a single move. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (57%), with development and tempo_loss as recurring tags — the player prioritizes piece development (moving a knight) while failing to notice an immediate tactical threat to an undefended piece. Maia's suggested move is always a queen move (100%), indicating the correct response was to address the queen's safety. The top boards confirm this: positions like Nf6 while the queen sits en prise on d6, or Nc3 while ignoring an attacked queen on d3. This is fundamentally a case of 'developing on autopilot' — making a natural-looking knight move without recognizing that a higher-value piece requires immediate attention.

1361.label: Pawn or rook moves that ignore a latent back-rank mating threat, allowing the opponent's rook to deliver decisive tactics.
1361.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a quiet pawn move (50%) or rook move (33%) that hangs material (56% hangs) while completely missing the opponent's rook-based tactical opportunity (Maia's response is always a rook move). The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and back_rank (50%), indicating the player overlooks a back-rank vulnerability or king safety issue. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 324cp), frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (50%) — suggesting these aren't positional inaccuracies but concrete tactical oversights. The top boards consistently show open files with enemy rooks poised to infiltrate, and the player makes an irrelevant pawn push (a4, b5, h5, h4) or misplaces a rook, ignoring the opponent's back-rank or mating threats. The common thread is a tempo-wasting move that fatally neglects defensive duties against rook penetration along the back rank.

1360.label: Playing f3 (or similar weakening pawn move) to chase a Bg4 pin instead of capturing the tactically available piece, squandering a winning advantage.
1360.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early-middlegame pattern where one side has a bishop pinning a knight on f3 (Bg4 or Bg5 scenarios) and the player responds with f2-f3 or ...f7-f6 to break the pin, instead of executing the correct tactical resolution (typically Bxf6/Bxf3 capture). The material signature shows pawn moves (88%) that are objectively safe but catastrophically misguided: Maia consistently recommends a bishop-takes-knight capture (Bxf6 or Bxf3) as the correct move. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions (88% winning→drawn, median 366cp lost), meaning the player throws away a decisive advantage. The tactical analysis reveals pins (20%), hanging pieces (30%), and tempo loss (20%) as dominant motifs, with 'missed_tactic' tagged in 9/10 positions. The concrete boards all feature Bg4/Bg5 pin structures where the weakening f-pawn push permanently damages pawn structure and misses the window to exploit the pin tactically. This is a classic move-order/prioritization error in well-known opening structures.

1362.label: Player makes a capture (often with a bishop) while ignoring an immediate threat to their own queen, losing significant material.
1362.description: This feature identifies positions where the player executes a capture or exchange—most frequently with a bishop (48%)—while completely overlooking a direct threat to their own queen or another high-value piece. The material signature shows 44% trades and 44% losses with a median net loss of -2.0 (roughly a piece), and the eval trajectory reveals devastating consequences: 48% of cases shift from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 358 centipawns. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), and the Opus analysis repeatedly highlights the pattern of 'threat ignorance'—the player focuses on executing their intended capture while their queen sits en prise to a knight fork, discovered attack, or direct piece threat. The top boards confirm this: Bxd7 while the queen on c2 is attacked by a knight on b4, Bxc6 while the queen on h5 is attacked by a knight on f6, and similar patterns where the player's attention fixates on the exchange they're making rather than the undefended major piece they're leaving hanging. Maia's recommended moves (56% queen moves) suggest the correct response was typically to move the threatened queen to safety first.

1363.label: Trading rooks (often with check) into a lost or drawn pawn endgame, squandering a winning or defensible position.
1363.description: This feature detects positions where a player executes a rook exchange (74% rook moves, 51% capturing an opposing rook, 89% with check) that transforms the position into a pawn endgame where their advantage evaporates or their position collapses. The material signature shows these are trades (64% equal exchanges, median net 0.0) rather than blunders—the player isn't hanging material but making a catastrophic simplification decision. The eval trajectory confirms massive positional cost (median 315cp lost), with 23% going drawn→losing and 14% winning→losing, indicating the rook was the piece providing all counterplay, defensive resources, or attacking potential. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly flags 'pawn_endgame' (60%) and 'simplification_error'/'premature_simplification' as dominant motifs, with example summaries consistently describing scenarios where the rook was the only piece maintaining the position's complexity or advantage. Maia's preferred moves (76% non-captures, only 41% checks) suggest the engine would maintain tension rather than simplify, confirming these exchanges are premature. The pattern is especially prevalent in middlegame-to-endgame transitions (76% middlegame phase) where players are lured by the forcing nature of a rook capture with check without calculating the resulting pawn ending.

1365.label: Player moves a minor piece in the opening that leaves another piece undefended, dropping material catastrophically.
1365.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase blunder where the player moves a knight or bishop (knight 43%, bishop 29%) without accounting for an existing threat to one of their own pieces. The material signature is stark: 57% of moves outright hang a piece with a median loss of 3 pawns' worth of material (median eval lost: 448 centipawns). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (83%), with common tags including 'ignored_threat' and 'undefended_piece.' The eval trajectory shows these are not minor inaccuracies but game-altering blunders—57% turn a drawn position into a losing one, and 29% squander a winning advantage to reach only a draw. The concrete positions illustrate the pattern clearly: a knight moves away from defending a bishop (Ng4 leaving Bc5 undefended), an aggressive knight lunge ignores an attacked bishop (Ne4 ignoring hanging Bf5), or a pawn move provokes a tactical sequence that exploits an unguarded piece (a3 allowing Bxc3/Nxc4). In all cases, the player prioritizes their own attacking idea or development while completely overlooking that one of their pieces has lost its defender or is under immediate threat.

1367.label: Player greedily captures material instead of pressing a winning king attack with a check or checkmate.
1367.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position (73% winning->winning, 18% winning->drawn) makes a greedy capture or quiet move with a bishop/queen/knight instead of delivering a devastating check or checkmate. The key signature is that Maia's recommended move gives check 100% of the time, while the player's move gives check 0% of the time—and 100% of positions involve missed winning material. The dominant motif is king_safety (100%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, material_greed, and missed_check. The example summaries make the pattern crystal clear: players capture a rook on a8, grab a pawn, or take hanging material when a forcing check (often winning the queen or delivering mate) was available. The median eval loss of 273 centipawns reflects how costly it is to let an exposed king escape. This occurs predominantly in the opening/early middlegame (55%/46%) where king safety is most exploitable. The material outcome being mostly 'safe' (64%) or involving captures (27% rook, 18% pawn) confirms that players are either making quiet developing moves or taking material while ignoring the opponent's fatally exposed king.

1366.label: Active-looking moves that leave pieces or pawns undefended, costing significant material or positional advantage.
1366.description: This feature captures middlegame moves where the player makes an active-looking but impulsive move (often with a queen, knight, or rook) that hangs material or squanders a winning advantage. The material signature shows 48% of moves result in hanging a piece with a median loss of ~1 pawn equivalent, while 65% miss winning material that was available. The eval trajectory is devastating: 30% go from winning to drawn and 17% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 323 centipawns—indicating these are game-changing mistakes rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 50%, king_safety 33%, tempo_loss 17%) and per-position analyses reveal the common thread: moves that appear active (checks, advances, piece relocations) but overlook that they leave something undefended or improve the opponent's position. Examples include an impulsive check that improves the opponent's king, a pawn push that gives back a winning advantage, and a king move that abandons defense of a critical pawn. The unifying pattern is prioritizing activity or initiative over concrete calculation of what's left hanging.

1368.label: Knight captures a pawn but fatally compromises king safety or piece coordination, squandering the position.
1368.description: This feature captures positions where a knight grabs a pawn (knight moved 86%, pawn captured 86%) in the opening or early middlegame (opening 57%, middlegame 43%), but the capture is speculative and self-destructive. The material signature shows the move is slightly_down or hangs material (net median -2.0), meaning the knight itself often becomes lost or trapped after the grab. The eval trajectory is devastating: 87% of the time the position shifts from winning/drawn to drawn/losing, with a median loss of 351 centipawns. The tactical motifs (king_safety 60%, tempo_loss, pawn_grab_punished, attack_without_follow_up) reveal why: the knight capture either removes a key defensive piece from the kingside (e.g., Nf6 leaving the king exposed on the h-file), activates opponent pieces, or wastes tempo without sufficient follow-up. The concrete positions confirm this—Nxg4 opening the h-file, Nxg6 without attacking resources, Ne3 hanging the knight. Maia's recommended moves (bishop 43%, non-captures 100%) suggest quiet consolidating alternatives existed. This is the classic 'greedy knight raid' that looks tempting but lacks tactical justification.

1369.label: In won endgames, player makes a passive king or piece move that hangs material instead of capturing or advancing a passed pawn.
1369.description: This feature fires on positions predominantly in the endgame (56%) or late middlegame (44%) where the player already has a winning advantage (78% winning->winning, 22% losing->winning) but squanders a median of 414 centipawns by making a passive move—often a king move (33%) or rook/queen/pawn move—that hangs a piece (67% hangs material) instead of executing the critical capture or passed pawn advance that Maia recommends (Maia captures 100% of the time, mostly pawns 56%). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%), passed_pawn (30%), and king_safety (20%), unified by the recurring tag of tempo_loss (appearing in 6/9 positions). The pattern is clear from the boards: players with dominant positions neglect immediate tactical obligations—like capturing a hanging piece, advancing a passed pawn, or addressing a critical threat—in favor of aimless piece repositioning that loses tempo and drops material. The player misses winning material 100% of the time, confirming these are won positions where the player fails to convert by ignoring the most forcing continuation.

1372.label: Player ignores a forced checkmate (usually via back-rank) and plays a non-checking move instead.
1372.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a forced checkmate—most often a back-rank mate—and plays an innocuous or materialistic move instead. The material signature shows the played move is typically a rook or queen move (or even a pawn push) that neither checks nor captures anything meaningful (68% no capture, 0% check), while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen check (60% queen, 100% check). The 97% 'missed winning material' rate and median eval loss of 344 centipawns confirm these are catastrophic oversights. The tactical motifs are dominated by back_rank (57%) and king_safety (43%), with explicit tags like back_rank_mate, missed_mate, and missed_mate_in_one/two. The per-position examples consistently show players choosing pedestrian moves (captures, knight retreats, pawn pushes) when a forcing queen check would have delivered checkmate in 1-4 moves. The eval trajectory shows most positions were already winning or drawn and became losing, reflecting the squandered decisive advantage.

1371.label: Giving an impulsive check instead of capturing a hanging piece or executing a clearly winning continuation.
1371.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check (100% of activating moves are checks) but misses a simple, decisive capture—typically of an undefended rook or other major piece. The Opus analyses repeatedly identify 'patzer sees a check' syndrome: the player reflexively gives check rather than calmly taking free material or maintaining a technically won endgame. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors (median 695cp lost), converting winning positions into draws or significantly less winning ones. The dominant tags—missed_capture, pointless_check, tempo_loss—all reinforce that the check accomplishes nothing constructive while squandering a concrete opportunity. The positions span rook endgames and middlegames where the board is relatively simplified, making the missed hanging piece especially egregious. The material signature (50% loses, 50% safe) reflects that sometimes the checking piece itself gets trapped or exchanged poorly, while other times it simply wastes a tempo without material loss but at enormous positional/eval cost.

1374.label: Player trades queens or simplifies when a deflection check first would have won decisive material.
1374.description: This feature fires when players execute queen trades or straightforward captures (queen moved 74%, captured queen 42%, trade outcome 47%) while missing a stronger intermediate deflection check. Maia's recommended moves (100% giving check) consistently involve inserting an intermediate check—often a rook or bishop deflection sacrifice—that forces the opponent's king off a defensive square, leaving a high-value piece unguarded. The dominant tags (missed_tactic, deflection, move_order, tempo_loss) and example summaries all converge on the same pattern: the player fails to insert a critical zwischenzug check before completing an exchange, costing a median of 404 centipawns and typically converting a winning position into a drawn one (winning->drawn 53%). The king_safety motif (50%) reflects that the missed tactic exploits the opponent's exposed king, while the tempo_loss tag captures the failure to use check as a forcing move to gain time. This is fundamentally a move-order/deflection error in middlegame positions where the player settles for an equal trade instead of first deflecting with check to win material.

1373.label: Impulsive pawn advances that leave pieces or squares fatally undefended, typically exposing the king.
1373.description: This feature identifies pawn moves (98% pawn played) that are non-captures (100% no capture) and hang material (67% hangs, median net material -1.0). The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic errors, with a median loss of 295 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (24% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: these are impulsive pawn pushes (h4, c4, f5, g6, h5) that compromise king safety (40% king_safety motif), leave pieces undefended (20% hanging_piece), or lose tempo (20% tempo_loss). The top boards consistently show positions in the opening/middlegame (100% combined) where the player pushes a pawn instead of developing or defending, often opening lines against their own uncastled king or abandoning pawn protection of critical squares. Maia's recommended moves are typically piece moves (bishop 29%, knight 16%, queen 18%), confirming that piece development or repositioning was called for rather than these weakening pawn advances.

1370.label: Giving a wasteful check with a rook that squanders a winning advantage by losing critical tempo in an endgame.
1370.description: This feature detects rook moves (72% of activations) that deliver check (56%) but are objectively terrible tempo losses in endgame positions (56% endgame). The material signature shows these moves hang material 83% of the time with a median loss of -1.0, and the eval trajectory reveals a devastating median cost of 265 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions to drawn ones (33% winning->drawn). The tactical analysis is dominated by 'tempo_loss' (50% of motifs) and 'pointless_check' tags, with recurring rook endgame contexts. The concrete positions show a clear pattern: players deliver flashy but purposeless checks with their rooks (e.g., Rb2+, Rb3+) that actually improve the opponent's king centralization while the player should instead be advancing their own king, addressing passed pawns, or executing proper endgame technique. Maia's recommended moves (king 50%, rook 33%) confirm that king centralization or more purposeful rook placement was correct. The feature captures a common amateur endgame failing: reflexively giving check rather than playing the slow, positional moves that maintain a winning advantage.

1375.label: A pawn advance that creates fatal structural or tactical vulnerabilities in the position.
1375.description: This feature identifies pawn pushes (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) that create exploitable weaknesses, most commonly in the opening and middlegame (50/50 split). The material signature shows these moves frequently hang material (57%) with a median cost of -1.0, meaning the pawn advance itself doesn't lose the pawn but exposes other pieces or squares to tactical exploitation. The eval trajectory is severe (median 268cp lost), with 36% turning drawn positions into losing ones and 21% throwing away winning positions. The tactical motifs reveal the mechanism: hanging_piece (38%) and king_safety (25%) dominate, with recurring tags like king_in_center and pawn_structure. The concrete examples are textbook cases—f6 weakening a diagonal with an uncastled king, f5 removing a pawn's defensive duty, e4 walking into a fork, d4 creating tactical vulnerabilities. These are aggressive-looking or prophylactic pawn pushes that actually tear open the player's own position, either exposing the king or leaving pieces undefended. Maia's recommended alternatives are typically piece moves (bishop 43%, knight 21%) suggesting development or repositioning was needed instead of these premature pawn thrusts.

1378.label: Player gives a flashy check instead of capturing or consolidating, allowing the opponent to escape or win material.
1378.description: This feature detects positions where a player delivers a check (100% of activations are checks) but the move hangs material or loses significant value (50% hang a piece, 17% lose material, median net -3.0 pawns). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 250 centipawns, often throwing away winning or drawn positions. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: tags like 'unnecessary_check' and 'tempo_gift' recur, and the example summaries explicitly describe players giving pointless checks that grant the opponent a crucial tempo to rescue hanging pieces or expose the checking piece to capture. The better move (Maia's recommendation) is typically a quiet capture or positional improvement rather than a check. The boards show queens, knights, and rooks lunging forward with check into squares where they are lost or where the check accomplishes nothing strategically, squandering tactical opportunities like free captures of undefended pieces.

1376.label: Player makes a routine capture or recapture instead of first inserting a critical check or castling to address king safety.
1376.description: This feature identifies positions where the player executes an otherwise reasonable-looking move (often a capture or recapture) but fatally neglects move order, specifically failing to prioritize king safety through castling or inserting an intermediate check first. The material signature shows trades and safe moves (not outright blunders of material), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 585cp), often converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones. The tactical analysis consistently flags 'move_order_error', 'uncastled_king', 'zwischenzug', and 'intermediate_check' as dominant tags, while king_safety is the primary motif. The concrete positions show uncastled kings on e1/e8 where the opponent has queen access to checking squares. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly queen checks (100%), confirming that the opponent punishes the move-order lapse with an immediate check that wins back material or more. The player captures a piece that 'isn't going anywhere' instead of first addressing their king's vulnerability or inserting a forcing intermediate move.

1364.label: Moving a piece to an apparently active square while leaving material hanging in a holdable position.
1364.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions (87%) where players move bishops (30%), rooks (20%), or queens (17%) to seemingly active squares but hang material (37% of moves result in a piece left en prise). The median loss is 383 centipawns, and the dominant trajectory is drawn->losing (33%), indicating these are holdable positions thrown away. Maia's recommended moves are often modest pawn moves (43%) or defensive rook repositions, suggesting the correct approach was patient/defensive rather than active. The concrete board positions show pieces being moved to aggressive-looking squares (capturing pawns, repositioning to open lines, giving checks) while overlooking that the move creates or exposes a tactical vulnerability. The pattern is one of misplaced aggression—choosing activity over safety in positions that demanded careful play.

1377.label: Suboptimal king moves in pawn endgames that lose critical tempo without immediate material consequence.
1377.description: This feature identifies king moves in pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player is already losing and makes a nearly imperceptible error (median 2 centipawns lost). The material signature shows exclusively king moves with no captures and no checks, all classified as 'safe'—nothing is hung or traded. The eval trajectory confirms these are losing->losing positions where the mistake barely worsens the evaluation. However, the tactical analysis reveals the subtle nature: the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (56%), tempo_loss (11%), and passed_pawn (11%), with recurring tags of king_activity, opposition, and pawn_race. The concrete examples show kings moving to wrong squares (Kd6 instead of maintaining opposition, Ke3 in a drawn-ish position, premature pawn pushes like a5 or h5 that concede tempo). These are positions where the precise king placement or move order matters enormously for opposition, tempo in pawn races, or controlling key squares, but the player wastes a tempo or chooses the wrong path—often nearly indistinguishable from the correct move in terms of immediate evaluation but potentially decisive in the long run.

1379.label: Moving the king to an inferior square in the endgame, missing critical tactical or positional resources that would hold or win.
1379.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (100% king moves, 0% checks, no captures) and catastrophically mishandles the position. The median eval loss of ~9177 centipawns reflects both missed mates and transitions from drawable to losing positions. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (44%), hanging_piece (22%), fork (22%), tempo_loss (11%)—along with recurring tags like king_activity, passed_pawn, and missed_tactic reveal that these king moves represent critical tempo or activity errors: the king walks to a passive or vulnerable square instead of maintaining opposition, supporting a passed pawn, or exploiting a tactical shot (e.g., a knight fork winning material, a capture of a hanging piece, or a key pawn advance). The boards confirm this pattern—positions with passed pawns, pawn races, or piece forks where the king move squanders a won or drawn position by losing a critical tempo or walking into a tactical vulnerability.

1380.label: King moves in endgames that lose tempo or activity, worsening an already difficult position.
1380.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a king move (70% king moves) that loses tempo or cedes critical king activity. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (91%) and the eval trajectory shows these moves primarily deepen already-losing positions (83% losing->losing) with a median cost of 145 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals tempo_loss (33%) and king_safety/king_activity as dominant motifs — the player retreats or wanders with the king when precise centralization or opposition was required. Maia would have played a king move 96% of the time too, suggesting these are subtle king placement errors rather than obvious blunders. The boards confirm sparse endgame positions (K+minor piece or K+pawns) where one wrong king step surrenders a critical tempo — allowing the opponent to activate, win a pawn, or penetrate decisively. These aren't hanging pieces but positional tempo errors specific to king maneuvering in the endgame.

1381.label: Trading away a critical defensive rook in an endgame, surrendering the position's only dynamic resource.
1381.description: This feature captures endgame positions where the player delivers a rook check that results in a trade (75%) or material loss (25%), eliminating their own crucial defensive piece. The material signature shows rook moves with checks (100%) that are exchanges rather than wins, and the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 509cp lost), often converting drawn or winning positions into losses. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: players trade away the very rook that was holding the position together—whether preventing a passed pawn promotion, maintaining a blockade, or providing essential counterplay. The Opus summaries repeatedly identify 'exchanging the only defensive piece' and 'pointless checks that waste tempo' as the core error. All positions are endgames featuring passed pawns and rook activity as central themes, where the rook's presence was the linchpin of the defense. The checks appear attractive but are strategically disastrous, as they invite or force an exchange that leaves the opponent with an easily winning pawn endgame or promotion race.

1382.label: Player makes a move that traps their own bishop (typically on g5/h4), allowing the opponent to win material.
1382.description: This feature identifies a highly specific tactical pattern where players trap their own bishop, predominantly in opening/middlegame positions involving the Bg5/Bh4 pin system. The material signature shows that 53% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) while the player's move is typically a knight or pawn move (not the bishop itself), confirming the piece is trapped indirectly. Maia consistently recommends a bishop retreat (100% bishop moves capturing a bishop - i.e., the forced unfavorable exchange that results from the trap). The eval trajectory is devastating (median 363cp loss), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (39% drawn->losing, 11% winning->losing). The Opus analysis confirms this with 'trapped_piece' (43%) and 'bishop_trapped' as dominant motifs, with specific examples showing moves like g3 or Nd2 that remove the bishop's escape squares or its defending piece, allowing the opponent to win the trapped bishop. The positions consistently feature a dark-squared bishop on h4/g5 in d-pawn opening structures where a seemingly natural developing move fatally compromises the bishop's retreat path.

1384.label: Moving a rook to a square where it is captured or trapped by an opponent's knight, dropping material.
1384.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a rook (54% of cases) to an unsafe square, resulting in a hanging piece (83% of outcomes) with a median material loss of -2.0 (consistent with losing the exchange or a full rook). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%), and the eval trajectory shows severe consequences: median 315 centipawns lost, often converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (25% drawn->losing, 17% winning->losing). The concrete positions reveal a recurring pattern: rooks are moved to squares attacked by enemy knights (e.g., Rc6-b6 into Na4, Nd5 leaving a rook hanging to Ne6, Rd7-c7 into Nc7). The opponent frequently has a knight on an active outpost (e6, a4, b7, c5) that controls the destination square. Maia's recommended moves (71% rook moves) suggest safer rook placements existed. The king_safety secondary motif (33%) indicates these rook moves sometimes also abandon defensive duties, compounding the error.

1383.label: King moves to the wrong square in a drawn pawn endgame, losing opposition or abandoning critical pawns and converting a draw into a loss.
1383.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame mistake: the player moves their king (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) in a pawn endgame (100% endgame phase) that was objectively drawn, but the move converts the position to a losing one (100% drawn->losing, median 540cp lost). The material outcome is 'safe'—nothing is immediately hung or traded—yet the positional damage is catastrophic. The Opus analysis and tags reveal the underlying mechanism: loss of opposition (tagged), tempo errors, moving the king away from critical passed pawns or promotion squares, or failing to execute the one precise king path that holds the draw. The top boards show pure or near-pure pawn endgames where a single king step to the wrong square (e.g., Kf6 instead of Kf4, Kb5 instead of staying near c4, Kh6 losing the g-pawn race) surrenders the theoretical draw. The motifs—pawn_endgame, promotion_error, passed_pawn—all point to the same theme: the king fails its dual duty of stopping enemy passers while supporting its own, a quintessential pawn endgame king-placement error.

1387.label: Playing a flashy check or capture instead of addressing a critical passed pawn about to promote.
1387.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a player, already losing, makes a bishop capture that gives check (100% check, 100% bishop captures knight, material appears 'safe') while ignoring an opponent's passed pawn that is one or two steps from promotion. The eval trajectory shows these are losing positions made catastrophically worse (median 428cp lost), consistent with a decisive tempo being squandered. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the 'patzer sees a check' syndrome — the player grabs material with tempo but overlooks that the opponent's advanced passer will queen immediately. Maia's recommended moves (capturing a pawn, no check) correspond to eliminating or blockading the promotion threat. The dominant motifs (passed_pawn 50%, promotion_error 25%, tempo_loss 25%) and tags (promotion_threat, critical_capture_missed) all converge: the player chooses a superficially attractive forcing move over the only defense against imminent promotion, turning a difficult but holdable (or slowly losing) position into an immediate catastrophe.

1385.label: Player wastes a critical tempo with a knight or rook move in a winning position, allowing the opponent to reorganize defenses or neutralize a decisive threat.
1385.description: This feature captures positions where the player, typically already winning or holding a significant advantage, makes a knight (50%) or rook (25%) move that squanders tempo rather than executing the most precise continuation. The material signature shows these moves are overwhelmingly 'safe' (88%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet 100% of the time the player misses winning material that was available. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (40%) and king_safety (40%), with passed_pawn appearing in 4 of 8 positions, indicating these are late-middlegame or early-endgame conversions where a passed pawn or mating attack demands immediate action. The eval trajectory confirms this: 62% of cases go winning->winning but lose a median of 99 centipawns, meaning the advantage shrinks substantially. The concrete positions show advanced passed pawns (d7, e6, d6), promotion threats, and pins that require immediate exploitation, but instead the player retreats a knight to a passive square or shuffles a rook without purpose. Maia's preferred moves (75% pawn pushes) confirm that the correct action was typically advancing a passed pawn or making a direct threat, not the temporizing piece maneuver that was played.

1386.label: In a hopelessly lost pawn endgame, the player makes inconsequential king moves or captures that fail to find the only defensive resource.
1386.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure pawn endgames where the player is already in a losing position and the move itself costs little or no material (median 0cp lost, 'trade' signature from king capturing a pawn while losing one). The trajectory is consistently losing->losing, meaning the position was already hopeless before the move. However, Maia's recommendation (a non-capturing king move 100% of the time) combined with the 'missed winning material' flag at 100% suggests these positions contain a narrow defensive or counterplay resource that the player overlooks. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame, tempo_loss, passed_pawn, king_activity—reveal that the critical error is one of king placement and tempo in zugzwang-rich positions. The player mechanically captures an available pawn or drifts with the king rather than finding the precise square that maximizes defensive chances (e.g., opposition, blockade of a passed pawn, or tempo triangulation). The boards confirm razor-thin pawn endgames with 1-3 pawns per side where a single tempo or king square decides the outcome.

1388.label: Player makes a move that abandons a winning king attack, missing a decisive check or mating sequence.
1388.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player has a winning attack against the opponent's king but plays a move that squanders the initiative. The material signature shows that 100% of cases missed winning material, and Maia's recommended moves deliver check in 100% of cases—indicating a forcing continuation was available but ignored. The dominant motifs are king_safety (43%), tempo_loss (29%), and back_rank (29%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, missed_mate, and exposed_king, all pointing to positions where the opponent's king was vulnerable and a decisive blow existed. The eval trajectory (median 363cp lost, with 50% winning->winning and 17% winning->drawn) shows these moves throw away significant advantage. The concrete examples reinforce this: Kf1 retreats instead of Qf5+; Qe7 self-blocks instead of exploiting a back-rank mate; Qxe7 captures with the wrong piece missing a forced mate; Rb4 withdraws from the 7th rank abandoning a king hunt. In each case, the player had a forcing attack on the enemy king and chose a passive or misguided alternative, losing the thread of the attack.

1391.label: Playing an aggressive queen check on a square directly controlled by an enemy minor piece, immediately losing the queen.
1391.description: This feature detects a highly specific and catastrophic tactical blunder: delivering a check with the queen (86% queen moves, 100% checks) on a square that is directly defended by an opponent's knight or other piece, resulting in the immediate loss of the queen (86% hangs, median material loss of -9.0, i.e., a queen). The eval trajectory confirms these are devastating mistakes (median 371cp lost), often turning drawn or even winning positions into losing ones. The OPUS analysis universally identifies 'hanging_piece' as the motif, with recurring tags like 'queen_blunder', 'premature_attack', and 'knight_captures_queen'. The top boards overwhelmingly show Qh5 or Qh4 checks where a knight on f6/f3 simply captures. This is not a complex tactical oversight but a one-move blindness pattern: the player sees the check and the apparent aggression but completely fails to verify that the destination square is controlled by an enemy piece. It occurs primarily in the opening (71%) when players launch premature attacks without basic piece-safety verification.

1389.label: Moving a piece away from king defense, allowing a devastating attack.
1389.description: This feature captures positions where players move pieces (especially queens, bishops, knights) away from defensive duties around their king, fatally weakening king safety. The material signature shows 41% of moves hang material (not through captures but by leaving pieces or the king exposed), with the player rarely capturing anything (91% no capture). The eval trajectory is severe—median 253cp lost, with 36% of cases converting drawn positions to losing ones and 9% throwing wins entirely. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and positional_mistake (50%), with tags like 'defensive_neglect', 'queen_misplacement', and 'kingside_attack'. The concrete examples illustrate this clearly: Black plays ...Qb6 removing the queen from kingside defense, or moves like ...Be7 in a position where the king is already under pressure. Maia's recommended moves (77% pawn moves, 41% pawn captures) suggest the correct responses were often simple defensive pawn moves or capturing attacking pieces, rather than the ambitious piece redeployments the players chose. The pattern is a player prioritizing activity or development over urgent king safety needs.

1392.label: Unsound knight sacrifice on f7 or f2 in the opening that loses material with no tactical follow-up.
1392.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake: a knight captures a pawn on f7 (against a castled king) or f2 (targeting the opponent's king/rook) that constitutes an unsound sacrifice. The material signature shows knight captures pawn 100% of the time with a net material outcome of slightly down (-2.0), meaning the knight is lost for just a pawn — a classic piece sacrifice. The eval trajectory (drawn->losing, median 360cp lost) confirms these are not sound sacrifices but premature attacks that swing the game decisively. The phase is exclusively opening (100%), and Opus analysis consistently tags these as 'unsound_sacrifice' with 'no supporting pieces developed' and 'no tactical follow-up.' The top boards reveal the concrete pattern: Nxf7 attacks against castled kings (g5f7, e5f7) or Nxf2 raids (e4f2, g4f2), all in early middlegame positions where the attacker lacks the piece coordination to sustain a king-hunt. The player is seduced by the apparent aggression of invading f7/f2 but the sacrifice simply drops a piece.

1394.label: Player makes a quiet developing or repositioning move, missing a concrete knight tactic (fork/capture) that would have won material.
1394.description: This feature fires on positions in the opening and early middlegame where the player chooses a safe, non-capturing move (95% safe, 100% no capture) — typically a queen or knight retreat/repositioning — while missing a knight tactic that wins a pawn or more. The Maia best-move is universally a knight capture of a pawn (knight 100%, captures pawn 100%), indicating a concrete tactical shot was available. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%), fork (25%), and hanging_piece (25%), and the common tags emphasize missed tactics exploiting geometric vulnerabilities, uncastled kings, or overextended pawns. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 241 centipawns, typically turning a winning position into a draw (43%) or a drawn position into a loss (38%). The top boards confirm the pattern: positions with active piece play where a knight can exploit a tactical weakness (diagonal, fork square, undefended pawn), but the player instead makes a routine developing move like Qe7, Bg5, O-O, or Rb1, losing the window for the concrete shot.

1390.label: Losing a won pawn endgame by making a passive or mistimed king/pawn move that surrenders the critical tempo advantage.
1390.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring mistake pattern: players in pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) who hold completely winning positions but throw them away with a single inaccurate move. The material signature shows safe pawn or king moves (no captures, no checks) — these aren't tactical blunders but subtle positional/tempo errors. The eval trajectory is devastating: 75% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 507 centipawns, indicating positions where the win evaporates entirely. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (50%) and tempo_loss (20%), with tags heavily emphasizing tempo_loss (9 occurrences), passed pawns (7), and king activity (5). The concrete positions show players retreating kings (d4-d3, f7-f6, e5-f5), making premature pawn pushes (h2-h4, c6-c5), or capturing the wrong pawn (a4xb5 instead of advancing a5 for promotion). In each case, the player had a narrow winning path requiring precise move order or tempo management, and instead made a natural-looking but fatally passive move that allowed the opponent to reach a drawing setup.

1395.label: Player grabs material or makes a passive move instead of delivering a forced checkmate or continuing a decisive king attack.
1395.description: This feature fires when a player in the middlegame abandons a winning attacking sequence—usually involving a forced mate or devastating king-side pressure—in favor of capturing material or making a passive move. The SEE signature shows queen and rook moves that often result in trades or hanging pieces (46% trade, 27% hangs), while Maia's recommended moves give check 100% of the time, indicating the engine saw a forcing continuation the player missed. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 257cp lost, with 96% missing winning material), and the Opus motifs consistently highlight king_safety, missed_mate, back_rank threats, and attack_abandoned/greed tags. The concrete examples show players grabbing rooks, retreating to passive squares, or trading when a forced mate was available—all cases where the player's attacking momentum was squandered by prioritizing material gain or safety over the lethal continuation.

1393.label: Wasting a critical tempo in a pawn endgame by making an aimless or self-blocking pawn/king move instead of the precise continuation.
1393.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame error pattern. All positions are pure pawn endgames (phase: endgame 100%) where the player moves either a pawn or king (50/50 split) without capturing, and the move hangs material 83% of the time—meaning the opponent can now win a pawn or promote decisively. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and passed_pawn (38%), with pawn_endgame as a consistent tag. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 191 centipawns, often turning a losing-but-defensible position into a trivially lost one (losing->losing 67%), or catastrophically blowing a win (winning->losing 17%). The concrete positions show scenarios like locking pawns head-to-head (a4 vs a5), moving the king away from the critical sector, or pushing a pawn that allows the opponent's passed pawn to advance. Maia consistently recommends capturing a pawn instead (Maia captures: pawn 100%), indicating the correct move involved an active pawn exchange or recapture. The unifying thread is that in these razor-thin pawn endgames, the player wastes exactly one tempo—either by a purposeless king move or a pawn push that blocks or ignores the critical race—and that single lost tempo is enough to lose the game.

1398.label: Quiet move that squanders a winning position by missing a one-move tactical opportunity.
1398.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing quiet move (94% safe, 93% no capture) in the middlegame (75%) while a decisive tactic existed. The eval trajectory shows these moves overwhelmingly throw away wins: 19% winning->drawn, 10% drawn->losing, 8% winning->losing, with a massive median cost of 316 centipawns. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (42% capture something) and knight moves (34%), indicating concrete tactical shots were available. The Opus analysis confirms this with 65% missed winning material, and motifs centered on tempo_loss (33%), forks (17%), overloaded defenders (17%), and trapped pieces (17%). The recurring pattern is a player who has built a winning position but plays a passive or retreating move instead of the single critical continuation—often a fork, en passant, or piece activation—that would have sealed the game. The top boards consistently show positions where only one truly strong move existed and the player chose something quiet instead.

1396.label: Premature or misguided pawn advances in king-and-pawn endgames that miss stronger alternatives involving piece activity or checks.
1396.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player pushes a pawn (50% pawn moves) or makes a king move (50%) that is materially 'safe' (nothing hangs, no captures involved) but misses a stronger continuation—typically a rook check or knight maneuver that Maia identifies (75% rook, 25% knight, 100% giving check). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame and passed_pawn, with recurring tags like tempo_loss and missed_tactic. The concrete positions show kings and pawns in simplified endgames where the player mechanically advances a passed pawn (h3-h2, f4-f3, g6-g5, a5-a4) instead of finding an active piece check or more precise king maneuver. The eval trajectory varies widely—from negligible loss to catastrophic blunders converting forced mates into merely winning positions—but the unifying pattern is choosing a passive, 'obvious' pawn push over a dynamic checking/active move in a pure or near-pure endgame.

1397.label: Moving a piece that fatally exposes one's own king to mating threats or back-rank attacks.
1397.description: This feature captures moves where a player relocates a piece (most often a rook, but also a king, bishop, or knight) that was serving a critical defensive role for their own king, leaving it catastrophically exposed. The material signature shows 75% of these moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece or worse), with a median net loss of -1.0 material units, while Maia's recommended response is almost always a rook move delivering check (100% check rate). The tactical analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif (62%), with recurring tags of forced_mate, back_rank vulnerability, mating_net, and deflection. The concrete positions show patterns like removing a knight that shielded against back-rank mates (Nb1-c3 examples), castling into a position where a piece is left hanging to a queen invasion, or moving a rook away from a defensive file while the king is already exposed. The eval trajectory (median 195cp lost) spans multiple game states—sometimes throwing a winning position, sometimes accelerating a loss—but the unifying thread is that the moved piece was the linchpin of king safety, and its relocation invites immediate tactical punishment via checks and mating threats.

1399.label: Playing a developing or routine move in the opening when an immediate tactical capture or piece-winning opportunity was available.
1399.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a non-urgent developing move (bishop repositioning, castling, knight development) while a concrete tactical opportunity—usually a hanging piece or a time-sensitive capture—goes unexploited. The material signature shows that 33% of moves outright hang a piece and 50% result in trades that could have been avoided or converted more profitably, with 100% of positions featuring missed winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly mistakes (median 294cp lost), predominantly turning winning positions into drawn ones (67%). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%) and tempo_loss (40%), with recurring tags like capture_urgency_missed and time_sensitive_tactic. The concrete positions show Italian Game and Scotch-type structures where an intermediate capture (like dxe7 or Bxe6) was available but the player instead made a slow move like Bd3, O-O, or Nf3, allowing the opponent to consolidate. The key pattern is prioritizing general development over a specific, time-critical tactical blow in the opening.

1404.label: Early queen development to an undefended square where it is immediately capturable by a minor piece.
1404.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: a player develops their queen early (queen moved 100% of the time) to a square where it hangs freely (hangs 100%, net material median -9.0, i.e., losing the queen). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic loss (median 591 centipawns lost), typically converting a drawn position into a losing one (75% drawn->losing).
