The concrete positions confirm the pattern—moves like Qb4 abandoning kingside defense against a knight on f5, Bd6 ignoring an attacked knight, or Ne5 landing on an unprotected square. The common thread is that the player makes a plausible-looking developing or active move while completely overlooking that the position demands an immediate tactical response to a concrete threat.

1462.label: King or rook moves in endgames that expose the piece to skewers, pins, or forks, turning drawn or winning positions into lost ones.
1462.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player moves their king (67%) or rook (25%) to a square that creates a tactical vulnerability—most commonly a skewer (33%), pin (11%), or fork—allowing the opponent to win material or force a decisive transition. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (92%) with no captures being made (100% non-capture moves), yet the median eval loss is a catastrophic 430 centipawns. The trajectory shows these are primarily positions that were drawn becoming lost (42%) or already losing positions made hopeless (50%), indicating the player fails to recognize that their king or rook placement walks into a tactical shot. The concrete examples reinforce this: Ke7 walks onto a file allowing a pin via Re2+, Kc4 allows a fork, Rg2 leaves the rook hanging after a deflecting check, and Kg3 allows a skewer. The common thread is misplacing the king or rook onto a tactically vulnerable square in simplified positions where one tempo-error is decisive.

1464.label: Hanging a critical piece in a pawn endgame by moving it to an undefended square where it is lost.
1464.description: This feature detects endgame positions where a player moves a piece (typically a bishop) to a square where it hangs undefended, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median -3.0 material, median 1101 centipawns lost). The positions are exclusively endgames involving passed pawns, pawn races, and promotion threats. The consistent pattern across the top activating positions shows players voluntarily placing their last remaining piece on an attacked square—often a bishop that was serving a critical defensive or offensive function (blocking a passed pawn, supporting promotion). The eval trajectory (winning->losing 50%, drawn->losing 50%) confirms these are game-deciding blunders that throw away the position entirely. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece, passed_pawn, tempo_loss, promotion_error) indicate that the mistakes arise from misjudging pawn race dynamics or failing to recognize that the piece is the essential resource holding the position together. Rather than calculated sacrifices, these are oversights where the player focuses on pawn advancement or king activity while neglecting that their piece lands on an attacked square.

1467.label: Trading a minor piece that fatally exposes one's own king to a mating attack.
1467.description: This feature fires on positions where a player trades or moves a minor piece (bishop 67%, knight 33%) in a way that catastrophically compromises their king's safety, converting playable positions into forced checkmates. The material signature shows exchanges (trades 67%) and hanging pieces (33%), but the defining characteristic is the massive eval loss (median ~9484 centipawns, i.e., forced mate). The dominant motif is king_safety (80%), with tags emphasizing exposed kings, missed tactics, and open files. The trajectory confirms these are positions that collapse into immediate forced mates—either throwing away a winning position (winning->losing 33%) or making a lost position instantly terminal (losing->losing 67%). The top boards consistently show kings on exposed squares (h7, g8, k-side) where the traded/moved piece was the last defensive resource against an incoming mating attack, particularly along open files or diagonals. Maia's recommended moves are uniformly king moves (100%), confirming that the critical need was to address the king's vulnerability rather than engage in piece exchanges.

1465.label: A knight delivers a flashy check that simply hangs the knight, squandering a winning or balanced position.
1465.description: This feature fires on knight moves that deliver check (100% knight moved, 100% gave check) but overwhelmingly hang the piece (62% hangs, median net material -3.0, i.e., losing a full knight). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders: 46% swing from winning to losing, with a median loss of 478 centipawns. Tags like 'pointless_check,' 'missed_tactic,' and 'piece_sacrifice_unsound' reinforce that these are not sound sacrifices but optical illusions where the check's forcing nature tricks the player into thinking it must be good. Maia's recommended moves (rook 25%, bishop 25%, pawn 25%) suggest quiet developing or consolidating moves were far superior. The positions are predominantly middlegame (79%) where complex piece interactions make it easy to overlook a defender covering the check square.

1463.label: Moving a critical defensive piece away from king protection, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
1463.description: This feature captures moves where the player relocates a piece that was serving a vital defensive role—particularly king safety—leaving their position fatally exposed. The material signature shows that 36% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) and the net material median is -1.0, indicating significant loss. The example summaries explicitly describe pieces being moved away from defensive duties (a bishop removed from kingside cover, a rook removed from the 7th rank exposing the king, a rook moved away from protecting a piece). Maia's recommended moves (73% queen moves, 73% giving check) suggest that the correct play involved active counterplay or defensive checks rather than the passive piece relocations the players chose. The moved pieces (rooks 36%, knights 27%, bishops 18%) are exactly the type of supporting defenders whose removal opens tactical floodgates.

1468.label: Queen retreats or diverts from a winning attacking position to grab a peripheral pawn or deliver an aimless check, surrendering a decisive initiative.

The material signature shows the move itself is usually 'safe' (no immediate material loss), yet the eval trajectory reveals a massive median cost of 336 centipawns, with 100% of cases missing a winning tactic. The dominant motifs — king_safety, tempo_loss, piece_activity, back_rank, and mating_attack tags — all confirm the same story: the player voluntarily relieved pressure on the opponent's king at the critical moment. The Opus summaries explicitly describe 'trading a crushing kingside attack for a single pawn' and 'decentralizing the queen at the precise moment when coordination was decisive.' This is not a material blunder or an exchange error; it is a positional/strategic collapse where the player fails to maintain attacking tension and instead pursues a low-value distraction, allowing the opponent to consolidate.

1469.label: Pawn or piece moves that open files or diagonals, exposing the player's back rank or pinned pieces to devastating tactics.
1469.description: This feature captures moves—most often pawn captures or advances (48% pawn, 24% bishop)—that inadvertently open critical lines (files, ranks, or diagonals) the opponent immediately exploits. The material signature shows 39% hangs and 30% loses with a median net loss of 4.0 material points, confirming these are not trades but outright blunders. The dominant motifs are back_rank (29%) and pin (29%), with tempo_loss and king_safety also prominent, indicating the player's move removes a key defensive barrier or creates an exploitable alignment. The eval trajectory (median 301cp lost, with 15% drawn->losing and 6% winning->losing) shows these mistakes are often game-decisive, turning playable or even winning positions into losses. The concrete examples reinforce this: dxc5 removing a pawn that shielded the back rank, captures that open the e-file for Rxe8+, and piece moves that leave back-rank or pin vulnerabilities fatally exposed. The common thread is that the player's move—often a tempting capture or natural developing move—structurally opens a line they failed to recognize as dangerous.

1466.label: Player makes a passive or retreating move that misses a critical tactical opportunity, turning a drawn or winning position into a losing one.
1466.description: This feature fires on moves where the player retreats or repositions a piece (bishop, rook, or knight) without capturing, in positions where a sharp tactical resource existed. The material signature shows all moves are 'safe' (nothing immediately hangs) and no captures are made, yet 100% of the time the player missed winning material — indicating the mistake is one of omission rather than commission. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 503cp lost), with positions swinging from drawn-to-losing (67%) or winning-to-losing (33%), confirming these are game-deciding errors. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves, suggesting the engine saw simple but committal continuations the player avoided. The motifs (tempo_loss, back_rank, hanging_piece) and tags (missed_tactic, king_safety, counterplay_abandoned) all point to players who sense danger and retreat defensively, missing that their position demanded immediate tactical action to survive or win.

1461.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet pawn or piece move that leaves another piece undefended and capturable.
1461.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame blunder pattern where the player makes a seemingly innocuous move (67% pawn moves, 33% bishop moves) that is not a capture or check, but critically leaves a piece hanging (67% of moves result in material being hung, with a median net loss of -3.0 material points, roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: a median of 741 centipawns lost, with positions swinging from winning to losing or drawn to losing in 67% of cases. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' in 100% of cases, with recurring tags of 'undefended_piece' and 'removed_guard'—the player makes a quiet move (like advancing a pawn or shifting a king) while ignoring that one of their pieces is tactically vulnerable to immediate capture. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (67%) where piece counts are low and every unit is critical, making such oversights immediately decisive. The Maia responses confirm exploitation via captures (pawn 33%, rook 33%). This is not a trade or positional misjudgment—it is a tactical oversight where the player simply loses awareness of a hanging piece.

1471.label: Knight captures a pawn in the opening with check but hangs the piece or loses major material due to overlooked defenders.
1471.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake (89% opening) where a knight (78% of moves) captures a pawn (78% captures) often with check (67%), but the move results in material loss (median -2.0, with 67% slightly_down and 22% hangs). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (78% drawn->losing) with a massive median cost of 381 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core error: players overlook defenders (hanging_piece 67%) — they see the attacked pawn and the check but fail to account for a defending piece that can recapture or that the resulting position leaves their knight or another piece en prise. The top boards confirm this pattern: aggressive knight forays to f7, c6, c7, f3 etc. that appear to win material or give devastating checks but actually lose the knight or more because a defender was overlooked. Maia's preferred moves (bishop 56%, pawn 22%) suggest quieter developing moves were available, reinforcing that these are premature tactical adventures in known opening positions where piece counting errors lead to catastrophic material loss.

1470.label: Capturing the wrong piece in an endgame, trading away a critical defender or allowing a decisive counterplay.
1470.description: This feature detects endgame positions where the player makes a capture (always taking a knight) that is objectively catastrophic despite appearing to be a reasonable trade or material exchange. The material signature shows trades or slight material losses—not outright blunders of hanging pieces—yet the eval trajectory reveals massive swings (median ~95 pawns lost), indicating these captures transition positions from drawn or slowly losing into completely lost. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs are passed pawns, pawn endgames, and wrong captures. The Opus summaries repeatedly describe players capturing the wrong piece—taking a knight instead of addressing a critical passed pawn threat, or exchanging a vital defensive piece (rook, bishop) for a less important one, thereby eliminating the only resource preventing promotion or king infiltration. The boards are uniformly endgame positions with few pieces where piece selection in captures is decisive. The player consistently picks a capture that looks natural but fails to address the actual winning threat (usually a passed pawn or king activity), collapsing what might have been a holdable position into a trivially lost one.

1472.label: Developing or moving a knight/piece in the opening that leaves another piece undefended, allowing a tactical refutation.
1472.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where the player makes a natural-looking developing move (knight 50%, pawn 25%, bishop 25%) that inadvertently hangs a piece (50% hangs, 50% slightly_down outcome, median net material -2.0). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (62%), with common tags including development, missed_tactic, and piece_activity — indicating moves that prioritize development or routine play while overlooking that a piece is tactically vulnerable. The eval trajectory is severe: 75% drawn->losing and 25% winning->drawn, with a median loss of 340 centipawns, meaning these moves transform playable positions into losing ones. The top boards confirm the pattern: positions from well-known openings (Petroff, Sicilian, Italian, Caro-Kann) where White or Black plays a developing move (d3, Bg5, Bd3, c3) while a knight on e5 or another piece is hanging or a pin exists. Maia consistently finds the knight recapture (Nxc6, Nxe5, etc.) that the player missed. This is not an exchange gone wrong but rather a failure to notice that a piece lacks adequate defense after a routine developing move.

1473.label: Player overlooks a forced checkmate in one move, typically a queen capture delivering mate on a vulnerable square.
1473.description: All three signals converge on a single, devastating pattern: missing checkmate in one. The Maia analysis confirms that in 100% of cases the best move was a queen move (often a queen capture of a pawn) that simultaneously delivered check—and in fact mate. The per-position tactical analysis is dominated by king_safety (80%) with explicit tags like missed_checkmate, one_move_mate, and smothered_king. The example summaries repeatedly describe queen captures on g2 or h7 delivering mate with the opposing king entombed by its own pieces. The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of ~93 pawns (consistent with dropping a forced mate to merely a large advantage or even losing the game), with many positions going from winning to still-winning but with the decisive blow squandered. The player's actual moves are distributed across piece types (queen, knight, rook, pawn) because they play essentially random developing or repositioning moves instead of the mating queen move. The 'safe' material outcome (58%) confirms these aren't blunders that hang material—they simply fail to deliver the killing blow. The boards show classic back-rank and smothered-king patterns where a single queen move ends the game immediately.

1475.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended square in the opening where it hangs to a knight fork or tempo-gaining attack.
1475.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake where a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) to an aggressive-looking but tactically vulnerable square, hanging it (net material median: -3.0, consistent with losing a minor piece). The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, and the move swings the evaluation from winning to losing (median 480cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the key motifs: tempo_loss (the bishop move wastes time or is immediately punished), hanging_piece (the bishop lands undefended), and fork (a knight can simultaneously attack the bishop and another target). The top boards show a clear pattern: bishops going to g4 or g5 where they are immediately exploitable—either by a knight fork (Nd4/Ng5 patterns threatening queen and bishop simultaneously), an intermediate check that wins the piece, or simply being left en prise to a tempo-gaining attack. The Maia model consistently recommends knight moves instead, confirming that the missed best move was a concrete knight tactic that punishes the bishop's exposed position. This is fundamentally a tactical oversight where apparent piece activity blinds the player to a concrete refutation.

1474.label: In rook endgames, capturing a far-advanced passed pawn with check rather than defending or blockading, trading into a lost position.
1474.description: This feature fires on a highly specific rook endgame pattern where a player uses their rook to capture an advanced passed pawn (often on the 7th rank) with check. The SEE signature shows 100% rook moves capturing pawns with check, yet the material outcome is 'loses' (median -4.0), indicating the rook is subsequently lost or the resulting position collapses. The top boards overwhelmingly feature positions with pawns on the 7th rank (e7, g7) where the opponent has a promotion threat, and the player captures the pawn with their rook giving check—but this either allows a back-rank tactic, loses the rook to a discovered attack, or simply trades into a hopeless position. The eval trajectory (losing->losing, 0cp median loss) confirms these are already lost positions where the capture doesn't change the evaluation much but represents the moment of final capitulation rather than prolonging resistance. The Opus analysis confirms several of these are actually engine-approved moves (0cp loss) in already-lost positions, while others trade into significantly worse endgames when better defensive resources existed. The dominant motifs—rook_endgame, passed_pawn, and piece_activity—all point to the critical endgame moment where a far-advanced passer must be addressed and the rook capture with check feels forcing but is strategically misguided.

1476.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing piece move that squanders a winning tactical opportunity.
1476.description: This feature fires when players make quiet bishop or rook moves (bishop 46%, rook 31%) that are non-captures (100% no capture) in middlegame positions (94%), missing crushing tactical continuations that Maia identifies—often involving checks (49%), queen moves (37%), or captures (queen 26%, pawn 14%). The median eval loss of 251 centipawns and 83% missed winning material rate confirm these are significant tactical oversights. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (33%), king_safety (22%), hanging_piece (22%)—reveal the pattern: players choose superficially reasonable developing or repositioning moves (Bd4, Bb5, Nh3, Kf8) instead of forcing sequences that exploit exposed kings or undefended pieces. The eval trajectory shows diverse starting positions (winning, losing, drawn) but consistent large drops, indicating the mistake isn't about misunderstanding who's ahead but rather failing to calculate concrete forcing lines. The example summaries consistently describe players choosing 'flashy' or 'slow' moves over simple winning captures or checks, losing tempo and allowing opponents to consolidate.

1477.label: Ignoring a pawn's direct attack on a knight in the opening, leaving it hanging for free capture.
1477.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a player either moves a piece other than the attacked knight (developing elsewhere like Nc3, d3, or Be2) or fails to address a pawn attacking their knight (e.g., ...exf3 threats or exf6 threats). The material signature shows 100% hangs with a median loss of -2.0 (a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic drops (median 323cp lost), typically converting drawn positions into losing ones (75% drawn->losing). The top boards almost exclusively feature positions from moves 2-4 where an advanced pawn (usually on e4 or e5) directly attacks a knight on f3 or f6, and the player ignores this threat entirely. The tactical motif is uniformly 'hanging_piece' with supporting tags of tempo_loss, development errors, and move-order miscalculations. Maia consistently recommends the knight move (100% knight), confirming the obvious defensive resource was available. This is a fundamental one-move oversight—a failure to notice the most basic pawn-attacks-piece threat in standard opening positions.

1478.label: Queen delivers a futile check in a winning endgame position, allowing the opponent to escape a forced mate or decisive advantage.
1478.description: This feature captures a highly specific and devastating endgame mistake: the player has a winning (often mate-in-N) position and plays a queen check that hangs material or squanders the entire advantage. All activating positions show a queen move delivering check that constitutes a 'hang' (non-capture losing ~5+ points of material equivalent in eval), occurring exclusively in endgame positions. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic damage—median loss of 10000 centipawns, converting forced mates or winning positions into draws or merely technical advantages. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss at 43%, promotion_error at 29%) and the Opus summaries consistently describe 'patzer sees a check' syndrome: the player gives an impulsive check that accomplishes nothing strategically, often when a quiet promotion-enabling move or a different capture order (e.g., Qxg2+ instead of Rxg2) would have delivered checkmate. The positions show complex endgames with passed pawns and promotion threats where the correct continuation required precision rather than reflexive checking.

1479.label: Player makes a quiet or developing move instead of capturing an opponent's undefended piece that is freely available.
1479.description: This feature consistently fires when a player ignores an opponent's hanging piece — typically a bishop or knight left en prise — and instead plays a quiet developing or repositioning move (often a bishop or pawn move, sometimes castling). The material signature shows 90% of the played moves are non-captures, yet Maia's recommended moves are captures 100% of the time (60% bishop captures, 16% knight, 13% rook, 10% queen). The motif is uniformly 'hanging_piece' across all top activations. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: 100% missed winning material, median cost of 489 centipawns, with 45% swinging from drawn to losing and 18% from winning to losing. The concrete positions reinforce this — e.g., failing to recapture on f3 after a bishop takes a knight, or ignoring a hanging queen. These occur overwhelmingly in the opening (71%), where players appear to prioritize development or routine moves over reading the board for free material.

1484.label: Giving a check in a won endgame that wastes tempo and disrupts the winning plan.
1484.description: This feature detects positions where a player in a clearly winning endgame delivers a check (100% played a check) that serves no constructive purpose—a classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' error. The material signature shows the moves are knights and pawns giving check without capturing anything, and the positions are exclusively endgames. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with tags emphasizing passed pawns, piece activity, and rook endgames—indicating the player had a concrete winning technique available but interrupted it with a purposeless check. The eval trajectory (winning->winning with median 9571cp loss) is misleading: several examples show 0cp loss (alternative winning paths), while the critical cases show catastrophic tempo losses that allow drawing resources. The pattern unifies around the concept of an unnecessary check that either disrupts mating geometry (Nf4 blocking Rxh4#), allows the opponent's king to escape to a better square, or wastes critical tempo needed to promote a passed pawn.

1480.label: In a winning endgame, the player captures material with the queen instead of forcing checkmate or a decisive transition via check.
1480.description: This feature fires on positions where, in a clearly won endgame, the player uses their queen to capture a pawn or rook (67% pawn, 33% rook captures) rather than playing the superior move that Maia identifies—always a queen move delivering check (Maia gives check: 100%). The material outcome is 'safe' (nothing is lost), and the eval trajectory shows minimal centipawn loss (median ~0cp), confirming these are minor inaccuracies rather than blunders. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss and pawn_endgame, with recurring tags around king_activity and conversion technique. The player is already winning but chooses a materialistic capture that wastes tempo, when the forcing check would accelerate the win or transition into a trivially won position. The boards consistently show simplified endgame positions with queens and minimal material, where the check would either drive the opponent's king into a worse position or enable a faster conversion. This is a subtle endgame technique error—prioritizing greed over tempo in positions where precision matters more than material accumulation.

1481.label: Premature bishop sacrifice on f7 with check but without sufficient attacking follow-up to justify the material investment.
1481.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring opening mistake: sacrificing a bishop on f7 (or f2 from Black's perspective) with check, typically from a light-squared bishop on c4. The material signature confirms it perfectly—bishop moves capturing a pawn with check, resulting in a net loss of approximately 2 pawns worth of material (the bishop-for-pawn exchange). The eval trajectory shows these positions go from drawn to losing (median 259cp lost), indicating the sacrifice is objectively unsound. The tactical analysis is unanimous: tags like 'insufficient_compensation,' 'premature_attack,' 'f7_sacrifice,' 'unsound_sacrifice,' and 'failed_sacrifice' all confirm that players are launching a speculative king-hunt without the necessary supporting pieces. The top 10 boards all show early opening positions (move 3-7) with Bc4xf7+ where White's remaining pieces are undeveloped, leaving no tactical infrastructure to exploit the exposed king. This is the classic beginner/intermediate trap of playing a flashy sacrifice that looks aggressive but simply loses material with no compensation.

1483.label: Moving a piece that fatally weakens one's own king position, missing an opponent's tactical capture opportunity.
1483.description: This feature identifies moves where the player neglects their own king safety, typically in the middlegame, resulting in a severe positional collapse. The material signature shows the player making non-capture moves (100% no capture) with pawns, kings, knights, or bishops that are nominally 'safe' (67%) or hang material (33%), while Maia consistently identifies a strong minor piece capture (92% knight capture) as the correct continuation. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 291 centipawns, frequently converting drawn or even winning positions into losing ones (33% drawn->losing, 17% winning->losing). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern through dominant king_safety motifs (40%), exposed king tags, and weakened kingside structures. The examples illustrate this clearly: h4 weakening dark squares around the king, Ne2 blocking escape routes and creating back-rank issues, and moves that provide illusory tempo while opening up fatal vulnerabilities. The player consistently prioritizes an aggressive or seemingly useful move while overlooking how it compromises their king's defensive structure, allowing the opponent's pieces (especially bishops and knights) to exploit the newly created weaknesses.

1482.label: Failing to address an opponent's passed pawn in a rook endgame, converting drawable or winning positions into losses.
1482.description: This feature captures a specific and recurring rook endgame mistake where the player neglects the critical threat of an opponent's passed pawn. The material signature shows all moves are 'safe' (no pieces hang or are traded), yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional collapse—38% of cases convert drawn positions to losing ones, and 15% throw outright wins, with a median cost of 270 centipawns. The dominant motif is overwhelmingly 'passed_pawn' (70%), and the boards confirm classic rook endgame structures with advanced passed pawns (c7, b5, a5, etc.) where the player makes passive or irrelevant moves (pushing kingside pawns, drifting the rook, or advancing the wrong pawn) instead of blockading or countering the passed pawn. The piece moved is typically a rook or pawn (84% combined), but critically NOT addressing the key passed pawn threat. Tags like 'tempo_loss', 'piece_activity', and 'promotion_error' reinforce that these are failures of endgame technique—wasting critical tempi when the position demanded precise prophylactic action against promotion threats.

1486.label: Aggressive knight move in the opening that hangs material by ignoring an existing threat.
1486.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake where the player lunges a knight forward aggressively (knight moved 100% of the time) without capturing anything, while ignoring an immediate tactical threat on the board. The material signature shows the move consistently hangs a piece (net material median: -3.0, i.e., a full minor piece lost), and the eval trajectory confirms the cost: positions that were drawn collapse into losing ones with a median loss of ~491 centipawns. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and tempo_loss (33%), with recurring tags like ignoring_threat, development issues, and missed_tactic. The top boards reinforce this: moves like Ne5 ignoring a threat to an undefended bishop on b5, or Ng5/Bf7 sacrificial lunges that are unsound, or Nd4 losing tempo. These are all opening-phase (100%) decisions where the player prioritizes an aggressive-looking knight jump over addressing a concrete positional or tactical obligation, resulting in immediate material loss.

1485.label: Player retreats or repositions a minor piece to a passive square, missing a concrete opportunity and losing critical tempo.
1485.description: This feature identifies moves where a player repositions a minor piece (bishop 50%, knight 25%, pawn 25%) to a passive or ineffective square without capturing anything, when a much stronger continuation existed. The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' (nothing is immediately hung), yet the median eval cost is 246 centipawns—indicating a serious positional or tactical opportunity was missed. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (an opponent's piece was free to capture), tempo_loss (the piece moved to a square from which it must move again or accomplishes nothing), and positional_mistake (the retreat abandons key defensive or attacking duties). Recurring tags like queenside_attack, closed_center, and missed_capture confirm the pattern: in closed or semi-closed positions where slow maneuvering matters, the player wastes a critical tempo by passively repositioning a piece (e.g., Bf5-h7 instead of Bxg4, Nd7-f6 losing a tempo when queenside defense was essential) rather than seizing a concrete opportunity. The eval trajectory (winning->drawn 25%, drawn->drawn 25%) shows these are often moves that squander a winning advantage or miss the moment to seize one, transforming active positions into passive ones through a single ill-timed retreat.

1489.label: Player makes an active-looking move while missing a critical king safety tactic, hanging major material or allowing mate.
1489.description: This feature fires when players make moves that appear purposeful (knight maneuvers, queen activity, king walks) but catastrophically overlook threats to their own king, resulting in massive evaluation swings (median 914 centipawns lost). The material signature shows 67% of moves hang a piece outright (non-captures that drop material), with the dominant motifs being king_safety (40%), back_rank threats, and forks—all pointing to the player ignoring immediate danger to their monarch. The trajectory confirms these are game-deciding errors: 50% convert a winning position into a losing one, and 33% turn drawn positions into losses. The tactical analyses reinforce this: players overlook forced sequences involving their exposed king (missed knight forks exploiting king position, back-rank mates, or simple captures made possible because the king is unsafe). Rather than defending or addressing the king's vulnerability, the player makes a 'normal' developing or active move, blind to the tactical refutation that the king's exposure permits.

1488.label: King moves (or other non-capturing moves) that ignore a free capture of an undefended enemy piece, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1488.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player makes a king move (100% king moved) that captures a knight (100% captured knight) in a seemingly safe transaction (net material +3 median), but critically overlooks that an enemy piece—almost always a rook—is hanging and could have been captured for free by a different piece (Maia recommends knight takes rook 100%). The eval trajectory shows these are drawn positions that become losing (median 427cp lost), indicating the player had equality but threw it away. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' with tags like missed_capture, hanging_rook, and missed_tactic appearing repeatedly. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows positions where a bishop or knight could capture an undefended rook (e.g., Bxh8, Nxa1, Bxa1), but instead the player makes a king move or other piece move that ignores this free material. The player often captures a lesser piece (knight) while leaving a much bigger capture (rook) on the table, effectively choosing the wrong capture priority and squandering a drawn position.

1487.label: Playing a purposeless or passive move that leaves a piece hanging when a winning tactic was available.
1487.description: This feature identifies positions where a player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (85% no capture) that hangs material (66% hangs outcome, median -2.0 net material) while missing a decisive tactic (85% missed winning material). The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 55% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 975 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), with missed_tactic (7) and tempo_loss (4) as top tags. The pattern across the top boards is strikingly consistent: players have a winning position with a concrete tactical shot available (often a capture or forcing check sequence winning material), but instead play a slow, purposeless move—a rook retreat, a pawn push, a king shuffle—that either directly hangs a piece or allows the opponent to seize the initiative. The Maia suggestions confirm the missed opportunities: rook captures (34%), queen captures (26%), and checks (17%) that would have been decisive. This is not an exchange error or positional misjudgment; it is a failure to recognize immediate tactical obligations, resulting in a piece left en prise while the player drifts with a tempo-losing move.

1490.label: King moves to a suboptimal square in a pawn endgame, losing a critical tempo and allowing the opponent's pawns to advance or promote.
1490.description: This feature captures king moves in pure or near-pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a tempo-losing king retreat or sidestep instead of the optimal king move. The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures, where 75% of the moves hang material (typically allowing a pawn to promote or be lost). The eval trajectory (losing->losing, median 339cp lost) indicates these players were already in trouble but made their position dramatically worse by choosing the wrong king square. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss, pawn_endgame, passed_pawn, and king_activity—paint a consistent picture: in razor-sharp pawn races where every single tempo matters, the player moves their king to a square that fails to contest the critical diagonal, file, or rank, allowing the opponent's passed pawn(s) to advance unchecked. Examples include moving Kf6 instead of capturing a critical pawn, moving Kf4 instead of Kf5 where the latter controls key squares, and moving Kd3 which abandons defense of a crucial pawn. The 50% missed winning material rate suggests that in half the cases, the correct king move would have actually turned the tables despite the deficit.

1491.label: Player makes a pawn capture that ignores a more critical tactical opportunity or threat, turning a winning position into a losing one.
1491.description: This feature fires when a player makes a pawn capture (often taking a knight) while completely overlooking a far more important tactical element in the position. The material signature shows pawn captures of knights that result in net material loss (median -3.0), indicating the capture is punished because it ignores something critical. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of cases go from winning to losing with a median loss of 689 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the pattern clearly — players reflexively grab material (a knight, a pawn) while missing forced checkmates, queen-winning threats along diagonals, or fork vulnerabilities that the opponent immediately exploits. The Maia suggestion (bishop moves, no captures) confirms that quiet developing/defensive moves were needed rather than greedy captures. Common tags like missed_mate, queen_hanging, bishop_attacks_queen, and ignored_threat all point to the same syndrome: the player's attention is captured by an available piece to take, blinding them to the opponent's far more dangerous tactical motifs. This occurs predominantly in the opening phase where such oversights are especially costly.

1492.label: Player makes a non-urgent move that fatally weakens their own king's defenses in a middlegame position where a queen attack is the critical threat.
1492.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player's move (often a rook, queen, pawn, or knight move) catastrophically neglects king safety when Maia consistently recommends a queen move to address the threat. The material signature shows 35% of moves hang material and 44% are 'safe' in immediate terms, yet 100% miss winning material—indicating the blunder is not about direct piece loss but about failing to use the queen defensively or offensively at the critical moment. The eval trajectory (median 250cp lost, with many drawn->losing and winning->drawn transitions) confirms these are game-changing mistakes rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly points to king_safety (50%) and related motifs like back_rank and exposed_king: players remove critical defensive pawns (fxe4 opening the f-file), self-block defensive diagonals (Rc6 interfering with bishop coverage), waste tempo on passive moves when immediate counterplay is required (Bb7 instead of Qxa2), or simply ignore forced mate threats. The common thread is that the player fails to recognize the urgency of their king's vulnerability and plays a structurally or materially motivated move while their opponent's queen-led attack delivers the killing blow.

1495.label: Retreating or passively developing a knight in the opening instead of exploiting a tactical window with an aggressive knight jump (typically Nb5 targeting weak squares).
1495.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player has a strong, often unique tactical shot involving an aggressive knight move (most commonly Nb5) that exploits weak squares like c7 or d6 with forking or invasion motifs. Instead of seizing this narrow one-move window, the player makes a routine developing move—retreating a knight (Nf3), developing a bishop (Be2, Bd3, Bb5), or pushing a pawn (h3)—that squanders a significant advantage. The material signature shows all moves are 'safe' (no pieces hang), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 224 centipawns, typically converting a winning position into a drawn one (89% winning->drawn). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (71%) and fork (14%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, piece_activity, and development. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, and Maia consistently recommends a knight move, confirming that the correct continuation involved an aggressive knight deployment that the player failed to recognize.

1493.label: Moving a rook to an unprotected square where it can be captured for free.
1493.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a rook (71% of activations) to a square where it is left hanging — 43% of moves result in a piece being hung with no compensation, and the median material loss is 3.0 pawns (roughly a full exchange or more). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly blunders, with a median loss of 300 centipawns, often converting drawn positions to losing ones (19%) or making already-losing positions worse (29%). The tactical analysis reinforces this: the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (40%), with examples describing rooks left completely unprotected and directly attacked along open files or ranks. The concrete positions show rooks being moved to ambitious but tactically oblivious squares — often overextending on open files (e3h3 walking into a mating net, d5d1 leaving a piece en prise, Rxd6 ignoring recapture). Unlike trade errors, these are predominantly non-captures (71% capture nothing) that simply place the rook where it can be taken for free, representing a failure to check whether the destination square is adequately defended.

1497.label: Player makes a developing or quiet move while missing a critical knight capture or knight-based tactical opportunity.
1497.description: This feature fires when players make quiet, non-capturing moves (90% no capture, 73% safe material outcome) in opening/middlegame positions where Maia consistently recommends a knight capture (100% knight move capturing a knight). The eval trajectory shows these are costly mistakes—median 284 centipawns lost, with 37% going from drawn to losing and 23% from winning to drawn. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (38%), hanging_piece (25%), and king_safety (25%), with tags like missed_tactic and ignored_threat recurring frequently. The concrete positions confirm this: players retreat bishops passively (Bb8), push pawns prematurely (d4-d5), develop pieces to quiet squares (Cb2, Rc1, Kb1), or castle/reposition—all while an opponent's knight sits exposed or a knight capture would win material or launch a decisive attack (e.g., Nxh4, Nxe4+Qh4, Nxf3+). The player loses critical tempo by ignoring the tactical urgency of the knight, allowing the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative.

1494.label: Ignoring threats to the king by making passive or irrelevant moves that hang material in positions where king safety is critical.
1494.description: This feature identifies moves where players neglect king safety concerns, resulting in significant material loss. The material signature shows 54% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -1.0 piece, and 75% involve no capture—indicating passive or misdirected moves rather than failed exchanges. The dominant tactical motif is king_safety (75%), with exposed_king and piece_activity tags recurring. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 358 centipawns, with many positions transitioning from drawn-to-losing or even winning-to-losing. The top boards confirm this: positions feature exposed kings (e.g., kings on open files, opponents with active queens/rooks bearing down) where the player makes a non-defensive move—often a knight or pawn push—that ignores the immediate king danger, allowing the opponent to exploit the vulnerability. Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve bishops and knights that address the king-side threats directly. The opening/middlegame phase distribution (34%/66%) aligns with positions where king safety is most tactically consequential.

1498.label: King moves in endgames that fail to address critical passed pawn threats, losing significant evaluation.
1498.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (85% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (62% king moves) in a way that is materially 'safe' (79% nothing immediately hangs) but strategically catastrophic, losing a median of 264 centipawns. The dominant motif is passed pawns (38%) combined with tempo loss (tagged 5 times), indicating the player mishandles passed pawn races or fails to stop opponent's passers. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting the correct response involved advancing or supporting one's own passer rather than making a passive or misdirected king move. The eval trajectories show drawn positions becoming lost (29%) and winning positions becoming drawn (14%), consistent with endgame positions where a single tempo on a passed pawn decides the outcome. The top boards confirm king-and-pawn or minor-piece endgames where passed pawns are the central strategic element, and the player's king move loses the critical tempo needed to queen or blockade.

1501.label: Minor tempo or activity concessions in simplified endgame positions that slightly reduce practical chances.
1501.description: This feature fires on positions that are entirely in the endgame phase (100%), where the player typically moves the king (67%) without capturing anything, and the move is materially safe (net material median 0.0). The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly minor inaccuracies: the median eval lost is only 2 centipawns, and the positions are mostly already losing (67% losing->losing), meaning these are not game-deciding blunders but subtle tempo or piece-activity concessions in simplified positions. The Opus analysis confirms this with dominant tags of 'tempo_loss' (6 occurrences), 'piece_activity' (6), and 'rook_endgame' (5), with summaries explicitly noting these are 'extremely minor inaccuracies' or moves losing 0-11 centipawns. The top boards show bare king endgames, rook endgames, and pawn endgames where the player chose a slightly suboptimal king retreat or rook placement, marginally reducing resistance rather than committing a true tactical or strategic error.

1500.label: King moves forward in pawn endgames/rook endgames, abandoning critical defensive or offensive duties around passed pawns.
1500.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player advances their king (100% king moves) instead of playing the correct pawn move (Maia consistently recommends pawn moves). The positions are exclusively endgames, typically rook endgames or pure pawn races involving passed pawns. The king move is often a tempo loss—the king goes to the wrong square or advances prematurely, allowing the opponent to exploit the misplaced king. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences (median 517cp lost), frequently converting winning positions into draws or holdable positions into losses. The tactical analysis confirms that these are narrow positions where only one move works (often a pawn advance like b6, h6, e6, or f7), and the king move squanders the position. The common tags (passed_pawn, tempo_loss, rook_endgame, pawn_race) all point to critical endgame junctures where precise calculation of tempi around passed pawns is essential, and the king wanders to an inferior square instead of supporting or pushing the decisive pawn.

1504.label: Player makes a quiet or positional move while missing a forcing rook check that leads to checkmate or decisive material gain.
1504.description: This feature identifies positions where the player had a winning rook check available (Maia's move is 100% rook with 100% check) that would exploit the opponent's exposed king, but instead played a quiet move with a different piece (rook 39%, king 18%, bishop 15%, knight 15%) that captured nothing (79% no capture) and was nominally 'safe' (76%). The missed opportunity cost a median of 361 centipawns, frequently converting wins into draws or losses (winning->drawn 11%, drawn->losing 10%, winning->losing 7%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is king_safety (75%), with recurring tags of missed_mate, exposed_king, mating_net, and rook_check. The concrete examples show players retreating bishops, castling, or making positional rook moves while a forcing rook check would have initiated a mating attack or won decisive material against a trapped king. The pattern is a failure to recognize that the opponent's king geometry permits a lethal checking sequence.

1496.label: Moving a key defensive or attacking piece away from a critical diagonal/square, allowing opponent's tactical threats to materialize.
1496.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player voluntarily relocates a piece (most often a bishop, but also queen or knight) that was performing a crucial defensive or offensive role, inadvertently enabling the opponent's latent tactical threats. The material signature shows 50% of moves are nominally 'safe' (no immediate capture loss) while 50% hang material—indicating the damage is indirect rather than an outright blunder of the moved piece itself. The eval trajectory (median 522cp lost, with 60% winning->winning but 30% winning->drawn) reveals these are overwhelmingly positions where the player squanders a significant advantage. The tactical motifs—discovered attacks, king safety collapses, hanging pieces exposed, and tempo loss—all point to the same mechanism: the moved piece was a linchpin holding the position together, and its removal unlocks opponent counterplay (discovered checks, knight invasions, diagonal/rank exploitation). The Opus analyses explicitly describe scenarios like 'removes the bishop from c4 which was preventing Nd5 with discovered check' and 'abandoned the lethal diagonal geometry.' Maia's recommended moves (capturing knights 50%, rooks 20%) suggest the correct approach was to press the attack with captures rather than passively repositioning.

1499.label: Knight captures a pawn on e5 where it becomes pinned or tactically vulnerable, losing material in the opening.
1499.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where a knight captures on e5 (or similar central squares) grabbing a pawn but walking into a tactical refutation—most commonly a pin along the e-file or a discovered attack. The material signature shows knights making 62% of the moves, capturing pawns 62% of the time, with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (75%) with uncastled kings, and the eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions into losing ones (50% drawn->losing), with a massive median eval loss of 453 centipawns. The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pins (40%) and discovered attacks (20%), with recurring tags of piece_activity, king_safety, and development neglect. The concrete boards show a clear pattern: Black's knight jumps to e5 capturing the e-pawn, but the king remains on e8, leaving the knight exposed to pins along the e-file (often from a bishop on c4 or queen on e2) or discovered attacks. The 'wrong knight' theme also appears—choosing the knight that abandons a strong post or leaves another piece undefended. This is a greedy central capture that ignores tactical vulnerabilities created by an uncastled king.

1505.label: A check (usually with a rook) that wastes tempo in an endgame, allowing the opponent to improve their position.
1505.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring mistake: giving a check—almost always with a rook (86%)—in an endgame (84%) that accomplishes nothing strategically and loses critical tempo. The material signature shows 100% of activating moves are checks, yet 93% capture nothing, and the opponent's response (Maia) is never a check back (0%), often simply a king move (27%) that lands on a better square. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (80%), and the tag 'pointless_check' appears explicitly. The eval trajectory reveals these checks are costly—median 237 centipawns lost—transforming drawn positions into losing ones (24%), winning into drawn (14%), or winning into losing (6%). The per-position analyses repeatedly describe the 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' pattern, where the player throws away a winning or holdable endgame by giving a meaningless check instead of improving their king position, advancing a passed pawn, or executing a concrete winning plan. The opponent's king simply steps to a better square, gaining the very tempo the checking side squandered.

1502.label: Moving the queen to a square where it is immediately captured or trapped by an opposing piece.
1502.description: This feature detects a highly specific and costly tactical blunder: the player moves their queen (100% queen moves) into a square where it is immediately hanging or capturable by an opponent's piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median net loss of -6.0 material, with 86% classified as 'loses' and 14% as 'hangs'). The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), with tags like 'blundered_queen', 'queen_for_rook_blunder', and 'bishop_diagonal_oversight' — all pointing to the queen landing on a defended or attacked square the player failed to notice. The eval trajectory shows these moves are game-deciding (median 529 centipawns lost), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (36% drawn->losing, 21% winning->losing). Concrete examples include queens capturing defended rooks (overlooking a back-rank defender), queens stepping onto open diagonals controlled by bishops, and queens taking pieces on squares immediately recapturable by rooks or minor pieces. The better moves (Maia suggestions) are typically non-queen moves (knights, bishops, pawns) that avoid the tactical oversight entirely, often with 86% non-captures, indicating the correct approach was a quiet developing or defensive move rather than the aggressive but fatal queen sortie.

1503.label: Developing a piece to an exposed square in the opening, ignoring tactical threats and losing significant material.
1503.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (79% opening) where a player develops a minor piece (bishop 31%, knight 29%) or pushes a pawn (19%) to an exposed or tactically vulnerable square, ignoring existing threats. The material signature shows 31% of moves hang a piece outright while 60% appear 'safe' only superficially—the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences with a median loss of 288 centipawns, often converting winning positions to drawn (36%) or drawn to losing (21%). The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 40%, fork 20%, tempo_loss 20%) combined with tags like 'piece_left_undefended', 'move_order_error', and 'development' confirm these are premature or misprioritized developing moves that walk into concrete tactics. Maia's recommended moves are always pawn moves (100%), suggesting the correct approach was a quiet preparatory move rather than an aggressive piece sortie. The top boards consistently show players lunging with knights or bishops (Nxe5, Ng5, Nxc7 forks missed, Bxf7 prematures) in sharp opening positions where patient play was required.

1506.label: Leaves a piece hanging to an enemy pawn in the opening, turning a drawn position into a lost one.
1506.description: This feature detects a specific and recurring opening blunder where the player moves a piece (most often a knight) to a square directly attacked by an enemy pawn, or ignores an existing pawn threat to one of their pieces. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' — these are non-capture moves that simply drop material, with a median loss of 2.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms the severity: every instance transitions from a drawn position to a losing one, with a median cost of 405 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (75%), supported by tags like 'pawn_captures_piece', 'undefended_knight', and 'opening_blunder'. Examining the top boards reveals positions featuring the e5 advance in various openings (Pirc, Philidor, King's Indian structures) where the player either moves a knight into the pawn's path (e.g., ...Nf6 into e5) or plays a developing move that ignores the pawn's threat to an existing piece (e.g., ...Nc6 when dxc6 is available). Maia's response is uniformly a pawn capture, confirming the pattern of a simple pawn-takes-piece punishment. This is a fundamental tactical oversight in the opening rather than a complex positional misjudgment.

1507.label: Playing a passive or non-forcing move in the opening/middlegame when the position demanded immediate tactical exploitation of an advantage.
1507.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a significant advantage (73% missed winning material, median 302cp lost) but plays a quiet, non-forcing move—typically a pawn push (32%), bishop move (20%), or knight move (18%)—that doesn't capture anything (89% no capture) and isn't a check (96%). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%), hanging_piece (33%), and fork (17%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, piece_activity, and development. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert winning positions to drawn (27%) or drawn to losing (14%), representing catastrophic squandering of advantages. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (55%) and middlegame (46%), where tempi are critical. The top board examples confirm the pattern: playing a5 instead of exploiting underdevelopment, castling instead of capturing material with Qxb7, retreating a queen (Qe2) instead of maintaining pressure, and making prophylactic pawn moves (e3, c3) when concrete tactics were available. The piece that should have been played was often identified by Maia as a capture (52% of Maia moves are captures vs only 11% of actual moves), confirming the player chose passivity over forcing action.

1508.label: Player moves a major piece to an inferior square while overlooking an opponent's undefended piece that could be captured for free.
1508.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move with a rook or queen (80% combined) that results in material loss (hanging 33%, loses 20%, slightly_down 20%, with a median net material of -2.0), while a free or advantageous capture was available. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 60%, and 80% of these positions involve missed winning material. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: players overlook undefended enemy pieces (a hanging rook on g2, a vulnerable queen on c4) and instead make purposeless or inferior moves. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 279 centipawns, with the mistake converting drawn positions to losing (20%) or making already-losing positions much worse (27%). The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (87%), where the board is complex enough that undefended pieces get overlooked. Rather than a positional or strategic error, this is a pure tactical oversight—the player simply doesn't see that an enemy piece is en prise and plays something else entirely.

1509.label: A knight check that wastes tempo by displacing the knight from a strong square while allowing the opponent's king to improve its position.
1509.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame error pattern: playing a knight check that serves no constructive purpose. The material signature shows knight moves (100%) that give check (100%) but frequently hang the piece or lose material (median -1.0, 57% hangs). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly mistakes (median 118cp lost), often worsening already difficult positions (57% losing->losing) or squandering advantages (14% winning->drawn, 14% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis is the clearest signal: the dominant tags are 'pointless_check' (5/7) and 'tempo_loss' (4/7), with per-position summaries consistently describing knights being displaced from excellent outposts (e3, e4, strong centralized squares) to passive squares after the opponent's king simply sidesteps. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (71%), where king activity and piece placement are paramount, making these tempo-losing checks especially damaging. Rather than maintaining the knight on a dominant square and improving king position, the player impulsively delivers a check that accomplishes nothing while permanently worsening their knight's coordination.

1511.label: Playing a showy check that ignores a critical tactical obligation, hanging material in the process.
1511.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player delivers a check (71% of moves are checks) — typically with a rook (43%) or other piece — that looks aggressive but fatally ignores a more urgent tactical need. The material signature is devastating: 57% of moves hang a piece outright, 29% lose material in exchange, with a median cost of -2.0 material and 318 centipawns of evaluation lost. The trajectory shows 43% of these turn a winning position into a losing one. The tactical motifs (discovered_attack, king_safety, counter_check) and the per-position analyses reveal a consistent pattern: the player has a forcing-looking check available but it is 'a hollow gesture' that fails to address the real threat or obligation in the position (e.g., capturing a queen, defending a hanging piece, or completing a combination in the correct move order). Maia's recommendations frequently involve capturing major material (queen 29%, rook 14%) rather than delivering the flashy check. The players are seduced by the visual drama of giving check while overlooking that the check accomplishes nothing structurally and leaves critical material en prise.

1510.label: Hanging a queen or major piece via a careless move in an already-winning position, throwing away a decisive advantage.
1510.description: This feature fires on positions where a player who is already winning (55% winning→winning, 9% winning→losing, 9% winning→drawn, 18% losing→winning with median eval loss of 9315 centipawns) makes a non-capture move that hangs a major piece—queen 64% of the time, rook 27%. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' (a non-capture that drops a piece) with a median net material loss of -6.0, consistent with losing a queen. The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of hanging_piece (50%) and king_safety (50%), with recurring tags like queen_hanging, unprotected_queen, winning_position_thrown, and missed_mate. The concrete examples reveal a consistent pattern: the player moves a queen or rook to an undefended square that is attacked by an opponent's piece (often a bishop on a diagonal), or moves a defender away from the queen, leaving it en prise. Many positions also feature a missed forced mate—the player had checkmate available but instead played a purposeless or flashy move (like a pointless check) that exposes their own piece. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (91%), where complex positions with many active pieces make it easier to overlook a single diagonal or defensive relationship.

1512.label: King moves that ignore or bungle critical pawn promotions in endgames, allowing the opponent to draw or deliver checkmate.
1512.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a 'safe' manner—not hanging material directly—yet catastrophically misses a pawn promotion or mishandles the promotion sequence. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 10000 centipawns, with half the cases converting a winning position into a draw, confirming these are game-throwing errors. The opponent's best response consistently involves checks (Maia gives check 100%), often connected to promotion or back-rank threats. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of promotion_error, king_safety, and tempo_loss: the king wanders to a square that either allows the opponent's promotion with check/checkmate, or forfeits the player's own promotion tempo. The top boards reinforce this—positions with advanced passed pawns (c7, f7, g7, a2) where a single promotion move wins, but the player instead makes a passive or misguided king move that squanders the win. The key pattern is a king retreating or sidestepping when the critical task was executing or stopping a pawn promotion.

1514.label: Player makes a losing move that misses a critical tactical opportunity, typically involving checks or captures that expose their own king.
1514.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move (usually with a rook) that loses significant material (median -4.0, net loss 408 centipawns) by missing a available tactic. The material signature shows 67% losses and 33% hangs, indicating these are not exchanges but genuine material hemorrhages. The eval trajectory spans all phases of advantage (winning->losing, drawn->losing, losing->losing), but the common thread is the tactical nature: tags consistently show 'missed_tactic' (appearing in all three examples), combined with 'exposed_king' and 'king_safety' concerns. The positions reveal a pattern where the player either delivers or walks into checks without calculating the full tactical consequences—67% of moves played are checks, yet they still lose material. The Opus analysis confirms players are making premature captures or failing to find forcing sequences (check-check-capture patterns, fork opportunities, pin exploitations). The positions are predominantly middlegame (67%) with complex piece interactions where a critical intermediate move or forcing sequence was available but overlooked.

1513.label: Player makes a passive or retreating move that leaves a piece undefended, squandering a winning or equal position.
1513.description: This feature captures moves where a player, typically in the middlegame with a winning or equal position, plays a quiet move (often a pawn push, queen retreat, or rook/bishop repositioning) that leaves one of their own pieces hanging and undefended. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in a hang (not a capture gone wrong, but a non-capture that drops a piece), with the dominant motif being 'hanging_piece' (60%) combined with 'tempo_loss' (40%). The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 484cp lost, with 42% going from winning to drawn and 33% from winning to losing—indicating these are not positional subtleties but concrete oversights. Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve captures (queen 33%, bishop 25%, knight 17%), confirming that after the blunder, the opponent can simply take the undefended piece. The concrete examples reinforce this: f3 ignoring an undefended bishop on b4, d3 instead of capturing a hanging knight with dxc3, queen retreats abandoning critical defensive posts. The common thread is that the player makes a move with some local logic (advancing, retreating, repositioning) while completely overlooking that one of their pieces is unprotected and can be taken for free.

1521.label: Player makes a king move instead of capturing an undefended enemy queen sitting on an open line.
1521.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a simple queen capture that would win the game. The material/position signature shows the player moves their king (57%) or queen (43%) instead of taking the opponent's queen, which Maia correctly identifies as capturable 100% of the time. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of cases, and the tags confirm missed_capture (5/7), undefended_queen, and queen_blunder patterns. The eval trajectory is devastating: median loss of 831 centipawns, with 43% of cases turning winning positions into losing ones and another 43% turning wins into draws. The board positions consistently show queen endgames or simplified middlegames where both queens share an open diagonal or file, yet the player makes an aimless king move (Kh2, Kh6, Kg1, Kg7, Kc7) completely missing the elementary queen capture. This represents a fundamental tactical blindness—failing to see that the opponent's queen is en prise—rather than a complex calculation error.

1515.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in the opening, missing a forcing queen check that wins material or delivers checkmate.
1515.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, non-forcing move (knight development or pawn push) while a devastating queen check (often with follow-up tactics) is available. The material signature shows the played move is 'safe' — nothing is immediately hung — but Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100%). The eval trajectory shows massive cost (median 260cp lost), flipping games from winning to drawn or losing to winning for the opponent. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are king_safety (62%) and tempo_loss (25%), with tags heavily featuring missed_tactic, queen_check, and even missed_mate. The boards show early opening positions where the opponent has weakened their king (often via aggressive pawn pushes like g4/f3 or premature pawn storms), creating diagonal or file vulnerabilities that a queen check would exploit decisively. Instead, players make natural-looking quiet moves (b6, Ne7, Bf5, c3) that squander the tactical window. The positions are universally in the opening phase, suggesting players are on 'autopilot' with development rather than calculating concrete forcing sequences.

1519.label: Playing a tempo-losing queen check in the opening that loses development time and hangs material.
1519.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) during the opening phase (100%) that turns out to be a costly tempo loss. The material signature shows these checks frequently hang the queen or leave it misplaced (57% hangs, median net material -1.0), while the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: 71% of cases convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 306 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with recurring tags of development problems, piece_activity issues, and misplaced_queen. The concrete positions (Qa4+, Qa5+, Qb4+) show a pattern of premature queen sorties delivering checks that look active but actually lose critical development tempi, allowing the opponent to gain initiative while the queen retreats or becomes trapped. Rather than developing pieces or castling, the player is lured by a superficially forcing check that ultimately costs significant material or positional compensation.

1517.label: Moving a knight to an undefended square where it is immediately captured for free.
1517.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: a player moves their knight (56% of activations) to a square where it hangs with no protection, and the opponent simply captures it. The material signature is overwhelmingly 'hangs' (73%) with a median loss of 3.0 pawns (i.e., a full piece), confirming these are not trades or exchanges but outright piece losses. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (80%), and tags like 'undefended_knight' and 'unprotected_knight' appearing explicitly. The eval trajectory shows devastating consequences: 33% of cases turn a drawn position into a losing one, with a median cost of 347 centipawns. The concrete positions illustrate the pattern vividly—knights moved to c4, f4, a5, g5, g4 where they land on squares with zero defenders and are immediately captured by a bishop or other piece. This occurs primarily in the opening (33%) and middlegame (67%), often when players aggressively reposition knights without checking if the target square is actually safe. Maia's recommendations also favor knight moves (65%) but to defended squares, confirming the error is specifically about neglecting piece safety rather than choosing the wrong piece to move.

1520.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king retreats or sidesteps when it should advance directly, losing a critical tempo in the pawn race.
1520.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a direction that wastes a tempo rather than taking the optimal direct path. The material signature shows these are 'safe' moves—nothing is captured or hung—yet the eval trajectory reveals they cost a median of 192 centipawns, always in already-losing positions (losing→losing 100%), making a bad situation significantly worse. The dominant tactical motifs are tempo_loss (40%) and pawn_endgame (30%), with recurring tags like king_activity and passed_pawn reinforcing that the critical resource being squandered is time (tempi) in a race between kings and pawns. Concrete examples show kings going to c2 instead of b4, or retreating to d2 instead of maintaining an active stance—moves that require two steps to reach what one correct step could have accomplished, often turning a difficult-but-resistable loss into a completely hopeless one.

1516.label: Player makes a passive or inferior move when a decisive material-winning capture (often queen taking a hanging piece) was available.
1516.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a winning capture that was clearly available. The material signature shows that 100% of the time, the engine's preferred move (Maia's move) involves the queen capturing major material (rooks or queens), yet the player instead makes a passive pawn push or misguided queen move. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (43%) and tempo_loss (29%)—confirm that the opponent had material en prise that went uncollected. The concrete examples reinforce this: in one position Black plays Qg5 instead of capturing a hanging queen with Qxg4+ leading to forced mate; in another, a player makes a quiet rook move while a decisive capture exists; in several positions pieces are left hanging while the player makes a slow pawn move or repositioning move. The eval trajectory is somewhat mixed (median 0.0 cp lost) because some positions were already winning or already lost, but the key unifying pattern is that a concrete, tactically winning capture was missed in favor of an inferior alternative. The 'missed winning material: 100%' signal is the strongest confirmation that every activation represents a position where significant material could have been won immediately.

1518.label: Giving an impulsive check that squanders a winning position instead of playing a quiet decisive move.
1518.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check (93% of activations) with a bishop or rook that hangs material (47% hangs, median net -4.0) instead of playing a stronger quiet move that would maintain or convert a winning advantage. The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly winning positions thrown away (67% winning->winning with massive centipawn losses, median 8856cp lost, and 87% missed winning material), indicating the player had a forced mate or crushing continuation available but chose a flashy check instead. The Opus tactical analysis explicitly identifies 'premature_check' as a recurring tag (3 occurrences), with tempo_loss and king_safety as dominant motifs — the check often allows the opponent to block with tempo, reposition a piece favorably, or escape to safety. Maia's recommended moves (queen 40%, rook 33%, knight 20%) notably give check 0% of the time, confirming that the correct continuations were quiet moves building the attack rather than premature checks. The concrete examples show patterns like checking when a mating net could be set up with a quiet bishop move, or giving a back-rank check that allows the opponent to interpose and consolidate.

1522.label: In won pawn endgames, the player makes an aimless king move instead of executing the winning queen check or promotion sequence.
1522.description: This feature detects a specific endgame error pattern where a player with a decisive advantage (winning→winning, but losing a massive median of 9467 centipawns—often converting mate-in-N into a much longer or less clean win) plays a safe king move instead of the optimal continuation. The material signature shows the player always moves their king with no capture and no check, while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capturing a pawn with check—indicating the player already has a queen but fails to use it decisively. The positions are universally pawn endgames or queen-vs-pawns scenarios featuring passed pawns and promotion threats. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss 30%, passed_pawn 40%, pawn_endgame 30%) and tactical tags (tempo_loss, king_activity, promotion_threat) confirm the pattern: the player retreats or wanders the king when precise queen checks or immediate pawn capture would resolve the position instantly. The boards show king moves like Ke3, Kd2, Kf5, Ke2 in positions where the queen should be actively checking and mopping up pawns. The colossal centipawn loss reflects not material hanging but the squandering of a forced mating sequence into a much longer technical conversion.

1523.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while opponent has a decisive tactical threat requiring immediate attention.
1523.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a move (often a rook, king, or pawn move) that ignores a critical immediate threat, resulting in catastrophic evaluation losses (median 834 centipawns). The material signature shows these are not capture-based errors—75% involve no capture—but rather moves that allow the opponent to execute a winning tactic. The Opus analysis reveals the common thread: tempo loss (tagged twice) combined with exposed king or promotion threats that demanded an immediate defensive or counter-tactical response. The top boards show middlegame positions where the opponent has a knight fork, a passed pawn about to promote, or a back-rank/king-safety threat, and the player wastes their move on something irrelevant (like h4-h5 when a pawn is on a2 about to queen, or Kb5 when Rxf7+ was the only resource). The eval trajectory spans all game states (winning→losing, drawn→losing, losing→losing) because the unifying factor isn't the starting position quality but rather the failure to address the single most urgent threat on the board.
