1586.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern where players make knight moves (65% of activations) that result in material loss—primarily hanging the piece (40%) or losing material in an unsound exchange (15%), with a median net material loss of -2.0 (consistent with losing a minor piece). The eval trajectory shows these moves are overwhelmingly costly, with a median loss of 269 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing (30%) or winning positions to drawn/losing (30%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), with tags like 'unsound_sacrifice' and 'missed_tactic' appearing repeatedly. Concrete examples include Nd5 sacrifices where the knight is simply captured with no real compensation (cxd5 leaves White a piece down), and knight jumps to squares where they are undefended or inadequately supported. Maia's recommended alternatives (rooks 20%, queens 20%) suggest the correct moves typically involved consolidating or activating major pieces rather than speculative knight lunges. The positions are predominantly middlegame (55%) and opening (35%), where premature knight aggression without calculating the tactical consequences leads to immediate material loss.

1588.label: Player makes a routine or developing move while missing a simple capture that wins material for free.
1588.description: This feature fires when players overlook elementary captures available on the board. The material signature shows 78% of these moves involve no capture by the player, while Maia's suggested moves capture pieces 58% of the time (knights 44%, pawns 8%, queens 6%), indicating a clear free capture was available but ignored. The 'hangs' rate of 28% reflects cases where the player's move additionally leaves material en prise. The devastating median eval loss of 313 centipawns confirms these are full-piece blunders, with 92% missing winning material. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%) and the recurring tags missed_capture and missed_tactic—confirm the pattern: pieces are literally available to be taken but the player plays something else (often a developing or routine move). The Opus analysis reinforces this with examples like 'missed the elementary tactic that the knight on f6 can simply be captured for free' and 'threw away a full piece by playing a routine developing move instead of the crushing capture.' The opening/middlegame phase split (50/50) and the trajectory showing winning->drawn (19%) and drawn->losing (17%) indicate these oversights occur when positions still have tactical richness that the player fails to notice, defaulting to autopilot development instead of calculating concrete captures.

1589.label: In won endgames, player makes an inaccurate move that hangs material or misses a simple winning continuation, squandering a decisive advantage.
1589.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player holds a winning or near-winning position but plays a move that hangs material (75% hangs) or makes a poor trade, with a devastating median eval loss of 1067 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows 50% of cases go from winning to drawn, indicating blown conversions. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging pieces (43%), promotion errors (14%), and missed captures/tactics, with recurring tags like missed_capture, missed_tactic, and promotion_error. The concrete positions confirm this: a player plays ...a2 instead of promoting immediately (losing a won pawn ending), another misses a free queen capture with axb4, another takes a pawn instead of the opponent's queen. These are not complex tactical oversights but rather simple endgame conversion failures where the player, perhaps rushing or relaxing in a won position, overlooks elementary winning moves—promotions, captures, or piece safety—allowing the opponent to draw or significantly reduce the deficit.

1592.label: Moves that fatally weaken king safety by hanging or losing material in positions where the opponent has attacking chances.
1592.description: This feature captures moves where players neglect king safety and lose substantial material as a result. The material signature shows 50% hangs and 41% loses with a median net loss of -4.0 (roughly a full piece or more), indicating these are not exchanges but outright material giveaways. The dominant motifs are king_safety (43%) and hanging_piece (29%), with tags like exposed_king and missed_tactic appearing frequently. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: 27% convert drawn positions to losing, 18% throw winning positions into losses, with a median eval loss of 348 centipawns. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: kings on e6, f2, f7 in open positions where the player makes a move that either exposes their own king or fails to address an existing king vulnerability, often missing a defensive or tactical resource (like Qxc4 or Qxe1+). The Maia recommendations heavily favor queen moves (55%) often capturing material, suggesting the correct responses involved active queen defense or counterattack that the players missed while making positionally naive moves that left their king exposed.

1593.label: Player makes a non-forcing move with a minor piece or rook when a queen check sequence wins material decisively.
1593.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a rook, bishop, or knight (50%/20%/20%) in a non-capturing way (70% no capture) while Maia consistently recommends a queen move with check (100% queen, 100% check, 70% capturing a pawn). The material signature shows 40% of these moves hang a piece or tempo, and the eval trajectory reveals massive cost (median 500cp lost), frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 30%, winning->losing 10%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant pattern: players confuse move order, choosing a piece development or repositioning move when a forcing queen check initiates an unstoppable tactical sequence. Tags like tempo_loss, check_sequence, and missed_tactic recur—players lose the initiative by failing to recognize that an immediate queen check creates threats that win material or deliver a mating attack. The concrete positions show complex middlegames where quiet-looking piece moves squander decisive tactical opportunities that required precise forcing sequences starting with queen checks.

1591.label: In the opening, moving a knight to a passive or retreating square when facing e5 pawn advances, wasting critical development tempo.
1591.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening mistake pattern where Black's knight on f6 is challenged by White's e5 pawn advance (a common theme in Italian Game and Two Knights Defense positions) and Black responds with a poor knight move — retreating to g8, jumping to h5, g4, or e4 — instead of the correct continuation. The material signature shows 64% knight moves that predominantly hang material (55%) with a median loss of -1.0 (a full piece), while Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (likely d5 counter-strikes). The eval trajectory is devastating: 73% of these moves convert a drawn position into a losing one, with a median 252cp loss. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with piece_activity and development as the most common tags — Black squanders development time by mishandling the knight, allowing White to consolidate the e5 pawn's spatial advantage. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, all featuring the e5 pawn thrust against Nf6 in Italian/Two Knights structures, making this a recognizable pattern of failing to meet the central challenge with the correct d5 pawn break.

1596.label: Pieces are moved to passive squares, losing critical tempo and converting a drawn position into a lost one.
1596.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where a player makes a piece move (knight or rook) that doesn't capture anything but fatally wastes tempo, converting a drawn position into a losing one (median 382cp loss). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), appearing consistently across the top activating examples. The concrete pattern shows pieces being relocated away from active squares to passive ones—a knight leaving a critical central outpost (e4→g5), a queen retreating from an attacking post, a bishop moving to a less useful diagonal—all in positions where the draw required maintaining piece activity or executing a specific tactic. The material signature shows no captures are made (100% non-capture), and 50% of the time the move outright hangs material, while the other 50% appears safe but is positionally catastrophic. Maia consistently finds pawn captures that exploit the lost tempo. The positions tend to be complex middlegames where maintaining piece coordination on active squares was essential to holding the balance.

1594.label: In lost endgames, moving a rook or king into a position where the rook becomes trapped or loses coordination, catastrophically worsening an already difficult position.
1594.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern in lost endgame positions (losing->losing 100%, endgame 100%) where the player makes a move—most often a rook move (67%) or king move (33%)—that doesn't immediately hang material (safe 100%) but catastrophically worsens the position (median 408cp lost). The dominant motifs are trapped_piece (30%) and king_safety (30%), with tempo_loss and hanging_piece also prominent. Examining the top boards reveals a clear pattern: rook endgames where a rook retreats or advances to a square where it becomes tactically trapped or loses all useful activity (e.g., Rf5-f6 repeatedly appearing as a trapped_piece motif against a centralized enemy queen). The player's pieces lose coordination—the rook blocks its own king or walks into a discovered attack/skewer. While the position was already losing, these moves convert 'difficult but defensible' situations into ones where the rook is immediately lost or mate is forced, as the Opus analysis confirms. The common tags (piece_activity, king_safety, tempo_loss) reinforce that these are moves where passive defense or active counterplay was available but the player instead made a structurally self-defeating move that trapped their own piece.

1595.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that hangs material while missing a forced queen capture or checkmate.
1595.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position makes a move (typically a rook or pawn push) that hangs material instead of finding a decisive tactical blow. The SEE signature shows 100% hangs with no captures, while Maia consistently identifies queen moves (often queen captures with check) as the correct continuation. The eval trajectory is devastating: all positions go from winning to still winning, but with a median loss of ~9471 centipawns—indicating missed forced mates being converted into merely large advantages. The Opus analysis confirms this with dominant tags of 'missed_mate', 'queen_capture_with_check', and 'hanging_piece', showing players who overlook that the opponent's queen or back rank is vulnerable, instead playing an irrelevant or tempo-losing move that leaves their own piece en prise. The common thread is a failure to calculate the critical forcing sequence (usually a queen capture or mate threat) in favor of a superficially reasonable but tactically oblivious continuation.

1597.label: Developing or moving a piece/pawn to a square where it immediately hangs to a simple tactical threat in the opening.
1597.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where a player moves a knight or pawn to an undefended or tactically vulnerable square, immediately hanging material to a one-move threat. The material signature shows 50% outright hangs and 50% trades resulting in a net loss (median -1.0, i.e., losing roughly a full piece), and the eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 437cp lost), with half going from winning to losing and half from drawn to losing. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (57%) and fork (29%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, piece_activity, and ignored_threat. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: knights developed to squares attacked by pawns (Nf3 into g4 pawn, Ne5 where it can be captured), pawns moved that ignore an immediate capture threat (e6 blocking defense of an attacked knight), and pieces placed on exposed squares vulnerable to forks or queen attacks along open lines. These are not complex multi-move oversights but simple one-move hanging blunders during development, where the player fails to notice an immediate tactical refutation of their piece placement.

1600.label: Developing a bishop in the opening that leaves a knight unprotected, allowing opponent to win it cleanly.
1600.description: This feature detects a specific opening blunder pattern where a player develops their bishop (100% bishop moves) without noticing that it leaves a knight hanging (material outcome: hangs 100%, median -3.0 pawns = a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions turning losing (100%, median 286cp loss). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is a hanging piece (60%), with recurring themes of pins and forks that prevent recapture. The top activating positions are overwhelmingly Sicilian/Open Game structures where White plays Bd3 or Bd2 on move 6-7, neglecting that a central knight on d4 is left undefended—often because a pin on the c3-knight (e.g., Bb4) removes the expected recapture. Maia consistently identifies the winning response as capturing the knight (100% knight captures knight). The common tags (development, missed_tactic, opening_trap) confirm this is a pattern of prioritizing piece development over tactical vigilance in familiar opening positions.

1599.label: Player moves their king or piece passively instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece.
1599.description: This feature fires when players overlook a simple hanging piece capture. The material signature shows the player mostly moves their king (56%) or rook (22%) without capturing anything (100% no capture), while Maia's recommended move captures a rook (89%) or queen (11%) — indicating a free capture was available. The 'missed winning material' tag fires 100% of the time, and the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%), with 'missed_capture' appearing in 6 of 9 tagged positions. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly winning positions that remain winning (89%) but shed a median of 155 centipawns — consistent with missing a free piece but retaining enough advantage to stay ahead. The concrete positions confirm this: players make routine king moves (Kg2, Kf5, Kb5) or passive piece moves (Re2, Be2, Rc1) while an opponent's piece sits en prise on an open diagonal or file. This is not a complex tactical oversight but rather a simple failure to notice an undefended piece that could be taken for free.

1598.label: Trading queens in winning positions where the queen was the primary attacking instrument, converting wins into draws.
1598.description: This feature fires on positions where the player initiates a queen trade (queen moved 86%, queen captured 57%) that squanders a winning advantage (winning->drawn 57%, median eval lost 411cp). The material signature shows 'trade' 57% — these are exchanges, not blunders — yet the positional consequence is catastrophic. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring theme: queens are traded away precisely when they are the key attacking piece against an exposed king or the instrument maintaining pressure. Maia's preferred moves (knight 43%, queen 43%) suggest quieter continuations or maintaining the queen on the board would have preserved the advantage. The 86% 'missed winning material' rate confirms these players had dominant positions with tactical opportunities they failed to exploit, instead simplifying into equality. The concrete examples show queen exchanges that relieve pressure on exposed kings (Qxg7 removing attack, Qxb3 trading into a drawable endgame, Qxe3 exchanging when the queen was coordinating an attack). The check rate (71%) suggests these trades often come with tempo-gaining checks that appear active but actually simplify the position fatally.

1602.label: Player makes a safe but passive knight move, missing a forcing tactical combination that wins major material.
1602.description: This feature identifies positions in the opening phase where a player moves a knight safely (no capture, no check, nothing immediately hangs) but completely misses a winning tactical combination—typically one that wins a queen for lesser material (Maia consistently shows queen captures of rooks as the missed best move). The material signature shows 100% 'safe' moves that aren't blunders in the traditional sense of hanging a piece, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 385cp), consistently converting winning positions into drawn ones. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (75%)—meaning the opponent had a piece that could be won through a forcing sequence—combined with tempo_loss (25%), where the knight retreat or passive move wastes critical development time. The top boards repeatedly show knight retreats from active squares (g5f3 appears multiple times) or quiet developing moves (d2d3, b1d2) when sharp tactical blows like Bxf7+ or Nxf7 were available. This is fundamentally a pattern-recognition failure: the player sees no immediate danger, plays a 'normal' move, and completely overlooks a concrete tactical shot that would have been decisive.

1603.label: Moves that fatally compromise king safety by opening lines, removing defenders, or ignoring tactical threats to the king.
1603.description: This feature captures moves where the player overlooks critical king safety considerations, resulting in massive evaluation losses (median 448 centipawns). The dominant motif is king_safety at 67%, with recurring tags like exposed_king, diagonal_attack, opened_line_toward_king, and removed_defender. The material signature shows these aren't simple piece-hanging blunders in the traditional sense—45% are 'safe' moves and 23% are trades—yet they catastrophically worsen the position because they open lines toward the king, remove key defensive pieces, or allow checks with tempo. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: winning positions become drawn or lost (29% combined), and the median centipawn loss of 448 indicates near-decisive swings. The concrete positions consistently show kings on open files or diagonals (e.g., king on c7 with opened dark-square diagonal, king on g1 with removed g2 defender, king on h6 exposed to queen attacks). Players are lured by material gains or seemingly reasonable moves while being blind to the opponent's tactical exploitation of their king's vulnerability.

1604.label: Bishop sacrifices on h2/h7 with check that lack sufficient follow-up pieces to sustain the attack.
1604.description: This feature detects the classic unsound Greek Gift sacrifice pattern. The material signature shows bishop captures pawn with check 100% of the time, with the outcome being 'slightly_down' (median -2.0 material), confirming the bishop is sacrificed for a pawn. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies king_safety motifs (100%) with explicit tags like 'greek_gift_failure', 'unsound_sacrifice', 'insufficient_attackers', and 'failed_attack'. The top boards all show Bxh2+ or Bxh7+ sacrifices in opening/middlegame positions where the attacking side lacks coordinated supporting pieces (e.g., knights on irrelevant squares, no queen lined up for follow-through). The eval trajectory shows a devastating median loss of 307 centipawns, with 47% of cases converting drawn positions into losing ones—the sacrifice not only fails to deliver checkmate but leaves the player down a full piece with no compensation. This is the quintessential amateur mistake of playing a memorized attacking pattern without verifying the concrete tactical prerequisites are met.

1601.label: Moving or leaving a queen on a diagonal where it becomes pinned to the king by an enemy bishop.
1601.description: This feature fires when players make moves that ignore or walk into a deadly diagonal pin, typically involving their queen being pinned to the king by a bishop. The material signature shows the move itself appears 'safe' (83%) — the player isn't capturing or losing material immediately — yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 426cp lost), with 29% of cases going from drawn to losing and 15% from winning to losing. The tactical analysis is overwhelmingly dominated by the 'pin' motif (89%), with recurring tags like queen_trapped, diagonal_vulnerability, and king_queen_alignment. The top boards consistently show positions where the player's queen and king sit on the same diagonal (often a7-g1 or similar), and the player either fails to notice this alignment or actively creates it (e.g., moving the queen to e3 with king on g1, or castling into an alignment), allowing the opponent to play a devastating bishop pin like ...Bc5. The moved pieces are often queens (37%) or pawns (24%), suggesting routine-looking moves that catastrophically overlook the geometric relationship between their own king and queen.

1606.label: King moves to the wrong square in a lost pawn endgame, wasting critical tempo near promotion.
1606.description: This feature fires on king moves (86%) in pure endgame positions (100%) where the player is already losing and makes things worse by a median of 87 centipawns. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (71%), with passed_pawn and promotion-related tags appearing frequently. The boards consistently show pawn endgames with advanced passed pawns (often on the 6th or 7th rank) where the losing side's king moves in the wrong direction—away from the critical pawns or failing to approach the promotion square. The material signature is 'safe' (no pieces are hung or traded), confirming this is purely a positional/tempo error rather than a tactical blunder. The eval trajectory (losing->losing, median 87cp lost) shows these aren't game-turning mistakes but rather acceleration of an already lost position by misplacing the king when precise defense was still required to maximize resistance against promotion threats.

1605.label: Queen retreats or repositions passively when an active queen exchange or simplification was required to survive.
1605.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their queen (88%) to a passive square instead of taking the critical queen exchange or active continuation. The material signature shows these are non-captures (100% no capture) that are frequently unsafe (38% hangs), while Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve queen captures (88% queen captures queen). The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 284 centipawns, with many positions transitioning from losing-but-playable to completely lost or even from winning/drawn to losing. The tactical analysis consistently identifies missed simplifications, refused queen exchanges, and defensive errors—the player retreats their queen to a passive square (Qf7, Qb7+, Qe6) when the only viable defense was to trade queens or simplify. The recurring motifs of king safety and back-rank threats confirm that these passive retreats leave the player's king fatally exposed to the opponent's continuing attack, which the queen trade would have neutralized.

1609.label: Passive or misplaced minor piece moves in the opening that overlook tactical vulnerabilities, turning equal positions into losing ones.
1609.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake (100% opening) where the player develops a bishop or knight to a passive or tactically vulnerable square (bishop 40%, knight 40%), missing a strong knight move recommended by Maia (90% knight). The material signature shows the move itself appears 'safe' (80%) — no immediate capture punishes it — but the eval trajectory universally shows drawn→losing with a median loss of 320 centipawns, indicating a serious tactical oversight. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 44%, king_safety 33%, fork 11%) combined with tags like development, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic reveal the pattern: in sharp opening positions (often involving Bc4 attacking f7), the player makes a natural-looking developing move (Bg4, Bd7, Nd7, Ne7) that either places a piece on an undefended square, blocks a critical defensive resource, or walks into a fork/tactical sequence. The boards confirm this — positions from Pirc/King's Indian/Sicilian setups where White has active central/kingside pressure and Black's careless development allows a concrete tactical blow.

1611.label: Trading queens with check when a more precise move order preserves a larger winning advantage.
1611.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position executes a queen trade (capturing the opponent's queen with check) but loses a median of 232 centipawns in the process—remaining winning but squandering significant advantage. The material signature shows 100% queen-takes-queen with check, yet Maia consistently preferred a rook capture of a bishop with check instead, indicating the engine saw a superior tactical sequence. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is tempo_loss (29%), with capture_order and missed_tactic also prominent: the player grabs the flashy queen exchange immediately rather than executing a precise intermediate move (often a rook check or bishop reposition) that would have won more material or created a decisive attack first. The positions show complex middlegames where multiple forcing sequences exist, and the player defaults to the 'obvious' queen capture with check rather than finding the optimal move order that extracts maximum value from the position before simplifying.

1613.label: Player makes a slow or irrelevant move while opponent's advanced passed pawn demands immediate attention.
1613.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (57% endgame, 43% middlegame) where the player makes a move—most often a pawn or king move (72% combined)—that ignores an urgent passed pawn threat. The dominant motif is 'passed_pawn' (57%), with 'tempo_loss' as the most common tag (5 occurrences), indicating the player wastes a critical tempo on an irrelevant advance or capture while the opponent's passed pawn races toward promotion. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' or 'hangs' moves (86% combined, rarely captures), meaning the player isn't trading or winning material but simply making a move that doesn't address the real threat. Maia's recommended moves (71% missed winning material) frequently involve checks or direct intervention against the passed pawn. The eval trajectory (median 202cp lost, with 57% losing->losing and 14% winning->drawn) confirms these are costly tempo losses that either squander a winning position or accelerate an already losing one. Concrete examples include h5 ignoring a d2 pawn about to promote, a5 allowing a mate-in-10 via promotion, and capturing a rook while a g3 pawn marches to queen.

1607.label: Moving a knight to a poor square in the opening, hanging material and turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1607.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening blunder pattern where Black, facing Italian Game or similar e4-e5 positions with White's bishop on c4 and knight on f3, makes a premature or misguided knight (or pawn) move that immediately drops material. The material signature shows 86% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that leave something en prise), with a median loss of ~1 pawn equivalent, and the eval trajectory uniformly converts drawn positions into losing ones (median 347cp swing). The top boards reveal the recurring concrete pattern: Black plays ...Na5 (chasing the c4 bishop but leaving pieces undefended), ...f5 or ...g5 (weakening the king while pieces are undeveloped), or ...Bf2+ (a premature attack). The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of king_safety and hanging_piece, with tags emphasizing tempo_loss, development neglect, and missed tactics. Maia consistently recommends natural developing knight moves (Nc6, Nf6) instead. This is fundamentally a tactical mistake—Black violates opening principles by making an aggressive-looking but tactically flawed move that leaves material hanging in well-known Italian/open game structures.

1610.label: In already-losing positions, player makes a move that fatally compromises king safety, allowing back-rank mates or discovered attacks.
1610.description: This feature fires on moves made in already-losing positions (losing->losing, 100%) that catastrophically worsen the situation by ignoring critical king safety threats. The material signature shows diverse piece moves (queen, king, bishop) that are predominantly non-captures, with a median net material loss of -1.0, but the true cost is positional/tactical: the median eval lost is a staggering 9431 centipawns, indicating these moves often allow forced checkmate. The dominant motifs are king_safety (43%), back_rank (29%), and discovered_attack (29%), with recurring tags including back_rank_mate, king_walk_blunder, and tempo_loss. Examining the concrete positions confirms the pattern: Ka8 walks into back-rank mate, Re6 misses a forced checkmate sequence, and several other moves ignore lethal threats along the back rank or discovered attack lines. Maia consistently recommends queen moves (100%), often capturing bishops, suggesting the engine sees active queen defense/counterplay that the player overlooks. The player, already in a difficult position, makes a panic or passive move that neglects an immediate king safety crisis, converting a bad-but-playable position into instant checkmate or decisive material loss.

1608.label: In the opening, a developing move leaves a piece (often a bishop) undefended on a vulnerable diagonal or square, allowing a fork or simple capture.
1608.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where the player moves a minor piece or queen (bishop 34%, knight 21%, queen 17%) without capturing anything (86% no capture), and the move hangs material (55% hangs, median net material -3.0, i.e., roughly a full piece lost). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses: 76% of cases shift from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 354 centipawns. The tactical motifs are hanging_piece (57%), fork (29%), and trapped_piece (14%), with recurring tags like tempo_loss, development issues, and missed_tactic. Maia's recommended moves are consistently bishop captures with checks (100% bishop capture, 55% giving check), indicating that the opponent had a forcing reply exploiting the newly undefended piece. The top boards show classic opening scenarios: bishops placed on b4 or b5 that become loose after pawn breaks open diagonals, knights jumping to squares that allow queen forks, and premature queen moves that leave pieces tactically vulnerable. The common thread is a developing or repositioning move in the opening that neglects piece safety, leaving material en prise to a simple tactic.

1614.label: Player makes a quiet, non-forcing move that squanders a winning or dominant position by failing to exploit concrete tactical or positional advantages.
1614.description: This feature captures positions where a player holds a significant advantage (100% missed winning material, median 291cp lost) but plays a passive or natural-looking move instead of pressing their advantage with the critical continuation. The material signature shows mostly non-capturing moves (93% no capture) with pawns and bishops being moved, and a striking 33% of moves simply hang material—suggesting the quiet move allows a counterattack the player didn't foresee. The trajectory confirms this is predominantly 'throwing a win' (40% winning->drawn, 7% winning->losing). The tactical analysis reinforces the positional nature: tempo_loss, released_tension, missed_simplification, and piece_coordination failures dominate. The example summaries are telling—Qe3 wastes a crucial tempo, a passed pawn is exchanged passively instead of being advanced to paralyze the opponent, and a developing move misses a crushing tactical shot. These are middlegame positions (87%) where the player had a dominant position but chose a slow, prophylactic, or routine move instead of the concrete action that would have maintained or converted their advantage.

1612.label: King moves to escape a knight attack but hangs material to a queen capture.
1612.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early middlegame pattern where a player's king is under pressure from an enemy knight (often on g5 after a Fried Liver or similar Italian Game attack) and the player retreats the king (100% king moves, no captures) but in doing so hangs a piece (100% hangs, median -3.0 material, i.e., a full minor piece). The best move was invariably to capture the attacking knight with the queen (Maia recommends Qxg5/Qxf5 type moves — 100% queen captures knight). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders converting winning positions into losing or drawn ones (62% winning->losing, 25% winning->drawn, median 626cp lost). The positional tags reinforce this: king_safety and hanging_piece dominate, with tempo_loss reflecting that the passive king retreat wastes the initiative. The boards all show a nearly identical tactical motif — an exposed king on f7/g6/e8 after ...Kxe7 or similar in Italian/Fried Liver structures where the correct defensive resource was a queen counter-capture on the intruding knight rather than a panicked king flight.

1615.label: Wasting critical tempo in winning endgames by retreating or misplacing pieces, allowing the opponent to escape or draw.
1615.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player holds a winning advantage but squanders it through tempo loss, the dominant motif at 40%. The material signature shows safe moves (no material is hung or traded—net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 545 centipawns, with 67% of cases converting winning positions into draws. The concrete positions confirm this: rook endgames and queen-vs-pawns scenarios where a single misplaced king move (Ke3 retreating from d4), a check from the wrong square (Qb4 instead of Qb3), or a passive rook move allows the opponent to reach a drawn fortress or escape a mating net. The player's moves are non-capturing and appear 'safe' by material standards, but they forfeit the one resource that matters most in these simplified positions—tempo. Maia consistently identifies forcing continuations (captures, checks) that maintain the win, highlighting how the human missed concrete winning tactics 67% of the time by choosing quiet, retreating moves instead.

1616.label: Giving a pointless or premature queen check that loses tempo and hangs material.
1616.description: This feature detects positions where a player delivers a check with the queen (100% checks, 98% queen moves) that is tactically unsound—59% of the time the queen is left hanging, and the median material cost is -1.0 (a full piece). The Opus analysis consistently tags these as 'pointless_check', 'premature_check', and 'tempo_loss' (60% of positions), indicating the check achieves nothing constructive: the opponent's king simply sidesteps to safety while the attacker's queen lands on a vulnerable square or loses coordination. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences (median 331cp lost), with many positions shifting from drawn to losing or winning to drawn. Maia's recommended moves (59% queen but often non-checking, 20% pawn pushes) suggest the correct plan was to improve position, advance passed pawns, or capture material rather than chase the king. The top boards repeatedly show queen checks to back ranks or open files where the king easily escapes, leaving the queen misplaced or trapped. This is the classic amateur mistake of 'checking because you can' rather than pursuing the objectively strongest continuation.

1617.label: Player makes a non-queen move that neglects the opponent's dominant queen, losing significant material or positional value.
1617.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a pawn, knight, or bishop (collectively ~71% of moves) while the best move overwhelmingly involved their queen (Maia recommends a queen move 98% of the time). The moves are mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense (70%) but 24% hang a piece, and nearly half (49%) miss winning material. The median eval loss is a massive 283 centipawns, with many positions transitioning from drawn-to-losing (16%) or winning-to-drawn (12%). The tactical motifs—hanging pieces (33%), tempo loss (22%), king safety (11%), and forks (11%)—reveal that by ignoring the critical queen action (whether defensive or offensive), the player loses tempo or leaves pieces undefended. The top boards consistently show positions where the queen needed to be actively deployed (capturing hanging material, defending critical squares, or exploiting tactical threats) but the player instead made a passive or irrelevant move with a minor piece or pawn, squandering the position. This is fundamentally a positional/tactical oversight where the player fails to recognize the urgency of queen involvement in the critical moment.

1618.label: Moving a piece that fatally exposes the king to tactical threats in already precarious positions.
1618.description: This feature identifies positions where players make moves (predominantly pawn pushes at 50% and rook moves at 28%) that critically expose their king to devastating attacks. The material signature shows 59% of moves hang material and the net median is -1.0, indicating these aren't trades but unforced errors. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly points to king_safety (71%) with tags like exposed_king, forced_mate, and king_walk_blunder dominating. The eval trajectory shows 44% losing->losing, meaning players in already difficult positions make their situation catastrophically worse by ignoring king vulnerability. Crucially, Maia's recommended move is always a rook move (100%), suggesting the correct response involved defensive rook placement or active counterplay, while players instead made passive or irrelevant moves (pawn pushes, king walks) that left their monarch fatally exposed. The top boards confirm this: kings on open files/diagonals getting mated after moves like Ke2, Kg2, or pawn pushes that ignore back-rank and diagonal threats.

1620.label: Moving a rook (or piece) to a passive square in the middlegame, losing tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit positional weaknesses.
1620.description: This feature captures middlegame positional mistakes where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material is immediately lost or exchanged) but squanders a balanced or manageable position into a losing one. The material signature shows rook moves (67%) that don't capture or give check, yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 293 centipawns, with 67% of cases turning a drawn position into a losing one. The tactical analysis confirms these are not tactical oversights but positional errors: pieces are moved to ineffective squares (Rdh1, Rh5, Bg4), losing tempo and failing to address critical positional demands like trapping an opponent's piece, maintaining central control, or advancing key pawns. The common tags (piece_activity, tempo_loss, missed_tactic) reinforce that the player chose non-urgent piece reshuffling over the one correct positional move, allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape from a bind.

1621.label: Player makes a quiet or materialistic move while missing a forced back-rank checkmate in one.
1621.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a devastating back-rank mate-in-one. The material signature shows the player making safe pawn or rook moves (no captures, no checks) while Maia consistently recommends a rook move delivering check — confirming the missed checkmate. The eval trajectory is extreme: positions swing from losing to winning (88%) with a median eval loss of ~105 pawns (i.e., missed mate), indicating the player was actually lost but had a forced mate available. The Opus tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies back_rank (89%) as the dominant motif, with tags like 'back_rank_mate', 'missed_mate_in_one', and 'king_safety' appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions show Black having a rook with access to the first rank (e.g., Rc1# or Ra1#) while White's king is trapped behind pawns, yet the player chooses a quiet king move, a pawn capture, or a positional rook move instead of delivering the lethal blow.

1619.label: Trading an active bishop for a knight with check, surrendering positional pressure in the opening.
1619.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: the player captures a knight with a bishop (94% knight captures), delivering check (100%), in what is materially an even trade (net 0.0). However, the eval trajectory reveals this trade is devastating positionally—49% of cases go from winning to drawn and 20% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 257 centipawns. The top boards show a recurring pattern: bishops on b4 or b5 capturing knights on c3 or c6 with check, typically in well-known opening structures (Nimzo-Indian, Scotch, Spanish). The tactical analysis confirms the key motifs are tempo_loss (38%), positional_mistake (38%), and hanging_piece (25%), with tags like 'premature_exchange' and 'move_order' dominating. The player surrenders a powerful, actively-placed bishop that was pinning or pressuring the opponent's position, trading it for a knight merely because check is available, when maintaining the tension or playing an intermediate move first would have preserved a significant advantage. The check creates an illusion of forcing play, but actually releases the opponent's positional bind.

1622.label: Premature or unnecessary pawn moves that fatally compromise king safety against an opponent's piece activity aimed at the king.
1622.description: This feature fires on moves—predominantly pawn advances (61%)—that create catastrophic king safety vulnerabilities in the opening and early middlegame. The material signature shows these are not capture-related blunders: 73% involve no capture, and the moves are often 'safe' in the immediate material sense (46%) or hang material indirectly (30%). The key pattern is that the player ignores a brewing kingside attack: Maia consistently recommends quiet pawn moves (100% pawn, 100% non-capture), suggesting the correct plan was modest development or prophylaxis rather than the ambitious/weakening move chosen. The eval trajectory is severe (median 305cp lost), with 42% of cases swinging from drawn to losing, indicating these moves cross a critical threshold where the opponent's attacking potential becomes decisive. The tactical analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif (56%), with supporting tags like greek_gift_sacrifice, piece_activity, and missed_tactic pointing to opponents having knights and bishops already aimed at the kingside (Ng5, Bc4, Bd3 patterns appear repeatedly in the top boards). The concrete positions show Italian Game and similar setups where one side has already committed pieces toward the king, and the mistake is a pawn move (h4, e5, b4xc3, etc.) that either opens lines, removes key defenders, or wastes a critical tempo while the opponent's attack is already in motion.

1624.label: Player makes a developing or pawn move in the opening while ignoring an undefended bishop that their queen could capture for free.
1624.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a bishop (typically on g4 or g5) is left completely undefended, and the opponent plays a routine developing move (knight, pawn, or bishop move) instead of capturing it with their queen (Qxg4 or Qxg5). The material signature shows 75% of moves hang material with a median loss of -1.0 (a full piece), and Maia consistently recommends a queen capturing a bishop. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: 75% of cases swing from winning to drawn and 25% from winning to losing, with a median 471 centipawns lost. The tactical tags unanimously identify hanging_piece, missed_capture, and undefended_piece motifs. The top boards reveal a near-identical recurring position—often after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.d4 Bg4 or similar lines where the bishop ventures to g4/g5 early without pawn support, and the opponent fails to notice the free capture available to their queen, instead making passive or irrelevant moves like Be2, f3, Nc3, or Ne7.

1625.label: Hanging or sacrificing a piece in an already losing position, often hoping for speculative counterplay that doesn't exist.
1625.description: This feature captures moves where a player, already in a losing position (78% losing->losing trajectory), hangs or sacrifices material (56% hangs, 22% loses) with a median cost of -4.0 material and ~197cp eval drop. The moves are predominantly knight and queen moves (55% combined) that leave pieces en prise. The Opus analysis reveals the common thread: players launch unsound sacrifices or ignore critical tactical threats (hanging_piece 40%, counterplay_illusion tag) while the opponent has a crushing continuation available—typically a queen capture with check (Maia's response is 89% queen moves giving check, 78% capturing a rook). The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (89%) with motifs of exposed/uncastled kings and open file tension. Rather than defending a difficult position, the player throws material at the opponent in hopes of generating an attack that doesn't materialize, accelerating an already bad situation.

1626.label: Ignoring a back-rank threat by moving a critical defender, allowing a devastating queen or rook invasion.
1626.description: This feature fires when a player, already in a losing middlegame position, makes a move that fatally neglects back-rank safety—removing a key defensive piece (rook, knight, or king step) that was the sole guardian of the back rank or critical escape squares. The material signature shows the played move is mostly 'safe' (no immediate material loss on that move), yet Maia's recommended response is always a queen capturing a rook, indicating the opponent can now exploit the exposed back rank with decisive force. The eval trajectory confirms these are already losing positions that become catastrophically worse (median ~93 pawns lost, i.e., forced mate). The tactical motifs—back_rank_mate, king_exposure, forced_mate, open_file_exploitation—and the per-position analyses consistently describe scenarios where the last defender of the back rank is moved (e.g., a rook leaving d8, a knight leaving e8, a king stepping into a worse square), instantly permitting a lethal back-rank combination. The mistake is not a material blunder in the traditional sense but a tactical oversight: failing to recognize that the moved piece was the linchpin of back-rank defense.

1627.label: Giving a pointless or counterproductive check (usually with the queen) that squanders a winning position by allowing the opponent's king to escape or improve its situation.
1627.description: This feature detects a highly specific recurring mistake: the player delivers a check (100% of activations) almost always with the queen (85%), but the check is premature or misdirected, costing an average of 330 centipawns. The material signature shows no capture is made (100% non-capture), meaning the check is purely a tempo move that gains nothing concrete. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with tags like 'premature_check' and 'patzer_sees_a_check' reinforcing the classic amateur error of checking just because it's available. The eval trajectory shows devastating consequences: 30% of the time a winning position becomes drawn, 11% winning becomes losing, indicating these checks throw away decisive advantages. The top boards consistently show queen checks (Qa8+, Qh8+, Qh1+) that give the opponent's king a flight square or allow favorable simplification, when quieter moves would have maintained crushing positions. This is the textbook 'patzer sees a check' phenomenon — an impulsive forcing move that feels strong but actually releases pressure.

1628.label: Player makes a safe-looking move that squanders a forced checkmate sequence available through a tactical capture or continuation.
1628.description: This feature fires when a player, in a middlegame position with a forced mate available, plays a 'safe' move (king retreat, quiet bishop move, or rook sidestep) instead of executing the winning tactical blow. The material signature shows the played moves are universally 'safe' (no material lost or gained), while Maia's recommended moves involve captures (100% capturing a rook) — indicating the player passed up a decisive tactical capture. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 9397 centipawns lost), with positions flipping from losing-to-winning or staying winning but dropping from forced mate to merely an advantage. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 67%, king_safety 33%) combined with tags like missed_mate, mating_net, and rook_on_seventh all point to situations where a lethal attacking pattern existed but the player chose a passive or irrelevant continuation — removing a piece from a mating net, allowing an attacked piece to escape, or missing a simple capture that wins decisive material. The player's moves feel natural or safe but catastrophically abandon a winning tactical sequence.

1623.label: Ignoring urgent threats (checks, captures, promotions) to play a slower or irrelevant move, losing significant material or positional value.
1623.description: This feature captures positions where the player fails to address the most urgent tactical threat on the board, instead making a move that is either passive, greedy, or structurally motivated but tactically irrelevant. The material signature shows that 46% of these moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave pieces en pris) while the opponent's best reply (Maia's move) frequently involves captures (54% capture something, including rooks and queens) and checks (38%). The median eval loss of 251 centipawns is severe, and the trajectory shows these errors often turn drawn or winning positions into losing ones (winning->drawn 15%, winning->losing 8%, drawn->losing 23%). The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: players capture an irrelevant piece instead of addressing Rxf8+ (Bxg2 example), advance a pawn breaking their own structure instead of defending (g5 example), or fail to execute a critical check/promotion sequence (Rc8 instead of Rxh7+). The dominant motifs—king_safety (40%), hanging_piece (20%), promotion_error (20%), and tempo_loss (20%)—all point to the same underlying error: the player loses sight of the most urgent demand of the position and plays a move addressing a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow.

1629.label: Moving a well-placed knight away from a strong square, losing tempo and allowing devastating tactical responses.
1629.description: This feature fires when a player moves a knight (100% knight moves) away from an active or well-placed square, typically resulting in a significant material or positional loss (median -2.0 material, median 504 centipawns lost). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn or even winning positions into losing ones (75% drawn->losing, 25% winning->losing), indicating catastrophic positional misjudgments rather than simple oversights. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the knight relocations lose tempo (50%) or leave pieces hanging (50%), with recurring motifs of abandoned outposts, intermezzo vulnerabilities, and zwischenzug punishments. The top positions consistently show knights leaving strong central or active squares (c4, c6, d4, c5) only to land on squares where their activity is nullified by intermediate moves or counterattacks. Maia's recommended moves (pawns, knights, queens that don't capture) suggest quiet consolidating alternatives were available, reinforcing that these knight moves represent unnecessary and self-destructive repositioning that invites tactical punishment.

1630.label: Player overlooks capturing an undefended enemy piece, typically a queen, losing massive material advantage.
1630.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move (usually with their queen or king) that hangs material (75% of moves result in hanging a piece) while completely missing an elementary capture of an undefended enemy piece. The material signature shows no captures made by the player (100% non-captures) while Maia's recommended moves capture high-value pieces (queen 75%, rook 25%), confirming the player missed winning free material. The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 9140 centipawns—often representing missed forced mates or lost queens—while the position remains nominally winning->winning (75%) because the advantage was so large it survived the blunder, or losing->losing (25%) where the missed capture would have been the saving resource. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (80%), 'missed_capture' tags appearing in all analyzed positions, and narrative descriptions consistently describing 'chess blindness' where trivially undefended pieces (especially queens sitting en prise) go uncaptured while the player makes irrelevant moves like prophylactic king moves or piece repositioning. This is pure tactical oversight of material sitting free on the board, not a positional misjudgment or trade decision.

1632.label: Player moves queen to an attacked square in a winning endgame, allowing it to be captured by a pawn.
1632.description: This feature captures a highly specific and costly mistake pattern: in endgame positions (75%) where the player has a winning advantage, they move their queen (75% queen moves) with check (75%), but place it on a square where it can be captured by an enemy pawn. The material signature shows the piece is 'hung' (75%) with a devastating median material loss of -8.0 (a queen's value). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions being thrown away—converting wins into draws (50%) or significantly degrading winning advantages (50%), with a median loss of 706 centipawns. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (80%) and 'queen_blunder' as the most common tag (3 occurrences), with specific examples showing queens placed on squares attacked by pawns (e.g., Qf5 captured by g6 pawn, Qe6 captured by f5 pawn). The check element appears to be what lures the player—they see an aggressive-looking check but overlook the simple pawn recapture that wins the queen outright.

1631.label: Knight captures a pawn in the opening with insufficient compensation, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1631.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where a knight captures a pawn (typically on f7 or f2) as a speculative sacrifice that lacks sufficient tactical or positional compensation. The material signature shows knight moves capturing a pawn 100% of the time with a net material loss of approximately 2 points (a full piece for one pawn), confirming these are unsound sacrifices rather than even trades. The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 310cp lost), indicating the player misjudged the attacking potential. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant tags of 'unsound_sacrifice,' 'insufficient_compensation,' and 'piece_for_pawn' — the knight lands on a square attacking the king or forking pieces, but with undeveloped remaining forces, there is no follow-up. The top boards are classic examples: Nxf7 'attacks' in Petroff/Philidor-type positions or Ne4xf2 lunges in French/Sicilian structures, all in the opening phase where the opponent's king is not actually vulnerable because the attacker has no supporting pieces developed.

1635.label: Playing a developing or advancing pawn move in the opening while a free piece capture (usually a knight) is available.
1635.description: This feature fires on opening positions (100% opening phase) where the player makes a safe pawn move (pawn played 100%, no capture 100%, nothing hangs) but misses a free piece capture that was available. The Maia-suggested moves show knight captures 100% of the time, and the tags confirm hanging_piece (78% dominant motif) and missed_capture as the recurring theme. The boards consistently show early game positions where an opponent's piece (typically a knight on d5 or a bishop) is en prise, but the player instead advances a pawn (d2d4, f2f4, f2f3, e7e5) or develops a piece without collecting the free material. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 303 centipawns, often converting a winning position into a drawn one (67% winning->drawn). The tactical summaries explicitly describe 'free piece captures' being overlooked in favor of routine developing moves or pawn pushes that attack pieces unnecessarily when simply capturing would be superior.

1634.label: Hanging or losing major material by ignoring king safety threats in already-difficult middlegame positions.
1634.description: This feature captures moves where a player, typically already in a losing or pressured position (52% losing->losing, 14% losing->winning flip suggests opponent blunders back sometimes), drops significant material (62% hangs a piece, 14% loses material, median net -3.0 pawns, median eval lost 180cp) by failing to address king safety concerns. The dominant tactical motifs are king_safety (44%), back_rank (22%), and fork (11%), with recurring tags like exposed_king, checkmate_in_one, and queen_infiltration. The played moves are predominantly rooks (30%) and queens (18%) being moved to squares that ignore defensive obligations—leaving back ranks unguarded, walking into forks, or missing forced mates. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (78%) where king vulnerability is acute. Rather than a simple oversight of a hanging piece, the common thread is that the player moves a piece for an ostensible purpose (attack, repositioning) while being blind to the lethal king safety threats that the opponent can exploit, often resulting in immediate material loss or checkmate. Examples include abandoning rook defense to allow back-rank mates, moving queens to squares that leave pieces undefended, and king moves that walk into mating nets.

1633.label: Player makes a quiet piece move while leaving or placing a high-value piece en prise, missing an available winning capture.
1633.description: This feature fires when a player, often in a winning position, plays a quiet knight or piece move that hangs major material (median net loss of -9.0, i.e., roughly a queen) instead of capturing an available high-value piece. The eval trajectory is uniformly winning->losing with a catastrophic median loss of 985 centipawns, indicating these moves throw away completely won games. The material signature shows 80% of moves are non-captures that hang a piece, while Maia's recommended move captures a queen 100% of the time—confirming the player overlooked a simple winning capture. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 60%, pin 20%, trapped_piece 20%) and tags (missed_capture, queen_capture_missed, undefended_piece) reinforce that the core error is tunnel-vision on a positional or developmental idea while ignoring a tactically available major capture. The board examples confirm this: a bishop can take a queen but instead develops passively (Be7), a queen sits en prise but the player makes a knight maneuver, a forced checkmate is abandoned for a slow improvement. The pattern is consistent: the player has a won position with a concrete tactical shot available (usually capturing or exploiting a hanging queen) but plays an aimless or 'improving' move that simultaneously leaves their own piece undefended.

1637.label: Player makes a move that fatally weakens their own king's position, missing critical defensive or tactical resources.
1637.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where the player neglects their own king's safety, resulting in a median loss of 228 centipawns. The material signature shows 50% of moves hang a piece and 50% involve trades, but critically 100% miss winning material — indicating the player overlooks tactical opportunities while making passive or self-destructive moves. The dominant motif is king_safety (86%), supported by tags like missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and forced_mate. The eval trajectory shows these errors often flip the position dramatically (50% losing->winning for the opponent, meaning the player was already under pressure and made it worse, or even transforming drawn/balanced positions into lost ones). Concrete examples include walking the king into a mating net (Kxg2), blocking defensive pieces with pawn captures (dxe4), and purposeless moves that abandon critical defensive duties. The common thread is that the player either moves their king into danger, removes a key defender of the king, or makes a structurally weakening move near their king while missing the opponent's tactical threats along diagonals and open lines.

1636.label: Player makes a seemingly active move that squanders a positional or material advantage by neglecting tempo or missequencing, typically costing 300+ centipawns.
1636.description: This feature fires on moves where a player in a favorable position (opening/middlegame) makes an impulsive piece move—often a bishop, pawn, or knight advance/capture—that surrenders a critical positional asset or misses the correct move order. The material signature shows 44% safe and 34% hangs, meaning the moves aren't outright blunders of pieces but rather positional concessions that the engine punishes severely. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: 15% swing winning→drawn and 13% drawn→losing, with a median cost of 301 centipawns—indicating thrown advantages rather than worsening already-lost positions. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are positional_mistake (33%) and tempo_loss (22%), with recurring tags around pawn structure, development, and piece activity. The concrete examples show patterns like advancing a key central pawn prematurely (d5-d4 surrendering a positional anchor), capturing without the preparatory tempo-gaining move first (taking on f5 without f4), or retreating a king to safety at the cost of a dominant position. Crucially, Maia's recommended moves are almost exclusively quiet pawn moves (99%), suggesting the correct continuation was patient positional play rather than the forcing or 'active' move the player chose.

1638.label: Moving a piece to a square where it is immediately captured for free or at significant material loss.
1638.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves a major or minor piece (most often a rook or knight) to a square where it is simply captured by the opponent, hanging the piece outright. The material signature shows 38% 'loses' and 38% 'hangs' outcomes with a median net material loss of -4.0 (roughly a full piece or rook), confirming substantial material is being donated rather than exchanged. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 275 centipawns, with half the cases being already-losing positions made decisively worse and some involving wins thrown away. The Opus tactical analysis identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (67%), with recurring tags like rook_blunder, material_loss, and unsound sacrifices. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: a rook moved to f2 captured by a queen with check, a rook placed on b6 taken by a knight, a rook moved to e2 left hanging—all cases where the player placed a piece on a tactically vulnerable square without calculating the opponent's immediate capture.

1640.label: Trading pieces in a lost endgame position instead of addressing critical passed pawn threats.
1640.description: This feature fires on rook trades in completely lost endgame positions where the player captures a major piece (queen or rook) but ignores the opponent's decisive passed pawn or promotion threat. The material signature shows 100% rook moves making trades, while Maia consistently recommends rook moves that give check—typically intermediate checks that address the real threat. The eval trajectory (losing->losing, 0cp median loss) confirms these positions are already lost, so the trade doesn't technically worsen the evaluation, but the player is capturing the wrong target. The Opus analysis and motif tags (passed_pawn 40%, promotion_error 30%, promotion_threat, pawn_race) reveal the core pattern: in pawn-race endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player reflexively trades or captures a piece rather than using tempo (often via an intermediate check) to stop or race the critical pawn. The boards consistently show positions with pawns on the 7th rank where the player takes a piece instead of prioritizing the existential promotion threat.

1642.label: Player makes a quiet or retreating move instead of capturing an undefended or tactically available piece that would have won material.
1642.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position fails to execute a winning capture, typically with the queen. The material signature shows the player's move is mostly 'safe' (77%) — meaning they didn't hang anything outright — but Maia's recommended move captures a piece (knight 69%, bishop 23%, rook 8%) in 100% of cases. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' across all positions, indicating an opponent's piece was available for capture. The played moves are often queen retreats, quiet developing moves, or rook moves that ignore the tactical opportunity. The eval trajectory (62% winning->drawn, 23% winning->losing, median 460cp lost) confirms these are cases where a decisive advantage evaporates because the player overlooked or declined a freely available capture. The concrete examples reinforce this: Qxc6 winning a piece was missed for Qb5, Qxd2 was missed, Qxd5 was missed — all cases where a hanging or inadequately defended piece went uncaptured.

1639.label: Capturing an enemy promotion pawn with a rook instead of using superior technique to stop or exploit it.
1639.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player uses a rook (86%) or queen (14%) to capture a pawn (100% pawn captures) — typically an advanced passed pawn near promotion — while delivering check (86%), but the capture loses significant material (net median -4.0, indicating the rook is lost for just a pawn). The boards universally show positions with advanced passed pawns on the 7th rank (a7, b7, c7, d7, g7) where the opponent has a promotion threat. Rather than employing correct endgame technique (e.g., using the king, maintaining piece activity, or finding tempo-gaining alternatives), the player impulsively captures the dangerous pawn, often allowing a recapture that nets a whole rook. The eval trajectory (57% losing→losing, 14% winning→drawn) shows this mostly worsens already difficult positions or squanders wins. The Opus analysis confirms motifs of promotion_error, tempo_loss, and pawn_endgame — the player panics about the passed pawn and sacrifices material unnecessarily rather than finding the patient defensive or winning technique.

1645.label: Developing or relocating a piece while ignoring critical central pawn tension, allowing a devastating pawn fork or advance.
1645.description: This feature fires on opening/early middlegame positions where the player makes a quiet developing move (typically a bishop move) that neglects urgent central pawn tension. The material signature shows mostly safe, non-capturing bishop moves (50%) with no checks, yet the eval trajectory consistently shows a drawn position collapsing into a losing one (median 311cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the opponent's central pawn advance (often ...d4 or e5) exploits the unresolved tension to create a pawn fork attacking two pieces simultaneously, or gains decisive tempo against a misplaced piece. Tags like 'center_tension_ignored', 'pawn_fork', and 'tempo_loss' dominate, and Maia consistently identifies the correct move as a central pawn capture or exchange. The player's error is a fundamental opening principle violation—prioritizing passive development over the critical need to resolve or maintain central tension—resulting in a position that immediately becomes tactically lost due to the opponent's forcing pawn thrust.

1641.label: Player captures material instead of delivering a faster or immediate checkmate.
1641.description: This feature fires when a player, already in a winning or near-checkmate position, opts to capture a rook (100% captures are rooks) rather than delivering checkmate or a more efficient mating sequence. The material signature shows the move is 'safe' with high net material (median +5.0), indicating the player is already up significant material — they're grabbing more rather than finishing the game. The Opus analysis is decisive: multiple examples describe missing checkmate-in-one (e.g., Rc8# missed for Bxb2), or choosing a slower mate (8 moves instead of 6) because the capturing move was more tempting. The dominant motifs (king_safety 40%, back_rank 20%) confirm the opponent's king was already fatally exposed. Maia's suggested moves give check 100% of the time, confirming a checking/mating continuation existed. The eval trajectory shows minimal centipawn loss in most cases (median 0.0) because the position remains winning, but the qualitative error — material greed over immediate checkmate — is consistent across all examples. This is a classic 'material greed' pattern where the player's pattern-matching prioritizes capturing a piece over recognizing the mating net already in place.

1644.label: Playing a slow pawn move instead of delivering a winning queen check on an exposed king diagonal.
1644.description: This feature fires consistently on opening positions where the player has a winning advantage (typically 300+ centipawns) thanks to Black's king being exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal after an early f-pawn capture. Instead of delivering the crushing Qh5+ check (Maia's recommended queen move with check in 100% of cases), the player wastes tempo with a non-forcing pawn move (f4, g4, d4) or a slow queen development (Qf3). The material signature shows the pawn move is 'safe' in isolation—nothing is immediately hung—but the eval trajectory reveals the catastrophic cost: every instance transitions from winning to drawn, losing a median of 343 centipawns. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss 25%, king_safety 38%, missed_tactic 12%) and tags (missed_check, tempo_loss) confirm the pattern: the player fails to exploit a one-move tactical window where the opponent's king is fatally exposed, allowing Black to consolidate. This is a pure tactical miss—ignoring an immediate forcing blow in favor of a 'developing' but non-forcing move.

1643.label: Pawn moves that fatally weaken the king's pawn shield, often allowing immediate checkmate.
1643.description: This feature fires on moves—predominantly pawn advances (80%)—that catastrophically compromise king safety. The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (80%), with a median cost of 207 centipawns but several instances showing mate-in-one losses (9748/9681 cp). The dominant motif is king_safety (75%), with recurring tags like pawn_shield_destruction, fatal_weakening, and checkmate_in_one. The concrete positions confirm this: multiple instances of g2-g3 or g7-g6 in front of a castled king facing a queen+piece attack on the kingside (often Qh4/Qh2 with knights on g4 or g6, bishops on c4). The eval trajectories are varied (losing->losing 40%, but also drawn->winning and winning->drawn) because the feature captures both positions where the player was already under pressure and cracked, and positions where they were fine but self-destructed with one weakening pawn move. The common thread is a pawn advance that removes a critical defensive square near the king, enabling an immediate tactical punishment—frequently checkmate.

1646.label: Player makes a passive move instead of capturing or checking with a rook, losing critical tempo against an exposed king.
1646.description: This feature identifies positions where the player had a strong forcing rook move available (typically Rxe4+ or a similar rook check/capture) but instead played a passive or slow alternative. The material signature shows the player moved various pieces (rook, king, queen, pawn) while Maia consistently recommends a rook move that gives check and often captures a pawn. The 100% 'missed winning material' rate combined with Maia always giving check confirms these are missed tactical shots. The eval trajectory (median 267cp lost, with winning->drawn and drawn->losing being dominant) shows these tempo losses are catastrophic, converting advantages into draws or losses. The Opus analysis repeatedly highlights the same pattern: an exposed or uncastled enemy king was vulnerable to an intermediate check, but the player chose a slow continuation (retreating, advancing a pawn, repositioning passively), allowing the opponent to consolidate. The dominant tags—missed_tactic, tempo_loss, exposed_king, intermediate_check—all point to the same failure: not exploiting a concrete forcing sequence when the opponent's king was temporarily vulnerable in the middlegame.

1647.label: Trading rooks into a lost pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawns decide.
1647.description: This feature fires on positions where a player (usually Black) initiates or allows a rook exchange that transforms a holdable or complex position into a hopelessly lost pawn endgame. The material signature shows rook moves (80%) frequently resulting in trades (60%), while the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 482cp), often converting drawn positions to lost ones (40%) or accelerating existing disadvantages (40%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (43%) and passed_pawn (29%), with recurring tags like 'simplification_error', 'connected_passed_pawns', and 'rook_trade_blunder'. The concrete positions consistently show late-game scenarios with advanced or connected passed pawns where the rook was the only piece providing sufficient defensive resources. Once the rooks come off, the resulting king-and-pawn endgame is trivially won for the side with the superior pawn structure or more advanced passers. Maia's recommendations (rook 60%, no captures 100%) suggest keeping rooks on the board to maintain defensive flexibility.

1648.label: Wasteful pawn moves (h3/h6/a6) in the opening that lose critical tempo and allow the opponent to seize the initiative.
1648.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: the player pushes a non-developing pawn (98% pawn moves, 88% opening phase) — typically h3, h6, or a6 — that wastes a crucial tempo. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (88%) in the immediate sense, meaning nothing is literally hung, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional damage (median 280cp lost, with 28% going from winning to drawn and 22% from drawn to losing). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, king_safety, and development. The top boards consistently show positions where a piece (usually a bishop on g4 or g5) is 'asking a question' and the player responds with a pawn nudge that either invites a favorable exchange (ruining pawn structure) or simply squanders development time in sharp opening positions where the center is contested and the king remains uncastled. Rather than playing the critical central or developing move, the player makes a slow prophylactic pawn push that hands the initiative to the opponent.

1649.label: Failing to handle critical pawn promotion threats in endgames, losing decisive tempo or allowing opponent's promotion to succeed.
1649.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a materially 'safe' move (no piece is immediately lost) but catastrophically mishandles a promotion-related situation. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (56%) and tempo_loss (22%), with passed_pawn being the most common tag (8 occurrences). The boards consistently show simplified endgames with advanced passed pawns where one or both sides have promotion threats (e.g., pawns on 7th rank, queens already promoted). The player's moves—king retreats, rook repositions, queen moves—are not tactically losing material directly but fail to address the critical tempo needed to either promote their own pawn or stop the opponent's. The eval trajectory shows massive centipawn losses (median 547cp), often converting drawn positions into lost ones (50% drawn->losing) or squandering winning advantages. Maia consistently recommends checks (100% check rate) suggesting the correct path involved gaining tempo through forcing moves. The pattern is a player who, in a razor-thin promotion race, plays a passive or misdirected move instead of the one precise forcing continuation that maintains the balance or winning edge.

1651.label: Player overlooks a concrete tactical opportunity (often a capture or active move), allowing the position to collapse from a favorable or equal state into a losing one.
1651.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that appears safe or routine but critically overlooks a tactical resource that was available — typically a winning capture or forcing move identified by Maia (which favors rook and bishop captures 33% each, often taking hanging or poorly defended pieces). The material signature shows 44% of moves are 'safe' (no immediate material loss) and 33% 'hangs' a piece, indicating the mistake isn't always an outright blunder but rather a passive or misguided move that leaves pieces undefended or ignores the opponent's tactical threats. The eval trajectory is devastating: 44% of cases turn a drawn position into a losing one, and another 22% throw a winning position into a loss, with a median cost of 576 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss' as the most common tags, with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (50%). The positions show a recurring pattern where one critical move existed (often a capture like Qxg5, Bxc5, or a recapture) and the player chose something else — a defensive move, a pawn push, or a capture on the wrong square — failing to recognize the concrete tactical shot that held the position together.

1652.label: Sacrificing a piece (usually knight) with check but without sufficient compensation, losing significant material.
1652.description: This feature fires on moves where players sacrifice a piece—most often a knight (41%)—frequently delivering check (52%) but leaving the piece hanging with no adequate follow-up. The material signature is stark: 52% of moves hang a piece outright, with a median net material loss of -3.0 (a full minor piece).
