The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors (median 386cp lost), with 44% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->losing 26%, drawn->losing 18%). The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players are seduced by flashy checks or apparent attacks (king_safety 25%, tempo_loss 25%) but the sacrifices are unsound—tagged explicitly as 'piece_sacrifice_unsound' and 'check_not_best'. The example summaries illustrate this clearly: a bishop sacrificed for a pawn with check but no follow-up, a knight moved to a fork square that fails to address the actual defensive need, and missed recaptures with tempo. Maia's recommended moves are typically quieter developing moves (bishop 30%, rook 22%, pawn 22%) that maintain material integrity. The pattern is a player lured by a tactical mirage—usually a check or apparent attack—into giving away a piece for nothing.

1650.label: Player delivers check with a bishop sacrifice (often on f7) that lacks sufficient attacking follow-up, losing significant material.
1650.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring chess mistake: delivering check with a bishop (75% bishop moves, 100% checks) that constitutes an unsound sacrifice. The material signature shows the move almost always loses material (median -3.0 pawns, with 34% 'loses' and 25% 'hangs'), typically capturing only a pawn (62%) while giving up the bishop. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors, with a median loss of 386 centipawns, frequently converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->losing 16%, drawn->losing 19%, winning->drawn 22%). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant pattern: king_safety-motivated bishop sacrifices on f7 (classic 'Greek gift' style attacks) that are refuted because no real attacking follow-up exists. The top boards show repeated Bxf7+ attempts in Italian Game structures and similar positions where the sacrifice is premature or simply unsound—White has no second-wave attack piece to justify the material investment. Maia's recommended moves (59% queen moves, often Qxd8+ or defensive queen moves) confirm that simple tactical exploitation or positional play was far superior to the speculative sacrifice.

1653.label: Playing slow developing or passive moves instead of seizing an immediately available winning tactic.
1653.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions where the player has a concrete winning tactic available (often a queen check or forcing sequence that wins material) but instead plays a quiet, non-capturing move—typically a pawn push or bishop development—that squanders the initiative. The material signature shows mostly safe non-captures (67% pawn moves, 33% bishop), meaning the player isn't blundering a piece outright but is simply failing to strike. The eval trajectory confirms severe consequences: a median loss of 348 centipawns spanning winning-to-losing, winning-to-drawn, and drawn-to-losing transitions. The tactical analysis reveals the consistent pattern: missed_tactic appears in every case, paired with tempo_loss (choosing slow moves over forcing ones) and king_safety themes (the missed tactics often exploit the opponent's exposed king). The top boards reinforce this—positions like the Scholar's Mate pattern (Qh5+ available but Bc4 played instead), or endgame checks on the wrong square—all cases where a precise forcing move existed but the player chose development or a 'natural' move, ceding the critical tempo that made the tactic work.

1654.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while leaving or creating a hanging piece, missing an elementary free capture of major material.
1654.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a simple, undefended piece that could be captured for free — most often a queen or rook — and instead makes a move that either hangs their own material or is simply irrelevant to the tactical situation. The material signature is stark: 62% of moves hang a piece, 90% involve no capture by the player, and 100% miss winning material. Maia's suggested best move captures a queen 73% of the time or a rook 24% of the time, confirming that the missed opportunity is almost always a major piece sitting undefended. The median eval loss of 362 centipawns reflects the cost of ignoring free major material. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (80%), with recurring tags like 'missed_capture' and 'hanging_piece_ignored.' The trajectory shows 40% winning->winning (the position remains won but advantage shrinks) and 15% winning->losing (the missed capture costs the game), indicating these are typically strong positions thrown away through simple tactical oversight rather than complex miscalculations. The board positions consistently show scenarios where an opponent's queen or rook is undefended on an open file or diagonal, and the player moves a different piece to an irrelevant square instead of taking the free material.

1655.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive role, leaving the position tactically vulnerable.
1655.description: This feature captures moves where a player relocates a piece (most often a bishop, 42%) that was serving a crucial defensive function—guarding a square, blocking a file, or protecting material—resulting in the piece being hung (67% of moves hang material) with a median loss of 204 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (50%), with tags like 'removing_defender,' 'blocked_file_defense,' and 'self_inflicted_mate' underscoring that the moved piece was the linchpin of the defensive structure. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes occur across various game states (losing->losing 33%, drawn->losing 25%), indicating players fail to recognize their piece's defensive importance regardless of the position's overall assessment. The Opus analyses explicitly describe scenarios like a bishop leaving a critical f-file blocking post or abandoning defense of a pawn, after which the opponent exploits the newly created tactical vulnerability. Unlike simple hanging pieces, the key pattern is that the piece itself often survives but its departure catastrophically weakens the position.

1656.label: Player makes a quiet or retreating move with a major piece, missing a forcing tactical continuation that wins significant material.
1656.description: This feature fires when a player moves a major piece (queen 50%, rook 25%) in a non-capturing, non-checking way that is objectively safe (material outcome 'safe' 75%) but catastrophically misses a winning tactic. The eval trajectory shows massive centipawn losses (median 565cp), with positions going from winning to losing 50% of the time — indicating the player threw away a won game. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve captures (pawn 75%) and checks (50%), confirming that concrete forcing moves were available but ignored. The tactical motifs (overloaded defenders, discovered attacks, hanging pieces) and tags (missed_tactic appearing in all 4 positions, tempo_loss in 3) reveal that these positions demanded precise calculation — discovered checks, exploiting overloaded pieces, or promoting passed pawns — but the player instead made passive or repositioning moves (Qd7 instead of Rxe5, Qh3 retreating, Rxd2 capturing the wrong piece). The positions are all middlegame with rich tactical content where only one good move existed, and the player's quiet continuation surrendered the initiative entirely.

1658.label: Capturing or trading with the wrong minor piece, surrendering a well-placed knight or bishop in an exchange that collapses the position.
1658.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a knight exchange (73% knight moves, 73% capturing a knight) that is objectively a material trade (55% trade outcome, median net 0.0) but strategically catastrophic (median 279cp lost). The eval trajectories show wins collapsing to draws or losses (36% winning->drawn, 18% winning->losing), indicating these are not material blunders but positional self-destruction through piece trades. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'captured with the wrong piece' and 'traded away the magnificently centralized knight' as the core error—players choose the wrong piece to recapture or initiate an exchange, surrendering their most active or strategically critical minor piece. The dominant motifs (60% positional_mistake, piece_activity tags, misplaced_piece) confirm this is about trading away a superior piece rather than a calculation error. The positions consistently feature centralized knights or active bishops being voluntarily exchanged when alternatives preserved the advantage.

1659.label: Moving a piece to a square where it loses tempo or hangs material, squandering a significant positional or material advantage.
1659.description: This feature detects middlegame positions where the player moves a minor piece or rook (knight 33%, rook 33%, bishop 11%) to an inferior square that results in hanging material (56% hangs) with a median cost of -3.0 material and ~417 centipawns of evaluation lost. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (100%), indicating these moves waste critical time rather than exploit existing advantages. The eval trajectory shows players frequently converting winning or drawn positions into drawn or losing ones (drawn->losing 33%, winning->drawn 22%), suggesting the player had a strong position but made a move that gave the opponent a free tempo to consolidate or counterattack. Maia consistently preferred rook moves (often rook captures), implying the correct continuation typically involved active rook play capturing material or maintaining pressure, while the player instead made a passive or misguided piece relocation that allowed the opponent to seize the initiative. The boards confirm complex middlegame positions where one side has clear advantages but squanders them through aimless piece shuffling rather than executing the winning plan.

1657.label: Player simplifies or captures prematurely, leaving a piece hanging that the opponent can exploit while missing a stronger tactical continuation.
1657.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a rook or queen move that results in hanging a piece (33% hangs) or trading down poorly (33% trade), with a median material loss of -2.0. The critical pattern is that in 100% of cases, the player missed winning material — typically a capture or tactical shot that was available. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), with recurring tags of 'simplification_error' and 'missed_capture'. The player attempts to simplify or reorganize pieces but does so in the wrong move order, either giving the opponent's piece an escape route (as in the exf3/Bxd4 example) or failing to neutralize a defender first (as in the Rxc1/Qxd4 example). The eval trajectory shows these are winning positions being squandered — 67% remain winning but at massive cost (median 515cp lost), while 33% drop all the way to drawn. The player had a concrete tactical win available (Maia's move gives check 100% of the time, suggesting forcing continuations were missed) but instead chose a premature simplification or capture that either hangs material or allows the opponent to equalize the exchange.

1661.label: Rook moves in endgames that waste critical tempo, missing checks or promotion-related priorities.
1661.description: This feature detects rook moves in pure endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player loses decisive tempo. The material signature shows rook moves (92%) that are mostly 'safe' (69%) — not outright blunders of material — yet miss winning material 92% of the time, costing a median of 88 centipawns. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (38%), with recurring tags of passed_pawn (7/13), rook_endgame (5/13), and promotion_threat (3/13). Maia consistently recommends rook moves that give check (85%), revealing that the human error is failing to use intermediate checks to gain tempo before executing their plan. The concrete positions show players grabbing pawns, making direct rook moves, or exchanging rooks when they should first deliver a check to deflect the opposing king, thereby securing promotion races or establishing critical blockades. The eval trajectory (46% losing→losing, 23% drawn→losing) shows these tempo mistakes often convert holdable or unclear endgames into losses.

1663.label: Trading rooks when the exchange removes a key attacking or defensive piece, squandering a winning or drawn position.
1663.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player initiates a rook exchange (rook captures rook in 100% of cases, with 98% resulting in a material trade) that critically damages their own position. The eval trajectory shows these trades are devastating: 26% convert drawn positions to losing and 22% throw winning positions to drawn, with a median cost of 258 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals why: the dominant motif is king_safety (57%), with recurring tags of removing_own_defender, premature_simplification, and tempo_loss. The player trades off a rook that was performing a vital defensive or offensive function—guarding a critical file, supporting an attack, or maintaining coordination—without recognizing that the opponent can recapture while sustaining or initiating a crushing attack. In 65% of cases the player missed a winning alternative (often a knight or queen move exploiting tactics), choosing instead to simplify into a worse position. The boards consistently show open positions with active pieces where the rook trade hands the opponent a tempo, opens a line to the king, or eliminates pressure on a key file.

1662.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while opponent has a decisive tactical threat involving back-rank or king safety.
1662.description: This feature fires when a player, often in a winning or at least tenable position, plays a move with their king, rook, or queen that completely ignores a lethal tactical threat. The material signature shows 76% of these moves hang material and 82% miss winning material, with a catastrophic median eval loss of 924 centipawns. The trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders: 29% swing from winning to losing and 12% from winning to drawn. The Opus analysis reveals the unifying thread: the opponent had a concrete mating or decisive tactical resource (back-rank mate, king walk into checkmate, coordination of queen+rook) that the player simply failed to address. Instead of capturing the opponent's attacking piece (Maia recommends captures 59% of the time, often with check), the player made a tempo-losing move—a purposeless king walk, a rook move that abandons defense, or a queen move that ignores the threat. The dominant motifs (king_safety 33%, promotion_error 33%, back_rank 17%) all share the pattern of a player who is blind to an immediate tactical crisis on the board, often involving exposed kings or advanced passed pawns requiring urgent attention.

1660.label: Developing a minor piece to a square where it becomes vulnerable to a knight fork or tactical exploitation in the opening.
1660.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players develop minor pieces (knights 41%, bishops 29%) or advance pawns (18%) to squares that leave them vulnerable to knight-based tactics. The Maia engine consistently recommends knight moves (100%) that capture pieces (94% knight captures), indicating the opponent's knight is delivering a decisive tactical blow—typically a fork—that the player's move failed to anticipate. The material signature shows moves are mostly 'safe' (76%) in isolation, meaning the piece isn't immediately hanging, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: 53% drawn->losing and 18% winning->drawn with a median loss of 350 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms fork (20%), hanging_piece (40%), and pin (10%) motifs, with recurring tags like missed_tactic, development, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions all feature Italian Game / Scotch-type structures where a centralized knight on d5 or d4 creates fork threats (e.g., Nxf6+ followed by d5 forking bishop and knight), and players carelessly develop pieces into the fork's path. The player overlooks that their 'developing' move walks into a prepared knight tactic that wins material or creates an overwhelming positional advantage.

1664.label: Premature pawn push in a drawn or winning endgame that fatally disrupts the pawn structure or loses a critical tempo.
1664.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn endgame positions (100% endgame phase, 80% pawn_endgame motif) where the player advances a pawn (100% pawn moves, no captures) that destroys a carefully balanced position. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic: 67% turn draws into losses and 33% turn wins into draws, with a median cost of 542 centipawns—essentially decisive in king-and-pawn endings. The dominant tags (passed_pawn, tempo_loss, pawn_structure, king_activity) reveal the mechanism: the player pushes a pawn that either breaks a holding structure (e.g., f4 leaving g4 undefended), wastes a critical tempo allowing the opponent's king to infiltrate, or prematurely advances a passed pawn when patient king maneuvering was required (e.g., e6 instead of Kd6). The opponent's best response is always a king move (Maia's move: king 100%), confirming that the pawn push gifts the opposing king decisive activity. These are not tactical oversights but positional misjudgments specific to pawn endgame technique—failing to recognize that in simplified positions, a single unnecessary pawn move can be the difference between a fortress and a loss.

1665.label: Player makes a non-capturing move while the opponent's queen hangs completely undefended, missing a trivially winning queen capture.
1665.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks an elementary queen capture that would win massive material. The material/position signature shows the player moves their queen (33%), king (33%), or rook (13%) WITHOUT capturing anything (player captured: none 100%), while Maia's recommended move captures a queen in 100% of cases. The 'hangs' category at 40% reflects that many of these non-capturing moves also leave the player's own pieces vulnerable, but the core mistake is the missed capture. The eval trajectory is devastating: 53% of cases go from winning to drawn, and 13% from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 734 centipawns—consistent with missing a free queen. The tactical analysis confirms this overwhelmingly: hanging_piece appears in 100% of positions, with tags like 'missed_capture' (9), 'queen_hanging' (4), and 'hanging_queen' (3). The board examples consistently show positions where the opponent's queen sits undefended on an accessible square, yet the player makes a completely different move—often a plausible-looking but irrelevant queen maneuver or king move—while the free queen capture goes unnoticed. This is not a complex tactic but a pure board-vision failure in spotting an unprotected queen.

1667.label: Player makes a move that fatally exposes their own king to a check or mating attack.
1667.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move—most often a pawn, rook, or king move (never a capture in 97% of cases)—that hangs material (70%) by leaving their king fatally exposed. The Maia-recommended move is overwhelmingly a rook or queen move that delivers check (100% of Maia moves give check), frequently capturing a pawn with check or initiating a forced mate sequence. The tactical motifs are uniformly king_safety (100%), with tags like exposed_king, forced_mate, king_walk_blunder, and check. The eval trajectory shows this often occurs in already-losing positions (40% losing->losing) but critically also converts losing positions into winning ones for the opponent via a missed defensive resource (37% losing->winning from opponent's perspective). The median eval lost is 0.0 centipawns because many positions were already lost, but the concrete pattern is clear: the player ignores an immediate check/mating threat on their king, plays a quiet or developing move, and gets punished by a forcing check that wins material or delivers mate. The top boards consistently show exposed kings (e.g., Kd6 walking into Qxf4+, king on open files facing rooks and queens).

1666.label: Player makes a quiet developing move while missing a powerful queen double-attack that wins material.
1666.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a seemingly natural developing move (pawn, bishop, or knight) while completely missing a devastating queen tactic available via Maia's recommendation (queen moves in 92% of cases). The material signature shows 41% of moves hang material and 100% miss winning material, with a median eval loss of 274 centipawns—indicating these are costly oversights, not subtle inaccuracies. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are forks (40%), tempo loss (40%), and hanging pieces (20%), with tags emphasizing missed double attacks and queen placement errors. The concrete positions show patterns like missing Qg5 double attacks, Qa5 captures on exposed pieces, or Qg4 multi-threat moves. Instead, players choose routine development (Bd6, Be7, Rb8, Qf3 without secondary threats) that fails to exploit the tactical tension in the position. The eval trajectory (26% winning→drawn, 23% drawn→losing) shows these missed queen forks frequently squander decisive advantages or tip balanced positions into lost ones, occurring primarily in openings and middlegames where tactical opportunities are abundant but easily overlooked.

1669.label: Moves that catastrophically ignore king vulnerability, turning winning positions into losses.
1669.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves where the player catastrophically overlooks king safety threats—either their own king's exposure or the opponent's counterattacking resources targeting the king. The material signature shows mostly safe or non-capturing moves (rook moves, knight moves, king moves) that aren't themselves losing material directly, yet Maia's suggested alternatives involve capturing pieces and giving checks, indicating the player missed aggressive tactical continuations. The eval trajectory is devastating: 60% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 692 centipawns, indicating these are positions where the player had a dominant advantage but threw it away in a single move. The tactical analysis confirms the unifying theme: king_safety and exposed_king are the dominant motifs, with back_rank_mate, deflection, and discovered_attack as the mechanisms. The concrete examples show kings walking into mating nets (Kf6 onto an open file), rooks grabbing material while ignoring back-rank mates, and moves that fail to anticipate checks and forced mating sequences. The player typically has a winning position but plays a 'reasonable-looking' move that catastrophically overlooks how their own king (or the opponent's tactical resources against it) changes the evaluation entirely.

1668.label: Player captures a queen (or trades queens) while missing a checkmate in one or critical king-safety tactic.
1668.description: This feature fires when a player, almost always in the endgame, captures the opponent's queen with a rook or queen (player captured queen 100%) but in doing so misses a forced checkmate or devastating king-safety tactic. The material signature shows the move appears 'safe' or is an even trade (net material median +9.0), yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 9420 centipawns—consistent with missing mate-in-one. The Opus analysis confirms: dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and back_rank threats, with recurring tags 'missed_mate_in_one' and 'queen_capture_distraction.' The pattern is tunnel vision on the high-value queen capture while the opponent's king is fatally exposed (trapped by own pieces, back-rank weakness, or open files). Maia's recommended moves are predominantly queen or rook moves that deliver check (100% give check), underscoring that the correct continuation was a mating attack rather than a material grab. The boards consistently show king positions with minimal cover and available mating squares that the player overlooked in favor of the tempting queen capture.

1670.label: Pushing g-pawn (g7-g6 or g2-g3) when a bishop on h6/h3 creates immediate tactical threats against the castled king.
1670.description: This feature captures a highly specific recurring blunder: a player pushes their g-pawn (g7-g6 for Black or g2-g3 for White) in response to a bishop placed aggressively on h6/h3, fatally weakening the kingside pawn shield around their castled king. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with 80% hanging material (median -2.0), meaning the pawn push itself isn't captured but it enables devastating tactical consequences. The missed moves are overwhelmingly knight moves (80%) that would have addressed the threat tactically rather than passively. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 530cp lost), with 40% converting drawn positions to losing and 20% throwing outright wins. The OPUS analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif (71%), with multiple examples showing the g-pawn push allows forced checkmate patterns (e.g., Qxg6+ mating nets) or decisive material loss. The positions consistently feature an opponent's bishop on h6/h3 combined with a queen on g3/g6 creating a battery, where the g-pawn push walks directly into the tactical threat rather than solving it.

1674.label: Greedy pawn capture in the opening that misses a crushing Qh4+ check exploiting a weakened kingside.
1674.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where the player captures a pawn (typically on e4) instead of playing the devastating Qh4+ queen check. The board positions consistently show open King's Gambit or similar structures where White's f-pawn is absent, leaving the e1-h4 diagonal fatally exposed. The material signature shows a safe pawn capture (nothing is lost immediately), but Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed tactics: every instance goes from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 410 centipawns. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags king_safety (71%) and missed_tactic (100%), with the specific pattern being a queen fork from h4 that simultaneously attacks the king and wins material (usually a rook). Players choose the routine, materialistic pawn grab over a spectacular tactical blow that would have been decisive.

1672.label: Passive or developing moves that overlook opponent's tactical opportunities involving king safety or hanging pieces.
1672.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes a seemingly reasonable but passive move (often a pawn push, piece development, or rook shuffle) while completely ignoring a critical tactical threat in the position. The material signature shows that 80% of the time the player doesn't capture anything, while Maia's recommended moves involve capturing knights (80%) or bishops (20%), indicating missed tactical opportunities. The eval trajectory shows severe consequences: 40% go from drawn to losing and 40% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 246 centipawns. The dominant motifs—king_safety (33%), hanging_piece (22%), and tempo_loss (22%)—combined with the 'missed_tactic' tag appearing in 6/10 positions, reveal that players are making moves that ignore concrete threats to their own king or leave pieces en prise. The concrete positions confirm this: f5 weakening the king, Ne5 leaving d4 hanging, Bd3 losing tempo while missing a defensive need, and gxh6 missing a fork combination. The pattern is consistently one of playing a 'natural-looking' move while being blind to the opponent's immediate tactical resources.

1671.label: Ignoring urgent threats in endgames by playing slow moves instead of immediate tactical captures or promotions.
1671.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a 'safe' move—neither capturing nor hanging material—but critically misses a winning capture or tactical resource that Maia identifies (100% missed winning material, with Maia's recommended moves being rook captures of pawns or bishops). The eval trajectory shows massive cost (median 335cp lost), with positions going from winning to drawn or from losing to hopelessly lost. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece, tempo_loss, passed_pawn, promotion_error) and recurring tags (tempo_loss, passed_pawn, material_win_missed) paint a clear picture: in complex endgames with passed pawns and hanging pieces, the player wastes a critical tempo on a slow pawn push, a passive rook move, or a king retreat, when an immediate capture of an undefended piece or a check-gaining capture was essential. The concrete positions show rook endgames and pawn races where one side ignores a free piece (Rxf7 missing a hanging bishop), pushes a pawn when connected passers demand action (h4 instead of addressing 7th-rank pawns), or loses the thread in promotion races by failing to capture with tempo.

1675.label: Player makes a non-forcing move while ignoring an available or incoming mating attack, gifting the opponent a crucial tempo.
1675.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player is winning but squanders a significant advantage (median 166cp lost) by playing a move that ignores a critical tactical opportunity—typically a mating threat or a forcing capture with check. The material signature shows 67% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that leave material en prise) and the remaining are merely safe but passive. Meanwhile, Maia consistently identifies queen captures of rooks with check as the correct continuation, pointing to missed back-rank or king-hunt tactics. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs: hanging pieces left unattended (50%), tempo loss (33%), and king safety neglect (17%). Tags like 'checkmate_in_one', 'mating_attack', 'ignored_threat', and 'catastrophic_blunder' reinforce that these players had lethal forcing sequences available but chose aimless or defensive moves, giving the opponent the tempo needed to escape. The boards consistently show positions with queens and rooks aimed at exposed kings (g2 weaknesses, back-rank themes) where one forcing move would have been decisive.

1673.label: Player makes a non-urgent move while their own king faces a mating attack or severe threats.
1673.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, often irrelevant move (typically a pawn push—62% pawn moves) while their king is critically exposed and under immediate tactical threat. The material signature shows these moves are split between 'safe' and 'hangs' (50/50), meaning the move itself doesn't always lose material directly, but it fatally wastes tempo. The dominant motif is king_safety (75%), with 'exposed_king' and 'tempo_loss' appearing as the most common tags. The Opus analysis repeatedly describes moves that ignore mating nets, fail to address rook invasions, or push passed pawns while checkmate looms. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures of major pieces (rook 62%, queen 38%), confirming that the correct response was to address the tactical crisis rather than play a slow move. The eval trajectory (62% losing->losing, 38% losing->winning) shows these occur in already-difficult positions where the player had a chance to fight back or was already lost but accelerated defeat. The median eval loss of 0.0 is misleading—several positions involve missed forced mates where centipawn swings are undefined. The pattern is consistent: the player is in a life-or-death king safety situation and plays a tempo-wasting move instead of addressing the immediate threat.

1676.label: Knight captures a d4 pawn in the opening but is immediately recaptured, losing a full piece for just a pawn.
1676.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake where a knight captures a pawn on d4 (97% knight moves, 97% capturing a pawn) but lands on an undefended or insufficiently defended square, resulting in the immediate loss of the knight. The material signature shows 'slightly_down' with a median net of -2.0 (knight lost for pawn = net loss of ~3 minus the pawn captured = ~-2), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: 47% of cases go from drawn to losing with a median eval loss of 333 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (70%), with recurring tags like 'pawn_grab_punished' and 'opening_trap'. The top boards almost universally show ...Nxd4 or Nxd5 positions in Scandinavian or Sicilian-like structures (80% opening phase) where the knight lands on a central square only to be recaptured with tempo—often by a queen that simultaneously attacks another piece. This is a classic opening trap where the tempting central pawn grab with the knight overlooks that the piece will be lost or won back with devastating positional compensation.

1678.label: Moving a bishop passively in the opening instead of playing a forcing queen move that exploits the opponent's exposed king.
1678.description: This feature detects opening positions where the player has a winning advantage (median ~200+ centipawns) but squanders it by making a safe but passive bishop move—often a retreat or development to a non-aggressive square (e.g., Bd2, Bd7)—when the position demanded an active queen move exploiting the opponent's king exposure or tactical vulnerabilities. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves that are materially 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost or traded), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (median 265cp loss). The tactical analysis reveals tempo_loss as the dominant motif (67%), with king_safety and missed_tactic as recurring tags: the player wastes a critical tempo on a slow bishop move while the opponent's king remains exposed, missing the narrow window (often only one good queen move within 50cp of optimal) to press the advantage decisively. The boards confirm this pattern across French Defense structures, open-center positions with exposed kings, and development decisions where Bd7/Bd2 is a natural but insufficient developing move compared to the engine's forcing queen continuation.

1679.label: Developing the bishop to an active square in the opening that loses tempo against a central pawn advance.
1679.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: playing a bishop development move (Bc5, Bc4, Bb4, or similar) in King's Pawn openings where the opponent has played f4 (Vienna/King's Gambit structures), when the correct move was a central pawn advance (Maia consistently recommends a pawn move, typically ...d5). The positions are all in the opening phase with central tension involving e4/e5/f4 pawn structures. The bishop move loses a critical tempo because the opponent can attack it with a pawn advance (like d4 or f5), forcing it to retreat and gaining time for development. The eval trajectory shows these moves uniformly convert drawn positions into losing ones (median 308cp lost), indicating the tempo loss is catastrophic in these sharp opening positions. The tactical analysis confirms tempo_loss as the dominant motif (60%), with development and piece_activity as key tags, showing the mistake is fundamentally about misunderstanding development priorities in sharp central positions where concrete pawn breaks must take precedence over natural piece development.

1677.label: King retreats or wanders in lost endgames, abandoning critical defensive tasks like blocking passed pawns or maintaining fortress positions.
1677.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions that are already losing but where the player makes the situation catastrophically worse (median 475cp loss). The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures, indicating the king is retreating or wandering rather than actively engaging with the position's demands. The eval trajectory (losing->losing 100%) confirms these aren't thrown wins but rather defensive collapses—positions that were difficult but had defensive resources that the player failed to find. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: passed pawns (dominant motif at 40%) need to be stopped, king safety concerns arise from the king being in the wrong zone, and tempo losses indicate the king moved to a square that loses a critical tempo in the race. Concrete examples like Kd8 instead of Bd8, Ke8 losing a defensible endgame, and Kc6 instead of Kxc8 (abandoning a fortress) all show kings fleeing to passive squares when active defense—blocking, capturing, or maintaining contact with key pawns—was essential. The player instinctively retreats the king rather than calculating the precise defensive requirements of the endgame.

1680.label: King moves to an unsafe square, hanging material or allowing immediate tactical punishment in drawn positions.
1680.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves their king (50% of activations) or queen (50%) in a way that hangs material (100% of moves result in hanging a piece) and converts a drawn position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing trajectory with median 10000cp loss, indicating many are outright mate-level blunders). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (75%) and back_rank (25%), while Maia consistently recommends capturing a rook instead. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: in rook endgames or simplified positions where one obvious capture was available (often winning a rook or major piece), the player instead makes a passive or active king/queen move that either walks into a back-rank mate (Ka8 allowing Rc8#), abandons defense of critical material, or gives the opponent a free tempo to consolidate. The common tags (rook_endgame, missed_capture, one_move_tactic, tempo_loss) confirm these are elementary one-move oversights in simplified positions where the player failed to see the single forced winning capture.

1681.label: Trading queens when holding a strong attack against an exposed king, squandering a winning advantage.
1681.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player initiates a queen trade (queen captures queen in 100% of cases) despite holding a significant attacking advantage, typically against an exposed or poorly placed enemy king. The material signature shows a clean exchange (net material median 0.0), confirming this is a trade decision rather than a blunder. The eval trajectory reveals the catastrophic cost: 50% of cases convert a winning position into a drawn one, with a median loss of 256 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant motifs of king_safety (40%) and positional_mistake (40%), and recurring tags like 'premature_queen_trade', 'attacking_potential_squandered', and 'attack_abandonment'. Maia's recommended moves (75% non-captures, 25% check) indicate the engine preferred maintaining pressure rather than simplifying. The concrete positions show exposed kings on e6, f2, d7, and k-side weaknesses where the queen was the primary attacking piece. By exchanging it off, the player eliminated their most potent weapon and allowed the opponent to consolidate into a survivable endgame.

1683.label: Player makes a slow or retreating move, missing a decisive knight fork that wins material.
1683.description: This feature fires when players miss powerful knight fork tactics, instead playing passive or tempo-losing moves. The material signature shows 37% hangs and a median loss of -1.0 material, indicating pieces are being left en prise by failing to execute the winning tactic. The Maia recommendations heavily favor knight moves (26%) and bishop moves (37%), often with captures (knight 16%, rook 16%) and checks (21%), consistent with missed forcing knight fork sequences. The OPUS analysis confirms this: 'fork' is the dominant motif (33%), with 'knight_fork' appearing as the most common specific tag (3 instances). The concrete positions show recurring Nf6+ fork patterns that win rooks or other material. The eval trajectory (median 312cp lost) shows these are game-changing misses—58% miss winning material outright—with the majority occurring in middlegame positions (79%). Players instead play quiet moves like rook retreats (Rd2→Rd1), pawn pushes (c2-c3), or piece captures on wrong squares, surrendering tempo and allowing opponents to escape the tactical threat.

1682.label: Failing to convert a winning endgame by missing simple captures or allowing unnecessary simplification.
1682.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player with a winning advantage makes an inaccurate move that squanders the win, typically converting it to a draw (67% winning->drawn). The material signature shows non-capture moves (100% no capture) that are mostly safe but occasionally hang material, while Maia consistently identifies captures (rook, bishop, queen) that would have maintained the advantage—67% of positions involve missed winning material. The tactical analysis reveals a dominant pattern of hanging_piece and capture_oversight motifs: pieces are left en prise or elementary captures are overlooked. The concrete examples reinforce this: missing Rxf7 taking an undefended bishop, allowing a queen trade that equalizes a winning position, and pushing pawns when simple captures win. The common thread is a player in a technically won endgame who loses focus on concrete material opportunities, instead making 'natural-looking' moves that allow the opponent to hold or equalize. The median cost of 322 centipawns reflects the transition from clearly winning to drawn or only slightly better.

1684.label: Moving a minor piece to a square where it is immediately captured for free in the opening.
1684.description: This feature fires on a very specific and fundamental opening mistake: moving a knight or bishop to a square where it is undefended and immediately capturable, converting a drawn/equal position into a losing one. The material signature shows minor pieces (knight 60%, bishop 40%) being moved, with the outcome being 'slightly_down' or 'hangs' (net material median -2.0, consistent with losing a minor piece worth ~3 pawns). The eval trajectory confirms drawn->losing with a median loss of 387 centipawns—almost exactly a full minor piece. The tactical analysis clinches it: 70% hanging_piece motif, with tags like 'unsound_sacrifice', 'piece_loss', and 'material_loss'. The top boards make the pattern concrete: Nxd5 where a pawn defends, Nxe5 where the knight is immediately recaptured, Bxa6 placing a bishop on an undefended square, and Bxf7+ sacrifices without compensation. All occur in the opening (100% opening phase) where beginners aggressively lunge pieces into enemy territory without checking if the square is adequately defended. Maia's suggested moves (knight 40%, pawn 40%) are quiet developing moves that don't hang material, confirming these are impulsive deviations from sound opening play.

1685.label: Developing pieces to passive squares or making aimless moves in the opening, ignoring central tension and losing critical tempo.
1685.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where players make knight or queen moves that are materially safe (no pieces hang, no captures) but squander tempo at a critical moment. The eval trajectory consistently shows drawn positions becoming losing (median 255cp lost), indicating these are decisive positional errors rather than minor inaccuracies. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (38%), supported by tags emphasizing development, piece_activity, and central_tension. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: players in well-known opening structures (King's Gambit, Catalan, Caro-Kann) make moves like premature Qf6, retreating Nh5, or passive Bd7 when the position demands addressing central pawn tension (e.g., playing ...d5 or ...exf4). Maia consistently recommends pawn captures that engage the center, confirming that the missed resource is almost always a concrete central pawn move. The mistake is not tactical blindness but a failure to prioritize opening principles—resolving tension, developing with purpose, and maintaining initiative—resulting in a permanently inferior position.

1686.label: Player makes a queen or rook move that overlooks a stronger tactical continuation, typically a discovered attack or winning capture.
1686.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a major piece (queen 52%, rook 27%) but misses a significantly stronger tactical option. The key signal is the 91% 'missed winning material' rate combined with a median eval loss of 310 centipawns — roughly a minor piece in value. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 40%, discovered_attack 20%, trapped_piece 20%) reveal that the board presented concrete winning tactics that were overlooked. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing pieces (bishop 24%, knight 15%, pawn 21%), confirming that the missed opportunities were material-winning captures or combinations. The concrete positions reinforce this: choosing the wrong discovered check, taking an en passant pawn instead of winning a knight, or moving the queen to a challenged square when a decisive capture was available. The player's move is often 'safe' (52%) or even gives check (27%), suggesting they chose a superficially reasonable or flashy move while missing the position's true tactical point — a stronger capture or combination that would have won material cleanly.

1687.label: Player makes a move that ignores a devastating back-rank or king-safety threat, often missing mate-in-one.
1687.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions (85%) where the player makes a move—often a rook capture or routine piece move—that completely overlooks a lethal back-rank or king-safety threat. The material signature shows 37% hangs and 26% trades, but the key signal is that Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen move (67%) delivering check (52%), indicating a missed queen-delivered mating or winning blow. The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of back_rank (40%) and king_safety (40%), with tags like back_rank_mate, missed_mate_in_one, and king_trapped. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 33% swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 701 centipawns, and 74% of positions involved missed winning material. The concrete pattern shows players capturing material or making seemingly active moves while their own king is fatally exposed on the back rank or an open file, blind to the opponent's mating/winning reply involving queen infiltration or pawn promotion with check.

1688.label: In endgames, the king moves away instead of capturing a hanging piece (typically a rook), turning a drawable or manageable position into an immediate loss.
1688.description: This feature detects a specific and devastating endgame mistake: the player moves their king (100% king moves, 0% captures) when Maia's recommendation is to capture a rook (100% king moves capturing a rook). The material outcome of the actual move is 'safe' — nothing is immediately lost on that square — but the missed capture costs everything, with a median eval loss of 10000 centipawns (i.e., mate or equivalent). The trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: positions go from drawn to losing (50%) or from already losing to hopelessly losing (50%). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (86%), with Opus analyses repeatedly describing scenarios where the king simply walks away from a free rook or piece. The boards confirm sparse endgame positions where a simple king capture was the only good move, and the player inexplicably sidesteps it — likely due to tunnel vision on king activity, promotion races, or failing to notice the piece is undefended in a simplified position.

1690.label: Player makes a non-forcing move that misses a decisive rook maneuver (infiltration, fork, or file control) in the middlegame.
1690.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player had a winning or strong advantage but played a passive or slow move (pawn 26%, queen 26%, bishop 21%, rook 18%) instead of the correct rook move (Maia's move: rook 100%). The material signature shows the moves are mostly 'safe' (65%) or 'hangs' (26%), meaning the player isn't directly losing material on the move itself, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: winning->drawn (38%) or winning->losing (21%) with a median loss of 338 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the missed rook moves involved forks (33%), tempo gains, king safety exploitation, and critical file control. Common tags include missed_tactic, released_tension, self_block, and critical_file_obstruction—all pointing to positions where a rook had a concrete tactical shot (infiltration on an open file, a fork, or a check-based combination) but the player chose a developing or positional-looking move that squandered the initiative. The concrete examples confirm this: Qc2 blocking a Rc5 fork, missing Rd3 infiltration, playing slow pawn advances when rook activity was decisive.

1691.label: Passive piece retreat or quiet move that overlooks an opponent's discovered attack, pin, or hanging piece tactic.
1691.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (92% no capture) with a piece (bishop, queen, rook, or knight) that appears safe on the surface (54% 'safe' material outcome) but actually hangs material (38% hangs) by ignoring a concrete tactical threat. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes are devastating: 46% shift drawn positions to losing and the median cost is 321 centipawns, indicating missed critical decision points rather than gradual positional drift. The Opus analysis reveals the underlying pattern: the opponent had available discovered attacks (17%), pins (17%), or pieces left hanging (33%), and Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing knights (46%) or bishops (31%)—the very tactical shots the player failed to see. The tagged motifs (tempo_loss, missed_tactic, discovered_check) and concrete examples (retreating a knight instead of capturing, allowing a devastating discovered check; playing a quiet rook move while a piece hangs) confirm that these are positions where the player chose a passive or developmental-looking move while blind to the opponent's immediate tactical resource exploiting piece coordination.

1689.label: Passive or unnecessary pawn moves in the opening that leave pieces or pawns hanging to tactical shots like forks.
1689.description: This feature captures a specific opening-phase mistake where the player makes a pawn move (60%) or quiet piece move (40%) that is not a capture, yet immediately hangs material (80% of cases). The positions are all well-known opening structures (Italian, French, Caro-Kann, Sicilian setups) around moves 3-5, where the correct approach involves active piece development or a critical central pawn exchange. Instead, the player chooses a passive or slow move (d7-d6, d2-d3, f2-f3, Be7 retreat) that fails to address a concrete tactical threat—typically a fork or hanging piece motif. The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 357cp lost), meaning these aren't positions where the player was already struggling but rather equal games thrown away by a single tempo-losing or structurally negligent move. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing a central pawn (exd4, cxd4 type moves), confirming that the correct response was to engage tactically in the center rather than play passively. The combination of development-related tags, tempo loss, and fork/hanging piece motifs indicates players who misunderstand the urgency of opening tactics and instead make 'safe-looking' moves that ignore immediate threats.

1694.label: Player delivers a showy check or premature capture that throws away a winning position by sacrificing material without adequate compensation.
1694.description: This feature identifies positions where a player, already winning, plays a flashy check or aggressive-looking move (75% checks, mostly with the queen or bishop) that actually loses significant material and converts a winning position into a drawn or losing one (median eval lost: 638 centipawns, with 75% winning->drawn and 25% winning->losing trajectories). The boards consistently show Italian Game and middlegame positions where simple captures (like Nxe5) were available, but the player chose spectacular-looking bishop sacrifices on f2 with check, premature queen trades, or checks that don't lead to meaningful attacks. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%) and positional_mistake/tempo_loss, with tags like 'premature_check', 'piece_sacrifice_for_pawn', and 'missed_winning_capture' reinforcing that these are cases where the allure of giving check or making a forcing move blinds the player to the fact they're giving away material (net median -2.0) for insufficient compensation. Maia's suggested alternatives (knight captures, quiet rook moves) confirm that calm, non-flashy continuations maintained the winning advantage.

1692.label: Rook moves to vulnerable squares allowing tactical exploitation of back-rank or hanging piece weaknesses.
1692.description: This feature captures positions where players move rooks (67% of moves) into tactically vulnerable squares, resulting in significant evaluation losses (median 264cp). The material signature shows the moves are often nominally 'safe' (67%) yet miss critical winning tactics (83% missed winning material). The motifs reveal the underlying vulnerabilities: back-rank weaknesses (33%), hanging pieces (33%), and passed pawn exploitation (33%), all occurring predominantly in the middlegame (83%). The eval trajectory shows these mistakes frequently convert winning positions to drawn ones (33%) or worsen already losing positions (33%). Examining the concrete positions, we see rooks being placed on squares where they are immediately captured (e.g., Rf7 walking into gxf7+, Rc2 allowing tactical refutation), or rook moves that abandon critical defensive duties on the back rank. The common thread is that the rook move appears active or useful but overlooks an immediate tactical consequence tied to structural weaknesses in the position.

1696.label: Pawn moves that leave pieces hanging by ignoring tactical threats in the position.
1696.description: This feature captures moves—predominantly pawn pushes (75%)—that hang material (75% of outcomes) by ignoring existing tactical vulnerabilities in the position. The median cost is a severe 316 centipawns, with positions going from drawn to losing (50%) or worsening already losing positions (50%). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), and the tactical analyses consistently describe scenarios where the player makes a pawn move that fails to address a critical tactical issue: an intermediate check exploiting an undefended piece, a knight left trapped, or a piece left en prise. The positions are primarily in the opening phase (75%) where piece safety is paramount. The common thread across all examples is that the player pushes a pawn (or occasionally makes another move) while being blind to the fact that a piece elsewhere on the board is tactically vulnerable—either through intermediate checks, discovered attacks, or simple lack of defense—resulting in material loss.

1693.label: Player makes a move that allows a back-rank checkmate instead of playing the defensive or offensive queen move that addresses it.
1693.description: This feature fires when players overlook a back-rank mate threat. The material signature shows diverse piece moves (pawns 25%, rooks 25%, queens 22%, knights 15%) that are overwhelmingly hanging pieces (55%) rather than captures (72% no capture), indicating the player is making a 'normal' move while missing a critical tactical threat. The Maia best-move signal is decisive: 98% of the time the correct move was a queen move, and 100% of the time it delivered check—strongly suggesting the missed opportunity was either a back-rank mating attack or a defensive queen move that simultaneously checked. The Opus tactical analysis confirms back_rank as the universal motif (100%), with trapped_king and king_safety as supporting tags. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 287 centipawns, with many positions going from losing-but-surviving to completely lost (28% losing->losing but much worse), and some catastrophic swings (winning->losing 2%, drawn->losing 10%). The top boards corroborate this: positions feature kings on back ranks with open files and rooks/queens aligned for mate threats. Players make routine-looking moves (castling into it, moving minor pieces, passive pawn pushes) while completely missing that their opponent's back rank is fatally weak or that their own back rank is about to be exploited.

1697.label: Player gives away a rook with a meaningless check in a losing position, accelerating defeat.
1697.description: This feature fires on positions where a player, already in a losing position (75% losing->losing), moves their rook (92% rook moves) to deliver check (58% played a check) but hangs the piece outright (83% hangs material, median net material loss of -5.0, consistent with losing a rook). The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: 'gave away their only remaining piece—the rook—for a meaningless check' and 'moved the rook to a square where it could simply be captured by the king.' Tags like desperation_check, hanging_piece, and tempo_loss reinforce that these are panic checks in lost positions where the player sacrifices their rook for no compensation. The eval trajectory shows a median 244cp loss, typically worsening an already losing position. The top boards show rooks moving to unprotected squares (f7f1, e1e2, c8c3, d8d2) where they can be trivially captured, often delivering a pointless check that doesn't improve the position at all. This is a classic desperation pattern in middlegame positions (92%) where a losing player throws away material with a spite check rather than finding defensive resources.

1695.label: Moving a knight away from a critical defensive or offensive post, allowing the opponent to win decisive material (typically a queen capture or promotion).
1695.description: This feature captures a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player moves their knight to an irrelevant square, hanging it or abandoning its essential defensive/offensive function. The material signature shows 100% knight moves that are non-captures resulting in a hung piece (median -3.0 material), while Maia's response is consistently capturing a queen—indicating the knight was guarding against a promotion or protecting a critical piece. The eval trajectory (losing->losing with massive centipawn losses) confirms these are positions already under pressure where the player compounds the deficit catastrophically rather than finding the one defensive resource. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring motif: passed pawns threatening promotion, pieces needing to stay on critical squares to block or contest, and tempo losses from moving the knight to irrelevant targets (grabbing pawns, retreating passively). The boards consistently show late endgames with advanced passed pawns or promotion threats where the knight was the sole piece capable of intervention, and its relocation immediately allows a decisive breakthrough.

1698.label: Hanging the queen in a winning position by making a purposeless or poorly calculated move.
1698.description: This feature identifies positions where a player, typically holding a winning advantage, blunders their queen (75% queen moves, 88% hangs material, median net material loss of -6.0 points). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes that convert wins into losses (50%) or draws (38%), with a median eval drop of 715 centipawns. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 67%, king_safety 33%) and tags (back_rank, queen_blunder, false_attack, trapped_piece) reveal the mechanism: players make queen moves that appear active—delivering checks, creating threats, or repositioning—but overlook that the queen becomes undefended or trapped after the opponent's reply. The board positions consistently show middlegame situations where the player's queen is placed on a square where it can be captured due to back-rank geometry, blocking by friendly pieces, or interposition-captures that win the queen. Rather than a miscalculated exchange, these are outright queen hangs from winning positions where a safer continuation would have maintained the advantage.

1702.label: Trading queens into a lost pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawns or pawn majority is decisive.
1702.description: This feature detects queen trades that transition into losing pawn or rook endgames. The material signature shows 100% queen moves capturing an opponent's queen (a trade, not a blunder), predominantly in endgame positions (75%). The eval trajectory reveals these trades cost a median of 250 centipawns, converting drawn or already difficult positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 50%, losing->losing 50%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (44%) and passed_pawn (33%), with recurring tags like 'queen_trade_error' and 'simplification_error.' The concrete pattern across boards shows players voluntarily exchanging queens only to find themselves in hopeless pawn endgames where the opponent has connected passed pawns, superior pawn majorities, or unstoppable promotion threats. The queen was typically their only source of dynamic counterplay, and its removal exposes a structurally lost position that was previously held together by tactical activity.

1699.label: King moves away from critical pawns in endgames, leaving them undefended or losing crucial tempo.
1699.description: This feature detects king moves in pawn endgames that hang material by abandoning defensive or offensive responsibilities. The material signature shows 100% king moves that are non-captures resulting in hung material (median -1.0, i.e., a pawn drops). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors—median 583 centipawns lost—often converting wins into draws. The tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant motifs of pawn_endgame, tempo_loss, and passed_pawn errors: the king walks away from a pawn it should protect (e.g., Kc4 leaving b6 en prise), captures the wrong pawn instead of promoting (Kxh6 instead of pushing a passed pawn), or loses a critical tempo that allows the opponent to reach a drawn or winning position. All positions are pure endgames where king placement relative to passed pawns is the decisive factor, and the recurring mistake is misjudging which pawn or square the king must attend to.

1700.label: Trading away an active bishop when the position demanded maintaining tension or pursuing a tactic.
1700.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players (predominantly with bishops, 88%) initiate exchanges—typically trading a bishop for a knight (38%) or another piece—that dissipate their positional or tactical advantage. The material signature shows 50% trades and 25% slightly_down outcomes, indicating these are voluntary exchange decisions rather than blunders. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% of cases go from winning to drawn and 12% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 343 centipawns—characteristic of throwing away a won game through simplification. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of 'positional_mistake' (60%) and tags like 'premature_exchange', 'releasing_tension', and 'missed_tactic'. The concrete positions show powerful bishops on active diagonals (Bb5, Bg3, Bc5) being traded off when the correct approach was to maintain pressure, preserve piece activity, or execute a concrete tactic that the active piece enabled. The Maia baseline (62% pawn moves, 25% knight moves) suggests the engine preferred quiet developing moves or tactical strikes rather than these premature exchanges.

1701.label: King or pawn moves in pure pawn endgames that waste a critical tempo, hanging material or ruining the race.
1701.description: This feature captures mistakes in king-and-pawn endgames where the player makes an innocuous-looking king move (67%) or pawn move (33%) that loses a crucial tempo. The material signature shows these are non-captures that 'hang' material (100%), meaning the move allows the opponent to win a pawn or promote without any exchange taking place. The eval trajectory shows these errors occur in already-difficult or drawn positions (losing->losing 67%, drawn->losing 33%), costing a median of 220 centipawns—often the difference between drawing and losing, or between a slow loss and an immediate one. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (67%) and tempo_loss (22%), with tags emphasizing king_activity, passed_pawn races, and move_order precision. The top boards are all pure pawn endings where a single tempo determines whether a king can blockade a passed pawn or whether a pawn race is won or lost. The Maia recommendations (100% pawn moves) suggest the correct continuations typically involve advancing pawns rather than making the king moves the players chose.

1703.label: In the opening, player makes a non-capturing move that leaves a piece hanging to a knight fork or tactical shot exploiting an uncastled/exposed king.
1703.description: This feature captures a specific pattern of opening-phase blunders (71% opening) where the player moves a knight or pawn (72% combined) without capturing anything, yet the move hangs material (71% hangs) worth a median of ~1 pawn. The critical context is that Maia's recommended move almost always captures a piece with a knight (86% knight captures), indicating the player missed an available knight fork or tactical combination. The dominant motifs—knight_fork (3 occurrences), king_safety (40%), and king_in_center/uncastled_king tags—reveal that the exposed king position enables these knight tactics. The trajectory (86% drawn->losing, median 335cp loss) shows these are game-defining mistakes that convert equal positions into losing ones. The recurring pattern is: player makes a passive or retreating move in the opening (e.g., Nd1 retreat, g5 weakening, Qe6 misplacement) while their king remains in the center, overlooking that the opponent has a devastating knight fork or tactic exploiting the king's exposure. The positions consistently show complex piece play around d4/d5 knight outposts in Sicilian/Open Game structures where fork vulnerabilities arise naturally.

1705.label: Player overlooks an elementary winning capture, hanging material or squandering a decisive advantage.
1705.description: This feature fires when a player fails to execute a straightforward capturing move that would win material outright. The material signature shows the player's move frequently 'hangs' a piece (50%) or makes a suboptimal trade (50%), with a median net material loss of 2.0 (roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: positions shift from winning to drawn or drawn to losing, with a massive median loss of 526 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (80%) as the dominant motif, with recurring tags of missed_capture, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions reinforce this: in multiple examples (e.g., missing dxc5 to capture an undefended bishop, or playing a king move instead of taking a free piece), the player makes an innocuous-looking move while a simple, obvious capture sits available. These occur across game phases (opening and endgame) and involve various piece types, but the unifying thread is always the same—a free or near-free piece left on the board because the player chose a different, inferior plan.

1704.label: Advancing a center pawn too early, hanging it or creating tactical vulnerabilities that turn a drawn or winning position into a losing one.
1704.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn advances (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) in the opening or early middlegame (54% opening, 46% middlegame) that push a central pawn forward prematurely. The material signature shows these pawns are frequently hung (65%) with a median net loss of -1.0, meaning the advanced pawn itself becomes indefensible. The eval trajectory is devastating: 58% of cases flip from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 249 centipawns—indicating these are not minor inaccuracies but game-changing mistakes. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: players with uncastled kings, development lags, or unstable pawn structures push d5 or e5 too aggressively, overlooking that the resulting pawn can be captured or that the opened lines expose their own king. Tags like 'premature_central_break', 'overextension', and 'development_lag' confirm that these pushes violate basic opening principles by prioritizing pawn aggression over piece coordination and king safety. The top boards uniformly show e4-e5 or d4-d5 pushes in positions where patience and development were required instead.

1707.label: King moves into a mating net in endgames, missing a critical capture that was the only defense.
1707.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (75% king moves) into immediate danger—walking into checkmate or a decisive tactical blow—rather than making the one saving move (usually a capture, as Maia's suggested moves involve capturing rooks 75% or queens 25%). The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (75% 'hangs'), and the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic swings: 75% flip from losing to winning for the opponent, with a median eval loss of ~106 pawns (i.e., forced mate). The dominant motifs are king_safety (57%) and the recurring tags 'mating_net', 'king_walk_blunder', and 'missed_capture' confirm the pattern: in each case an exposed king steps onto a fatally wrong square where checks, forks, or immediate checkmate await, when the only viable alternative was to capture a piece that would disrupt the opponent's coordination. The positions uniformly occur in endgames with minimal material, where king placement is decisive and one wrong step is instantly terminal.

1708.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while missing a critical king safety tactic or decisive capture, converting a drawable or winning position into a losing one.
1708.description: This feature fires on positions where the player overlooks a serious king safety threat or decisive tactical opportunity, instead making a quiet or passive move that catastrophically worsens their position. The material signature shows 56% of moves are 'safe' (non-captures that don't immediately hang material) and 68% capture nothing, yet 56% miss winning material — indicating the mistake is one of omission rather than commission. The dominant motif is king_safety (43%), with supporting tags of missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and missed_capture. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 380 centipawns, with the most common pattern being drawn->losing (32%), meaning these quiet moves squander holdable positions. The concrete examples reinforce this: retreating a queen to g7 instead of capturing an undefended queen, playing h3 in a position requiring active defense, moving a rook passively when a queen trade could be forced, or losing tempo with moves like Rb8 when the position demands immediate tactical engagement. The player consistently fails to recognize the urgency of the position — particularly around king safety — and plays a 'do-nothing' move while the opponent's threats or available captures go unaddressed.

1711.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured, squandering a winning or competitive position.
1711.description: This feature consistently fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a bishop or rook to a square where it hangs undefended (material outcome: 'hangs' 50%, 'loses' 50%, median net material loss of -3.0). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (60%), and the Opus analysis repeatedly identifies pieces placed on squares where they can be captured for free. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 760 centipawns lost), with 50% converting winning positions into losing ones. Maia consistently recommends bishop moves that give check instead—active developing moves that maintain piece safety. The common tags (missed_tactic, hanging_piece, tempo_loss) confirm that players are overlooking opponent threats to their pieces, placing them on undefended squares without considering immediate captures. The boards show patterns like Bd1 where the queen captures freely, or Rc6 where the piece is unprotected. This is not a complex tactical oversight but a basic failure to check whether the destination square is defended.

1710.label: Advancing a pawn speculatively that hangs material and squanders a winning or equal position by losing tempo and weakening the king.
1710.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn advances (96% pawn moves) that are not captures (93% no capture) and result in hanging material (66% hangs, median -1.0 net material). The trajectory shows these moves frequently throw away winning or equal positions (winning->drawn 18%, drawn->losing 16%, winning->losing 7%), with a severe median eval loss of 275 centipawns. The Opus analysis reveals the positional layer: these are tempo-losing, self-weakening pawn pushes (tags: tempo_loss, self_weakening_pawn_advance, premature_attack, king_safety) that open lines for the opponent or waste critical time on speculative attacks. The top boards show patterns like ...g3, ...h3, b6, ...c3, ...b3—pawns lunging forward without tactical justification, often near the player's own king or on the wrong side of the board, leaving pieces undefended and handing the opponent initiative. Maia's suggested alternatives (queen, rook, bishop moves) confirm that piece activity or defensive moves were called for, not speculative pawn thrusts.

1709.label: Player makes a safe or materialistic move instead of pursuing a decisive king attack.
1709.description: This feature detects positions where a player abandons a winning attack on the opponent's king in favor of a passive, safe, or materialistic alternative. The material signature shows that 50% of moves are 'safe' and 69% involve no capture—these aren't greedy grabs but rather quiet moves that fail to press a decisive advantage. The king_safety motif dominates at 56%, combined with tags like missed_mate, missed_mating_attack, and materialism_over_attack, indicating the player had a crushing initiative against the enemy king but chose something else. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: a median loss of 483 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing. Maia's preferred moves (57% queen moves, 0% checks) suggest the engine wanted aggressive queen maneuvers the player avoided. The top boards consistently show middlegame positions with exposed kings where the player played a purposeless pawn push (f4, a3, g3, h4) or retreated a piece instead of delivering a forced mating sequence or maintaining overwhelming pressure. The common thread is a failure of attacking nerve—seeing the position as requiring consolidation when it actually demanded a finishing blow.

1712.label: Player captures a queen with check but overlooks a forced checkmate, settling for a trade instead of delivering mate.
1712.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a check that captures the opponent's queen (100% capture queen, 100% check) but in doing so misses a forced checkmate — typically a back-rank mate or short mating sequence. The material signature shows a 'trade' (median net +6.0, consistent with winning a queen but losing equivalent material back or entering a simplified position), yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 198 centipawns, indicating a dramatically superior continuation was available. The dominant motifs (back_rank 40%, hanging_piece 40%) and recurring tags (missed_mate, back_rank_mate, mating_net) confirm the pattern: the player reflexively grabs the queen with check — a superficially attractive move — rather than calculating 1-2 moves deeper to find a forced mate. The Opus analyses explicitly describe this: 'greed of taking material with check blinded White to the far superior back-rank mate' and 'missed a forced checkmate in two by playing the superficially attractive capture.' The positions span middlegame and opening, with Maia sometimes suggesting quieter moves (bishop, queen without capture) that would have delivered the mate instead.

1706.label: Pawn exchanges or advances that leave other pieces undefended, turning solid positions into losing ones.
1706.description: This feature fires on pawn moves (95% pawn played) that are predominantly exchanges (68% trade, 65% capturing pawns) but which inadvertently leave other pieces or squares undefended. The eval trajectory shows these are costly mistakes (median 231cp lost), frequently converting drawn positions to losing (32%) or winning to drawn (18%). The tactical analysis reveals the consistent pattern: the pawn recapture or advance looks natural but ignores that it was the pawn's defensive role holding the position together. The dominant motifs—positional_mistake (50%), hanging_piece (25%), king_safety (25%)—combined with tags like piece_activity, central_control, and undefended_pawn confirm that these pawn trades remove critical support from other pieces or key squares. The top boards reinforce this: c3-c4 leaving d4 undefended, fxe4 opening lines dangerously, cxd4 abandoning a winning tactical sequence. Maia's recommended alternatives (knights 30%, bishops 18%) suggest developing or repositioning pieces was correct rather than committing to the pawn exchange. Players are lured by the apparent symmetry of the trade while missing that their pawn was performing a crucial defensive or structural duty.

1713.label: Passive or tempo-wasting moves that leave pieces undefended against tactical threats like forks.
1713.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a move (often a quiet king, bishop, or queen move) that loses a critical tempo, leaving a piece hanging to a tactical motif—most commonly a fork or an exploitation of an undefended piece. The material signature shows 67% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0, while Maia's recommended moves involve capturing rooks (100%), indicating the opponent immediately wins material. The dominant motifs are forks (40%) and hanging pieces (40%), with 'tempo_loss' being the most frequent tag (appearing in 4 of 6 examples). The eval trajectory is mixed (winning->drawn, winning->winning, losing->losing), suggesting these aren't always game-deciding but consistently cost material through inattention to tactical threats.
