The board positions consistently show situations where the player ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability—such as a knight fork on the next move or an undefended piece—in favor of a passive repositioning move that wastes the tempo needed to address the threat.

1716.label: Knight captures a central pawn that is defended by a recapturing piece, losing a full minor piece for a pawn.
1716.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake where a knight captures the e-pawn (Nxe5 or Nxe4) prematurely, winning a pawn but leaving the knight hanging to immediate recapture by a defending piece (typically another knight on c3 or c6). The material signature confirms knights capturing pawns with a net loss of approximately 2 pawns (i.e., losing a minor piece worth ~3 for a pawn worth ~1). The eval trajectory shows these moves turn drawn/balanced positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 254 centipawns—consistent with dropping a full minor piece. The top boards reveal this pattern occurs almost exclusively in common opening positions (Petrov-like, Four Knights, Italian setups) where the e-pawn appears undefended or where the player confuses the position with a legitimate tactical pattern (like the true Petrov Defense 3...Nxe4). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' because after the capture, the knight itself is immediately lost. Tags like 'unsound_sacrifice' and 'development' reinforce that players are making a pseudo-aggressive capture without noticing the defending piece covers the square.

1714.label: Greedy captures or active moves that fatally ignore back-rank mate threats.
1714.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a move that appears materially safe or even favorable (73% safe, 27% trade, median net +1.0 material) but catastrophically overlooks a back-rank checkmate vulnerability. The dominant motif is back_rank at 88%, with recurring tags of back_rank_mate, one_move_checkmate, and greed_punished. The player typically moves a queen (46%) or rook (27%) to capture material or reposition actively, but in doing so removes the last defender of their back rank or ignores the opponent's access to the first/eighth rank via an open file. The eval trajectory confirms these are devastating errors: the median centipawn loss is -9422 (essentially losing a won or drawn game outright), with 18% going from winning to losing. Maia's recommended moves (king 27%, pawn 27%) suggest simple prophylactic measures like creating luft or blocking the file would have prevented mate. The concrete positions consistently show kings on g1/g8 with pawns on f2-g2-h2/f7-g7-h7 unadvanced, open e-files or d-files, and opponent rooks poised to deliver checkmate once the critical defender is lured away.

1715.label: In knight/pawn endgames, playing a passive king or knight move that squanders a critical tempo, missing a forcing check or tactic that was required to maintain the position.
1715.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players make passive king moves (32%) or knight retreats (39%) that waste a crucial tempo, when the position demanded an immediate forcing move—almost always a knight check (Maia recommends knight moves with check 100% of the time). The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (84%) featuring knights and passed pawns, where a single tempo decides whether a passed pawn promotes or a piece is saved. The material signature shows moves are mostly 'safe' (79%) meaning no piece is immediately dropped, yet the eval loss is severe (median 293cp), indicating these are positional/tempo catastrophes rather than simple blunders. The trajectory (29% drawn->losing, 29% losing->losing, 7% winning->losing) shows players failing to find the one saving or winning resource. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (30%), tempo_loss (20%), passed_pawn (10%)—and the example positions consistently show situations where a check-delivering knight move would have forked, blockaded, or gained the tempo needed to deal with a passed pawn or rescue a hanging piece. Instead, the player makes a 'natural' but passive move that allows the opponent to consolidate a decisive advantage.

1717.label: Player retreats a piece passively instead of executing a winning tactical shot, squandering a significant advantage.
1717.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a safe but passive move—typically retreating a queen, knight, or bishop to a non-threatening square—while missing a decisive tactical opportunity such as a fork, winning exchange, or crushing attack. The material signature shows 77% safe moves with no captures (89% no capture), meaning the player chose a quiet, non-committal move rather than striking. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of tempo_loss (75%) and fork (25%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, passive_retreat, and piece_activity, confirming the player moved a piece backward or sideways when an aggressive continuation was available. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 317 centipawns, with many positions swinging from winning to losing (6%) or drawn to losing (17%), indicating these retreats squander substantial advantages. The top boards reinforce this: Ng8 instead of Ng6 forking pieces, Bf8 instead of Qc1 winning material, quiet queen moves instead of Bc3 winning the exchange. The common thread is that the player sensed danger or uncertainty and reflexively retreated rather than calculating the concrete tactical blow that would have decided the game.

1719.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty, allowing the opponent to win material.
1719.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons its defensive responsibilities, leaving material unprotected. The material signature shows 70% of moves result in hanging material (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0 (approximately a pawn), and 57% of positions had winning material available that was missed. The eval trajectory (median 271cp lost, with 21% drawn->losing and 17% winning->drawn) confirms these are game-changing errors rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical analysis reveals a dominant pattern of 'removed_defender' and 'hanging_piece' motifs alongside 'positional_mistake' and 'tempo_loss' tags. The concrete examples reinforce this: Bh3 removes a bishop defending c6, Kd3 abandons defense of the e5 pawn, and Qxf3 uses the wrong move order leaving pieces undefended. These are middlegame positions (87%) where players relocate a piece for an ostensibly active purpose (attack, simplification) without recognizing it was the sole guardian of a critical square or pawn, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the newly undefended target.

1721.label: Trading queens or rooks into a lost position by ignoring back-rank vulnerabilities.
1721.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where players initiate or accept piece trades (92% trade outcomes, median net material 0.0) involving queens (65% captured) and rooks (25% captured), but catastrophically misjudge the resulting position due to back-rank weaknesses. The dominant motif is back_rank (44%), with king_safety (22%) as a secondary theme. The eval trajectory shows these trades cost a median of 499 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions to losing (22%) or drawn to losing (15%). Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (92%) that often give check (40%), suggesting the correct play was to maintain tension and exploit the opponent's back-rank vulnerability rather than trade into it. The top boards consistently show positions where the player exchanged heavy pieces (particularly queens on e8 or rooks) only to discover that the resulting position leaves their own back rank fatally exposed or eliminates the attacking potential they needed. The player trades away their attacking piece, failing to recognize that the trade relieves pressure on the opponent's vulnerable back rank or exposes their own.

1718.label: Rook retreats to passive or tactically vulnerable squares in simplified positions, abandoning active posts or exposing back-rank/tactical weaknesses.
1718.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their rook (71% of activating moves) to passive or tactically vulnerable squares in middlegame-to-endgame transitions. The positions are predominantly rook endgames (tag: rook_endgame appears frequently) where the rook abandons an active post—such as the 7th rank or a defensive square—for a square that either hangs the rook to a tactic (40% hangs material) or creates a fatal positional weakness. The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic errors (median 292cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (26%) or accelerating already difficult positions into hopeless ones (23%). The motifs reveal the underlying tactical punishment: back-rank mates become possible when the rook leaves its defensive post, pieces get trapped on their new squares, and tempo is lost. The top boards consistently show rooks moving laterally or backward to squares where they become targets (Rd2 walked into a deflection, Re3 abandoned back-rank defense, Rb4 gave up the 7th rank). The 97% non-capture rate confirms these are voluntary repositioning moves rather than exchanges, and the fact that Maia's recommended moves are more diverse (involving pawns, knights, kings) suggests the correct plans involved other pieces entirely.

1720.label: King moves to a suboptimal square in a lost pawn endgame, failing to address the critical passed pawn or tempo requirements.
1720.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern in pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the losing side plays a king move (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) that significantly worsens an already losing position (100% losing->losing, median 427cp lost). The positions are all king-and-pawn endgames featuring passed pawns (50% dominant motif), tempo-sensitive maneuvering (tempo_loss 20%), and critical king activity decisions. The tactical analyses reveal that the king consistently moves in the wrong direction—away from stopping dangerous passed pawns, losing critical tempi, or failing to maintain opposition. Rather than blundering material outright (the moves are 'safe'), the errors are positional: the king simply goes to the wrong square, violating fundamental endgame principles about pawn races, opposition, and the priority of addressing the opponent's most advanced passed pawn. The large centipawn losses despite already-lost positions indicate these moves transform positions with practical defensive chances into immediately hopeless ones.

1722.label: Player makes a non-checking move while missing a knight check that wins significant material via fork.
1722.description: The three signals converge clearly: (1) Maia's recommended move is a knight 94% of the time and delivers check 100% of the time, while the player's actual move is spread across rooks, pawns, kings, and queens—never the knight check. The player's move hangs material 33% of the time and is otherwise 'safe' but passive. (2) The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 291 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn (20%) or winning to still-winning but with drastically reduced advantage (20%), indicating a massive missed tactical opportunity. (3) The board positions confirm this: in nearly every case there is a knight available that can deliver check while simultaneously attacking a queen, rook, or other high-value piece (a fork), but the player instead makes a routine developing or defensive move, completely overlooking the tactical shot. The 92% 'missed winning material' rate confirms the pattern—these are not positional subtleties but concrete knight fork checks that win material immediately.

1724.label: Giving a check in a won endgame that wastes tempo and prolongs the win without improving piece placement.
1724.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check (100% of activations) in an endgame (100%) using a rook or queen, but the check is strategically pointless—it doesn't improve the checking piece's position or drive the opponent's king to a worse square. The material signature shows these are safe moves (75%) that don't hang anything, yet they cost a median of 109 centipawns in already-winning positions (winning->winning 100%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with recurring tags like 'pointless_check' and 'unnecessary_check' confirming the pattern. The Opus analysis explicitly invokes the 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' adage—these checks often improve the opponent's king position or delay forced mating sequences. The better moves (identified by Maia giving check only 25% of the time) typically involve quiet improving moves like advancing passed pawns or restricting the opposing king without check. The positions are overwhelmingly rook endgames with passed pawns where precise technique matters more than forcing moves.

1727.label: Knight captures a pawn or moves to an undefended square in the opening, leaving itself en prise to a queen or other piece.
1727.description: This feature fires on opening-phase knight moves (100% knight, 100% opening) where the knight lands on an undefended square—often capturing a pawn—and is immediately capturable for free. The material signature shows the move is slightly_down or hangs (median net: -2.0 pawns), indicating the knight is lost or traded very unfavorably. The eval trajectory confirms these are drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (drawn->losing, median 335cp lost), consistent with a full piece being dropped. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (90%) with 'undefended_knight' and 'queen_capture' as top tags. The concrete positions show a recurring pattern: in Scotch/Center Game-style structures, White plays Nf3xd4 when the knight on d4 is left completely unprotected (no other piece guards it), or Black develops a piece to an immediately capturable square. The key error is a one-move tactical oversight where the player fails to notice their knight will be undefended after landing.

1725.label: Failing to properly support or execute pawn promotion in endgames, often by premature queening or misplacing the king relative to passed pawns.
1725.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players mishandle critical pawn promotion decisions. The material signature shows pawn and king moves (50% each) with 50% hanging material, indicating moves that leave pieces or pawns en prise. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (75%), and the dominant motifs are passed_pawn (50%) and promotion_error (40%), with tempo_loss as a frequent tag. The tactical analyses reveal a consistent pattern: players either promote immediately without proper king support (e.g., queening on f8 without first positioning the king to recapture), or move the king away from critical passed pawns instead of toward them. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes occur in already-losing positions (losing->winning 50% means the opponent benefits, losing->losing 50% means compounding existing disadvantage), suggesting players in desperate endgame positions rush promotion or misplace their king under pressure. The top boards consistently feature advanced passed pawns (7th rank) alongside kings that need precise coordination, and the errors stem from failing to sequence king moves and pawn advances correctly.

1723.label: Moving a developed knight to an aggressive but undefended square in the opening, hanging it for free.
1723.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a knight (100% of cases) to an attacking square—almost always Nf3-g5 or similar aggressive lunges—without adequate support, hanging the piece outright. The material signature confirms no capture was made and the knight is simply left en prise (hangs 100%, median loss of -3.0 material, i.e., a full piece). The eval trajectory shows these positions go from dead equal (drawn) to completely lost, with a median cost of 414 centipawns—consistent with dropping a minor piece for nothing. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies 'hanging_piece' as the motif, with supporting tags of 'tempo_loss,' 'premature_attack,' and 'development,' indicating the player sacrifices a well-developed piece for a speculative attack that has no tactical justification. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show Italian Game or similar open-game structures where White plays Ng5 prematurely (or Black plays ...Nh5), attacking f7 or a bishop but leaving the knight capturable. Maia's suggested moves are pawn moves (100%), suggesting the refutation is a simple pawn capture of the hanging knight.

1728.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move while a forced checkmate (often via back rank or queen delivery) sits available on the board.
1728.description: This feature fires when a player, in a winning middlegame position, plays a non-capturing, non-checking move with their queen or bishop while Maia identifies a forcing queen check that delivers or leads to checkmate. The material signature shows the player's move is mostly 'safe' (no material lost directly) yet misses winning material 100% of the time—because the missed resource is not a piece win but a mating sequence. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: a median loss of ~95 pawns (i.e., mate lost), with 33% of cases flipping from winning to losing outright. The tactical motifs—back_rank_mate, missed_mate, one_move_checkmate, queen_delivery, king_entombed—all point to the same pattern: the opponent's king is fatally restricted (often entombed on the back rank or in a corner), and a simple queen check ends the game, but the player instead makes a developing or positional move, completely overlooking the immediate tactical finish.

1726.label: Moving a minor piece to a square where it hangs to a tactical fork or discovered attack exploiting king position.
1726.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move a knight or bishop (81% minor pieces) to an apparently active square, only to hang it outright (81% hangs, median -1.0 material lost, ~288cp eval drop). The dominant motifs are fork (33%), hanging_piece (33%), and king_safety (33%), with recurring tags like king_in_center, open_file_exploitation, and removal_of_defender. The positions cluster in the opening/middlegame (100%) where kings are often uncastled or centralized, and the piece relocation ignores latent tactical threats—typically a knight fork, a queen check exploiting an open file, or a recapture that fails due to a discovered attack on the king. Maia's suggested response is overwhelmingly a king move (94%), indicating the computer sees the opponent must deal with a check or king-safety crisis that the hanging piece enables. The eval trajectory shows most positions were already difficult (44% losing->losing) or balanced-to-losing (25% drawn->losing), suggesting players in pressure tried an active piece move that overlooked a concrete tactical refutation involving their king's vulnerability.

1729.label: Moving the queen to a passive or vulnerable square in a queen endgame, enabling forced trades into lost pawn endings.
1729.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player makes a queen move (100% queen moved, 0% captures) in a late-game position (67% endgame) that hangs material (67% hangs) and converts a drawn or already difficult position into a losing one (drawn->losing 67%, median eval loss 227cp). The boards consistently show queen-and-pawn endgames where both sides have queens and sparse pawn structures. The dominant motif is pawn_endgame (67%), indicating that the critical error enables a queen trade leading to a trivially won pawn ending for the opponent—as explicitly noted in the tactical analysis ('enables a queen trade that leads to a trivially won pawn endgame'). King safety and tempo loss tags further indicate that the queen move either exposes the king or loses a critical tempo. The Maia response is always a king move (100%), suggesting the opponent calmly consolidates after the blunder. The pattern is not a tactical oversight in a complex middlegame but rather a failure to recognize that the queen's new square allows forced simplification into a hopeless pawn ending.

1730.label: Trading queens by recapturing on e2 instead of playing a critical intermediate move that wins material or tempo.
1730.description: This feature fires when a player uses their queen to recapture a bishop (typically on e2), completing a trade, while missing a crucial zwischenzug (intermediate move) that would have maintained a winning or equal position. The material signature shows queen takes bishop as a trade (net 0), but the eval trajectory reveals this costs a median of 369 centipawns, shifting positions from winning to drawn (60%) or drawn to losing (40%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant pattern: the player overlooks that their queen was defending a key piece elsewhere (hanging_piece motif in 67% of cases), or that an intermediate capture with tempo (zwischenzug/intermediate_move tags) should have been inserted before the routine recapture. The boards overwhelmingly show Qxe2 positions in the opening/middlegame where moves like Bxe7 or other interpositions exploit mutual threats before completing the exchange. The player defaults to the 'obvious' recapture rather than recognizing the move-order dependency that makes the position tactically rich.

1733.label: Promoting a pawn to a queen when underpromotion or preparation was required, hanging the newly promoted piece or allowing a decisive tactical response.
1733.description: This feature fires on endgame pawn promotions to queen that immediately lose material. All top activating positions show a pawn move (100%) that hangs material (100% hang rate, median -6.0 material loss), with the dominant motif being 'promotion_error' (89%). The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently throw away winning or drawn positions (winning->drawn 38%, winning->losing 12%, drawn->losing 12%), with a massive median eval loss of 389 centipawns. The concrete board positions universally show passed pawns promoting to queens (c8q, b8q, a1q, d1q, etc.) in endgame scenarios where the queen promotion either allows an immediate fork/skewer of the new queen, or where an underpromotion (typically to knight) was necessary to deliver check or avoid stalemate. The Opus analysis confirms 'premature_promotion' and 'missed_tactic' as recurring tags, indicating players reflexively chose queen without calculating the tactical consequences.

1736.label: Queen checks that trade into drawn or worse pawn endgames, squandering winning advantages near promotion.
1736.description: This feature detects endgame positions where the player delivers a queen check (100% checks, 100% queen moves) that results in either a trade or material loss, typically converting a winning position into a draw (median 534cp lost). The boards reveal a consistent pattern: advanced passed pawns near promotion where one side has a queen, and instead of nursing the pawn advantage or maintaining queen activity, the player impulsively checks with the queen, often capturing on the promotion square or allowing a queen exchange. The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of pawn_endgame (44%) and promotion_error (33%), with tags emphasizing passed pawns, tempo loss, and missed tactics. Maia's recommended alternatives (quiet queen moves without captures) suggest the correct approach was maintaining piece activity rather than forcing a premature queen interaction. The trajectory (winning->drawn 50%) combined with the trade/loses material signature shows these are not tactical brilliancies but panicked checks that simplify away a decisive advantage in technically won pawn endgames.

1732.label: Wasting a move on a non-urgent or aimless piece shuffle instead of executing a concrete plan in a winning middlegame position.
1732.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player holds a significant advantage (median ~350cp) but squanders it by playing a slow, purposeless move—often a queen retreat, a pawn push, or a piece repositioning that lacks tactical or strategic urgency. The material signature shows 94% safe moves (no material is lost directly) and 100% missed winning material, indicating the player overlooked a concrete continuation that would have maintained or increased their edge. The eval trajectory confirms this is overwhelmingly a 'throwing the win' pattern: 62% winning→drawn and 19% drawn→losing, with a median cost of 256cp. The Opus analysis is dominated by tempo_loss (60%) and piece_activity tags, revealing that the mistake is not a tactical oversight per se but a failure to use the initiative—moves like Qd2, c3, Nb1, or Kh7 that develop nothing, challenge nothing, and allow the opponent to consolidate. Maia consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), suggesting the correct plans involved pawn breaks (f4, c4, d6) that would have exploited the positional bind, while the player instead drifted with a non-committal move.

1737.label: Moving a knight to a tactically inferior square in the opening, abandoning better tactical continuations and leaving pieces or key squares vulnerable.
1737.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player typically moves a knight (50%) to a square that either hangs material or results in a suboptimal trade, while missing stronger bishop or queen moves (Maia prefers bishop 75%). The eval trajectory shows a substantial median cost of 262 centipawns across varied swing types (drawn->losing, winning->drawn), indicating these are serious errors rather than minor inaccuracies. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (38%), tempo_loss (25%), and discovered_attack (12%)—combined with tags like missed_tactic and king_in_center reveal that these knight moves abandon tactical opportunities (e.g., Bxf7+ sacrifices, maintaining pressure on diagonals) in favor of superficially aggressive but strategically flawed relocations. The top boards confirm this: knights jump to squares like f5 or c6 where they either lose tempo, expose critical defensive coverage, or walk into discovered attacks, while the opponent's king remains in the center as an unexploited target.

1734.label: Player makes a non-capture move that ignores a knight fork or direct threat, hanging a major piece.
1734.description: This feature fires when a player makes a developing or quiet move (bishop, king, knight, or pawn) that completely ignores an opponent's knight delivering a fork or direct attack on a high-value piece. The material signature shows 100% hangs (non-captures that drop material) with a median loss of 6.0 points (approximately a queen), and 100% of positions had missed winning material available. The eval trajectory is devastating: 64% swing from winning to losing with a median cost of 762 centipawns. The tactical motifs confirm this pattern: 71% hanging_piece and 29% fork, with recurring tags of queen_loss, ignored_threat, and queen_blunder. The concrete positions reinforce this clearly—opponent knights on f7, h7, f6, or e6 deliver forks or attacks on queens/rooks, and instead of addressing the threat (e.g., capturing the knight with Kxf7 or moving the attacked piece), the player makes an irrelevant developing move like ...Bb7, ...Bg7, ...d6, or castles into the tactic. This occurs overwhelmingly in the opening phase (73%), suggesting players are on autopilot with development rather than recognizing the immediate tactical emergency posed by the opponent's knight.

1731.label: Playing a passive or slow developing move in the opening instead of capturing a critical central pawn, squandering a significant advantage.
1731.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (79% opening) where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (93% no capture) — typically a pawn push, queen development, or bishop placement — that fails to seize a concrete tactical opportunity, usually a pawn capture in the center. The material signature shows 50% of moves hang material and the median cost is -1.0 (a full pawn), with 68% missing a winning material opportunity. Maia's recommended moves strongly favor pawn captures (68%) and knight captures (21%), confirming that the missed best move was almost always a central pawn take. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'dxc6', 'dxe5', or similar central pawn strikes as the missed continuation, while the actual moves played are passive retreats (Nc3), slow development (Bc4, Qe2, e3), or premature pawn advances (d5) that close the position. The dominant motifs — tempo_loss (50%), trapped_piece, king_safety, hanging_piece — and tags like 'development_advantage_squandered' and 'central_tension' confirm the player is releasing central tension passively rather than exploiting it. The eval trajectory (32% winning→drawn, 25% drawn→losing, median 349cp lost) shows these are not minor inaccuracies but game-changing failures to strike at the critical moment in the opening.

1738.label: In won endgames, player advances a pawn or king instead of capturing a hanging piece that was the only winning move.
1738.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player has a completely winning advantage but fails to capture a hanging or vulnerable piece (bishop, rook) with their king, instead making a 'safe' pawn push or king move that throws away the win. The material signature shows 100% safe moves (no material lost immediately) yet 100% missed winning material—the player's move doesn't hang anything but ignores the critical capture. Maia consistently recommends king captures (Kxb5, Kxg7, etc.), confirming the pattern. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 1072cp lost), converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones. The board positions uniformly show endgames with passed pawns and piece activity where one precise capture was required, but the player chose a natural-looking but losing pawn advance or king shuffle, often mishandling promotion races or leaving pieces en prise for the opponent to exploit.

1739.label: Moving the queen away from a critical defensive or coordinating square, releasing pressure or exposing the king.
1739.description: This feature fires when a player moves their queen (100% queen moves) to a square that abandons a vital defensive or coordinating role. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (75%) rather than outright blunders—the queen isn't immediately lost—but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional consequences (median 400cp lost, with 50% going from winning to losing). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the queen leaves a post where it was guarding key squares (h2, e-file battery support) or maintaining piece coordination, and the opponent immediately exploits the vacuum. Tags like 'king_safety_pressure_released', 'queen_placement', 'simplification_allowed', and 'back_rank_weakness' all point to the queen departing from duty. Concrete examples include abandoning e2 (breaking an e-file battery against an exposed king), moving away from f2 allowing Qxh2#, and pawn-grabbing with Qxb7 that permits a devastating queen trade. The common thread is not material loss on the move itself, but the positional collapse that follows when the queen's defensive/coordinating function is removed.

1735.label: Playing a slow or passive move instead of exploiting a concrete tactical opportunity in a sharp opening position.
1735.description: This feature detects positions where a player wastes a critical tempo with a passive or purposeless move (pawn push, quiet piece shuffle, or unnecessary prophylaxis) when the position demanded immediate active play—typically a knight jump to a dominant outpost. The material signature shows the played move is usually 'safe' (56%) or 'hangs' material (28%), meaning the move itself doesn't lose a piece directly but creates a positional collapse; meanwhile Maia's recommended move is a knight move 100% of the time, indicating a missed knight tactic or outpost occupation. The eval trajectory confirms these are serious errors (median 258cp lost), often converting winning or drawn positions into drawn or lost ones (winning->drawn 16%, drawn->losing 18%). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with recurring tags like development_advantage_squandered, king_safety neglect, and missed_tactic. The positions are predominantly in the opening (66%) or early middlegame (34%), featuring sharp structures where one side has attacking chances against an uncastled or weakened king. The player chooses a quiet consolidating move (Qe1, Rc1, a6, f3, Qe2) instead of the concrete knight strike (Nd5, Ne5, Nd4, Ne3) that would have maintained or increased the advantage.

1741.label: Player makes a routine developing move in the opening instead of exploiting the exposed king with Qh4+.
1741.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where the opponent's king is exposed along the e1-h4 diagonal (typically after a kingside pawn has advanced or captured away from the king), and the player misses a crushing Qh4+ queen check. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (no material lost immediately) but Maia consistently identifies a queen check as the best move. The eval trajectory shows 100% winning-to-drawn transitions with a median loss of 278 centipawns, indicating a substantial squandered advantage. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags king_safety (86%) with exposed_king, queen_check, and missed_tactic as recurring themes. The FEN positions all share a common structure: early opening positions (typically King's Gambit or similar lines) where White's f-pawn is missing, creating a fatal diagonal to the king, and Black plays passive knight retreats or routine development (Nc6, Nb6, Bc5, Ng6) instead of the punishing Qh4+.

1740.label: Player makes a routine move in the opening, missing a devastating queen check that wins material via fork or deflection.
1740.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing move (typically a pawn advance or minor piece development) while completely overlooking a crushing queen check available on the board. The material signature shows safe moves (80%) with no captures (74%), yet Maia consistently identifies a queen move with check (100% queen, 100% check) as the correct alternative. The tactical motifs are overwhelmingly fork (62%) and hanging_piece (38%), indicating the missed queen check simultaneously attacks the king and an undefended piece. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 423cp lost, with 49% of cases going from winning to drawn and 13% from winning to losing—confirming these are game-changing missed tactics. The positions are almost entirely in the opening (92%), where weakened diagonals (often from ...f6 or early pawn pushes) and undeveloped kings create queen check opportunities that exploit multiple targets at once. Tags like deflection, diagonal_exploitation, and undefended_piece confirm the queen check serves as a multi-purpose tactic the player simply didn't see.

1744.label: Trading rooks in endgames that eliminate critical defensive or winning resources.
1744.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players exchange rooks in endgame or late-middlegame positions, voluntarily simplifying when keeping the rooks on the board was essential. The material signature shows 74% rook moves capturing rooks (trades, not blunders—net material median is 0.0), while Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (90%), indicating the engine wanted to maintain piece activity rather than trade. The eval trajectory (74% losing->losing, median 129cp lost) shows these are predominantly positions where the player was already worse and the rook trade made a difficult defense impossible—removing counterplay resources like perpetual check threats, active rook defense, or pressure against passed pawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are rook_endgame (70%) with tags like simplification_error, endgame_technique, and rook_activity, and example summaries explicitly describe eliminating 'the one piece providing all defensive counterplay.' The concrete positions show rook-vs-rook endgames where one side initiates an exchange that hands the opponent a technically winning king-and-pawn ending or removes drawing chances.

1743.label: Developing a bishop to a square that abandons defense of a piece on the long diagonal, allowing the opponent's fianchettoed bishop to win material.
1743.description: This feature fires on opening positions where a player develops their bishop (82% of cases) to a natural-looking square (commonly Bd6, Be7, or Bd3) but inadvertently hangs a piece on the long diagonal. The boards consistently show a fianchettoed bishop on b2 (or g7) controlling the long diagonal, and the player's move either blocks or removes a defender from that diagonal, leaving a rook or other piece en prise. The material signature confirms this: 91% of moves are non-captures that hang a piece (median loss of ~1 piece worth, -1.0 material), and the eval trajectory shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (77% drawn->losing) with a massive median swing of 367 centipawns. Maia consistently recommends a knight move instead (96%), suggesting the correct plan was piece development that maintained diagonal defense. The tags (long_diagonal, king_safety, development, piece_activity) and example summaries confirm this is a pattern of 'developing into a tactic' — the bishop move looks logical for development but fatally weakens the long diagonal geometry, typically allowing the opponent's already-placed fianchetto bishop to strike.

1742.label: In endgames, plays a pawn move or piece move that hangs material by missing a critical move-order or tempo, allowing the opponent to exploit the lost time.
1742.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a move (most often a pawn push) that hangs material or squanders a decisive advantage due to a tempo or move-order error. The material signature shows 67% hangs (non-captures that drop a piece or pawn) with a median net material loss of -1.0, and 100% of positions are in the endgame phase. The eval trajectory reveals that most positions were already winning (67% winning->winning, 33% losing->winning), yet the player lost a median of 83 centipawns—indicating these aren't game-losing catastrophes but costly inaccuracies that complicate or nearly throw away wins. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (57%) and tempo_loss (14%), with recurring tags of passed_pawn, move_order errors, and blockade themes. The concrete examples reinforce this: pushing g2 before capturing a bishop gives the opponent a critical tempo to blockade a passer; playing f6 instead of capturing an undefended rook on a4; advancing a pawn when a simple king capture wins material outright. The common thread is an endgame position where the player rushes a pawn advance or makes an impatient move, overlooking that precise move-order (typically a capture or king move first) was required to maintain the advantage.

1746.label: Playing a showy knight check that hangs the piece instead of maintaining a perpetual or winning capture.
1746.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a knight check (100% knight moves, 100% checks) that hangs the knight (100% hangs, median -3.0 material), when a stronger alternative existed—typically a perpetual check drawing line (Nb5+) or a winning capture (Nxc7+). The eval trajectory shows these checks convert drawn positions into losing ones (60%) or squander large advantages (40%), with a median cost of 262 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core error is tempo loss (50%): the flashy check looks aggressive but the knight lands on an undefended square where it can simply be captured, while the opponent's king escapes to safety. Discovered attack motifs (30%) appear because the better moves often involved the knight enabling or executing discovered threats. Maia's recommended alternatives consistently involve the knight capturing material (pawn 80%, rook 20%) while also giving check, showing that the correct check was one that won material rather than simply displacing the king. The recurring pattern across the top boards—particularly the repeated Na6+ instead of Nb5+ perpetual—confirms this is a systematic preference for an impressive-looking but unsound check over a concrete tactical continuation.

1745.label: Player develops or repositions a knight instead of capturing an active enemy bishop, losing tempo and allowing the opponent's piece to dominate.
1745.description: This feature fires when a player moves a knight (50% of cases) or another piece in the opening/middlegame while ignoring a clearly superior pawn capture of an enemy bishop (Maia recommends pawn captures bishop in 100% of cases). The boards show a recurring pattern: an enemy bishop has landed on an aggressive square (often h3 or h6, disrupting king safety), and the player has the simple recapture available (e.g., gxh3, gxh6) but instead plays a developing or repositioning move. This constitutes a tempo loss—the opponent's bishop remains active or the opponent gains a free tempo—and frequently compromises king safety. The eval trajectory (median 276cp lost, with 40% winning→drawn and 30% drawn→losing) confirms these are game-changing mistakes, not minor inaccuracies. The material signature shows 'safe' moves (90%), meaning the player isn't hanging a piece outright but is simply choosing the wrong priority: piece movement over a free capture that would neutralize an enemy attacker. Tags like king_safety, tempo_loss, and missed_capture consistently reinforce that the core error is neglecting an available recapture of a threatening bishop in favor of an inferior developing move.

1747.label: Pushing a pawn in a won endgame instead of delivering a decisive rook check or forcing promotion with tempo.
1747.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, no captures, material outcome 'safe') but catastrophically misses a winning rook move that delivers check (Maia's recommendation is always a rook move with check). The eval trajectory shows a complete collapse from winning to losing (median 10,459 centipawns lost), typically converting a forced win into immediate checkmate or a lost position. The dominant motifs—promotion_error, tempo_loss, and passed_pawn—reveal the core mistake: the player advances a passed pawn one move too early, squandering a critical tempo that should have been used for a rook check to deflect the opponent's king, win material, or force promotion with check. The concrete positions confirm this pattern: advancing b6 instead of c8=Q+, pushing h7 instead of Rg8+, playing g4 instead of maintaining perpetual check pressure, and pushing d7 instead of a winning rook maneuver. In each case, the pawn push feels natural but hands the opponent a crucial tempo to counterattack or escape.

1752.label: Throwing away a completely won endgame by allowing back-rank tactics or exposing the king to perpetual check instead of simplifying.
1752.description: This feature captures positions where a player with a decisive advantage in the endgame (67% endgame phase) makes a move that throws away the win—median eval loss of 511 centipawns, with 33% swinging from winning to losing and 11% from winning to drawn. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (80%) combined with king_safety (20%), and the recurring tags include rook_endgame(4), tempo_loss(3), and missed_capture(3). The Opus analysis reveals a consistent pattern: players avoid the winning simplification (often a queen trade like Qxe3 that leads to a trivially won pawn endgame) and instead play an active-looking but fatally flawed move—either exposing their king to perpetual check or placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (e.g., the e-file controlled by an opponent's rook). Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing major pieces (rook 67%, queen 33%), confirming that the correct play was to simplify into a won ending. The positions show players choosing 'fancy' or aggressive continuations over clean technique, converting a won position into a disaster.

1750.label: Playing a slow pawn move that ignores urgent tactical threats, allowing the opponent to exploit pins, forks, or loose pieces.
1750.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive pawn move (50% pawn moves, 83% no capture) during the opening or early middlegame (67% opening, 33% middlegame) that constitutes a critical tempo loss. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic: 67% swing drawn positions to losing, with a median cost of 366 centipawns. The Maia analysis reveals what was missed — primarily captures of knights (58%) and checks (58%), indicating the opponent had concrete tactical threats (trapped pieces 40%, pins 20%, forks 20%) that demanded immediate attention. The common tags reinforce this: tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and piece_activity appear repeatedly. The players chose quiet developmental or structural pawn moves (b6, h6, d5, e5f4) while their positions required urgent defensive or tactical responses to threats along diagonals, against uncastled kings, or to loose pieces. The material outcome is mostly 'safe' (83%) because the pawn move itself doesn't immediately drop material — but it grants the opponent a free tempo to execute a winning combination.

1749.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move (often pawn or king) while the opponent's rooks dominate open files or ranks, allowing decisive material loss.
1749.description: This feature captures positions where the player neglects the critical importance of rook activity and file control. The material signature shows the player moved pawns (38%), kings (31%), or rooks (23%) in non-capturing moves that hang material 69% of the time (median net loss of -3.0), while Maia consistently identifies a rook move (often a rook capture) as the correct response. The eval trajectory confirms these are severe errors (median 279cp lost), predominantly occurring in already-losing positions (54%) or converting drawn positions to lost ones (31%). The tactical analysis reveals the recurring theme: overloaded defenders, rook endgame mishandling, and failure to contest open files. Concrete examples show players pushing pawns (f5, f6), wandering kings (Kb7, Kf6, Kd7), or making irrelevant moves while the opponent's rooks exert crushing pressure on open files (c-file, e-file). The common thread is a failure to prioritize neutralizing or contesting the opponent's rook dominance—whether through exchanges, counterplay, or defensive coordination—resulting in immediate tactical losses along the files and ranks the opponent controls.

1751.label: King moves that abandon a critical pawn race or passed pawn advance in a winning endgame, allowing the opponent to draw.
1751.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames where the player had a winning position but threw it away by moving the king passively instead of advancing or supporting a passed pawn. All activations occur in the endgame phase (100%), involve king moves (100%) that are materially 'safe' (no pieces hang or are traded), yet cost a median of 616 centipawns—converting winning positions into draws (100% winning->drawn trajectory). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is passed_pawn (88%), with recurring tags like pawn_race, promotion_race, and pawn_endgame. The concrete positions show pure king-and-pawn endings where the correct move was a precise pawn push (e.g., e3!, a5, e6, f4) to create or advance an unstoppable passed pawn, but instead the player made a temporally wasteful king move that surrendered the critical tempo needed to win the promotion race. The Maia engine consistently recommends pawn moves (100%), confirming that the missed resource was always a pawn advance rather than a king maneuver.

1748.label: Retreating or repositioning an active piece to a passive square, losing critical tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
1748.description: This feature captures a recurring middlegame mistake where the player voluntarily moves an already-active piece (most often a bishop, 44% of moves) to a passive or irrelevant square, squandering tempo and initiative. The material signature shows that 78% of the time no capture is involved and the move is nominally 'safe' (56%) or hangs material (28%), yet the median eval loss is a devastating 275 centipawns—indicating the damage is positional/tactical rather than a simple piece drop. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (75%), with tags like 'active_piece_retreat', 'bishop_sidelined', 'lost_initiative', and 'piece_misplacement' reinforcing that the core error is pulling back a well-placed piece instead of pressing an advantage. The eval trajectory (33% drawn->losing, 22% winning->losing) shows these moves frequently convert holdable or winning positions into lost ones. The Opus analyses confirm: pieces like a bishop on c2 that could create decisive threats are instead retreated to a4; captures are made that hand the opponent powerful squares; pieces are rerouted when a concrete tactic was available (missed_tactic at 78%). The pattern is a player who, in a critical middlegame moment, fails to maintain piece pressure and instead makes a passive reorganizing move that hands the opponent decisive tempo.

1754.label: King moves to a square where surrounding pawns create a mating net or trap.
1754.description: This feature detects king moves that walk into pawn-constructed cages, typically in endgame or late middlegame positions. The material signature shows 81% king moves with no captures, and 38% of these moves hang material (the king itself, via checkmate). The eval trajectory is striking: 33% flip from losing to winning (for the opponent) and 14% from drawn to losing, indicating these moves often throw away holdable or even defensible positions. The tactical analysis is unanimous: 100% king_safety motif, with dominant tags including 'exposed_king', 'king_walk_blunder', and 'pawn_cage'. The concrete positions show kings stepping to squares like h4, g5, or g4 where fixed pawns (both friendly and enemy) form an inescapable enclosure, allowing the opponent's queen or advancing pawn to deliver checkmate or force a decisive tempo-gaining check. The median eval lost of 0.0 is misleading—many of these are already difficult positions, but the catastrophic ones (drawn->mate) reveal the true danger of voluntarily entering a pawn cage.

1755.label: Player makes a developing or quiet move while leaving a piece hanging to an enemy knight capture.
1755.description: This feature fires when players make quiet, non-capturing moves (92% no capture) in the opening phase (85%) that leave a piece en prise to an opponent's knight. The material signature shows Maia's recommended move is always a knight capture (100% knight moves, capturing bishops 77% or queens 23%), confirming the opponent had a concrete knight tactic available. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), and the common tags reveal players chose development or positional ideas over addressing immediate tactical threats ('development_over_tactics', 'missed_capture'). The eval trajectory shows these oversights are devastating: 46% swing from winning to drawn and 23% from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 292 centipawns. The board examples consistently show positions where a knight can exploit an undefended or poorly defended piece (e.g., Nxe5 capturing a hanging pawn/piece, Nxd5 exploiting lack of support), but the player instead plays a slow developing move like Bd7, Qc7, or Re8 that ignores the immediate tactical vulnerability.

1753.label: Moving a piece away from its active post, losing a critical tempo and leaving other pieces or squares undefended.
1753.description: This feature captures middlegame moments where a player relocates a piece (most often a knight, rook, or bishop) to a square that accomplishes little or nothing strategically, while forfeiting the tempo needed to address a concrete tactical threat. The material signature shows 47% of these moves hang a piece and 73% involve no capture—these are not exchange errors but non-capture repositioning blunders that leave material or key squares unguarded. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences (median 328cp lost), with positions swinging from winning to drawn or losing in nearly a quarter of cases. The motif analysis is dominated by king_safety (50%) and tempo_loss (25%), indicating the moved piece was typically performing a defensive or attacking duty near the king, and its relocation grants the opponent a decisive tactical blow—often a check, a fork on a newly opened square, or a winning attack against the exposed king. The Maia recommendations (knight 43%, bishop 32%) suggest the correct moves were typically developing or repositioning those same pieces to genuinely useful squares, underscoring that the error is not in which piece to move but in choosing a purposeless destination that squanders a vital tempo.

1757.label: Capturing a bishop with a pawn while overlooking critical tactical threats that turn a winning position into a losing one.
1757.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player captures a bishop with a pawn (pawn moved 100%, bishop captured 100%) in what appears to be an even exchange or slight material loss, but catastrophically overlooks hanging pieces, back-rank threats, or forks. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 852 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the player's pawn capture is a move-order error—they grab material before addressing urgent threats (hanging pieces 38%, king safety 25%, back-rank 12%, fork 12%). Maia's recommended moves (rook 50%, knight 50%) suggest non-capturing defensive or active piece moves were required instead. The common tags (piece_activity, missed_tactic, hanging_piece, move_order, tempo_loss) paint a picture of a player who snatches a bishop with a pawn while their own pieces are uncoordinated or exposed, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical vulnerabilities. The capture itself looks reasonable in isolation but ignores the broader position's demands.

1756.label: In a losing position, trading a critical defensive rook exposes the king to a mating attack or allows decisive threats to break through.
1756.description: This feature identifies a specific recurring mistake where a player in an already losing middlegame position executes a rook trade (SEE shows rook moved 100%, rook captured 100%, net material 0 — a trade) that catastrophically worsens their position. The eval trajectory confirms these are losing->losing moves but with a staggering median cost of 93+ pawns (indicating missed mates or allowing forced mate), meaning the trade accelerates defeat from 'difficult but fightable' to 'immediately hopeless.' The tactical analysis reveals the core mechanism: the traded rook was serving a critical defensive function — typically back-rank defense or king safety coverage (king_safety 40%, back_rank tag recurring). Driven by material greed (capturing an opponent's rook that appears 'free' or 'equal') or panic exchanges, the player removes their own defensive anchor. The Maia recommendation of quiet pawn moves (100%) suggests the correct approach was patient defense rather than reactive trading. The positions consistently show exposed kings (often on h8/k-side) where the traded rook was the sole piece preventing mating threats, and the opponent has queens/rooks poised to exploit the opened lines.

1758.label: A quiet piece move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a tactic or decisive threat.
1758.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material immediately lost or exchanged) — typically a rook or knight relocation — that squanders a crucial tempo. The material signature shows no captures and no checks, yet Maia's recommended reply consistently involves capturing a knight, indicating that the player's move neglected an available tactic or left a piece en prise to a follow-up. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 285 centipawns, often converting a winning position into a drawn one or making a losing position significantly worse. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' as dominant motifs: the player repositions a piece to a passive or vulnerable square (e.g., Rd4 walking into ...c5, or ...Kf8 retreating when a concrete continuation existed). Rather than executing the one critical move the position demanded, the player makes a plausible but inert developing/repositioning move, handing the opponent the tempo needed to consolidate or counterattack decisively.

1760.label: King moves in endgame that leave a piece unprotected, missing a critical capture or defensive resource.
1760.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a way that leaves a piece hanging or misses a decisive tactical opportunity. The material signature shows these are non-capture king moves that are mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense (67%) but occasionally hang material directly (33%), yet universally miss winning material (100%). The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences—median 331 centipawns lost—transforming drawn positions into lost ones or making losing positions hopeless. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%), with consistent tempo_loss and missed_tactic tags. The concrete positions show kings wandering away from defending pieces (Kb4 leaving Nd4 unprotected, Ke5 leaving Nd5 hanging) or missing the one critical capture/defensive move available. The player instinctively moves their king for activity or safety but fails to notice that the piece left behind becomes a free target or that a tactical capture was the only good move.

1759.label: Playing a slow move in an endgame instead of addressing a critical passed pawn (own or opponent's) that demands immediate action.
1759.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material lost immediately — 100% safe) but catastrophically misses the urgency of a passed pawn situation. The material signature shows mostly pawn pushes (60%) or king moves (20%) that are tempo-wasting, while Maia consistently recommends rook moves (80%) or queen moves (20%) that capture pawns — the critical passed pawns demanding attention. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (67%), with tempo_loss as a secondary tag, and the Opus analysis repeatedly describes moves that 'waste a critical tempo' instead of addressing promotion threats or eliminating dangerous passed pawns. The eval trajectory (median 503cp lost) shows these are game-deciding errors: 40% make a losing position worse, but 40% convert winning or drawn positions into losing ones, reflecting how a single wasted tempo in a pawn race endgame is fatal. All positions are pure endgames with advanced passed pawns where the correct move involves immediately capturing or blocking the passed pawn, often with a rook sacrifice or capture-with-check.

1761.label: A quiet pawn move that misses a forcing tactic, leaving pieces hanging or creating fatal weaknesses.
1761.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly quiet pawn advance (86% pawn moves, 0% checks, 100% no captures) that constitutes a serious tactical oversight. The material signature shows 62% of these moves hang material (median -1.0), and 81% miss winning material that was available. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 277cp lost), with many positions shifting from drawn to losing (29%). The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: instead of playing forcing moves (Bxh7+ checks, Rxe6 sacrifices, captures exploiting forks), the player makes passive pawn moves like c3, g4, f6, g6, f3 that either weaken their king, drive opponent pieces to better squares, or simply ignore concrete threats. The common motifs—hanging_piece (38%), king_safety (25%), missed_tactic tags—show these pawn moves fail to address urgent tactical demands in the position, representing a fundamental disconnect between the quiet nature of the chosen move and the sharp tactical requirements of the position.

1762.label: Placing or leaving a piece on a square where the opponent's queen can capture it for free.
1762.description: This feature detects moves where the player hangs a piece (46% hangs, 17% loses material) with a median cost of -3.0 material and 547 centipawns of eval loss, frequently turning winning or drawn positions into losing ones (33% winning->losing, 29% drawn->losing). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (100%), with recurring tags like 'piece_hanging_to_queen' and 'double_attack_on_square'. The player most often moves a queen (38%) or bishop (25%) to an undefended or insufficiently defended square, while Maia's recommended response frequently involves a queen capture (38%) or bishop capture (25%). The concrete examples confirm this pattern: bishops placed on f5 where the opponent's queen captures them, queens left en prise, and pieces moved to squares under multiple attacks. The player typically overlooks that their piece destination is controlled by the opponent's queen, sometimes distracted by apparent counterplay (checks in 29% of cases) that proves insufficient compensation.

1769.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended square in the opening where it is immediately captured for free.
1769.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder where a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) to an unprotected square deep in enemy territory, hanging it outright (100% hangs, median material loss of -3.0, consistent with a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: positions shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 557 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (78%), with supporting tags like opening_blunder, undefended_piece, and board_vision_failure. The top activating positions overwhelmingly show Bf4-c7 in the opening where the bishop lands on a square immediately capturable by the opponent's queen, with no tactical justification. This is a pure board-vision failure in the opening phase—an aggressive-looking but tactically unsound bishop deployment that simply drops a piece.

1764.label: Removing or displacing a key defensive piece, fatally weakening king safety in the middlegame.
1764.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves where the player removes, trades, or repositions a critical defensive piece—often a knight or bishop guarding the king—leaving their king exposed to attack. The material signature shows that 43% of moves are 'safe' (no immediate material loss) and 81% involve no capture, yet the median eval loss is a devastating 228 centipawns, indicating a deep positional/tactical concession rather than a simple blunder. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%), with supporting tags like exposed_king, removing_defender, and tempo_loss. The Opus examples confirm this: a knight guarding the kingside is captured for a pawn, a rook is passively placed allowing a kingside onslaught, or a piece is moved that was shielding the king. Maia overwhelmingly recommends pawn moves (99%), suggesting the correct play was quiet prophylaxis or pawn defense rather than the active but self-weakening piece move the player chose. The trajectory (often winning->drawn or drawn->losing) shows these are game-changing positional errors that hand the opponent a decisive attack.

1765.label: Rook exchanges or sacrifices in winning endgames that convert into drawn positions due to misjudged resulting pawn/piece structures.
1765.description: This feature captures a specific endgame error pattern where a player with a winning position uses their rook to make an exchange or sacrifice (rook moved 100%, capturing pawns or knights 50% each) that simplifies into a drawn endgame. The eval trajectory is strikingly consistent: winning->drawn 100% of the time with a median loss of 484 centipawns, indicating these moves completely throw away the win. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (50%) with key tags including king_activity, pawn_structure, and passed_pawns — the player misjudges the resulting simplified position. The concrete examples confirm this: Rxg6 allowing fxg6+ converting R+N vs N+P into a drawn K+N vs K endgame; Rxb2+ cxb2+ Kxb2 failing to recognize Black's dominant king activity in the resulting pawn endgame; and Rb2 in a complex pawn endgame. The player consistently overvalues material capture while underestimating the resulting positional dynamics (king proximity, passed pawn races, piece activity) in the simplified position.

1763.label: Slow or purposeless developing moves in the opening that forfeit critical tempo against an opponent's active plan.
1763.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of tempo-wasting moves in the opening and early middlegame (60% opening, 40% middlegame) that transform drawn positions into losing ones. The material signature shows these are predominantly non-capturing pawn and knight moves (37% pawn, 26% knight) that are objectively 'safe' (80%) in the sense that no piece is immediately hanging, yet they catastrophically misallocate time. The eval trajectory is stark: 66% of activations swing drawn positions to losing, with a median loss of 236 centipawns—substantial positional deterioration without any material exchange. The tactical layer confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with supporting themes of king_safety neglect and missed tactics. The top boards consistently show players making passive reorganizing moves (Ng3, a3, Qc8, Bh2) while their opponent has an urgent attacking plan (pawn storms, piece coordination) that needed immediate counterplay. Rather than responding to the concrete threat—capturing to open lines, challenging the center, or initiating counterattack—the player dawdles, allowing the opponent's initiative to become decisive.

1767.label: Premature pawn capture with check in endgames that squanders a winning or drawn position by giving the opponent tempo or key squares.
1767.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a player makes a pawn capture that delivers check (100% pawn moved, 100% pawn captured, 100% check given), resulting in a material trade (net 0) that nonetheless devastates their position (median 431 centipawns lost). The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly thrown wins (winning->drawn 50%, winning->losing 17%) or drawn positions turned into losses (17%). The tactical analysis reveals the core issue: the check is a tempo-losing move that superficially looks forcing but actually grants the opponent's king access to critical squares or eliminates key pawn structure. The boards confirm this—positions like hxg5+, fxg4+, dxc4+ where the pawn recapture with check appears active but hands the opponent an outpost, simplifies favorably for them, or disrupts the player's own pawn chain. The player is seduced by the 'free' check into making an exchange that destroys their positional advantage in a won or balanced endgame.

1766.label: Advancing a pawn in the endgame instead of maintaining a winning rook, allowing the opponent's rook to capture decisive material.
1766.description: This feature identifies a recurring endgame mistake where a player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) when they should instead be using their rook actively, resulting in hanging material worth a median of -5.0 (the rook itself becomes lost or the position collapses). The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic errors converting winning positions into losing ones (100% winning->losing, median 1207cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: in rook endgames or positions transitioning to pawn endgames, the player confuses move order—pushing a passed pawn prematurely instead of first exchanging rooks on favorable terms or maintaining rook activity. Maia consistently finds the correct rook move (100% rook moves, 100% rook captures), indicating the engine sees the rook exchange or rook activation as critical. The motifs (rook_endgame, tempo_loss, pawn_endgame, passed_pawn) and tags (move_order, rook_exchange_timing, simplification_error) confirm that these players misjudge when to simplify or advance pawns, fatally giving up their rook's defensive/offensive role one tempo too early.

1768.label: Player makes a quiet developing or pawn move in the opening, missing a powerful Bxf7+ bishop check that wins material with tempo.
1768.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern. The material signature shows the player moving pawns (34%), bishops (20%), or kings (18%) in safe, non-capturing moves (93% no capture, 82% safe), while Maia's recommended move is universally a bishop capture (100% bishop, 96% capturing a pawn) that delivers check (100%). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (86%), and the eval trajectory shows these quiet moves cost a median of 258 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions to drawn (43%) or drawn to losing (14%). The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and missed_tactic (12%), with multiple example summaries explicitly citing missed Bxf7+ zwischenzugs and bishop sacrifices on f7 that win material with tempo against an uncastled king. The top boards consistently show positions with a bishop on c4/b3 aimed at f7, an uncastled black king, and the player choosing a passive developing move (h3, Bg5, Nd2) instead of the decisive Bxf7+ strike. This is a classic opening tactical oversight where the player prioritizes routine development over a concrete forcing blow against the vulnerable f7 square.

1772.label: King moves that ignore urgent tactical threats, worsening an already difficult position.
1772.description: This feature fires on king moves (73%) and occasional rook moves (27%) in positions that are predominantly already losing (64% losing->losing), where the player drops a median of 253 centipawns. The material signature shows these are not captures or trades—82% capture nothing—but 36% hang material by moving. The key pattern from the tactical analysis is that the player moves their king passively (tempo_loss, king_safety, king_exposure tags dominate) without addressing immediate tactical threats such as forks, hanging pieces, or forced mates. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), suggesting the correct defense required active piece play rather than king relocation. The positions are middlegame/endgame scenarios where the opponent has dominant attacking pieces (queen_dominance, piece_activity), and the king drift exposes the player to even greater tactical vulnerabilities—walking into forks, abandoning defensive coordination, or shortening the opponent's mating sequence. The consistent thread is a king retreating or wandering when the position demanded concrete defensive resource calculation.

1770.label: In a won endgame, plays a meaningless queen check that leaves the queen hanging to a king or pawn capture.
1770.description: This feature detects a highly specific and catastrophic endgame blunder pattern. The material/position signature shows the player moves their queen (100%), delivers a check (100%), but the move hangs material (100%) with a median net loss of -9.0 (a full queen). The eval trajectory confirms this converts a winning position into a draw or loss (winning->drawn 100%, median eval lost: 10000 centipawns — often a missed forced mate collapsing to a draw). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (90%), with tags like rook_endgame, stalemate_material, and queen_blunder reinforcing that these are simplified positions where the player had a trivially won game. The concrete board positions show king+queen vs lone king or near-bare positions where the player delivers a pointless check, placing their queen where it can be captured for free (often by the opposing king), instantly throwing away a forced win. The promotion_error variant (10%) shows a related pattern where advancing a pawn to give check similarly throws away the win. This is the classic 'hallucination check' in won endgames — the player sees a check and plays it reflexively without noticing the queen is undefended on the checking square.

1771.label: Player makes a routine move while missing a forcing back-rank checkmate or mating net available in one to three moves.
1771.description: This feature fires when players overlook a decisive back-rank or king-safety-based checkmate. The material/position signature shows the player's actual move is often a queen or rook move (65% combined) that is objectively 'safe' (58%) or even 'hangs' material (26%), while Maia's recommended move delivers check 97% of the time—overwhelmingly with queen (52%) or rook (36%) captures on key squares (rook captures at 45%). The players missed winning material 81% of the time, with a median eval loss of 197 centipawns. The dominant motifs are back_rank (50%) and king_safety (38%), with recurring tags of missed_mate_in_one, back_rank_mate, and mating_net. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly positions where the player was already winning (45% winning->winning, meaning they stay ahead but squander a knockout) or even flips from losing->winning (32%, suggesting the opponent blundered first and the player failed to capitalize on the back-rank weakness). The concrete examples confirm the pattern: reflexive captures or quiet moves that ignore a fatally trapped king on the back rank, where a simple rook or queen check would have delivered immediate or short-sequence checkmate.

1773.label: Moving a major piece to a passive or misplaced square that abandons critical defensive duties, worsening an already difficult position.
1773.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where a player moves a major piece (queen 30%, rook 20%, bishop 20%) without capturing anything (94% non-captures) to a square that either hangs material (46%) or is nominally safe but positionally catastrophic. The eval trajectory shows these overwhelmingly occur in already-difficult positions (drawn->losing 31%, losing->losing 26%) with a steep median cost of 294 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: pieces are moved away from critical defensive squares (king_safety 50%, hanging_piece 25%), abandoning guard duties or blocking escape routes. The Opus summaries consistently describe pieces being relocated to squares that ignore urgent threats—a rook leaving a back-rank defense, a knight self-blocking an escape square, a queen retreating to a passive square instead of trading into survivable endgames. Maia's recommended moves are almost always captures of major pieces (queen 37%, knight 36%, rook 15%), indicating the position demanded active counterplay or material exchanges rather than the passive repositioning that was played. This is fundamentally a positional error of piece coordination under pressure—misplacing defenders when the position requires precise prophylaxis.

1774.label: Player makes a slow or irrelevant move, missing a decisive back-rank tactic (often mate-in-one or a crushing rook check).
1774.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a rook or minor piece to a safe but purposeless square, while Maia (representing the engine's best move) overwhelmingly recommends a rook move delivering check (73% of Maia's moves are checks, 86% are rook moves). The dominant motif is 'back_rank' (75%), and the tags repeatedly flag missed_tactic, missed_mate_in_one, and back_rank_mate. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (86%) — nothing is hung — yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic cost: 55% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 266 centipawns. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: in one case White misses Rd8# and plays a2a4; in another the player misses Rf8 (a back-rank invasion) and plays Rf4 losing 344cp. The player is not blundering material directly but is failing to recognize an immediate back-rank threat or checkmate, instead making a tempo-losing 'nothing' move while the opponent's back rank is critically weak.

1775.label: Rook moves that fatally weaken back-rank defense, allowing decisive tactical punishment.
1775.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a rook (85% of cases) away from a critical defensive post, most commonly exposing a back-rank weakness. The dominant tactical motif is back_rank (67%), with hanging_piece (33%) as a secondary consequence. The material signature shows the move itself often appears 'safe' (60%) — the rook isn't immediately captured — but the resulting position collapses tactically, as shown by the severe median eval loss of 469 centipawns. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing mistakes across all game states (losing→losing 25%, drawn→losing 20%, winning→drawn 15%, winning→losing 10%), indicating the player fails to recognize that their rook's departure permits a lethal back-rank invasion or exposes hanging pieces. The concrete examples reinforce this: Rxa7 removes the back-rank guardian allowing Re1+; Rxe5 triggers a sequence leaving pieces undefended; Rdxd2 abandons defense of a knight. Maia's suggested moves (queen 40%, pawn 30%) are typically quiet defensive or consolidating moves that maintain back-rank integrity, contrasting sharply with the player's aggressive but fatally loosening rook sorties.

1776.label: Knight moves in endgames that hang material or walk into tactical shots, converting winning/drawn positions into lost ones.
1776.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake pattern where players move their knights (50% of activating moves) into squares that either hang the piece or allow a devastating tactical reply. The material signature shows 62% of moves result in hanging a piece with a median net loss of 2.0 (roughly a full piece), and the phase is overwhelmingly endgame (88%). The eval trajectory is severe: 50% convert winning positions to drawn and 38% convert drawn positions to losing, with a median cost of 402 centipawns. The tactical layer reveals the common mechanism: knights land on squares that walk into forks (Kf5 allowing Nd4+ winning the bishop), fail to account for passed pawn support (Nb6+ trading into a structure that supports an unstoppable passer), or simply abandon critical defensive duties (Nd6 leaving a piece undefended). The tags tempo_loss and missed_tactic appear frequently, indicating these knight moves not only lose material but also surrender the initiative in positions where precise piece placement was essential. The common thread is that in simplified endgame positions, the knight's limited mobility makes repositioning errors catastrophic—one wrong square and the game swings decisively.
