1777.label: Playing a slow developing or repositioning move when a concrete tactical opportunity (capture or forcing move) was available.
1777.description: This feature fires when players make quiet, non-capturing piece moves (bishops 30%, knights 25%, pawns 20%) that are objectively safe (65% safe, 0% checks, 80% no capture) but miss a strong tactical opportunity. Maia consistently recommends capturing moves (knight 65%, rook 25%, queen 10%), indicating the best move was a concrete capture. The eval trajectory shows these passive moves are extremely costly (median 257cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing (30%) or winning to drawn/losing (35%). The OPUS analysis confirms the pattern: dominant motifs are tempo_loss (33%) and king_safety (33%), with tags like missed_tactic (5), concrete_over_general (2), and missed_capture (1). The examples consistently show players choosing routine developing moves (Bd6, Bd3, Be3, h3) when forcing tactical shots were available—capturing undefended pieces, exploiting weak king positions, or executing forks. This occurs primarily in the opening/early middlegame (55%/45%) where development tempi are critical and one missed concrete opportunity can squander an entire positional advantage.

1778.label: Player moves a bishop or minor piece while overlooking an undefended enemy knight that could be captured by the queen.
1778.description: This feature fires in opening positions where the player moves a bishop (54%) or knight (23%) while completely missing that an enemy knight is hanging and capturable by the queen (Maia recommends queen captures knight in 100% of cases). The material signature shows the player's move is technically 'safe' (85%) — they aren't losing their own piece — but they forfeit a free piece capture, as confirmed by 100% missed winning material. The eval trajectory is devastating: 69% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 463 centipawns (roughly a full piece). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' in every case, with recurring tags like 'undefended_knight' and 'queen_capture'. The top boards reveal a specific recurring pattern: knights on h4, h5, or h6 that have jumped to the rim early in the opening and are left undefended, while the player focuses on developing or retreating their bishop (often along the f5-g6 or f4-g5 diagonal) rather than simply taking the free knight with their queen.

1783.label: Player makes a quiet move while their opponent's queen hangs undefended, turning a winning position into a losing one.
1783.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position completely overlooks an elementary one-move tactic to capture the opponent's undefended queen. The material/position signature shows that the player's move is mostly safe (70%) with no captures (80%), while Maia's recommended move captures a queen 100% of the time — indicating the queen was freely available to take. The eval trajectory is devastating: 90% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of ~1089 centipawns, consistent with missing a free queen (~900cp piece). The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging_piece (88%), and tags like missed_capture, queen_hanging, one_move_tactic, and blunder appearing repeatedly. The board positions consistently show an opponent's queen sitting undefended on an open line while the player moves a piece elsewhere — a rook retreating passively, a knight hopping to a non-critical square, or a king shuffling — all while a simple capture (Rxc2, Nxd1, Rxd7) would win the queen outright.

1779.label: Bishop captures a seemingly free pawn in the opening that turns out to be a tactical trap, costing significant material or positional value.
1779.description: This feature identifies a specific opening mistake pattern where a bishop captures what appears to be a safe pawn (material outcome registers as 'safe' since nothing is immediately hanging), but the capture walks into a tactical refutation. All activating positions occur in the opening phase, with the player's bishop capturing a pawn 100% of the time. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (median 360cp loss), indicating severe tactical consequences. The Opus analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of forks (43%), hanging pieces (43%), and discovered attacks (14%), revealing that the bishop capture exposes the piece to tactics—commonly Qa5+ forks, discovered attacks along diagonals, or piece traps. The recurring concrete pattern shows bishops greedily snatching g5/g4 pawns or venturing to exposed squares (Bb4, Bb5, Ba3) where they become vulnerable. Tags emphasizing tempo_loss, piece_activity, and missed_tactic confirm these are cases where development priorities were violated for a pawn grab, and the opponent's superior piece coordination punishes the greedy capture.

1782.label: Player makes a routine move while their queen hangs to an invading bishop on c7.
1782.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where an opponent's bishop has invaded c7 (or a similar square), directly threatening the player's queen, but the player ignores this threat entirely and plays a routine pawn move or development move instead. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves that lose material (median -5.0, consistent with losing a queen for a bishop), while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capturing the hanging bishop. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders—100% swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 998 centipawns. The tactical tags (ignored_threat, hanging_queen, queen_blunder, opening_trap) and the board positions all converge on the same motif: a bishop has landed on c7 attacking the queen in the opening, and the player fails to address it, often making a natural-looking but irrelevant move like ...Nf6, ...Bg7, ...d6, or a pawn capture elsewhere. The pattern is overwhelmingly concentrated in the opening phase where an early bishop invasion creates a one-move tactical crisis that the player simply overlooks.

1780.label: Player makes a routine developing move while overlooking that their pawn can capture an undefended enemy knight for free.
1780.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where a player's pawn has a clean capture available on an enemy knight (Maia always recommends pawn captures knight), but the player instead makes a routine developing or non-capturing move. The material signature shows 100% hangs (the player's move leaves their own piece or pawn undefended) with a median loss of 1.0 material, and the eval trajectory shows the player going from winning to drawn, losing a median of 518 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, with 'missed_capture' and 'pawn_takes_piece' as recurring tags. The top boards almost all feature positions from the English/Queen's Pawn openings where a d-pawn can capture a knight on c3 or c6 (e.g., dxc3 or dxc6), but the player plays autopilot development instead. This is a classic opening blindness pattern where players fail to notice a free piece capture with a pawn because they are focused on standard development.

1781.label: Player moves queen to a passive or irrelevant square, missing that the opponent had a forcing check or tactic that wins material.
1781.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their queen (73%) or rook (18%) to a square that appears safe (73% safe, no captures made) but critically misses the opponent's best reply—which Maia identifies as a queen check (100% Maia gives check). The missed winning material rate is 100%, meaning every activation involves overlooking a concrete tactical opportunity or threat. The eval trajectory is devastating: 46% of cases swing from drawn to losing, 18% from winning to drawn, and 9% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 343 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals motifs of hanging pieces and threat ignorance—the player repositions their queen without recognizing that the opponent's pieces (often a knight or the opponent's queen) create immediate tactical threats. In the top boards, we see patterns like queens placed on squares where they become tactically vulnerable, or quiet queen moves that ignore the opponent's ability to deliver a check that wins material or creates a decisive advantage. The core error is a failure to check the opponent's forcing replies (especially checks) before committing the queen to a new square.

1784.label: In a winning endgame, the player pushes a pawn (or makes a quiet move) instead of capturing an undefended piece sitting en prise.
1784.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player in a clearly winning endgame (winning->winning, but losing a massive median of ~95 pawns worth of eval, often missing forced mate) plays a safe pawn push or quiet move while an enemy piece—most often a rook—is hanging and can be trivially captured (typically by the king). The material signature shows the played move is always a non-capturing pawn move rated 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet Maia's recommended move is always a king capturing a rook. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (90%) with recurring tags like 'missed_capture' and 'forced_mate_missed.' The boards show king-and-pawn endgames or simplified positions where an opponent's piece is left undefended, and the player advances a passed pawn or makes a positional move without first collecting the free material, often converting a forced mate into a much longer or even drawn game.

1785.label: King moves in endgames that ignore an opponent's bishop capturing an undefended piece along a diagonal.
1785.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a passive or tempo-losing king move while leaving a piece (typically a rook) undefended and vulnerable to capture along a bishop diagonal. The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures, rated 'safe' in isolation—meaning the king move itself doesn't immediately drop material by SEE—but Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a rook, confirming the player missed a one-move tactical shot. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of cases go from drawn to losing with a median loss of 509 centipawns, indicating these were holdable positions thrown away by a single oversight. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), with recurring tags like 'missed_capture' and 'bishop_geometry.' The concrete pattern across the top boards shows endgame positions where a bishop has a clear diagonal line to an undefended rook or major piece, and the player simply moves their king without noticing the threat or failing to execute the defensive/equalizing capture themselves.

1786.label: Pawn captures a minor piece in the opening that leaves another piece hanging or exposes a tactical vulnerability.
1786.description: This feature fires on opening/early middlegame positions where a pawn captures a knight or bishop (appearing as a trade or slight material loss), but the exchange is premature and tactically flawed. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves capturing minor pieces (57% knight, 43% bishop), with the outcome classified as a trade (86%) — yet the eval trajectory reveals these are catastrophic decisions, with a median loss of 292 centipawns and 71% of cases collapsing from winning to drawn. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (78%), indicating that after the pawn exchange, a piece is left undefended. The concrete positions confirm this: moves like exf3, c4xb3, d5xc6, e5xf6, and a5xb6 are all pawn captures of minor pieces that superficially appear to win or trade material but actually expose hanging pieces or abandon critical positional advantages. Maia's recommended responses (86% bishop moves, no captures) suggest the AI wanted quiet developing moves rather than premature exchanges. The common tags (piece_activity, missed_tactic, tempo_loss, development) reinforce that these pawn captures squander development and activity advantages built up in the opening.

1788.label: Squandering a winning opening advantage by making a slow or passive move that allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
1788.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player makes a seemingly safe move (75% safe material outcome) that nevertheless costs a massive ~304 centipawns median, typically converting a winning position into a drawn or losing one (75% winning->drawn, 25% drawn->losing). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (30%) and hanging_piece (30%), with development and piece_activity as top tags, indicating the player wastes a critical tempo in the opening rather than exploiting their advantage. The concrete positions show patterns like retreating a bishop to b3 instead of maintaining pressure, playing passive pawn moves (h6, d6) when tactical strikes were available, or moving a knight to a square that loses coordination. In each case, the opponent had a concrete vulnerability (fork, hanging piece, king safety issue) that required immediate action, but the player chose a developing or repositioning move that let the opponent consolidate. The 75% 'missed winning material' rate confirms these are positions where a tactical blow existed but the player opted for a quiet move, hemorrhaging their opening advantage through inactivity rather than through a direct blunder.

1787.label: Moving a major piece (usually the queen) to an undefended square where it can be captured, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
1787.description: This feature captures moments where players move their queen or rook to an unprotected square, hanging it to an opponent's piece. The material signature shows 50% queen moves and 25% rook moves with no captures (85%), and 45% of these moves result in a hung piece — the most common outcome. The median material loss is -1.0 (a full piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings: 30% go from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 408 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (40%), supplemented by tempo_loss (20%) where the piece is placed where it loses time to attack. Concrete examples include Black placing the queen on e5 directly in front of a rook, and positions where the only saving move was a forcing capture (like Rxf6 or Qxf8+) that was missed in favor of a passive piece relocation. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (knight 20%, pawn 20%, bishop 15%) and checks (25%), indicating the player missed active tactical continuations and instead made a quiet move that left material en prise.

1791.label: Hanging a major piece by ignoring immediate king safety threats in the middlegame.
1791.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a queen or rook (86% combined) without capturing anything, yet the move hangs material (100% hang rate, median -5.0 material loss). The dominant motif is king_safety (100%), with tags like exposed_king, checkmate_in_one, and deflection appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions show pieces being moved away from critical defensive duties around the king—e.g., Qd6 removing the defender of f7 allowing checkmate, or Rb4 ignoring a mating net. The eval trajectory shows this occurs across various standings (43% losing->losing, 29% losing->winning suggests some positions where the opponent also erred), but the median 124cp loss confirms these are consequential mistakes. The pattern is consistently a middlegame scenario (86%) where the player moves a major piece for some purpose (attack, repositioning, or flight) while failing to recognize that their own king's vulnerability means the moved piece is effectively hanging to a tactical sequence exploiting king exposure.

1792.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while their own high-value piece (often a queen) hangs undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it for free.
1792.description: This feature identifies positions where the player overlooks that one of their own major pieces—most frequently a queen—is left undefended (hanging_piece motif in 89% of cases). The material signature shows 67% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a queen's value), and Maia's recommended response captures a rook (56%) or queen (44%) in every case. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 56% flip from winning to losing with a median centipawn loss of 1110, while the remaining 44% severely damage an already-winning position. The moves themselves are typically passive king retreats, purposeless knight maneuvers, or pawn pushes that ignore the immediate tactical crisis of an undefended piece on the board. Common tags like 'missed_capture', 'queen_hanging', and 'diagonal_oversight' reinforce that the player simply failed to notice their piece was en prise, often in positions where both sides had hanging pieces and capturing first was the only critical priority.

1790.label: Passive or slow pawn/bishop moves in the opening that lose tempo and allow opponent to trap pieces or seize initiative.
1790.description: This feature detects opening-phase mistakes where a player makes a seemingly safe pawn or bishop move (no material is immediately lost or exchanged) that squanders critical tempo, allowing the opponent to gain a decisive positional advantage. The material signature shows 100% safe moves (nothing hangs immediately) with pawn (46%) and bishop (36%) being the primary pieces moved, yet the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 254 centipawns, with 91% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and trapped_piece (50%), which are deeply connected: by wasting a move on a slow retreat (like Bb6 retreating from an active diagonal) or an unnecessary pawn push (like h3 or c3 when development is urgent), the player allows the opponent to execute tactical sequences that trap pieces or dominate key squares. The boards consistently show Italian Game and similar open-game structures where White has an active Bc4 and the critical question is whether to maintain tension or develop efficiently—the blundering side chooses passive consolidation over necessary active play, and gets punished.

1793.label: Player overlooks an available queen capture, typically by a pawn, while making an inferior move that collapses a winning position.
1793.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that completely overlooks the opportunity to capture the opponent's queen, most often with a pawn. The material/position signature shows Maia's recommended move captures a queen 75% of the time (frequently via pawn captures queen), while the player instead makes various other moves (captures of minor pieces, quiet moves, or trades). The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 75% of cases go from winning to losing with a median loss of 837 centipawns, indicating these are game-deciding oversights. The dominant tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' (71%), and the Opus analysis consistently tags 'missed_queen_capture', 'tunnel_vision', and 'en_prise_queen'—the player focuses on an alternative plan or capture while the opponent's queen sits undefended in a direct capture path. The concrete positions confirm this: in multiple cases, the e5 pawn could capture a queen on f6 (exf6), but the player instead makes a rook or knight capture on e4. This is pure tunnel vision—the player sees one tactical idea and completely misses the far stronger queen capture available.

1789.label: Developing or advancing a piece in the opening that leaves material en prise to an obvious one-move capture.
1789.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening blunder pattern (100% opening phase) where a player develops or advances a piece (pawn 40%, knight 40%, bishop 20%) without capturing anything, yet leaves material hanging (60% hangs) to a simple one-move capture. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly mistakes (median 265cp lost), typically turning drawn positions into losing ones (80%) or winning positions into drawn ones (20%). The tactical analysis is dominated by hanging_piece motifs (50%) with tempo_loss (30%) as secondary — the player makes a 'natural-looking' developing move (Nf3, Bf4, e3, b3, d5) that ignores a direct one-move threat to their own piece, often in well-known d4/e4 pawn center structures. The top boards show a recurring pattern: positions with central pawn tension (especially ...d5/e5 vs d4) where the opponent's center pawn directly attacks a piece the player just placed or left undefended. Maia's suggested moves consistently capture material (80% pawn captures), confirming these are straightforward tactical oversights rather than deep positional errors.

1796.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of playing a pawn fork that wins material by attacking two pieces simultaneously.
1796.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player misses a tactical pawn fork opportunity, typically in the opening or early middlegame. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (85% no capture, 88% safe) while Maia consistently recommends a pawn move (100% pawn). The eval trajectory reveals these are predominantly game-changing errors—48% convert a winning position to drawn and 6% to losing, with a massive median loss of 291 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: 57% fork motifs with 'pawn_fork' as the most common tag, often exploiting a queen-bishop alignment on diagonals like a4-c4. The top boards repeatedly show the same structural theme—White's queen on a4 and bishop on c4 creating a vulnerable geometry that can be punished by ...b5, but the player instead develops a piece naturally (Nf6, Be7, O-O). The player's actual moves are bishops (27%), pawns (21%), and knights (21%)—all natural developing moves that ignore the concrete tactical shot available.

1795.label: Knight recaptures in the opening that miss stronger forcing moves, throwing away a winning position.
1795.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a seemingly natural knight capture (often a recapture or exchange) instead of a stronger tactical continuation. The material signature shows knight moves that are objectively safe or result in trades (median net +3.0), but 100% of the time the player missed winning material available through a superior alternative. The eval trajectory is severe: every instance goes from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 447 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the missed opportunities involve king safety exploitation (exposed kings in center, open files), discovered attacks, forks, and tempo-gaining moves. The common thread is that players default to routine piece exchanges (Nxe4, Qxf3 recaptures, Nc3 development) when forcing moves like checks, discovered attacks, or even checkmate were available. The opening phase and 'king_in_center' tags confirm these are positions where the opponent's king is vulnerable but the player chose a safe-looking capture over a punishing tactical blow.

1797.label: Moving king or rook in an endgame that inadvertently leaves a major piece undefended and hanging.
1797.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame blunder pattern where the player moves their king or rook (93% of positions are endgames) and in doing so leaves a piece completely unprotected. The material signature shows 53% of moves hang a piece outright and 33% lose material via a bad exchange, with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a rook). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%) and rook_endgame (40%), with concrete examples showing kings stepping away from rooks they were defending, or rooks moving to squares directly attacked by the opponent's king. The eval trajectory shows most of these occur in already-losing positions (53% losing->losing) but with a massive median cost of 303 centipawns, indicating these moves accelerate defeat dramatically. Notably, 20% convert drawn positions to losing ones, representing critical endgame collapses. The pattern is distinctly about spatial awareness failures in simplified positions—players miscalculate piece protection relationships when few pieces remain on the board.

1798.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move that wastes a winning attacking tempo against a vulnerable king.
1798.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe but passive move (pawn or bishop development) that costs critical tempo in positions where the engine strongly recommends an aggressive, forcing continuation—typically a queen check or capture exploiting an exposed king. The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe' (nothing hangs immediately), yet the eval trajectory consistently shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (median 352cp lost), indicating the window for decisive action has closed. The Opus analysis and tags heavily emphasize tempo_loss (appearing in 4/4 examples) alongside king_safety and missed_tactic: in each case, the opponent's king was vulnerable (often uncastled or centralized), and the player chose a slow preparatory move (b4, c3, g3, Bg2) instead of the one critical forcing line. Maia consistently identifies the missed move as a queen check capturing a knight, confirming that a concrete tactical blow was available. The positions span opening-to-middlegame transitions where development tempo is at its most valuable, and the mistake pattern is fundamentally about prioritizing quiet consolidation over the unique moment to strike.

1794.label: Player moves a knight to an active square but misses that a knight check (often with fork) was available, losing significant material or position.
1794.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a knight (50%) or other piece to a seemingly active square, but misses a critical knight check that would fork enemy pieces or safely reposition with tempo. The Maia signal is striking: 100% of the time the best move was a knight move delivering check, and 100% of the time winning material was missed. The median eval loss of 252 centipawns confirms these are substantial tactical oversights. The motif analysis shows a 50/50 split between 'fork' and 'positional_mistake' — in the fork cases the player places a piece where it gets forked by an opponent's rook or misses their own forking check; in the positional cases the player makes a passive move when a forcing knight check would have won material or seized initiative. The concrete examples reinforce this: Nf2+ check was available but missed (example 2), pieces land on squares where they become fork targets (example with Rf5+), and knights move to squares that lack the forcing quality of the available check. The material signature shows 'safe' (61%) and 'hangs' (29%) — the played moves often look reasonable but either hang the knight or simply forfeit the tactical opportunity of a winning check/fork.

1800.label: King moves that waste tempo or choose slightly inferior paths in won pawn endgames near promotion.
1800.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure pawn endgames (endgame 100%) where the player has a winning position and retains it (winning->winning 100%), but plays a king move (king 100%) that is marginally suboptimal—typically losing a tempo or choosing a less precise path toward promoting a passed pawn. The material outcome is 'safe' (no pieces hang or are exchanged), and the eval loss is minimal (median 3cp), but the dominant motifs (tempo_loss 30%, passed_pawn 30%, promotion_error 20%, pawn_endgame 20%) reveal the recurring pattern: these are positions with advanced passed pawns where the king needs to support promotion, and the player either steps to a square that delays mate by a few moves, allows the opponent's king to gain opposition, or fails to use the most efficient triangulation. The top boards confirm this—nearly all are king-and-pawn vs king positions with pawns on the 6th or 7th rank where precise king placement is the only remaining question. Maia consistently recommends a pawn push instead, suggesting the AI recognizes these as moments where the pawn should advance rather than the king repositioning.

1799.label: In the opening, player makes a developing or non-capture move while leaving a piece en prise, allowing the opponent to win material for free.
1799.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring opening-phase blunder pattern. The material signature shows that 90% of the time the player makes a non-capture move (pawn 37%, knight 31%, bishop 22%), and 29% of these moves directly hang a piece — yet the player isn't trading or capturing anything. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic: 69% go from winning to drawn and 21% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 471 centipawns (roughly a full piece). The tactical analysis shows 'hanging_piece' as the motif in 100% of cases, with Maia's recommended moves being captures of bishops (47%), knights (29%), and queens (22%) — the very pieces the player left undefended. The top board examples reinforce this: players make routine-looking development moves (Be2, O-O, Nf3, d5, f4) in the opening while completely ignoring that an opponent's piece is attacking one of their own undefended pieces. The 98% opening phase and 98% missed-winning-material rate confirm these are players who had a significant advantage (often from the opponent's own earlier mistake) but then blindly played a 'normal' move without noticing a tactical threat on the board, effectively gifting back a full piece.

1801.label: Moving a knight to an unprotected square that fatally compromises king safety, often enabling mating attacks.
1801.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves a knight (59% of cases) to a square where it hangs (69% of moves result in a hung piece), catastrophically undermining king safety in the middlegame. The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and hanging_piece (33%), with recurring tags like back_rank, exposed_king, and king_hunt. The median centipawn loss is 312, and the per-position analyses reveal patterns where knight moves vacate critical defensive squares or sacrifice pieces without tactical justification, enabling forced mating sequences or devastating discovered attacks. The eval trajectory shows 38% occur in already-losing positions being made decisively worse, consistent with defensive desperation moves that collapse the position entirely. The material signature (net median -3.0, i.e., a full piece lost) combined with the king safety motif distinguishes these from ordinary piece blunders—the knight move specifically opens lines or removes defenders around the king.

1804.label: Losing critical tempi with king moves in pawn endgames where precise timing determines the outcome.
1804.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes where players squander decisive tempi, primarily in pawn endgames. The material signature shows king moves (67%) that are materially 'safe' or involve trades (not blunders of pieces), but the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 123 centipawns—converting wins to draws or drawn positions to losses. The dominant motifs are overwhelmingly pawn_endgame (78%) with tempo_loss and king_activity as the recurring tags. The concrete positions are almost all king-and-pawn endings where the player moves their king to the wrong square or in the wrong sequence, failing to calculate that a pawn break or direct advance was required immediately. Examples include Ka4 instead of f4 (wasting a critical tempo), Kd5 allowing the opponent's king to reach a key square, and misjudging resulting pawn endgames after piece exchanges. The common thread is that these are positions requiring precise endgame calculation where one lost tempo is fatal, but the error appears innocuous because no material is immediately dropped.

1803.label: Player moves king or piece while opponent's queen has an undefended capture available, hanging major material.
1803.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a non-capture move (100% no capture) that hangs significant material (88% hangs, median -5.0 material), predominantly by moving their king (47%) or queen (24%) while completely overlooking that the opponent's queen can capture a hanging or undefended piece (Maia's response is queen capture 100% of the time, with queen moves 82%). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 1165 centipawns lost), with 35% converting a winning position into a losing one and 41% making an already-losing position decisively worse. The tactical motifs confirm this: 60% hanging_piece, with tags like 'queen_capture_oversight', 'undefended_queen', and 'hanging_piece'. The board positions reveal a consistent pattern—players make seemingly purposeful but irrelevant moves (king retreats, pawn pushes, piece repositioning) while a queen capture on an undefended piece sits plainly on the board. The moves suggest tunnel vision on one aspect of the position while ignoring the opponent's most forcing threat.

1805.label: In won endgames, player makes a passive king move instead of capturing a hanging or checking piece, turning a win into a loss.
1805.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame blunder pattern. The material/position signature shows the player always moves their king (100%) without capturing anything, while Maia consistently identifies a rook capture as the correct move (100%). The positions are universally endgames (100%) where the player had a winning advantage but transitions to losing (100%), with a catastrophic median eval loss of ~1006 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the motif: players flee with their king or make purposeless moves instead of simply taking a hanging or checking piece (often a rook). The Opus summaries explicitly describe cases like 'fled from check with Kb3 instead of capturing the checking rook with Kxc5' and 'played a purposeless check instead of the crushing Rxf3 which wins White's rook.' The common tags—missed_capture, hanging_piece, tempo_loss—all reinforce that the player overlooks a straightforward capture in a simplified position, likely due to time pressure or tunnel vision on king safety rather than material collection. The boards confirm rook endgames and pawn endgames where one clean capture would clinch the game.

1808.label: Player makes a natural-looking developing or active move while overlooking an opponent's undefended piece that could be captured for free.
1808.description: This feature fires when players make routine-looking moves (typically bishop or queen moves) during the opening phase while missing a free capture of an undefended enemy piece. The material signature shows 50% of moves are 'safe' (non-captures that don't immediately lose material themselves) yet 75% miss winning material according to Maia's evaluation, with Maia frequently recommending queen moves to snatch hanging pieces. The eval trajectory is severe (median 417cp lost), often converting winning positions to drawn or losing ones (38% winning->drawn, 25% winning->losing). The tactical motifs are dominated by hanging_piece (50%) and trapped_piece (33%), with tags emphasizing missed_tactic and missed_capture. The concrete positions confirm this: pieces like undefended knights on g5, bishops vulnerable to trapping after center breaks, and queens that could exploit unprotected pieces are all overlooked in favor of 'natural' developing moves. Players prioritize routine development or positional ideas (development_over_tactics tag) while failing to scan for tactical opportunities involving opponent's loose pieces.

1806.label: Suboptimal king moves in pure pawn endgames that waste tempo or cede opposition.
1806.description: This feature fires on king (and occasionally pawn) moves in pure pawn endgames where the player makes a small but meaningful tempo or opposition error. The material signature shows 80% king moves with no captures and overwhelmingly 'safe' outcomes—nothing is hung, no pieces are traded—yet the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 37 centipawns, typically making a losing position slightly worse (80% losing->losing). The positions are exclusively endgame phase, almost all king-and-pawn(s) vs king-and-pawn(s) structures. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (50%) and tempo_loss (30%), with recurring tags of king_activity, passed_pawn, and positional concerns. The concrete boards show bare king-pawn positions where the critical resource is tempo and opposition—moving the king to the wrong square loses a crucial tempo needed to stop or promote a passed pawn. Many of these are near-trivial in centipawn terms (0-2cp in some cases) but the feature consistently identifies the pattern of tempo-losing king maneuvers in simplified pawn endings.

1809.label: Queen moves to a passive square, ignoring tactical threats and losing significant material or positional advantage.
1809.description: This feature fires when players make queen moves (87% queen moves) that are passive or misguided, failing to address critical tactical threats on the board. The material signature shows these are not captures (97% no capture) but rather repositioning moves where the queen ends up on a square that either hangs material (43%) or is nominally safe but misses a crucial tactic (50% missed winning material). The eval trajectory shows devastating consequences: median 250cp loss with 30% of cases converting drawn positions to losing ones and 10% throwing winning positions to drawn. The tactical analysis reveals the queen moves ignore hanging pieces (40%), forks (20%), and tempo-gaining threats, often placing the queen on squares where it blocks development or abandons defensive duties (e.g., Qe2 removing protection from a rook, Qd2 ignoring tactical strikes). The common tags—development issues, missed tactics, tempo loss, and king safety—confirm these are premature or aimless queen deployments in the opening/middlegame (96% combined) that surrender the initiative or leave tactical vulnerabilities unaddressed.

1802.label: Moving the king into a mating net or fatal exposure when a tactical defense or material capture was available.
1802.description: This feature captures positions where a player in an already losing position makes a fatal king move that dramatically worsens their situation—typically walking into a forced mating net or abandoning a critical tactical resource. The material signature shows 100% king moves that hang material (median -1.0 net), while Maia consistently identifies a pawn capturing a queen as the correct move, indicating the player missed a major material recovery opportunity. The eval trajectory confirms these are losing positions made catastrophically worse (median 9141 centipawns lost), meaning the player accelerated their own demise. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant king_safety motifs (60%), tags like 'king_walk_blunder', 'mating_net', and 'forced_mate', and example narratives describing kings walking into coordinated piece attacks. The concrete positions show exposed kings on open boards where the player moved the king (e.g., Kb4-a3 into a Q+R mating net, Kb5-b6 leaving a queen en prise) instead of capturing available material that would have prolonged resistance.

1807.label: Player captures or trades material while leaving a critical piece or king fatally unprotected.
1807.description: This feature fires on moves where the player initiates an exchange or grabs material (42% trades, 29% hangs) but in doing so abandons the defense of a more important piece or exposes their king. The material signature shows a median loss of 1.0 pieces with 525 centipawns median eval drop, often swinging from winning to losing (23%) or drawn to losing (13%). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (40%), king_safety (20%), and tempo_loss (20%)—reveal that the underlying error is not miscalculating the immediate exchange but failing to see that the move leaves something else undefended. The concrete examples confirm this: a rook leaves c7 to grab a pawn on c5, exposing the king to Rxg3+; a queen lands on d3 in the firing line of a rook; a pawn push on h3 leaves a rook on c3 unguarded. The player is drawn to material or active-looking moves (queen 29%, bishop 26%) but overlooks the tactical consequence of removing a defender or stepping into a pin/skewer. Maia's recommended moves are largely quiet (74% non-captures), suggesting the correct approach was to maintain piece coordination rather than grab material.

1811.label: Moving a minor piece or pawn that leaves another piece undefended against an immediate tactical threat.
1811.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a pawn (38%) or knight (33%) that hangs material (95% of moves result in a 'hang' classification) with a median cost of ~269 centipawns. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece, tempo_loss, and back_rank—reveal that the player ignores an existing tactical threat (often to a rook or queen) by making a move that doesn't address the critical danger. The eval trajectory shows these errors frequently throw away winning or drawn positions (winning->drawn 19%, winning->losing 10%), while Maia's recommended moves typically involve the queen (33%), bishop (19%), or rook (19%), often capturing material or resolving the threat directly. The concrete examples confirm this: Ng8 loses tempo while a winning capture exists, Be6 leaves a rook hanging to a simple queen capture, and f4 ignores an immediate back-rank mate. The common thread is that the player makes a non-urgent pawn push or knight retreat while a critical hanging piece or mating threat demanded immediate attention.

1810.label: Trading or losing the queen when it was the key piece maintaining the player's attacking or defensive advantage.
1810.description: This feature identifies positions where the player's queen—overwhelmingly the moved piece at 71%—is either traded away or hung in circumstances where it was the linchpin of their position. The material signature shows 56% hangs and 44% loses with a devastating median net loss of -9.0 (roughly a queen's value), confirming the queen is being given up without adequate compensation. The eval trajectory shows massive damage: median 675 centipawns lost, with 15% of cases converting winning positions to losing and another 15% converting drawn positions to losing. The Opus tactical analysis is the clinching signal: recurring tags like queen_trade_error, queen_trade_blunder, and queen_blunder appear alongside positional_mistake (50%) and hanging_piece (50%). The example summaries repeatedly describe scenarios where the queen was the foundation of an attack or defense—pressuring weak squares, threatening the opposing king, or restraining passed pawns—and the player either offered a trade, captured on a square inviting the trade, or placed the queen where it could be won. This is not a simple blunder of leaving a piece en prise; it is a strategic error of relinquishing the most powerful piece precisely when the position demanded its presence.

1812.label: Player makes a move in the wrong sequence, losing critical material by neglecting immediate tactical threats.
1812.description: This feature captures mistakes where the player executes moves in the wrong order, typically losing substantial material (median -4.0, with 60% losing and 20% hanging outcomes). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: 40% convert winning positions to drawn, 20% winning to losing, with a median loss of 796 centipawns. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (40%) and king_safety (40%), with 'move_order' as the most common tag (appearing 3 times). The pattern across positions is consistent: players prioritize a secondary goal (capturing material, completing a sequence) while ignoring an immediate tactical threat—an undefended queen on a diagonal, a back-rank infiltration, or a king-safety collapse. Maia's recommended moves (80% queen moves, 80% queen captures) suggest the correct continuation typically involved addressing the queen-level threat first. The positions span opening and middlegame (40%/60%), where complex piece interactions make move-order precision critical. Players consistently grab material or advance plans one move too early, before neutralizing the opponent's tactical shot.

1813.label: Player makes a move that walks into a devastating knight fork, typically losing a queen or converting a winning position into a lost one.
1813.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player's move places a piece (most often the queen) on a square vulnerable to a knight fork. The material signature shows these are not simple blunders of hanging pieces—50% are trades and 50% are 'safe' moves—yet the eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 1238 centipawns lost, with 75% going from winning to losing). The tactical analysis is dominated by fork motifs (33%) with 'knight_fork' appearing in 3 of 4 tagged examples, and the detailed summaries repeatedly describe queens being placed on squares where a knight can simultaneously attack the queen and deliver check. The boards confirm this: positions feature knights on active squares (Nf5+, Ne3) ready to exploit the misplaced piece. Maia's recommended moves (75% king moves) suggest the correct response was often a prophylactic king move to deny the fork's check component. This is a pure tactical oversight where the player fails to see the knight's dual-threat geometry.

1814.label: Missing winning tactical shots (skewers, hanging pieces) in rook endgames, turning wins into losses.
1814.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern in rook endgames where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material lost immediately) but catastrophically misses a winning tactic. The material signature shows the player's move is materially safe (100%), yet Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing rooks (67%), indicating a massive tactical opportunity was overlooked. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-losing mistakes: 67% go from winning to losing with a median eval loss of 1016 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging pieces (50%) and skewers (33%), with the common thread being rook endgame positions (4/5 tagged) where simple forcing sequences—check-then-capture skewers, taking undefended rooks, or exploiting hanging pieces—were missed in favor of passive or irrelevant moves (like pushing a pawn, retreating a bishop, or making a quiet king move). The player appears to lose concentration or tactical awareness in simplified endgame positions where the winning move requires only 1-2 move calculation.

1815.label: Player makes a slow or aimless move instead of executing a winning knight fork (typically with check) that would win material.
1815.description: This feature consistently fires when a player misses a decisive knight fork opportunity. The material/position signature shows that Maia's recommended move is always a knight move delivering check (100% knight, 100% check), while the player's actual move is often a knight move but without the critical tempo-gaining check, or a slow pawn/king move. In 100% of cases the player missed winning material, and the median eval loss of 232 centipawns confirms a significant tactical oversight. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'fork' as the dominant motif (80%), with recurring tags like knight_fork, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show knights ideally placed to deliver forks on kings and rooks/bishops, but the player either gives a pointless check, plays a positional move, or moves the knight to a square that attacks something without the forcing check. The trajectory (87% winning->winning) indicates these players maintain their advantage but squander a clean tactical conversion, while the 7% winning->losing cases show that missing the fork can sometimes be fatal.

1816.label: Trading bishops into a lost pawn endgame where the bishop was needed to hold the position.
1816.description: This feature detects a specific endgame error where a player in an already losing position voluntarily exchanges bishops, transitioning into a pure pawn endgame that is even harder to defend. All activating positions are endgames (100%) where the player trades their bishop for the opponent's bishop (material outcome: trade, net 0.0). The eval trajectory shows these are losing->losing positions with a median 48cp further deterioration, indicating the trade makes a bad position worse rather than throwing a win. The tactical analysis is unanimous: the dominant motif is pawn_endgame (100%), with tags like simplification_error, wrong_exchange, and passed_pawn appearing frequently. The bishop was serving a critical defensive role—blockading passed pawns, covering multiple weaknesses simultaneously, or restraining a pawn majority—and its removal leaves the king unable to cope alone. Maia consistently recommends keeping the bishop (bishop move, no capture), confirming that the engine-preferred defense involves preserving the piece rather than simplifying. The concrete board positions all show opposite-colored or same-colored bishop endgames where one side has dangerous passed pawns or a pawn majority that becomes unstoppable once bishops leave the board.

1817.label: Playing non-urgent pawn or minor piece moves that neglect critical kingside threats against an uncastled or vulnerable king.
1817.description: This feature consistently fires on opening/early middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable developing or expanding move (pawn 50%, knight 25%, bishop 25%) that is objectively safe in material terms (75% safe, no captures) but catastrophically ignores immediate kingside tactical threats. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 522 centipawns, typically converting drawn positions to losing ones (75%) or winning to drawn (25%). The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is king_safety (60%), with overloaded defenders and tempo loss as secondary themes. The concrete positions show a striking pattern: the opponent has a queen on h5 and bishop on g4 creating a battery against f3/f2, while the player pursues queenside expansion (b5, c5), premature attacks (Nb5, dxe5), or passive moves (Kh1, Qd2) instead of addressing the immediate kingside crisis. Tags like 'king_in_center', 'neglecting_castling', 'hanging_rook_h1', and 'premature_attack' confirm the player is prioritizing long-term plans while their king position is tactically collapsing.

1819.label: Hanging or losing major pieces by ignoring threats to the exposed king in middlegame positions.
1819.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders where players move high-value pieces (queens 38%, knights 25%) without recognizing that their king is critically exposed, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median -3.0 material, 62% hangs) and massive eval drops (median 483 centipawns). The king_safety motif is present in 100% of cases, with recurring tags like exposed_king, forced_mate, and defensive_piece_removal. Players capture a seemingly attractive piece or make a natural-looking move, but fail to see that the move removes a critical defender or allows a devastating check/mating attack. Maia's recommendations (100% non-captures) suggest quiet defensive moves were available. The trajectory (50% losing->losing, 25% drawn->losing) shows these errors often occur in already pressured positions where the player cracks under tactical complexity, making a move that fatally compromises their king's safety rather than addressing the primary threat.

1818.label: Passively retreating the queen to a vulnerable square, allowing back-rank or tactical exploitation.
1818.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (41% of moves) passively or retreats it to an inferior square, when the engine strongly preferred an active queen move (Maia suggests queen 83% of the time). The back-rank motif dominates (40%), with tempo_loss and king_safety also prominent, indicating the queen retreats abandon critical defensive or offensive duties. The material signature shows 41% of moves hang material (not through captures but by leaving pieces undefended after the retreat) while 45% appear superficially safe—yet the median eval loss of 344 centipawns reveals these are severe tactical oversights. The trajectory (48% losing→losing, with other cases converting drawn/winning positions into losses) shows players in already difficult positions compounding their troubles by pulling the queen back rather than finding the one active defensive resource. Concrete examples include Qd8 walking into a back-rank skewer, Qg2 abandoning all central activity, and retreats that allow forced mating nets or devastating invasions on the back rank.

1820.label: Delivering a tempting but catastrophic check with a rook or queen that leaves the checking piece hanging or simplifies into a lost position.
1820.description: This feature captures the classic 'patzer sees a check' blunder pattern. The material signature shows 100% of these moves are checks, delivered predominantly by rooks (77%) or queens (23%), yet 62% hang the piece outright and 31% lose material, with a devastating median loss of 5.0 points of material. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-ruining mistakes: 31% flip from winning to losing, 23% from winning to drawn, with a median eval swing of 678 centipawns. The tactical analysis tags explicitly include 'unnecessary_check' and 'patzer_sees_a_check', with example summaries describing players succumbing to the temptation of a check that leaves their rook undefended, or throwing away forced mates by delivering rook checks that allow the opponent to capture with tempo. Maia's recommended moves (which are checks only 54% of the time) suggest the better alternative was often a quiet move maintaining pressure rather than an impulsive check. The boards confirm the pattern: positions with powerful rook or queen setups where the player delivers a check that walks into a capture or disastrous simplification.

1822.label: Moving a piece to or from a square where it leaves another piece undefended and capturable.
1822.description: This feature captures a recurring middlegame mistake where players move a minor piece (knight 44%, bishop 22%) that results in hanging material (44% hangs, 33% slightly down, median -2.0 material). The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly thrown wins (56% winning->drawn, 33% winning->winning but losing significant eval, median 340cp lost), indicating players who had strong positions but made a careless piece move. The OPUS analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (71%), with supporting tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'piece_coordination' failures. The concrete examples reveal the pattern clearly: retreating a bishop severs indirect defense of another piece, castling while a knight hangs unprotected, placing a knight on an undefended square within capture range, or capturing prematurely without noticing what's left unguarded. The key distinction is that these aren't exchange decisions—44% involve no capture at all—but rather positional or developing moves that inadvertently leave a piece en prise, typically because the player overlooked a defensive relationship between their own pieces.

1824.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while missing a decisive tactical blow against the opponent's exposed king.
1824.description: This feature fires when players abandon or overlook winning attacks targeting the opponent's vulnerable king. The material signature shows the player's moves are often trades or quiet moves (queen 40%, pawn 30%, rook 30%) rather than aggressive continuations, while Maia's recommended moves heavily feature checks (90%) with bishops and queens—pieces ideally suited for king attacks. The eval trajectory is devastating: 30% of cases go from winning to losing, 20% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 469 centipawns, indicating these are critical moments where the win was fully available. The dominant motifs (king_safety 50%, back_rank 25%, tempo_loss 25%) and tags (exposed_king, missed_tactic) confirm the pattern: positions feature an exposed enemy king ripe for tactical exploitation (often via checks, sacrifices like Rxc3 or Rxg5+, or back-rank threats), but the player instead chooses a passive, positional, or exchanging move that squanders the attack entirely. The board positions consistently show open king configurations with tactical combinations available involving checks and piece coordination that the player simply misses.

1825.label: A pawn or piece move that fatally weakens the king's defenses, allowing a dangerous attack.
1825.description: This feature fires on moves that critically compromise king safety, turning drawn or slightly worse positions into losing ones. The material signature shows the player most often moves a pawn (35%) or minor piece, and in 85% of cases no capture is made—these are quiet, positional moves rather than tactical exchanges. Yet the median eval loss is a devastating 265 centipawns, with 43% of cases converting a drawn position into a losing one. The Opus analysis confirms king_safety as the dominant motif in 100% of positions, with tags like greek_gift_sacrifice and missed_tactic appearing alongside. The concrete positions reinforce this: moves like ...f5, ...f6, g4, and ...c4 all push pawns or reposition pieces in ways that open critical diagonals or files toward the king, often enabling Greek Gift-style sacrifices (Bxh7+) or other kingside attacks. Maia overwhelmingly recommends bishop moves (97%), suggesting the correct plan involved developing or repositioning a bishop defensively rather than making the weakening move played. The 38% 'hangs' rate reflects that after the weakening move, existing pieces become tactically vulnerable due to the compromised king position.

1826.label: In the opening, player makes a safe but passive move (often castling or a slow pawn push) instead of seizing an available tactical or central breakthrough.
1826.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions where the player has a significant advantage (often winning or at least equal) and squanders it by playing a 'safe' but tempo-losing move instead of exploiting a concrete tactical window. The material signature shows no captures and no material hung—the moves are objectively safe (96%) but cost a median of 296 centipawns, indicating a missed tactical opportunity rather than a blunder. The eval trajectory confirms this: 52% of cases go from winning to drawn, representing thrown wins. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, central_breakthrough, and missed_central_break. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: players castle (e1g1) or play routine developing/preparatory moves (Nc3, c3, Be2) when a forcing central pawn break (typically d5 or d4) or a tactical piece move would have exploited the opponent's piece placement. Maia's preferred moves are overwhelmingly pawn pushes (83%), confirming the engine wanted an aggressive central advance. This is the classic opening mistake of prioritizing king safety or 'development' over a time-sensitive tactical opportunity.

1823.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from a critical square, leaving other material undefended or tactical resources lost.
1823.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where a player relocates a piece (most often a rook, knight, or pawn) away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive or tactical function. The material signature shows that 79% of moves involve no capture and 33% result in hanging material—these aren't exchange decisions but positional retreats/redeployments that inadvertently leave pieces unguarded or abandon critical tactical threats. The eval trajectory is severe (median 344cp loss) with 60% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into drawn or lost ones, indicating these moves throw away significant advantages. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (33%) and positional_mistake (22%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss and piece_activity. The concrete examples are textbook cases—a knight leaves c3 abandoning central control for a peripheral pawn raid, a knight leaves d5 surrendering a fork threat and leaving a rook hanging, a king steps onto a dangerous diagonal, a rook moves off a critical file. In each case the player prioritizes a secondary plan over maintaining a piece's essential role in the position.

1821.label: In endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player moves a rook or king without first inserting a critical intermezzo check, allowing the opponent's pawn to promote favorably.
1821.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves a rook (75%) or king (25%) in a way that loses critical tempo in a passed-pawn race or promotion battle. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (75%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 423cp lost), with 67% of cases being already-losing positions made dramatically worse. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs: passed pawns (50%), tempo loss (38%), and promotion errors (12%). The recurring pattern from the per-position summaries is that players capture or reposition their rook without first inserting an intermediate check (intermezzo) that would disrupt the opponent's promotion sequence. Maia's recommended moves are all rook moves (100%) that frequently give check (67%), confirming that the missed resource is typically a forcing check that gains tempo against the enemy king before the pawn promotes. The player's moves are fundamentally sound-looking rook maneuvers that miss the narrow tactical window requiring precise move ordering in pawn-promotion endgames.

1828.label: Moving a major piece away from defensive duties, exposing the back rank or leaving pieces hanging to tactical shots.
1828.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where the player moves a major piece (rook 36%, queen 29%) in a way that ignores critical tactical vulnerabilities, particularly back-rank weaknesses and hanging pieces. The material signature shows 64% of moves are non-captures that either hang material (29%) or appear safe but miss a devastating tactical reply. The eval trajectory is severe (median 419cp lost), with 35% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones, indicating these are game-deciding oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are back_rank threats (33%), missed tactics (33%), and hanging pieces (33%), with recurring themes of removing defenders and tempo loss. Maia's suggested moves frequently involve capturing (bishop 36%, queen 36%) and giving check (36%), revealing that the best moves involved active tactical strikes the player completely overlooked. The concrete positions show pieces being moved to passive squares (Rac1, Ne2, Qd2) while the opponent has forcing tactical resources available, often exploiting the weakened back rank or undefended pieces left behind.

1827.label: Moving a rook that leaves a critical piece or pawn undefended, turning a winning position into a losing one.
1827.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player, holding a winning middlegame position, makes a rook move (62% of activating moves) that hangs material (75% of outcomes), typically leaving a queen, key pawn, or the rook itself undefended. The median material loss is -4.0 (roughly a full piece or more), and the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic swing of ~1200 centipawns, with 88% going from winning to losing. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (dominant at 50%), tempo_loss, and king_safety—reveal that the rook move either abandons a defensive duty (e.g., the only piece guarding the queen) or misses a forcing intermediate move that would have maintained the advantage. Maia's recommended moves consistently involve capturing the hanging queen (100% captures are queen takes), confirming that the opponent has an immediate tactical refutation. The concrete positions show patterns like Rge6 leaving a queen en prise, Re2/Re1 leaving a central pawn or piece unguarded, and rook moves that ignore back-rank or tempo-based threats. The core mistake is a passive or developing rook move that overlooks the immediate tactical consequence of leaving something hanging.

1831.label: Queen captures a pawn or piece on an open file, landing on a square where it becomes pinned to the king.
1831.description: This feature identifies a highly specific and recurring mistake: the player moves their queen (79% of cases) to capture material (typically a pawn, 50%), believing it to be safe (79% 'safe' outcome by simple material count), but in doing so places the queen on a file or diagonal where it becomes pinned to the king. The dominant motif is 'pin' (70%), and the common tags emphasize uncastled kings, open files, and open file exploitation. The eval trajectory is devastating—median loss of 327 centipawns—with 86% of cases missing a winning alternative. The pattern is most clearly seen in positions where the queen greedily captures on the e-file (Qxe4, Qxe5) in front of an uncastled or exposed king, allowing the opponent to exploit the pin with a rook or bishop. The phase is early (50% opening, 50% middlegame), consistent with kings that haven't yet castled. Maia's recommended moves are typically non-queen moves (knight, king, bishop) suggesting the correct play was to address king safety or develop rather than grab material.

1830.label: King moves to an exposed square, hanging material and allowing forced mate.
1830.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) into a fatally exposed square rather than addressing immediate threats, resulting in hanging material (net -3.0 median) and typically shortening the opponent's path to forced mate. The OPUS analysis consistently highlights 'king_safety', 'exposed_king', 'forced_mate', and 'king_walk' as dominant tags, with example summaries describing kings walking into lethal corridors, pawn checks, and mating nets. The eval trajectory shows positions that were already difficult (losing->winning 50%, winning->winning 50% with median 0.0 cp lost suggests the positions often involved forced mates where centipawn eval is unreliable), but the king move catastrophically accelerates the opponent's attack. In the top boards, we see kings on c4, b3, a3, d3, d4—all central or exposed squares where they become vulnerable to coordination attacks from queens, rooks, and pawns. The missed winning move (Maia's bishop capturing a rook, 100%) indicates that a defensive or material-recovering capture was available but the player instead made a panicked or misguided king retreat that worsened their position dramatically.

1829.label: Knight moves that ignore critical passed pawns in won endgames, allowing the opponent to advance or exchange pawns favorably.
1829.description: This feature captures a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player, already in a winning position, makes an aimless or misguided knight move (100% knight moves) that hangs material (median -1.0 net) instead of addressing the critical passed pawn dynamics on the board. The positions are exclusively endgames (100%) with passed pawns as the dominant motif (70%), and Maia consistently recommends simple pawn captures (100% pawn takes pawn) that would maintain the winning advantage. The eval trajectory shows these are all winning→winning transitions, but with a massive median loss of 303 centipawns, meaning the player squanders a decisive advantage into one requiring precise technique. The tactical analyses reveal a consistent theme: the knight maneuver loses tempo or abandons control of key squares, allowing the opponent's passed pawn to become more dangerous or enabling favorable pawn exchanges. The boards confirm this—nearly all feature advanced passed pawns where the correct plan involves direct pawn play rather than knight repositioning.

1833.label: King retreats or sidesteps passively instead of capturing or actively engaging in a pawn endgame, missing the chance to stop or capture a piece supporting a passed pawn.
1833.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king passively (100% king moves, 0% captures) in positions that are already losing, making the loss significantly worse (median 306cp lost, losing->losing trajectory). The Maia engine consistently recommends capturing a knight instead (100% knight captures), indicating the player missed a concrete piece win. The dominant motifs—passed pawns (43%), king safety (29%), and pawn endgames (14%)—reveal that the passive king move fails to address the critical threat of an advancing passed pawn or fails to activate the king when material recovery was available. The position summaries confirm the pattern: kings retreat to squares that appear useful (blockading, staying safe) but actually allow the opponent's passed pawn to advance or preserve the opponent's key supporting piece. These are not losing positions turned into draws, but already difficult positions made hopeless by choosing king safety over active king play and material recovery.

1832.label: Misplaying king or pawn moves in pawn endgames by losing a critical tempo, turning drawn or winning positions into lost ones.
1832.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame error pattern. The material/position signature shows predominantly pawn (52%) and king (37%) moves with no captures in 74% of cases, occurring in endgame (59%) and middlegame (41%) phases—consistent with pure pawn endgames or near-pawn endgames. The eval trajectory is devastating: 41% of cases convert drawn positions into losing ones, and 37% make already-losing positions worse, with a median loss of 215 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (40%) and tempo_loss (30%), with recurring tags including pawn_structure, tempo_loss, passed_pawn, and king_activity. The top boards universally show locked or semi-locked pawn structures where a single king retreat (Kg2, Kb3, Kd7) or premature pawn advance (f4, c5+, g5, exd4) squanders a tempo that is critical in the race to promote or blockade passed pawns. The mistake is not about hanging material but about subtle positional timing—moving the king to a passive square or advancing a pawn that creates targets rather than threats, allowing the opponent to seize the opposition or outflank.

1834.label: Leaving a piece undefended in the opening by playing a slow pawn or bishop move that ignores an immediate tactical threat.
1834.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening-phase blunder (95% opening) where the player makes a pawn move (42%) or bishop move (37%) that hangs material (79% hangs) rather than addressing an immediate tactical threat. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically convert a drawn position into a losing one (79% drawn->losing) with a massive median cost of 313 centipawns. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece (33%), fork (33%), discovered_attack (11%), skewer (11%)—reveal that the player ignores concrete threats on the board, often leaving a piece undefended or failing to neutralize a tactical combination. The top boards consistently show Italian Game and Sicilian-type positions where the player makes a developing or prophylactic move (like Nc3, b6, a6, g6, or Bb5) that is a 'tempo-losing luxury' while the opponent has a direct tactical shot available. Maia strongly preferred bishop moves (95%), suggesting the correct response was typically a bishop retreat or interposition to address the threat. The common tags—ignored_threat, premature_attack, diagonal_exploitation—confirm these are cases where players prioritize their own plan over responding to the opponent's immediate tactical resources.

1835.label: Placing or leaving a piece on a square directly attacked by an enemy pawn in the opening, hanging material for free.
1835.description: This feature fires on early-game moves (100% opening phase) where the player makes a non-capture move (100% no capture) that hangs a piece (67% hangs material, median net -2.0 pawns), typically moving a knight (67%) to a square controlled by an opponent's pawn. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (67% drawn->losing, median 369cp lost), confirming they are serious blunders rather than speculative sacrifices. The tactical analysis corroborates this: the dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), with common tags including pawn_captures_piece, opening_principle_violation, and piece_loss. The concrete positions reveal a highly specific pattern—knights being developed to squares attacked by advanced central pawns (e.g., Nc3 into a d4 pawn, Nf6 into an e5 pawn), or positionally catastrophic opening moves like Ke2 that forfeit castling. Maia's response is consistently a pawn capture (100%), confirming the opponent simply takes the hanging piece with a pawn. This is a fundamental tactical oversight in the opening where players fail to account for pawn control of their target square.

1837.label: Player gives a check with the queen but places it on a square where an opponent's rook can simply capture it.
1837.description: This feature detects a highly specific and catastrophic one-move oversight in the middlegame: the player moves their queen to deliver check, but in doing so places it on a line (rank, file, or diagonal) where it is unprotected and can be captured by an enemy rook. The material signature confirms that 100% of cases involve a queen move that is a non-capture check which hangs material (median net loss of -4.0, consistent with losing a queen for nothing or for a minor piece). The eval trajectory shows a massive swing from winning to losing (median 1299 centipawns lost), indicating these were won positions thrown away by a single blunder. The tactical analysis and board positions reinforce this: tags like 'rook_captures_queen' and 'hanging_piece' dominate, and the concrete positions consistently show a queen landing on a square attacked by the opponent's rook. The player is likely focused on the aggressive idea of giving check without noticing the rook's coverage of the destination square.

1836.label: Trading a bishop for a rook while missing a stronger tactical continuation that would have won decisively.
1836.description: This feature fires when a player exchanges a bishop (90%) or knight (10%) for a rook (100% capture rook), gaining nominal material (median +2.0, consistent with the bishop-for-rook exchange value), but catastrophically misses a much stronger tactical opportunity. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 332cp), with 35% going from winning to losing and 25% from drawn to losing — indicating the exchange itself isn't bad in isolation, but it squanders a decisive advantage. The tactical motifs (discovered attacks, hanging pieces, king safety, tempo loss) and tags (missed_tactic, checkmate_in_2, exposed_king) reveal that in these positions, the opponent's king was vulnerable or pieces were hanging, and instead of delivering a knockout blow, the player greedily grabbed the rook. The top boards confirm this: bishops capture on a1/a8 taking corner rooks while missing discovered attacks, checkmates, or winning combinations. Maia's suggested moves (queen 20%, knight 20%, bishop 25%) with no captures in 45% of cases suggest the correct moves were often quiet tactical shots or piece redeployments rather than material grabs. This is fundamentally a 'material greed' error where the temptation of winning the exchange blinds the player to superior tactical resources.

1839.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of executing the classic Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice that exploits Black's uncastled king.
1839.description: This feature fires consistently in opening positions where White has a bishop on c4 aimed at the vulnerable f7 square, Black's king remains uncastled (often with a knight on d7 blocking coordination), and the classic Bxf7+ sacrifice is available—frequently followed by a knight fork winning material. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (castling, developing a knight, retreating the bishop) rather than the aggressive Bxf7+ capture that Maia consistently identifies. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that collapse to drawn (median 346cp lost), indicating a significant tactical opportunity squandered. The tactical analysis tags (f7_weakness, knight_fork, bishop_sacrifice, king_in_center) and example summaries all converge on the same pattern: players default to autopilot development moves and miss the devastating Bxf7+ sacrifice that exploits the precise tactical configuration of the Italian Game / Philidor-type structures. This is a pattern-recognition failure where the player doesn't recognize the classic sacrificial motif despite having all the pieces optimally placed for it.

1838.label: Knight captures pawn on f2/f7 in the opening with insufficient compensation, losing a piece for a pawn.
1838.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: a knight captures a pawn on f2 (or f7), typically targeting the opponent's king, but the sacrifice is unsound. The material signature shows knight moves capturing a pawn 94% of the time with a net material outcome of 'slightly_down' (median -2.0, i.e., piece for pawn). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors—74% swing a drawn position to losing, with a median loss of 264 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players launch premature attacks expecting the exposed king (on f2 after Kxf2) to provide lasting compensation, but the position doesn't support it. Tags like 'unsound_sacrifice' (6), 'insufficient_compensation' (5), 'premature_attack' (4), and 'piece_for_pawn' (4) all converge on this pattern. The top boards confirm it—nearly all show a knight on g4 or e4 jumping to f2 in the opening (94% opening phase), hoping for a kingside attack that simply doesn't materialize against accurate play.

1841.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while an undefended enemy piece (often a queen) sits available for capture.
1841.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a free capture of an undefended high-value piece. The material signature shows 100% of moves are non-captures that hang material (56% hangs, median net -1.0), while Maia's recommended moves capture a queen 78% of the time or a bishop 22% — indicating the opponent had a hanging piece that went untouched. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (50%), reinforced by tags like 'missed_capture' (appearing in 4/9 positions) and 'missed_tactic' (3/9).
