The tactical analyses consistently describe scenarios where a queen or major piece sits undefended (e.g., queen on c3, queen on h1, queen along the third rank) and the player instead makes a king move, a quiet rook move, or a knight retreat that accomplishes nothing. The eval trajectory shows this mostly occurs in already-losing positions (56% losing->losing) where the missed capture was the last chance to stay competitive or even win (33% losing->winning, 11% drawn->winning), with a median cost of 114 centipawns. The phase is predominantly middlegame (78%), where tactical awareness of hanging pieces is most critical.

1840.label: Player makes a quiet king or pawn move while a free queen capture (pawn takes queen) sits on the board.
1840.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks an elementary pawn capture that wins the opponent's queen outright. The material signature shows the player moved a king (67%) or pawn (33%) with no capture, while Maia's recommended move is always a pawn capturing a queen — indicating a completely unprotected queen left hanging. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame, and 100% of them involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory (median loss of 232 centipawns, with most cases going from losing to deeper losing or occasionally losing to winning when the capture was the only saving resource) confirms these are catastrophic oversights rather than subtle positional errors. The Opus analyses repeatedly describe the same pattern: a specific pawn capture (dxc5, exf6) that wins the queen is available, yet the player makes an aimless king shuffle or pawn push instead. Tags like 'hanging_queen', 'hanging_piece', and 'missed_capture' reinforce this. The board positions show Black queens sitting en prise on c5 or f6 where a central pawn can simply take them, but the player's attention drifts to irrelevant king-side pawn moves (h2h3, g2g3, f2f3).

1845.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move when a queen check wins decisive material or delivers checkmate.
1845.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player (across various piece moves—pawns, rooks, queens) plays a safe, non-capturing, non-checking move while Maia consistently identifies a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) as the correct continuation. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 9332 centipawns lost), often converting a winning or drawn position into a losing one. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the missed moves are diagonal checks, bishop captures with check, and forcing sequences that win material or deliver checkmate. The common thread across all top-activating positions is that a powerful queen check exploiting the opponent's king placement was available but overlooked in favor of a quiet continuation—often an advancing pawn or a repositioning rook that ignores the tactical emergency on the board.

1843.label: Playing a flashy bishop sacrifice (typically Bxf2+) in the opening instead of capturing the hanging knight on e5, throwing away a winning position.
1843.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake where players choose a showy but unsound bishop sacrifice—almost always Bxf2+ check—instead of the simple and strong Nxe5 capture. The material signature shows bishops and pawns being moved (57% bishop, 29% pawn), with the outcome being slightly_down or hanging material (median -1.0), while Maia consistently recommends capturing the knight (100% knight moves, 86% capturing a knight). The eval trajectory is devastating: 71% winning->drawn and 29% winning->losing, with a median loss of 484 centipawns, confirming these players are throwing away completely won positions. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: sacrificing a bishop (~3 pawns) for a mere f2 pawn (~1 pawn) plus a check that leads nowhere meaningful. Tags like f7_weakness, tempo_loss, and opening_tactics confirm this happens in well-known Italian Game / Two Knights Defense positions where the knight on e5 is genuinely hanging but the allure of a check on f2 proves irresistible. The boards confirm this: multiple instances of Bxf2+ from c5 in standard Italian positions, plus similar premature tactical attempts that ignore the simple winning capture.

1844.label: Player makes a materially tempting trade or capture while ignoring a critical king safety threat that leads to a devastating attack or checkmate.
1844.description: This feature fires when a player executes a trade (86% of the time) — typically involving a knight (57%) or queen (29%) capture of an enemy piece — that appears materially sound (median net +2.0) but catastrophically neglects king safety. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 410 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing (43%) or winning positions to losing (29%). The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies king_safety (83%) as the dominant motif, with tags like 'greedy_capture', 'exposed_king', and 'king_safety_neglect' recurring. The concrete positions show a clear pattern: the player grabs material on the periphery (e.g., Nxh8 capturing a rook in the corner, or taking a bishop/knight) while their own king is fatally exposed, allowing the opponent — who typically responds with a queen move (43%) rather than recapturing — to launch an immediate mating attack or decisive infiltration. Maia's recommended moves (86% non-captures) confirm that the correct response was a defensive or prophylactic move rather than the greedy material grab.

1842.label: Moving the king or a piece to an unprotected square that allows forced checkmate or decisive tactical blow.
1842.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders where the player makes a move (often a king move or a rook/piece relocation) that fatally exposes their king or hangs material to a forcing sequence. The material signature shows 60% of moves hang a piece with no capture involved, and a median loss of 1.0 in material — but the eval trajectory reveals the true cost is much deeper (median 214 centipawns lost), with 40% of cases converting a drawn position to losing. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is king_safety (50%), with recurring tags of forced_mate, exposed_king, and king_walk. The concrete examples show kings walking into mating nets (Kb4 into forced mate, Ke2 onto exposed diagonals), impulsive checks that drop queens, and missed defensive necessities. The player fails to recognize that their move creates fatal tactical vulnerabilities — checking diagonals, open files against their king, or forks — where the opponent has a forcing sequence. This is not a trade gone wrong but rather a pure tactical oversight where the player's move actively creates the losing condition.

1848.label: Player gives a queen check that hangs the queen or loses major material, throwing away the game.
1848.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that catastrophically loses material (67% hangs, 33% loses; median net material: -9.0, i.e., roughly a queen's worth). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders with a median cost of 771 centipawns, often flipping winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->losing 17%, drawn->losing 33%, losing->winning 33% reflects opponent's perspective gains). The Opus tactical analysis highlights 'check_obsession' and 'hallucinated_tactic' tags—players fixate on delivering check without verifying the queen's safety on the destination square. Multiple board examples show queens moving to squares where they can be simply captured by the opponent's king or other piece. The dominant 'hanging_piece' motif (80%) confirms the queen is left en prise after the check. Maia's suggested alternatives (50% queen moves, 33% pawn moves) indicate quieter, safer continuations were available. This is a classic pattern of prioritizing the psychological appeal of check over board safety.

1847.label: Player gives a tempting check with a knight or bishop that simply loses the piece.
1847.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) predominantly with a knight (55%) or bishop (32%), but the checking piece is immediately captured or left hanging—43% of moves result in a hung piece, with a median material loss of 2.0 (a full piece). The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' pattern: the player is lured by a seemingly forcing move (a fork or discovered check) that is cleanly refuted because the checking piece lands on a square covered by the opponent. Maia (the engine's predicted human move) almost never gives check (0%), preferring quiet developing moves, confirming that the check is the deviation from sound play. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 268 centipawns—consistent with dropping a minor piece—and the tags 'check_is_not_always_best', 'premature_attack', and 'piece_sacrifice_unsound' reinforce that these are not calculated sacrifices but impulsive tactical errors. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (81%), where the board complexity tempts players into pseudo-active checks that backfire.

1849.label: Playing a casual or developing move while leaving a piece undefended and en prise.
1849.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make moves—often developing or repositioning pieces—while failing to notice that one of their own pieces is hanging or has just become undefended. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' outcomes (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full minor piece), occurring predominantly in the opening phase. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (75%), supplemented by 'undefended_piece' and 'tempo_loss' tags, indicating players prioritize development or positional goals over immediate piece safety. The eval trajectory shows a substantial median loss of 311 centipawns, with cases ranging from throwing away a winning position to deepening an already losing one. The concrete examples reinforce this: a developing move while a knight on b7 hangs to a queen, removing a defender that leaves a bishop hanging to a queen with check, and capturing a defended pawn while leaving one's own rook unprotected. The common thread is a failure to perform basic piece-safety checks before executing an otherwise logical-looking move.

1846.label: Recapturing a pawn in the opening that fatally opens a diagonal toward the king, missing a knight development move.
1846.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player recaptures a pawn (most often fxe5) that appears materially safe but catastrophically opens a diagonal — typically the e8-h5 or related king diagonal — allowing devastating tactics like Qh5+. The material signature shows a 'safe' pawn capture (net +1.0 median), yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 294 centipawns, often swinging from drawn or slightly worse to clearly losing. The dominant motif is king_safety (57%), and the Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the f-file/diagonal exposure as the root cause. Maia consistently recommends a knight move instead (knight 100%, no capture), indicating the correct plan was piece development rather than the greedy-looking pawn recapture. The top boards confirm the recurring pattern: positions with pawns on f6 recapturing on e5 in the first few moves, opening lines before the king has castled. Tags like development, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic reinforce that the player chose a superficially logical recapture over a developing move that maintained king safety.

1850.label: Reckless rook moves (often checks) that squander a winning position by hanging material or entering a lost endgame.
1850.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes an aggressive rook move (78% rook moves, 67% giving check) that appears forceful but actually throws away a winning or drawn position. The material signature shows the move predominantly hangs a piece (56%) or loses material (28%) with a median net loss of 5.0 points, indicating these are not subtle positional errors but catastrophic material oversights disguised as active play. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-ruining mistakes: 28% convert winning to losing, 22% drawn to losing, and 17% winning to drawn, with a median cost of 455 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: players attempt pseudo-sacrifices or premature attacks with their rooks (often involving false sacrifices, as tagged), missing that the forced continuation leaves them down material. The 'rook_endgame' motif (33%) and 'patience_required' tag indicate positions where maintaining pressure was correct but the player impatiently lunged with a rook check or capture that simplified into a lost or drawn endgame. Maia's preferred moves (44% rook, 22% pawn) suggest quieter rook repositioning or pawn advances were superior, and the 72% missed winning material rate confirms concrete tactics were available that the flashy rook move overlooked.

1851.label: Passive bishop retreat in the opening that wastes tempo and allows tactical punishment, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1851.description: This feature detects a specific opening mistake where the player moves a bishop passively (100% bishop moves, 0% captures, 0% checks) in a way that loses critical tempo during development. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase, and the eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 225cp loss). The tactical analyses reveal a consistent pattern: bishops that were actively placed (often on b4 in Nimzo-Indian or similar structures) retreat unnecessarily (e.g., Bb4-e7, Bc5-e7, Bb4-d6), wasting two tempi without achieving their strategic purpose (like doubling pawns). The material signature shows these moves are nominally 'safe' (83%) — the piece isn't immediately lost — but Maia's recommended responses involve captures and checks that exploit the tempo loss. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss, trapped_piece, king_safety) confirm that these passive bishop moves leave the player underdeveloped and vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation, particularly discovered attacks and pawn forks that trap the misplaced bishop.

1853.label: Player captures or moves with the wrong piece/sequence, leaving another piece hanging.
1853.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a capture or move without first addressing a tactical prerequisite—typically capturing with the wrong piece or in the wrong order, leaving one of their own pieces undefended and hanging. The material signature shows 50% trades and 17% hangs, indicating the player often initiates an exchange but executes it incorrectly, resulting in net material loss. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 436cp lost, with 50% drawn->losing and 25% winning->losing), showing these are game-changing errors that throw away objectively held or equal positions. The Opus analysis is unanimous: 100% hanging_piece motif with recurring tags of wrong_capture, move_order, and undefended_piece. The correct moves (often bishop or rook captures/checks per Maia, with 33% giving check) reveal that an intermediate move or different capture order would have maintained material balance. The player repeatedly fails to recognize that their chosen sequence leaves a piece en prise, often missing a zwischenzug, intermediate check, or removal-of-defender tactic that the opponent can exploit between moves.

1854.label: Trading pieces when ahead or equal, overlooking that the exchange surrenders a critical attacking or defensive resource.
1854.description: This feature captures positions where a player initiates a seemingly equal material trade (60% of moves result in trades with median net material of 0.0) but suffers devastating positional consequences—median eval loss of 334 centipawns, with 33% of cases going from winning to drawn and 27% from drawn to losing. The piece moved is typically a bishop or queen exchanged for an opponent's piece of similar value, but the trade eliminates a key piece needed for attack or defense. The Opus analysis reveals king_safety (50%) and exposed_king as dominant motifs: players trade off a defensive piece (like a bishop covering key squares) or an attacking piece (like a queen needed for initiative), failing to recognize that the simplified position fatally shifts the balance. Maia's recommended moves (queen 40%, rook 33%) often maintain tension or deliver checks (27%), suggesting the correct approach was to keep pieces active rather than simplify. The concrete positions show patterns like trading a bishop that guards the king, exchanging queens when holding an attack, or capturing material that opens lines against one's own king—all cases where an objectively equal trade is strategically catastrophic.

1855.label: Moving the king to an unsafe square in the endgame, ignoring tactical threats or losing critical tempo.
1855.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their king (64% of activating moves) into danger or waste tempo in late-game positions (55% endgame, 46% middlegame). The material signature shows 55% of moves hang material and the median cost is -1.0, indicating these king moves directly allow tactical punishment. The eval trajectory (73% losing->losing, 27% losing->winning from opponent's perspective) shows players already in difficult positions making things worse by misplacing their king—median 70cp lost per move. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of king_safety (25%) and back_rank (25%), plus tags like exposed_king, checkmate_in_2, and tempo_loss. Concrete examples show kings walking into mating nets (Kg5 into Rxg3+/Nf5#), moving away from the action (Kg1 losing tempo), or stepping onto squares that allow devastating checks (Kxa6 allowing Qxc6+). Maia preferred pawn moves 73% of the time, suggesting the correct approach was usually quiet pawn play rather than premature king activity. The pattern is a king that moves when it shouldn't—either into tactical danger or away from where it's needed—costing material or allowing forced sequences.

1857.label: Advancing a passed pawn prematurely or passively instead of using king activity to convert a winning endgame into a decisive result.
1857.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player in a clearly winning position (median 532 centipawns lost) makes a pawn move that appears safe but throws away the win, resulting in a draw. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures and no material lost immediately ('safe'), yet the eval trajectory is devastating: winning->drawn in every case. The phase is exclusively endgame, and the tactical analysis highlights pawn_endgame, king_activity, and tempo_loss as dominant themes. The top positions reveal king-and-pawn endgames where the player pushes a passed pawn (e.g., g3-g2) instead of making the critical king maneuver (e.g., Kg4) that maintains the winning advantage. The pattern is one of impatience or autopilot in won endgames—choosing the 'obvious' pawn advance over the precise king move that actually wins, often in positions where only one move preserves the advantage.

1859.label: Moving a pawn or knight to a square where it is immediately captured, often collapsing a defensible position into a loss.
1859.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player advances a pawn or knight (50/50 split) without capturing anything, and the piece is immediately lost (100% 'hangs' outcome, median -2.0 material). The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median ~93 pawns lost), with half the cases converting a winning position into a drawn one and the other half making a losing position dramatically worse. The tactical motifs center on hanging pieces (50%), forks (33%), and king safety issues (17%), with common tags emphasizing missed tactics, tempo loss, and piece activity collapse. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: knights placed on squares where they are captured by pawns (Ne5 taken by f-pawn), pawns advanced to squares where they are tactically exploited, all in situations where a much stronger alternative existed (often a check or capture that maintained the position). The players consistently overlook that their moved piece lacks support or that the move creates a tactical vulnerability the opponent immediately exploits.

1852.label: In pawn endgames with passed pawns, the losing side's king retreats to the back rank, allowing a forced checkmate sequence instead of prolonging resistance.
1852.description: This feature fires on a very specific endgame catastrophe: the player (who is already losing, with evals around -550) moves their king backward (king moves 100%, no captures, no checks) in a pure pawn endgame (endgame 100%) with passed pawns on the board. The critical signature is the eval trajectory: positions shift from 'losing but no forced mate' to 'forced checkmate' (losing->winning from opponent's perspective, median eval loss ~10547cp). The top boards all show king-and-pawn endgames where the defending king retreats to the first/eighth rank (d2d1, f2f1, e2e1, e7e8, d7d8, a7a8) rather than staying active to contest the passed pawn's promotion square. The motifs (passed_pawn 60%, tempo_loss 30%, promotion_error 10%) confirm the mechanism: by retreating, the king loses a critical tempo, cedes opposition or key squares, and allows the opponent's passed pawn to promote with checkmate. Maia agrees these are king moves (likely the natural-looking retreat), but the correct defense required keeping the king active and contesting the pawn's advance. The move itself loses no material ('safe' 100%) — the catastrophe is entirely positional/endgame technique.

1858.label: King or pawn moves in pure pawn endgames that fatally lose a critical tempo, turning drawn or close positions into lost ones.
1858.description: This feature fires on king and pawn moves (king 60%, pawn 30%) in pawn endgames (70% endgame phase) where no material is exchanged or immediately hung (safe 90%), yet the move costs a devastating median of 273 centipawns. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (60%) and tempo_loss (40%), with recurring tags for king_activity, passed_pawns, and pawn_structure. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into lost ones (40%) or worsen already losing positions (40%), often with only one correct move available. The concrete positions are locked pawn structures where a single wasted tempo—a king retreat to g7/g6/h6 instead of the critical advance, or a pawn push like c5 or f4 that permanently forfeits a key option—allows the opponent's king or passed pawns to break through decisively. These are not material blunders in the traditional sense but positional tempo errors uniquely punishing in king-and-pawn endgames.

1856.label: Queen or piece left hanging in the opening due to missed forks or recapture oversights, turning equal positions into lost ones.
1856.description: This feature captures a specific opening-phase blunder pattern where the player moves their queen (75%) or a pawn (25%) to a square where it hangs material with no compensation. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The eval trajectory is strikingly uniform: 100% of cases transition from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 572 centipawns — indicating these are game-deciding mistakes from otherwise balanced positions. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are forks (50%) and hanging pieces (25%), with recurring tags of missed tactics, queen hanging, and failed recaptures. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: queens repeatedly land on e3 where they are forked by knights on d4 via Nxc2+, or pieces are left unrecaptured (like the d2d3 instead of bxc3). These are all opening disasters where a developing or repositioning move overlooks an immediate tactical threat — typically a fork or simply forgetting to recapture — leaving a piece en prise and collapsing the position from equality into a lost game.

1860.label: Taking back on c3 with a pawn in the opening instead of developing a piece, leaving material hanging.
1860.description: This feature fires on a specific opening pattern where the player recaptures a pawn (almost always dxc3 in Scotch/Italian/Advance French structures) rather than developing a piece. The material signature shows pawn-takes-pawn trades with a net loss of about a piece (-1.0 median), and the eval trajectory consistently shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 322cp lost). The top boards reveal a striking concrete pattern: positions with a Black pawn on d4 and White's c3 pawn, where Black mechanically recaptures dxc3 instead of playing a developing move (Nc6, e6, Nd5, etc.). The Opus analysis confirms that Maia consistently recommends knight development moves, and the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece'—after the pawn trade on c3, Black's pieces (often knights on exposed squares) or key squares become tactically vulnerable. The tempo spent on the pawn recapture allows White to seize the initiative with threats that weren't present before. Tags like 'tempo_loss', 'development', and 'piece_activity' reinforce that this is fundamentally a development-tempo error disguised as a natural recapture.

1863.label: Trading a dominant rook for an inferior knight, converting a winning endgame into a draw.
1863.description: This feature detects a specific endgame exchange error where the player captures a knight with a rook (player captured: knight 100%, player moved: rook 78%), voluntarily surrendering their most powerful remaining piece. The material signature shows 'slightly_down' (median -2.0), consistent with a rook-for-knight exchange rather than a blunder. The eval trajectory reveals this trade is catastrophic positionally: 44% go from winning to still-winning (but much worse), 33% from winning to drawn, and 11% from drawn to losing, with a massive median cost of 382 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is entering a theoretically drawn pawn endgame (71% pawn_endgame) after needlessly exchanging the rook—the piece with decisive superiority—for a passive or trapped knight. The positions consistently show late endgames (78%) where the rook's long-range dominance over the knight should guarantee a win, but the player simplifies into a king-and-pawn ending where the advantage evaporates. Tags like 'incorrect_exchange', 'material_superiority_squandered', and 'drawn_pawn_endgame' reinforce that this is a classic failure to maintain the winning piece imbalance.

1864.label: King or rook moves that waste a critical tempo in simplified endgames, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
1864.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a king or rook move (50% king, 50% rook) that is materially safe (no pieces hang or are lost) but squanders a decisive tempo in a simplified position. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic cost (median 489cp lost), with positions going from winning to drawn or drawn to losing. The dominant motifs—pawn endgame (40%), tempo loss (30%), rook endgame (20%)—combined with the top tags (tempo_loss appearing 7 times, king_activity 5 times) reveal that these are not tactical oversights but failures of endgame technique: kings blocking their own pawns (Kf3 blocking f4), retreating when infiltration was required (Ka4-a5 abandoning a breakthrough), or making aimless rook moves when precise calculation was needed. All positions are endgames (100% endgame phase) and the missed winning material rate is 100%, indicating the correct move always involved concrete pawn promotion or king infiltration sequences that the player failed to find.

1861.label: Moving a knight (or minor piece) that ignores a critical tactical obligation, weakening king safety or losing tempo and allowing the opponent a forcing capture.
1861.description: This feature fires when a player redeploys a minor piece—most often a knight (50%) or bishop (21%)—without capturing anything (93% non-captures), in a position where the opponent had a strong forcing move available (typically a knight or bishop capture, as shown by Maia's preferred responses capturing knights 71% and bishops 14%). The move itself doesn't immediately hang material (86% 'safe'), but it catastrophically misses the tactical obligation in the position: resolving tension, defending a critical square, or maintaining king safety. The Opus analysis confirms that 50% of cases involve king_safety degradation and 50% involve tempo_loss—the player makes a developing or repositioning move that either weakens their own king's pawn cover (e.g., ...g5 opening dark-square holes) or allows the opponent to execute a forcing sequence with check or capture that the piece move failed to prevent. The eval trajectory (43% drawn→losing, 36% winning→drawn, median 211cp lost) shows these are game-changing mistakes that squander advantages or tip balanced positions into lost ones, all because the player chose a quiet minor-piece move instead of addressing the immediate tactical demand in the position.

1862.label: Moving a bishop to an aggressive but undefended square, hanging it while abandoning defensive duties.
1862.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players impulsively lunge a bishop (53% of moves) or queen (29%) to an attacking square—most commonly along a diagonal toward the opponent's king (h6, h3, h5, b5)—only to hang the piece outright (65% hangs, median material loss of -1.0 piece). The eval trajectory shows these are not desperate attempts from losing positions: 35% go from winning to drawn and 18% from winning to losing, meaning players are throwing away strong positions on speculative attacks. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (56%), combined with tempo_loss (22%) and premature_attack tags—the piece lands on an aggressive square but lacks support, giving the opponent a free tempo to capture it. The concrete positions show bishops going to h3/h6 attempting kingside pressure or pin ideas, but the piece simply hangs because the attacker misjudged the tactical justification. This is not a positional misjudgment or a trade gone wrong—it's a tactical oversight where aggressive intent blinds the player to the elementary fact that their piece is undefended on its new square.

1865.label: Aggressive checks or attacks that miscalculate forced sequences, losing significant material or the game.
1865.description: This feature captures positions where the player launches a superficially attractive aggressive move—typically a queen check or piece sacrifice aimed at the opponent's king—that badly miscalculates the resulting forced sequence. The material signature shows queen and knight moves (often with check, 75% of the time) that result in net material loss (median -1.0), while Maia's recommended moves are quieter knight or pawn moves that maintain the position. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 50% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 407 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of hanging pieces (50%) and back-rank vulnerabilities, combined with recurring tags of tempo_loss, premature_attack, and missed_capture. The concrete positions reinforce this: multiple Qxf7+ Italian Game traps where the exchange sequence leaves the attacker down material, a king walk into back-rank mate when a simple capture was available, and a promotion error. The common thread is initiating forcing moves (checks, captures) that look dangerous but leave the attacker worse after the forced reply sequence resolves.

1866.label: Playing a non-urgent or passive move when a winning attacking continuation (usually a queen maneuver) was available.
1866.description: This feature detects positions where a player has a winning advantage but squanders it by making a slow, non-threatening move (tempo loss) instead of pressing the attack with the queen. The material signature shows the player's moves are mostly quiet pawn or piece moves (no checks, no captures in 70% of cases), while Maia consistently recommends queen moves (100% queen). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions thrown away: 60% transition from winning to drawn and 20% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 330 centipawns. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), supported by king_safety and missed_tactic tags, indicating the player had attacking opportunities against the opponent's king but chose passive moves (like a7a5, b7b5, O-O, or quiet exchanges) instead of the critical aggressive queen continuation. The concrete positions show repeated patterns of players making queenside pawn pushes or routine developing moves when a forcing queen attack (e.g., Qh3, Qh6) would have been decisive.

1867.label: Player makes a quiet or non-capturing move when an opponent's high-value piece (often a queen) is immediately capturable.
1867.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player has a winning capture available—typically taking an undefended or hanging queen—but instead plays a quiet pawn or bishop move that fails to collect the free material. The material/position signature shows 100% missed winning material with no captures made by the player, while Maia's recommended moves involve capturing a queen 100% of the time. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 67%, promotion_error 33%) and tags (missed_capture, threatening_vs_capturing, undefended_queen, hanging_queen) all confirm the player chose to threaten, reposition, or advance when a decisive capture was sitting on the board. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 484 centipawns lost) with positions going from winning to losing or drawn, consistent with squandering a won game by overlooking a simple take. The concrete examples reinforce this: moving a bishop to threaten a queen instead of capturing it, playing a king move when a rook can take an undefended queen, and pushing a pawn instead of promoting with check to win immediately.

1868.label: Player moves a bishop to an irrelevant square instead of capturing an opponent's undefended bishop that is threatening material.
1868.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves their own bishop (100% bishop moves, 0% captures) while an enemy bishop sits undefended and actively threatening material (typically a rook). The material signature shows the move 'hangs' material with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a rook), and Maia consistently identifies capturing the hanging bishop as the correct response (Maia captures bishop 100%). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights, swinging from winning to losing positions with a median loss of 941 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (89%), with tags like 'free_material_ignored' and 'opening_blunder' reinforcing that players are overlooking an immediate tactical threat in the opening. The board positions consistently show an enemy bishop deep in the player's position (e.g., Bg7 threatening Rh8, Bb7 threatening Ra8) where the simple recapture with the player's own bishop was the only correct move, but the player instead develops or repositions their bishop to an unrelated square.

1869.label: Player captures a rook (often with queen) while missing a back-rank mate or decisive back-rank tactic that would have won immediately.
1869.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning middlegame position plays a queen or rook capture (taking an enemy rook 100% of the time), resulting in what looks like a reasonable trade or material gain (median +2.0 material), but catastrophically overlooks a back-rank mating threat or combination. The dominant motif is back-rank vulnerability (75%), with tags including back_rank_mate, checkmate_in_one, and missed_forced_mate. Maia's recommended moves (bishop 40%, knight 40%, queen 20%) frequently deliver check (60%) and target the queen (80%), indicating the missed moves exploit king exposure via back-rank geometry. The eval trajectory is uniformly winning->drawn with a massive median loss of 615 centipawns, showing these players had decisive advantages but threw them away by reflexively capturing hanging or traded material instead of delivering or setting up back-rank checkmates. The concrete positions confirm this: kings trapped by their own pawns on h1/g1/g8, open back ranks, and the player grabs a rook exchange rather than playing the killing blow (e.g., Re1#, Qg8#, or forcing sequences via back-rank pressure).

1873.label: Moving a knight that leaves another piece undefended, dropping material.
1873.description: This feature detects positions where the player moves a knight (63% of cases) that results in hanging a piece (47% hangs, with median material loss of -2.0 and median eval loss of 321 centipawns). The Opus analysis confirms 100% hanging_piece motif, with tags like 'removed_attacker' and 'piece_coordination_collapse' indicating that the knight move disrupts the defensive coordination of the position—either the knight was defending another piece, or its move exposes a previously protected piece. The eval trajectory shows these are costly errors across all game states (26% losing->losing, 26% drawn->losing, 16% winning->losing), meaning players make this mistake regardless of their standing. The concrete examples reinforce this: pushing e4 leaves a knight undefended, capturing on e6 leaves a bishop hanging, and moving Nxe5/Nxc6 type captures ignore that a piece back home becomes unprotected. Maia's recommended moves (58% pawn, 21% bishop) suggest simpler, safer alternatives that maintain piece coordination rather than the ambitious but tactically flawed knight maneuvers.

1872.label: King or pawn moves in won endgames that mishandle promotion timing or king placement, often allowing counterplay or missing forced wins.
1872.description: This feature fires on positions that are exclusively endgames (100%) where the player moves their king (67%) or pawn (33%) in a materially safe way (no pieces hang, net material 0.0), yet misses winning material opportunities (100%). The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly already-won positions (winning->winning 67%, drawn->winning 33%) with minimal centipawn loss (median 0.0), indicating trivial inaccuracies rather than catastrophic blunders. The tactical analysis reveals dominant motifs of king_safety (29%), tempo_loss (29%), and passed_pawn (14%), with recurring tags including passed_pawn, promotion_error, self-block, and king_walk_blunder. The concrete positions all feature advanced passed pawns near promotion, where the player makes suboptimal king moves (e.g., walking into dangerous squares like Kh7 enabling back-rank mates) or delays promotion by one tempo. These are won endgames where imprecise king placement or promotion sequencing costs a tempo or, in rare cases, allows forced checkmate — the quintessential 'won but sloppy' endgame technique error.

1871.label: Wasting a critical tempo in endgames with passed pawns near promotion, allowing the opponent to neutralize the advantage.
1871.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (61% endgame, 39% middlegame) where a player has a passed pawn close to promotion but squanders the advantage by making a non-urgent king or pawn move instead of the decisive advancing or promoting move. The material signature shows mostly safe, non-capturing moves (84% no capture, 68% safe) with king (32%) and pawn (16%) being the most common pieces moved, while Maia strongly recommends pawn moves (97%). The dominant motifs—passed_pawn (50%), tempo_loss (25%), and promotion_error (25%)—combined with tags like promotion_threat, promotion_threat_missed, and pawn_endgame paint a clear picture of failing to execute a won promotion race. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors in otherwise winning positions: 61% remain winning but at enormous cost (median 317cp lost), while 20% see the position collapse from winning to drawn or losing. The top boards consistently show positions with advanced passed pawns (d6, f6, c6, d7 pawns) where the player chose a king retreat, wrong pawn push, or aimless rook/knight move instead of the critical tempo-gaining promotion advance.

1875.label: Playing a queen check that squanders a forced checkmate or decisive winning sequence by losing tempo.
1875.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that misses a forced mate or winning tactical blow. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert winning positions into dramatically worse ones (median loss of ~10773 centipawns, with 100% losing->winning flips from the opponent's perspective), indicating thrown wins of catastrophic magnitude. The material signature shows the checks themselves are 'safe' or 'hang' material—they aren't capturing anything (0% captures), while Maia's recommended moves capture pieces (knights/bishops) without giving check. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant pattern: purposeless checking sequences that squander forced mates (missed_mate appears 3 times in tags, 'checking_without_purpose' is explicitly tagged). Specific examples include missing Qe3# by playing Qc6+, and losing a mate-in-10 by playing a tempo-losing check. The motifs of tempo_loss (43%) and king_safety (43%) reinforce that these checks chase the king without purpose, allowing defensive resources that didn't previously exist.

1874.label: Player makes a passive or retreating piece move, missing a decisive check or forcing sequence available.
1874.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a knight, rook, or queen to a passive or retreating square while completely missing a forcing check-based tactic that was available. The material signature shows 100% non-captures (no piece taken) that are mostly 'safe' in the immediate sense but miss winning tactics — Maia's recommended moves are 100% checks (queen checks in 64% of cases), and 100% of positions involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: the median cost is 400 centipawns, with 29% going from winning to losing and 21% from drawn to losing. The tactical analysis reinforces this with motifs of missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and fork — players retreat well-placed pieces (e.g., knight from c4 to e3, knight from e5 to g4) or make quiet rook moves when devastating queen checks, queen forks with check, or forced promotion sequences with check were available. The common thread is choosing a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move over a forcing check that wins immediately.

1870.label: Queen captures a piece on a square where it is immediately vulnerable to recapture or counterattack, losing the queen.
1870.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves where the player uses their queen to capture a bishop (100% queen moved, 100% captured bishop), but the capture lands the queen on a tactically poisoned square. The material signature shows a consistent net loss of approximately 6 pawns (median -6.0), which corresponds to losing a queen for a bishop—a catastrophic material deficit. The eval trajectory confirms these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones (100% drawn->losing, median 513cp lost). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the queen lands on a square attacked by an opponent's piece (common tags: queen_hanging, piece_capture_on_attacked_square, knight_recapture), allowing immediate recapture. Board examples confirm this—e.g., Black plays Qxg5 where White's Nf3 immediately recaptures, or the queen captures on b5 where it can be won. These are opening-stage greedy queen captures that overlook elementary tactical responses, typically knight forks or simple recaptures on the destination square. Maia's suggested alternatives (knight or bishop moves, no captures) indicate quiet developing moves were correct rather than the tempting but poisoned capture.

1877.label: King moves to an unsafe square, allowing immediate or forced checkmate that was avoidable.
1877.description: This feature fires when a player makes a king move (100% king moved) that hangs catastrophic material (median -9.0, i.e., equivalent to losing a queen) by walking into a forced checkmate sequence. The eval trajectory shows these positions flip from losing to winning for the opponent (losing->winning 100%), with a staggering median eval loss of ~104 pawns (forced mate). The tactical motifs are dominated by king_safety (80%) and back_rank themes (20%), with recurring tags like exposed_king, immediate_checkmate, and king_walk_blunder. In every case, the player had a better defensive resource available—often a forced queen trade (Maia recommends queen captures 100% of the time)—but instead moved the king into a square where coordinated enemy pieces deliver checkmate. The positions are all middlegame scenarios where the player's position was already difficult but playable, and the king move converts a survivable disadvantage into immediate forced mate.

1876.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move instead of exploiting the opponent's exposed king with a decisive checking/mating sequence.
1876.description: This feature fires when a player, typically with a queen or bishop, plays a safe but passive move (75% safe material outcome) while missing a crushing queen check or mating attack that Maia identifies (Maia plays queen 96% of the time, always with check). The dominant motif is king_safety (75%), with tags like exposed_king, missed_mate, checking_sequence, and forcing_moves_missed consistently appearing. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 428 centipawns, often converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->winning 43% reflects positions so good they survive the mistake, but winning->drawn/losing accounts for 18%). The concrete positions confirm this: in nearly every case, the opponent's king is exposed or vulnerable, and the correct move is a forcing queen invasion or check sequence that wins material or delivers mate, but the player instead chooses a quiet repositioning, peripheral capture, or non-forcing developing move. The mistake is fundamentally one of failing to recognize the urgency of a direct king attack when all the tactical prerequisites (exposed king, queen access, forcing checks) are in place.

1880.label: Pawn or piece moves that catastrophically weaken the player's own king, allowing forced checkmate or decisive attack.
1880.description: This feature fires on moves that fatally compromise the player's king safety. The material signature shows 60% of moves hang material (often the king itself via checkmate) with a median net loss of -1.0, and the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic swings (median 225cp lost), including positions going from losing-but-defensible to immediate checkmate. The dominant motif is king_safety at 80%, with supporting tags like king_exposure and diagonal_weakness. The concrete positions confirm this: f6 weakening the e8-h5 diagonal allowing Qh5+, f3 blocking the king's escape square enabling Qd2#, Kg2 walking into a mating net, and c3 failing to address king vulnerability on an open file. These are predominantly middlegame errors (70%) where the player makes an innocuous-looking pawn or piece move that ignores an immediate king safety crisis, converting survivable positions into forced mates or decisive material loss.

1881.label: Trading a rook for a knight+pawn when winning, allowing the opponent to simplify into a drawn position.
1881.description: This feature captures positions where a player initiates a rook capture (always taking a pawn in the process) that results in an approximately equal material exchange — specifically, the opponent recaptures with a knight taking the rook. The material signature shows a 'trade' (net 0.0), meaning the player loses their rook in return for capturing material of roughly equivalent value. However, the eval trajectory uniformly shows a winning position collapsing to drawn (median 538cp lost), indicating these exchanges catastrophically simplify the position. The tactical analysis reveals hanging pieces and missed tactics — the player had stronger continuations available (often involving piece activity or passed pawns) but chose to exchange into a position where their winning advantage evaporates. The boards confirm middlegame positions where one side has active pieces and pressure, but voluntarily trades down into simplified positions where the opponent's knight proves sufficient for a draw. This is a classic case of premature simplification — exchanging a dominant rook when maintaining tension would have preserved a winning advantage.

1879.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king moves away from or fails to approach a critical passed pawn, allowing it to promote or losing the race.
1879.description: This feature consistently fires on pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player's king move is the mistake. The material signature shows king moves with no captures that are usually 'safe' in the immediate sense (89%), meaning no piece is literally hung—but the positional damage is catastrophic. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs: pawn_endgame (30%), tempo_loss (20%), passed_pawn (20%), and king_safety (20%), all pointing to the same pattern—the king steps in the wrong direction relative to an enemy passed pawn or abandons a critical blockade square. The eval trajectory (44% losing→winning from the player's perspective, i.e., the opponent was losing but the player's blunder flipped it) combined with the concrete positions shows kings moving to edge squares (Kh3, Kg4, Ke2) or retreating (Kb3, Kc2) instead of approaching or blocking passed pawns. The Opus summaries explicitly describe kings moving toward pawns that 'advance away' or getting trapped in 'passive cages' while enemy pawns promote. This is a fundamental endgame error of king misdirection in pawn races.

1878.label: Moving the king (or queen) to an unsafe square, leaving pieces undefended and dropping significant material.
1878.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their king or queen (63% combined) in a way that hangs material (69% of moves result in a hang), typically losing a full piece or more (median net material: -1.0, median eval lost: 428 centipawns). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (38%), king_safety (25%), and tempo_loss (25%)—reveal that these king/queen moves abandon defensive duties: they either remove a piece that was guarding something critical, walk into tactically vulnerable squares, or waste tempo while the opponent has active threats. The trajectory shows this pattern spans all game states (26% losing->losing, 14% drawn->losing, 9% winning->drawn), but the common thread is a middlegame (91%) position where the player's king or queen move exposes a tactical vulnerability—unguarding a piece, opening a diagonal, or neglecting a back-rank threat—that Maia would have addressed with a developing or defensive piece move (rook 37%, bishop 23%). The concrete examples confirm this: Kc6 leaving pieces unguarded, f4 removing a critical pawn shield, d5 undefending a bishop.

1882.label: King moves passively in endgame instead of capturing an undefended rook.
1882.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player moves their king (100% king moves) in a safe manner (no material lost on the move itself) but completely overlooks that they could capture an undefended enemy rook (Maia's recommendation is king captures rook in 100% of cases). The positions are exclusively endgames with passed pawns and simplified material, where a hanging enemy rook is available for a simple king capture. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 1102 centipawns lost, converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (50% winning->losing, 50% winning->drawn). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (80%), with tags like missed_capture, hanging_piece, and rook_endgame recurring throughout. The concrete board positions show endgames where the opponent's rook sits en prise to the player's king (e.g., Kxf6, Kxb5), yet the player makes an aimless king move or advances a pawn instead, throwing away a completely won position by failing to notice the trivially available capture.

1883.label: Trading a bishop in the opening that exposes the king to a devastating knight fork or mate.
1883.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening mistake where the player initiates a bishop trade (bishop captures bishop 100%) that appears materially neutral (net material 0.0, classified as a trade) but catastrophically overlooks a knight tactical blow. The eval trajectory shows these positions go from winning to losing with a massive median loss of 955 centipawns, indicating the trade isn't the problem per se—it's what it enables. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are knight forks (Ng5+, Ne6+, Nd6#) exploiting an exposed king, with tags like knight_fork, exposed_king, and checkmate_in_one appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions confirm this: players play moves like ...Be6 or ...Bxf6 that seem developing or simplifying, but the bishop move either removes a defensive piece or places it on a square that creates a knight fork/mating geometry. Maia's recommended moves (pawn captures knight) suggest the correct response was to address the knight threat rather than initiate the bishop exchange. The opening phase confirms these are early-game tactical oversights where development priorities blind the player to concrete knight tactics.

1884.label: Trading rooks in drawn endgames that fatally misjudges the resulting pawn endgame.
1884.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player initiates or accepts a rook trade (100% rook moves capturing rooks, net material 0.0 indicating an equal exchange) that converts a drawn position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing trajectory, median 541cp loss). The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (67%), passed_pawn, connected_passers, and tags like rook_trade_error, simplification_mistake, and endgame_misjudgment—reveal that the player misevaluates the resulting pawn endgame after the rooks come off. The rook was providing dynamic counterplay (blockading passed pawns, maintaining activity), and its removal leaves the opponent's structural advantages (connected passers, advanced pawns, superior king position) decisive. Maia's recommended moves (100% rook moves with no capture) suggest maintaining the rook on the board was critical to holding the draw.

1885.label: Playing a quiet pawn move in the opening that ignores a tactical threat or misses a developing opportunity, leaving pieces hanging or conceding a positional advantage.
1885.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn moves (100% pawn played, 100% opening) that appear safe on the surface (material outcome: safe, no captures, no checks) but cost significant evaluation (median 249 centipawns lost, 67% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the underlying problem: these pawn pushes ignore hanging pieces (60% hanging_piece motif) or create positional weaknesses (30% positional_mistake). The common tags—piece_activity, hanging_piece, tempo_loss, development—paint a clear picture: players push pawns when they should be developing, capturing, or addressing threats. The top boards confirm this: moves like c3-c4 instead of capturing on d4, ...c6-c5 ignoring a superior developing move, ...b6-b5 creating targets, or quiet bishop/knight developing moves that ignore an opponent's hanging piece. Maia's alternatives consistently involve more active piece development (67% pawn but 33% bishop moves, 33% captures). The player wastes tempo on non-urgent pawn advances while concrete tactical opportunities or threats go unaddressed.

1888.label: Player makes a mundane move in the opening while opponent's queen hangs undefended on the board, missing a free queen capture.
1888.description: This feature identifies a specific and dramatic opening blunder pattern: the player has a bishop that can capture the opponent's hanging queen (Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a queen), but instead plays an innocuous developing move—a pawn push, a quiet queen move, or a knight retreat. The material signature shows 75% of moves hang material (non-captures that leave pieces en prise) with a median loss of ~1.0 piece value, yet the missed opportunity is far larger: 100% of positions had winning material available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic, with positions swinging from winning to drawn or losing by a median of 989 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is a hanging piece, with tags emphasizing missed_tactic, missed_capture, and queen_capture. The boards consistently show early-game positions where a diagonal is open for a bishop to snatch an undefended queen (often on d1 or d8), but the player overlooks this concrete tactical shot in favor of routine development like ...e6, O-O, or Qd2.

1892.label: In drawn endgames, plays a passive king or knight move instead of the one available capture that holds the draw.
1892.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player has exactly one good move—typically a capture (Maia's recommended moves capture queens 67% or pawns 33%)—but instead plays a passive king (67%) or knight (33%) move that neither captures nor creates meaningful threats. The material outcome of the played move is 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost), yet the eval trajectory shows a consistent drawn->losing swing (median 402 centipawns), indicating the player squandered a theoretical draw by failing to take the one critical capture. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' motifs (67%) and universal 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss' tags, reinforcing that the opponent left material en prise (often a queen) and the player simply walked away from it. The positions show sparse endgame boards where the single correct capture would maintain equality, but the player's instinct to move the king or reposition a knight—perhaps seeking activity or opposition—overlooks the concrete tactical requirement.

1889.label: Player makes a slow or purposeless move, missing a bishop check (often Bxh2+ or Bxf2+) that wins the opponent's queen through deflection or discovered attack.
1889.description: This feature fires when a player squanders a winning tactical shot involving a bishop sacrifice with check. The material signature shows the player's move is mostly 'safe' (72%) and non-capturing (77%), meaning they played a quiet, non-forcing move instead of the critical tactic. Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a bishop (54%) or knight (36%) that delivers check (100%), and 54% of activations involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory is devastating: 28% go from winning to drawn and 28% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 630 centipawns—indicating these are game-changing missed opportunities. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss 38%, discovered_attack 12%, overloaded_defender 12%) and tags (deflection_sacrifice, clearance_sacrifice, queen_win) confirm the pattern: the player had a forcing sequence beginning with a bishop check that deflects a defender or creates a discovered attack to win the queen, but instead played a slow move (king retreats, pawn pushes, rook lifts) that surrenders the initiative entirely. The top boards consistently show positions where Bxh2+ or Bxf2+ wins material through deflection, but the player chose a non-tactical alternative.

1886.label: Moving a piece to an unprotected square or abandoning defense of a key piece, allowing the opponent a winning tactical shot.
1886.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player makes a move (most often with a rook, queen, or minor piece) that leaves a piece undefended or abandons a critical defensive duty, allowing the opponent a powerful tactical reply—typically a back-rank or rook-based tactic involving a check (Maia's reply is a rook capture 87% of the time, with 72% giving check). The material signature shows the move itself often doesn't capture anything (79% non-capture) yet 28% of the time it outright hangs a piece, and the median eval loss is a devastating 359 centipawns. The dominant Opus motifs (hanging_piece 43%, overloaded_defender 14%) confirm that the core error is placing or leaving a piece where it lacks protection, or moving a defender away from a critical task. The eval trajectory (drawn→losing 32%, winning→losing 6%, winning→drawn 13%) shows these are often game-deciding mistakes that swing the position sharply. The concrete examples—abandoning queen defense of f1, placing a bishop on an unprotected square before forced exchanges, moving a rook away from a critical file—all share the common thread of leaving material tactically vulnerable to an immediate forcing reply.

1890.label: Trading away a key bishop before exploiting the tactical tension it supports, losing significant eval in the opening.
1890.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player exchanges a bishop (67% bishop moves, 67% capturing a knight) prematurely, before leveraging the tactical pressure that bishop was generating. The material signature shows these are mostly trades (67%) rather than outright blunders—the player gets material back but destroys their own position. The Opus analysis is strikingly consistent: move-order errors where the bishop is exchanged (typically Bxf6 or similar) before executing the tactic the bishop was supporting (e.g., Nxe4 exploiting a weak pawn). Tags like 'move_order_error' (3/4), 'premature_exchange', and 'bishop_pair_concession' confirm this pattern. The eval trajectory is severe—drawn→losing (67%) or winning→losing (33%) with a median loss of 457 centipawns—indicating these trades catastrophically release tension and leave pieces (often knights on f3 or c3) hanging to previously-blocked threats. The top boards reinforce this: positions with Bg5 pinning/pressuring f6 where the bishop is cashed in too early, or positions where exchanging reveals an undefended piece.

1893.label: Moving the queen to a passive square that allows the opponent to gain tempo or exploit a tactical motif.
1893.description: This feature fires when a player retreats or repositions their queen (83% queen moves) to a square that loses critical tempo or releases tension, allowing the opponent's queen to exploit the position (Maia's best response is always a queen capture, 100%). The material signature shows 50% of these moves hang material outright while 50% appear superficially safe, but the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 301 centipawns—often converting drawn positions to losing ones (50%) or throwing away winning advantages (17%). The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 50%, fork 33%, tempo_loss 17%) combined with tags like 'tension_release' and 'queen_misplacement' confirm the pattern: the player moves their queen away from an active or tension-maintaining post to a passive square, inadvertently allowing the opponent to win material through forks, discovered attacks, or simply capturing now-undefended pieces. The concrete positions consistently show queens retreating to squares like g6, g3, e2, d2, or a7 where they either lose tempo to developing pieces or vacate critical defensive/offensive lines.

1887.label: Minor piece captures a pawn far from safety, leaving it trapped or creating devastating tactical vulnerabilities.
1887.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern where a player's minor piece (knight 60%, bishop 40%) captures a pawn (80% of captures) in a way that loses significant material or position. The material signature shows the move is 'slightly_down' (80%), with a median net of -2.0, indicating the piece that grabbed the pawn gets trapped or the capture exposes critical weaknesses. The eval trajectory is severe (median 363cp lost), with 60% of cases swinging from drawn to losing and 20% from winning to losing—these are game-ruining mistakes in the opening (80%). The tactical analysis reveals the core mechanism: the capturing piece becomes trapped (14% motif) or the capture neglects king safety (29%) and leaves hanging pieces (29%). The per-position summaries are strikingly consistent: Nxh2 trapping the knight, Nxf2 leaving the queen unsupported, Bxb7 walking into a trap, and premature Bxf7/Nxf7 sacrifices that are tactically unsound. The common tags of 'unsound_sacrifice', 'tempo_loss', and 'trapped_piece' confirm these are greedy captures where the minor piece ventures too far from coordination for a single pawn, only to be punished by concrete tactics exploiting the overextension.

1891.label: Queen delivers check while leaving itself or major material hanging, causing catastrophic loss.
1891.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player moves their queen (100%) to deliver check (100%), but the check is unsound, resulting in severe material loss (median -8.0 material, with 61% 'loses' and 17% 'hangs' outcomes). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-ruining blunders (median 647cp lost), often turning winning or drawn positions into lost ones (26% winning->losing, 9% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the underlying cause: players are seduced by the forcing nature of a check but overlook that after the king moves or interposes, their queen is trapped (25% trapped_piece), hanging (50% hanging_piece), or captured by an overlooked defender. The top boards consistently show queens capturing pawns with check (70% capture pawns) on squares where they have no escape or where the 'won' pawn was actually defended by a piece the player didn't notice (e.g., Qxf7+ overlooking Bxf7, Qxg7+ walking into a trap). Maia's preferred moves are typically quiet developing moves (rooks 35%, bishops 17%) that maintain the position rather than grabbing material with tempo, confirming these checks are impulsive rather than calculated.

1894.label: Rook moves (often capturing h-pawns) that leave the rook trapped or overextended, turning equal/drawn positions into losing ones.
1894.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: rook moves—frequently Rxh7 or rook lifts to the back rank—where the rook becomes trapped or loses coordination after the capture. The material signature shows 100% rook moves with 83% pawn captures, and while 67% appear 'safe' immediately, the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median 254cp lost), with 67% converting drawn positions into losing ones. The trapped_piece motif dominates (44%), and the top boards overwhelmingly show Rxh7 moves or rook invasions where the rook has no escape route. The Opus analysis confirms this: rooks capturing h-pawns that become trapped after forced responses, leaving the player down a full piece with no compensation. Maia preferred quieter pawn moves (67%), suggesting the AI recognized these rook expeditions were unsound. This is not a simple hanging piece—the rook captures material but then cannot retreat, a classic amateur tactical oversight where the immediate capture looks tempting but the piece has no safe squares afterward.

1897.label: Playing a passive or non-developing move in the opening when a concrete tactical shot or initiative-seizing continuation was available.
1897.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player makes a 'safe' move—typically a pawn or knight move that captures nothing and gives no check—while missing a strong tactical opportunity (75% missed winning material). The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 215 centipawns, most commonly converting a winning position into a drawn one (62%) or a drawn position into a losing one (25%). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (40%) and missed tactics, with tags like 'initiative_squandered', 'development_neglect', and 'unnecessary_prophylaxis' recurring. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: players choose prophylactic pawn pushes (f4, f5, h4), passive piece repositioning (Nf3, Bd3), or retreating moves when the position demanded immediate exploitation of tactical vulnerabilities such as exposed kings, hanging pieces, or forcing sequences including missed checkmates. Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve queen moves and checks (38% check rate, 50% queen moves), reinforcing that the missed continuations were aggressive, initiative-maintaining moves rather than quiet development.

1896.label: Rook moves in won endgames that hang the rook to the opposing king, converting a forced win into a draw.
1896.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame catastrophe: the player moves their rook (100% rook moves) in a position where they had a winning advantage (often mate-in-N), but the rook move hangs material (net median -5.0, i.e., losing the rook) without capturing anything. The eval trajectory shows these are universally losing->drawn swings of enormous magnitude (median -10000 centipawns), meaning forced mates are being thrown away into dead draws. The opponent's response is always a king move (100%), consistent with the king simply capturing the hanging rook. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and endgame themes (pawn_endgame, passed_pawn), with tags emphasizing tempo_loss and insufficient_material after the blunder. Concrete examples show positions like KR vs K or KQ+N vs K where the player carelessly places their major piece within capture range of the opposing king, instantly converting a trivially won position into a theoretical draw. This is a pattern of endgame technique failure—specifically, neglecting the enemy king's reach when maneuvering the winning piece.

1895.label: Passive rook move in a drawn endgame that loses a critical tempo, allowing opponent's passed pawn(s) to advance decisively.
1895.description: This feature captures a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player moves their rook to a passive or aimless square (100% rook moves, 0% captures, 0% checks) in a drawn position, converting it into a loss (100% drawn->losing, median 392cp lost). The material signature shows the rook move 'hangs' something—not the rook itself typically, but the positional resource of holding the draw, as the opponent's passed pawns or promotion threats become unstoppable. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are tempo_loss (appearing in 5/7 tagged positions) and passed_pawn (5/7), with rook_endgame and promotion_error also present. The top boards show classic scenarios—rook retreats to passive ranks (g3->g7, h3->h7) when only one precise rook placement held the draw, or rook moves that fail to prevent pawn promotion. The Maia response is always a king move (100%), suggesting the opponent's king calmly advances or sidesteps once the critical tempo is gifted. This is fundamentally an endgame technique failure where the player misidentifies which rook square maintains the drawing fortress against advanced passed pawns.

1900.label: In won rook endgames, advancing the king passively instead of delivering a decisive rook check that wins material.
1900.description: This feature captures a specific endgame mistake pattern where the player, holding a clearly winning position (evaluations around +600-700), advances their king (king moved 100% of the time) instead of playing a forcing rook check that captures a knight (Maia's move: rook captures knight with check, 100%). The positions are all late endgames featuring a rook vs knight imbalance where a tactical rook capture with check cleanly wins material. The king moves are 'safe' (nothing hangs immediately) but represent tempo losses—the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%)—because the passive king advance allows the opponent to reorganize defensively. The eval trajectory shows winning->winning with a median loss of 120 centipawns, indicating these are not game-losing blunders but meaningful missed opportunities to convert more efficiently. The concrete pattern across all four boards is identical: a rook is positioned to capture a knight with check, but the player chooses a slow king advance (Kf4, Kh3, Kf4, Kf5) that squanders the forcing nature of the position.

1899.label: Player makes a move that allows the opponent to force perpetual check or escape via perpetual, squandering a winning or drawn position.
1899.description: This feature fires when players make moves that fatally expose their king to perpetual check sequences, or fail to deliver checkmate when available, allowing the opponent to draw via perpetual. The material signature shows the player often moves pawns or kings (not delivering checks themselves), while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen move delivering check (86% queen, 100% check). The 'hangs' category at 46% reflects moves that don't capture but leave the position collapsing—here not by losing a piece, but by allowing a drawing mechanism. The king_safety motif (80%) and perpetual_check tags confirm the pattern: players either walk their king into perpetual check territory (Kf4 into exposed position), abandon defensive posts that prevent mate/perpetual (Qc3-f6 abandoning a5 defense), or miss forced mates and allow the opponent perpetual instead. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 209 centipawns with winning->drawn and winning->winning drops, consistent with converting decisive advantages into draws or near-draws through king exposure. The endgame/middlegame split and queen-heavy positions confirm these are simplified positions where perpetual check is the primary defensive resource the opponent exploits.

1898.label: Queen captures a piece instead of delivering or enabling checkmate, fatally breaking a mating net.
1898.description: This feature detects positions where the player uses their queen to capture material (usually a rook or knight) while missing a checkmate-in-one or a forced mating sequence. The material signature shows the queen making captures that are objectively losing or slightly down (median net -2.0), indicating the capture itself isn't even a clean trade—it often removes a piece that was serving a defensive function in the opponent's position OR abandons the queen's own critical attacking role. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median ~97 pawns lost, with 67% going from drawn to losing), confirming these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-ending blunders. The tactical analysis is decisive: 100% king_safety motifs, with tags like checkmate_in_one, missed_mate_in_one, overloaded_defender, and back_rank_pattern appearing repeatedly. Maia consistently recommends a rook move delivering check instead. The concrete positions show queens greedily snatching material while the opponent has an immediate mating reply—often a back-rank or diagonal mate that the captured piece or the queen's former position was preventing. The player's queen was the linchpin of a mating attack or defensive cover, and by capturing, it abandons that role entirely.

1902.label: Trading or exchanging rooks in endgames when maintaining piece activity would preserve a winning advantage.
1902.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their rook to make an exchange or trade (rook moved 100%, material outcome is trade 67% or slightly down 33%). The eval trajectory shows that 33% of the time this converts a winning position into a losing one, with a median loss of 141 centipawns, and 67% of positions miss winning material. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players simplify by exchanging rooks when their rook was actively placed and needed for attacking purposes—as explicitly noted in one example where 'the rook on a2 was far more valuable alive, delivering Ra1+ to initiate a lethal king-hunt.' The dominant motifs (passed pawns 25%, pawn endgames 25%, hanging pieces 25%) confirm that these rook trades prematurely transition into pawn endgames where the opponent's passed pawns or superior king activity become decisive. Maia's preferred moves (rook 67%, pawn 33%) suggest the engine often wanted to keep rooks on the board or advance pawns instead of trading down.

1904.label: Trading queens into a lost endgame where the opponent holds structural or passed-pawn advantages.
1904.description: This feature fires on positions where a player initiates a queen trade (queen moved 100%, queen captured 100%, net material 0.0 confirming an exchange) that transforms a drawn or competitive position into a losing one (drawn->losing 67%, median eval loss 288cp). The tactical analysis consistently identifies queen_trade_error and simplification_error as dominant tags, with the resulting positions being pawn endgames or rook endgames where the opponent has decisive structural advantages—typically outside passed pawns, superior king activity, or crippled pawn structures. The boards confirm this pattern: in nearly every case, the player trades queens on an open file or central square, failing to recognize that the queen was either maintaining defensive resources or providing attacking potential that masked an inferior endgame structure. The positions are predominantly middlegame-to-endgame transitions where keeping queens on the board preserved drawing chances or even winning prospects, but the trade crystallizes latent positional disadvantages into concrete losses.

1903.label: Trading a bishop for a rook in the opening when a stronger continuation existed, squandering a winning advantage into a draw.
1903.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where the player executes a bishop-takes-rook exchange (bishop moved 100%, rook captured 100%) that registers as a 'trade' in material terms (net ~2 pawns, the standard exchange value). However, the eval trajectory reveals this trade is premature: 100% of cases go from winning to drawn, losing a median of 215 centipawns. The tactical analysis shows the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and king_safety (38%), with tags heavily featuring missed_tactic and move_order errors. The concrete positions confirm that players are grabbing the exchange (winning the rook for a bishop) when instead they should be pursuing a more forcing continuation—often involving threats to the exposed king or maintaining piece activity. The best move was typically a quiet pawn capture or development move (Maia recommends pawn takes pawn 100%). By prematurely taking the exchange, the player loses tempo, relieves pressure on the opponent's king, and allows the opponent to consolidate, converting what was a winning attack or positional bind into a level position.

1906.label: Moving a minor piece passively when a forcing mating sequence or decisive tactical blow was available.
1906.description: This feature fires when players move bishops (56%) or knights (24%) to squares that are either hanging (52%) or merely safe but passive (36%), squandering positions where a forced checkmate or winning tactical sequence existed. The median eval loss of 346 centipawns and the 56% missed-winning-material rate confirm these are not minor inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights.
