The eval trajectory shows these trades convert winning positions to drawn (50%) or drawn positions to losing (50%), with a median cost of 407 centipawns—indicating the exchange itself destroys a latent advantage. The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant tags are 'premature_exchange', 'simplification_error', and 'wrong_simplification', where players choose natural-looking captures instead of maintaining tactical tension. In 83% of cases, a superior move existed that preserved winning material chances. The concrete examples show players trading off active pieces (bishops, knights) when a more precise move order—often involving an intermediate tactic, a forcing sequence, or maintaining piece pressure on the opponent's king—would have preserved a decisive advantage. The motifs (hanging_piece, overloaded_defender, king_safety) reveal that the trades relieve tactical pressure the opponent was struggling to handle.

1966.label: Ignoring critical passed pawn or tactical threats in endgames to make an aimless move that converts a drawn or close position into a loss.
1966.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players make passive or irrelevant moves (often king moves or pawn advances) while ignoring an urgent tactical or strategic threat. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (55%) and 'hangs' (30%) with no captures (85%), indicating these aren't exchange errors but rather quiet moves that overlook something critical. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% of cases turn a drawn position into a losing one, with a median cost of 324 centipawns—consistent with losing a whole piece or allowing an unstoppable promotion. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (80%), and the OPUS analysis reveals the dominant motifs: passed pawns about to promote (29%), forks (14%), and hanging pieces (14%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss and ignoring_threat. The concrete examples confirm this pattern: a bishop retreats while a passed pawn is two squares from queening, a king steps onto a fork square, a rook captures a pawn on a square directly attacked by the opponent's king, and pawn advances fatally weaken structure while ignoring promotion threats. The common thread is a failure to recognize the urgency of the opponent's concrete threat in a simplified position.

1969.label: Player makes a non-capturing move with a major piece or king while their opponent's queen or rook is hanging, throwing away a winning position.
1969.description: This feature identifies positions where a player, holding a winning advantage in the middlegame, plays a move with a rook, queen, or king that completely ignores a simple high-value capture available on the board. The material signature shows 91% of these moves are non-captures, yet Maia's recommended move captures a queen (65%) or rook (32%) — indicating the opponent's major piece was freely available to take. The 'hangs' outcome (47%) confirms the played move often leaves the player's own piece en prise as well, compounding the error. The eval trajectory is devastating: 56% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 921 centipawns, representing a complete game-deciding reversal. The per-position analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif and examples explicitly describing missed captures of hanging queens. The pattern is a player who, perhaps focused on their own plan (king walk, rook lift, passed pawn advance), suffers a tactical blindness to the simplest possible capture on the board — typically a free queen — and instead plays an irrelevant or self-destructive move.

1972.label: Pawn moves in the opening that ignore an imminent knight fork, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
1972.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) during the opening phase (100%) that either hangs material (56%) or appears superficially safe (44%), but critically overlooks a devastating knight fork. The eval trajectory is uniformly drawn->losing with a massive median loss of 378 centipawns, indicating these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic tactical oversights. The dominant motif is fork (78%), and the per-position analysis reveals the recurring theme: moves like ...a6 or ...c6 that 'attack' a knight on b5 without recognizing it can jump to c7 forking king and rook, or pawn moves like c2-c3 that inadvertently open a square for an enemy knight fork. The common tags (opening_trap, knight_fork, tempo_loss) confirm these are well-known opening traps where the player wastes a tempo on a pawn move while a tactical blow is available for the opponent. Maia's recommended responses are predominantly knight moves (56%), confirming the fork execution.

1974.label: Player makes a trade or non-capture move while overlooking a freely available winning capture or forced checkmate.
1974.description: This feature fires when a player has a clearly winning tactical opportunity—often a hanging piece to capture or a forced checkmate sequence—but instead plays a move that trades material or makes a neutral/losing move. The material signature shows 67% trades and the moves are primarily rook/queen moves, but critically 100% of positions involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 9420cp), with positions collapsing from winning to losing or from forced mate to unclear. The tactical analysis confirms this: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%) and the common tags repeatedly cite missed_tactic and missed_capture. The concrete examples show a king moving instead of capturing an undefended queen, a check given instead of capturing a vulnerable rook, and premature exchanges when forced mates were available. The player sees an 'active' move (a trade, a check, a recapture) but is blind to the much stronger simple capture or mating continuation that was immediately available.

1975.label: Playing a routine pawn move while a queen (own or opponent's) hangs undefended, losing massive material in the opening.
1975.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) while a critical tactical obligation—almost always involving a hanging queen—goes completely unaddressed. The material signature shows these moves uniformly 'hang' material with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a queen's value), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (median 914 centipawns lost), sometimes converting a winning position into a losing one. The OPUS analysis and top boards reveal the recurring scenario: a queen (often White's on h7/g6 or Black's exposed piece) is en prise, and instead of capturing it or addressing the threat, the player makes an irrelevant developing or preparatory pawn move. Tags like 'hanging_piece' (dominant at 90%), 'missed_capture', and 'hanging_queen' reinforce that these are not positional misjudgments but pure tactical oversights—failing to see that a major piece can be taken for free. The opening phase (100%) suggests these occur in sharp, early-game positions where queens have ventured forward aggressively.

1970.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square where it can be captured or leaving another piece unprotected by relocating its defender.
1970.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves where the player relocates a major or minor piece (primarily rooks at 43%, queens and knights at 21% each) without capturing anything (71% non-captures), resulting in material being hung (57% of outcomes) with a median loss of 2.0 material units and a massive median eval drop of 469 centipawns. The trajectory shows these errors occur across all eval states—50% in already-losing positions making things worse, but critically 21% turning winning positions into losing ones and 14% converting draws into losses. The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (40%), with recurring themes of pieces being placed on tactically vulnerable squares (e.g., a bishop placed on a skewer square, a rook moved away from a critical defensive file, a queen relocated severing a key tactical connection). The positions consistently show the player ignoring immediate threats or vacating defensive posts, leaving pieces or squares fatally unprotected. Unlike trade errors, these are overwhelmingly non-captures where the moved piece or a piece it was guarding becomes tactically exploitable.

1973.label: Player makes a non-critical move when a forced checkmate sequence was available, squandering a winning mating attack.
1973.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced checkmate (typically mate-in-2 to mate-in-4) but plays a quiet or irrelevant move instead—often a pawn recapture, a rook shuffle, or a defensive-looking move that completely ignores the mating attack. The material signature shows mostly safe/non-capturing moves (pawn 60%, queen 20%, rook 20%) rather than the aggressive queen moves Maia recommends (queen 100%), confirming the player failed to deliver the decisive blow. The eval trajectory is devastating: median loss of ~9610 centipawns, representing the collapse from a forced mate to merely a large or even modest advantage. The positions share a consistent king_safety motif (57%) with mating_attack and missed_mate tags, and the boards show classic mating patterns—bishops on f6/h6 pinning or attacking near a castled king with queens on h4/h6/f6 poised to deliver checkmate. The player loses tempo by making a move that addresses something irrelevant (recapturing a piece, developing passively) while the opponent's king was fatally exposed. This is not a material blunder or a trade error—it is a failure to recognize and execute a short forced checkmate sequence in a middlegame attacking position.

1977.label: Playing a check or promotion that looks forcing but surrenders a critical positional asset or simplifies into a lost position.
1977.description: This feature fires on endgame and middlegame positions where the player delivers a check (83% of activations) or promotes a pawn, but the move is materially costly (median -4.0 net material, 50% loses, 17% hangs) and strategically destructive. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 324 centipawns, turning drawn positions into losing ones (50%) or worsening already-losing positions (50%). The tactical analysis reveals a consistent theme: the player prioritizes an immediately forcing continuation—a rook check capturing the wrong piece, a premature pawn promotion, or a rook capture with check—over a quieter move that would have maintained counterplay or neutralized the opponent's threats. Tags like passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and counterplay_destruction confirm that these moves trade long-term positional assets (doubled rooks on the 7th, promotion sequencing, piece coordination) for a superficially attractive but strategically ruinous forcing move. The Maia engine's preferred alternatives (67% non-captures, often king or knight moves) suggest the correct play was patient rather than forcing.

1976.label: In the opening, player makes a developing or safe move instead of the crushing Qh5+ check that exploits Black's missing f-pawn to win material.
1976.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern, predominantly arising from the Latvian Gambit or similar lines where Black has moved the f-pawn early, leaving the e8-h5 diagonal fatally exposed. The FEN positions almost all show White with a knight on e5 and Black's f-pawn absent, creating the classic Qh5+ tactical shot. Instead of delivering this devastating queen check (Maia's recommendation in 100% of cases), the player makes a 'safe' developing move—Nc3, d3, Bc4, or Nxd3—that is materially non-losing in the immediate sense but squanders a winning advantage. The eval trajectory confirms this: 100% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 141 centipawns. The dominant motif is king_safety (88%), and the recurring tags (missed_tactic, queen_check, exposed_king, latvian_gambit) all point to the same pattern: failing to punish a weakened king position with the immediate forcing Qh5+ that wins material through a combination. The tempo_loss tag also appears because moves like Bc4 allow Black to gain time with d5, erasing White's tactical opportunity entirely.

1978.label: Ignoring immediate mating threats by making irrelevant moves while the king is fatally exposed.
1978.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move (typically a queen move or irrelevant pawn push) that completely ignores a critical king safety crisis, often resulting in forced checkmate. The material signature shows 44% of moves 'hang' something (not a capture, but enabling the opponent's attack) while the player rarely captures or checks—indicating passive or irrelevant moves rather than defensive ones. The eval trajectory shows 44% losing->losing (failing to extend survival in already-lost positions) and 44% losing->winning (likely mislabeled due to mate-score conversions where the opponent's forced mate gets shorter). The Opus analysis overwhelmingly identifies king_safety (70%) as the dominant motif, with tags like exposed_king, missed_tactic, and defensive_failure. The concrete positions consistently show scenarios with back-rank threats, multiple enemy queens/rooks bearing down on the king, and the player making moves like pawn pushes (a4a5, g3g4) or aimless queen moves instead of addressing immediate mating nets. The median centipawn loss of 0.0 is misleading—these are positions already evaluated as forced mate where the move merely accelerates the inevitable, converting survivable-but-lost positions into immediate checkmate sequences.

1979.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (typically a pawn push or king move) when the position demands an immediate tactical capture with a rook.
1979.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'safe' but passive move—usually a pawn push (35%) or rook move (35%) that captures nothing—while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a rook capture (90% rook moves, 55% capturing pawns, 35% capturing bishops). The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic tempo losses: 40% go from winning to drawn, 20% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 389 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the core motif is tempo_loss (appearing in 33% of positions and tagged 3 times), where the player wastes a critical move on an irrelevant pawn push or king shuffle when the position demands an immediate tactical strike—typically a rook capturing an undefended or strategically critical piece/pawn. The boards show complex middlegame positions (95%) with passed pawns and hanging pieces where one precise rook capture was the only strong move, and the player instead made a quiet, non-urgent move that allowed the opponent to consolidate or escape.

1980.label: Retreating the Nimzo-Indian bishop to a5 where it gets trapped by b4.
1980.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake in Nimzo-Indian and similar structures where Black plays ...Ba5 (or makes an analogous bishop move) that leaves the bishop stranded and trappable. The material signature shows bishop moves (78%) that are technically 'safe' at the moment of playing (89%) but the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic loss (median 344cp, drawn->losing 89%), indicating the piece is about to be won. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of trapped_piece (50%) and tags like bishop_misplacement, pawn_advance_wins_piece, and opening_trap. Nearly all positions are in the opening phase (100%) with Nimzo-Indian structures (a3/b4 pawn advances trapping the bishop on a5). Maia consistently recommends capturing the knight on c3 (Bxc3) instead, often with check, which is the standard theoretical continuation. The player fails to recognize that retreating to a5 allows b4 to trap the piece with no adequate escape square.

1981.label: Player makes a king or queen move that ignores an existing mating threat, converting a survivable position into immediate or forced checkmate.
1981.description: This feature identifies positions where the player (predominantly moving their king at 58% or queen at 23%) completely overlooks a lethal mating threat on the board. The material signature shows 73% of moves 'hang' material with a devastating median loss of -4.0 material units, while the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 9369 centipawns—essentially the cost of getting mated. The dominant motifs are king_safety (75%) and discovered_attack (25%), with recurring tags like mating_net, checkmate_threat_ignored, forced_mate, and exposed_king. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing major pieces (queen 31%, rook 27%, bishop 23%), suggesting the correct defense often required taking an attacking piece to defuse the threat. The concrete board positions confirm this: kings stepping into mating nets (Kg8 allowing Qe6+, Kh8 walking into a queen mate), or queen moves ignoring Qxg7# threats. Most positions (54%) are already losing-to-losing, meaning the player was in trouble but still alive until they played the fatal move that allowed immediate mate. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (92%), where mating attacks are most common and king safety is paramount.

1984.label: Exchanging a minor piece that exposes a devastating tactical fork or mating attack.
1984.description: This feature fires when a player initiates a minor piece exchange (bishop or knight capture, with 'trade' as the dominant material outcome) that fatally overlooks a tactical refutation—most commonly a fork (67% of motifs) or a king safety collapse (33%). The material signature shows the player capturing a bishop in every case, suggesting they are drawn to an apparently fair exchange, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: median eval loss of ~95 pawns (i.e., checkmate or decisive material loss), with positions going from drawn-to-losing or losing-to-losing. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: the exchange removes a defensive piece or vacates a critical square, enabling knight forks on the king+queen, back-rank mates, or battery-based checkmates (e.g., Greek gift patterns, Qd3+Bc2 batteries). The player focuses narrowly on the piece trade while missing that the resulting position contains a forced tactical blow. Maia's recommended moves (rooks, queens, pawns) are all non-capturing and defensive/prophylactic, confirming the correct approach was to address the lurking tactic rather than initiate the exchange.

1983.label: Playing a slow or retreating move when a concrete winning tactic (often a queen capture or attack) was available.
1983.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a quiet, passive, or repositioning move—often with a rook or queen—while completely overlooking a concrete tactical opportunity that would win material or deliver a decisive attack. The material signature shows that 87% of moves are non-captures classified as 'safe' (no immediate piece loss), yet Maia's suggested best moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (93%) that capture material (80% capture pawns or knights). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: 47% convert a winning position into a draw, and 20% turn a win into a loss, with a median cost of ~4 pawns. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss 43%, hanging_piece 29%, fork 14%) and example summaries consistently show the player retreating a piece or making a slow positional move (Nb3, Bb3, Rdd2, b5, Re8) when a forcing queen move exploiting hanging pieces, king vulnerability, or undefended pawns was immediately available. The 'missed_tactic' tag appearing in 5/10 positions and 'king_safety' in 4/10 further confirm that these are positions rich in tactical potential that the player failed to calculate, instead defaulting to a non-urgent positional continuation.

1986.label: Pointless queen/bishop checks in the opening that lose tempo and hang material.
1986.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake pattern: delivering a check (100% of activations) with the queen (66%) or bishop (34%) that accomplishes nothing concrete. The material signature shows these checks frequently hang the checking piece (53%) with a median loss of -1.0 material, occurring overwhelmingly in the opening phase (84%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with recurring tags like 'premature_check', 'pointless_check', and 'development'—the opponent simply blocks or interposes with a developing move, gaining tempo. The eval trajectory shows these checks are game-changing blunders (median 280cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing (32%) or winning to drawn/losing (18%). The top boards reveal the classic pattern: early Qa5+ or Qe7+ checks that allow the opponent to develop with tempo (e.g., Bd2 blocking while completing development), or bishop checks that leave the piece stranded and vulnerable. Maia's suggested alternatives are quiet developing moves (knights, pawns, bishops) that maintain the position rather than forcing the opponent to improve their piece placement for free.

1982.label: King castles into an unsafe position where tactical threats immediately exploit its placement.
1982.description: All top activating positions show the player moving their king (100% king moves), specifically castling (O-O or O-O-O), with no captures involved (100% non-capture). The material signature shows 44% of these moves hang material and 56% are 'safe' in the immediate sense, but the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 269 centipawns, with 30% of cases going from drawn to losing and 26% making a losing position worse. The dominant motifs—king_safety (25%), hanging_piece (38%), and overloaded_defender (12%)—combined with tags like king_safety(5), missed_tactic(4), and tempo_loss(4) confirm that these are castling decisions that walk the king directly into tactical danger. The top boards explicitly show O-O and O-O-O moves where the king lands on a square exposed to existing attacks, pawn storms, or piece activity. Maia's suggested alternatives (pawns 33%, bishops 30%, queens 26%) indicate that developing, defending, or counterattacking moves were available instead. This is a positional misjudgment: the player castles reflexively or to 'safety' but actually places the king on a more vulnerable square where opponent's forces are already aimed.

1985.label: In winning endgame positions, player makes a queen or rook move that either hangs the piece or allows a devastating counterattack, squandering a won game.
1985.description: This feature captures a specific pattern of endgame collapses where a player with a winning or drawn position makes a careless major piece move (queen 46%, rook 36%) that throws away the advantage. The eval trajectory shows winning->drawn (36%) or winning->losing (9%) with a massive median loss of 242 centipawns, indicating these are game-changing errors rather than minor inaccuracies. The material signature shows moves are mostly 'safe' (73%) — meaning the player isn't making captures but rather repositioning pieces — yet Maia's recommended responses involve capturing major pieces (rook 46%, queen 46%) with check (91%), revealing that the player's move leaves their piece hanging or walks into a fork/skewer. The dominant motifs of pawn_endgame (56%) and hanging_piece (33%) combined with tags like 'simplification_error' and 'tempo_loss' confirm this: players in simplified endgame positions make passive or aimless major piece moves (often queens wandering to squares controlled by the opponent's rook, or rooks moving away from critical files) that overlook immediate tactical refutations. The concrete positions show queen and rook endgames where the player's piece lands on an undefended square or blocks a critical line, allowing the opponent to win material with check.

1987.label: Failing to properly address passed pawn promotion threats in late-game positions, allowing forced wins or mates.
1987.description: This feature fires on endgame and late-middlegame positions where the player makes a king, rook, or pawn move that fatally mishandles a passed pawn situation. The material signature shows no captures (100% non-capture moves) with mostly 'safe' outcomes—meaning nothing is immediately hung—yet the eval trajectory reveals a massive median cost of 312 centipawns, often converting drawn positions into lost ones (30%) or accelerating already-losing positions (50%). The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (56%) and promotion_error (22%), with tempo_loss (11%) also prominent. Examining the boards confirms this: nearly every position features advanced passed pawns (on the 7th rank or supported) where the player either fails to blockade, fails to promote their own passer, or makes a tempo-losing move that allows the opponent's pawn to queen or enables a mating net. The king_safety and piece_activity tags reflect how misplacing the king or rook relative to the promotion square is the core error. These are not tactical oversights in the traditional sense but rather endgame technique failures where the player doesn't appreciate the urgency of promotion threats.

1988.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of executing a winning Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7/h2.
1988.description: This feature fires when a player misses a classic Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+ or Bxh2+) during the opening phase. The material signature shows the player moved a knight (31%) or bishop (27%) safely (88% safe moves, no captures in 96% of cases), while Maia consistently recommends a bishop capture on a pawn with check (bishop 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%). The Opus analysis confirms king_safety as the universal motif with explicit tags for greek_gift, greek_gift_sacrifice, and Bxh7_sacrifice appearing repeatedly. The eval trajectory shows this costs a median of 246 centipawns, often converting a winning position into merely drawn (46%) or reducing the winning advantage (38%). The board positions consistently show French Defense and similar pawn structures where a bishop on d3 has a clear diagonal to h7, a knight on f3 is ready to follow up with Ng5+, and the opponent has castled kingside—the textbook Greek Gift setup that the player fails to recognize, opting instead for routine development (Be3, Qc2, O-O, etc.).

1989.label: Player makes a move that ignores a lethal queen-bishop battery or diagonal mating attack, allowing checkmate or decisive material loss.
1989.description: This feature fires when players overlook an existing or imminent mating threat along a diagonal, typically involving a queen-bishop battery targeting weakened king-side squares (especially g2/g7 or back-rank adjacent squares). The material signature shows that 62% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) while the rest are trades that lose material (median net -1.0), indicating moves that fail to address the real threat. The eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of ~94 pawns (checkmates), with many positions going from winning or drawn to immediately lost. The tactical analysis confirms this: 75% involve king_safety motifs, 25% back_rank threats, with recurring tags like 'checkmate_in_one', 'queen_bishop_battery', 'long_diagonal_weakness', and 'g2_weakness'. The concrete positions consistently show bishops on long diagonals (b7, b2) paired with queens targeting weakened king positions, where the player makes a superficially reasonable developing or attacking move but catastrophically ignores the diagonal mate threat. Maia consistently recommends bishop moves (100%), suggesting the AI recognizes the diagonal defense/attack that the player missed.

1993.label: Player makes a move that ignores an immediate tactical threat, leaving pieces hanging or undefended.
1993.description: This feature captures positions where the player ignores a critical immediate tactical threat to pursue an unrelated plan. The material signature shows 67% of moves hang material (non-captures that drop pieces) with a median net loss of -5.0 material, and 100% of positions had winning material available that was missed. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), with recurring tags of undefended_piece, check_exploitation, and missed_tactic. The example summaries consistently describe players who ignore immediate threats (Qxh1+ with check, Qxc3+ capturing an undefended knight) to pursue positional ideas or passive moves that don't address the crisis. The eval trajectory shows most positions (67%) go from losing to losing, suggesting players already under pressure compound their difficulties by failing to address the most urgent tactical problem on the board, losing a median of 290 centipawns. The phase is predominantly opening/early middlegame (67% opening) where king safety issues and undeveloped positions create tactical vulnerabilities that demand immediate attention.

1990.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn move in the opening that squanders a significant advantage by losing tempo and allowing the opponent tactical counterplay.
1990.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a player, often holding a winning or near-winning position in the opening phase (76% opening), plays a passive pawn advance (81% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) instead of the one critical move that maintains their advantage. The eval trajectory shows these moves are devastating—median 279cp lost, with 38% going from drawn to losing and 19% from winning to drawn—indicating the player is throwing away substantial edges. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss 43%, hanging_piece 29%, fork 14%) reveal that these slow pawn pushes either waste critical tempo needed for development or leave pieces tactically vulnerable to forks and attacks that weren't possible before. The top boards confirm this: positions like 8...c6 instead of d4, or e6-e5 instead of a more active piece move, where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' but passive pawn move that either fails to challenge the center decisively or leaves pieces uncoordinated and exposed. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve bishops (38%) and captures (19%), suggesting the correct play was active piece deployment or a tactical strike, not a quiet pawn push.

1991.label: Passive or misdirected king moves in pawn endgames that surrender critical opposition, tempo, or key squares.
1991.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame mistake pattern: the player makes a king (or minor piece) move that appears safe materially (100% 'safe' outcome, no pieces hang or are traded) but catastrophically misplays king activity in a pawn endgame. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 480 centipawns, often converting drawn positions into losses (50%) or throwing away wins (25%). The tactical analysis consistently flags king_activity (6 occurrences), tempo_loss (4), opposition (3), and passed_pawn (4) as the dominant themes. The concrete positions are all pure or near-pure pawn endgames where the correct move involved seizing opposition, maintaining central king control, or advancing toward a critical square, but instead the player moved the king passively, retreated a piece pointlessly (Nc1, Be5), or walked to the wrong flank (Ka5, Kf4 instead of maintaining centralization). Maia's recommended moves are universally king moves, confirming the correct plan was always about king positioning. This is a classic amateur endgame error: failing to recognize that in king-and-pawn endings, every tempo and every square of king activity is decisive.

1992.label: Trading the active bishop for a knight on c6 when a tactical continuation (typically Nxd5) wins material outright.
1992.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake where White prematurely exchanges the Bb5 for the Nc6 (or makes a similarly passive bishop/queen move) instead of exploiting a concrete tactical opportunity—almost always Nxd5 exploiting an overloaded Black queen on b6. The material signature shows bishop moves (71%) executing trades (57%) with a median net material of 0.0, confirming these are exchanges rather than blunders. However, the eval trajectory reveals these trades uniformly convert winning positions into drawn ones (100% winning->drawn, median loss 256cp), indicating the player squanders a decisive advantage. Maia's recommended moves are always knight moves (100%) capturing pawns (86%), consistent with the Nxd5 tactic that exploits tactical motifs like overloaded defenders, hanging pieces, and tempo loss. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies that the d5 pawn is effectively free because the knight fork on d5 attacks the queen, but instead the player releases central tension with the premature bishop exchange. The positions are uniformly opening-phase Semi-Slav/QGD structures with the characteristic Bb5, Nc3, d4 vs ...Qb6, ...Nc6, ...d5 configuration.

1996.label: Moving a piece (often king or rook) that leaves another piece unprotected, resulting in catastrophic material loss.
1996.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their king (33%) or rook (29%) and inadvertently leave another piece completely undefended — a classic hanging piece blunder. The material signature is stark: 75% of moves result in a hang (non-capture that drops a piece), with a median net material loss of -3.0 (roughly a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding errors: 42% convert winning positions into losing ones, with a median eval swing of 712 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (57%), supplemented by tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'tempo_loss'. The concrete positions show kings stepping away from pieces they were defending (e.g., Kc5 abandoning a knight on a5), rooks moving to passive squares while leaving bishops or pawns en prise, and generally failing to account for the defensive duties of the piece being moved. Maia's suggested alternatives (bishops 33%, knights 21%) indicate that developing or repositioning minor pieces was typically the correct plan rather than the king/rook moves actually played.

1995.label: Moving a piece to a square where it or another piece is left undefended, allowing the opponent to win material by capturing a hanging piece.
1995.description: This feature captures moves that leave a piece hanging (48% of moves result in a hang), typically costing substantial material (median -1.0, median eval lost 358 centipawns). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (40%), supplemented by trapped_piece (20%) and overloaded_defender (20%), indicating the player makes a move that either leaves their own piece unprotected or fails to notice that another piece has become tactically vulnerable. The trajectory shows these errors frequently occur in already-losing positions (43% losing->losing) but also catastrophically convert drawn or winning positions into losing ones (24% drawn->losing, 10% winning->losing). Maia consistently recommends a rook move capturing a rook (100%), suggesting that in nearly every case, the correct response was to capture the hanging piece with a rook. The concrete examples confirm this: players make developing or attacking moves (bishop retreats, pawn pushes, knight maneuvers, king moves) while overlooking that a piece—often a rook on an open file—is left undefended and can be captured. This is a classic tactical oversight where the player's move has a plausible positional purpose but ignores an immediate hanging-piece threat.

1994.label: Playing a slow or routine move when the position demands immediate tactical action, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
1994.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a passive, non-urgent move (often a pawn push, quiet king move like castling or Kh1, or a piece retreat) when concrete tactical action was required—typically a knight capture or tactical strike (Maia recommends knight captures 100% of the time, usually taking a bishop). The tempo_loss motif appears in 100% of cases, and the Opus analyses consistently describe situations where the player chose a 'routine' or 'slow' move instead of executing an immediate tactic that would have justified a previous aggressive piece placement. The material signature shows the played moves are mostly 'safe' (64%) or 'hangs' (29%)—meaning the player either did nothing or actually left a piece en prise by ignoring the forcing continuation. The eval trajectory (median 229cp lost, with 43% winning->drawn and 21% drawn->losing) confirms these are substantial positional collapses rather than minor inaccuracies. The pattern is clear: in sharp opening/middlegame positions with pieces already aggressively deployed (especially knights on outposts like g5, f5, e6), the player plays a slow developing or prophylactic move, allowing the opponent to consolidate, reposition, or seize the initiative that was rightfully the player's.

1998.label: Player makes a safe-looking move that squanders a winning position by missing a forcing tactical shot (discovered attack, fork, or combination).
1998.description: This feature fires when players in winning middlegame positions make quiet, non-capturing moves (often bishop or king moves that appear safe) while missing a decisive tactical blow. The material signature shows 71% safe moves with no captures, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic losses (median 517cp), with 71% going from winning to drawn and 14% from winning to losing. Maia consistently recommends piece captures (86% pawn captures) that deliver check (100%), indicating the missed moves were forcing tactical shots. The dominant motifs—discovered attacks (33%), forks (17%), and tempo loss (33%)—along with tags like deflection, combination, and overloaded defender confirm these are positions where a concrete forcing sequence wins material or delivers a mating attack. The players instead chose passive moves (Kf1, Rd1, f4) that surrendered all initiative and allowed the opponent to consolidate.

2000.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive or restraining role, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a devastating tactical response.
2000.description: This feature captures moves where a player relocates a minor piece, bishop (60%), rook (20%), or knight (20%) away from a square where it was performing a crucial defensive or restraining function. The material signature shows these moves predominantly hang material (40%) or end up slightly down (40%), with a median loss of 2.0 material units—indicating the player isn't making a deliberate exchange but rather abandoning a key post. The eval trajectory is severe (median 403cp lost), with 40% converting drawn positions to losing and 20% throwing wins entirely. The tactical motifs center on king_safety (67%) and fork (33%), confirmed by the per-position analyses: releasing restraint on a file allows doubled rooks on the 7th, removing a key defender enables an unstoppable fork (Nb5 on c7), or an unsound sacrifice fails because the piece was needed defensively. The common thread is that the moved piece was the linchpin holding the position together—its departure creates immediate tactical catastrophe through forks or king-side attacks that didn't exist one move prior.

1999.label: King moves that waste tempo in lost or critical endgame positions with passed pawns and promotion threats.
1999.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player loses tempo in positions involving passed pawns and promotion threats. The material signature shows exclusively king moves with no captures (100% king, 100% no capture), and the positions are overwhelmingly already losing (86% losing->losing). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with passed_pawn and king_safety as supporting themes. Examining the top boards reveals a consistent pattern: positions with advanced passed pawns (often on the 2nd rank about to promote) where the player's king retreats or sidesteps to a less optimal square, wasting a critical tempo. The median eval loss is modest (28cp), suggesting these are subtle inaccuracies rather than game-losing blunders—the player is typically already losing but makes the opponent's conversion easier by misplacing the king rather than maximizing resistance or maintaining proximity to key squares. The positions frequently feature queen vs. pawn endgames or mutual promotion races where every tempo counts.

1997.label: Missing a critical tempo move (often a check or pawn advance) in a won pawn endgame, allowing the opponent to improve their position.
1997.description: This feature detects a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a 'safe' king or pawn move in a pawn endgame instead of the precise continuation (usually a pawn advance delivering check or creating a promotion threat). The material signature shows king moves (75%) and pawn moves (25%) that don't capture or give check, while Maia consistently recommends a pawn move that delivers check (100%). The positions are all endgames (100%) featuring passed pawns and critical tempi. The tactical analysis highlights tempo_loss (3 tags), passed_pawn (4 tags), and pawn_endgame (3 tags) as dominant motifs—the player fails to exploit the forcing nature of checks or promotion threats, instead making a natural-looking but imprecise king maneuver. The eval trajectory confirms these are positions where the missed move would have been decisive: 100% of cases miss winning material, and the median eval loss in the losing->drawn cases is catastrophic (-10000cp, i.e., converting a win into a draw by missing a forced promotion sequence). The concrete positions (e.g., Kc5 instead of advancing a passed pawn, or a5 instead of c3+) all show the same pattern: the player's move looks reasonable but squanders a tempo that was essential for the promotion race or opposition battle.

2002.label: Trading an active bishop relieves tension and squanders a positional or tactical advantage.
2002.description: This feature fires when a player makes a bishop exchange (83% bishop moves, capturing knights/bishops/rooks at roughly equal material — 89% trades) that constitutes a premature simplification. The eval trajectory shows these trades are costly: median 266 centipawns lost, with 28% going from winning to drawn and 22% from drawn to losing, indicating the player is throwing away an advantage. The tactical analysis confirms this is overwhelmingly a positional mistake (56%) centered on releasing tension (tagged 4 times), premature exchange (4 times), and piece activity loss (4 times). The concrete positions show active bishops on diagonals (g4, b5, e5, c5) being traded into positions where the opponent's king was vulnerable or where the bishop was exerting significant pressure. Rather than maintaining the tension and exploiting the bishop's activity, the player simplifies into an equal or worse position. Maia's preferred moves (rooks 33%, knights 28%) suggest better alternatives existed that maintained pressure rather than exchanging.

2004.label: In the opening, player moves a bishop or pawn to a square that leaves a piece hanging, missing an obvious recapture of an opponent's hanging bishop.
2004.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a non-capture move (75% bishop, 25% pawn) that hangs material (75% of moves result in a piece being left en prise), while Maia's recommended move captures a hanging bishop in every case. The eval trajectory is devastating and consistent: all positions swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 492 centipawns—roughly a full minor piece. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 38%, tempo_loss 38%) combined with the tags (missed_tactic, tempo_loss, development) tell a clear story: in opening positions where the opponent has left a bishop hanging (often on c3 after a Winawer/exchange-type structure), the player ignores the free capture and instead develops passively or makes a positional move (like Bd2, Bd3, d3, or Qb3), failing to collect the available material. The top boards confirm this—multiple positions feature an opponent's bishop sitting undefended on c3, and the player moves elsewhere, gifting the opponent a full piece advantage.

2001.label: Giving a purposeless queen check that wastes tempo and allows the opponent to improve their position.
2001.description: This feature fires on queen checks (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that serve no constructive purpose—classic 'checking for the sake of checking.' The material signature shows these aren't capturing moves (87% no capture) and roughly half the time the queen itself becomes hanging (47% hangs), yet the median net material is 0.0, indicating the immediate material loss is often avoided but at severe positional cost. The eval trajectory confirms substantial damage: a median of 232 centipawns lost, with many positions going from winning to drawn or drawn to losing. The tactical analysis is definitive: 75% are tagged with tempo_loss, and the recurring tags include 'premature_check,' 'pointless_check,' and 'king_improves_after_check.' The OPUS summaries explicitly describe these as 'checking for the sake of checking' where the opponent's king escapes to a safer square or interposes with a developing/useful move. Meanwhile, Maia's recommended moves (rook 40%, queen 23%, pawn 17%) suggest that constructive developing or attacking moves were available instead of the wasteful check. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (90%), where tempo is critical and a misplaced queen check squanders the initiative.

2003.label: Moving minor pieces or pawns while ignoring critical king safety threats, allowing devastating attacks on exposed kings.
2003.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes seemingly reasonable minor piece or pawn moves (pawn 42%, bishop 33%, knight 17%) that fatally ignore king safety vulnerabilities. The material signature shows these moves frequently hang material (42%) or result in trades (50%) with a median cost of 272 centipawns. The dominant motif is king_safety (60%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, king_in_center, and open_file_exploitation. The trajectory shows these mistakes are catastrophic: 33% convert winning positions to losing ones, and 42% accelerate already-losing positions into hopeless ones. The concrete positions reveal kings stuck in the center on open files (d6, e1 without castling), while Maia's recommended moves frequently involve king retreats (42% king moves) or queen activity exploiting the exposed king. The player's moves place pieces on vulnerable squares (open files, undefended diagonals) without recognizing that the opponent's next move exploits the king's exposure with checks, discovered attacks, or file-based tactics. The pattern is consistently one of positional/tactical blindness to king danger rather than simple material miscalculation.

2005.label: Developing or moving a bishop to a square directly controlled by an enemy knight, hanging a full piece.
2005.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening-phase blunder where the player moves a bishop (75% of activations) to a square attacked by an opponent's knight, immediately hanging it. The top activating positions overwhelmingly show the pattern ...Bg4 played into a knight on e5 (Nxg4), a simple piece-hanging oversight. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in a hang, and the eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 489cp lost), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones. Opus analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, with repeated notes about pattern-recognition errors where the player instinctively develops the bishop to g4 without registering the knight's control of that square. The tags (tempo_loss, missed_tactic, development) reinforce that this is a development-phase oversight rather than a complex positional misjudgment.

2006.label: Player makes an inferior queen/rook move while overlooking an available winning capture of undefended material.
2006.description: This feature fires when a player moves their queen or rook (60%/40%) without capturing anything (40% no capture) or capturing something minor, while a much stronger capture was available. The Maia best-move analysis shows 80% of the time the correct move was capturing a queen or significant material (80% Maia captures queen), indicating the player consistently overlooks free or loosely-defended pieces. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic costs (median 280cp lost), with positions shifting from winning to losing/drawn in 60% of cases. The tactical motifs—hanging_piece, overloaded_defender, and undefended material—combined with tags like 'queen_capture' and 'hanging_piece' all point to the same pattern: the player ignores an available winning capture (often of an undefended queen or major piece) in favor of a move that looks active but accomplishes far less. The per-position summaries explicitly describe overlooking 'free captures' and 'undefended' pieces, confirming this is a visibility/awareness failure rather than a strategic misjudgment.

2007.label: Moving a rook or pawn away from a critical defensive post, fatally exposing the king to back-rank or mating threats.
2007.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves a rook (47%) or pawn (35%) in a way that hangs material (65%) with a median cost of ~190 centipawns. The dominant motif is king_safety (57%), supplemented by back_rank (14%) and tempo_loss (14%). The Opus analysis consistently describes scenarios where the moved piece was performing a vital defensive function—guarding a back rank, covering a key square, or shielding the king—and its relocation allows immediate tactical exploitation (forced mates, devastating checks, or piece wins). The eval trajectory shows these mostly occur in already-losing positions (53% losing->losing), suggesting players under pressure make the final critical error of abandoning their defensive anchor. The concrete examples (Re2 abandoning back-rank defense, Rc1 abandoning second-rank coverage, Kg5 walking into a tactical zone, rook moves leaving kings exposed) all share the pattern of a piece leaving its defensive duty, transforming a difficult but resistant position into an immediately lost one.

2008.label: Playing a flashy check that hangs or sacrifices material without sufficient compensation in the opening.
2008.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake where players deliver a check (100% check rate) by moving a minor piece (knight or bishop) into an exposed square, sacrificing or hanging it for at most a pawn and one tempo of king displacement. The material signature shows the move either hangs a piece outright (50%) or comes out slightly down (50%), with a median net loss of 2.0 pawns—far from a sound exchange. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: positions go from winning to drawn or drawn to losing, with a median loss of 424 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant tags like 'premature_attack,' 'check_is_not_always_good,' 'unsound_sacrifice,' and 'piece_sacrifice_unsound.' The concrete positions (e.g., ...Bxf2+ against a castled king, ...Nf3+ where Bxf3 recaptures trivially) all show the same pattern: the player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check but the resulting position offers no follow-up, leaving them down material with nothing to show for it. This is the classic amateur trap of 'patzer sees a check, patzer plays a check.'

2012.label: Moving a bishop to a square where it is immediately captured or trapped, losing a full piece.
2012.description: This feature fires when a player moves their bishop (90% of cases) to a square that is directly controlled by an opponent's piece or pawn, effectively hanging it for no compensation. The material signature shows 90% 'hangs' with a median net loss of -3.0 (a full piece), confirming these are non-capture moves that simply drop material. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—37% go from drawn to losing and 10% from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 456 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (67%) and trapped_piece (33%), with tags like 'board_vision_error' and 'pawn_captures_piece' indicating the player overlooked that the destination square was covered by a pawn or minor piece. The top boards reinforce this: Bg4 into an h3 pawn, Be7 freeing a trapped piece, and multiple instances of bishops landing on g4/g5 where they are immediately captured. These occur in the opening (42%) and middlegame (58%), suggesting hasty development or impulsive bishop sorties without checking basic square control.

2011.label: A minor piece move that blocks a friendly piece's defensive line, leaving another piece hanging.
2011.description: This feature detects a highly specific tactical blunder pattern where a player moves a knight (49%) or bishop (24%) to a square that physically interferes with a friendly piece's defensive coverage, causing another piece to hang. The material signature is stark: 83% of moves result in a hung piece with a median loss of 3.0 material units (typically a full piece), and 83% are non-captures—meaning the player isn't trading but simply dropping material through self-inflicted geometric interference. The Opus analysis confirms this with 100% 'hanging_piece' motif and recurring tags like 'self_block,' 'geometric_interference,' and 'piece_coordination_collapse.' Concrete examples show knights blocking queen defense of rooks along files, bishops blocking rook defense of knights along ranks, and knights obstructing diagonal defense lines. The eval trajectory (median 424cp lost, with 18% drawn->losing and 14% winning->losing) shows these are game-deciding blunders that frequently throw away advantageous or balanced positions. These moves often appear aggressive or purposeful (tagged 'aggressive_looking_blunder') but fatally overlook that the moved piece now obstructs a critical defensive geometry between two other friendly pieces.

2009.label: Player makes a move that leaves a piece undefended and immediately capturable, typically losing major material.
2009.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player makes a move (most often a pawn advance) that either directly hangs a piece or removes a critical defender, leaving material en prise. The material signature is stark: 67% of moves hang a piece outright and 33% lose material through an exchange imbalance, with a median net loss of 6.0 pawns worth of material—indicating queens and rooks being dropped. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders (median 649cp lost), with 50% converting winning positions into losing ones. The Opus tactical analysis reveals the universal motif is 'hanging_piece' (100%), with tags like 'ignored_threat', 'hanging_queen', 'removing_the_guard', and 'unprotected_piece' reinforcing that these are one-move oversights where the player fails to notice their own piece is undefended or that their move removes a crucial defender. The concrete positions show pawn advances that open diagonals to undefended queens (d3-d4 leaving Qa4 hanging), pawn pushes that remove guards from rooks (d4-d5 unprotecting Re5), and moves made while ignoring an immediate capture threat on an exposed piece. Maia's recommended moves (67% queen moves) confirm the engine sees obvious captures of the hanging material.

2010.label: Player makes a move that leaves a piece undefended, allowing the opponent to win material through a simple capture or tactical shot.
2010.description: This feature identifies positions where the player overlooks a hanging piece or an insufficiently defended piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss. The material signature shows 33% 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) and 43% trades that likely represent unfavorable exchanges, with a median net material of -1.0. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 67%, combined with 'overloaded_defender' at 33%, indicating the player fails to notice that a piece is unprotected or that a defender is taxed beyond its capacity. The eval trajectory is devastating: 24% of cases swing from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 527 centipawns, indicating these are game-deciding oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The concrete positions confirm this pattern—pieces left en prise on exposed squares (rook on d1 hanging to a knight, pieces left undefended after a move), where the player makes a developing or repositioning move without noticing the immediate tactical threat to their own material. Maia's recommended moves (often rook or knight captures) confirm that simple captures of hanging pieces were available. The middlegame phase (81%) is consistent with complex positions where piece safety is easy to overlook amid multiple threats.

2013.label: Active piece moves that fatally ignore back-rank mate vulnerability due to an entombed king.
2013.description: This feature fires when a player makes a materially 'safe' move (82% safe, often a rook capture of a pawn for +1 material) that catastrophically overlooks a back-rank checkmate threat. The positional signature is unmistakable: Opus analysis tags back_rank in 100% of cases, with recurring themes of kings entombed behind f2-g2-h2 pawns with no luft. The player typically moves a rook (55%) to capture a pawn (48%) or reposition a piece, while the best move (Maia's recommendation, 82% pawn moves) would have been creating an escape square or addressing the back-rank weakness. The eval trajectory is devastating—median loss of ~101 pawns (i.e., checkmate)—with 35% flipping from losing to winning for the opponent and 18% from drawn to winning, confirming these are game-deciding oversights. The boards consistently show endgame-approaching middlegames where the player greedily grabs material or activates a piece while their back rank is fatally exposed, allowing immediate or near-immediate mate via rook invasion on the first/eighth rank.

2015.label: King moves that squander tempo in won pawn endgames instead of advancing or supporting passed pawns.
2015.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player is already winning but makes a slight tempo-wasting king move instead of the optimal pawn advance (Maia consistently recommends a pawn move). The material signature shows safe king moves with no captures—nothing is hung or traded—yet the tactical analysis reveals recurring tempo_loss (8 tags), passed_pawn (9 tags), and king_activity (8 tags) motifs. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning->winning positions with minimal centipawn loss (median 7cp), meaning the mistake is a subtle inaccuracy rather than a game-losing blunder. The top boards are all king-and-pawn endgames where precise tempo and opposition matter: the player shuffles the king or moves it to a suboptimal square when a direct pawn push or better king placement would maintain or increase the winning margin. The pattern is a failure to calculate pawn-race tempi precisely in simplified positions.

2020.label: A queen check that wastes tempo, leaving the queen misplaced or trapped while hanging material.
2020.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check with the queen (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that results in hanging material (100% hangs, median -2.0 net material). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 386cp lost), often converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (50% drawn->losing, 33% winning->losing). The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (67%), with recurring tags of premature_queen_sortie, king_safety concerns, and missed tactics. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show early-game Qh4+ or Qh5+ checks—classic beginner moves that look aggressive but allow the opponent to develop with tempo by attacking the exposed queen. The queen ends up displaced on h4/h5 where it accomplishes nothing after a simple g3 or similar defensive move, while the opponent consolidates development advantage and often traps or wins the queen outright.

2014.chip: King Tempo Loss in Pawn Endgame
2014.label: King moves to the wrong square in a pawn endgame, losing critical tempo or opposition and squandering a winning advantage.
2014.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring endgame error: the player moves their king (75% of activating moves are king moves) in a pure pawn endgame (78% pawn_endgame motif, 100% endgame phase) to a square that loses a critical tempo or the opposition. The material signature shows these are 'safe' moves—nothing is immediately hung or captured—yet the median eval loss is a devastating 550 centipawns, with 50% of cases converting a winning position into a draw. The dominant tags (tempo_loss, king_activity, opposition) confirm the positional mechanism: the king retreats or sidesteps when it needed to advance or maintain opposition, allowing the opponent to blockade passed pawns or achieve a drawn position. The Opus analysis repeatedly highlights that only one or two king moves maintain the win, and the chosen square fatally mismanages the tempo battle that governs pawn endgame outcomes. This is not a tactical oversight but a failure of endgame technique—specifically, choosing a king square that looks natural but violates the precise tempo/opposition requirements of the position.

2016.label: Pawn moves that waste critical development tempo in the opening, leaving pieces hanging.
2016.description: This feature captures a specific class of opening mistake where the player makes a pawn move (100% pawn moves) that constitutes a severe tempo loss, allowing the opponent's knight (Maia's response is 100% knight moves) to exploit the position. The material signature shows these are non-captures that hang material (net median -2.0, approximately a full piece), and the eval trajectory consistently shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 259cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (62%), with development and piece_activity as recurring tags. The top boards illustrate this clearly: moves like 3.d4 (instead of saving a threatened knight), 7...b6 (slow preparation instead of challenging the center), Ng1 (undeveloping a piece), a2a3 (a do-nothing pawn move), and Gh3 (a purposeless bishop move) all represent moments where the player chose a passive or preparatory pawn/piece move instead of addressing an immediate tactical obligation. The opponent's knight then exploits the wasted tempo to win material or seize a decisive positional advantage.

2017.label: Losing critical tempo in endgame positions by making passive or purposeless moves instead of the one precise move required.
2017.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern. All positions are endgames (100%) where the player typically moves a pawn (58%) or rook (25%) without capturing anything (92% no capture). The moves are objectively 'safe' in that nothing is immediately hanging (83%), yet they miss winning material 75% of the time and cost a median of 446 centipawns — often converting winning positions to drawn (33%) or drawn positions to losing (33%). The dominant motif is tempo_loss (33%), supported by tags like passed_pawn, king_activity, and endgame_technique. The concrete positions reveal scenarios where only one precise move exists (e.g., activating the king, blocking a passed pawn, or saving an exposed piece) but the player wastes a crucial tempo on an irrelevant pawn push or passive rook move. This is not a material blunder in the traditional sense — nothing is captured or immediately dropped — but rather a fatal loss of timing in positions where every single tempo determines the outcome of the endgame.

2021.label: Moving the king when urgent tactical threats (hanging pieces, back-rank mates, or king-safety crises) demand a different response.
2021.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their king (54% of activations) in the middlegame (88%) while ignoring a more critical tactical issue—typically a hanging piece, back-rank vulnerability, or king-safety crisis. The material signature shows that 42% of these moves hang material outright, with a median net loss of -1.0 piece and a massive median eval drop of 288 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (25%), indicating that the king move either worsens the king's own safety or neglects a piece left en prise elsewhere. The eval trajectory shows 38% go from losing to deeper losing and another 12% from drawn to losing, suggesting these are not speculative king walks but panicked or misguided king moves that overlook the real tactical priority. Maia's recommended alternatives frequently involve piece moves (queen 19%, knight 12%) or captures (pawn 23%, rook 15%), confirming that the correct response was addressing material or tactical threats rather than relocating the king. Concrete examples include Ke1 ignoring a hanging bishop, Kf8 walking into a rook loss, and king moves that allow forced checkmate sequences.

2019.label: Moving a piece without noticing an impending knight fork that wins material.
2019.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a non-capturing move (typically king, rook, or bishop) that appears safe but fatally overlooks a knight fork. The material signature shows 50% of moves hang a piece outright while the rest appear superficially safe, yet 100% miss winning material (Maia consistently suggests pawn moves, indicating the engine saw simple alternatives). The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 598 centipawns lost, with 50% swinging from winning to losing and 33% from drawn to losing. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is fork (80%), with 'knight_fork' and 'hanging_piece' as the most common tags. Examining the boards reveals a consistent pattern: a white or black knight on an aggressive square (e5, d4, g5, e4) has access to a forking square with check, and the player's move either places a piece on the fork square or removes a defender. Examples include placing a rook on d8 where Nc6+ forks king and rook, castling queenside allowing Nxf2 forking rook and king, and moving king to g7 where a knight can exploit the exposed position. The player consistently fails to calculate the opponent's knight geometry one move ahead.

2018.label: Trading down pieces in already-losing positions, often removing key defensive resources or enabling opponent's passed pawns.
2018.description: This feature fires on exchanges (65% trades, median net material 0.0) made in already-losing positions that worsen the situation further (78% losing->losing, 17% drawn->losing, median 215cp lost). The player captures high-value pieces (queen 35%, rook 35%) primarily with rooks (48%) and queens (22%), but these trades are strategically catastrophic. The Opus analysis reveals the pattern: players trade away their most important defensive pieces (bishops controlling key diagonals, queens providing counterplay, knights blocking invasion routes) in exchange for nominally equal material, but the resulting simplified position is hopeless. Tags like passed_pawn(6), pawn_endgame(2), and promotion_error(22%) show that after the trade, opponent's passed pawns or promotion threats become unstoppable. The concrete examples confirm this: trading a bishop for a pawn removes a blockader, trading queens enters a lost pawn endgame, capturing a knight removes the piece blocking a back-rank mate. Maia's preferred moves (70% non-captures) suggest the correct approach was maintaining piece tension rather than simplifying. These are not blunders in the traditional sense—the material exchange is equal—but the player fails to recognize that their specific pieces serve irreplaceable defensive functions in an already difficult position.

2023.label: Giving a purposeless check in a critical endgame position instead of addressing an urgent promotion threat.
2023.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern where a player delivers a check (100% of activating moves are checks) that serves no constructive purpose, squandering critical tempo needed to combat an advancing passed pawn or promotion threat. The material signature shows the move itself is 'safe'—nothing is immediately lost—but the eval trajectory reveals a median cost of 252 centipawns, often converting winning or drawn positions into drawn or lost ones. The tactical analysis confirms this through dominant motifs of tempo_loss (38%) and promotion_error (25%), with recurring tags like 'pointless_check,' 'passed_pawn,' and 'promotion_threat.' The concrete positions all involve late endgames with advanced passed pawns (typically on the 7th rank) where the opponent's promotion is imminent. Instead of blockading or capturing the dangerous pawn (usually with a rook), the player moves a bishop or rook to deliver a visually attractive check that actually improves the opponent's king position or wastes the one tempo needed to stop promotion. Maia's suggested moves (100% rook, no checks) consistently point to direct anti-promotion prophylaxis rather than the flashy but counterproductive check.

2022.label: Moving the queen to an exposed square where it gets traded off, surrendering dynamic compensation or counterplay.
2022.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their queen (80% of moves involve the queen) to an exposed or vulnerable square, enabling the opponent to force a queen exchange that eliminates the player's key dynamic resource. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (60%) rather than outright blunders—the queen isn't immediately lost but is placed where it can be traded under unfavorable circumstances. The eval trajectory (median 250cp lost, with 40% winning->drawn and 40% drawn->losing) confirms these are game-changing errors that squander advantages or tip balanced positions. The tactical analysis and tags reinforce this: 'queen_exchange_error' appears twice, and position summaries repeatedly describe queens landing on exposed squares where trades are forced (Qg4, Qd3, Qc2), removing the attacking piece needed for compensation. Maia's responses frequently involve checks (60%) or captures (including queen captures at 20%), indicating the engine immediately exploits the exposed queen. The common thread across all top positions is that the queen move abandons a superior post or counter-threat, allowing the opponent to simplify into a winning or drawing position.

2025.label: Player moves bishop (or other piece) aimlessly while a free capture of an opponent's knight is available, throwing away a winning position.
2025.description: This feature identifies a highly specific and costly endgame/middlegame blunder pattern. The material signature shows the player moves a bishop (100%) without capturing anything, and this move hangs material (net -1.0), while Maia's recommended move captures a knight (100%) — indicating a completely free piece was available. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes: 100% go from winning to losing with a median loss of 793 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (83%) and tags like 'missed_capture' and 'undefended_piece'. The concrete positions show locked or simplified structures (mostly endgames despite being tagged middlegame) where a knight is en prise — often capturable by the king or bishop — but the player instead makes an irrelevant move (advancing a pawn, retreating a bishop, wandering the king). The blunder is not a complex tactical oversight but a simple failure to notice an undefended piece, converting a won position into a loss or draw.

2024.label: A rook check in the endgame that abandons a winning passed pawn promotion sequence, converting a won position into a draw.
2024.description: This feature identifies a highly specific endgame mistake pattern where a player delivers a rook check (rook moved 100%, check given 100%) that is materially 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost) but catastrophically squanders a winning position, with the eval dropping a median of 448 centipawns from winning to drawn (100% winning->drawn trajectory). The concrete pattern visible across the top boards is consistent: these are rook endgames (tagged rook_endgame) with advanced passed pawns near promotion. The player delivers a tempting but purposeless check instead of executing the winning promotion or supporting the passed pawn's advance. The dominant motifs—promotion_error (25%), passed_pawn (38%), tempo_loss (12%)—and recurring tags like 'pointless_check' and 'sacrifice_missed' confirm that the check disrupts the rook's critical role in the promotion mechanism. Maia's preferred move (pawn 100%, no check) shows the engine wanted to simply push or promote the pawn. The player chose flashy king harassment over the prosaic winning technique of pawn promotion, a classic endgame tempo error.

2026.label: Moving a piece that exposes the player's own king or major pieces to a discovered attack along a newly opened line.
2026.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player's move inadvertently opens a line (diagonal, file, or rank) that enables the opponent to deliver a discovered attack or discovered check. The material signature shows that 50% of moves hang a piece and 25% lose material outright, with a devastating median eval loss of ~95 pawns, indicating these are catastrophic tactical oversights rather than subtle positional errors. The Opus analysis confirms 'discovered_attack' as the dominant motif (40%), with supporting tags like 'discovered_check' and 'removal_of_defender.' Concrete examples show kings stepping onto fatal diagonals (Ke1 walking into a discovered checkmate, Kh8 stepping onto the bishop's diagonal), and pieces moving off critical defensive squares that unmask devastating discoveries. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve queens and checks (50% check rate), confirming that the opponent had powerful tactical follow-ups exploiting the opened lines. The trajectory (75% winning->winning but with massive eval drops, 25% winning->losing) shows these are positions where the player had a strong advantage but threw it away by failing to notice the geometric relationship between their own pieces and the opponent's attacking potential along shared lines.

2027.label: Knight captures in the opening that allow a devastating fork or leave pieces hanging, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
2027.description: This feature identifies a specific opening mistake pattern where a player recaptures or exchanges with a knight (player moved knight 100%, captured knight 75%) when a bishop recapture was correct (Maia recommends bishop 100%, capturing knight 100%). The material signature shows these are mostly trades (75%) rather than outright blunders, but the eval trajectory reveals they are catastrophic: 100% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median cost of 424 centipawns—a full piece. The tactical analysis confirms the mechanism: the wrong piece recapture (tagged 'wrong_piece_capture') leaves other pieces vulnerable to forks (43% fork motif) or hanging (29%). The FENs show this occurring repeatedly in well-known opening structures (e.g., French/Caro-Kann setups with knights on e5/c6) where taking with the knight instead of the bishop exposes a piece to a pawn fork or removes a defender. The positions are all in the opening phase, typically around moves 7-9, where piece coordination is critical and one wrong recapture sequence can unravel the entire position.

2030.label: Moving the king or other piece while the opponent's queen hangs free for capture.
2030.description: This feature fires when a player makes a king move (70%) or other non-queen move in positions where the opponent's queen is undefended and directly capturable. The material signature shows these moves overwhelmingly 'hang' material (74%) with a catastrophic median loss of -9.0 points and median eval drop of 1283 centipawns. Maia's recommended move is almost always a queen capture (100% captures, 78% queen moves), confirming the missed opportunity is a simple queen take. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'queen_hanging' and 'hanging_piece' motifs—players overlook open diagonals or lines where their queen could capture the opponent's undefended queen. The eval trajectory (56% winning->losing) shows these are typically won positions thrown away by a single catastrophic oversight. The board positions confirm the pattern: positions with queens on open lines where one queen is en prise, yet the player moves their king or makes an irrelevant move instead of taking the free queen.

2031.label: Failing to address an opponent's passed pawn promotion threat in endgames, allowing promotion (often with check) that converts a winning or drawn position into a loss.
2031.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a slow or incorrect move—typically a king move (60%) or pawn move (20%)—that ignores a critical pawn promotion threat. The dominant motif is promotion_error (75%), with passed_pawn appearing as the most common tag (7 occurrences). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings: winning→drawn (40%), drawn→losing (40%), and winning→losing (20%), with a median eval loss of 669 centipawns. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: players move their king to a square that either allows the opponent to promote with check (placing the king on the promotion file/diagonal), play a non-forcing move when an immediate tactical solution exists, or promote their own pawn prematurely without first neutralizing the opponent's counter-promotion. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (80%)—these aren't captures or trades gone wrong, but positional tempo errors where the player simply fails to recognize the urgency of stopping or correctly handling a promotion race.

2029.label: Trading or sacrificing a well-placed knight with check, surrendering a positional or material advantage for a tactically empty forcing move.
2029.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a knight check that voluntarily exchanges or hangs their knight, resulting in a significant evaluation loss (median 402 centipawns). The material signature shows 100% knight moves delivering check, yet the outcomes are overwhelmingly negative: 46% are trades where a dominant knight is exchanged for an inferior piece, and 38% simply hang the knight. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors—29% swing from drawn to losing, 25% from winning to drawn, and 8% from winning to losing outright. The tactical analysis reveals the common thread: players are seduced by the forcing nature of a check, exchanging knights that occupy dominant outposts (d5, e4, f5) for passive bishops or pawns, or playing 'forks' that are trivially refuted. Tags like 'premature_exchange', 'piece_activity', and 'positional_mistake' confirm that the knight being traded was the player's most active piece. The boards consistently show centralized knights on strong squares (d5, e4, f5) being thrown away with check against castled kings, where quieter moves would have maintained a large advantage.
