2034.label: Trading queens with check when holding a winning position, squandering the attacking advantage.
2034.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a queen trade via check (100% queen moved, 94% captured opponent's queen, 100% gave check) but the exchange is strategically premature. The eval trajectory shows these moves predominantly convert winning positions into drawn or lost ones (56% winning->drawn, 6% winning->losing), with a median loss of 286 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core error: players are reflexively trading queens when they have active attacking chances—often against kings stranded in the center (king_in_center tag), with hanging pieces available to exploit (hanging_piece motif), or with fork sequences that would have netted material. The tags 'premature_queen_trade' and 'premature_simplification' recur, and 81% of these positions had winning material available via alternative moves. The check aspect makes the trade feel forcing and 'safe,' but it actually abandons the player's attacking initiative and simplifies into equality or worse.

2028.label: Moves in the opening that leave pieces vulnerable to knight forks or tactical combinations exploiting blocked/pinned pieces.
2028.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player makes a seemingly safe move (100% safe material outcome, no captures) but catastrophically overlooks a tactical vulnerability—primarily knight forks (50% fork motif) combined with pins and self-blocking patterns. The moves are typically quiet developing moves (pawns 38%, knights 25%, bishops 25%) that fail to address an opponent's knight-based tactical threat. Maia consistently recommends a knight capture (100% knight taking knight), indicating the correct response was to eliminate the tactical piece before it strikes. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors (median 367cp lost), converting drawn positions to losing (50%) or winning positions to drawn/losing (50%), characteristic of falling into opening traps (tagged twice). The positions all share a Sicilian/classical opening structure where piece coordination is critical, and the player's passive or routine move allows a devastating tactical blow—whether a smothered mate threat, an absolute pin on the e-file, or a fork gaining material.

2032.label: Capturing or advancing a pawn while leaving a more valuable piece hanging or a critical tactical shot unaddressed.
2032.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a pawn move or pawn capture (75% pawn moves, 100% pawn captures) that overlooks a much more important tactical obligation. The material signature shows these pawn captures result in trades or losses (not gains), while Maia's recommended moves involve queens (58%) and bishops (33%) — often capturing rooks, knights, or bishops — indicating the player missed a significant tactical opportunity. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of cases miss winning material, with a median loss of 295 centipawns, frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 33%, winning->losing 25%, drawn->losing 25%). The tactical motifs confirm the pattern: hanging pieces (50%) are left unaddressed, king safety threats (33%) are ignored, and tempo is lost (17%). The concrete positions show recurring hxg6/fxg3-type pawn recaptures that address a minor pawn threat while completely overlooking that a major piece (often a bishop or queen) is left en prise on another part of the board. The player fixates on the local pawn tension rather than scanning for the globally critical tactic.

2038.label: Moving a bishop while ignoring an existing checkmate threat against one's own king.
2038.description: This feature consistently fires when a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) in a way that hangs material (100% hangs, median -1.0 net material) while completely overlooking a lethal checkmate threat already present in the position. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 9987 centipawns lost), indicating these moves typically result in immediate checkmate. The dominant motifs are king_safety (86%) and back_rank (14%), with the most common tags being checkmate_in_one (appearing in all top examples), exposed_king, and missed_tactic. The concrete pattern across the top boards is remarkably consistent: the player makes an aggressive-looking or developing bishop move—often attacking an opponent's piece—while being completely blind to an existing mate-in-one threat. Examples include moving a bishop to f6 while Qxf7# or Qxf8# is available, or retreating a bishop while Qxg2# hangs over the position. These are middlegame/opening positions where the player's king is fatally exposed but they focus on irrelevant attacking ideas rather than addressing the immediate survival crisis.

2035.label: In winning endgames, plays a slow or passive move that misses a critical tactical tempo, allowing the opponent to equalize or win.
2035.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (75% endgame phase) where the player holds a winning advantage but squanders it through a tempo-losing or strategically passive move (median eval lost: 594 centipawns, with 50% staying winning but 25% dropping to drawn and 25% to losing). The moves are predominantly safe pawn or king moves (not captures, not checks) that miss a decisive tactical continuation—often a deflection, a forcing pawn advance, or a king activity move that would have been immediately winning. The Opus analysis highlights missed deflection tactics, wrong exchanges that eliminate dynamic pieces, and slow king moves instead of immediately decisive pawn pushes. The common thread is that the player had a concrete winning line requiring precise tempo (e.g., d7+ deflecting the king, f4+ luring the king away, exploiting a passed pawn) but instead played a natural-looking but non-forcing move that allowed the opponent to consolidate. Tags like critical_tempo, deflection_missed, and pawn_endgame_transition confirm this is fundamentally about failing to seize the critical moment in an endgame.

2036.label: Player makes a routine developing move in the opening instead of capturing the undefended g7 pawn with a bishop on the long diagonal, winning material.
2036.description: This feature fires consistently on opening positions where a bishop on the long diagonal (typically b2 or a fianchetto square) has a clear tactical shot capturing an undefended g7 pawn (Bxg7), often winning the exchange by exposing the h8 rook. The material signature shows safe, non-capturing moves (pawns, bishops, knights developing routinely) while Maia consistently recommends a bishop capturing a pawn. The 'missed winning material' rate is 100%, and the eval trajectory shows a devastating median loss of 359 centipawns, with 74% of cases going from winning to drawn. The tags (hanging_piece 80%, undefended_pawn, long_diagonal, long_diagonal_exploitation, exchange_win) and the example summaries all converge on the same pattern: the player plays a natural developing move on autopilot—Nf3, Bg2, Qe2, f4, d3—completely overlooking that Bxg7 exploits the open a1-h8 or b1-h7 diagonal to win a pawn and often the exchange against the exposed rook. This is a classic opening tactical oversight where pattern blindness to the long diagonal opportunity costs substantial material.

2033.label: Ignoring central knight captures to play passive or premature moves in the opening, losing tempo and hanging material.
2033.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where players choose bishop or pawn moves (60%/40%) instead of the clearly superior knight captures (Maia recommends knight moves capturing pawns 100% of the time). The positions are almost exclusively standard open-game openings (Italian, Scotch, King's Gambit structures) where a knight capture on a central pawn (typically Nxe4 or Nxd4) is available but ignored. Instead, players make passive developing moves (Bd6, Be2, Bd3), tempo-wasting moves (h6, b3, b6), or unsound sacrifices (Bxf7+) that lack tactical justification. The eval trajectory is severe—median loss of 282 centipawns—frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (60% drawn->losing). The dominant motifs of hanging_piece (44%) and tempo_loss (33%) confirm that by declining the free central capture, players leave material en prise or fall behind in development. The recurring tags (tempo_loss, missed_tactic, development, piece_activity) all point to the same pattern: in critical opening moments where a concrete knight capture wins material or seizes the center, these players choose 'natural-looking' but inferior alternatives that squander their position.

2037.label: Delivering a check with a rook that leads to a losing exchange or sacrifice rather than pursuing a stronger non-checking continuation.
2037.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players deliver a rook check (88% rook moves, 100% checks) that appears forcing but is actually self-defeating. The material signature shows these checks predominantly hang material (50%) or result in unfavorable trades (25%), with a median cost of -1.0 material and 249 centipawns of evaluation lost. The eval trajectory (62% losing->losing, 25% drawn->losing) reveals these aren't throwing wins but rather making already difficult positions worse or converting holdable positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis confirms the 'check is not always best' tag recurring across positions—players reflexively choose a forcing check over quieter but superior moves. The concrete positions show rooks charging into enemy territory with check, only to be captured in exchanges that simplify to hopeless endgames (e.g., Rxg2+ leading to lost material, Rf8+ forcing unfavorable rook-for-queen trades, Rb7+ allowing defensive consolidation). The positional_mistake motif (50%) and hanging_piece tag (38%) underscore that these checks abandon attacking potential or defensive coordination for a superficially forcing but strategically empty move.

2040.label: Trading queens in drawn endgames where perpetual check was available, creating a lost pawn endgame.
2040.description: This feature fires when a player trades queens (100% queen captures queen with check) in positions that were objectively drawn, transforming them into losing endgames (drawn->losing trajectory with a median loss of 542 centipawns). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: players had perpetual check resources (perpetual_check_missed tag) that maintained the draw, but instead chose to exchange queens, entering pawn endgames where the opponent's king activity or passed pawns prove decisive. The Maia engine consistently recommends a non-capturing queen check (queen move, no capture, gives check), confirming that the drawing resource was a continuing queen check sequence rather than the trade. The resulting positions are overwhelmingly pawn endgames (22% pawn_endgame motif) with passed pawns (22%), where the opponent's king is better placed to support promotion. The FENs confirm this: sparse endgame positions with queens and pawns where one side's king is fatally misplaced after the trade.

2039.label: Capturing a pawn or minor piece in the opening that leaves a queen or major piece hanging on an exposed square.
2039.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake where the player makes a pawn capture (75% pawn moves) that appears to win material but catastrophically overlooks a tactical consequence—typically leaving their queen hanging or exposed. The material signature shows the player captures a piece (knight 50%, queen 25%, bishop 25%) but the net outcome is a severe loss (median -6.0 material, 75% losing), indicating the capture triggers a much larger material loss in return. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders (median 635cp lost), converting winning or drawn positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (70%), with recurring tags of hanging_queen, missed_tactic, and queen_capture. The concrete positions show a clear pattern: in early opening positions with undeveloped pieces, players capture on tempting squares (especially BxQ captures on d1, or pxN on c3) only to leave their own queen undefended or walk into a fork/discovery. The king_safety motif (20%) appears in cases where capturing the queen on d1 leaves the king fatally exposed. All positions are in the opening phase where development advantage punishes greedy captures.

2041.label: Moving the king to a more exposed square, allowing forced mating attacks or devastating check sequences.
2041.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves their king (50% of moves are king moves) into greater danger, typically in the middlegame (88%), resulting in catastrophic evaluation losses (median 493 centipawns). The dominant motif is king_safety (100% of positions), with recurring tags of exposed_king, forced_mate, king_walk, and queen_checks. The trajectory shows positions swinging from survivable to lost (winning->losing 25%, drawn->losing 25%), indicating that the king move transforms a tenable position into one with unstoppable mating threats. The top boards confirm this pattern: Kg4 walking into check sequences, Kg7 leaving shelter, Ke4 stepping into open files—all cases where the player's king abandons relative safety for a fatally exposed square. Even the non-king moves (queen retreats, rook captures) share the same signature of neglecting king safety while the opponent has active attacking pieces. Maia's recommended moves (75% missed winning material) frequently involve captures or checks that exploit the opponent's position, suggesting these players overlooked immediate tactical threats to their own king.

2042.label: Player makes an irrelevant move while opponent's advanced passed pawn promotes or delivers mate.
2042.description: This feature fires when a player, already in a losing position, makes a move that ignores a critical promotion threat, resulting in a catastrophic material or mating loss. The material signature shows 75% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -5.0, indicating the player's move isn't engaging with the opponent's threat at all. Maia consistently recommends capturing a pawn with a rook—likely the advancing passed pawn itself. The dominant motif is 'promotion_error' (67%), with recurring tags of 'passed_pawn', 'promotion_threat', and 'ignored_threat'. The eval trajectory confirms these are mostly losing positions made catastrophically worse (losing->losing at 75%, with median 503cp lost), often converting from a difficult-but-playable deficit into forced mate. The concrete positions all feature advanced passed pawns on the 7th rank (f7, g7, b7, P on a-file) where the player plays a passive or irrelevant pawn push or king move instead of addressing the imminent promotion, allowing the opponent to queen or deliver mate.

2043.label: Advancing a passed pawn one square too early in the endgame, allowing the opponent to gain tempo or establish a winning response.
2043.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players push passed pawns (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) prematurely toward promotion. The positions are exclusively endgame (100%) and the dominant motifs are promotion_error (40%) and passed_pawn (30%), with tempo_loss also appearing frequently. The boards show advanced passed pawns being pushed (d7, c7, g7, f2, e2, h2, b2, d2) where the player rushes promotion without adequate preparation. The eval trajectory shows most cases occur in already-losing positions (67% losing->losing), meaning these pushes often fail to create the necessary counterplay and sometimes catastrophically worsen the position (one example drops 9000+ centipawns into forced mate). The material signature shows 50% of moves hang material — the pushed pawn becomes indefensible or the promotion attempt is refuted — while Maia's response is typically a king move (83%), indicating the opponent calmly repositions to intercept or exploit the tempo. The median eval loss of 4 centipawns reflects that many pushes are near-irrelevant in already-decided positions, but the catastrophic outliers reveal the true danger of mistiming pawn advances in critical endgame moments.

2044.label: Player makes a non-urgent move while opponent's passed pawn is about to promote, losing decisive material or the game.
2044.description: This feature fires when a player ignores an imminent pawn promotion threat, typically in endgame or late middlegame positions with advanced passed pawns. The material signature shows the player's move is often a pawn or king move (non-captures, 100% no capture) that is 'safe' in isolation but catastrophically misses the real threat — 67% of the time Maia's recommended move involves capturing a pawn (addressing the promotion threat directly). The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (57%) and promotion_error (29%), with tempo_loss (4 occurrences) underscoring that the played move wastes a critical tempo.
